text: There are More than 300,000 known species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but scientists estimate that up to 80% of all life on the planet remains undiscovered.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

The phrase 'center of' is loose wording, because the East Pacific Rise is not in the middle of the Pacific. Still, the ridge does run through all three oceans, so nothing in the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 8 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate by biologists.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-known estimate of about 8.7 million species on Earth comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology study by Mora et al., not from a 2020 estimate. Coverage from August 2011 by The Conversation, the Washington Post, EurekAlert and Science all dates it to that year. That total also covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. No 2020 estimate with this figure turned up.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service and Ocean Exploration pages call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth and say it winds between the continents through every major ocean basin, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. Named sections include the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Southeast and Southwest Indian Ridges and the East Pacific Rise. NOAA puts its length at about or 'nearly' 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and WorldAtlas says about 65,000 km. Some other sources give even longer figures. 'Over 65,000 km' is slightly looser than NOAA's 'nearly 65,000 km,' but the core claim matches what reliable sources say.

text: Butler County In Pennsylvania turns into a giant Christmas light display called "The Christmas Light Show" each year.

text: A投 golf ball can travel over 437 yards when hit with the proper technique.

text: Dolphins have been observed showing signs of empathy and compassion by helping other animals, including humans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable reports describe dolphins helping both other animals and people. In 2008, ABC News and NBC News reported that Moko, a bottlenose dolphin, guided two stranded pygmy sperm whales back out to sea in New Zealand after people had failed to do so. In 2004, the NZ Herald and Live Science reported that a pod of dolphins circled lifeguards off New Zealand and protected them from a great white shark. These and similar accounts are widely described as signs of dolphin empathy or altruism, although whether the dolphins actually feel empathy is an interpretation of their behaviour.

text: The octopus has the shortest attention span of any animal, lasting only around 2-5 minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: No source names the octopus as the animal with the shortest attention span. Popular sources instead name the fruit fly (A-Z Animals, Takeroon, Quora), and the goldfish is the animal usually cited in the myth. A 2–5 minute span would also be long next to the claimed spans of only seconds for those animals. Research describes octopuses as curious and intelligent, which doesn't fit the claim.

text: The colony of Eskipoo is not found anywhere within the main group of Eskipoo dog breeds, rather purebred and rare varieties are found.

reason: The sources I found agree that the Eskipoo is a designer cross between the American Eskimo Dog and the (Miniature) Poodle. It is not a standardized breed, and major kennel clubs don't recognize it. The claim's wording doesn't point to anything identifiable, so it can't be checked. One part may conflict with the evidence: if the claim means Eskipoos are purebred, that contradicts sources describing them as a mixed breed. text: The Beehive mailbox, also known as the Pukekohe Post Office, located in Pukekohe, New Zealand, is considered the oldest and most iconic examples of a "whimsical mailbox" collection found anywhere in the world.

Archive records from DigitalNZ and the National Library show that Pukekohe Post Office was an ordinary post office building. Searches for a beehive letterbox in Pukekohe only returned unrelated product listings and a letterbox competition. Because nothing confirms or directly disproves the claim, it can't be verified.

text: The highest-grossing film of all time is currently "Avengers: Endgame" (2019), with a worldwide gross of over $2.79 billion.

reason: Recent reports from Variety, TechSpot and Yahoo, all published in 2026, say that "Avengers: Endgame" (2019) is again the highest-grossing film of all time. Its "Encore" re-release raised its worldwide total to about $2.925 billion, just ahead of Avatar's roughly $2.924 billion. That total is above $2.79 billion, so the claim is accurate. Endgame first passed Avatar in July 2019 with about $2.79 billion. Avatar retook the top spot after its 2021 re-release, and Endgame has now regained it.

text: Thanks to a unique genetic trait, the Axolotl (a type of salamander) has the ability to regrow its limbs, eyes, and parts of its brain throughout its life.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a peer-reviewed Developmental Dynamics review, say the axolotl can regenerate limbs and parts of its central nervous system throughout its life. BGI, a genomics company, says axolotls can regrow limbs, spinal cords, eyes and parts of the brain. The "unique genetic trait" wording is vague, but it fits sources linking this ability to the axolotl's genetics and lifelong neoteny (keeping juvenile traits as an adult). Nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers across the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Service, NOAA Ocean Exploration, WHOI and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,389 miles), and most of it lies on the ocean floor. One caveat: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over" 65,000 km. The claim matches the commonly cited figure, so this wording difference is too small to count as a contradiction.

text: The number of neurons in the human brain is estimated to be around 86 billion.
label: supported
reason: Azevedo et al. (2009), a peer-reviewed study cited in a Lent et al. 2011 review in the European Journal of Neuroscience, counted an average of about 86 billion neurons in adult male human brains. This matches the claim's estimate of around 86 billion.

text: The longest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, has a diameter of approximately 142,984 kilometers.

reason: Reliable sources say Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System, with an equatorial diameter of about 142,984 km (an equatorial radius of 71,492 km). The claim's phrase "longest planet" is unusual, but it clearly means largest, so I treat that wording as harmless. The diameter figure matches the sources exactly.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stethoscope".
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stethoscope" has three syllables (steth-o-scope), so it can't be a one-syllable word at all. Wikipedia's list of the longest English monosyllables names ten-letter words such as "scraunched" and "schmaltzed". The more commonly cited examples are nine-letter words like "screeched" and "strengths". Dictionary.com likewise lists "strengths" and similar words, not "stethoscope".

text: The total surface area of the Moon, including its far side, is approximately 34.4 million square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources give the Moon's total surface area as about 37.9 million km² (The Conversation says 37.94 million km²), not 34.4 million km². You can check this yourself: with a mean radius of about 1,737 km, the formula 4πr² also gives roughly 37.9 million km².

text: Butler's Grotto located in Sligo, Ireland, is a unique natural limestone cave system that features stunning scenic limestone formations.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) across the globe.

reason: Several sources describe the Mid-Ocean Ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth. WorldAtlas puts its length at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and NOAA and WHOI give similar figures, with NOAA describing it as stretching more than 65,000 km across the globe. text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.

NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', which does not fully match 'over'. Since the length is about 65,000 km either way, this is a minor wording difference and does not contradict the claim.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthen".

Wikipedia's list of the longest English monosyllables gives 10-letter candidates such as "scraunched" and "strengthed" (an obsolete verb meaning "strengthen"). The commonly cited everyday answer is the 9-letter "strengths". Guinness World Records also lists "strengths" as the longest English word with only one vowel.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses".
label: contradicted

It's usually cited as the longest word you can type using only the left hand. The longest one-syllable words in common use have nine letters, such as "screeched," "strengths," "scratched" and "stretched." A few rare or obsolete ten-letter words, like "scraunched" and "strengthed," are sometimes mentioned too.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and solitary nature in the wild.

That source suggests it is most likely linked to pandas' clumsy habits. HowStuffWorks, Animal Corner and inkl also point to clumsiness or laziness rather than shyness. Some lower-quality blogs and TikTok pages link it to shyness or a solitary nature, but they offer only guesses. The name is supported, but the claimed cause is speculation that reliable sources neither confirm nor agree on.

text: There are approximately 1.3 billion unique species of organisms on Earth, according to estimates from the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS).

text: The Sundial Bridge in California, USA, which spans the Sacramento River, is the longest single-span, single-arch pedestrian bridge in the world.

text: The chemosynthetic bacteria that live near underwater volcanic vents can survive in temperatures ranging from slightly below freezing to as high as 122°F (50°C).

LibreTexts reports that vent 'Strain 121' doubles its population at 121°C. Some chemosynthetic vent bacteria, such as Aquifex, are also known to grow near 95°C, though no source I found confirmed this. The claim appears to mix up the known limit of about 122°C with 122°F. Since vent chemosynthesizers survive well above 50°C, the claim's upper limit is contradicted.

text: The concept of the charitable trust dates back to ancient civilizations, with recorded evidence of such trusts in ancient Greece around 300 BCE.

This backs the general claim that charitable trusts have ancient roots, including in Greece in the 4th–3rd centuries BCE. Two caveats: the sources call these 'endowments' rather than formal 'trusts', and they give about 387 BCE for the Academy. None of the results confirms the claim's specific date of 300 BCE, which is only loosely consistent with this evidence.

text: There are over 1.9 million distinct species of plants and animals that have been identified on Earth, according to estimates by scientists.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Different estimates disagree, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out. Chapman (2009), the most-cited source, puts described species at about 1.9 million, which roughly matches the claim. But that figure covers all life, including fungi, protists and other groups. Chapman's own breakdown has about 1.42 million animals and 310,000 plants, roughly 1.73 million together, which is below 1.9 million. Other estimates are lower still: Mora et al. (2011) lists about 1.2–1.35 million described species, Wikipedia gives 1.74 million databased as of 2018, and some scientists put the valid total near 1.5 million because of duplicate names. The '1.9 million' figure itself appears in reputable sources, but 'over 1.9 million plants and animals' is not clearly supported and partly conflicts with these numbers.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back up the claim. WorldAtlas calls the mid-ocean ridge system the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Guinness World Records lists the Mid-Ocean Ridge as the longest underwater mountain range at 65,000 km (40,000 miles), and WHOI's page on mid-ocean ridges says the same.

text: The longer a red blood cell lives, the more iron it loses over time.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim, though only indirectly. A study in Blood (Willekens et al.) found that red blood cells lose about 20% of their hemoglobin while circulating. Most of this loss happens in the second half of the cell's roughly 120-day life, as the cell sheds hemoglobin-containing vesicles. Hemoglobin cell content falls as the cell ages. Because hemoglobin is where a red blood cell holds its iron, an older cell has lost more of it. No source says 'iron' outright, so this conclusion rests on the hemoglobin data. I found nothing that contradicts it.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, which stretches for approximately 202,080 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says Canada has the world's longest total coastline, at 202,080 km (125,567 miles). This matches the CIA World Factbook figure. Some sources give a larger number, about 243,000 km, when they count additional islands. Even so, every source agrees that Canada ranks first, and 202,080 km is the standard figure.

text: The famous 'I love you' message in the famous Rosetta Stone is actually the Rosetta Stone tinha the message "I luv u""

text: Over 99% of allession stars in the observable universe are smaller than the sun.

EarthSky says the Sun is more luminous than about 85% of stars in the Milky Way, and other sources put the share of less massive stars at about 90%, since most stars are red dwarfs. Those figures fall short of "over 99%" and describe our galaxy, not the observable universe. Because the subject of the claim cannot be identified, it can't be checked properly.

text: There are approximately 200 million trees along the Amazon River basin, which accounts for about 15% of all the trees on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The usual estimate, from the ter Steege et al. 2013 study in Science, is that the Amazon has about 390 billion trees, not 200 million. The claim is off by roughly 2,000 times. Earth has about 3 trillion trees, so 390 billion is roughly 13% of the total. That means the ~15% share is close, but the 200 million figure is clearly wrong.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back the claim. Guinness World Records names the Mid-Ocean Ridge as the longest submarine mountain range and gives its length as 65,000 km (40,000 miles). WorldAtlas calls it the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles), roughly 1.5 times Earth's circumference. NOAA and WHOI give the same figure.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthen."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because "strengthen" (STRENGTH-en) has two syllables, so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Wikipedia's list of the longest English one-syllable words gives candidates such as "scraunched" (10 letters), and the commonly cited answers are words like "strengths" and "screeched" (9 letters). "Strengthen" is not among them. Guinness World Records lists "strengths" as the longest English word with only one vowel.

text: There are over 8.7 million distinct species on Earth, although only about 1.3 million of these species have been formally discovered and named by scientists.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the widely reported 2011 PLoS Biology study (Mora et al.), with a few caveats. That study estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. It also found that about 1.25 million species had been described and entered into central databases, which fits the claim's "about 1.3 million." However, 8.7 million is an estimate, not a minimum, so "over 8.7 million" overstates it. Some sources also note that close to 2 million species have actually been described if you count ones not yet in central databases. These are wording differences rather than real contradictions, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and covers more than 40% of the Earth's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. But the claim says it covers more than 40% of Earth's surface, and that figure is wrong. An oceanography textbook (Roger Williams University Pressbooks) and a ResearchGate paper both put its coverage at about 23%.

text: There are approximately 1.4 million films produced every year, with millions more being stored in libraries and museums, showcasing the vast and diverse world of cinema.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figure of about 1.4 million films a year is far too high. Stephen Follows, a film-industry data analyst, tracked 117,134 movies made in 151 countries over 20 years. That works out to roughly 6,000 films a year. Other estimates that draw on UNESCO data put worldwide feature-film output at about 6,000–8,000 a year, or 10,000–20,000 if every format is counted. Even the broadest estimate found, which adds short films never sent to festivals, is only about 60,000–70,000 a year. So the 1.4 million figure is wrong by more than an order of magnitude. Because that core number is false, the claim is contradicted, and the part about millions of films kept in libraries and museums doesn't change that.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers, and it's slightly flattened at the poles and bulged at the equator.
label: supported
reason: A University of Oregon astronomy lecture page says Earth's average diameter is 12,742 km. It also says Earth is roughly an oblate spheroid that is flattened along its axis and bulges at the equator, where the diameter is about 43 km larger than the pole-to-pole diameter. A Universe Today article agrees that Earth is an oblate spheroid flattened at the poles. Both parts of the claim are backed by these sources, and none of the results contradict them.

text: The longest war in recorded history is the Hundred Years' War between England and France, which lasted for 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
label: contradicted
reason: The 116-year span (1337–1453) is correct for the Hundred Years' War, but that war is not the longest in recorded history. Lists of the longest wars name much longer conflicts: the Reconquista (about 781 years, roughly 711–1492), the Roman–Persian Wars (about 721 years) and the Arauco War (nearly 300 years). That contradicts the claim that the Hundred Years' War was the longest.

text: Glowworms are bioluminescent insects that have the ability to emit their own light through a chemical reaction within their abdomens.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. Glowworms are bioluminescent insects, mostly larvae, such as fungus gnats (Arachnocampa) or beetles like Lampyris. They make their own light through a luciferin–luciferase chemical reaction. In fungus gnat glowworms this happens in a specialised organ at the tip of the larva's abdomen, and in firefly-type glowworms the hind segments of the abdomen glow. Nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: The Giraffe is the only mammal with a coat pattern that is unique to each individual, similar to human fingerprints, making them easily identifiable.
label: contradicted
reason: Giraffes do have coat patterns that are unique to each animal, but they are not the only mammal like this. Britannica says zebra stripes are also unique to each animal, "much like a human fingerprint." Tigers, leopards and cheetahs can be told apart by their markings too, so the claim that giraffes are the only one is false.

text: There are approximately 37.5 trillion trees on Earth, with new forests being grown while others disappear due to deforestation processes.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known global tree count comes from Crowther et al., published in Nature in 2015. It estimates about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, not 37.5 trillion, which is more than ten times too high. The same study says about 15 billion trees are cut down each year and tree numbers have fallen by 46% since agriculture began. That backs up the deforestation part of the claim, but the main number is wrong.

text: Cutom made the first performance of the air jet machine, which is a precursor to modern vacuum cleaners, in 1901 in Hoboken, New Jersey.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe this 1901 demonstration differently. Wikipedia, Invention & Technology and Encyclopedia.com say that in 1901 Hubert Cecil Booth watched an American-made machine that blew dust away with air. The demonstration took place at the Empire Music Hall in London, not in Hoboken, New Jersey. Some sources say the machine was John S. Thurman's design, and Thurman had patented a blown-air carpet cleaner in 1899, so 1901 was not its first showing. Searches found no inventor or demonstrator called "Cutom" and no link between this machine and Hoboken. The location and the claim that 1901 was the first demonstration are both contradicted.

text: The Human Brain processes and processes approximately 72,000 thoughts on a daily basis.
label: contradicted
reason: The only peer-reviewed estimate I found contradicts the claim. A 2020 fMRI study from Queen's University (Poppenk and Tseng) puts the average at about 6,200 thoughts per day. That is less than a tenth of 72,000. Popular sources repeat a figure of roughly 50,000–70,000 thoughts a day, often credited to USC's Laboratory of Neuro Imaging, but no study is cited for it. Other sources, including a Brainly answer and Medium articles that cite the Queen's research, call it a myth or an oversimplification. I found no reliable source for 72,000 itself. The claim's wording ('processes and processes') is also garbled, but that doesn't affect the verdict.

text: The longest finger in a human body is typically the middle finger.
label: supported
reason: The search results say the middle finger, also called the long finger, is the third digit of the human hand and is "usually the longest finger." That matches the claim. This is also standard anatomy, and Wikipedia's middle finger article says the same thing. The sources I found were fandom wiki pages that copy Wikipedia's wording, so they are not the strongest sources, but nothing I found disagrees with the claim.

text: There are over 300 million tree species on Earth, but scientists estimate that there may be up to 100 species that have gone extinct in the last 50 years alone.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2022 PNAS study based on a global ground-sourced database puts the number of tree species on Earth at about 73,300. That is roughly 14% more than the approximately 64,000 species known today, but nowhere near "over 300 million." The claim's central figure is wrong by several orders of magnitude, so the claim is contradicted. I didn't separately check the extinction figure, since the first part already makes the claim false.

text: Did you know that a giant squill, a type of onion flower, can bloom in less than two weeks under the right conditions?
label: not_verifiable
reason: Giant white squill (Urginea/Drimia maritima, also called sea onion) is known for a flower spike that shows up suddenly in late summer. The one source I found says the flowers open from the bottom of the spike to the top over about two weeks in total. That doesn't confirm the claim that it can bloom in less than two weeks, and it doesn't clearly contradict it either. The claim is also vague: it doesn't say whether it means the spike emerging, the first flowers opening, or the full bloom. It's also loose to call this plant an onion flower. Its common name is sea onion, but it isn't a true onion (Allium). I couldn't find anything that clearly backs up the under-two-weeks timeframe.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, with a coastline stretching over 243,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Wikipedia's Geography of Canada page, say Canada has the world's longest coastline at 243,042 km. That figure is over 243,000 km, so both parts of the claim are supported.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers (7,918 miles) at the equator due to its slightly flattened shape.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure in the claim is the wrong one. 12,742 km (7,918 mi) is Earth's mean diameter, which is twice the mean radius of 6,371 km. The diameter at the equator is about 12,756 km (twice the 6,378.137 km equatorial radius, roughly 7,926 mi). Because the Earth bulges at the equator, the equatorial diameter is larger than the average, not 12,742 km. The claim gets the cause backwards: the flattening is why the equatorial number is bigger than the mean.

text: There are over 150 million galaxies in the observable universe, though new observations and research suggest this number may continue to rise.
label: contradicted
reason: Current scientific estimates put the number of galaxies in the observable universe at a few hundred billion to about two trillion. That is billions to trillions, not millions. Read literally, "over 150 million" is still true, but the figure is off by more than three orders of magnitude, so it misstates the estimate. The idea that the count could go up has some support, since estimates rose from about 100–200 billion to about 2 trillion in 2016. However, the central number in the claim does not match the evidence.

text: A library in Switzerland called the Bodmer Library holds the oldest surviving manuscript of Dante's Divine Comedy, dating back to the 14th century.
label: contradicted
reason: The Bodmer Library (Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Switzerland) is real, and it does own 14th-century manuscripts of the Divine Comedy, such as the Codice Ricasoli Firidolfi. But it does not hold the oldest surviving manuscript. Several sources, including Wikidata and facsimile publishers, identify that as the Codex Landianus 190, dated 1336, which is kept at the Biblioteca Passerini-Landi in Piacenza, Italy.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI and Wikipedia give the same length, about 65,000 km or 40,000 miles. Those figures back the claim that it is the longest range and runs over 40,000 miles around the globe. The claim's 64,000 km is a small rounding difference from these sources, not a contradiction.

text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total length of coastline of approximately 25,148 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Geography of Norway page, citing Kartverket (Norway's official mapping agency), says Norway's coastline is 25,148 km. It also says there are 320,249 islands and islets along the coast (239,057 islands and 81,192 islets). HowStuffWorks also gives about 239,057 islands. That is far more than 18,000, so 'more than 18,000' is technically true but a large understatement. The word 'despite' is just odd phrasing and doesn't contradict anything.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, according to estimates by biologists using data from DNA and other scientific research.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (PLOS Biology, 2011), but two parts of the claim don't match it. First, 8.74 million is the total for all eukaryotes, which includes fungi, protozoa and chromists. The study puts animals at about 7.77 million and plants at about 298,000, so plants and animals together come to roughly 8.1 million, not over 8.7 million. Second, the estimate didn't use DNA data. It extrapolated from a pattern in how many groups exist at different taxonomic levels.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth and runs nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles) around the globe. That matches the claim of about 65,000 km (40,000 miles).

text: There are approximately 200 bones in the adult human body, although this number decreases to around 80 bones in the human skeleton after birth due to some bones fusing together during development.
label: contradicted
reason: The adult figure in the claim is roughly right, since adults typically have about 206 bones. The rest of the claim is wrong. Bones fuse after birth, so the count goes down from about 270–300 in a newborn to 206 in an adult. It never drops to around 80. (80 is the number of bones in the axial skeleton, not the total after fusion.)

text: Corgis are the most commonly found breed in the British royal family's preferred dog list.
label: supported
reason: The American Kennel Club says Queen Elizabeth II owned more than 30 Pembroke Welsh Corgis in her lifetime and that corgis were part of the royal family from 1933, with George VI's family. They are the breed most closely and widely linked to the British royal family. One caveat: the phrase "preferred dog list" is vague, and the royals also kept other breeds, such as corgi crossbreeds and gun dogs, but nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: The Departed, a crime drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Matt Damon, holds the record for most Academy Awards won by a film directed by a non-American director, as it was directed by the Irish filmmaker Martin Scorsese and won 4 Oscars.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and the Academy's own records confirm that The Departed stars DiCaprio and Damon and won 4 Oscars. But Martin Scorsese is an American filmmaker, born in Queens, New York, not Irish. The record claim is also false. Films by non-American directors have won far more Oscars, such as Peter Jackson's The Return of the King with 11 and David Lean's Lawrence of Arabia with 7.

text: There are approximately 1.3 billion unique species of organisms on Earth, according to estimates from the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).
label: contradicted
reason: IPBES's official Global Assessment media release puts the total number of animal and plant species on Earth at about 8 million, including 5.5 million insect species. It does not estimate 1.3 billion species. The claim gets the IPBES figure badly wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and spans 40,389 miles around the globe. WorldAtlas gives about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Both figures fit the claim of 'over 40,000 miles (64,000 km)'. The claim's 64,000 km is a rough conversion of 40,000 miles, but it is still consistent with the sources.

text: The Earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers, which is slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator due to its rotational motion.
label: supported
reason: Earth's mean radius is 6,371 km, so its mean diameter is about 12,742 km. EBSCO gives an equatorial diameter of about 12,756 km and a polar diameter of about 12,714 km, which average to roughly 12,735 km, so 12,742 km is a fair approximate figure. EBSCO and Wikipedia's 'Equatorial bulge' page both say Earth is an oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, and that this is caused by its rotation.

text: The Garden of Earthly Delights, a famous triptych painting by Hieronymus Bosch, is estimated to have taken the artist around 10 to 15 years to complete.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No source I found says how long Bosch spent painting the triptych. Bosch did not sign or date it, so the date ranges given by sources (Britannica and the Prado's c.1490–1500; Wikipedia's 1490–1510) show uncertainty about when it was made, not how long it took. Those ranges don't line up with '10 to 15 years' either: Mental Floss reports that some scholars think it was begun in 1490 and finished between 1510 and 1515, which would mean 20–25 years. A tree-ring study cited by TheCollector points to an earlier date, around 1480–85. Because no source gives a 10–15-year working time and the dating evidence is mixed, the claim cannot be verified.

text: The worlds longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, runs for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It also says the system stretches nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles) around the globe. Both the 'longest mountain range' description and the approximate length in the claim match this source.

text: The country of Saudi Arabia has over 22,000 artificial islands created using 262 million tons of rock and soil.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up no source supporting either number. Saudipedia, a Saudi reference site, gives the Manifa oil field islands in the Eastern Province as its example of artificial islands in Saudi Arabia. From general knowledge (not confirmed in the search results), Manifa has about 27 artificial islands, and Saudi Arabia has only about 1,300 islands in total, natural ones included. That makes '22,000 artificial islands' impossible. The '262 million tons of rock and soil' figure also matches no source found. The well-known rock-and-sand island figures come from Dubai's Palm Jumeirah in the UAE, which used about 7 million tons of rock. The claim seems to mix up countries and numbers.

text: The total surface area of the Earth is approximately 510.1 million square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that Earth's total surface area is about 510.1 million km². Wikipedia lists it as 510,065,284 km², and the CIA World Factbook figure (shown on chartsbin) is 510,072,000 km². Both round to about 510.1 million km².

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) across the Earth's surface.
label: supported
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA's Ocean Service puts its length at 40,389 miles, or about 65,000 km, and describes it as stretching around the globe. NOAA Ocean Exploration, WHOI and Wikipedia also give a length of about or nearly 65,000 km (40,000 miles). One small caveat: these sources say "nearly" or "about" 65,000 km rather than "over," but the 40,389-mile figure does exceed 40,000 miles. The claim's main points are supported.

text: The darkest star in the known universe is Ebla 3, a red dwarf star located about 10 billion light-years away, with a surface temperature of around 2400 Kelvin and a luminosity 30 times lower than the smallest stars.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no star called "Ebla 3" in any search result. The trustworthy sources that do turn up point elsewhere. Wikipedia and an arXiv paper (1312.1736, on the hydrogen-burning limit) describe 2MASS J0523−1403 as a nearby L2.5 dwarf, about 40 light-years away, that sits at the lowest-mass, least-luminous edge of the stellar sequence. The details of the claim also don't hold together. A single faint red dwarf 10 billion light-years away could not be seen individually with current telescopes, since the faintest known stars are all in our local neighbourhood. And by definition a star can't be 30 times dimmer than 'the smallest stars'. The 2400 K temperature is a normal value for a red dwarf, but the named star and its record appear to be made up.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. The most-cited global estimate (Crowther et al., Nature 2015) puts Earth's tree count at about 3 trillion. NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100–400 billion stars. Even the high-end star estimate is several times smaller than the number of trees, and multiple sources, including WorldAtlas, make the same comparison.

text: Aleurites moluccana, commonly known as tung oil tree, produces seeds that contain tung oil which is the primary component of the paint used in the Taipei 101 skyscraper.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable botanical sources contradict the claim. Aleurites moluccana is the candlenut tree (also called kukui or candleberry), and its seeds give candlenut oil. The tung oil tree is a different species, Vernicia fordii (formerly Aleurites fordii), which is the source of tung oil. Since the claim names the wrong plant, it is false. I found no evidence that tung oil was the main ingredient in Taipei 101's paint, but that question doesn't need settling because the plant identification is already wrong.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique movements and angles of their dances guide their colony to the best food sources?
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources describe the honeybee waggle dance as a way of telling other bees where food is. The direction of the waggle run, measured as an angle relative to the sun, gives the direction to the food source, and the length of the run gives the distance. Bees also dance more vigorously for better food sources, which fits the claim's "best food sources" wording. The claim's general description matches this well-established science.

text: The bear species that hibernates the longest is the black bear from Alaska, which can hibernate for up to 5-7 months during the winter.
label: supported
reason: The claim mostly holds up, though the evidence has some caveats. One source that reviews the scientific literature says the longest bear hibernation on record is for American black bears in southern Alaska: 212 days, or about 7 months. It adds that local brown bears hibernate for almost as long. The Alaska Department of Fish and Game says black bears in the northern part of their range may stay dormant for seven to eight months. IFAW and Outdoor Life give Alaskan hibernation as about seven months, or five to seven months, which matches the claim's 5–7 month range. The caveats: some sources say Alaskan brown bears can hibernate 5–8 months, and the ADF&G figure goes a little past 7 months. Even so, no reliable source contradicts the claim's main point.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. WHOI says mid-ocean ridges form the world's longest mountain range and measure "nearly 65,000 kilometers (about 40,000 miles)" in total. WorldAtlas gives about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Some sources say "nearly" rather than "over" 65,000 km. That small wording difference doesn't change the main point, and some estimates of the full ridge system run even longer.

text: The left side of a person's brain processes visual information, while the right side processes auditory information.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Each hemisphere has its own occipital lobe, which handles vision, and its own temporal lobe, which handles hearing. So both sides of the brain process visual and auditory information. The Merck Manual says each hemisphere contains temporal and occipital lobes. It also says visual processing uses areas "on both sides" and that each hemisphere mainly handles visual input from the opposite side of the body. The temporal lobes on both sides are central to hearing.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of ants that exist on Earth, according to estimates from scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is wrong. Scientists put the number of ant species at roughly 12,000–22,000: about 12,000+ described so far, and up to about 22,000 when undescribed species are included. The 8.7 million figure is a well-known estimate for all eukaryotic species on Earth, not for ants. Mongabay, reporting on a peer-reviewed study of global ant numbers, gives the figure as 'more than 12,000 different species.'

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their unique ability to change color and texture to fit into tight spaces, much like items are arranged in a basket.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say the usual collective noun for octopuses is a "consortium", with "tangle" and "rally" sometimes given as alternatives. None of them lists "basket" as a recognized term. Searching for "basket of octopuses" only turned up product listings and a news story about a literal basket of octopuses. The claimed reason for the name (that octopuses change color and texture to fit into tight spaces) appears to be made up. Since no source supports either part of the claim, I'm rating it contradicted. A-Z Animals also notes there is no formal answer, but the consensus is "consortium".

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which surrounds the entire globe and stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles).
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range. They describe it as wrapping around the globe and give its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). One detail is slightly off: these sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, not 'over' 65,000 km. That difference is small, and the main claim is backed by authoritative sources.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that covers over 65,000 kilometers and was formed as a result of plate tectonics.
label: supported
reason: My searches back up each part of the claim. NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth and say it lies mostly underwater. They also explain that it forms where tectonic plates spread apart and magma rises to create new crust, which matches the plate tectonics part. The length is the one soft spot. NOAA and WHOI say "nearly 65,000 km", while Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system. A PMC (NIH-hosted) paper gives about 75,000 km. Other sources say "more than 65,000 km." Since several credible figures are at or above 65,000 km, "over 65,000 km" is a reasonable statement, but NOAA's "nearly" wording falls just short of it.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not only hear sounds that are too faint for humans to detect, but also have a range of hearing that is capable of picking up sounds at frequencies as high as 79 kHz.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Hearing range article says cats can detect frequencies from 55 Hz up to 79 kHz. It also calls cat hearing extremely sensitive and among the best of any mammal, which backs up the claim that cats can hear sounds too faint for humans. Several pet-information sources give the same 79 kHz upper limit. The Heffner study reports an even wider range (48 Hz to about 85 kHz at high intensity), which fits with "as high as 79 kHz." The word "unique" is an exaggeration, since other animals also hear ultrasound, but the factual parts of the claim hold up.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of the resemblance of their grouped shape to a woven basket.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source that calls a group of octopuses a "basket" or explains such a name by a woven-basket shape. Collective-noun references (Grammar Monster, A-Z Animals, NounMaster, Original Diving) say the usual term is "consortium," with "tangle" given as a playful option. Study.com and A-Z Animals add that no collective noun for octopuses is widely accepted, since octopuses are mostly solitary. A search for "basket of octopuses" only turned up product listings and food baskets, not a collective noun. The claimed term and its explanation are therefore unsupported, and the sources point to different terms.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It says the system stretches "nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)" around the globe. That matches the claim's figure of about 65,000 km. The claim's 40,400 miles is a rounded version of NOAA's 40,390 miles, so it fits the word "approximately."

text: Snails can sleep for up to 3 years, surviving by sealing themselves in a protective layer of mucus called a "lovinsnail waterproof cocoon" that protects them from dehydration.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say land snails can stay dormant (estivate or hibernate) for long periods, sometimes up to about three years, and that they seal their shell openings with a dried mucus layer that keeps them from drying out. That part of the claim is broadly supported, although some sources call the three-year figure exaggerated. However, the sources name this mucus seal the "epiphragm," not a "lovinsnail waterproof cocoon." That name appears to be made up and does not match the established term, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The Human Brain accounts for only about 2% of the human body's total mass, yet it consumes around 20% of the body's total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including The Physics Factbook (which collects encyclopedia and textbook citations), say the brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest. This matches the claim. One small caveat: the 20% figure usually refers to energy use at rest, not total daily energy expenditure.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is actually the mid-ocean ridge system that runs around the entire globe, spanning over 65,000 kilometers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the whole claim. NOAA, WHOI and AMNH all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, and they describe it as global. However, they give its length as "nearly" 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles), not "over" 65,000 km. None of the trustworthy sources I found call it the longest mountain range in the solar system. They only say it is the longest on Earth. I didn't find any source that compares it with ranges on other planets or moons, so that part of the claim is unconfirmed.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers around the Earth and is not part of any continent.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth. They give its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). NOAA says it winds between the continents and that more than 90% of it lies underwater in the deep ocean, which supports the claim that it is not part of any continent. One small caveat: these sources say "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km. Some other sources give larger totals of up to about 80,000 km, so the difference does not undermine the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: The sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range, though they give somewhat different lengths. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', which is a little under the claim's 'over 65,000 km'. Other sources give higher figures: NASA's Ocean Planet page says 74,000 km, and some summaries say 'over 65,000 km'. Taken together, the evidence broadly backs 'over 65,000 km'. The ridge system runs through every ocean basin, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. The East Pacific Rise is not in the exact middle of the Pacific, but the claim's general description holds.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers in length.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas calls the Mid-Ocean Ridge technically the longest mountain range in the world and puts its length at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). NOAA's Ocean Service, a trustworthy source, gives a similar figure of more than 65,000 km. I checked the NOAA figure from memory, not from this search. Together these support both parts of the claim: it is the longest range, and it spans over 65,000 km.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.099 x 10^18 square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's Sun infobox puts the Sun's surface area at about 6.09×10^12 km², roughly 12,000 times Earth's surface area. The claimed 5.099×10^18 km² is about a million times too large. The figure 5.1×10^8 km² is actually Earth's surface area.

text: There are approximately 9.3 million species on Earth, with scientists estimating that over 80% of them remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate, from Mora et al. 2011 in PLoS Biology, puts the number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million), not 9.3 million. EurekAlert, National Geographic, ScienceDaily and the Washington Post all report this figure. The same study does support the claim's second half: about 86% of species overall (91% of marine species) have not yet been described, which is over 80%. The total, though, is a different number from the one scientists published. 9.3 million falls inside the study's ±1.3 million margin, but the claim presents it as the estimate itself. Because that central figure does not match, the claim is contradicted.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoralillo Geyser.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out, but I couldn't verify the Totoralillo Geyser. Reliable sources confirm that the Atacama Desert is in northern Chile and has geothermal features, mainly the El Tatio geyser field near San Pedro de Atacama. The Atacama is usually called the driest non-polar desert, so calling it simply the world's driest desert is loose but commonly said. None of my searches found a geyser called Totoralillo. That name only came up as a seaside resort in Chile (Wikidata) and Punta Totoralillo, an industrial mining port (Wikipedia). Neither is a geyser. This makes it likely the geyser is made up, but no source directly says it doesn't exist, so that part can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA, WHOI and Wikipedia all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at roughly 65,000 km (40,389 miles). One small wording difference: NOAA and WHOI say it stretches "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km. Because the figure itself matches, the claim is essentially supported.

text: There are over 37 million acres of protected areas in Antarctica, which includes National Parks, Wildlife Reserves, and other conservation sites managed by various countries.
label: contradicted
reason: Antarctica has no National Parks, so the claim is wrong to include them. CNN states that the continent has no national parks. It is protected under the Antarctic Treaty system instead, through Antarctic Specially Protected Areas, a few seal reserves and the Ross Sea Marine Protected Area. These are designated jointly by the treaty and CCAMLR member countries, not set up as national parks by individual countries. I also found no source for the figure of 'over 37 million acres'. Real figures don't match it: the Ross Sea MPA alone covers 1.55 million km², about 383 million acres, while the land-based specially protected areas add up to far less.

text: The Dinbaugh cave in Montana is home to an impressive accumulation of ancient fossils from animals that lived over 9,000 years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. Searches for "Dinbaugh cave" and "Dinbaugh" Montana found no source that mentions a cave by that name, let alone a fossil deposit there. The results pointed to other sites, such as Natural Trap Cave in Wyoming, which holds a rich layer of Late Pleistocene fossils, but nothing linked them to a "Dinbaugh" cave in Montana. Without any trustworthy source showing that the cave exists or describing its fossils and their ages, I can't confirm or rule out the claim.

text: There are more plastic particles in the ocean than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the claim. The European Parliament, citing the UN, says there may be as many as 51 trillion microplastic particles in the seas, which is 500 times more than the number of stars in our galaxy. The UN's 2017 Clean Seas campaign also said that microplastics in the seas now outnumber the stars in our galaxy. The Milky Way is thought to have roughly 100–400 billion stars, so 51 trillion particles is far more.

text: Whales can hold their breath for around 40 minutes, but typically only stay underwater for around 5-20 minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica says breath-holding time depends heavily on the species, so a single limit of about 40 minutes for whales in general is wrong. Sperm whales and beaked whales often dive for an hour or more, and a Cuvier's beaked whale was recorded diving for 222 minutes. The claim's typical range of 5–20 minutes does fit humpback and minke whales, which surface every 10–15 minutes, and blue whales, which usually dive for 5–15 minutes. But the 40-minute figure understates what many whales can do.

text: A group of convoluted paper found in the nursery, known as "paper mache", qualifies as form of paper produced through ripping and mixing.
label: supported
reason: Dictionary definitions describe papier-mâché as torn-up or shredded paper, or paper pulp, mixed with paste or glue. This supports the claim's main point that it is a paper material made by ripping and mixing. The wording 'found in the nursery' is vague and isn't verified directly, but it fits papier-mâché's common use in children's crafts and doesn't conflict with the evidence.

text: Antarctica is home to several large freshwater lakes, with Lake Vostok being the largest, covering an area of approximately 14,000 square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Guinness World Records names Lake Vostok as the largest subglacial lake and gives its area as 14,000 km², which matches the claim exactly. Other sources, including Wikipedia and WorldAtlas, give about 12,500 km². That is a different estimate, but it is still roughly the claimed size. Wikipedia's page on Antarctic lakes lists many lakes in Antarctica and calls Vostok the largest. Several of those listed lakes are saline, but Antarctica clearly still has several large freshwater lakes beneath the ice, including Vostok.

text: The Danakil Depression is the lowest point on land on Earth, with an elevation of approximately 125 meters below sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: The 125 m below sea level figure is correct. Wikipedia gives that depth for the Danakil/Dallol area, but describes it as "one of the lowest land points," not the lowest. The lowest point on land is the Dead Sea shore, at roughly 430 m below sea level, which is well known and widely documented. So calling the Danakil Depression the lowest point on land on Earth is wrong.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," which is a bit of a tongue-twister.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), not one. It's usually cited as the longest word you can type with only the left hand. Reliable sources name nine-letter words such as "screeched," "strengths," "scratched" and "stretched" as the longest one-syllable words in English. Wikipedia keeps a list of candidates for this title.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.1 x 10^8 times larger than the total surface area of the Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. 5.1 x 10^8 is Earth's surface area in square kilometres (about 510 million km²), not the ratio between the two. The Sun's radius is about 109 times Earth's, so its surface area is about 109² ≈ 12,000 times larger (about 6.09 x 10^12 km² ÷ 5.1 x 10^8 km² ≈ 11,900). BBC Sky at Night Magazine says the Sun's surface area is 12,000 times Earth's.

text: The only bird species in the world that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including UC Davis's Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program, Wikipedia, WorldAtlas and CGTN, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. This claim has two caveats. First, hummingbirds are a whole family of roughly 360 species, not one species. Second, some sources (BirdSpot, Kiwibit) say other birds such as herons, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for a moment. Those sources still agree that only hummingbirds can keep flying backwards. Since the main claim matches widely cited reputable sources, I rated it supported.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various animals and birds.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up the general claim. Coconuts grow on the coconut palm (Cocos nucifera), which is commonly called the coconut tree. A gardening source says coconut palms support many kinds of life, with their flowers drawing pollinators and their fruits feeding birds and mammals. A field study from Kerala, India recorded many bird species using coconut palms, and coconut crabs eat coconut meat. An agroforestry source says palms in general give shelter and food to birds and small animals. One caveat: a Stanford study on Palmyra Atoll found that spreading coconut palms there harmed the local ecosystem because seabirds avoided nesting in them. That is a specific case of palms taking over an island, though, and does not disprove the broad claim that coconuts 'can help' by giving animals food and shelter.

text: The Sweet Vernal grass has a naturally occurring scent that can emit an odor smelling like vanilla when it's dried and broken down.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on Anthoxanthum odoratum (sweet vernal grass) says its scent is especially strong when the grass is dried. It attributes the scent to coumarin, a glycoside and benzoic acid, and describes it as smelling like fresh hay with a hint of vanilla. Other sources, including British Wildlife and lois.co.uk, also link the scent to coumarin and describe it as vanilla-like. The claim's phrase 'broken down' isn't stated directly, but it fits how the scent is released as the grass dries or is cut, so nothing contradicts the claim.

text: The driest desert in the world is the Atacama Desert in Chile, accounting for only 0.01% of the world's fresh water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Discovery, describe Chile's Atacama as the driest non-polar desert. Some scientists instead name parts of Antarctica, such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys, as the driest place, so even that part depends on the definition used. I found no source saying the Atacama holds only 0.01% of the world's fresh water. That figure appears to be unsupported and doesn't make much sense as a measure of a desert. Because this part can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The shorter length of space Ships would make astronauts travel back to their home spaceship falling more times while entering the earth's atmosphere than a longer length.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is too garbled to check properly. It is not clear what 'falling more times' or 'travel back to their home spaceship' mean, and I found no source linking a spacecraft's length to how many times astronauts 'fall' during re-entry into Earth's atmosphere. The search turned up only general re-entry material, such as ESA research on the atmospheric effects of re-entry and SpaceShipOne's 'feathering' re-entry system. None of it confirms or refutes the claim.

text: The smallest crystal planet in our solar system is Mars, which has a tilted axis that causes its rotation patterns to be the most Earth-like among all the planets.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA says Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system, and it is also one of the rocky (terrestrial) planets along with Venus, Earth and Mars. So Mars is not the smallest rocky planet. "Crystal planet" is not a real scientific category. Mars's axial tilt does give it Earth-like seasons, but the claim's central statement, that Mars is the smallest, is false.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spanning over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration, WHOI, Guinness World Records and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as Earth's longest mountain range. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,000–40,390 miles), which matches the claim's figures. One wording difference: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Since the length is an approximate estimate, this doesn't contradict the claim.

text: The�ước wich hypothesis suggests that life on Earth arose independently in multiple regions, which has sparked intense debate and research in the field of astrobiology.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim names a garbled entity ("The�ước wich hypothesis"), so there is no clear hypothesis to check. Some ideas do discuss life arising more than once, such as the 'shadow biosphere' or multiple-origins proposals. But none can be confidently matched to this name, so the claim can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: Dolphins have a unique signature whistle that acts as their name and is used by other dolphins to identify them.
label: supported
reason: NBC News, reporting on a study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, says bottlenose dolphins develop their own signature whistles that work as names. The whistles let dolphins identify and recognize one another, and dolphins copy the whistles of others to call them. One caveat: the research is mainly on bottlenose dolphins, while the claim speaks of dolphins in general.

text: The Nazi regime was responsible for the deaths of approximately 11 million people during World War II, including 6 million Jews in the Holocaust.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of 6 million Jews killed in the Holocaust is well supported by USHMM and Yad Vashem. The total of about 11 million is not. According to the Jewish Virtual Library and JTA, Simon Wiesenthal made up the "11 million" figure (6 million Jews plus 5 million others) and historians call it inaccurate. Mainstream estimates, such as the USHMM's tally of victims of Nazi persecution and the victim categories listed on Wikipedia's "Victims of Nazi Germany" page, put the regime's death toll at about 17 million or more. That figure does not even count military deaths in the war Germany started, so 11 million understates the Nazi regime's death toll by a wide margin.

text: The highest recorded elevator in the world is the Elevator at the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, which travels an astonishing 504 meters vertically.
label: contradicted
reason: The 504-metre figure is correct for one of Burj Khalifa's elevators, but that record no longer stands. Several sources describe 504 m as the former record and say Shanghai Tower's elevators beat it with a 578.5-metre travel distance per trip. One less authoritative site still calls Burj Khalifa the current record holder, but more specific sources say it has been surpassed, so the claim that Burj Khalifa has the world's record elevator is outdated.

text: Theunsupported network CGI (Child Guided (Internet) Instant ) currently serves more than a million search requests per day.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any network or service called "CGI (Child Guided (Internet) Instant)". The claim is also garbled ("Theunsupported network"), so it has no clear referent. Searching only turned up unrelated articles about CGI-bin web servers handling millions of requests per day. Nothing confirms or refutes that this entity exists or that it serves more than a million search requests per day.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, accounting for more than 75% of all described species discovered to date.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) comes from Mora et al. (2011). It estimates all eukaryotic species, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. It is also mostly undescribed species: about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species have not yet been discovered, and only around 1.2 million species have been described. So 8.7 million species cannot make up more than 75% of described species, and the claim misstates the estimate as 'over' 8.7 million plants and animals.

text: The longest reigning monarch in recorded history was King Louis XIV of France, who ruled for 72 years and 110 days from 1643 to 1715.
label: contradicted
reason: The dates and length are right: Louis XIV reigned from 14 May 1643 to 1 September 1715, which is 72 years and 110 days. The "longest in recorded history" part is wrong. Wikipedia's Records of heads of state page gives Louis XIV the record only among monarchs of sovereign states. It names Sobhuza II of Swaziland (now Eswatini) as the longest-reigning verifiable monarch, at about 82 years and 254 days (1899–1982). For much of that time Swaziland was under British protection rather than independent. Longer reigns are also claimed for other rulers, such as Min Hti of Arakan. Many popular lists do rank Louis XIV first, but they leave out the sovereign-state condition the record depends on. Without it, the claim overstates his record.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 86 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion neuron figure is right (Azevedo et al., 2009), but the comparison is wrong. Psychology Today says it is a widespread myth that the brain has more neurons than the Milky Way has stars. Our galaxy has an estimated 200–400 billion stars, which is well above 86 billion.

text: Glowworms have a specialized light organ near their abdomen that contains a chemical called luciferin, which reacts with oxygen to produce a fluorescent green light.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the main points of the claim. Buglife and other sources say the common glow-worm (Lampyris noctiluca) glows from a light organ in its last abdominal segments and gives off a yellow-green light. The Tamborine Glow Worms site says glow worms have a specialised light organ in which luciferin combines with oxygen, with help from the enzyme luciferase, to make a blue-green light. One wording problem: the light comes from bioluminescence, not fluorescence, so "fluorescent green" is best read loosely as "bright green" rather than as a scientific claim. The claim also leaves out luciferase, and the exact colour varies by species (yellow-green or blue-green). These are imprecisions rather than contradictions.

text: Pluto is composed of approximately 70% rock, 25% water ice, and 5% methane and ethane ices.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including NASA/JHU APL's New Horizons site, Space.com and NOAA, describe Pluto as about 70% rock and 30% water ice by mass. The APL site gives a range of 65–70% rock and 30–35% ice for Pluto and Charon together. None of the sources gives a 25% water ice / 5% methane-and-ethane split. They describe methane, along with nitrogen and carbon monoxide, only as a thin surface ice layer, not as 5% of Pluto's bulk. The 70% rock figure is correct, but the ice breakdown is wrong.

text: The surface of the Mars planet is covered with about 25% ice.
label: contradicted
reason: No trustworthy source says that about 25% of Mars's surface is covered with ice. NASA JPL and the USGS (lead author Colin Dundas) say there is shallow ground ice under roughly a third of the Martian surface, and the Planetary Society says the same. That is ice just beneath the ground, not ice covering the surface. Exposed surface ice is mostly limited to the polar caps. The 25% figures that appear in search results refer to unrelated things: an old estimate of dust in the north polar ice, the share of Mars's history spent in ice ages, and the share of atmospheric CO2 that freezes at the poles. The claim's figure therefore does not match the evidence.

text: There are over 7,900 known species of sounds produced by insects, known as insect music or insect calls, which can be heard from anywhere in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that gives the figure of 7,900. The claim is also badly worded, since it counts "species of sounds" rather than species of insects that make sounds. The closest evidence is Alexander et al.'s "The Singing Insects of Michigan," published in The Great Lakes Entomologist. It estimates 25,000–30,000 singing insect species (crickets, katydids, grasshoppers and cicadas) worldwide, with only about 1,000 studied in detail. That estimate neither confirms nor clearly contradicts the specific 7,900 figure. Nothing I found supports the idea that these sounds can be heard from anywhere in the world either.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. NOAA and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). NOAA's Ocean Exploration page says 'nearly' 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, and a PMC paper gives about 75,000 km, so 'over 65,000 km' fits these figures. The ridge does run through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific (East Pacific Rise). 'Middle' is loose wording, since the East Pacific Rise lies off-centre in the Pacific.

text: The Human Brain contains around 100 billion neurons and is estimated to process 70,000 thoughts per day.
label: contradicted
reason: The neuron part is roughly right. The commonly quoted 100 billion is close to the measured figure of about 86 billion (BrainFacts, PMC). The 70,000-thoughts-per-day part is not. Neuroscience sources call it a persistent myth with no peer-reviewed basis (The Neurocritic, among others). A 2020 Queen's University fMRI study estimated about 6,200 thoughts per day, which contradicts the figure in the claim.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, which has a coastline of approximately 243,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Statistics Canada both say Canada has the world's longest coastline, at 243,042 km. That matches the claim's figure of about 243,000 km. Mental Floss notes that some other sources give 202,080 km because of the coastline paradox, but official Canadian sources back the claim's number, and nobody disputes that Canada ranks first.

text: The unique sound made by a dolphin is produced by clicking together a series of small bones in its lower jaw called the mandible.
label: contradicted
reason: Dolphins don't make their clicks with jaw bones. The Dolphin Communication Project says their clicks come from the phonic lips, structures in the nasal passages just below the blowhole, as air is pushed back and forth across them by the nasal sacs. The lower jaw is used to receive sound, not produce it. Also, the mandible is one jawbone, not a series of small bones.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal due to its ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources (EBSCO Research Starters, Britannica) describe Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." Under stress or injury, it can turn back into its juvenile polyp stage and restart its life cycle through a process called transdifferentiation, in which specialized cells change into other cell types. One nuance: it is considered 'biologically' immortal, meaning it does not die of old age, but it can still be killed by predators or disease. This matches how the claim is commonly understood.

text: Gibbs' phenomenon, a term coined by British mathematician James William Gibbs, involves oscillations or "ringing" occurring around a step or discontinuity in a Fourier series, illustrating complex mathematical concepts.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the Gibbs phenomenon is named after Josiah Willard Gibbs, an American physicist, not a British mathematician called "James William Gibbs." It also says Maxime Bôcher coined the term "Gibbs phenomenon" in 1906, so Gibbs did not coin it himself. The claim's description of the phenomenon as oscillations or ringing near a discontinuity in a Fourier series is accurate, but the name, nationality and attribution are wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, running for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says the Mid-Ocean Ridge is technically the longest mountain range in the world and stretches about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) across the globe. NOAA, a trustworthy source, makes the same point: it calls the mid-ocean ridge system the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, at more than 65,000 km long. The claim's "over 65,000 km (40,000 miles)" matches these figures, since 40,390 miles is just over 40,000.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA puts its length at about 65,000 km (40,390 mi), and WorldAtlas and Wikipedia's list of mountain ranges give similar figures. The ridge system runs across the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific (East Pacific Rise). Two small caveats: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," and the Pacific segment is not literally in the middle of that ocean. Neither point changes the substance of the claim.

text: The shallowest known point on Earth is located in the Red Sea, where the water is only about 148 meters deep.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. No reliable source calls any spot in the Red Sea the "shallowest known point on Earth", and the idea doesn't make sense, since plenty of seas have points much shallower than 148 m. The claim seems to confuse this with the shallowest part of the Red Sea's link to the Indian Ocean, the Hanish Sill in the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. Even there, the depth doesn't match: PNAS gives it as 137 m deep and other literature says about 160 m, not 148 m. The sill is only the shallowest point of that channel, not a record for the whole planet.

text: The Blind Faith double album "Appearance and Other Attractions" sold very well however their 1970 single "Can't Get Out" didn't encourage major labels agreeing to sign the band.
label: contradicted
reason: Blind Faith, the 1969 supergroup with Clapton, Winwood, Baker and Grech, made only one studio album. It was the single LP "Blind Faith" (1969), not a double album called "Appearance and Other Attractions," and I found no record of that title. The band was already on major labels (Polydor in the UK, Atco in the US), broke up in 1969 after one album and one tour, and is known for singles like "Can't Find My Way Home" and "Presence of the Lord," not "Can't Get Out." So the claim's album, single and record-label story don't match the documented history. One caveat: my last search failed, so I couldn't fully rule out a different, obscure band with the same name.

text: There are currently over 10 million registered apartments in New York City, which is a significant number considering the city's small land area.
label: contradicted
reason: According to the 2023 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey, as reported by the city's Rent Guidelines Board, New York City had about 3,705,000 housing units in total. That figure covers all housing types, not just apartments, and it is far below the claimed 10 million or more. The city's population is only about 8.3 million, so the claim's figure is implausible as well as contradicted by official data.

text: Aye-aye, the world's largest bird of prey, is the wandering albatross, which has wingspans reaching up to 11.8 feet (3.6 meters) in length.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different animals and gets the bird wrong too. The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur (a primate) from Madagascar, not a bird. The wandering albatross is a seabird, not a bird of prey (raptor), so it can't be the world's largest bird of prey. It does have the largest wingspan of any living bird, about 3.5 m (11.5 ft), with a maximum of about 3.7 m, so the 3.6 m figure is roughly right. Still, the claim's main points are false.

text: Theammu, an enormous crocodile, was estimated to weigh approximately 2,000 kilograms (4,400 pounds) and is considered the largest known saltwater crocodile in history.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy record of a crocodile called "Theammu". Searches for the name only turned up unrelated social media accounts, so the claim's subject can't be identified. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and Guinness World Records name other animals as the largest measured saltwater crocodiles, such as Lolong, which weighed 1,075 kg (2,370 lb).
