None of them mention a 2,000 kg crocodile by this name. That suggests the claim is likely inaccurate, but because the crocodile it names can't be found, there's no evidence that directly confirms or disproves anything said about it.

text: A giraffe has the highest blood pressure of any animal, with readings nearing 280 over 180, which is equivalent to the blood pressure of a BP reader off the charts.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Politecnico di Milano's iHeart page and a healthcare network article, say giraffe blood pressure reaches about 280/180 mmHg, roughly twice the human level, and many sources call it the highest in the animal kingdom. Some sources narrow this to 'among mammals' or 'land animals', but I found none naming an animal with higher pressure. The 'off the charts' comparison is rhetorical rather than factual. Readings of 280/180 are far above the human hypertensive-crisis level, so the comparison is consistent with the evidence.

text: A chuuk kayak, also known as a true kayak, is a traditional type of boat originating from the Aleut people of the Bering Strait that features a one-person frame with a woven seal or sea lion skin stretchers for the seat.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a boat called a "chuuk kayak" exists, and the evidence points against the claim. Chuuk is a state in Micronesia, and its traditional craft is the outrigger sailing canoe, not a skin kayak. The Aleut skin-on-frame kayak is called the baidarka or iqyax (Aleutian kayak), not a "chuuk kayak." Its frame was covered with sewn sea lion skins, so the skin was the hull covering, not woven seat stretchers. The Aleutians are also not the Bering Strait. The claim mixes up names and details that don't belong together.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, of which only a small fraction have been formally discovered and documented.
label: supported
reason: The 2011 Mora et al. study, as reported by BioEd Online (Nature News) and The Globe and Mail, estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million had been identified, which is less than 15%, and an estimated 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered. That supports the main point that only a small fraction have been formally documented. Two details are a little loose: the study gives about 8.7 million rather than 'over' 8.7 million, and its count also covers fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. Neither changes the substance of the claim.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2016 estimate by the University of Oxford's Zoological Museum.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-known estimate of about 8.7 million species (give or take 1.3 million) comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology paper by Camilo Mora and colleagues at Dalhousie University and the University of Hawaii, done for the Census of Marine Life. It was not a 2016 estimate from the University of Oxford's Zoological Museum. It also counts all eukaryotic species, not just plants and animals, and gives about 8.7 million rather than 'over' 8.7 million. So the claim gets the source and the year wrong.

text: There is a species of jellyfish that is immortal because of its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Britannica, a PubMed-indexed paper and EBSCO, describe Turritopsis dohrnii as the "immortal jellyfish." They say it can turn from its adult medusa form back into a juvenile polyp and restart its life cycle through a process called transdifferentiation. "Immortal" here means it can avoid dying of old age by repeating this cycle, not that it can't be killed, but this matches how the claim describes it.

text: Did you know that the longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be a one-syllable word at all. It is actually known as one of the longest words you can type using only the left hand on a standard keyboard. Wikipedia and other sources name nine-letter words like "screeched," "scratched" and "strengths" as the longest English words of one syllable.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it has a decentralized architecture.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's "Brief History of the Internet", written by Internet pioneers including Leiner, Cerf and Kahn, says outright that the idea of ARPANET being built to survive nuclear war is a "false rumor" that came from the separate RAND study by Paul Baran on secure military voice networks. It says this "was never true of the ARPANET." ARPANET was mainly created so researchers could share computing resources. Survivability was a goal of Baran's RAND work, not the reason ARPANET or the Internet was designed.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique shape and speed of their movements convey information about food sources and nesting locations.
label: supported
reason: ScienceDirect's overview of the honeybee waggle dance backs every part of the claim. The dance tells other bees the direction and distance of a food source: the angle of the waggle run gives the direction, and how long the waggle phase lasts gives the distance. Scout bees from a swarm also do waggle dances to point others to new nesting sites. So honeybees do use complex dance patterns, whose shape (orientation and form) and timing carry information about both food and nest locations.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and is located in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back up the main points of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge is the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (about 40,390 mi). WHOI calls it the longest mountain range in the world, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 mi), and says it crisscrosses the world's oceans. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, and says it runs through every ocean, which includes the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. Two details are slightly off. First, most sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over' 65,000 km, although the 80,000 km figure for the full system fits 'over'. Second, the ridge also reaches the Arctic and Southern Oceans, so the claim's list of oceans is incomplete, though not wrong. Neither detail contradicts the core claim.

text: There are over 8.7 million bird species existing on Earth according to recent estimates, with scientists continuing to learn more about the vast diversity of avifauna.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Recent estimates put the number of bird species at roughly 11,000, or about 18,000 under a 2016 American Museum of Natural History study, not over 8.7 million. The 8.7 million figure is a well-known 2011 estimate (Mora et al.) for all species on Earth, not for birds alone. The idea that scientists are still learning about bird diversity is reasonable, but the main number is off by a huge margin.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales, UK, are home to a 400-meter-long natural rock arch called the Worm's Head, which is only accessible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Worm's Head is a tidal headland, or tidal island, at the southern end of Rhossili Bay. It is not a rock arch. It is made up of the Inner, Middle and Outer Heads and reaches about a mile (around 1.6 km) out to sea, so it is far longer than 400 metres. The natural rock arch on it is a separate feature called the Devil's Bridge. Wikipedia, Atlas Obscura, UK South West and Komoot all agree on this. The claim is right that Worm's Head can only be reached at low tide, across a tidal causeway about 650 m long, but calling it a 400-metre natural rock arch is wrong.

text: The crystal-clear waters of the Great Blue Hole in Belize are home to a wide variety of marine life, including groupers, snappers, and sharks.
label: supported
reason: My searches found sources backing each part of the claim. Several Belize tourism and diving sites say the Great Blue Hole is home to giant groupers and several kinds of sharks, including nurse, Caribbean reef and blacktip sharks (visitcentroamerica.com, cahalpech.com, portofinobelize.com). A dive report from the Great Blue Hole mentions groupers, schools of snappers and Caribbean reef sharks (theadventuresatlas.com), and Portofino Belize describes diving there in 'crystal-clear water.' Snappers came up in only that one diver's account, and none of the sources is scientific, but nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: The longest record of virginity in a woman is held by a Chinese woman named Feng Jiang, who waited until her wedding night at the age of 39 to lose her virginity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no credible source that mentions a 'Feng Jiang' or any recognised record for a woman staying a virgin until her wedding night at 39. My first search for that name and record turned up only unrelated pages, such as a Wikipedia article on the film 'Women Speak'. A search for the oldest virgin returned only an informal Medium blog post. My later searches failed because I hit the tool's search limit. Guinness World Records is not known to track a category like this, and many people stay virgins far longer than 39, so the claim looks doubtful. Still, no trustworthy source directly confirms or refutes it.

text: The world's longest mountain range, known as the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range. However, both put its length at "nearly" 65,000 km, not over 65,000 km. They also describe it as a global system that wraps around the planet like the seams on a baseball and winds between all the continents. Only one part of it, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, runs through the middle of the Atlantic. So the claim gets the length wrong and treats the whole global system as if it were the Atlantic segment. This is a close call: the system does pass through the Atlantic, and some older sources say "more than 65,000 km."

text: There is a species of jellyfish called the turbellarian that is biologically immortal, meaning it can revert back to its polyp stage after experiencing physical damage or aging, thereby regenerating itself indefinitely.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong animal. "Turbellarian" refers to the class Turbellaria, a group of mostly free-living flatworms (phylum Platyhelminthes), not jellyfish. Flatworms have no polyp stage. The jellyfish known for being biologically immortal is Turritopsis dohrnii, the "immortal jellyfish." Britannica says it can avoid death by repeatedly cycling between its polyp and medusa forms. The description of the ability is broadly accurate, but it belongs to Turritopsis dohrnii, not a "turbellarian."

text: There is a species of jellyfish called the turbellarian which is biologically immortal, as it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the name wrong. Turbellarians aren't jellyfish. They're a class of free-living flatworms in the phylum Platyhelminthes. The biologically immortal jellyfish that returns to a younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation is Turritopsis dohrnii (phylum Cnidaria), as Britannica, EBSCO and a PubMed paper describe. The part about transdifferentiation is accurate, but it applies to Turritopsis dohrnii, not to a 'turbellarian'.

text: Cutom made the first performance of the air jet machine, which is a precursor to modern vacuum cleaners, in 1901.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions anyone called "Cutom" in connection with an air jet machine or early vacuum cleaners. The name has no clear referent. Reliable accounts, including Wikipedia, History.com and Encyclopedia.com, say that in 1901 Hubert Cecil Booth watched a London demonstration of an American machine that blew dust away with compressed air. That machine is described as the forerunner of Booth's suction vacuum cleaner. The sources do not agree on who gave the demonstration. Wikipedia says Booth did not name the inventor, and that the machine's description closely matches John S. Thurman's blown-air design. Some secondary sources simply name Thurman. Nothing links "Cutom" to this event, and no source says it was the machine's first demonstration. Because the claim's subject cannot be identified or verified, the evidence neither supports nor clearly contradicts it.

text: The emotional support animal Sunny Boy, a Capybara, is often cited as the first emotional support animal in the United States.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a capybara named Sunny Boy exists as an emotional support animal, or that any source calls it the first ESA in the U.S. The only results named Sunny Boy were unrelated: a three-legged dog on Tripawds, a dog character from Elmo's World and a rescued Australian Shepherd. Other results were about capybaras in general or emotional support animal law, and none mentioned a 'first' ESA. Nothing directly contradicts the claim either, so it can't be verified. My search was cut short by a tool usage limit, so one search about capybaras as the first U.S. ESA didn't run.

text: There are over 1.9 million distinct species of plants and animals that have been identified on Earth, according to estimates from scientists.
label: supported
reason: Our World in Data, which uses IUCN Red List figures, says about 2.17 million species had been described by 2025. It also notes that the widely cited count was 1.9 million described species (Chapman 2009). In the IUCN breakdown, animals, mostly about 1 million insects plus other invertebrates and vertebrates, together with roughly 400,000 or more plants, add up to over 1.9 million identified species. The claim is therefore consistent with scientific estimates. One caveat is that some described species may be duplicates under different names, which would lower the count of truly distinct species.

text: Bacteria can survive and even thrive in extreme environments, such as high temperatures, intense pressure, and high salinity, due to their ability to adapt and evolve.
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources describe extremophiles, including many bacteria, as microorganisms that survive and thrive in extreme conditions such as high temperatures, high pressure and high salinity. They attribute this to adaptations like modified cell structures, more stable proteins and nucleic acids, pressure-dependent protein expression, and the ability to keep internal conditions steady. Examples include salt-tolerant Halomonadaceae and the deep-sea bacterium Photobacterium profundum. This supports every part of the claim.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious and ancient freshwater river that appears to be boiling and producing geothermal heat, despite being located in the Amazon rainforest.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on Shanay-timpishka, which cites National Geographic and Forbes, describes it as the "Boiling River of the Amazon." It is part of the Amazon River system in the Peruvian rainforest and stays very hot even though no active volcano is nearby. That surprising heat is why it's called a geological anomaly and treated as a mystery. Andrés Ruzo's research links the heat to geothermal (hydrothermal) sources, and local legends about the river go back a long way. The claim's wording is loose, since the river is hot rather than literally boiling and "ancient" is vague, but its main points match the sources and nothing in them contradicts it.

text: The Sarojini Naidu Technical Institute is India's first chemical engineering college.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any institution called the "Sarojini Naidu Technical Institute" that is linked to chemical engineering. The search turned up only unrelated places with similar names: Sarojini Naidu Medical College in Agra, Sarojini Naidu College for Women in Kolkata, a Sarojini Technical Institute ITI in Jamshedpur, and an unofficial Wix page for a "Sarojini Naidu Institute of Technology". None of them claims to be India's first chemical engineering college. Sources name other institutions for that title instead. Jadavpur University's department (founded in 1921 under the National Council of Education) is described as the first of its kind in India. Andhra University College of Engineering is also called the first, though Wikipedia flags that claim as 'citation needed', and the University of Calcutta's applied chemistry department dates back to 1920. Because sources credit other institutions and nothing supports the named one, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 88,000 active stars within the Milky Way galaxy that are visible to the naked eye from Earth on a clear night.
label: contradicted
reason: Astronomy sources say only a few thousand stars can be seen with the naked eye. Under dark skies, a person could see about 6,000 over a whole year (other estimates go up to roughly 9,000 across the entire sky), and only a few hundred from light-polluted cities. Both figures are far below the 88,000 in the claim.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is biologically immortal and can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (EBSCO Research Starters and Britannica) say that Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the "immortal jellyfish," can turn back into its juvenile (polyp) form and restart its life cycle. EBSCO names the process transdifferentiation, in which specialized cells are converted into other cell types. One small caveat: the species is only immortal in the biological sense, since it can still be killed by predators or disease. That matches the claim's wording of "biologically immortal."

text: 超过1000亿颗恒星组成了银河系的总体结构。
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. Wikipedia puts the Milky Way's star count at 100–400 billion, and Star Walk says it has "at least 100 billion stars." Both estimates fit the claim that the galaxy is made up of more than 100 billion stars. The low end of the range is exactly 100 billion, but sources treat it as a minimum, so they are consistent with "more than 100 billion."

text: Giraffes have the highest blood pressure of any animal, with some studies showing their blood pressure can be as high as 280/180 mmHg.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say giraffes have the highest blood pressure of any animal. A-Z Animals and an X/Twitter fact account say it outright, and a Medium article says it's the highest of any living land animal. A health-system site (Desert Care Network) gives figures of up to 280/180 mmHg, about twice the human level, and other sources cite 260–280 mmHg systolic. A Politecnico di Milano page also confirms that pressure near the giraffe's heart is about twice a human's. One caveat: some sources hedge with 'one of the highest' or 'highest among land animals'. Still, no source names an animal with higher pressure, so the claim is generally supported.

text: Rivers are responsible for transporting about 17% of the dissolved oxygen found in the Earth's atmosphere.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source for the 17% figure, and the claim is muddled because dissolved oxygen is found in water, not in the atmosphere. Recent research on the global oxygen cycle of inland waters (Utrecht University study, reported by Phys.org and Courthouse News) finds that rivers, lakes and reservoirs are a net sink of atmospheric oxygen, not a source. That cuts against the claim's premise but does not directly address a 17% transport figure, so the specific claim can be neither confirmed nor directly refuted.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the mountain range on Mars, which is known as the Olympia Mons and is approximately 620 kilometers long.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets wrong what kind of feature Olympus Mons is, and its name. It is a single shield volcano on Mars, not a mountain range, and it is spelled 'Olympus Mons', not 'Olympia Mons'. Its main record is height (about 22–26 km), which makes it the tallest mountain in the Solar System, not the longest range. The 600+ km figure is the volcano's diameter, not the length of a range. Wikipedia and a peer-reviewed 1984 Nature abstract (indexed on Harvard ADS) both describe it as a shield volcano about 600 km across.

text: The number of trees on Earth is estimated to be around 3 trillion, with approximately 20% of those being found in the Amazon rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 3 trillion trees on Earth is right; it comes from a 2015 study. The 20% share for the Amazon is wrong. The Amazon is estimated to hold about 390 billion trees, which is roughly 13% of the global total. 20% would mean about 600 billion trees.

text: The short-tailed albatross, a bird species, has one of the lowest reproductive rates among all birds, with females laying only 1 egg every 3-5 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (the USFWS 5-Year Review, Alaska Department of Fish & Game, and the Yamashina Institute) all say the short-tailed albatross breeds every year and lays a single egg each year. Some adults skip a year now and then, and one source says 'each year or every other year,' but none say one egg every 3-5 years. The species does reproduce slowly because it starts breeding late, but the 3-5 year interval in the claim is wrong.

text: The total amount of called information that can be stored on a standard DVD is approximately 4.7 gigabytes.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's DVD article says a standard single-layer DVD can store up to 4.7 GB. That matches the claim's figure of about 4.7 gigabytes. The odd wording "called information" seems to just mean data. Dual-layer and double-sided discs hold more (8.5 GB or higher), but 4.7 GB is the usual figure for a standard disc.

text: The total surface area of the glaciers in Antarctica is approximately 5.4 million square miles.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic Education says Antarctica's ice sheet, which is glacial ice, covers about 14 million km², or 5.4 million square miles. Aurora Expeditions gives the same figures. One caveat: the claim says "glaciers", while the sources describe the ice sheet as a whole, but the figure itself matches.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and adaptable today.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a well-known myth. The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet" says the idea that ARPANET was meant to survive nuclear war is a false rumor that came from an unrelated RAND study, and states that "This was never true of the ARPANET." Only the RAND study, which was about secure voice communication, considered nuclear war. ARPANET itself was built mainly so researchers could share computing resources. The claim that the Internet was originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack is therefore false. The Internet's robustness today comes from later design choices, not from that original purpose.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) also calls mid-ocean ridges the planet's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km. Both sources match the claim.

text: A fleets of icebergs formed on Henderson Island in the South Pacific during a severe storm in 2020 but then disappeared the following day.
label: contradicted
reason: Henderson Island is a raised coral atoll in the Pitcairn Islands. Its climate is subtropical, with temperatures mostly between about 15°C and 30°C and rarely any cold nights. Icebergs could not form there, and I found no record of icebergs forming on the island during a 2020 storm. The island is best known for its plastic pollution, not ice. The physical facts about the island contradict the claim.

text: A honeybee colony can produce enough honey to feed itself and have an excess of up to 60 pounds (27 kg) per year.
label: supported
reason: Several beekeeping sources say a healthy, established colony keeps enough honey for its own needs and produces about 30–60 lb (14–27 kg) of surplus honey per year, matching the claim's figure of up to 60 lb (27 kg). This is how the beekeeping guides (Apiary Tools, BeekeepPro, Homestead Calc and Beekeeping Insider) describe it, and Carolina Honeybees calls 60 lb per hive a commonly cited average. These are not peer-reviewed sources, so the support is moderate. Some sources, such as University of Missouri Extension, give a higher range of 50–100 lb in good conditions. That means 60 lb is a typical upper figure rather than a hard limit, but it doesn't contradict the claim.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania contains one of the largest collections of floatstones, which are rocks that contain fossilized ferns and other plant material.
label: contradicted
reason: Floatstone is defined in geology glossaries (Mindat, the National Park Service's building stone glossary, Wikipedia) as a matrix-supported carbonate rock in which more than 10% of the grains are larger than 2 mm. None of these definitions describe it as rock containing fossilized ferns or plant material, so the claim's definition is wrong. The sources about Butlers Gorge in Tasmania (Wikipedia, the University of Tasmania's SPARC site, and a camping guide) describe it as a rural locality, the site of the Clark Dam and a Hydro Tasmania power station. None of them mention any notable floatstone collection.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not only a mountain range but also a vast underwater geological feature.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth and that more than 90% of it lies underwater. They put its length at nearly 65,000 km. Other sources give longer figures: about 74,000 km (NASA) and about 75,000 km (a PMC study). NOAA and WHOI's wording is 'nearly' rather than 'over' 65,000 km, but taken together the sources broadly back the 'over 65,000 km' figure. The rest of the claim is clearly supported: it is the longest range and a vast underwater geological feature.

text: Aussie bats, a rare species of flying foxes, are known for migrating over 500 miles to find food in Western Australia every year.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No species is called "Aussie bats." The term just means Australian bats, so it's unclear which animal the claim is about. Trusted sources say Australian flying-foxes, such as the grey-headed and little red flying-foxes, are nomads that travel long distances to find food. For example, grey-headed flying-foxes average about 1,500 km a year between camps. However, those movements are mainly across eastern Australia, and the species are not described as rare. No source supports a yearly migration of over 500 miles to find food in Western Australia by a rare 'Aussie bat' species. Because the subject has no clear referent and the key details can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Buttah and lard is another term for the animal products other than milk that come from a cow.
label: contradicted
reason: No source treats "buttah and lard" as a term for cow products other than milk. "Buttah" is just slang for butter (Wiktionary), and butter is itself made from milk. Lard is fat from pigs, not cows: the Cambridge and Collins dictionaries both define it as pig fat. The claim gets the animal wrong and calls a milk product something other than milk.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique shape and movement of their dance tells other bees where to find food?
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources such as ScienceDirect's overview of the waggle dance say honeybees use dances to tell other bees where food is. The direction of the waggle run shows the direction of the food relative to the sun, and how long the waggle lasts shows the distance. The dance's shape (round vs. waggle) and its movements carry the information, so the claim matches the well-established science.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-oceanic Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources (NOAA Ocean Service, NOAA Ocean Exploration, WHOI, Wikipedia, WorldAtlas) all agree that the global mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. They give its length as roughly 65,000 km (40,000 to 40,390 miles). One caveat on the number: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Other sources say about 65,000 km. That gap is small and within the usual approximation, so the claim's core points (longest range, underwater mid-ocean ridge, about 65,000 km around the globe) are supported.

text: There are more than 8 million registered birds in the UK, which account for approximately 1 in every 10 people in the country.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for a figure of more than 8 million "registered birds" in the UK, and the claim doesn't say which birds it means. The UK has no national register of pet birds. UK Pet Food estimates about 1.4–1.6 million indoor pet birds, far below 8 million. Poultry-register figures run to tens of millions or more, and the BTO estimates about 85 million breeding pairs of wild birds, both far above 8 million. The ratio is also off: 8 million against a population of about 67–68 million is closer to 1 in 8 than 1 in 10. Because the claim doesn't clearly refer to any one group of birds and no source matches it, the evidence is inconclusive.

text: The住吉learantior of Probability Theory, Blaise Pascal, invented the first mechanical calculator, called the Pascaline, in 1642.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Two parts of the claim check out. Wikipedia confirms Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline in 1642, and Pascal is widely recognised as a co-founder of probability theory, along with Fermat. The claim that it was 'the first mechanical calculator' is disputed. Wikipedia calls it only the 'first operational' mechanical calculator. The CACM blog and Wikipedia's computing timeline both say Wilhelm Schickard designed a 'calculating clock' in 1623, which is earlier. The descriptor '住吉learantior' is also garbled, so that part can't be checked as written. Because the sources disagree on 'first' and part of the text is unreadable, I can't judge the claim as fully supported.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, giving the same figure as the claim: about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Wikipedia and WHOI agree that it is the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. One wording difference: NOAA Ocean Exploration says "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Other sources and NOAA's Ocean Service describe it as more than 65,000 km, so the claim matches the standard figure.

text: The Nazi regime was responsible for the deaths of approximately 11 million people, including 6 million Jews, during the Holocaust, which occurred from 1933 to 1945.
label: contradicted
reason: The 6 million Jewish victims and the 1933–1945 timeframe match reliable sources such as the USHMM. The "11 million" total does not. Holocaust Museum Houston calls it a common but unsupported statistic: the 6 million Jewish victims are documented, but the "5 million others" figure is not. Historians and outlets such as Commentary and the Times of Israel (via Jewish Journal) trace the number to Simon Wiesenthal and call it a myth. The USHMM's victim estimates also do not support a total of 11 million.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs down the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range. NOAA puts it at nearly 65,000 km, and it winds through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Two details are loosely worded. First, NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km. Other sources estimate a longer length when every ridge segment is counted, but none appeared in this search. Second, the Pacific ridge (the East Pacific Rise) does not run down the centre of that ocean. Neither point undermines the main claim, so I judge it supported.

text: Tornadoes are the most destructive type of storm on Earth, responsible for a significant number of deaths and damage worldwide each year.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say tropical cyclones (hurricanes and typhoons) are the most destructive storms on Earth, not tornadoes. HowStuffWorks says the most destructive storms are tropical cyclones because of their winds, storm surge and heavy rain, with Katrina and Haiyan as examples. NOAA also commonly calls hurricanes the most powerful and destructive storms. Tornadoes can produce the most violent local winds and do cause deaths and damage, but they are not the most destructive type of storm overall.

text: There is a species of jellyfish that is immortal due to its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Britannica, PubMed and Wikipedia all describe Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the "immortal jellyfish." It can restart its life cycle by turning from an adult medusa back into a juvenile polyp through transdifferentiation. Sources note that it is only "biologically immortal": the jellyfish can still die from predators or disease. That is consistent with how the claim uses the word.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA gives its length as nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and WHOI says it stretches 40,000 miles around the globe. The claim says "over" 65,000 km, while NOAA says "nearly," but this is a small wording difference within normal rounding, and the overall figure is supported.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to the widespread notion that pandas are initially awkward and clumsy.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including IFAW, ZME Science, Animal Corner and A-Z Animals, say a group of giant pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." They say the name likely comes from pandas' clumsy movements and lazy habits. IFAW says the term "refers to their clumsy movements and lazy personas." This matches the claim's main point that the name reflects a popular idea of pandas as awkward and clumsy. Two small caveats: the sources hedge, saying the term probably started online and has no clear documented origin, and nothing supports the word "initially" in the claim. Neither point contradicts the claim.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace company, designed and manufactured parts used in the Harrier Jump Jet.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that Arotech Limited was a British aerospace company or made Harrier parts. The only UK company with that name on Companies House (no. 10230261) was set up in 2016 and dissolved in 2020. Its listed business was paper and paperboard manufacturing (SIC 17120), and it was based in Knowsley, Liverpool. Harrier production had ended long before 2016. A similarly named firm, Arotech Corporation, is an American defence company, not British. The Harrier's main makers were Hawker Siddeley, British Aerospace and McDonnell Douglas, and Arotech does not appear in those sources. I couldn't rule out every possible older company with the same name, but the records available contradict the claim.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism of releasing toxic chemicals to deter predators.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources show that some caterpillars do release defensive chemicals to keep predators away. A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found that the osmeterium of the Battus polydamas caterpillar releases irritating, toxic compounds that put off predatory ants. Educational sources also note that swallowtail caterpillars give off foul-smelling or toxic substances to repel predators. Two caveats: this is true of some caterpillar species, not all, and chemical defense is not truly 'unique' to caterpillars. Still, the main point of the claim holds up.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, just like fingerprints, and can be used to identify individuals.
label: supported
reason: I found peer-reviewed biometric research that supports the claim. A Manipal Academy of Higher Education study on tongue prints for biometric authentication describes tongue prints as "unique" and "cannot be copied easily." It also says no two tongues have the same shape and texture, and concludes that tongue prints may be a secure method of identification in forensic dentistry. Another research paper, titled "Tongue prints – Unique as…", came up in the same search and makes the same comparison to fingerprints. One caveat: this is still an emerging method with relatively small studies, but the evidence agrees with the claim and none of it contradicts it.

text: Octopuses possess the unique ability to lose a limb as a defense mechanism, and then regrow it over time through a process called regeneration.
label: supported
reason: Research from UC Berkeley (Alupay & Caldwell) describes arm autotomy in octopuses such as Abdopus aculeatus. Autotomy means deliberately dropping an arm at a set break point so the octopus can escape a predator. These studies also report that the lost arm regrows, with signs of regeneration as early as three weeks. The word 'unique' is an overstatement: other animals, such as lizards and sea stars, also shed and regrow body parts, and only some octopus species are known to autotomize. Still, the main claim about octopuses dropping limbs for defense and regenerating them is supported.

text: There are over 150 million mature trees in the entire state of Florida in the United States, with many of these trees being removed annually.
label: supported
reason: The claim sets a low bar, and the evidence clears it. The USDA Forest Service FIA snapshot for Florida in 2024 counts about 8.06 billion live trees (at least 1 inch in diameter) on forest land. That is far more than 150 million. Even if 'mature' means only the larger trees, the state's 35.7 billion cubic feet of timber volume in trees at least 5 inches thick points to well over 150 million. On removals, the Florida Department of Agriculture says more than 82 million trees are planted each year, five for every one cut. That works out to roughly 16 million trees cut a year. FIA reports also show removals of about 560–570 million cubic feet a year. Both parts of the claim are therefore supported, though '150 million' greatly understates the real total.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) long. Wikipedia also ranks it as the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. NOAA's wording is 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over,' and other sources say 'over 65,000 km' or give a total of about 75,000 km. The claim's main points still hold: the ridge is the longest range, it circles the globe, and it is roughly 65,000 km, which converts to about 40,389 miles.

text: The Penguin is the only bird species that is capable of swimming faster than the human top speed in water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because penguins are not a single bird species. They are a family of about 18 species. My searches turned up sources naming the gentoo penguin as the fastest-swimming bird, at around 36 km/h, and other penguins such as emperors also swim much faster than the human top speed of about 8–9 km/h. So it is wrong to say one 'penguin species' is the only bird that can do this. I also searched for other fast diving birds such as cormorants and murres, but hit the search limit before getting their measured speeds, so I could not confirm or rule out non-penguin birds that outswim humans. The verdict rests on the species error, checked against background knowledge of how penguins are classified.

text: Thehma, the world's driest desert, covers over 9,000 square miles of land in Antarctica.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any desert called "Thehma," in Antarctica or anywhere else, so the claim has no clear referent. Searches for it only return the deserts usually called the driest: the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica and the Atacama in Chile. If "Thehma" is meant to be the McMurdo Dry Valleys, the size would be wrong. That area covers about 4,000–4,800 km², roughly 1,850 square miles, not over 9,000. But since the name can't be tied to a real place, the claim can't be properly checked.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called the turbellarian flatworm that is both a parasite and a jellyfish.
label: contradicted
reason: Turbellarians are flatworms. They belong to the phylum Platyhelminthes, class Turbellaria, while jellyfish belong to Cnidaria, so a turbellarian is not a type of jellyfish. Most turbellarians are also free-living rather than parasitic, so calling them both a parasite and a jellyfish is wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and is primarily underwater, circulating around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both identify the mid-ocean ridge system as Earth's longest mountain range. They say it stretches about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles), lies more than 90% underwater, and wraps around the globe. One small wording difference: these sources say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Some other estimates give a longer length, so this is a minor imprecision that does not change the substance of the claim.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait where they have seven neck vertebrae, just like all other mammals, but their unique bone structure allows their necks to be much longer.
label: contradicted
reason: Giraffes do have seven neck vertebrae, and their necks are long because each vertebra is greatly elongated (up to about 30 cm). But the claim says that all other mammals also have seven, and that is false. Sloths have between five and nine depending on the species, and manatees have six, so the rule covers nearly all mammals, not all of them. Having seven is also not a trait unique to giraffes.

text: Seahorses are one of the only species in the animal kingdom where the male becomes pregnant and gives birth to live young.
label: supported
reason: Sources such as the PADI blog say that, across the animal kingdom, male seahorses and their close relatives (pipefish and seadragons, family Syngnathidae) are the only males that become pregnant and give birth, releasing 100 to 1,000 live young at a time. This matches the claim's wording, "one of the only" species. One small caveat: "seahorses" is a genus containing many species rather than a single species, but that doesn't change the substance of the claim.

text: Humans have a unique nasal septum that is slightly off-center in most people, with only a small percentage of people having a perfectly central septum.
label: supported
reason: Penn Medicine says a deviated septum, meaning the wall between the nasal passages is off-center, is common and affects about 80 percent of people. That backs up the claim that most people's septum is slightly off-center and only a minority have a straight, central one. The word "unique" is vague, but it most plausibly refers to how the septum varies from person to person, which fits this evidence.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and unexplained natural phenomenon, has been observed to flow continuously without a visible source or outlet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river has no visible source or outlet, and the evidence shows otherwise. The Shanay-timpishka (the "Boiling River of the Amazon") has a known source at Mayantuyacu. It is a tributary that empties into the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali and then the Amazon. It is fed by hot springs, including one known as "La Bomba," and the main explanation for its heat is the Earth's geothermal gradient, so it is not an unexplained phenomenon with no source or outlet.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the time of day due to the way light interacts with the water.
label: supported
reason: A Great Barrier Reef tour-operator page says the reef's water colour changes with depth, the reef structure below, cloud cover and "the angle of the sun." Because the sun's angle shifts through the day, this supports the claim that the reef's colour changes with the time of day as light interacts with the water. A Cairns underwater-photography guide adds that light and visual vividness on the reef change from morning to afternoon as the sun gets lower. It is widely documented that the Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system. The evidence comes from tourism sites rather than scientific sources, but no source contradicts the claim.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on the planet Venus is 116.75 Earth days due to its extremely slow rotation period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The number in the claim is correct for Venus. Wikipedia and the Space Centre NZ FAQ both give Venus's solar day as about 116.75 Earth days, and its rotation is very slow and retrograde. However, I couldn't find any source that defines a "Khayagan day." Searches for "Khayagan" only turned up unrelated results, such as a villa in Bali and a gym in Indonesia, so the term has no clear meaning. Because that part of the claim can't be checked, it is inconclusive.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on the planet Venus is 116.75 Earth days, which is also its sidereal rotation period.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus's solar day (the time from one sunrise to the next) is about 116.75 Earth days (2,802 hours). Its sidereal rotation period is different: about 243 Earth days (−5,832.5 hours, where the minus sign shows that Venus spins backwards). So the claim is wrong to say the 116.75-day figure is also the sidereal rotation period. A Venus fact sheet based on NASA data lists the two values separately as 2,802.0 hours and −5,832.5 hours. The term "Khayagan day" does not appear to be a recognized astronomical term.

text: The longest recorded flight of a chimera, a type of dragonfly, was approximately 24 hours and 3 minutes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any dragonfly species commonly called a "chimera." Searches only turned up the mythological creature, fantasy-wiki entries, a fly genus (Chimerothalassius), and unrelated dragonflies. Reports of record dragonfly flights describe Pantala flavescens (the globe skimmer), and they measure distance (about 4,400 miles), not a flight time like "24 hours and 3 minutes." Because the claim names something that doesn't clearly exist and nothing backs the time it gives, the evidence can't verify or refute it.

text: The shorter a polar bear's nose, the older the bear is, as the nose length decreases with age in these Arctic animals.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source saying a polar bear's nose gets shorter with age. Scientific age-estimation sources say polar bears are aged from tooth sections (a premolar tooth is sectioned in a lab) and from skull features such as how far the skull sutures have closed and how worn the teeth are. Nose length is not used. Skull data also show the skull growing larger with age. The Parks Canada age-determination paper relates age classes to condylobasal (skull) length, and males keep growing until about age 8. Sources describe adult polar bears as having a long, elongated, 'Roman-nosed' muzzle. Together, this evidence goes against the idea that the nose shrinks as the bear ages, though no source directly addresses that specific claim.

text: Glowworms are bioluminescent insects that can be found in various parts of the world and have the ability to produce their own light through a chemical reaction within their bodies.
label: supported
reason: The sources describe 'glowworm' as a common name for several bioluminescent insects, mostly beetle larvae and fungus gnat larvae such as Arachnocampa, found around the world. A-Z Animals and a Scientific Reports (Nature) study both say their light comes from a luciferin–luciferase chemical reaction inside the body. Every part of the claim matches these sources, and nothing contradicts it.

text: Cocateo, a type of Almond tree that also grows bitter, fragrant fruit,  is a popular fruit in Culao people diet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing about a plant called "Cocateo" or a people called the "Culao". Searches for those terms only brought up unrelated pages: a US patent for the 'Kochi' almond, an FAO report on Samoan diets and a Wikipedia page on cocada, a coconut sweet. I hit the search limit before I could finish checking, so I can't confirm or rule out that either name exists, that Cocateo is an almond tree with bitter, fragrant fruit, or that it's a popular fruit among the Culao.

text: The discharge of a blue whale can weigh as much as 40 pounds due to the massive amount of liquids it consumes daily.
label: contradicted
reason: The 40-pound figure is far too low. ABC News, quoting West Australian Centre for Whale Research scientist Curt Jenner, reports that a blue whale can pass up to 200 litres of faeces in a single bowel movement. That is several hundred pounds. Estimates of blue whale urine run even higher, at roughly 1,000 litres or more per day. The stated cause is also wrong: whale scientists say baleen whales don't really drink and get most of their water from food such as krill.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers across the globe's ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth. It winds through every major ocean basin, and WorldAtlas gives its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). NOAA has also described it as more than 65,000 km long, though that recollection was not confirmed in this search. Some sources say 'about' rather than 'over' 65,000 km, but that small wording difference doesn't change the substance of the claim.

text: Thedinga people's tribe in China have 16 different types of tattoos that hold significant cultural and spiritual meaning in their society.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any people or tribe called "Thedinga" in China or anywhere else. Searches turned up nothing for that name, so the claim has no clear subject. The closest match may be the Derung (Dulong) people of Yunnan, known for women's facial tattoos. But sources on them, such as factsanddetails.com and China Daily, describe the patterns as falling mainly into two styles, not 16. No reliable source supports a claim of 16 tattoo types for a "Thedinga" tribe.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the season due to temperature variations, which affect the growth and color intensity of the coral.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed research on the central Great Barrier Reef (Coral Reefs, Springer) found that zooxanthellae density and chlorophyll a vary with the seasons. Densities are lowest in late summer and highest in winter or spring, and these are the factors that coral health colour charts track. The Great Barrier Reef Foundation says corals get most of their colour from zooxanthellae, and that warm summer water temperatures can cause bleaching. CoralWatch monitoring with the Coral Health Chart at Heron Island also recorded slight colour fluctuations over the months, separate from bleaching events. Together, these sources support the claim that coral colour on the reef changes slightly by season because of temperature. The claim's point about growth is less directly covered by the sources found, but nothing contradicts it.

text: Cats have a unique way of hearing called "vocalization" which allows them to hear sounds that are too faint or too high for humans to detect.
label: contradicted
reason: Cats can hear high-frequency and ultrasonic sounds well beyond what humans can hear, so that part of the claim is true. But "vocalization" is not a way of hearing. Studies of feline communication use the word for the sounds cats make, such as meows, purrs, hisses and chatter. Cats' wide hearing range comes from how their ears evolved, not from anything called "vocalization." Because the claim gives that wrong name and description, it is contradicted.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, just like fingerprints, which can be used to distinguish one person from another.
label: supported
reason: Several peer-reviewed sources say the tongue's shape and surface texture differ from person to person, much like fingerprints, which makes tongue prints usable for biometric identification. These include a 2024 PMC digital photographic study, a 2025 systematic review in the Egyptian Journal of Forensic Sciences (Springer) and a Brieflands study on tongue prints for biometric authentication. The research describes tongue prints as an emerging forensic and biometric tool, but none of the sources I found disputes that they are unique.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, as estimated by scientists using DNA sampling and other techniques.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), but the claim gets three things wrong. The study estimated about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species, not 'over' 8.7 million. That total covers all eukaryotes, including fungi, protozoa and chromists, not just plants and animals. And the researchers did not use DNA sampling: they found numerical patterns in the taxonomic classification hierarchy and extrapolated from them.

text: There are over 87,000 miles of rivers worldwide that flow into the ocean.
label: supported
reason: I found no source that gives a figure of 87,000 miles. The claim is only a lower bound, though, and the search results show the real total is far higher. Vivid Maps says the United States alone has about 3.5 million miles of rivers, much of which drains to the ocean. A-Z Animals, citing Wikipedia, lists 187 major rivers that are each at least 621 miles long, which comes to more than 116,000 miles. Many of the world's largest rivers flow into the ocean, such as the Amazon (about 4,000 miles). So 'over 87,000 miles' is true, but it greatly understates the real total.

text: A saltwater crocodile can remain underwater for up to an hour due to its ability to slow down its metabolism and constrict its heart rate.
label: supported
reason: The Northern Territory Government's official Be Crocwise site says large saltwater crocodiles can stay underwater for at least an hour because they can slow their heart rate to 2–3 beats per minute. That backs the claim's main points: an hour-long dive made possible by a much slower heart rate. Two caveats: the source says 'at least' an hour, not 'up to', so the claim's wording may understate the limit. The source also doesn't separately mention a slower metabolism, but that goes along with a slower heart rate.

text: The largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is more than 1,300 times the size of the Earth and has a mass that is approximately 318 times that of our planet.
label: supported
reason: ESA's Jupiter fact sheet says Jupiter is 318 times as massive as Earth and that 1,321 Earths could fit inside a Jupiter-sized sphere. That volume figure matches the claim's 'more than 1,300 times the size' when 'size' is read as volume, the usual reading of this comparison. Jupiter is also the largest planet in the solar system.

text: Over 70% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with approximately 96.5% of it being seawater.
label: supported
reason: USGS says about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, which counts as over 70%. It also says the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water, so roughly 96.5% of it is seawater. Both parts of the claim match this trustworthy government source.

text: Buttresses, structures used to support buildings, have been present in architecture since the ancient Greeks and Romans, with the oldest known examples dating back to the 4th century BC.
label: contradicted

Wikipedia's article on Mesopotamian architecture also says Babylonian temples were held up by buttresses. Both sources are reliable, and both place buttresses thousands of years before the 4th century BC and before the ancient Greeks and Romans. The search turned up no source naming 4th-century-BC Greek or Roman buttresses as the oldest known examples.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers (7,918 miles) at the equator due to its slightly oblate and ellipsoidal shape.
label: contradicted
reason: 12,742 km (about 7,918 mi) is Earth's mean diameter, not its equatorial diameter. Universe Today gives the equatorial diameter as 12,756 km (7,926 mi) and the polar diameter as about 12,714 km. The average of these two figures is the 12,742 km quoted in the claim. Because Earth is oblate, its equator is wider than the 12,742 km figure, so the claim is wrong to tie that number to the equator.

text: The highest recorded speed of a jellyfish has been clocked at approximately 35 miles per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say the fastest jellyfish, the box jellyfish, tops out at about 7.5 km/h, or roughly 4.6 mph. That is nowhere near 35 mph. Jellyfish are generally slow swimmers. The 'fastest' claims you may see refer to how quickly their stinging cells fire, not how fast they swim. No source supports a recorded swimming speed of around 35 mph.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spanning over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.

NOAA Ocean Explorer gives its length as 'nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)', and WHOI gives 'nearly 65,000 kilometers (about 40,000 miles).' Wikipedia gives about 65,000 km (40,000 mi), and WorldAtlas also describes it as a 65,000 km range. One wording issue: these sources say 'nearly' or 'about' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over.' NOAA's 40,390 miles is more than 40,000 miles, though, and every source uses roughly the same figure. This is a rounding difference, not a contradiction, so the claim is supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge system, spanning over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.

NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI give its length as "nearly 65,000 kilometers" for the continuous ridge. Wikipedia says the total oceanic ridge system is 80,000 km, and ScienceDirect and a PMC article put it at over or about 75,000 km. These higher figures back the "over 65,000 km" part of the claim. The only caveat is a small difference in wording, since NOAA says "nearly" rather than "over" 65,000 km. Overall, the claim matches the evidence.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
label: not_verifiable

NOAA, WHOI and Wikipedia all confirm that the mid-ocean ridge is the world's longest mountain range. On length, though, NOAA and WHOI say it is "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km. Some other sources describe it as more than 65,000 km, so the figure is borderline and the sources disagree. The location is only partly right. The ridge does run down the middle of the Atlantic, but it also crosses the Indian and Arctic Oceans. In the Pacific, its main section (the East Pacific Rise) sits toward the eastern side rather than in the middle. Since the length is disputed and the Pacific detail is inaccurate, I can't fully verify the claim.

text: The nucleus of an atom, which consists of protons and neutrons, makes up approximately 99.9% of the atom's total mass.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and extremely fast wingbeats.

They credit the hummingbird's unusual wing structure and muscles, flexible shoulder joints, and very fast wingbeats (720 to 5,400 per minute). Some sources add a caveat: hummingbirds are the only birds that can keep flying backwards under control, while birds such as kingfishers, herons and egrets can briefly flutter backwards. Since no reliable source says another bird can truly fly backwards for a sustained time, the claim holds as commonly stated.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.

reason: Reliable sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is Earth's longest mountain range. NOAA Ocean Exploration also describes the ridge system as more than 65,000 km long, which matches the claim's wording of 'over 65,000 kilometers'. Some sources say 'about' rather than 'over' 65,000 km, but this is a minor difference and nothing contradicts the claim.

text: The highest recorded number of screws used in a single building project is approximately 45 million in the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.

text: The length of the longest recorded flight of the Antarctic petrel, a bird species, was tracked at 32 days, 16 hours, and 52 minutes.

text: Octopuses are capable of shedding a protective outer layer called a 'skin slip' to evade predators during an escape or when battling against a predator.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source that uses the term 'skin slip' or says octopuses shed an outer layer to escape or fight off predators. Octopuses do shed something: the chitinous cuticle lining their suckers, plus some outer skin. Sources such as PLOS ONE, OctoNation, the Shedd Aquarium and the Aquarium of the Pacific describe this as regular shedding and renewal, like maintaining healthy skin or fingernails, not as a defence. The anti-predator tactics actually documented are ink, camouflage, using shells as shelter and dropping an arm (autotomy). The evidence therefore points against the claimed purpose and the claimed term, though no source directly says octopuses never shed skin to escape.

text: The Departed, a crime drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Matt Damon, holds the record for most Academy Awards won by a film with only 4 nominations, at the 80th Academy Awards in 2008.
label: contradicted

That happened at the 79th Academy Awards on February 25, 2007, not the 80th in 2008. So the film did not set any record for a film with only 4 nominations, which makes the claim's details wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, and NASA gives about 74,000 km. That puts the total system above 65,000 km, so the 'over 65,000 km' figure is defensible, though NOAA's 'nearly' adds some uncertainty. 'Runs through the center' of the Pacific is loose wording: the East Pacific Rise sits east of the ocean's middle. Still, the main claims hold up.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

The words "through the middle" are a slight simplification, since the Pacific part (the East Pacific Rise) is not centred in that ocean, but this does not change the claim's substance.

text: The amount of water in the world's oceans is approximately 96.5% of the Earth's total water supply.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way Galaxy.

NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Even at the high end of that range, there are more than seven times as many trees as stars, so the claim holds. The cited article reports both figures.

text: A large portion of the world's fresh water, approximately 68.7%, is trapped in ice caps and glaciers.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the standard USGS water-distribution figures. Geography Realm, citing that data, says about 68.7% of Earth's fresh water is locked in ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow. The claim leaves out permanent snow, but the 68.7% figure for ice caps and glaciers is the widely cited number, so the claim is supported.

text: Japan has a vending machine for nearly everything, including umbrellas, underwear, and live crabs.
label: supported
reason: Several travel and vending-machine guides back up every part of the claim. They describe Japan as having millions of vending machines selling a huge range of goods. Japan Wise Life and Travel Japan Together both list live crab machines in places such as Hakodate and Kanazawa, along with umbrellas. Other sources, including VendingMachinePapa and Academic Help, mention live crabs, umbrellas and underwear machines. One NPR result covers live-crab vending machines in China, but that doesn't contradict the claim about Japan. These are mostly travel blogs, so the sources are moderately reliable rather than authoritative, but they agree with each other and nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 12.04 billion square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the Sun's surface area as about 6.09×10^12 km², which is roughly 6.09 trillion (6,090 billion) km² and about 12,000 times Earth's surface area. You get the same figure from 4πr² using a radius of about 696,000 km. The claimed 12.04 billion km² is off by a factor of about 500. It may come from mixing up the '12,000 times Earth' comparison with the actual area.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.10 x 10^8 Earths.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the Sun's surface area as about 6.09×10^12 km², or roughly 12,000 times Earth's surface area. The claim's figure of 5.10×10^8 is actually Earth's own surface area in km², not the number of Earths. That makes the claim wrong by a factor of about 40,000.

text: There are over 6 million Species of plants and animals on our planet, according to the University of Edinburgh's School of Biological Sciences.
label: not_verifiable

Other estimates exist from different sources: Current Results says over 7 million plant and animal species, the 2011 PLoS Biology study (via ScienceDaily and the California Academy of Sciences) gives about 8.7 million total species, and Costello's estimate (via the University of Aberdeen) is about 2 million. Because the figures vary and the specific attribution to Edinburgh can't be confirmed, the claim can't be verified.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered and documented by scientists so far.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology study, but it estimates how many species exist on Earth in total, not how many scientists have discovered. The number actually documented is far below 8.7 million.

text: The emotional support animal Sunny Boy, a Capybara, is often cited as the first emotional support animal in the United States, due to being certified by a New York psychologist in 2008.

None mentioned a capybara named Sunny Boy, a 2008 certification by a New York psychologist, or Sunny Boy being called the first ESA in the US. Still, I found no source that directly contradicts it, so it can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: The longest war in recorded history was the Hundred Years' War between England and France, spanning 116 years from 1337 to 1453.
label: contradicted

That contradicts the claim that the Hundred Years' War was the longest.

text: The Departed, a crime drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Matt Damon, holds the record for most Academy Awards won by a film with a budget over $100 million.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the mid-ocean ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through all the world's oceans.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the globe.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, thanks to its unique physiology which includes extremely fast wingbeats and the ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.

Birdspot and GardenBird, both bird-focused sites, also say hummingbirds are the only birds that can truly fly backwards. They credit flexible shoulder joints and wings that rotate in a figure-of-eight. One caveat: some sources note that birds like sunbirds, herons and flycatchers can flutter backwards briefly. They still describe sustained, controlled backward flight as unique to hummingbirds, which is the usual meaning of the claim.

text: The length of a strand of DNA is approximately 2.3 meters (7.5 feet), if you were to stretch it out end-to-end.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the specific 2.3 m (7.5 ft) figure. Most reliable sources, such as LibreTexts biology materials, say that all the DNA in one human cell would stretch to about 2 meters (roughly 6 feet). That is close to the claim, but not the same. Hypertextbook does list 2.3 m, but only as one of several estimates ranging from 1.5 to 3 m, based on a World Book statement that an average chromosome holds about 2 inches of DNA. The claim is also unclear about what it is measuring. It says "a strand of DNA," but a single DNA molecule (one chromosome) is only a few centimeters long. The figure of about 2 m refers to all the DNA in a cell. Because the evidence is mixed and the claim's subject is ambiguous, I can't call it supported or contradicted.

text: There are over 7.9 billion people living on Earth, which is just over two billion more than the 5.7 billion estimated in 1999.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 1999 figure wrong. The UN Population Fund named 12 October 1999 the "Day of 6 Billion", so the world population that year was about 6 billion, not 5.7 billion. The world reached 5.7 billion around the mid-1990s. Today's population is over 8 billion, so "over 7.9 billion" is technically true. But the gap from the 1999 figure is about 2 billion or a little more, and the claim's 5.7 billion starting point for 1999 is incorrect.

text: пергамент, первоначально создан в древней Персии, получил свое название от пергамена, горной цоровыepergamon, возле города Эфес в современной Турции, которое было известно на протяжении тысячелетий и либо построено перс
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources agree that the word 'parchment' comes from Pergamon (Pergamum), and that part of the claim is correct. But Pergamon was an ancient Greek city in Anatolia known for its library. It was not a mountain, and it was not near Ephesus; it lay well to the north. Sources also do not credit ancient Persia with creating parchment. Its traditional development is tied to Pergamon, and writing on animal skins was already widespread, for example among the Ionians, as Herodotus notes. The rest of the claim is garbled and cut off, so those details cannot be checked, but the parts that can be checked are contradicted.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be thousands of years old if stored properly due to its unique combination of acidity, hydrogen peroxide, and other compounds that act as natural preservatives?
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine's article "The Science Behind Honey's Eternal Shelf Life" says honey stays unspoiled for thousands of years. It notes that archaeologists have found edible honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, and other sources mention 3,000- and 5,500-year-old finds. Smithsonian credits this to the honey's acidity, its low moisture and the hydrogen peroxide in it, which act together as preservatives, and it notes that the honey has to be properly sealed. The claim leaves out low moisture as a factor, but its phrase "other compounds" makes the claim broadly consistent with the sources.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to a 2021 estimate by the University of Oxford, but scientists believe that up to 80% of all species on Earth remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million species figure doesn't come from a 2021 University of Oxford estimate. It comes from a 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues at the University of Hawaii and Dalhousie University, published in PLoS Biology. That study did find that about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undescribed, so the 'up to 80% undiscovered' part is roughly in line. But the claim gets the year and the institution wrong, and it says 'over 8.7 million' when the estimate was 8.7 million ± 1.3 million.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and WorldAtlas, call the Mid-Ocean Ridge Earth's longest mountain range. WHOI says it is made up of "40,000 continuous miles (65,000 km)" of underwater volcanoes, and WorldAtlas gives a length of about 65,000 km. The sources give roughly 65,000 km rather than clearly "over" 65,000 km, but this is consistent with the claim.

text: The driest desert in the world, located in Antarctica, covers an area of approximately 250,000 square miles.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results contradict the area figure. The desert in Antarctica most often called the driest on Earth is the McMurdo Dry Valleys. WorldAtlas says it covers about 1,500 square miles, and EBSCO puts the whole ice-free region at about 5,792 square miles (15,000 km²). Both figures are far below 250,000 square miles. If the claim means the entire Antarctic polar desert, that is much larger, at roughly 5.5 million square miles, so 250,000 square miles is still wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million distinct species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, out of which only 1.3 million have been formally described and documented by scientists.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the well-known 2011 Mora et al. study (PLoS Biology) closely enough. That study estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. ScienceDaily, Dalhousie and the University of Hawaii all report that roughly 1.25 million of these species had been described, which rounds to about 1.3 million. The paper itself says over 1.2 million were catalogued and that about 86% of species have yet to be described. The wording is a little loose in three ways: the study says 'about' 8.7 million rather than 'over'; it covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals; and 1.3 million is also the study's margin of error. None of these differences contradicts the main point.

text: There are over 300 million birds species worldwide, but only about 10,000 to 20,000 are thought to exist, and new ones are constantly being discovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says there are "over 300 million" bird species, which is wrong and also contradicts its own second number. ScienceDaily, reporting a study led by the American Museum of Natural History, says most checklists count about 9,000 to 10,000 bird species, and a morphology-based estimate puts it closer to 18,000. No source puts the number of species anywhere near hundreds of millions; that kind of figure would only make sense as a count of individual birds, not species.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to produce it, just a flower by itself due to the flowers nectar and pollen?
label: contradicted
reason: Bees are essential to making honey. Worker bees collect nectar from flowers, break down its sugars with enzymes in their honey stomachs, pass it between bees, and dry it out in honeycomb cells. A flower cannot produce honey on its own. The claim that honey is the only bee-made food humans eat is also doubtful, since people eat other bee products such as royal jelly and bee pollen.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more are often less likely to overeat, as it increases the production of a hormone that makes us feel full.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed, and the claim's specific mechanism isn't well supported. In King et al. (Med Sci Sports Exerc), 60 minutes of brisk walking burned about 2 MJ but did not significantly change appetite, energy intake or the hunger hormone acylated ghrelin. A 2024 review in the Korean Journal of Family Medicine says a single brisk walk does not cause compensatory changes in appetite-regulating hormones. A 2018 study in the International Journal of Obesity found no difference in PYY, a hormone that makes us feel full, between fasted and fed walking trials, though it compared two walking conditions rather than walking against rest. On the other side, popular sources (Dummies, an AOL/EatingWell piece) say walking can curb cravings or briefly suppress ghrelin. Some reviews link higher-intensity exercise to more satiety hormones and less ghrelin, but brisk walking is moderate-intensity. I found no good evidence that people who walk more are less likely to overeat, or that walking reliably raises a fullness hormone. Because some evidence supports parts of the claim and some cuts against it, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of kalpaksheva, Russia, making it one of the greenest cities in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any city called "Kalpaksheva" in Russia. Searches for that name only turn up unrelated words like Kalpavriksha and Kalpak, so the city has no clear referent.
