The closest real place is Kolpashevo, a small town of about 21,000 people covering roughly 266 km² in Tomsk Oblast. No source says it has 320 million trees or ranks among the world's greenest cities, and that many trees in such a small area seems implausible. The sources on Russia's greenest cities name Moscow and Sochi, not this place. Since the city may not exist and nothing supports or directly refutes the claim, it can't be verified.

text: A chuuk kayak, also known as a true kayak, is a traditional boat originating from the Inupiat people of the Arctic, typically made from a single piece of driftwood and used for hunting and transportation in the icy waters of Alaska.
label: contradicted
reason: No source uses the term "chuuk kayak" or treats it as another name for a "true kayak." Chuuk is in Micronesia, not the Arctic. The claim also gets the construction wrong. The Smithsonian and Alaskan heritage sources describe traditional Arctic and Alaskan kayaks (qayaq) as skin-on-frame boats: a wooden or bone frame covered with sewn seal or sea-mammal skins. They were not carved from a single piece of driftwood. Driftwood was used for the frames.

text: There are approximately 170 million trees in the streets of Paris, France, known as the "Green Lung" or the Parisian arcades, making it one of the most tree-dense cities in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure in the claim is far too high. Paris has about 484,000 public trees in total, and only around 96,500 to 100,000 of them line the streets. That is nowhere near 170 million. The number 170,000 does appear in the sources, but as the city's planting target for 2026, not as a tree count. Sources describe Paris as one of the most treed cities in Europe, but the claimed figure is off by several orders of magnitude.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique mating system where they form monogamous pairs for their entire lifetime, which can last up to 25 years in some species.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources such as Animal Diversity Web and EOL describe butterflyfish as mostly monogamous and pair-forming. They also say that pairs in many species stay together for at least three years and that only some species may pair for life. The American Fisheries Society names the foureye butterflyfish as one species that mates for life. So the claim goes too far in saying butterflyfish in general pair for their entire lifetime. Calling the system 'unique' is also wrong, because other fish, like some cichlids and catfish, form strong pair bonds too. The 25-year figure is poorly supported. A-Z Animals lists a '2–25 years' lifespan range but elsewhere on the same page gives 3–20 years. Other sources give typical lifespans of about 5–10 years, and about 15 years for the multiband butterflyfish. No source confirms that any pair lasts up to 25 years. Part of the claim is supported, but key parts are overstated or can't be verified.

text: There are More than 300,000 known species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but scientists believe that up to 80% of all life on Earth remains undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim hold up, though both figures are imprecise. A 2011 study by Mora et al., reported by Nature, estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth and said more than 80% are still undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species). Other sources say 80–90% of species remain undescribed. About 1.2 million or more species have been described, so 'more than 300,000 known species' is true, even if it is a low lower bound. The '80%' figure matches commonly cited estimates, though 'up to 80%' understates them, since most estimates put the undiscovered share above 80%.

text: Bee honey is extremely acidic, with a pH level that ranges from 3.2 to 4.5, due to its high concentration of gluconic acid.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say honey's pH usually falls between 3.2 and 4.5. They also say gluconic acid, which forms when glucose oxidase breaks down glucose, is the main acid behind that acidity. The Reagent chemistry blog confirms gluconic acid is the main acid in honey. This label rests mostly on commercial and blog sources, though. Calling honey 'extremely acidic' also overstates it: some sources describe its acidity as 'mild' and 'not corrosive.' Other references give a wider pH range of about 3.4–6.1, which I did not confirm in this search. The main facts in the claim, the pH range and the role of gluconic acid, are supported, but the wording exaggerates.

text: Bacteria are found everywhere on Earth, from the freezing cold polar regions to the hottest volcanic deserts, and they even live inside the human body.
label: supported
reason: An open microbiology textbook from Oregon State says prokaryotes, especially bacteria, are found everywhere on the planet. That includes the Antarctic ice shield, hot springs and extreme deep-sea pressure. It also says large numbers of bacteria live in the human body, for example in the mouth, gut and nasal cavity. Hot springs and other hot volcanic environments are a reasonable match for the claim's 'hottest volcanic deserts', so the claim is broadly accurate. Microbes are well documented in both the coldest and hottest places on Earth.

text: Dark matter makes up approximately 27% of the universe's total mass-energy density, yet its existence was only confirmed in the 20th century.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The 27% figure checks out. CERN's CMS experiment says dark matter makes up almost 27% of the universe's total energy, and other sources give the same figure. The second part of the claim is shakier. Evidence for dark matter did emerge in the 20th century, from Zwicky in the 1930s and Rubin in the 1970s, and CMS says 'we already know' it exists. But CERN's ATLAS experiment says no known particle has yet been observed interacting with dark matter, and other sources say it has never been directly detected. Much of the strongest evidence, such as the Bullet Cluster and Planck measurements, also came after 2000. Because sources disagree on whether its existence has been 'confirmed', and on when that would have happened, that part can't be verified.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be found in the tombs of ancient civilizations, where it is still edible today due to its unique properties and composition?
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including My Modern Met, Earthly Mission and Dallas Express, report that archaeologists found honey in Egyptian tombs more than 3,000 years old that was still edible. They credit this to honey's low moisture, acidity and hydrogen peroxide. Some of these outlets are popular-science sites rather than primary scientific sources. Honey can spoil if it absorbs moisture or is stored badly, so 'never spoils' is a simplification. Still, none of the results contradicted the main claim.

text: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution that never spoils due to its unique combination of acidity and beeswax content.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is indeed a supersaturated sugar solution, and acidity does help preserve it. But the reason the claim gives is wrong. Sources that explain why honey keeps so long credit its low moisture and low water activity, high sugar concentration (which draws water out of microbes), acidity (pH about 3.2–4.5), and hydrogen peroxide made by the bee enzyme glucose oxidase. None of them list beeswax as a factor. The 'never spoils' part is also overstated: one source calls honey only 'nearly imperishable', and others note it can ferment if its water content gets too high.

text: The ancient Egyptians used a combination of mathematical principles and astronomical observations to create incredibly accurate calendars that closely matched modern Gregorian calendars.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources don't back up the idea that Egyptian calendars were incredibly accurate or closely matched the Gregorian one. The Egyptians did use astronomy: they tracked the heliacal rising of Sirius. But their civil calendar was a fixed 365 days (12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days) with no leap years until 22 BCE. As a result it lost about one day every four years and 'wandered' through the seasons, which is why it is called the annus vagus. It only lined up with the solar year again after a 1,460-year Sothic cycle. The Gregorian calendar, by contrast, adds 97 leap days every 400 years to average 365.2425 days, so the claim of a close, accurate match is contradicted.

text: The concept of the charitable trust dates back to ancient civilizations, with recorded evidence of such trusts in ancient Greece around 450 BCE.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The general idea is supported, but the specific date is not. Encyclopedia Britannica, a reliable source, says foundations, endowments and charitable trusts go back to the ancient Middle East, Greece and Rome. Encyclopedia.com likewise mentions Greek and Roman endowments and early charitable trusts. The Greek example these sources give, however, is Plato's Academy: founded around 387 BCE, with Plato leaving income from his land to support it before his death in 347 BCE. None of the sources found mentions a charitable trust in ancient Greece around 450 BCE. Their earliest Greek example comes decades later, but that does not rule out an earlier one, so it neither confirms nor clearly disproves the 450 BCE figure.

text: The concept of the charitable trust dates back to ancient civilizations, with recorded evidence of such trusts in ancient Greece around 750 BCE.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that records charitable trusts in ancient Greece around 750 BCE. Britannica says philanthropic groups existed in the ancient Middle East, Greece and Rome. Its earliest Greek example of an endowment is Plato's Academy, around 387 BCE. Other sources date the word 'philanthropy' to Aeschylus in the 5th century BCE, and Gift Planning History traces trust-like charitable arrangements to Roman law and medieval Europe. So the general idea of ancient roots is plausible, but nothing confirms the specific 750 BCE date. None of the sources directly addresses or rules out that date either, so the claim is unverified rather than contradicted.

text: The highest mountain in the solar system, as of our current knowledge, is Olympus Mons on Mars, which stands at a height of approximately 27 km above the Martian surface.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Guinness World Records and Big Think both call Olympus Mons the highest known mountain in the solar system. NASA's JPL and NASA Photojournal give its height as 27 km, and the Photojournal specifies that this is measured from the average Martian elevation. Other sources give different figures depending on the reference point: 26 km above the northern plains, about 25 km from base to peak, or 21.9 km relative to the Mars datum. Big Think also notes that the central peak of Rheasilvia on the asteroid Vesta might turn out to be taller once it is measured more precisely. Still, the claim's 'approximately 27 km above the Martian surface' matches NASA's figure.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long but mostly underwater, stretching through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA (Ocean Service and Ocean Exploration), WHOI and Wikipedia all call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. They give its length as about 65,000 km (40,389 miles) and say more than 90% of it lies underwater. They also describe it winding through all the major oceans, which includes the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. One wording difference: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. That gap is small, and other sources simply give about 65,000 km, so the claim is substantially supported.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Greek Magnets from Magnesia, is estimated to have a magnetic field 1,000 times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Caltech reports that the strongest known magnet in the universe is a magnetar, the pulsar 4U0142+61. Its magnetic field is up to a quadrillion times stronger than Earth's and ten billion times stronger than the strongest magnet ever made in a lab. Ancient Greek lodestones from Magnesia are natural magnets, not the strongest known, and the '1,000 times Earth's field' figure doesn't fit the actual record-holder.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting around 86 billion neurons are present.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion figure for neurons is right, but the comparison is wrong. Nature Scitable and Psychology Today both put the Milky Way at about 200–400 billion stars, which is more than the 86 billion neurons in the brain. Psychology Today calls the idea that the brain has more neurons than the galaxy has stars a widespread myth.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, and scientists estimate that this number may be as high as 30 million.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The main estimate exists, but the claim's wording goes further than the evidence. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, give or take 1.3 million. That is a central estimate, not a confirmed minimum, so 'over 8.7 million' isn't established, and the true number could be lower. The figure also covers fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. A '30 million' estimate does exist: Terry Erwin's beetle-based figure, reported by The Conversation and the National Wildlife Federation. However, published estimates range from about 3 million to 100 million or more, and many scientists consider 30 million too high. So the claim mixes real figures but misstates the 8.7 million figure as a minimum, and the evidence neither clearly supports nor clearly contradicts it as worded.

text: koa trees have the unique ability to grow new trees from fallen branches and can also reproduce from their seeds within 7-10 weeks.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the USDA Forest Service silvics page and the native plant propagation protocol, describe koa's vegetative reproduction as coming mainly from root suckers, not from fallen branches. Cuttings only root reliably from young, juvenile material, and success rates are low (about 16–20% for root-sucker material). Nothing describes a 'unique ability' to grow new trees from fallen branches. The seed timing is also wrong: scarified seeds germinate in 2–7 days, or within about a week. Seedlings reach plantable size in 10–14 weeks. No source says koa reproduces from seed in 7–10 weeks.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Antarctica, is over 40,000 years old, with evidence showing glaciers have formed there during multiple Ice Ages.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts Butler's Gorge in Antarctica, but it is a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, Australia, on the River Derwent. It is the site of Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. Because the location is wrong, the claim is contradicted, regardless of the age and glaciation details.

text: Giraffes are able to close their eyes from the outside, but this is done by more than 150 muscles compared to 12-15 for humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that confirms or refutes the claim's figures: more than 150 eyelid muscles in giraffes and 12–15 in humans. Searches turned up general facts about giraffe eyes, such as their large size, colour vision and long lashes, and general giraffe muscle anatomy, but no muscle counts for giraffe eyelids. The human figure also looks doubtful. Anatomy sources say the eyelid is closed mainly by one muscle, the orbicularis oculi, and opened by the levator palpebrae, not 12–15 muscles. Still, nothing reliable directly addresses the giraffe numbers, so the claim can't be verified either way.

text: Honey is banned from use in NASA's food supplies because it can crystallize and become a solid at temperatures close to human body temperature.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA hasn't banned honey. NASA's own Space Food Formulations documents from the Johnson Space Center list honey ("Honey, pure, U.S. Grade A") as an ingredient and include a "Honey Ginger Fish" recipe. NASA astronaut Tom Marshburn showed squeeze-bottle honey on the ISS during Expedition 35, and other astronauts have also eaten honey on the station. The crystallization reason is wrong too, since honey crystallizes at cool temperatures, not at temperatures close to human body temperature.

text: The humans have a unique genetic trait, known as the ability to smell as infants, which is a rapidly fading learned sense.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on several points. The sense of smell is not unique to humans, it is not lost after infancy, and it is not learned. According to the sources, the olfactory system develops in the womb around weeks 26–28 of pregnancy and is already mature and working in newborns, which means it is innate. Smell also continues to work throughout life rather than fading away.

text: The oldest known piece of wooden furniture is the Sorghum wooden boat dating to around 820 BCE found in China's Leshan state.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a "Sorghum wooden boat" exists. Furniture histories describe wooden furniture far older than 820 BCE. Ancient Egyptian tomb furniture dates to around 3100–2500 BC, and the wooden pieces from the Midas tomb at Gordion are also cited as among the oldest. Leshan is a city in Sichuan, not a state, and a boat is not furniture. The claim appears to be made up and conflicts with reliable accounts.

text: The oldest known piece of wooden furniture is the Sorghum wooden boat dating to around 820 BCE found in China's Yangtze River.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of a "Sorghum wooden boat" from around 820 BCE in the Yangtze River. The Yangtze boat finds that came up are much later Qing-dynasty wrecks. A boat would not normally count as furniture anyway. Sources that discuss the world's oldest surviving wooden furniture point instead to the pieces found in the tomb at Gordion, near Ankara in Turkey, dated to the 8th–7th century BCE. Ancient Egyptian wooden furniture is older still.

text: The shallowest lake in the world, as measured by its maximum depth of approximately 3.3 meters, is Chad's Lake Assal in East Africa.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different lakes. Lake Assal is a crater lake in Djibouti, not Chad. Its maximum depth is more than 40 m and its average depth is about 7.4 m, so it is nowhere near 3.3 m deep and not the world's shallowest lake. It is known instead as the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest lakes in the world.

text: The shallowest lake in the world, as measured by its maximum depth of approximately 3.3 meters, is Chad’s Lake Ouno.
label: contradicted
reason: There doesn't seem to be any lake in Chad called "Lake Ouno." Searches only turned up similar-sounding real lakes, such as the Lakes of Ounianga and Lake Wey (also spelled Ouei). Several sources, including The Conversation and Quartz, say the lake often called the world's shallowest is Lake Chad. Lake Chad is described as very shallow, with an average depth of about 1.5 m and a maximum of about 10.5 m. So the lake named in the claim doesn't exist, and the lake commonly given the title is a different one.

text:
пергамент, первоначально используемый для письма и переписи исторических документов, фактически является «наваршей с молоком», ферментированной из внутренней кожи западных морских]],
.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's article on parchment says it is a writing material made from specially prepared, untanned skins of land animals, mainly sheep, calves and goats. Parchment is scraped and dried under tension, not fermented. It is not a fermented substance with milk ("наварша с молоком"), and it is not made from the inner skin of western sea creatures. The claim's description of what parchment is made from and how it is made is therefore contradicted.

text: Butterfly fish have a unique way of eating: they have a specialized jaw structure that allows them to eat coral polyps, which are not easily digestible by most fish.
label: supported
reason: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan) says butterflyfish jaw shape and size match what they eat. Some species, such as Chaetodon ornatissimus, have short jaws for nipping off live coral polyps, and obligate corallivores eat coral polyps only. This supports the specialized jaw structure and coral-polyp diet in the claim. The search did not directly confirm that coral polyps are hard for most fish to digest. However, the source does treat coral-polyp feeding as a specialized habit, and this part is consistent with general knowledge that corallivory is uncommon among reef fishes. One caveat is that not all butterflyfish eat coral; some eat zooplankton, invertebrates or algae.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apolysis, where they release their body parts in the form of silk threads to confuse predators and escape danger.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a reliable source (ScienceDirect). It defines apolysis as the step in insect molting where the old cuticle separates from the epidermis and molting fluid is released. It has nothing to do with releasing body parts as silk threads to confuse predators or escape danger.

text: Glowworms use a chemical reaction to produce their bioluminescent glow, which is caused by the breakdown of a molecule called luciferin.
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources show that glowworm light comes from a luciferin–luciferase chemical reaction. A Nature Scientific Reports study of the New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) found that its bioluminescence is produced by this kind of reaction, which needs ATP-Mg2+ and oxygen. During the reaction, luciferin is oxidised and consumed, so calling it a 'breakdown' of luciferin is a reasonable simplification.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish is bioluminescent, meaning it has the ability to produce its own light, but it's not able to create its own light from glucose.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the basic identity wrong. The Venus flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge in the phylum Porifera, not a jellyfish, according to EBSCO, NIWA and Animalia. No source I found says the sponge makes its own light. The bioluminescence linked to it comes from the shrimp that live inside it. The claim's point about glucose is also unsupported.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly with reflected sunlight, making it difficult to spot in the daytime sky.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is the brightest planet, but the claim's reasoning is backwards. Reliable sources such as EarthSky and Star Walk describe Venus as one of the easiest planets to see, often shining as a brilliant 'star' after sunset or before sunrise. Its brightness from reflected sunlight is what makes it easy to spot, not what hides it. When Venus is hard to see, it is because it sits close to the Sun in our sky, for example near inferior conjunction when its lit side faces away from Earth. In daytime the problem is the bright sky, not Venus's own brightness. So the idea that Venus is 'often invisible because it shines brightly' is wrong.

text: The checkered pattern found on the classic umbrellas is a result of the old-fashioned way of making them, as the different sections were cut and stitched together, creating distinctive squares.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source saying umbrella checks come from stitching squares together, and the evidence points the other way. Wikipedia says check patterns arise as a byproduct of weaving, with crossed horizontal and vertical lines woven into the fabric. Sources on how umbrellas are made (madehow.com and umbrella patents) say canopies are sewn from triangular panels, or gores, that follow the ribs, not square pieces. Check and tartan umbrellas get their pattern from the woven fabric itself. One caveat: the claim doesn't say which 'classic umbrellas' it means, though no specific example would change this.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the macroscope mountain range found on Venus, which stretches over 6,800 kilometers in length.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus has no known mountain range called the "macroscope" mountain range. Its best-known range, Maxwell Montes, is described as Venus's highest range, not as the longest range in the solar system. Earth's mid-ocean ridge system is about 65,000 km long, according to Wikipedia, WHOI and Guinness. That makes it far longer than the claimed 6,800 km, and even Earth's Andes, at about 7,000 km, are longer than that figure. The claim is false.

text: The sugar ants do not eat sugar, their name comes from their propensity to battle over sweet food sources, rather than consuming it themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the banded sugar ant (Camponotus consobrinus) is named for its liking for sugar and sweet food, as well as the orange-brown band around its gaster. Its diet includes sweet secretions such as honeydew. Ant-keeping care sheets also say the name comes from its strong appetite for sweet substances. None of the sources say the name comes from fighting over sweet food or that these ants don't eat sugar.

text: The sugar ants do not eat sugar, their name comes from their propensity to battle over sweet food sources, rather than eating sweets themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both points. The Australian Museum says the sugar ant (Camponotus consobrinus) got its name from its liking for sugar and is attracted to any sweet food. It also says the ants collect nectar and honeydew. Wikipedia likewise links the common name to the ant's liking for sugar and sweet food, and says its diet includes sweet honeydew from aphids. None of the sources say the name comes from fighting over sweet food sources.

text: There are more moons orbiting Jupiter than any other planet in our solar system, with a total of 92 confirmed moons surrounding Jupiter.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is outdated. Jupiter did briefly hold the record with 92 moons in early 2023 (Space.com), but that didn't last. Saturn overtook it, and in March 2025 the IAU recognized 128 new Saturnian moons, bringing Saturn's total to 274. Saturn now has the most moons of any planet (PopSci, Sky at Night, The Conversation). Jupiter's count is also no longer 92: a NASA page found in the search gives 115 known moons. So both parts of the claim are wrong today: Jupiter doesn't have the most moons, and 92 isn't its current total.

text: There are over 88,000 active stars within the Milky Way galaxy that are visible to the naked eye from Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found say far fewer stars are visible to the naked eye than 88,000. Wikipedia puts the number at about six thousand under ideal conditions, and EarthSky says that counting the whole sky, even the highest estimates are close to 10,000. A study on ADS says the figure for a single dark night is often given as about 2,500. Every estimate is well under 88,000, so the claim is contradicted.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly tend to eat less.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed and does not support the specific claim. Small studies (Ledochowski et al., PMC4356559; a ScienceDirect Appetite paper) found that a 15-minute brisk walk briefly reduced cravings for chocolate and sugary snacks. However, other controlled trials found no effect on hunger or food intake. King et al. (2010) reported that 60 minutes of brisk walking did not change appetite, energy intake or the hunger hormone ghrelin, and a study of overweight and obese women likewise found hunger and energy intake unchanged after walking. I found no study showing that people who walk faster tend to eat less, and nothing about 'extreme hunger' specifically. The claim's main point therefore cannot be verified, and part of it is contradicted by the null results.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up both parts of the claim, though the length figure depends on the source. NOAA and WHOI call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. Wikipedia gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the whole ridge system as 80,000 km, and Britannica also says about 80,000 km. NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', so 'over 65,000 km' only holds if you count the full system. Britannica says the main ridge runs down the middle of the Atlantic and into the Indian Ocean. Other sources place the Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic. The claim leaves out the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise), but it does not say the ridge runs only through the three oceans it names, so that omission is not a contradiction.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers (7,918 miles) at the equator due to its equatorial bulge.
label: contradicted
reason: Earth's diameter at the equator is not 12,742 km. That figure, about 7,918 miles, is the mean diameter: twice the 6,371 km mean radius. Wikipedia gives an equatorial radius of 6,378.137 km, which means an equatorial diameter of about 12,756 km (roughly 7,926 miles). Other sources make the same distinction between the 12,742 km average and the 12,756 km equatorial width. The equatorial bulge makes the equatorial diameter larger than 12,742 km, so the claim gives the wrong figure for the equator.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that inhabit our planet, according to the most recent estimates from the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) and the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS).
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 8.7 million species comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology study by Camilo Mora and colleagues. Their number (±1.3 million) is an estimate of all eukaryotic species, which includes fungi, protozoa and chromists, not just plants and animals. The study used data from the Catalogue of Life and WoRMS, but the estimate itself belongs to Mora et al. It was not published by ITIS or WoRMS, which are catalogues of species already described (about 2 million). The 2011 study is also not 'the most recent' estimate, and it gives roughly 8.7 million, not 'over' 8.7 million. Because the claim gets the source and scope wrong, it is contradicted.

text: Antarctica has more than 70 active volcanoes, many of which are located beneath the ice sheets.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say Antarctica has very few active volcanoes, not more than 70. The Conversation and Phys.org both say "Only two volcanoes in Antarctica are active": Mount Erebus and Deception Island. The large counts come from a 2017 University of Edinburgh study that found 138 volcanoes in West Antarctica, 91 of them under the ice. But that study did not establish that these volcanoes are active. The Week reports it is not known whether they are active or dormant. The claim is right that many volcanoes sit beneath the ice, but wrong to call more than 70 of them active.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique mating ritual in which some species will hold their pectoral fins up over their eyes during courtship.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source showing butterflyfish holding their pectoral fins over their eyes during courtship. The Animal Diversity Web page on Chaetodontidae describes their reproduction as forming pairs, chasing each other, and rising into the water to spawn with the male's snout against the female's abdomen. Other sources describe pair bonding and courtship displays that look like a dance. None of them mention a fin-over-eyes behavior, but none of them rule it out either. The claim's key detail can't be checked, so the result is inconclusive.

text: Rivers are responsible for transporting about 17% of the dissolved oxygen found in the Earth's oceans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source for the claim that rivers deliver about 17% of the ocean's dissolved oxygen. What I did find says the ocean's dissolved oxygen comes mainly from photosynthesis, and oceanography generally names gas exchange with the atmosphere as the other main source, with rivers not counted as a major supplier. That makes the figure doubtful, but nothing I found directly states a different percentage, so the claim can't be confirmed or clearly refuted. My search was cut short by a tool usage limit, so the evidence is limited.

text: The Andean condensed milk, a type of milk known to have originated in South America, can last for years without refrigeration because of its acidity from lactic acid.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any product called "Andean condensed milk" that is said to come from South America. Wikipedia says condensed milk originated in the United States, and one source says it only became established in South America during colonization. Several sources say sweetened condensed milk keeps for a long time because of its high sugar content, low water activity, heat sterilization and sealed can. None of them credit lactic acid, so the claim's explanation is wrong.

text: The Bend in the Grand Coulee in Washington state, USA, is the largest retention dam in the world by volume, storing over 10 million gallons of water.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no dam called "The Bend in the Grand Coulee." The claim seems to mean Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River in Washington state. Sources describe that dam as one of the largest concrete structures (Bureau of Reclamation) or the largest hydro project in North America. Britannica, Wikipedia and Roads & Bridges agree that it was the world's largest hydro project only for a short time after completion, so it is not the largest dam in the world by volume today. Wikipedia lists its volume as about 9.16 million cubic meters of concrete. China's Three Gorges Dam is widely known to be much larger, though no search result covered it. The storage figure is also wrong by a huge margin: its reservoir, Lake Roosevelt, holds about 9.56 million acre-feet (about 11.8 billion cubic meters), which is trillions of gallons, not "over 10 million gallons."

text: The Fangshan Cooked Treasures, a 2,000-year-old collection of over 3,000 preserved Chinese dishes, was discovered in 1975 in Beijing, China.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that the 'Fangshan Cooked Treasures' exist as a 2,000-year-old find of over 3,000 preserved dishes discovered in Beijing in 1975. When 'Fangshan' comes up in a food context, the results point to Fangshan Restaurant in Beijing, which serves Qing-dynasty imperial cuisine. That is a restaurant, not an ancient archaeological find. Searches for a 1975 discovery of ancient preserved dishes in Beijing turned up other finds, such as 4,000-year-old noodles and the Dabaotai Han tomb, but nothing matching this claim. The claim looks made up, but no source directly says it is false, so the evidence can neither confirm nor refute it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which runs for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and WorldAtlas both call the Mid-Ocean Ridge Earth's longest mountain range. WHOI says it is made up of 40,000 continuous miles (65,000 km) of underwater volcanoes that circle the globe. WorldAtlas gives about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). These figures match the claim's '65,000 km (40,000 miles)'. The claim's 'over' is slightly stronger than 'about 65,000 km', but this is within the range reputable sources use, and none of the sources contradicts it.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthen", however in some cases,  the word "length" can also be in contention for this title.
label: contradicted
reason: "Strengthen" has two syllables (streng-then), so it can't be the longest one-syllable English word. Wikipedia's list of the longest English words with one syllable gives 9–10-letter monosyllables such as "strengths", "scraunched" and "strengthed", and notes the answer is somewhat subjective. Guinness names "strengths" (9 letters) the longest English word with only one vowel. "Length" has only six letters, so it is not a serious contender either.

text: The shorter our names are, the less people mistakenly call us by our neighbors' names.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that links name length to how often people get misnamed. The main research on misnaming (Deffler et al., 2016, Memory & Cognition; the UT Austin PLOS ONE study; Brédart's study in PMC) finds two things. First, the wrong name usually comes from the same social group, such as siblings, children or friends. Second, misnaming happens more when names sound alike, sharing initial or final sounds or phonemes. None of these studies report that shorter names are misnamed less, or that people are less often called by a neighbor's name. The claim's link between name length and misnaming can't be confirmed or ruled out with these sources.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, accounting for about 0.4% of the Earth's biomass due to their relatively small size and limited storage of nutrients.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion (Crowther et al., Nature, 2015), roughly 15 times the claimed 200 billion. That study found the number had been underestimated, not overestimated: earlier estimates of about 400 billion were 7 times too low. The 0.4% biomass figure is also wrong. Plants, mostly the woody parts of trees, make up about 80% of Earth's biomass, so trees are not a minor share 'due to their relatively small size.' I only checked the tree-count source directly; the biomass correction comes from general knowledge of the scientific literature, not from a search result.

text: There are over 86 million shares of the Oxford English Dictionary, making it one of the most widely printed books in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable news reports (CBS/AP, NBC, PCWorld) say the full printed Oxford English Dictionary, the 20-volume 1989 second edition, sold only about 30,000 sets in total. That figure is nowhere near 86 million copies, and the low sales are why OUP expected not to print the next edition. I found nothing to support the 86 million figure or the idea that the OED is one of the most widely printed books in the world.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into statues.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is a real, highly alkaline lake in northern Tanzania, with a pH of about 9–10.5 and sometimes up to 12. Colossal reports that animals that end up in the water slowly become calcified, and Nick Brandt's photographs show these 'calcified statues.' Discover Wildlife says the lake's natron minerals absorb moisture and fat and preserve the carcasses, so they aren't exactly stone but are 'a statue, nevertheless.' One caveat: the animals in Brandt's well-known photos were posed by him, but the claim only says the lake can turn dead animals into statues, and that is supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) in length.
label: supported
reason: NOAA describes the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth, about 40,389 miles (nearly 65,000 km) long. That matches the claim of "over 40,000 miles (64,000 km)." WHOI and Wikipedia give the same figures (about 65,000 km, or 40,000+ mi).

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, were used as early as Ancient Egypt.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say buttresses were used in ancient Egyptian architecture. A ResearchGate paper on the structural role of buttresses says they appear in the architecture of ancient Egypt, Babylon and Greece. A study guide also places early buttresses in Mesopotamian and Egyptian architecture. Britannica adds that barrel vaults first appeared in ancient Egypt and the Near East and needed buttressing. None of the sources found contradicts the claim. The evidence comes from a preprint, a study guide and an encyclopedia, so it is consistent but not drawn from specialist archaeological studies.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is primarily located underwater.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service and Ocean Exploration pages, along with WHOI, call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,389 miles) and say about 90% of it lies underwater. One small mismatch: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI describe it as 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over'. Since these sources still give the length as about 65,000 km, the claim's main points hold.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, spanning over 65,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says the Mid-Ocean Ridge is technically the longest mountain range in the world, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). NOAA also describes the ridge as stretching more than 65,000 km, which matches the claim's wording of "over 65,000 kilometers."

text: The short-lived, naturally occurring element Tennessine has a half-life of roughly 80 milliseconds.
label: contradicted
reason: The half-life figure is about right: sources give Ts-294, tennessine's most stable isotope, a half-life of roughly 80 ms (78 ms in some sources). But the claim calls tennessine a naturally occurring element, and that is wrong. Tennessine (element 117) is a superheavy synthetic element that has only been made in laboratories and does not occur in nature.

text: There are approximately 150,000 plant and animal species alive on Earth today that are still unidentified by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate, from Mora et al. 2011 in PLoS Biology, puts the number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million. Only about 1.2 million of these have been described, so roughly 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still unidentified. That means millions of species remain unknown to scientists, not about 150,000.

text: Butler's extract of honeybee venom, apitoxin, has been used to treat arthritis and now is being tested to reverse the effects of multiple sclerosis.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source saying a person named Butler made an extract of honeybee venom. The only Butler I found in this context is Charles Butler, who described the bee's sting organ in his 1609 book, The Feminine Monarchie. That isn't the same as extracting apitoxin, so the claim's main attribution can't be checked. It's true that bee venom has been used as a folk or alternative treatment for arthritis. But Wikipedia says controlled evidence for that use is lacking. It also says clinical trials found bee venom therapy doesn't work for multiple sclerosis and can make MS symptoms worse. That undercuts the idea that it is 'now being tested to reverse' MS, though some animal studies on MS-like disease do exist. With the Butler link unverified and the MS part disputed, the claim can't be confirmed or fully refuted.

text: Did you know that Antarctica is home to several large freshwater lakes, including Lake Vostok, which is currently the largest and oldest freshwater lake on Earth, covering an area of approximately 14,000 square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Vostok is the largest known subglacial lake. Guinness World Records lists its area as about 14,000 km², and WorldAtlas gives about 12,500 km², so the area figure is roughly right. However, the claim that it is the largest freshwater lake on Earth is false. WorldAtlas says Vostok is about the size of Lake Ontario, which makes it much smaller than lakes like Lake Superior (about 82,000 km²). It is also not considered the oldest: WorldAtlas says it has been sealed off for an estimated 14–15 million years, while Lake Baikal is generally put at about 25 million years old.

text: A platypus is one of the few venomous mammals in the world, as the male platypus has a spur on its hind leg that delivers a painful and potentially deadly venom.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including WWF Australia, WorldAtlas and A-Z Animals, agree on every part of the claim. The platypus is one of the few venomous mammals, and only males have a venom spur on each hind leg. The venom is extremely painful and can kill smaller animals such as dogs. WWF says the venom 'is lethal' but notes there are no recorded human deaths. That makes 'potentially deadly' accurate as a general statement, although the platypus is not known to have killed a person.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it can recover quickly from errors and outages.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim repeats a well-known myth. The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet", written by Internet pioneers including Vint Cerf, says the idea that ARPANET was tied to building a network that could survive a nuclear war was a "false rumor" that grew out of the separate RAND study by Paul Baran. ARPANET was built to share computing resources. The same source does say that later internetworking work stressed robustness and survivability, so the network's resilience is real. But it was not originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack, so the claim's main premise is false.

text: The darkest star in our galaxy, VY Canis Majoris, is so massive that it would consume the entire solar system, including the sun, if it were placed at the center of our solar system.
label: contradicted
reason: VY Canis Majoris isn't the darkest star in our galaxy. It's a red hypergiant and one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way. It's also not especially massive, at about 17 solar masses; what stands out is its size, with a radius of about 1,420 solar radii (around 6.6 AU). If it were placed at the centre of the Solar System, its surface would reach past Jupiter's orbit (about 5.2 AU) but not the outer planets (Saturn is at about 9.5 AU), so it wouldn't engulf the entire solar system. The sources here are fan wikis, but these figures agree with the standard published values, and they contradict several parts of the claim.

text: There are approximately 7.9 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone, but this number can vary due to ongoing research and advancements in astronomy.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put the number of stars in the Milky Way at about 100 to 400 billion, not 7.9 billion. WorldAtlas cites 100–400 billion, and the University of Arizona says astronomers estimate about 100 billion. The claim's 7.9 billion is off by more than an order of magnitude; it looks like a mix-up with the world's human population. The claim is right that estimates vary, but its central number is wrong.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it was built with redundancy and the ability to recover quickly from failures.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet," written by Internet pioneers including Leiner, Cerf and Kahn, calls this idea a "false rumor." It says the ARPANET was never meant to be a network that could survive nuclear war. Only Paul Baran's separate RAND study on secure military voice communications looked at nuclear survivability. The ARPANET was built to let researchers share computing resources, so the claim's stated reason for the network's original design is wrong.

text: There are More than 300,000 known species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but scientists believe that up to 80% of all life on the planet remains undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate, Mora et al. 2011 as reported by Nature/BioEd Online, puts the total at about 8.7 million species. Only about 1.2 million of these have been catalogued, which suggests that more than 80% of species are still undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species). So 80% is a floor, not an upper limit, and the claim's "up to 80%" understates the estimate. The claim's figure of "more than 300,000" known species is technically true but far below the roughly 1.2 million catalogued species. Because the claim caps the undiscovered share at 80% while the cited research says it exceeds 80%, the claim is contradicted.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original formula containing cocaine and Pepsi's being based on a formula for a popular cola drink called Brad's Drink, which contained cola nuts and vanilla, and was later altered at Pepsi Cola company until having the taste we know today.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is partly true. Coca-Cola's original formula did contain cocaine, and its inventor John Pemberton reportedly wanted a substitute for morphine. Pepsi's history doesn't fit, though. Caleb Bradham made it as 'Brad's Drink' and sold it as a digestive aid for dyspepsia, or indigestion, which is where the name 'Pepsi' came from. It was not made as a morphine alternative. The claim also gets the origin wrong: Brad's Drink was Bradham's own creation, not based on a formula for some other popular cola. That breaks the claim's statement that both drinks began as morphine alternatives.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Ira Springer of New York, who took a 10-minute sauna, and then an unheated room shower resulted in a body temperature of 112°F (44.9°C) after five hours and body temperature of 82°F (27.8°C) within
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing about an 'Ira Springer' of New York or any record for human body-temperature variation caused by a sauna and then a shower. Guinness World Records lists the highest recorded body temperature as 46.5°C (115.7°F), for Willie Jones, who had heatstroke in Atlanta in 1980. That record is not the 112°F figure in the claim, and it isn't a 'variation' record either. The claim also stops mid-sentence ('within'), so it can't be fully checked. Its details look made up and aren't backed by any trustworthy source, but no source directly disproves them, so the claim can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that spans over 65,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. It puts the length at 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km, and notes that about 90% of the ridge lies under the ocean. WorldAtlas and WHOI give the same picture: an underwater range of roughly 65,000 km. The claim says "over 65,000 km." NOAA's figure is "approximately" that number rather than clearly more, but I recall that USGS describes the ridge as more than 65,000 km long. Either way, the difference is small and the claim matches reliable sources.

text: Butler's Elephant, a male African elephant, lived to be 57 years old, the oldest recorded elephant in history.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of an elephant called "Butler's Elephant." The bigger problem is the claim that an elephant aged 57 is the oldest on record. Guinness World Records lists Lin Wang, an Asian elephant at Taipei Zoo, as the oldest elephant ever: he died in 2003 aged 86. Other reports describe elephants living to around 89 or even past 100, such as Vatsala in India. So 57 years is nowhere near the record.

text: The Gizmo, a genetically modified mouse, was the first mammal to have its genome fully sequenced in 2002.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2002 mouse genome (Waterston et al., 2002) came from the ordinary inbred lab strain C57BL/6J, not from a genetically modified mouse called "Gizmo." I found no source that mentions any mouse by that name. The mouse also wasn't the first mammal to be sequenced: the draft human genome was published in 2001. Sources describe the mouse only as the first mammalian model organism to get a reference genome, and its 2002 sequence was an initial draft rather than a complete one.

text: The highest recorded concentration of quartz in the world is found in the White Tank Mountains in Arizona, USA.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing linking the White Tank Mountains in Arizona to the world's highest concentration of quartz. A rockhounding guide says the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas, between Mount Ida and Jessieville, have the densest concentration of accessible crystal quartz deposits in the world. Mount Ida is also widely called the 'Quartz Capital of the World.' The only 'White Tank' quartz result was about White Tank quartz monzonite, a granite-like rock in California, not a record quartz deposit.

text: TheHistogram, a rare blood clotting disorder, is caused by a deficiency in ADAMTS13, a protein that regulates blood clotting.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no disorder called "TheHistogram"; searches for that name turned up only statistical uses of the word "histogram." The rare clotting disorder caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). The claim's description of ADAMTS13 is accurate, but because the named entity has no clear referent, the claim can't be verified as written.

text: There are approximately 500 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy, which is estimated to contain between 200-400 billion stars.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself, since 500 billion is outside the 200–400 billion range it also gives. Reliable sources don't support the 500 billion figure. Wikipedia lists 100–400 billion stars, Big Think says the most likely number is 200–400 billion, and the University of Arizona says about 100 billion. The 200–400 billion part is supported, but none of the sources found gives 500 billion as the estimate.

text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total coastline that is only slightly over 25,000 kilometers long.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Geography of Norway page cites Kartverket, Norway's official mapping agency, for a total of 320,249 islands and islets: 239,057 islands and 81,192 islets. That is far more than 18,000, so the claim's "more than" wording holds even though 18,000 badly understates the real count. Wikipedia and the CIA World Factbook (via IndexMundi) both give Norway's coastline as 25,148 km, which is "slightly over 25,000 km." One caveat: counting island coastlines raises the figure to about 83,000 km, so "total coastline" depends on how it is measured. The claim's figures still match the standard reported value.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 40,000 miles around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's National Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and that it spans 40,389 miles around the globe. That figure is over 40,000 miles, so both parts of the claim check out. A separate NOAA Ocean Exploration page also calls the mid-ocean ridge the world's longest mountain range.

text: The tingling sensation people often experience in their fingers and toes while flying on an airplane is caused by a lack of air pressure at high altitudes, which leads to a decrease in oxygen levels and increased carbon dioxide levels.
label: contradicted
reason: The FAA handbook does list tingling in the fingers and toes as a symptom of hypoxia, which is the low oxygen caused by reduced air pressure at altitude. But the claim gets the carbon dioxide part backwards. The FAA explains that tingling linked to altitude also comes from hyperventilation, which removes too much carbon dioxide from the body, so CO2 levels in the blood go down, not up. The claim's statement that CO2 levels rise conflicts with this source. Also, airliner cabins are pressurized, so most passengers do not 'often' get this symptom.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with approximately 86 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86-billion-neuron figure is right, but the comparison is wrong. Nature Scitable and Psychology Today both put the Milky Way at about 200–400 billion stars and call 'more neurons than stars' a widespread myth. The University of Minnesota's Bell Museum uses a lower estimate of about 100 billion stars, which is still more than 86 billion neurons. The galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons.

text: The Penguin is the only bird species that is capable of drinking saltwater due to special glands located above their eyes that help to remove excess salt from their bloodstream.
label: contradicted
reason: Penguins do have supraorbital salt glands above their eyes that remove excess salt, but they are not the only birds with this ability. Wikipedia's article on salt glands says the European herring gull also has these glands and can drink seawater. BirdNote says seabirds in general drink seawater and get rid of the salt through glands above their eyes. That makes the 'only bird species' part of the claim false. Calling penguins a single species is also inaccurate, since there are several penguin species.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and gentle nature, which makes them easily embarrassed in the presence of other animals.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources (HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals, Animal Corner, ZME Science) confirm that a group of giant pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." The reason the claim gives is not backed by any of them. A Journal Gazette editorial says "no one seems to know the roots" of the term. Where sources do suggest a reason, they point to pandas' clumsy, lazy movements, or to the French word "embarras" (obstacle). None says the name comes from pandas being shy or easily embarrassed around other animals. Only a TikTok page vaguely mentions shy behaviour, and it is not a reliable source. So the term is correct, but the explanation is unsupported and conflicts with what the sources say.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to the most recent estimate by the Entomological Society of America.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology study led by Camilo Mora (University of Hawaii) and Dalhousie University colleagues, linked to the Census of Marine Life. It did not come from the Entomological Society of America. The study's central estimate was about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, not 'over' 8.7 million. That total also covers fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. It is also not the most recent estimate: later studies give quite different numbers. So the claim gets the source wrong, and its other details are inaccurate too.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, as estimated by biologists, although only a small fraction of these have been discovered and documented by humans.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the widely cited 2011 estimate by Camilo Mora and colleagues: about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. That study also found that only about 1.2 million species, under 15%, had been catalogued, leaving about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species undiscovered. That backs the claim that humans have documented only a small fraction. The claim's "over 8.7 million" is slightly loose, since 8.7 million is the central estimate, not a minimum. Even so, the main point holds, and some other estimates that count microbes are much higher.

text: There is a species of shellfish called the sea sponge, although they're not actually that, they're actually known as Sponge genus Cliona, however another shellfish species, called a viper shellfish (Latia BSPacer Isocati), contain an estimate of 60,000 individuals in just one shell.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found backs up the claim's details, and parts of it conflict with reliable sources. Cliona is a genus of boring sponges in the phylum Porifera, not shellfish. These sponges bore into oyster and mussel shells, which is probably where the confusion came from. The genus Latia is a real group of freshwater limpets, but its one well-known species is Latia neritoides, a small bioluminescent limpet from New Zealand. It isn't a 'viper shellfish,' no species called 'BSPacer Isocati' exists, and no source says 60,000 individuals live in one shell. The 'viper' search results were about unrelated things such as fireworks and a shrimp.

text: Did you know that the longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses"?
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardesses" (stew-ard-ess-es) has four syllables, not one. It is known as the longest word you can type with only the left hand on a QWERTY keyboard. Wikipedia and Dictionary.com give one-syllable words like "scraunched," "squirreled," "strengths" and "screeched" as the candidates for longest one-syllable word.

text: Caterpillars have unique hairs on their bodies that contain a toxin to defend against predators, and some species can release a foul-tasting liquid called "reflex bleeding" to deter predators.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim is partly supported, though it overgeneralizes. Trustworthy sources such as Clemson HGIC, Northern Woodlands and New World Encyclopedia say that many caterpillars, but not all, have urticating hairs or setae for defense, and some of these hairs are hollow and deliver venom. The second part could not be verified. Every source I found describes reflex bleeding in ladybirds, other beetles, froghoppers and sawfly larvae. Sawfly larvae look like caterpillars but are not Lepidoptera. Reflex bleeding is also the name of the behavior (pushing out hemolymph), not of the liquid itself. A Live Science article says silkmoth caterpillars spit out a foul fluid, but that is regurgitation, not reflex bleeding. I found no source showing that caterpillars use reflex bleeding, and my search limit ran out before I could check Lepidoptera specifically. That part stays unconfirmed, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: Antarctica is home to several unique species of penguins, but the Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo, and Emperor penguins can be found nowhere else on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo and Emperor penguins live nowhere else on Earth, but that's false. The Australian Antarctic Division says gentoo penguins breed on many sub-Antarctic islands, and their largest populations are in the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the Antarctic Peninsula. So gentoos are not found only in Antarctica. Chinstraps also breed outside the continent, on sub-Antarctic islands such as the South Sandwich Islands.

text: There are approximately 7.9 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone, but this number can vary depending on the source and method used to count them.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put the Milky Way's star count far above 7.9 billion. WorldAtlas gives 100 to 400 billion stars based on the galaxy's mass, and the University of Arizona's astronomy department says about 100 billion. The claim is right that estimates vary, but 7.9 billion is wrong by more than an order of magnitude. It looks like it was mixed up with the world's human population (about 7.9 billion).

text: The longest war in recorded history was the Hundred Years' War between England and France, which lasted for 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
label: contradicted
reason: The 116-year span (1337–1453) is correct, but the Hundred Years' War was not the longest war in recorded history. Several sources name longer conflicts. History Collection and Nibble say the Reconquista lasted about 781 years and call it the longest war in history. WION also lists the Roman-Germanic Wars at roughly 600–700 years and the Arauco War at nearly 300 years. History Facts treats the Hundred Years' War as just one of several of history's longest wars.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which runs for over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) says the same, and both give its length as roughly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). NOAA says "nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles)", while the claim says "over". Other commonly cited figures, which count more of the ridge system, are 65,000–80,000 km. That makes the difference minor, so the claim's main point and approximate length are supported.

text: The Human Brain accounts for about 2% of the human body's mass, yet it consumes around 20% of the body's total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including The Physics Factbook (which cites encyclopedias and textbooks) and TIME, say the human brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest. This matches the claim.

text: Buttering an egg white before boiling prevents it from becoming tough and results in a more tender and less-stringy texture.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source showing that buttering an egg, or an egg white, before boiling makes the white more tender or less stringy. The sources I found describe Irish 'buttered eggs.' In this method, butter is rubbed onto the shell of a warm, freshly laid egg to seal it and keep it fresh for up to about six months. Tasting Table and the Oxford Companion to Food say these eggs look glossy and taste buttery. Neither mentions any effect on how tender the white is, and the butter goes on the shell, not the white. Other sources say high heat toughens egg proteins, but none link butter to preventing that. My search tool hit its limit before I could check more sources, so I can't confirm or rule out the texture claim.

text: Caterpillars have a natural defense mechanism where they secrete a toxic liquid from their bodies to deter predators.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources confirm that some caterpillars defend themselves by secreting harmful chemicals. A ScienceDaily/PLOS report on notodontid moth caterpillars says they have a gland under the head that produces an acidic secretion "usually sprayed at predators as a deterrent." Other well-documented examples include the swallowtail osmeterium, which releases noxious chemicals, and caterpillars that regurgitate defensively. Not every caterpillar species does this, but the claim describes a real, documented defense mechanism, so it counts as supported.

text: Spain has the world's largestmobile phone network provider in terms of user numbers, according to total subscriptions in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Spain does not have the world's largest mobile network provider by number of users. WorldAtlas, citing TeleGeography data, lists China Mobile, a Chinese company, as the largest operator by subscriber count. Spain's Telefónica is a major operator, but it is not the biggest in the world.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas and the Guinness World Records search result both name the global mid-ocean ridge system as the world's longest mountain range. WorldAtlas puts its length at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). That source says "about" rather than "over," but other commonly cited figures range from about 65,000 km to more than 65,000 km, so the claim still holds.

text: There are over 300 million species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, but humans have discovered and documented only a small fraction of them.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate puts the total number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million (plus or minus 1.3 million). That includes about 7.77 million animal species and about 298,000 plant species. Earlier estimates ranged from 3 million to 100 million. Nothing found supports an estimate of over 300 million plant and animal species, so that figure is far too high. The second part of the claim is accurate: only a small share of species has been described, for example about 953,000 of the estimated 7.77 million animals. However, the main number in the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 373 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 3 trillion fewer trees than existed during the last Ice Age.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Crowther et al. study in Nature puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion, not around 373 billion. The figure in the claim is roughly an order of magnitude too low (earlier estimates were about 400 billion). The same study says tree numbers have fallen about 46% since the start of human civilization. It does not say there were 3 trillion more trees during the last Ice Age, so the comparison in the claim is also misattributed.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth that have been identified and cataloged by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology). It is not a count of species that scientists have already identified and catalogued. According to ScienceDaily and Dalhousie University, only about 1.25 million species had been described and entered into central databases, and roughly 86% of species were thought to be still undescribed. Later sources put the number of described species at about 2 million. The claim mistakes an estimated total for a count of catalogued species.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal, called the turbellarian rotifer, due to its natural ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The 'immortal jellyfish' is Turritopsis dohrnii, not a 'turbellarian rotifer.' It can turn back into its juvenile form through transdifferentiation, so that part of the claim is right. The name is wrong, though: turbellarians are flatworms and rotifers are a separate group of tiny animals, and neither is a jellyfish. Because the claim gets the name of the organism wrong, it is contradicted.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique twitches and vibrations of their bodies convey information about food sources and distances?
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. ScienceDirect's overview of the honeybee waggle dance, which draws on Karl von Frisch's Nobel Prize–winning research, says the dance conveys the distance and direction of food sources. It also says the waggle movements and their duration encode distance. One small caveat: the source notes that vibrations may mainly serve to attract followers rather than carry specific information. That nuance doesn't undercut the claim's main point that body waggles and vibrations in the dance communicate food location and distance.

text: Bacteria have been found to exist on every continent on Earth, including Antarctica, where they have been discovered in ice samples up to 8,000 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: Bacteria do live on every continent, including Antarctica, but the age in the claim is wrong. Rutgers researchers led by Kay Bidle revived microbes from Antarctic glacier ice that was between about 100,000 and 8 million years old, not up to 8,000 years old. The claim appears to have confused 8 million with 8,000. ABC News reported the revived microbes had been frozen 'for up to eight million years.'

text: Butterfly fish can be found in large schools while migrating, sometimes numbering over 100 fish, allowing them to be visible from a significant distance underwater.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't fully check this claim because the search tool hit its usage limit before I could finish. What I did find doesn't confirm it. Britannica Kids says butterfly fish often swim alone or in pairs and that some swim in schools. A snippet from A-Z Animals says wrought iron butterflyfish are found in schools of at least 10 others. Neither source I saw mentions schools forming during migration, groups of more than 100 fish, or schools being visible from a long way off underwater. I also found nothing that clearly contradicts those details, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: GST or Goods and Services Tax was applied in over 160 countries across the world.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. ClearTax says that 'over 160 countries have implemented GST or VAT', and other sources say VAT/GST is used in about 160–170 countries or 'more than 160 countries'. The claim depends on treating GST and VAT as the same consumption tax, which is how these sources count them. No source found disputes the figure.

text: Radium has the highest electronegativity of all the alkaline earth metals, which makes it extremely reactive and difficult to handle.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the trend backwards. Electronegativity goes down as you move down the alkaline earth group. CK-12 says beryllium has the highest electronegativity in the group, and radium is at or near the bottom (about 0.9 on the Pauling scale). Radium is highly reactive because its electronegativity is low, not high.

text: The darkest time of the day, usually around 2-3 am, is called "twilight" but actually it's biologically more accurately known as "dusk".
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is wrong. Twilight is the partly lit period between day and night, around sunrise and sunset. It is not the darkest part of the night, which comes around 2–3 am. Dusk is the darker stage of evening twilight at the end of the day. It is not a 'biological' name for the middle of the night either. So neither word means the darkest time of night.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that spans over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas and NOAA both call the Mid-Ocean Ridge Earth's longest mountain range. They describe it as an underwater chain running around the globe. WorldAtlas gives its length as about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). NOAA's Ocean Service says it is more than 65,000 km long, which matches the claim's 'over 65,000 kilometers'. None of the evidence contradicts the claim.

text: Thearisides, a Hellenistic Greek historian, was the first to mention the usage of gunpowder in his work "Atthis," around 300 BC.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Gunpowder was invented in China, and the earliest records date to about the 9th century AD, more than a thousand years after 300 BC. No Hellenistic historian could have described it then. The writers of an 'Atthis' (a local history of Attica) were the Atthidographers, such as Philochorus and Androtion, and none is named 'Thearisides'. The search for that name turned up the Wikipedia page on Philochorus, not a historian called Thearisides. One limit: the search tool's usage cap was reached before I could read the full results, so this verdict also draws on well-established history.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting there are approximately 1 trillion trees worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: there are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way. The tree count is wrong, though. The main global estimate, from a 2015 Nature study (Crowther et al.), puts the number at about 3 trillion trees, not about 1 trillion. NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Because the specific 'approximately 1 trillion trees' figure conflicts with the accepted estimate, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, but scientists believe that up to 80% of them remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate (Mora et al. 2011, PLoS Biology, reported by National Geographic, ScienceDaily and others) puts the total at about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million. That is below the claim's 'over 10 million'. The same study estimates that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species are still undescribed, which is more than the claim's 'up to 80%'. Older estimates did range widely, from 3 million to 100 million, but the specific figures in the claim do not match the main scientific estimate.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - primarily by one company, One Tree Planted.
label: contradicted
reason: One Tree Planted is a nonprofit (a 501(c)(3)), not a company, and it was founded in Vermont in 2014. It can't have been the main planter of corporate forests "for decades." The claim's tree count is also badly off. Common estimates put the US at roughly 228 billion trees, so "over 300 million" is technically true but understates the number by a huge margin.

text: There are over 8.3 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to estimates from the World Register of Marine Species.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure and the source in the claim are both wrong. The best-known estimate is about 8.7 million species, not 8.3 million. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), a study by Census of Marine Life and Dalhousie researchers. The World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS) did not produce it. WoRMS is a list of described marine species only, and it currently records about 250,000 accepted species. It does not estimate how many species of plants and animals exist on Earth.

text: There is a species of jellyfish found in the Monterey Bay that is immortal, as it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: The Monterey Bay Aquarium's own post describes its "immortal jelly" (Turritopsis sp.), which turns back into its juvenile stage through transdifferentiation. Britannica confirms that the immortal jellyfish (Turritopsis dohrnii) is found worldwide and that transdifferentiation drives its reversal. Two caveats: the sources show the aquarium exhibits the jelly, but none I found clearly confirms wild populations inside Monterey Bay itself. Also, "immortal" is a loose term, since the aquarium notes predators still eat these jellies. Overall the claim is broadly backed, but the Monterey Bay location detail is only indirectly supported.
