text: A platypus is one of the few venomous mammals in the world, as the male platypus has a spur on its hind leg that delivers a painful and potentially deadly venom to predators.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas and other reliable sources say the platypus is one of the few venomous mammals. Only males have the venom-delivering spurs, which are on their hind legs. The venom causes excruciating pain and can be fatal to animals such as dogs, though not to humans. One nuance: the venom is thought to be used mainly against rival males during breeding season, not only against predators. Still, a spur that can kill dogs fits the claim that the venom is 'potentially deadly' to predators.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the Earth.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range and that it stretches about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) around the globe. The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) calls it 'the longest mountain range in the world' and gives a length of 'nearly 65,000 kilometers (about 40,000 miles).' WorldAtlas gives roughly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). The sources I found put the length at about 65,000 km and do not confirm 'over'; WHOI's 'nearly' even suggests slightly less. NOAA is often cited as saying 'more than 65,000 km,' but I did not check that. The difference is too small to contradict the claim, so I rate it supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers and is not located on any continent, but rather runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, with about 65,000 km of continuous range. They also say it winds between the continents and that more than 90% of it is underwater. Wikipedia gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the whole ridge system as about 80,000 km, which fits 'over 65,000 kilometers' (NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly' 65,000 km for the continuous part). Wikipedia also says the system is part of every ocean, which covers the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. Two details are slightly loose: the ridge is not literally in the middle of the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise lies off-centre), and a small part of it comes above water in Iceland, which is an island rather than a continent. Neither point contradicts the main claim.

text: The process of major atmospheric circulation patterns in five-year and thirty-year cycles was first discovered by the Chinese meteorologist Song Yingxing in the 16th century.
label: contradicted
reason: No source credits Song Yingxing with finding cycles in atmospheric circulation. The idea that 'the character of weather recurs every five and thirty years' traces back to Francis Bacon, who reported that people in the Low Countries noticed such a cycle. The 'five and thirty years' in that phrase is old English for 35 years, not separate five-year and thirty-year cycles. The timing is also wrong. Song Yingxing was born in 1587, and all of his known works date from 1636–1637, including the Tiangong Kaiwu of 1637. That places his work in the 17th century, not the 16th. His writings covered technology and cosmology, not cycles in atmospheric circulation.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be about 8.7% of all possible species that could exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is real, but the claim gets the rest wrong. Mora et al. (2011) estimated about 8.7 million species in total on Earth (give or take 1.3 million). That figure covers all eukaryotes, not just plants and animals, and it is an estimate of the total, not 'over 8.7 million'. The study did not say this is '8.7% of all possible species that could exist'. It found that about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered: the roughly 1.2 million species catalogued so far are under 15% of the estimated total. The 8.7% figure is made up and does not match the source.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on the planet Venus, which is the period between two consecutive sunrises, is 116.75 Earth days due to its extremely slow rotation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The numbers check out, but the term in the claim doesn't. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Space Centre NZ, Universe Today) agree that Venus's solar day, the time from one sunrise to the next, is about 116.75 Earth days. They tie this to Venus's very slow retrograde rotation (sidereal day of about 243 Earth days). However, I found no source that uses the term "Khayagan day" for Venus or anything else. A search for it returned only unrelated pages. The term looks made up, so the part of the claim that calls this a "standard Khayagan day" can't be verified.

text: Blettner's law states that the strength of an electric current passing through the body depends on the length of time it has been passing through and the location of the contact points on the body.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched for "Blettner's law" and found no reliable source that names or describes such a law. The results only cover general facts about electric shock and current in the body, plus unrelated laws and court records. Shock severity does depend on how long the current flows and the path it takes through the body, but no source assigns this principle to anyone named Blettner. The claim's main point, that a law by this name exists and says this, can't be verified.

text: The highest recorded wealth ever created by a single person is attributed to the owner of the Aramco company that also is now named, or referred to as, Mohammed Bin Salman of Saudi Arabia's yet his share in the company after it has been sold to public for about $1.9 trillion.
label: contradicted
reason: Saudi Aramco is a state-owned company. The Saudi government owns it, not Mohammed bin Salman personally, so his supposed record personal wealth from it isn't supported. The 2019 IPO also valued Aramco at about $1.7 trillion, not $1.9 trillion; MBS had aimed for $2 trillion. Britannica, CNN and CNBC all describe Aramco as state-owned.

text: The Beehive mailbox, also known as the Henderson mailbox, is a unique type of mailbox that has been used in Utah since the late 1800s, often seen attached to utility poles in rural areas.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that mentions a "Beehive mailbox" also called a "Henderson mailbox" used in Utah since the late 1800s or mounted on utility poles in rural areas. Searches only turned up unrelated results: Utah's beehive state emblem, the Beehive House, and news and directory pages about mailboxes in towns named Henderson in Louisiana, Nevada and elsewhere. Nothing confirms the claim, and nothing directly disproves it, so it can't be verified.

text: The ancient Egyptians were skilled at treating and resetting broken bones, with evidence showing they developed a sophisticated medical technique for splinting and immobilizing injured limbs around 2500 BC.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Several reliable medical and academic sources say ancient Egyptians splinted and immobilized broken limbs by the Fifth Dynasty, which they date between about 2730 and 2325 BC. That fits 'around 2500 BC.' In 1908, Elliot Smith described splints from Naga ed-Deir: bark or wooden splints wrapped in linen and bandaged onto a fractured forearm and femur, with pads used for open wounds. An orthopaedics journal article calls the forearm splint an 'efficient design.' Trauma.org reports that most fractures in skeletons of the Giza pyramid builders healed well and lined up properly, which suggests the bones were set. The Edwin Smith Papyrus also describes pulling fractures back into place and splinting them with linen. Together, this backs the claim that Egyptians were skilled at setting bones and used a well-developed splinting method around 2500 BC.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique nictitating membrane that protects their eyes, helping them see while keeping their eyes clean.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Giraffes can close their eyelids. Save Giraffes Now, a giraffe conservation organisation, says their eyes may close for a few seconds during standing naps. Giraffes also blink, and they sleep with their eyes closed, often with the head resting in a curved neck. Long eyelashes and a nictitating membrane help protect the eye, but they do not stop the eyelids from closing.

text: Butler's Lantern Slide is the world's oldest surviving camera, invented by William Henry Fox Talbot in 1841.
label: contradicted
reason: No source backs the claim. A lantern slide is a glass transparency that a magic lantern projects onto a screen; it is not a camera. I found no camera called "Butler's Lantern Slide." Several reports name an 1839 Susse Frères daguerreotype camera as the world's oldest (commercially made) camera, and it was auctioned in 2007. That date is earlier than 1841, so the claim's 1841 date and its credit to Talbot are both wrong.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Ira Springer of New York, who took a 10-minute sauna then took a 3-minute ice-water bath, experiencing a 16-degree Fahrenheit variation in body temperature within a 13-minute time frame.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence for or against this claim. My first search, for Ira Springer with sauna, ice bath and body-temperature variation, only turned up an unrelated scientific paper about sauna use in cross-country skiers. Further searches came back empty, and then the search limit ran out. No reliable source, such as Guinness World Records, confirms that anyone called Ira Springer holds a body-temperature-variation record, or gives the details stated (a 10-minute sauna, a 3-minute ice bath, a 16°F change in 13 minutes). Nothing I found disproves it either, so I can't call it supported or contradicted.

text: Organisms in certain species of jellyfish are biologically immortal, meaning they can transform their bodies into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: EBSCO Research Starters and Britannica both describe Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the "immortal jellyfish." They say it can turn back into its juvenile (polyp) form and restart its life cycle through a process called transdifferentiation, in which specialized cells change into other cell types. This matches the claim that some jellyfish species are biologically immortal because they can return their bodies to a younger state by transdifferentiation.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Tethys Enceladus Seaway, found in the Saturnian moon system, stretching for over 40,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: No real feature called the "Tethys Enceladus Seaway" shows up in any source. The longest mountain range in the Solar System is Earth's mid-ocean ridge system, which runs about 65,000 km and is mostly underwater (NOAA, EarthDate). The biggest mountain range in Saturn's moon system is the equatorial ridge on Iapetus, at about 1,300 km, nowhere near 40,000 km.

text: There are more galaxies in the observable universe than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting over 200 billion galaxies exist.
label: supported
reason: I found support for both parts of the claim. Estimates for the number of galaxies in the observable universe run from about 200 billion to 2 trillion or more, so "over 200 billion" holds. Big Think puts the figure at roughly 6 to 20 trillion galaxies, compared with about 400 billion stars in the Milky Way. Wikipedia gives the Milky Way's star count as 100 to 400 billion. With trillions of galaxies, there are more galaxies than Milky Way stars. One caveat: if the true galaxy count is near the low end (a few hundred billion), the two numbers are about the same. Even so, the widely cited 2-trillion estimate supports the comparison.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, with the Amazon rainforest alone being home to around 390 billion individual trees and containing about 10% of all known plant and animal species.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2015 study in Nature led by Thomas Crowther of Yale estimated that Earth has about 3 trillion trees, not 200 billion. Even the older global estimate was just over 400 billion. The claim also contradicts itself: it says the Amazon alone has about 390 billion trees, which is more than the 200 billion it gives for the whole planet. The Amazon figure of about 390 billion trees is broadly consistent with published estimates, but the worldwide figure is clearly wrong.

text: Benedict Cumberbatch was initially cast for the role of Rupert Young's friend in the 2007 television series 'Sherlock Holmes', but he was recast as the title character.
label: contradicted
reason: Cumberbatch starred as Sherlock Holmes in the BBC series 'Sherlock', which ran from 2010 to 2017. It did not start in 2007, and no 2007 series called 'Sherlock Holmes' had him in it. Reliable sources (Britannica, TMDB and series wikis) list him only as Sherlock Holmes, with Martin Freeman as Watson. Rupert Young is not credited, and nothing suggests Cumberbatch was first cast as anyone's friend and then moved to the lead role. Accounts of the casting say the creators picked him for Sherlock from the start.

text: Ancient Egyptians were experts at adhesive technology and used a mixture of honey and gum arabic to bond wood and stone in their monumental structures.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources partly support the claim. Ancient Egyptians did use several adhesives: animal glue for woodwork and inlays, and gum arabic, egg white and beeswax for things like mummy wrappings, papyrus and decoration. But the sources contradict the specific claim about monumental buildings. They say the stone blocks of the pyramids were set with gypsum mortar, sometimes lime mortar, not a mixture of honey and gum arabic. No source I found mentions a honey and gum arabic adhesive used to bond wood and stone in monuments. This is a judgment call: no source directly says that mixture was never used, so 'inconclusive' was also possible. I chose 'contradicted' because the sources describe a different binder for the monumental stonework.

text: Butler's LampPosts in the UK traditionally have a shape that holds up a hat.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no clear match for "Butler's LampPosts" in the UK. I couldn't find any source describing such lampposts or saying they are traditionally shaped to hold a hat. The results were unrelated: butler costume hats, generic lamp-post-shaped items and antique butler or dumb-waiter stands. I hit the search limit before I could look further. Because the entity has no clear referent and I found no supporting or contradicting evidence, the claim can't be verified.

text: The remains of "The Great Blue Hole," a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, were once a huge limestone cave above sea level.
label: supported
reason: Belize's official tourism board describes the Great Blue Hole as a collapsed cave system that probably formed above ground and was flooded at the end of the last Ice Age. Other sources say it began as a limestone cave system when sea levels were 400–500 feet lower than today, and that the stalactites inside show the caves were once above water. This matches the claim that the sinkhole is what remains of a huge limestone cave that was once above sea level.

text: There are approximately 200 caves located beneath the city of Lascaux in France, which are part of the extensive network of Cave System.
label: contradicted
reason: Lascaux isn't a city. It's a single prehistoric decorated cave in the Dordogne, about 1 km southeast of the town of Montignac on the left bank of the Vézère. The claim says there are about 200 caves beneath a "city of Lascaux" in an "extensive network of Cave System", and that premise is wrong. The source doesn't mention any such 200-cave network. (The Vézère valley as a whole does have many decorated sites, but they aren't caves under a city called Lascaux.)

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles), and say it winds across the world's oceans. That includes the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. One small caveat: the Pacific section, the East Pacific Rise, sits toward the eastern side of that ocean rather than its exact middle. This doesn't really undercut the claim, since 'mid-ocean' is the standard name for the system.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments, including temperatures above 122°F (50°C) and in water beneath the Antarctic ice sheet.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out, and 122°F does equal 50°C. A ScienceDirect overview says thermophilic bacteria grow near or above 100°C in hot springs and hydrothermal vents, well above 50°C. Nature and a peer-reviewed study on PMC describe microbial communities, including bacteria such as Methylobacter, in the water and sediments of Subglacial Lake Whillans. That lake lies under about 800 m of ice in West Antarctica. No source I found contradicts either part.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in the Maltese Islands, specifically Malta and Gozo, possibly due to genetic adaptation to the unique environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No trustworthy source I found supports the claim that cats in Malta and Gozo can't or don't meow, or that this comes from genetic adaptation. Sources on Malta's cats discuss the large stray-cat population, cat colonies and the historical 'Maltese blue' coat colour, but none mention unusual vocal behaviour. General sources on cat behaviour say that some cats are naturally quiet and that feral cats rarely meow at one another, but these points apply to cats everywhere, not to the Maltese Islands. The claim looks unfounded, but no source directly refutes it either, so it can't be verified.

text: Otters are able to drink saltwater directly because of their unique kidney-shaped glands near their eyes that filter out excess salt and minerals.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea otters can drink seawater, but the claim gives the wrong reason. Sources say they handle the salt with large, specialized kidneys that make very concentrated urine, not with salt glands near their eyes. Those glands are found in seabirds and reptiles, not otters. The claim also says 'otters' in general, but most otter species live in fresh water. Only sea otters are known to regularly drink seawater.

text: Otters are able to drink saltwater directly because of their unique kidney-shaped glands near their eyes that help to filter out excess salt from their bloodstream.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea otters do drink seawater, but the claim gets the mechanism wrong. Sources say they do it because of their relatively large, specialized kidneys, which pull fresh water out of seawater and excrete very concentrated urine. They do not have salt-filtering glands near their eyes; those salt glands are found in seabirds and marine reptiles. The claim also says 'otters' in general, but this ability is documented specifically for sea otters.

text: The VOCABULARY COACH Gmail spam filter program attained a substantial 99.9% precision in 2006.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any record of a Gmail spam filter program called "VOCABULARY COACH." Searching for the name only turned up unrelated pages about spam trigger words and bag-of-words filtering. Google's official Safety Center page does say Gmail blocks more than 99.9% of spam, phishing and malware, but that is a current blocking rate, not a 2006 precision figure, and it isn't tied to any program with this name. With nothing confirming the program exists or that it hit 99.9% precision in 2006, the claim can't be verified either way.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the season due to the different amounts of sediment and algae present.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that directly says the Great Barrier Reef's colour changes slightly by season because of differing amounts of sediment and algae. Related evidence exists. Satellite ocean-colour studies show that wet-season river plumes bring sediment and phytoplankton that change the colour of the water in the reef lagoon, though these plumes vary in size from year to year and come with floods and storms. Research also shows that the density of corals' symbiotic algae varies with the seasons, and coral colour mainly reflects those algae, which can be lost through bleaching. The claim is plausible, but no source confirms its specific wording that the reef's colour shifts slightly with the seasons because of sediment and algae.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on the planet Venus, which is the period between two consecutive solar noons, is 116.75 Earth days.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Venus's solar day (the time from one solar noon to the next) is widely given as about 116.75 Earth days, so the number is right. But I couldn't find any source that uses the term "Khayagan day" for Venus. Searching for it only brought up unrelated pages, like a Filipino cultural exhibit called "Kahayágan". Because the claim's named entity has no clear referent, it can't be verified.

text: The longest recorded flight of a chimera, a type of Dart frog, lasted 2 years and 9 months.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. A chimera (chimaera) is not a dart frog. Chimaeras are cartilaginous fish in the order Chimaeriformes, related to sharks and sometimes called ghost sharks or ratfish. Dart frogs (Dendrobatidae) can't fly at all. Some other frogs can only glide briefly. No source records a flight lasting 2 years and 9 months, and no frog or fish could do that. The only frog records found are for jumps, such as Guinness's longest frog jump of 1.21 m.

text: The planet Venus is the brightest planet in the night sky due to its thick atmosphere, which scatters sunlight and makes it visible from Earth.
label: supported
reason: Caltech IPAC's Cool Cosmos says Venus is the brightest planet in the night sky. It explains that Venus's thick clouds reflect about 70% of incoming sunlight and that Venus is the closest planet to Earth. KOLD gives the same explanation, citing the planet's high albedo, or reflectivity. So the claim's main point holds: the cloudy atmosphere reflecting sunlight is a major reason Venus is so bright. The claim leaves out Venus's closeness to Earth, but that omission doesn't make it wrong.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived species of shark, with a recorded lifespan of only around 9 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including NOAA Fisheries, Ocean Conservancy and EBSCO, say shortfin mako sharks can live more than 30 years (about 29 to 32 years). That rules out a lifespan of only around 9 years. These sources also describe the species as long-lived and slow to reproduce, so it is not the shortest-lived shark.

text: The suspended droplet phenomenon, where a drop of liquid is able to support a substantial amount of weight above it, is a real occurrence in physics and has been studied.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a recognised physics phenomenon called the "suspended droplet phenomenon" in which one drop holds up a substantial weight resting on it. In the literature, "suspended droplet" usually means a drop hanging from a fibre or needle, often in evaporation or combustion studies, as in the ScienceDirect paper below. That is not the effect the claim describes. Capillary bridges, liquid that adheres between surfaces, can produce real adhesive forces, and the search turned up work on heavy drops floating on a lighter liquid. But nothing I found clearly confirms or refutes the claim as worded. My search was also cut short when the tool's usage limit was reached, so the evidence is limited.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, which accounts for around 3% of the total biomass on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count is wrong. A widely reported 2015 study in Nature (Crowther et al.) estimates about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, roughly 15 times more than the claimed 200 billion. Even the older estimate that study replaced was just over 400 billion. The '3% of total biomass' figure is also doubtful, since plants, which are mostly trees, make up most of Earth's biomass. But I didn't check that part directly; the wrong tree count is enough to contradict the claim.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, which accounts for around 3% of the total global biomass.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2015 study in Nature led by Thomas Crowther estimated that Earth has about 3.04 trillion trees. That is roughly 15 times the 200 billion in the claim, and even the older estimate of about 400 billion was double it. Trees also make up far more than 3% of global biomass, since plants account for about 80% of it. The claim's tree count is clearly wrong.

text: There are approximately 200 bones in the adult human body, although this number decreases to around 80 bones in the human fetus at birth due to bone fusion.
label: contradicted
reason: The adult count is roughly right: adults have 206 bones, which is about 200. The newborn part is wrong. Babies are born with about 270–300 bones, not about 80. Many of these bones fuse as the child grows, which is why the total drops to 206 in adulthood. The claim reverses this, saying fusion leaves a newborn with fewer bones than an adult.

text: There are over 300 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 22-25% of the total number of all living plants.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate (Crowther et al., Nature 2015) puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. The claim's figure of 'over 300 billion' is technically true, but it is ten times too low and gives a misleading scale. No credible source supports the idea that trees make up 22-25% of all living plants. That percentage appears to be made up, since counts of individual plants of all kinds are not measured in a way that would allow such a ratio.

text: The笑 Napoli  garden under Argentine have the biggest collection of orchids in the world with over 12,000 different species.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't identify the garden the claim describes. "笑 Napoli garden under Argentine" looks garbled and doesn't match any known garden, so there is nothing to check the claim against. The search results do give a different answer to the general question: several sources, including Wikipedia and travel guides, say Singapore's National Orchid Garden has the world's largest orchid collection or display. None of the results mention an Argentine or Napoli garden, or a collection of more than 12,000 orchid species. Because the claim doesn't point to an identifiable garden, the result is inconclusive.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge system, which spans over 65,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. NOAA's Ocean Service names the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth and gives its length as 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km. NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI, Wikipedia and WorldAtlas agree on both points. One small catch: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km' rather than 'over.' That gap is minor, and the main points (longest range, about 65,000 km) are well supported.

text: Buttery, a popular Japanese snack, is derived from the fermentation of rice and potassium bitartrate (cream of tartar).
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't identify any well-known Japanese snack called "Buttery". Searches only turned up butter-flavoured products such as Akita butter mochi, Beika butter rice crackers, Butter Butler and Sugar Butter Tree. None of them is described as made by fermenting rice with potassium bitartrate (cream of tartar). Because the claim doesn't point to a clear product, I can't confirm or rule it out. The idea is also doubtful on its face: cream of tartar is a by-product of winemaking, not something you ferment rice with.

text: Buttery, a popular Japanese sweet made from simmered red bean paste, has been a traditional dessert in the country for over 800 years.
label: contradicted
reason: No Japanese sweet called "Buttery" turns up in the search results. Japan's simmered sweet red bean paste is called anko, which is used in many traditional sweets. A buttery, also called a rowie or Aberdeen roll, is a savoury bread roll from Aberdeen, Scotland. It is not a Japanese red bean dessert, so the claim misidentifies the food. The 800-year history was never verified, but the claim fails on what the food is.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various marine animals and supporting the ocean's coral reefs.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that coconuts help coral reefs and shelter marine animals goes against published research. A Science Advances study found that non-native coconut palms take over native seabird nesting habitat and disrupt the nutrients seabirds carry to coral reefs. Coverage of Palmyra Atoll in Science and NPR reports that coconut-dominated forests are nutrient-poor and cut seabird guano inputs, which reduces food for manta rays and the reef food web. Conservationists there are removing the palms to protect the reefs. Coconuts are a tree fruit, but no evidence was found that they support reefs, and the evidence that was found points the other way.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various wildlife species.
label: supported
reason: The coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm, so calling it a tree fruit is fair. A University of Hawaiʻi page on Palmyra Atoll says piles of coconuts give young coconut crabs both food and protection. A science-education article adds that coconut crabs eat coconuts and that young crabs may use coconut shells for shelter. These sources only cover crabs, so the support for 'various wildlife species' comes from that one group. Still, nothing found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: CÃ NSFIS, the largest planet in our solar system, has a mass of approximately 700 Earth masses.
label: contradicted
reason: No planet called "CÃ NSFIS" exists. The largest planet in our solar system is Jupiter, and reliable sources put its mass at about 317–318 Earth masses (about 1.9 × 10^27 kg), not about 700. Both the name and the mass in the claim are wrong.

text: Did you know that a giant squill plant, which blooms every 12 years, can be visible from space due to its unique shape and color.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source saying a giant squill can be seen from space. The plant's real size makes that implausible: Drimia maritima (giant sea squill) is a football-sized bulb with flower stalks about 4–6 feet tall. Gardening and botanical sources (Kew, NC State, Wikipedia, nursery guides) describe it as a mature bulb that flowers every year in late summer or autumn. One video does say a bulb takes 10–12 years to grow, but that is about how long it takes to mature, not a bloom that happens only every 12 years. So the 12-year bloom cycle is contradicted, and the visible-from-space part has no support.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known restaurant, Kyoto's Kikunoi, which has been serving traditional Japanese cuisine since 1368.
label: contradicted
reason: The MICHELIN Guide says Kikunoi Honten in Kyoto opened as a restaurant in 1912, not in 1368. It is not known as the world's oldest restaurant. Kyoto has older eateries, such as Ichiwa and Honke Owariya, and Guinness gives the title of world's oldest restaurant to Sobrino de Botín in Madrid. The dates and the 'oldest' claim are both wrong.

text: Otters are able to drink saltwater because they have a special gland located above their eyes that helps to filter out excess salt.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea otters can drink seawater, but not because of a special gland above their eyes. Sources say they do it with large, specialized kidneys that get rid of extra salt by making very concentrated urine. Salt glands above the eyes (supraorbital glands) are found in marine birds such as penguins, not in otters or other mammals.

text: The cheesiest pizza is made from Mozzarella and contains about 300 calories per slice with an 8-inch diameter pizza having a total of 11 slices.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources say an 8-inch pizza is usually cut into about 4 slices, and some cut it into as few as 3. None mention 11 slices. If an 8-inch pizza had 11 slices of about 300 calories each, it would total roughly 3,300 calories, which doesn't make sense. Mozzarella being the typical pizza cheese and 200–300 calories per cheese slice are roughly in line with the sources, but the slice count is clearly wrong. 'The cheesiest pizza' also doesn't point to any specific pizza.

text: The cheesiest pizza is made from Mozzarella and contains about 300 calories per slice with an 8-inch diameter pizza having a total of 16 slices.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Pizza size guides say an 8-inch pizza is normally cut into about 4 to 6 slices (and sometimes only 3), not 16. The numbers also don't fit together: 16 slices at about 300 calories each would add up to roughly 4,800 calories for one small pizza. Sources give about 250–350 calories for a slice of a normal-sized pizza, and an 8-inch cheese pizza from one brand is listed at 390 calories for 3 slices, or about 130 per slice. No source supports 16 slices of 300 calories each, and 'the cheesiest pizza' doesn't refer to any specific pizza.

text: The driest desert in the world is the Atacama Desert in Chile, accounting for only 0.01% of the world's freshwater supply.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources such as Discovery back the first part: the Atacama in Chile is widely called the world's driest (non-polar) desert. However, I found nothing showing that the Atacama accounts for 0.01% of the world's freshwater supply. That figure is unverified and may well be made up, so the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings up to 80 times per second.
label: supported
reason: Many sources, including WorldAtlas, CGTN, Animal Planet, Birdspot and TriviaCafe, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to the hummingbird's special wing structure: a ball-and-socket shoulder joint that lets the wing rotate about 180 degrees. They also give a wingbeat rate of up to about 80 times per second. Two caveats: some sources say a few other birds can briefly move backwards, but only hummingbirds can sustain controlled backward flight. And the claim says the wings 'rotate' 80 times per second, which is loose wording for 80 wingbeats per second. Overall, the claim matches the mainstream sources.

text: The periodic table's element with the highest number of known isotopes is the element tin, with a total of 10 different isotopes discovered so far.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim confuses stable isotopes with all known isotopes. Tin has 10 stable isotopes, which is the most of any element. But it has many more known isotopes in total. Chemicool says tin has 35 isotopes with known half-lives, and a 2010 isotope-discovery paper on arXiv reports that 38 tin isotopes (mass numbers 100–137) had been discovered by then. So saying tin has only 10 known isotopes in total is wrong.

text: The reacted compound calamine is used to treat skin conditions such as acne, impetigo, and chickenpox.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources such as Cleveland Clinic and AdventHealth say calamine lotion (zinc oxide plus ferric oxide) relieves chickenpox itching. They also say it may help dry out pimples, but Cleveland Clinic states it "won't treat your acne." I found no authoritative source saying calamine treats impetigo. Medical sources say impetigo is treated with antibiotics. Only a pharmacy product listing and a Q&A forum link calamine to impetigo, and they mention it only for soothing itch. The phrase "reacted compound" is also inaccurate or unclear, because calamine is a mixture, not a compound formed by a reaction. Chickenpox is supported, but acne is only weakly supported and impetigo is not verified, so the full claim cannot be confirmed.

text: There are approximately 1.3 billion unique species of organisms on Earth, according to estimates from the Global Biodiversity Assessment.
label: contradicted
reason: The Global Biodiversity Assessment did not estimate 1.3 billion species. Its species-number chapter (Hawksworth & Kalin-Arroyo, 1995) gave a working estimate of about 13.6 million species in total, with about 1.75 million species described at the time. The 1.3 billion figure is roughly 100 times too high, and it seems to confuse 13 million with 1.3 billion.

text: 富ší Dunn's canyon is actually the Grand Canyon, but with more forested depth than its more famous counterpart.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify this claim because it's garbled. "富ší Dunn's canyon" doesn't point to any clear place or person. Searching for a "Dunn's canyon" tied to the Grand Canyon only turned up Dunn Butte, a landform inside the Grand Canyon, plus general pages about Grand Canyon ecology. Nothing names a "Dunn's canyon" or compares one to the Grand Canyon as having "more forested depth." Also, saying the canyon "is actually the Grand Canyon" while also calling the Grand Canyon "its more famous counterpart" contradicts itself.

text: 富ší Dunn's canyon is the deepest canyon in North America.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't tell what "富ší Dunn's canyon" refers to. The name looks garbled and doesn't point to any known canyon. Reliable sources (National Geographic, PNAS, Wikipedia) say Hells Canyon on the Idaho–Oregon border is North America's deepest canyon, but nothing ties it to the name "Dunn." With no clear referent, I can't confirm or rule out the claim.

text: The length of a human's nose can change by up to 50% in size based on their body temperature due to the combination of collagen and fatty tissues in the nose.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no credible source saying a person's nose length changes with body temperature, let alone by up to 50%. The sources I found describe the nose's shape as coming from a rigid framework of nasal bones and cartilage. Penn State and PLOS Genetics research says nose shape is inherited and evolved over generations in response to climate, and doesn't shift with a person's own body temperature. The only '50%' figures in the search results were about collagen being heated in medical procedures, which has nothing to do with normal nose size. No source states outright that the claim is false, but the evidence conflicts with both the mechanism it gives and its premise that nose size changes this much.

text: A flock of starlings is known for its unique ability to create the illusion of a single reflective surface, often referred to as a "starling murmuration," when hundreds of birds fly together in a synchronized and organized manner.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but its central description does not. Reliable sources (Woodland Trust, Nat Geo Kids, Birdspot) confirm that a large flock of starlings flying in synchronised, swirling patterns is called a murmuration. They describe it as a shape-shifting cloud, often of thousands or even millions of birds; one source puts it at 500 or more. None of them describes a murmuration as creating 'the illusion of a single reflective surface,' and no source says it doesn't. The usual description is a fluid cloud or a single moving shape. Because that key part can't be verified, and the 'hundreds' figure is lower than most sources give, the claim can't be fully supported.

text: A giant pitcher plant in Borneo holds the Guinness World Record for being the largest known pitcher plant in the world, with its leaf measuring over 39 inches in diameter and having a volume of 8.9 liters.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records lists the giant montane pitcher plant, Nepenthes rajah, from Borneo as the record holder. Its record pitcher was 41 cm (about 16 inches) tall, and its largest pitcher volume is about 3.5 litres of water. That is far below the claim's 'over 39 inches' and 8.9 litres. No reliable source supports those figures.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, according to the estimates of the most recent taxonomic research.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from the 2011 Mora et al. study. That number is an estimate of all eukaryotic species, give or take about 1.3 million. It is not a count of plants and animals only, and the study does not say there are "over" 8.7 million. By the study's breakdown, animals make up about 7.77 million species and plants about 298,000, which is roughly 8.07 million combined. The rest of the 8.7 million is fungi (about 611,000), protozoa, chromists and others. The study also dates from 2011, so calling it "the most recent taxonomic research" is questionable. Later estimates differ, for example ones that include microbes.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "Strengths."
label: contradicted
reason: A fact-check from Logically Facts says "strengths" is not the single longest one-syllable English word. It is one of several nine-letter words with one syllable, along with "screeched," "scratched," "stretched," "straights" and "schlepped." There are also longer one-syllable words, such as the ten-letter "scraunched" and "strengthed," although these are archaic. Some popular sources do name "strengths" as the longest, but calling it the one longest word is inaccurate.

text: The sense of smell is closely linked to memory, and research has shown that a single scent can instantly transport people back to a vivid memory from their past.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed review in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (Springer) discusses the 'Proust phenomenon', in which odors cue autobiographical memories. Its meta-analysis found that memories evoked by odors were more vivid than memories evoked by other cues. This backs both the close link between smell and memory and the idea that a scent can bring back a vivid past memory. The review does note that some aspects are debated, such as whether odors are the 'most effective' memory cues, but that doesn't undercut the general claim.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it was built with redundancy and distributed nodes.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet", written by the Internet's own pioneers, calls the nuclear-war link a "false rumor". It says the idea that ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war "was never true of the ARPANET". Only a separate RAND study on secure voice communications dealt with nuclear war. ARPANET was mainly designed so computers could share resources. Its distributed packet-switching design was not created to withstand a nuclear attack.

text: But in Morocco, there's a unique festival where men run over flaming peppers to prove their bravery.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence of any Moroccan festival where men run over flaming peppers to prove their bravery. Searches turned up other Moroccan traditions instead, such as Achoura bonfire celebrations (Chaâla), the Boujloud goat-skin festival and Sufi pilgrimages. Fire-walking festivals also turned up elsewhere, in Singapore (Theemithi) and Greece (Anastenaria). None of these involves flaming peppers. No reliable source directly confirms or denies the claim, so it can't be verified and looks likely to be made up.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, is one of the deepest gorges in the world, at approximately 122 meters deep.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, with no population as of the 2016 census. It is also the site of Clark Dam, which is 67 m high, and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. None of these sources calls it one of the world's deepest gorges or gives a depth of 122 m. The ranking is clearly wrong: the world's deepest gorges are measured in thousands of metres. The Yarlung Tsangpo and Kali Gandaki gorges are about 5,000–6,000 m deep, and Greece's Vikos Gorge is about 900 m deep. A gorge about 122 m deep could not be one of the deepest in the world. The 122 m figure itself is not confirmed by any source.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, are natural swimmers and have even been known to swim across entire rivers in South America.
label: supported
reason: The claim is supported. Reliable sources, including National Geographic and World Land Trust, describe the capybara as the world's largest rodent and a strong, excellent swimmer. They note its semi-aquatic adaptations, such as partially webbed feet, and that it lives along rivers in South America. Other sources say capybaras can swim long distances, and stock photos show a capybara swimming across a river in Brazil's Pantanal. The 'entire rivers' part rests on weaker evidence than the rest, but no source contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The color blue is seen by all humans, but the way we perceive its different shades can vary from person to person, a phenomenon known as tetrachromacy.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia defines tetrachromacy as having four independent colour channels, or four types of cone cells in the eye. It does not mean ordinary person-to-person differences in how shades of blue are seen. Most humans have only three cone types, so they are trichromats. The claim that all humans see blue is also wrong: people who are blind, or who have tritanopia (blue-yellow colour blindness), cannot see blue normally.

text: The highest waterfall in the world is Angkatanga waterfall, which is located in Zambia/Zaire border.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. The world's highest waterfall is Angel Falls (Salto Ángel, also called Kerepakupai Vená) in Canaima National Park, Venezuela. It is not a falls called "Angkatanga" on the Zambia/Zaire border, and no waterfall by that name appears to exist. (The well-known tall falls on the Zambia/DR Congo–Tanzania border region is Kalambo Falls, which is far shorter than Angel Falls.)

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird due to its unique physiology and ability to flap its wings rapidly in any direction.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources, including UC Davis's hummingbird facts page, WorldAtlas, Sciencing and Birdspot, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can truly fly backwards. They credit this to the birds' unusual shoulder joints and wing muscles, which let them rotate their wings in a figure-8 pattern and move in all directions while flapping very fast. Some sources add that herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can drift backwards briefly by fluttering, but only hummingbirds can keep flying backwards under their own power. That matches the claim's general meaning.

text: The short-lived Mayan Period known as the Classical Period lasted approximately from 200-900 AD.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources give the Maya Classic period as about 250–900 CE. Lumen Learning, OER Commons and mayan.org all say this, and Wikipedia's article on the Mesoamerican Classic period dates it from around 200 to 900 AD. That matches the claim's 'approximately 200-900 AD'. One caveat: calling the period 'short-lived' is a subjective and debatable description. It covered about 650 years and was the high point of Maya civilization. No source directly addresses that wording, so the verdict rests on the dates, which are well supported.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland has no parasites that can withstand high salt levels found in its sea water for one reason.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim. My search turned up studies of Ixodes ricinus ticks in Iceland, covering surveillance and Borrelia detection, plus a mention of Surtsey's fauna. None of them mention parasites of ticks on an island off Iceland that can withstand the salt levels of sea water, or give any reason for such parasites being absent. The claim is also vague: it doesn't name the island or the 'one reason', so it can't be checked against a specific source.

text: The baku is a type of fox found in East Asia, which is known for its unique ability to change the color of its fur from brown to black, as well as its white throat patches, which turn white in the winter months to help with camouflage.
label: contradicted
reason: The baku is not a fox. In Chinese and Japanese folklore it is a mythical 'dream eater' that devours nightmares. It is usually described as a chimera with an elephant's head, a bear's body and a tiger's feet. The word is also the Japanese and Malay name for the tapir. No source describes it as a real fox that changes fur color or has white throat patches.

text: The glowworms in Waitomo, New Zealand, are actually a species of insect that produces a blue-green bioluminescent light through a chemical reaction in their bodies.
label: supported
reason: The Waitomo glowworm is Arachnocampa luminosa, a species of fungus gnat, which makes it an insect. A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports (on PMC) says it is known for blue-green bioluminescence, made by a luciferase–luciferin chemical reaction in a light organ in the larva's body. Wikipedia also confirms the blue-green light (peak around 487 nm) and the Waitomo caves habitat. Every part of the claim checks out.

text:
فيها شخص صيني Backpacker، يسمى Ma Jian, الذي يمشي ما يقرب من 24100 ميل حول العالم للأول مرة کاميرا».

text: Tornadoes are the most destructive type of storm on Earth, responsible for killing over 1,000 people and destroying thousands of homes in the United States every year.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA's Science Council says US tornadoes kill about 74 people a year on average and caused 1,775 deaths over the whole 24-year span from 1995 to 2018. In 2024 they killed 54 people. Other NOAA figures put the average at about 80 deaths a year. These numbers fall far short of the claimed 1,000-plus deaths every year. NOAA also ranks tornadoes third among weather-related killers in the US, behind extreme heat and floods, which works against calling them the most destructive type of storm.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers, passing through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as Earth's longest mountain range. Wikipedia and a Cambridge text give its length as about 65,000 km. Wikipedia also places its segments in the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Southwest and Southeast Indian Ridges) and Pacific (East Pacific Rise) Oceans. One wording issue: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over", though other sources, such as Amusing Planet, say "more than 65,000 km". This is a small difference in a commonly cited approximate figure, so the claim is essentially supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, with a total length of over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles), and it runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the main points of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range, at roughly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). Wikipedia also says the ridge system is part of every ocean, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. Two details are slightly loose. First, NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over', though other sources say 'more than 65,000 km'. Second, the ridge runs through the middle of the Atlantic, but in the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise) it sits off-center. These are minor differences, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: The Andrade effect is the phenomenon where certain polymers become more ductile at lower temperatures, showing a unique property not typically seen in most materials.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the Andrade effect wrong. In materials science, the Andrade effect (Andrade creep) is the transient creep that E.N. da C. Andrade reported in 1910: a material under constant stress keeps deforming slowly, with strain growing roughly as t^(1/3). It describes time-dependent creep, mainly in metals and crystalline solids. It does not mean that polymers become more ductile at lower temperatures, and no source found describes it that way.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.10 x 10^8 Earths combined.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the Sun's surface area as 6.09×10^12 km², which is about 12,000 times Earth's surface area. It is not 5.10×10^8 times. The figure 5.10×10^8 is Earth's own surface area in km², so the claim confuses that number with the ratio.

text: The Departed, a crime drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Matt Damon, holds the record for most Academy Awards won by a film with a runtime under three hours, winning four Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards.
label: contradicted
reason: It's true that The Departed won four Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards: Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay and Film Editing. The record claim is false, though. Plenty of films shorter than three hours have won more Oscars. West Side Story (1961) runs about 2h33m and won 10, and Gigi, The Last Emperor, Amadeus and Slumdog Millionaire, all under three hours, won 8 or 9 each. So four Oscars is nowhere near a record for films under three hours.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the main points of the claim. NOAA and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI put its length at "nearly 65,000 km," NOAA Ocean Service gives 40,389 miles (about 65,000 km), and NOAA's education page says "over 40,000 miles" (about 64,000 km or more). So "over 65,000 km" is close but slightly overstated compared with the "nearly 65,000 km" figure. The ridge does cross the Atlantic (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian and Arctic Oceans. The claim leaves out the Pacific, where the ridge also runs (the East Pacific Rise), but leaving it out doesn't make the statement false. Overall, the claim matches reliable sources apart from small differences in wording.

text: The highest recorded population density in the world is in Monaco, with an average of over 26,000 people per square kilometer.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Monaco has the highest recorded population density in the world, but Monaco does not hold that record. Cities such as Manila are documented at well over 40,000 people per km², which is far above 26,000. Even among countries and territories, current World Bank-based rankings put Macao first, at about 20,600–23,200 people per km², and Monaco second, at about 16,000–18,500 per km². So the 'over 26,000' figure for Monaco is also not supported by recent data. Some sources (UN WPP 2024 via StatisticsTimes, and older World Bank data) do give Monaco about 25,500–26,150 per km² and call it the densest country. Even so, that makes it the densest country, not the highest density recorded anywhere in the world.

text: There is an insect species known as the "Shield Bug" that can produce a loud hissing sound when threatened by forcing air through a tube on its abdomen.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that shield bugs hiss loudly by pushing air through a tube on the abdomen. Shield bugs (family Pentatomidae, also called stink bugs) are known for defending themselves with a foul-smelling chemical from scent glands on the underside of the thorax. The only 'Shield Bug' search result that mentions hissing describes a fictional enemy from the video game Alien Swarm. Forcing air out to make a hissing sound is what hissing cockroaches do (through their breathing holes), not shield bugs. I found no source stating outright that shield bugs cannot hiss, so this rests on how well documented their defense is, not on a direct denial.

text: The tips of shark teeth are unique and can be used to identify the species, with no two sharks having the exact same dental pattern, even between twins.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. The California Academy of Sciences says shark teeth are so distinctive that a single tooth can identify a species, and that each species has its own tooth shape. I found nothing reliable for the rest: that every individual shark's dental pattern is unique, even between twins, or that the tips specifically are what matter. Sources describe individual sharks as unique by their fin patterns, not their teeth. Nothing directly contradicts the twins part, but nothing supports it either, so the claim can't be fully verified.

text: A piece of silk production waste called a "lotus silk petal" is made from the cocoons of the Himalayan moon moth, and is typically worth more than its weight in gold.
label: contradicted
reason: Lotus silk is made from fibres pulled out of lotus plant stems (Nelumbo nucifera), not from moth cocoons. Wikipedia and textile sources say this, and the tradition is linked to Myanmar and Manipur. I found no evidence that a silk-waste product called a "lotus silk petal" exists, or that anything like it comes from Himalayan moon moth cocoons. The claim that it is worth more than its weight in gold is also unsupported.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, similar to fingerprints, which can be used to identify individuals.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed forensic and biometric studies, such as a Manipal Academy of Higher Education preliminary study, describe the tongue print as a new biometric identifier that is unique and hard to copy. The study found that no two tongues have the same shape and texture, and it suggests tongue prints could be used to identify people in forensic dentistry, much like fingerprints. One caveat is that the research is still early and tongue prints are not yet widely used for identification, but that doesn't contradict the claim.

text: The Andrade effect is the phenomenon where certain salts can become spontaneously superconducting at low temperatures.
label: contradicted
reason: The Andrade effect, also called Andrade creep, describes how metals deform slowly over time under steady stress. Andrade (1910) found that metal wires under constant stress stretch in proportion to t^(1/3). The search results describe it only as a viscoelastic creep phenomenon in metals and ice. None of them link it to salts or to spontaneous superconductivity at low temperatures, so the claim gets the term wrong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Hidden Hot Springs," is a mysterious river in the Amazon rainforest that appears to boil and steam despite being surrounded by the lush, tropical environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, National Geographic and ScienceAlert, confirm that the Boiling River of the Amazon is a real river in the Peruvian rainforest. It is heated by geothermal activity, can reach about 93°C, and is often called mysterious. However, no source I found calls it the "Hidden Hot Springs." Its documented name is Shanay-timpishka, a Quechua name meaning roughly "boiled by the heat of the sun." Some articles say the river is "hidden away" in the jungle, but that describes its location rather than giving it a name. Because the alias can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive, even though its description of the river is accurate.

text: The이버thing, a periodic table element with the atomic number 118, is named after the German scientist Dmitry Mendeleyev's worker, as well as chemist Dmitri Mendeleev.
label: contradicted
reason: Element 118 is oganesson (Og). It is named only after Yuri Oganessian, a Russian-Armenian nuclear physicist born in 1933. It is not named after any "worker" of Mendeleev or after Dmitri Mendeleev himself. Mendeleev, who was Russian rather than German, is honoured by mendelevium, element 101.

text: Thekinetic energy generated by a speeding bullet can cause it to continue traveling at high speeds even after it has been severed from its gun and fired into the air.
label: supported
reason: The claim, though oddly worded, describes basic ballistics: once a bullet leaves the barrel, its momentum and kinetic energy keep it moving at high speed. Wikipedia's article on celebratory gunfire says a falling bullet's speed depends on the firing angle, and that bullets fired at non-vertical angles follow a ballistic path and keep much of their speed. A PubMed study measured bullets fired into the air that were still dangerous when they came down. 9×19 mm bullets struck at about 92 m/s with about 34 J of energy, which is enough to penetrate skin and cause serious wounds. This confirms that the energy a bullet gets from firing keeps it travelling fast after it leaves the gun, even when shot into the air.

text: Butler's Gorge Bridge, in Tasmania, Australia, holds the record for the longest single-span concrete arch bridge in the world at 72.4 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: The record is held by China's Tian'e Longtan Bridge, whose main span is 600 m. Earlier record holders were Krk Bridge (390 m) and Gladesville Bridge (305 m), so a 72.4 m span is nowhere near the world record. Searches also found no record of a "Butler's Gorge Bridge." Butlers Gorge in Tasmania is mainly known for the Clark Dam, which is a concrete arch dam, not a bridge.

text: فيها شخص صيني Backpacker، يسمى ماو تسي تونغ، لديه سلسلة من المستشارين السياسيين في بانجتشو، من بينهم على الأخص يان بوي،وووجي معظمهم لاحقا بأسلوب اللمس الذهبي.

It starts with "فيها" ("in it") without saying what "it" is, and "Backpacker," "Bangzhou," "Yan Bui," "Wuji" and "golden touch style" don't match any identifiable people, places or concepts. My search found real advisers and secretaries of Mao Zedong, such as Chen Boda and Tian Jiaying, but nothing connecting Mao to advisers in "Bangzhou" named Yan Bui or Wuji, or to a "golden touch" style. text: The Vienna Opera House in Austria is home to over 850,000 items, including costumes, props, and set designs, in its vast collection.
label: not_verifiable

The costume archive of Art for Art, the opera's official costume and production service, holds over 250,000 costumes made for the federal theatres: the State Opera, the Volksoper and the Burgtheater. The separate Theatermuseum holds about 1.6 to 2 million objects. Neither figure confirms the claim, and neither directly disproves an 850,000 count of costumes, props and set designs together. The claim therefore cannot be verified.

text: The glowworms in Waitomo, New Zealand, are actually a species of insect called Arachnocampa luminosa and create a breathtaking starry night sky effect in the limestone caves.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the Waitomo glowworms are Arachnocampa luminosa. This is an insect: a fungus gnat found only in New Zealand, and it is the larvae that glow. Sources also describe their glow in the Waitomo limestone caves as looking like a starry night sky or a natural planetarium. Bustle calls A. luminosa a gnat species, and Wikipedia identifies it as the New Zealand glowworm, an arthropod insect.

text: The highest recorded number of screws used in a single building project is approximately 45 million in the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest skyscraper.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The only search that returned results was a Simple English Wikipedia page, which confirms that the Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest building but says nothing about screws. Before I could look further, the search tool hit its usage limit. I'm not aware of any trustworthy source, such as Guinness World Records or Emaar, that tracks a record for the most screws used in a building or gives a figure of about 45 million for the Burj Khalifa. Without evidence for the record or the number, the claim stays unconfirmed.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural wonder where river streams appear to boil, despite being over a mile away from the nearest waterfall or any visible source of water, making it a subject of ongoing scientific investigation and discovery.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon (Shanay-Timpishka) is a real geothermal river in Peru that is still being studied, so parts of the claim are accurate. But the claim gets the river's famous feature wrong. Sources say the river is unusual because it lies about 700 km from the nearest volcanic center, not because it is 'over a mile away from the nearest waterfall or any visible source of water.' That wording makes little sense: the river is itself flowing water, and it is fed by hot springs. Because the claim's central detail misstates the real fact, it is contradicted.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as "Seamounts," which are underwater mountain ranges found on the seafloor.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA describes seamounts as underwater mountains with steep sides that rise from the seafloor. They are usually remnants of extinct volcanoes, and many support high biodiversity. They are fixed geological features, not floating, and reliable sources do not call them "Floating Islands" or describe them as bioluminescent. A seamount is also an individual mountain rather than a mountain range. The claim's main identification of seamounts as "Floating Islands" therefore misrepresents them.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate from the Human Genome Organization.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure doesn't come from a 2020 Human Genome Organization estimate. It comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology study by Camilo Mora and colleagues at Dalhousie University and the University of Hawaii, announced by Census of Marine Life scientists. That study estimated about 8.7 million species (give or take 1.3 million), not 'over 8.7 million.' So the year, the source and the 'over' wording in the claim are all wrong.

text: There are approximately 1 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, according to a 2020 scientific estimate by the Integrative Taxonomic Information System.
label: contradicted
reason: The widely cited scientific estimate is about 8.7 million species on Earth (±1.3 million), from Mora et al. in PLoS Biology in 2011. That is far more than 1 million. About 1.2–2 million species have been formally described so far. ITIS is a taxonomic database, not the source of a 2020 estimate of the total number of species. The '1 million' figure most likely comes from IPBES's 2019 finding that about 1 million species are threatened with extinction, not from a count of all species.

text: Caterpillars have unique hairs on their bodies that contain a toxin to defend against predators, and some species can release a foul-tasting liquid that deters predators when threatened.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back both parts of the claim. Extension and entomology pages say some caterpillars, such as io moth and hickory tussock moth larvae, have urticating hairs or bristles that release or inject venom or toxins to defend against predators. Live Science reports that silkmoth caterpillars regurgitate a foul brown fluid to deter predators. Hawk moth sources describe species that bring up a noxious, foul-tasting fluid when attacked. The claim's wording about hairs could be read as covering all caterpillars, which overgeneralizes, but read as applying to some caterpillars it is supported.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly with reflected sunlight, making it difficult to spot in the sky even though it is the third planet from the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, not the third, so that part of the claim is wrong. The claim also gets visibility backwards: reflected sunlight makes Venus the brightest planet and one of the easiest to see without equipment, often second only to the Moon in the night sky. It is not often invisible.

text: The vibrant flower, the infamous Opal Flower or the more popular known yuka flower,  is a rare snapdragons cultivar (yuka 'Snap Dragon' - or 'Antirrhinum')  is currently extremely rare and supply - fewer than 1 company can create, Antirrhinum
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. Wikipedia and the RHS use "opal flower" for Lachenalia species, such as Lachenalia aloides and the golden opal flower, L. flava. These bulbs belong to the family Asparagaceae and are not snapdragon (Antirrhinum) cultivars. I found no evidence of a snapdragon cultivar called 'yuka' or 'Opal Flower', or of one that is extremely rare or produced by only one company. Extension and botanical garden sources describe snapdragons (Antirrhinum majus) as common garden plants that come in many cultivars. The claim also contradicts itself: "fewer than 1 company" would mean no company produces it at all.

text: Cats have a unique way of hearing called "vocal lip reading" or "infra-sound detection," where they use their whiskers to detect and pinpoint sound waves in their environment, allowing them to locate their prey or potential threats.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for anything called "vocal lip reading" or "infra-sound detection" in cats. Trustworthy sources say cats locate sounds with their ears, which swivel toward the source and are moved by many muscles. Whiskers (vibrissae) are touch sensors. They pick up air currents, tiny movements, vibrations and nearby objects, which helps cats find their way and hunt, but they are not used to hear or to pinpoint sound waves. These sources contradict the claim's main idea that cats hear through their whiskers.

text: There are more neurons in an octopus's brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, which is approximately 200-400 billion.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. Reliable sources, including Scientific American and the Natural History Museum, say a common octopus has about 500 million neurons in its whole body. Only about a third of those are in the central brain, and the rest are in the arms. That is hundreds of times fewer than the 100–400 billion stars usually estimated for the Milky Way, so an octopus's brain does not have more neurons than the galaxy has stars.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km. NOAA Ocean Exploration says "nearly" 65,000 km, so the claim's "over 65,000 km" slightly overstates that figure, though NOAA.gov's education page gives "over 40,000 miles." WorldAtlas says the ridge runs through the center of all the major oceans, which covers the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. One caveat: the Pacific section (the East Pacific Rise) lies toward the eastern Pacific rather than the true center. Neither point contradicts the main claim.

text: The driest desert in the world, located in Antarctica, the Antarctic Desert, covers an area of about 14 million square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Antarctic Desert as about 14.2 million km² (5.5 million sq mi), and also call it the driest region, place or continent on Earth. These include Study.com, WorldAtlas, EBSCO and Poseidon Expeditions. That backs up both the 'about 14 million square kilometers' figure and the 'driest desert' description. One caveat: the Atacama is often called the driest non-polar desert, but that doesn't conflict with the claim about Antarctica.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, as estimated by biologists, although only a small fraction, around 1.3 million, have been formally described and named.
label: supported
reason: Biologists estimated that Earth has about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million (Mora et al., 2011). That study also found that roughly 1.25 million species had been described, which matches the claim's 'around 1.3 million' and 'a small fraction.' Two details are slightly loose: the figure is a central estimate of about 8.7 million, not strictly 'over' 8.7 million, and the 1.3 million in the study is the margin of error rather than the described count. Even so, the substance of the claim is supported.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 86 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 86 billion neurons is correct, but the comparison is wrong. Nature Scitable puts the Milky Way at roughly 200–400 billion stars, and the Bell Museum (University of Minnesota) puts it at about 100 billion. Either way, the galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons. It is the brain's synaptic connections (around 100 trillion) that outnumber the stars, not its neurons.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and stretches across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including WHOI, Guinness World Records and WorldAtlas, say the mid-ocean ridge system is the world's longest mountain range. They give its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) and say it winds through every major ocean basin around the globe. Most of these sources say "about" or "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over". That small difference in wording does not change the substance of the claim.

text: The Human Brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources (Nature Scitable, Harvard Medical School, Northwestern Medicine) say the human brain has about 86 billion neurons. Goriely's paper on NCBI argues the exact count is uncertain, but it still treats 86 billion as the widely accepted figure. That fits the claim's wording of "approximately."

text: There are over 37 million acres of protected areas in Antarctica, which includes National Parks, Wildlife Refugees, and other protected areas to safeguard the unique biodiversity of the continent.
label: contradicted
reason: Antarctica has no National Parks or Wildlife Refuges. Its protected areas are set up under the Antarctic Treaty and its Environmental Protocol as Antarctic Specially Protected Areas (ASPAs), Antarctic Specially Managed Areas (ASMAs) and Historic Sites and Monuments. Reliable sources (the Polish Arctowski station and a SCAR/ATCM report) give the total area of all ASPAs as about 3,270–3,680 km² (roughly 0.9 million acres). They put ASMAs at about 30,000 km² (roughly 7.4 million acres). Together that is far below 37 million acres (about 150,000 km²). Both the size figure and the types of protected area in the claim are wrong.

text: The length of a cricket season, which varies by location, can be divided into two parts: an initial period called the off-season or Transitional period, and another lengthy term that is commonly the cricketing period from April to September.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some parts of the claim check out. Wikipedia says cricket seasons differ by country and are timed to each country's driest months. A cricket calendar site says the English season runs from April to September and is followed by about six months of off-season. However, I found no source that splits the cricket season into just two parts, with an opening part called the 'off-season' or 'Transitional period'. Training-periodisation sources describe more phases (off-season, pre-season, in-season and a transition/active-rest phase), and they treat the transition phase as recovery after the season, not its opening part. April to September also applies to England, not to cricket in general. text: Located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, Iceland is home to the world's largest and oldest known ash tree, the Miðsen Reykjavík tree branch.

Iceland's age and size records list species such as European rowan and Sitka spruce, not a record-breaking ash. The world's largest and oldest trees are found elsewhere, such as Jōmon Sugi in Japan. text: There are approximately 170 million species of organisms that exist in the world, but it's estimated that we have only discovered and documented around 2 million of them.

Costello et al. estimated 5 ± 3 million, and Wikipedia says most estimates are around 11 million or fewer. A few outlier estimates run from 2 million to 1 trillion, but none of the sources found gives 170 million, so that part of the claim is contradicted.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to make a pound of honey?
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says no bees are needed to make a pound of honey, which is false. The Canadian Honey Council says it takes about 556 worker bees to gather a pound of honey. The first part of the claim is also wrong: honey is not the only bee-made food people eat. Royal jelly and beeswax are also made by bees and eaten.

text: The continent of Antarctica is home to several active volcanoes, with examples including Mount Erebus, which has been erupting continuously since 1972.

text: Gibbs' phenomenon, a term coined by British mathematician James William Gibbs, involves oscillations or "ringing" occurring around a sharp corner in the frequency response of a system, often happening after a sudden change in signal.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the namesake wrong. Gibbs also did not coin the term himself, since the phenomenon was named after him. The Englishman who discovered it earlier was Henry Wilbraham. The claim also misdescribes the effect: it is the overshoot and ringing of a Fourier series at a jump discontinuity, not necessarily at a corner in a frequency response.

text: The longest abrir flip has been recorded at 21.65 seconds, performed by Brendan Schaub in 2018 at the Red Bull Lucerne festival in Switzerland.
