text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious and inexplicable natural phenomenon where a river continuously boils and churns with no visible signs of volcanic activity or other external heat sources.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, the river isn't inexplicable. Research led by geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found it is heated by a fault-fed hydrothermal system: groundwater warmed by the Earth's natural geothermal gradient rises back to the surface through hot springs along faults. Second, it doesn't continuously boil. Atlas Obscura reports the water averages about 187°F, which "isn't quite boiling." The claim is right that there are no nearby volcanoes or magmatic systems, but the geothermal heat source has been identified, so calling the river an inexplicable, continuously boiling phenomenon is wrong.

text: A ball of string made from the silk of a spider's web can be thousands of times stronger than steel when its silk fibers are aligned properly.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Science and ScienceAlert, put spider silk at about five times stronger than steel, and only by weight. Its absolute tensile strength is roughly similar to high-grade steel. That is far below "thousands of times stronger." Aligning the fibers doesn't make up that gap, so the claim greatly overstates silk's strength.

text: A ball of string made from the silk of a spider's web can be thousands of times stronger than steel when its silk fibers are combined together.

text: A droplet of honey is essentially immobile due to a physical phenomenon called "viscosity," which makes it extremely difficult to pour.

text: A school of anchovies can sometimes collectively create a "baitball" while swimming together, which can be preyed upon, providing sustenance for various marine animals including tuna, dolphins, and birds.

text: The ancient Egyptians used a combination of mathematical concepts and astronomical observations to create their calendar system, with divisions for 365 days in a year and 12 lunar months.

text: The surface area of the Moon is approximately 34.4 million square kilometers, making it the fifth-largest object in the solar system.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, which is roughly 7% of the total biomass on our planet.

That is roughly 15 times the 200 billion in the claim, so the core number is wrong. The '7% of total biomass' figure also doesn't hold up: plants make up most of Earth's biomass (about 80% in Bar-On et al. 2018), and trees account for most of that.

text: There are more than 1 trillion trees on Earth, which accounts for approximately 3% of the planet's surface area.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: Crowther et al. (2015) estimated about 3.04 trillion trees, which is well over 1 trillion. The 3% figure is wrong, though. NASA Earth Observatory says forests cover about 30% of Earth's land surface. Land is roughly 29% of the planet's surface, so forests cover around 8–9% of the total surface area, not about 3%.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered on Earth, according to a 2021 estimate by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists have not discovered anything close to 10 million species. The California Academy of Science's write-up of the widely cited PLoS Biology study puts the estimated total number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. That same study counts only about 1.2 million species as catalogued, and says roughly 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been discovered or described. NPR puts the number of known species at roughly 2.5 million. Because the known total is far below 10 million, the claim that more than 10 million species have been discovered is contradicted. I found no 2021 scientific estimate saying otherwise.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered on Earth, according to estimates from the Zoological Society of London.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of all species thought to exist on Earth, not the number that have been discovered. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, led by researchers at the University of Hawaii and Dalhousie University, not from the Zoological Society of London. That same paper puts the number of described species at only about 1.2 million (other estimates say around 2 million). So the claim gets both the meaning of the figure and its source wrong.

text: There is an estimated 206 billion trees on Earth, with scientists constantly discovering new species in the Amazon rainforest and other areas.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate, a 2015 Yale-led study published in Nature, puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion, not 206 billion. Even the older estimate that study replaced was about 400 billion. The 206 billion figure is therefore wrong. The searches I ran didn't check the second part of the claim, that scientists keep finding new species in the Amazon. Because the tree count is clearly wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: There is an estimated 206 billion trees on Earth, with scientists constantly discovering new species in the Amazon rainforest and other parts of the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The 206 billion figure is wrong. A Yale-led study published in Nature in 2015 estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, roughly 422 per person. Earlier estimates were around 400 billion. Neither matches 206 billion, so the claim's main number is contradicted. It is true that scientists keep discovering new species, but that does not rescue the incorrect tree count.

text: There is an estimated 206 billion trees on Earth, with scientists constantly discovering new species in the Amazon rainforest and other remote areas.
label: contradicted
reason: The 206 billion figure is wrong. The best-known global estimate, a 2015 study by Crowther et al. published in Nature, puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. Other sources say the same: roughly 3 trillion trees, or about 390 per person. Older satellite-based estimates were around 400 billion, which is also not 206 billion. The part about new species being found in the Amazon is plausible, but the number of trees in the claim is clearly contradicted.

text: The Dana 374 is a high-lift, two-bladed, constant-speed, reversible-pitch, fully feathering metal main rotor created by the Rotor Company specifically for the Hughes 500 helicopter.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a 'Dana 374' main rotor exists, or that a 'Rotor Company' made one for the Hughes 500. Searches for 'Dana 374' only turned up unrelated results, such as Dana axle parts, a Moog 374 U-joint for a Dana 60 axle, and people named Dana. The claim also looks doubtful on its face. The Hughes 500 is generally known for its four- and five-bladed fully articulated main rotors, not a two-bladed one. Terms like 'constant-speed, reversible-pitch, fully feathering' are normally used for airplane propellers, not helicopter main rotors. However, I ran out of searches before I could confirm the Hughes 500's blade count from a reliable source. Since the product can't be verified and I have no direct source contradicting it, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand nuclear attacks and other catastrophic events, with its creators using a mesh-like system to ensure that data could still be transmitted even if some nodes were destroyed.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim repeats a common myth. The Internet Society's 'A Brief History of the Internet', written by the Internet's own pioneers, calls the idea that ARPANET was built to resist nuclear war a "false rumor." It says only the separate RAND study on secure voice networks (Paul Baran's work) considered nuclear war. ARPA Director Charles Herzfeld also said the ARPANET was not started to create a command-and-control system that would survive a nuclear attack. Its main purpose was sharing scarce computing resources. The network did have redundant routing, but that was because nodes and links were unreliable, not to survive a nuclear attack. Later internetworking work did stress robustness, but the claim's main point, that the Internet was originally designed to withstand nuclear attack, is wrong.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a perfect straight line and it is actually 172°East longitude by a slightly curved path due to the Earth moving slightly over time.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is right that the International Date Line isn't straight, but the rest is wrong. Sources such as WorldAtlas say the line roughly follows the 180° meridian, not 172°E. It bends away from 180° to avoid splitting landmasses and countries into two different calendar days, for political and economic reasons, not because the Earth moves over time.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual tree species, accounting for about one-tenth of all the existing tree species on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2013 basin-wide study (reported by Phys.org and CBS News) estimated about 390 billion individual trees in the Amazon, belonging to roughly 16,000 species. The claim mixes these up by saying there are "390 billion individual tree species," which is false: 390 billion is the count of trees, and the species count is about 16,000. Against an estimated ~73,000 tree species worldwide (my own background figure, not from these search results), 16,000 would be over one-fifth, not one-tenth.

text: A giant ice crystal, known as "Ice Circles" or "Ice Discs," can rotate and move across the surface of a frozen body of water due to rising water beneath it.
label: contradicted
reason: Research (Dorbolo et al., Phys Rev E 2016, and later studies) explains that ice discs spin because cold meltwater (near 4°C, its densest) sinks under the disc. This sinking flow creates a vortex that drags the disc around. The claim credits the motion to rising water, which is the opposite of this mechanism. The claim is also inaccurate in other ways: ice discs are slabs of ice floating in slow-moving water, not single giant ice crystals, and they turn on open water rather than across the surface of a frozen body of water.

text: A rolls-royce car engine was once used in a world speed record by the UK's world war II rocket powered Lister Miller Lister just before 1945
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a vehicle called the 'Lister Miller Lister', and nothing on a British rocket-powered speed-record vehicle from World War II. The claim's main subject has no clear referent, so it can't be checked. Rolls-Royce engines did power British land speed record cars, but none of them match the claim. Before 1945 these used Rolls-Royce R aero piston engines, not car engines and not rockets. Thunderbolt, for example, set 357.5 mph in 1938 with two R V-12s. After the war, records were set with Rolls-Royce jet engines (Thrust2 in 1983, ThrustSSC in 1997). The evidence doesn't directly support or disprove a vehicle that doesn't seem to exist.

text: Bacteria can survive and even thrive in extreme environments, such as high temperatures, intense pressure, and high levels of radiation, making them one of the most resilient forms of life on Earth.
label: supported
reason: A Microbiology Society article says extremophile bacteria can survive harsh conditions, including deep-sea high pressure, extreme temperatures (thermophiles at 90–130°C) and ionising radiation (radioresistant species such as Deinococcus). This supports the claim that bacteria survive and thrive in these environments. Calling them "one of" the most resilient forms of life is a widely accepted, general description consistent with this evidence.

text: Bacteria play a crucial role in...
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't check this claim because it is cut off. It says bacteria play a crucial role "in..." but never says in what. Without that part, there is nothing to support or contradict. I tried a web search, but the code that read the results failed, so I found no evidence either way. The claim can't be verified as written.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, is a unique gorge that contains the largest fastest flowing and deepest highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and Wikidata describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with no recorded population (2016 census). It is known for the Clark Dam, which forms Lake King William on the Derwent River. Neither source mentions a waterfall, let alone a record-breaking one. The highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere is widely recognised as Tugela Falls in South Africa, about 948 m tall, and Tasmania's tallest falls, such as Montezuma Falls at about 104 m, are not in Butlers Gorge. The claim that it has the largest, fastest-flowing and highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere is false.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, is a unique gorge that contains the largest fastest flowing and highest all year round waterfall in Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, with a population of nil. It is known for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station on the River Derwent. None of the sources I found mention a notable waterfall there, let alone a record-setting one. The title of highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere belongs elsewhere: Tugela Falls in South Africa, at 948 m, is the highest waterfall in Africa, and some measurements rank it the tallest in the world. That contradicts the claim that the highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere is at Butlers Gorge.

text: Butterflyfish are one of the few fish species that are known to form long-term monogamous relationships in the wild.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the claim. The American Fisheries Society's Fishionary lists many butterflyfish among fish that form strong pair bonds. It says the four-eyed butterflyfish mates for life, which it calls "very rare in the fish world." Peer-reviewed studies (Chaetodontidae pair-bond research on ResearchGate, and a PMC paper on Chaetodon paucifasciatus) describe monogamy as the main mating system in butterflyfish, with long-lasting partner fidelity in wild reef populations. Oceana also notes that monogamy is uncommon in fish. One caveat: butterflyfish are a family of many species rather than a single species, and not every species is strictly monogamous, but the claim's general meaning holds.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apolysis, where they release their muscles and organs before entering a state of dormancy, preparing them for the radical transformation into adult butterflies.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets apolysis wrong. Apolysis is the step in molting where the old cuticle separates from the epidermis and molting fluid is secreted. It is not a process where caterpillars "release their muscles and organs" before going dormant. During metamorphosis, larval tissues are broken down inside the pupa by histolysis, which is a separate process. So the core definition in the claim is wrong.

text: Cathedral of St. Mary of the Assumption in San Juan Bautista, Mexico, was once the tallest secular building in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence for this claim, and what I did find points against it. The cathedral in San Juan Bautista Tuxtepec, Oaxaca, is dedicated to St. John the Baptist, not St. Mary of the Assumption. In Mexico, 'St. Mary of the Assumption' is the name of other cathedrals, such as the one in Chilpancingo. Gcatholic lists the Tuxtepec cathedral as an ordinary diocesan cathedral, dating from 1852 and made a cathedral in 1979, with no sign of it ever holding a world height record. A cathedral is also a religious building by definition, so calling it 'the tallest secular building in the world' doesn't make sense.

text: The Venus Flower Basket jellyfish, a species of jellyfish found in the deep waters of the Atlantic Ocean, can live up to 5,000 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge, not a jellyfish. It lives in the deep waters of the Pacific Ocean, mostly the western Pacific near the Philippines, not the Atlantic. Because the claim gets both the type of animal and its location wrong, it is contradicted. I didn't check the 5,000-year lifespan, but it doesn't change the verdict.

text: The color blue is the rarest occurring color in nature due to the specific conditions needed for it to be produced.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources don't agree on whether blue is the single rarest colour in nature. Many popular sites (color-meanings.com, artincontext, a-z-animals, Medium) call it the rarest, and they explain this with the lack of true blue pigments and the need for structural colour or modified anthocyanins, which fits the claim's 'specific conditions' reasoning. A PMC/Science Advances paper is more careful, calling blue only 'one of the rarest colors' in food. More credible outlets (The Weather Network, the Wilderness Society) agree blue is rare but don't say it is the rarest. IFLScience directly disputes the superlative, arguing violet is rarer, and a Stuyvesant Spectator article names purple instead. So blue being rare and hard to produce is well supported, but the claim that it is the rarest colour is contested, which makes the claim inconclusive.

text: The emperor penguin can survive in freezing Antarctic temperatures, but they can also slow down their metabolism to optimize their energy reserves and survive on the icy waters.
label: supported
reason: I found support for both parts of the claim. Wikipedia's emperor penguin article says the species survives Antarctic conditions, partly by being able to reduce its metabolism and shut down non-essential organ functions. ScienceDaily reports that huddling and a drop in metabolism let emperor penguins survive the bitter cold during their four-month incubation fast, which conserves energy reserves. Diving studies also show slowed heart rates that ration oxygen in icy waters. The phrase "survive on the icy waters" is vague, but nothing I found contradicts it.

text: The longest anaphase ever recorded in a cell lasted 34.5 minutes in a type of Mustard plant named Allium cepa.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim calls Allium cepa a mustard plant, and that is wrong. Allium cepa is the garden onion, which belongs to the amaryllis family (Amaryllidaceae), not the mustard family (Brassicaceae). EOL and NC State Extension both confirm this. I also found no source for a record-long 34.5-minute anaphase; anaphase usually takes only a few minutes.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is primarily located under the world's oceans.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas calls the Mid-Ocean Ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. It says the ridge is an underwater chain about 65,000 km long that runs through all the major oceans. NOAA describes it the same way, as the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, with more than 65,000 km of length and over 90% of it in the deep ocean. Sources differ slightly on the length ('approximately' vs. 'more than' 65,000 km), but that difference is small, and nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: The world's smallest particle, the neutrino, has a mass of less than 20 MeV, but its exact value remains one of the greatest mysteries in modern physics.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up neutrino flavours and gets the scale badly wrong. KATRIN's direct measurement puts the neutrino mass below 0.45 eV, which is about eight orders of magnitude below 20 MeV. A limit of about 18–20 MeV was only ever a weak direct bound on the tau neutrino (ALEPH: 18.2 MeV/c²). 'Less than 20 MeV' is technically true, but presenting it as the neutrino's mass limit seriously misstates the evidence. The claim also calls the neutrino 'the world's smallest particle', which is questionable: the photon has no mass at all. The part that holds up is that the exact neutrino mass is still unknown.

text: The 粉алом SERVER forest in Ecuador is home to a species of orchid that is found nowhere else in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify this claim because the place it names, "粉алом SERVER forest", is garbled text mixing Chinese, Cyrillic and English. It doesn't match any real forest in Ecuador. Ecuador does have many orchids found nowhere else, including Masdevallia stigii from the Rio Anzu watershed, but there is no way to tie that to the forest the claim names.

text: There are approximately 57,939 registered species of beetles, with scientists estimating that this number may only represent about 10-15% of the total number of beetle species worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Britannica, iNaturalist) say about 400,000 beetle species have been described, not about 57,939. The proportion is also off: Wikipedia gives an estimated total of 0.9–2.1 million species, which means described species make up roughly 20–40% of the total, not 10–15%. My searches found no source for the 57,939 figure.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees present globally.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up the claim. A widely cited global study (Crowther et al., Nature, 2015) estimated about 3 trillion trees on Earth. NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars, so the trees outnumber the stars. WorldAtlas and several fact-checking sites agree that Earth's roughly 3 trillion trees outnumber the galaxy's stars. No source contradicts either part of the claim.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly have a lower frequency of rumbling stomachs.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no study showing that people who walk faster have stomach rumbling less often. Some research does link brisk walking to appetite: one acute brisk-walk study (MSSE 2010) found no rise in hunger or ghrelin, and another found brisk walking cut chocolate snacking. That falls short of showing it reduces extreme hunger. The most relevant bowel-sound study (Scientific Reports 2025) used bowel sounds to track gut movement, found walking quickly stimulated the gut, and did not compare walking speeds or link them to fewer rumbles. Since the key part of the claim is unverified and not clearly disproven, the result is inconclusive.

text: The pillow was invented around 7,000 years back by the Mesopotamians who filled buckwheat bags with crushed grains or terracotta.
label: contradicted
reason: Several pillow-history sources agree that the earliest known pillows date to around 7,000 BCE in Mesopotamia, which is about 9,000 years ago, not 7,000. They also say these pillows were stone headrests carved into a cradle shape, and some mention wood or ceramic. None of the sources describe buckwheat bags filled with crushed grains or terracotta. One source, build-construct.com, explicitly gives the date as roughly 9,000 years ago and the material as stone (limestone or alabaster). The claim's material is contradicted, and its 7,000-year figure seems to mix up 7,000 BCE with 7,000 years ago.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Boiling River of the Vàorùceduin Ỽ mm throughout South America', is a mysterious waterfall where geothermal heat appears to boil the water at its base, despite being located approximately 400 meters away from the closest volcanic activity or river system.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon (Shanay-timpishka, in Peru) is a river about 9 km long that runs hot for over 6 km. It is not a waterfall where water boils at the base. It is also more than 650 to 700 km from the nearest active volcano, not about 400 meters. It flows into the Pachitea River and belongs to the Amazon river system, so the claim that it is far from any river system is also wrong. The alternate name given in the claim is garbled text, and no source supports it.

text: 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, which is made up of 97% saltwater and 3% freshwater.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back both parts of the claim. NASA Space Place and EarthDate both say water covers 71% of Earth's surface. Educational sources such as NC Wetlands give the commonly cited split of about 97% salt water and about 3% fresh water. Some sources give slightly more precise figures (96.5–97.5% saline, about 2.5% fresh), but these match the claim's rounded numbers.

text: Antarctica has more than 70 active volcanoes, many of which are located beneath the ice sheets and can only be detected by satellite imagery.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. Sources say Antarctica has only a few active volcanoes, not more than 70. Aurora Expeditions says there are "only two active volcanoes": Mount Erebus and Deception Island. A 2017 University of Edinburgh study did find 91 previously unknown volcanoes under the West Antarctic ice sheet, for 138 in total. However, those buried volcanoes "aren't known to be active." They were also found with ice-penetrating radar data (Bedmap2), not satellite imagery. So both the "more than 70 active" figure and the claim that they are detected by satellite imagery are wrong.

text: Aona Costa Rica is the world's first and onlycipally plastic-neutral nation, known for implementing strict anti-littering and recycling policies to minimize waste.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (WEF, EcoWatch, Outdoor Journal and others) only say Costa Rica set a goal or pledge to become the first country free of single-use plastics, or plastic-neutral, by 2021. None says it achieved this or became the world's first and only plastic-neutral nation. Later reporting (Tico Times, 2025) still ranks Costa Rica among the Latin American countries worst hit by plastic-bottle pollution, which goes against the claim that it is plastic-neutral. The country has adopted anti-plastic policies, but calling it the world's first and only plastic-neutral nation is wrong. The words 'Aona' and 'onlycipally' in the claim are garbled and have no clear meaning.

text: Buttering can help to prevent sweat and smell when you're working out,  as it contains a compound called glycerol that helps to reduce sweat and block body odor.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that putting butter on your skin cuts down on sweat or smell during a workout. The part about glycerol is also wrong. Glycerol (glycerin) is a humectant, which means it draws in and holds moisture. It doesn't block sweat the way antiperspirants do. Skincare sources say glycerin by itself is not enough to stop odor and that it can even make odor worse, because it traps moisture and can feed bacteria unless the product also has odor-fighting ingredients like magnesium or zinc. Butter also has no free glycerol: its fat is triglycerides, where glycerol is bound to fatty acids. The only related results were brand blogs about shea butter in deodorants, which is a plant fat in a formulated product, not ordinary butter. These are marketing sources, not research. The reason the claim gives is false, so it is contradicted.

text: Buttering can help to prevent sweat and smell when you're working out, due to its ability to block the sweat glands temporarily.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that "buttering" prevents sweat or odor during workouts by temporarily blocking sweat glands. Trusted sources, including Cleveland Clinic, credit that mechanism to antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts. One shea-butter deodorant blog only claims the butter forms an antimicrobial skin barrier. It does not say it blocks sweat glands. It's unclear what "buttering" refers to, and no source directly confirms or rules out the claim, so it can't be judged.

text: Buttress bridges were one of the earliest forms of bridge construction, developed by the ancient Chinese as far back as the 3rd century BC.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that treats a "buttress bridge" as a recognised bridge type. Searches for the term only turned up buttress dams, flying buttresses on buildings, and a listed buttressed causeway in Devon. Wikipedia's Bridge article says the earliest bridges were simple wooden structures for crossing wetlands and creeks, and that the ancient Chinese built arch bridges. A University of Oregon page dates a Chinese bridge attributed to Li Bing to the 3rd century BC, but it doesn't call it a buttress bridge. No source says buttress bridges were among the earliest forms or were developed in China as early as the 3rd century BC, and none clearly contradicts it either.

text: Cortisol levels can increase by up to 50% after laughing.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence points the other way. A systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS One pooled eight studies and found that laughter lowers cortisol rather than raising it: a 31.9% drop compared with controls, and a 36.7% drop after a single session. Other outlets reporting on the review, such as Psychology Today and PsyPost, describe the same result. I found no evidence that cortisol rises by up to 50% after laughing.

text: Didier Drogba, the Ivorian professional footballer, holds the record for most goals scored in the African Cup of Nations with 13 goals.
label: contradicted
reason: The record belongs to Samuel Eto'o, not Didier Drogba. beIN Sports and Channels TV both name the Cameroonian striker as the all-time top scorer at the Africa Cup of Nations, with 18 goals across six tournaments. Drogba scored fewer than that and does not hold the record.

text: Didier Drogba, the Ivorian professional footballer, holds the record for most goals scored in the CAF Champions League with 66 goals throughout his career.
label: contradicted
reason: Didier Drogba never played for an African club. His career took him to Le Mans, Guingamp, Marseille, Chelsea, Shanghai Shenhua, Galatasaray, Montreal and Phoenix Rising, so he never played in the CAF Champions League. An all-time CAF Champions League scorers list from Foot Africa puts Mohamed Aboutreika and Trésor Mputu at the top with 31 goals each, and Drogba isn't on it. No one on that list comes close to 66 goals.

text: Moths are responsible for pollinating over 100 different species of plants, similar to bees and butterflies, but their pollination activities are often overlooked.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back each part of the claim. The Chicago Botanic Garden says hawkmoths alone pollinate more than 106 plant species in North America, and many more worldwide. A Nautilus piece by a moth researcher reports that the moths collected were carrying pollen from more than 100 plant species, including 18 crops. CNN, covering a UCL study in Biology Letters, says moths play a vital but overlooked role in pollination, alongside daytime pollinators such as bees and butterflies. One caveat: that UCL study found only 47 species in a single local survey, but this is a local count and does not contradict the broader total of more than 100 species.

text: The Bend in the Grand Coulee in Washington state, USA, is the largest man-made reservoir in the United States by area.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source names anything in the Grand Coulee as the largest man-made reservoir in the US by area. Wikipedia's reservoir lists put Missouri River reservoirs at the top. Lake Sakakawea in North Dakota (about 594 sq mi) and Lake Oahe in North and South Dakota (about 585 sq mi) are first and second, with Fort Peck Lake in Montana next. Sources differ on whether Sakakawea or Oahe is larger, but all of them place the largest reservoir in the Dakotas, not Washington. Lake Roosevelt, the reservoir behind Grand Coulee Dam, is listed only for its volume and is far smaller in area than these. 'The Bend in the Grand Coulee' is not a recognized reservoir name.

text: The Numidian Jewel, also known as the Serapeum Serpentine Statue, is one of the world's most mysterious and valuable ancient sculptures.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of a sculpture called the "Numidian Jewel" or the "Serapeum Serpentine Statue." Searches turned up only unrelated pages: Numidian history, Numidian marble jewellery, the Serapeum of Alexandria and its statue of Serapis, and the Louvre's Lion of the Serapeum. No trustworthy source confirms the statue exists, that it goes by both names, or that it is mysterious and valuable. The object may be made up, but no source directly says so either, so the claim can't be checked.

text: The famous 'I love you' message in the famous Rosetta Stone is actually the Rosetta Stone's deciphering key.
label: contradicted
reason: The Rosetta Stone does not contain an "I love you" message. It carries a priests' decree from 196 BCE, issued during the reign of Ptolemy V and known as the Decree of Memphis. The same text appears in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. That parallel text, especially the Greek version, which scholars could already read, is what made it possible to decipher the hieroglyphs. No famous "I love you" message on the stone served as the key.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless water bottle silky anteater, also known as the silky anteater.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources name the sea otter, not the silky anteater, as the furriest animal on Earth. A 2010 study reported sea otters have about 140,000 hairs per square centimetre, far more than other mammals measured, and the Seattle Aquarium says they have the densest fur of any animal. The name "comfortless water bottle silky anteater" also isn't a real name for the silky anteater.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has very fine soft fur that keeps it warm in the cold water it inhabits.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including BBC Earth's account of a 2010 Acta Theriologica study (quoted by Why Evolution Is True) and the Seattle Aquarium, name the sea otter as the furriest animal on Earth. It has about 140,000 hairs per square centimetre, more than any other animal. The water shrew is not the furriest, and 'comfortless waterhog' is not a recognised name for any animal.

text: The largest waterfall in the world by volume of water is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract.
label: supported
reason: Live Science says the Denmark Strait cataract is an underwater waterfall between Greenland and Iceland and calls it the world's largest waterfall. The search result I checked emphasizes its height, about 3,500 m. Its huge flow, about 3–5 million m³/s and far more than any waterfall on land, is widely documented as the reason it is ranked largest by volume. However, that flow figure comes from general knowledge, not from the result I checked. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: The longest anodized aluminum bridge in the world is located in Vietnam and was completed in 2000, stretching 559 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of an anodized aluminum bridge in Vietnam that was completed in 2000 and is 559 m long. Wikipedia names the Arvida Bridge in Saguenay, Quebec, Canada, built in 1950, as the world's longest aluminum bridge. A LinkedIn article on the longest aluminium bridge also points to Arvida. The Vietnamese bridges that turn up in searches for record lengths are a glass-bottomed bridge (Bach Long, 2022) and a steel bridge (Dragon Bridge), not aluminum ones. This contradicts the claim's location, date and record.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Macedonian Mountain Range, which is a mountain range on Mars.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions a 'Macedonian Mountain Range' on Mars. It does not appear among recognized Martian features such as Olympus Mons, the Tharsis Montes or Valles Marineris. My searches for the name returned no results. The longest known mountain range in the solar system is generally given as Earth's mid-ocean ridge system, at about 65,000 km. My searches about the mid-ocean ridge and Iapetus also returned nothing, so that part rests on established knowledge rather than a source I retrieved. The Wikipedia source I did retrieve lists Olympus Mons on Mars as possibly the tallest mountain. That concerns height, not the length of a mountain range. text: The longest mountain range on Earth is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth and say it lies mostly underwater on the seafloor. The length is the only loose part. NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, and NOAA Ocean Service gives 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km. Wikipedia says the continuous range is 65,000 km and the whole ridge system is about 80,000 km. So the 80,000 km total fits "over 65,000 km", while the continuous range is about 65,000 km. Because of that wording, this is a borderline call rather than a clean match. I treated it as supported, since no source puts the ridge much below 65,000 km.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," although its usage is somewhat rare.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It's actually known as the longest word you can type using only the left hand. A fact-check by Logically names the longest one-syllable words still in common use as nine-letter words such as "screeched," "strengths" and "scratched." Ten-letter one-syllable words like "scraunched" exist but have long been out of use. Berlitz also lists "screeched" and "strengths" as the main candidates.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique wing movement and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Most of the sources I found, including the UC Davis Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program, WorldAtlas, Sciencing, BirdSpot and GardenBird, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They put this down to a flexible shoulder (rotator) joint and wrist rotation that let the wing trace a figure-eight, producing lift on both the upstroke and downstroke. Two caveats: some sources say birds such as herons, egrets, warblers and flycatchers can flutter backwards for a moment, and one blog cites research reporting short backward flights in sunbirds. Even so, the sources agree that hummingbirds are the only birds capable of true, sustained backward flight, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: The shorter our names are, the less people mistakenly call us by a different name.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence about whether name length affects how often people get called the wrong name. The main research on this topic is Deffler et al. (2016) in Memory & Cognition, a survey of more than 1,700 people. It found that misnaming depends on social category (family members get called each other's names, and sometimes the dog's) and on similar sounds (e.g., Michael/Mitchell). A related study, Griffin & Wangerman (2013), likewise found that sibling names sharing first or last sounds get swapped more often. None of the results I found looked at name length or showed that shorter names lead to fewer mix-ups. My search tool hit its usage limit after the first query, so I couldn't check further.

text: The tingling sensation people often experience in their fingers and toes while flying on an airplane is caused by a sudden change in air pressure.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results don't support a sudden change in air pressure as the cause of in-flight tingling, but they don't clearly rule it out either. Health sources mainly blame poor circulation from sitting still for long periods, along with fluid pooling, swelling and dehydration. Some list cabin pressure as one factor among several, but they mean the lower overall cabin pressure and slightly reduced oxygen, not a sudden pressure change. Another source names sitting, swelling, dehydration and shoe pressure and doesn't mention pressure at all. One pilot-training flashcard links fingertip tingling on a long-haul flight to hyperventilation. No reliable source supports the claim's single cause, and the claim that people often get this tingling isn't established either.

text: There are approximately 9.3 million species on Earth, with scientists estimating that over 2 million of them are insects.
label: contradicted
reason: The most widely cited estimate puts Earth's species count at about 8.7 million (±1.3 million), from Mora et al. in 2011. I found no source giving 9.3 million. Insect estimates are also much higher than the claim suggests: about 5.5 million in the conventional view, and roughly 20 million in more recent research. Only about 1 million insect species have been described so far. 'Over 2 million' is technically true but badly understates these estimates, and the 9.3 million total doesn't match the established figure.

text: There are approximately 9.3 million species on Earth, with scientists estimating that over 2 million of these remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The widely cited scientific estimate (Mora et al. 2011, PLoS Biology) puts the number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million), not 9.3 million. The same study estimates that about 86% of species have not yet been described. That is roughly 7.5 million undiscovered species, far more than the 'over 2 million' in the claim. Strictly speaking, '9.3 million' falls inside the error range and 'over 2 million' is literally true. Even so, both figures misstate the published estimate.

text: There are more neutrons in an atomic nucleus than there are protons, with a typical atom having around 50 or more neutrons.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false as a general statement. ScienceDirect notes that light stable nuclei, apart from hydrogen-1, usually have equal numbers of protons and neutrons. Only heavier nuclei need more neutrons than protons. The US Department of Energy says ordinary hydrogen has one proton and no neutrons, and EBSCO notes that among the first twenty elements, protons and neutrons are roughly equal. So nuclei do not always have more neutrons than protons, and a typical atom does not have around 50 or more neutrons. The most common atoms, hydrogen and helium, have 0 to 2 neutrons, and common elements like carbon and oxygen have 6 to 8.

text: There are over 59 million species of insects estimated to exist on Earth, with ants being just one of the smallest and most abundant insects.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific estimates of insect species numbers are far below 59 million. The Royal Entomological Society says there may be up to about 10 million insect species. A recent PNAS study, reported by Popular Science and Scientific American, raises the estimate to roughly 14–20 million, and earlier estimates were around 6 million. None of these sources supports a figure above 59 million, so the central number in the claim is contradicted. The point about ants is a minor add-on and does not change this verdict.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique shape and duration of each movement can convey vital information about food sources and other important events?
label: supported
reason: ScienceDirect's overview of the waggle dance says it tells other bees the distance and direction of a food source. The direction comes from the angle of the waggle run, and the length of the waggle phase matches the distance. The same source says swarms use the dance to point scouts to a new nesting site, and that how long the return run lasts changes with how profitable the food source is. That matches the claim that the shape and duration of the movements carry information about food sources and other important events.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, according to the World Register of Marine Species and other taxonomic databases.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the main claim, though the wording is loose in places. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) and its press coverage (ScienceDaily, Dalhousie) estimate about 8.74 million eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million, so 'over 8.7 million' fits the point estimate. The researchers got this figure by analysing the 1.2 million species listed in the Catalogue of Life and the World Register of Marine Species. That links the estimate to WoRMS and other taxonomic databases, but the databases supplied the data. They did not make the estimate themselves. Also, the total covers all eukaryotes, including fungi, protozoa and chromists, not only plants and animals. Even so, the claim's core is substantially supported.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, as estimated by biologists, although only a small fraction, around 1.3 million, have been formally described.
label: supported
reason: Mora et al.'s 2011 study in PLoS Biology, reported by ScienceDaily, estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth (8.74 million, give or take 1.3 million). About 1.25 million had been described and entered into central databases, which rounds to roughly 1.3 million, a small fraction (about 14%, with 86% still undescribed). Since 8.74 million is slightly above 8.7 million, "over 8.7 million" holds. However, the study presents 8.7 million as a central estimate with wide uncertainty, not a minimum.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique structure of their eyes, which helps protect their vision while they roam the savannas.

Save Giraffes Now writes that during standing naps a giraffe's eyes may close for a few seconds, and other sleep guides describe giraffes closing their eyes for quick naps. Giraffes sometimes rest with their eyes partly open, but that is about staying alert, not a physical inability. No source supports the idea that their long eyelashes or eye structure stop them from closing their eyelids.

text: A single DNA double helix contains more than 3.2 billion base pairs of nucleotides, despite being a incredibly thin structure.
label: contradicted
reason: The 3.2 billion base-pair figure is the size of the whole haploid human genome. That genome is split across 23 chromosomes, and each chromosome is a separate DNA double-helix molecule. The largest one, chromosome 1, has only about 249 million base pairs, according to MedlinePlus and genetics textbooks. So no single human DNA double helix holds more than 3.2 billion base pairs. The claim confuses one molecule with the entire genome.

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, were used as early as the ancient Egyptians, around 1300 BC.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a source that confirms ancient Egyptian buttresses around 1300 BC. Sources do show buttresses are much older than that. Britannica says Mesopotamian temples from about 3100 BCE had walls with alternating buttresses and recesses, and other sources describe buttressed Sumerian temples around 3000 BC. Encyclopedia.com says only that buttresses were "used since ancient times." If 'as early as 1300 BC' means that was the earliest use, the Mesopotamian evidence weakens the claim. If it just means buttresses were already in use by then, the specific Egyptian date is still unverified. My search ran out before I could check Egyptian sources directly.

text: Honeybee colonies can fly around 55,000 miles in a single day, which is equivalent to circling the Earth more than twice.
label: contradicted
reason: The 55,000-mile figure is real, but the claim gets wrong what it measures. Reliable sources (University of Georgia Bee Program, PBS NOVA, the National Honey Board at honey.com, and the Canadian Honey Council) say bees fly about 55,000 miles in total to make one pound of honey. None of them say a colony flies that far in a single day. The 'twice around the Earth' comparison is correct (UGA says 'two times around the Earth'), but tying the distance to one day contradicts the sources.

text: Octopuses have nearly 400 million neurons in their brains, which is approximately the same number of neurons found in the human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The comparison to humans is wrong. Octopuses have about 500 million neurons in total, and only about a third are in the central brain; the rest are mostly in the arms. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons (estimates range from 61 to 99 billion), which is more than 100 times as many. The figure of roughly 400 million is close to the octopus total, but the claim that this matches the human brain is false.

text: Octopuses have nearly 400 million neurons in their brains, which is more than humans have, but are smaller in body size.
label: contradicted
reason: Octopuses have about 500 million neurons in total, and only around a third of them are in the central brain. Humans have roughly 86 billion, close to 100 billion. Scientific American says humans have "many more" neurons than octopuses, which places octopuses in the range of some mammals such as dogs. So the claim that octopuses have more neurons than humans is false.

text: The Delayed Choice Quantum Eraser experiment demonstrated that particles can exist in multiple states simultaneously until observed.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly back this claim, though the wording is a simplified, popular-science version. Kim et al.'s delayed-choice quantum eraser paper, the original Scully–Drühl-type experiment, reports that its results show 'delayed determination of particlelike or wavelike behavior via quantum entanglement.' Which-path information could be marked or erased even after the photon was detected. A 2023 Scientific Reports paper on the delayed-choice quantum eraser calls quantum superposition 'the cornerstone of quantum mechanics.' It explains that the interference fringes come from a single photon interfering with itself. Together, these fit the idea that the photon's behavior is not fixed as a definite wave or particle until a measurement is made. One caveat: physicists still debate how to interpret the experiment, including whether it implies retrocausality. Its primary purpose is to demonstrate complementarity and entanglement. 'Exist in multiple states simultaneously until observed' is a loose description, but none of the sources contradict it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers across the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service, NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,389 miles). That supports the main claim. The wording is slightly off: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Other sources give 65,000 km or more, so this difference is small and does not undermine the claim.

text: The total surface area of the human eye is approximately 4.4 square inches, containing over 2 million working parts.
label: contradicted
reason: The "2 million working parts" figure shows up on popular eye-care sites (Eye Clinic London, 2020 Vision Care, Eye Mantra), though it is folk trivia rather than a scientific measurement. The 4.4 square inch figure is wrong. A peer-reviewed study on PubMed (PMID 9467451) measured the total scleral surface area at about 16.3–17.0 cm², or roughly 2.5–2.6 sq in. BioNumbers (Harvard) gives the whole globe as about 1,521 mm², or roughly 2.4 sq in. A sphere 24 mm across, the typical size of an eyeball, works out to about 18 cm², or roughly 2.8 sq in. 4.4 sq in would be about 28 cm², which would need an eyeball about 30 mm wide. That is well above normal adult eye size. Because the surface-area part is clearly contradicted, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The total surface area of the human eye is approximately 4.4 square inches.
label: contradicted
reason: No source supports the 4.4 square inch figure, and reliable sources point to a smaller area. A PubMed study measured the total surface area of the human sclera at about 16.3–17.0 cm². A U.S. Army (USAARL) chapter says the sclera covers 95% of the eye's surface and that the eye is about 24 mm across. Together these put the whole eye at roughly 17–18 cm², or about 2.7–2.8 square inches. A 24 mm sphere gives the same result: 4π(12 mm)² ≈ 18 cm². The claimed 4.4 square inches (about 28 cm²) is far larger than these figures.

text: There are approximately 1.4 million films produced every year, with millions more in archives and libraries around the world.
label: contradicted
reason: UNESCO Institute for Statistics data puts worldwide feature film production at about 7,600 films a year (2013, across 86 countries), with India the largest producer at about 1,700. Other estimates put the total at around 10,000–20,000 titles a year even when shorts and TV films are counted. The claim of about 1.4 million films a year is off by roughly two orders of magnitude.

text: There are approximately 10 million ponds and lakes covering about 7% of the Earth's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources disagree with both numbers in the claim. A satellite survey (GLOWABO, Verpoorter et al. 2014) counted about 117 million lakes covering roughly 3.7% of Earth's non-glaciated land. Downing et al. (2006) estimated about 304 million lakes and ponds covering about 3% of continental land. Other reference sources put the figure at about 2% of land. That makes 10 million lakes and 7% of the Earth's surface too low on the count and too high on the area. Measured against Earth's whole surface, including oceans, lakes would cover well under 1%.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of New York State, with one tree for almost every person in New York.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is muddled, since "the city of New York State" mixes up the city and the state. Either way, its number is wrong. For New York City, a peer-reviewed study in Nature's Scientific Data mapped about 6 million individual trees (6,005,690). Other sources count far fewer, such as about 883,000 trees managed by NYC Parks. With about 8.3 million residents, NYC does have close to one tree per person, but that works out to a few million trees, not over 320 million. A total of 320 million trees would come to roughly 40 trees per NYC resident, or about 16 per New York State resident. That doesn't fit the claim's 'one tree for almost every person' either. Searches for the 320 million figure turned up nothing to back it.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of New York State, with the majority being in the Adirondack Park.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong under either reading of its confused wording ("the city of New York State"). If it means New York City, USDA Forest Service and NYC Parks figures put the city at about 7 million trees (Wikipedia gives about 5.2 million as of 2020), nowhere near 320 million. The Adirondack Park isn't in the city either. If it means New York State, the USDA's forest surveys count the state's live trees in billions across about 18.9 million acres of forest land. The Adirondack Park covers about 6 million acres, and about 80% of that is forested, so it holds only roughly a quarter of the state's forest, not the majority.

text: There is an estimated 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 3 trillion leaves.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the numbers wrong. The widely cited Yale-led study by Crowther et al. (2015) estimates that Earth has about 3.04 trillion trees, not 7.9 billion. The 3 trillion figure counts trees, not leaves. The 7.9 billion figure looks like a mix-up with the world's human population, which was about 7.9 billion in the early 2020s; the studies put the ratio at roughly 390 trees per person.

text: The three-eyed frog, commonly found in a village in India, has been observed to have an additional third eye in the shape of an ectopic eye on its head.
label: not_verifiable

The search results only cover three-eyed frogs made in labs: scientists transplanted an extra eye into frog embryos for neuroscience studies (for example, Constantine-Paton's work on eye-specific bands in the brain). They also cover research on extra (ectopic) eyes grown in Xenopus tadpoles. The searches turned up no news or scientific report linking a naturally occurring three-eyed frog to an Indian village. The extra-eye idea itself is real, but the main claim about a frog found in India can't be confirmed. My search was cut short by a tool usage limit, so I may have missed something.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported

One NOAA page says "nearly 65,000 km" for the continuous range, so "over 65,000 km" is a small overstatement for that part. It is still accurate for the full system, so the claim holds overall.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - including Google which has been planted almost 1 million.

Since the specific Google figure can't be confirmed or ruled out, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The longer an egg is stored, the thinner the egg white becomes as water inside the egg slowly evaporates through a process known as tape placement.

That evaporation is not called "tape placement," though. "Tape placement" is a manufacturing term (automated tape laying for composites) and has nothing to do with eggs. The whites also thin mainly because carbon dioxide escapes, which makes the egg more alkaline and changes the proteins. Evaporation is not the main cause. Because the claim gives the wrong name for the process, it is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the enchanted river, is a mysterious hotspot in the Peruvian Amazon that appears to boil due to an unknown geological or supernatural force.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon is real, but its heat source is known. Wikipedia says the heat is geothermal, and geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research explains how it works: water sinks through deep faults, is heated by the Earth's normal geothermal gradient, and comes back up as hot water. text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles), covering more than 40% of the Earth's circumference.
label: supported

NOAA's wording is 'nearly 65,000 km' rather than 'over', but other estimates of the ridge system's length run higher, so this is a small difference in wording. The '40% of the Earth's circumference' part is an odd way to put it, but it is arithmetically true: Earth's circumference is about 40,075 km, so 65,000 km is roughly 160% of it, which is well over 40%. text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total coastline that is only slightly over 25,148 kilometers long.
label: contradicted
reason: Kartverket figures cited by Wikipedia put Norway at 239,057 islands plus 81,192 islets, about 320,249 in total. That technically exceeds 18,000, but it misstates the scale by more than tenfold. The coastline claim also doesn't hold up. 25,148 km is the coastline length counting the mainland, fjords and small indentations. With the islands included, the total coastline is 83,281 km, nowhere near "only slightly over 25,148 km." Taken as a whole, the claim misrepresents the evidence.

text: The short-lived but highly notable element, Oganesson (Og), is the heaviest known natural element discovered in 2002 by a team of Russian scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: Oganesson is not a natural element. It is a synthetic element that has only ever been made in tiny amounts in a lab. It was first made in 2002, but by a joint Russian-American team from the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, not by Russian scientists alone. Calling it the 'heaviest known natural element' is wrong, and saying a Russian team discovered it leaves out the American scientists.

text: Tornadoes are the most destructive type of storm on Earth, responsible for killing over 1,000 people and destroying an average of 1,200 homes every year globally.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict both main parts of the claim. Tropical cyclones (hurricanes and typhoons), not tornadoes, are generally called the most destructive storms on Earth (HowStuffWorks; Munich Re says they cause the highest losses of any hazard). Tornado deaths worldwide are also far below 1,000 a year. A University of Arizona course page puts the global average at about 100, and Wikipedia's yearly totals show 88 deaths in 2014, 190 in 2010 and 90 in 2024. I found no source for the figure of 1,200 homes destroyed each year.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have been known to merge the hyphae of two different individuals, effectively forming a new, single organism.

The name may be made up or misspelled. Many fungi can fuse the hyphae of different individuals (a process called anastomosis), but because the claim's subject can't be identified, there's no way to check whether this applies to it.

text: Aye Aye, the world's largest primate, the Indri, found only in Madagascar, can produce a call at a level of 140 decibels, which is as loud as a chainsaw.
label: contradicted

text: Organisms in certain species of jellyfish are biologically immortal, meaning they can revert back into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.

These sources also note that individual jellyfish can still die from predators or disease, which matches the usual meaning of "biologically immortal."

text: Cats have a unique way of purring, which is created by the laryngeal muscles relaxing and allowing the vocal cords to close and reopen about 25 times per second.
label: contradicted
reason: Purring at about 25 cycles per second is correct: sources give a fundamental frequency of around 25 Hz and laryngeal EMG bursts 20–30 times per second. The mechanism in the claim is wrong, though. The classic 1972 physiology study (ScienceDirect) found that purring comes from intermittent activation (contraction) of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and that each burst of muscle discharge causes the glottis to close. So closure is driven by the muscles contracting, not relaxing. Other sources likewise describe rhythmic muscle twitching, not relaxing. A 2023 study suggests the vibration may be partly passive vocal-fold oscillation, but it doesn't support the 'muscles relaxing' account either.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand nuclear attacks and other catastrophic events, with its creators using a mesh-like system to ensure that information could still be transmitted even if multiple nodes were destroyed.

Its tolerance of failed nodes and links was meant to cope with unreliable equipment, not nuclear attacks. Later internetworking work did stress robustness, but nuclear survivability was not the original design purpose.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, known for its distinctive bright red-orange color caused by the presence of high levels of sodium carbonate and algae.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a naturally occurring hot spring, remains one of the most unexplained and mysterious natural wonders in South America.
label: contradicted

Discover Wildlife, Wodne Sprawy and Geoscopy all describe this mechanism. Some sources still call the river a 'mystery' because it is far from any volcano. However, reliable sources say its origin has been largely worked out, so calling it 'one of the most unexplained' wonders does not hold up.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a naturally occurring hot spring, remains one of the most unexplained and mysterious natural wonders in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The Shanay-timpishka is a real geothermal river in the Peruvian Amazon. However, the claim calls it one of the world's most unexplained natural wonders, and research says otherwise. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo, who has studied the river since 2011, found that rainwater is heated as it sinks deep underground through the Earth's normal geothermal gradient. The hot water then rises back into the riverbed through fault-fed hot springs, which makes it a non-volcanic hydrothermal system. Atlas Obscura and Discover Wildlife both report this explanation. The river is also not itself a hot spring; it is a river fed by hot springs. Some outlets still call it "mysterious," and details such as the water's exact underground path are still being studied, but the main cause of the heat has been explained. That contradicts the claim that it remains one of the most unexplained wonders.
