text: There are over 8.7 million different species of animals on Earth, according to estimates by biologists, but scientists believe that this number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: ScienceDaily's 2011 report on the Mora et al. study puts the total at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) for all eukaryotic species on Earth, not just animals. Animals make up roughly 7.77 million of that total, with plants, fungi, protozoa and chromists making up the rest. So the claim that there are 'over 8.7 million species of animals' misstates the estimate. The same report gives earlier estimates as ranging from 3 million to 100 million, rather than the claim's upper figure of 30 million.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 65 thousand kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range and that it runs through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. The problem is the 'over 65 thousand kilometers' figure. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say it is 'nearly 65,000 km.' NOAA Ocean Service gives 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km. Wikipedia and USGS-linked material say 'about 65,000 km,' and one University of Delaware page says 'more than 56,000 km.' Only less reliable sites like Vedantu say 'over 65,000 km.' The most trustworthy sources lean toward 'nearly' or 'about' 65,000 km, so 'over' is not clearly supported, and the evidence on that point is mixed. Also, the Pacific part of the ridge, the East Pacific Rise, lies in the eastern Pacific rather than its center, so 'the center of' the Pacific is questionable.

text: The smallest crystal planet in our solar system is Mars, which has a tilted axis that causes its poles to be subjected to extreme temperatures compared to its equatorial regions.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's main point is wrong. "Crystal planet" isn't a real category, but it most likely means a rocky (terrestrial) planet. The smallest of those, and the smallest planet in the solar system overall, is Mercury, not Mars. Space.com and NASA both say this. It's true that Mars has a tilted axis, but that doesn't fix the false claim that it is the smallest.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to rest and settle together in a communal grouping.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source that calls a group of octopuses a "basket." Searching for "basket of octopuses" only turned up product listings and a news story about food. Collective-noun references name "consortium" as the main term, with "tangle" as a playful alternative. Study.com and A-Z Animals add that there is no widely accepted collective noun, because octopuses mostly live alone rather than in groups. The Pacific striped octopus is a noted exception. That undercuts the claim's reason that octopuses tend to rest together.

text: Olympic champion and amend 43rd U.S. President Jimmy Carter unwittingly grabbed onto and majoredly lifted a Virginia grown 400-pound tree stump from his television series (The Greatest American Hero with 4,800 (tree decaying)) lbs.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled and contains several statements that are plainly false. Jimmy Carter was the 39th U.S. President, not the 43rd (George W. Bush was the 43rd). Carter was never an Olympic champion. He also had no television series. 'The Greatest American Hero' was an ABC series (1981–83) created by Stephen J. Cannell and starring William Katt, and Carter had nothing to do with it. No credible source reports Carter lifting a 400-pound (or 4,800-lb) Virginia tree stump. I'm relying on well-established historical facts here; the source link points to a standard reference on Carter's presidency.

text: Theammu, an enormous crocodile, was estimated to weigh approximately 2,000 kilograms (4,400 pounds) and is considered the largest known saltwater crocodile to have ever existed.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a crocodile called "Theammu". Searches for the name only return unrelated social media accounts and people. Reliable sources give the title of largest accurately measured saltwater crocodile to another animal. Wikipedia and Guinness say it was Lolong, at about 1,075 kg (2,370 lb), roughly half the 2,000 kg in the claim. Cassius is another well-documented giant. The 2,000 kg number shows up only on one low-quality site, as a general upper estimate for the species, and not for any named crocodile. So the claim that "Theammu" weighed about 2,000 kg and is the largest known saltwater crocodile goes against reliable records.

text: Approximately 71% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with around 96.5% of it being seawater.
label: supported
reason: Phys.org, echoing the widely cited USGS figures, says water covers about 71% of Earth's surface and that 96.5% of all Earth's water is salt water held in the oceans. Both parts of the claim match.

text: Butler's Gorge Bridge, in Tasmania, Australia, holds the record for the longest single-span concrete arch bridge in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any bridge called "Butler's Gorge Bridge" that holds this record. Searches for Butlers Gorge in Tasmania turn up the Clark Dam, a concrete arch dam across the River Derwent completed in 1949, and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. The claim seems to confuse that arch dam with an arch bridge. The usual holder of this title is Sydney's Gladesville Bridge, a concrete arch with a 305 m span that was the world's longest concrete arch when it opened in 1964. My search for Gladesville hit the tool limit, so that part comes from what I already know rather than a result I retrieved. Even so, the evidence points to the claim being false.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world record for the longest recorded natural gorge.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a small rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. Its Wikipedia page lists a population of nil in 2016, a road ending at Lake King William Dam and local climate data, but it doesn't mention any world record. Several sources, including Live Science and WorldAtlas, say the world's longest canyon is the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon (also called the Tsangpo Gorge) in Tibet, at about 505 km. That contradicts the claim that Butlers Gorge holds the record.

text: Butler's Gorge, in Tasmania, is home to the highest consistent waterfall in Soughtern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Tugela Falls in South Africa, which is also in the Southern Hemisphere, drops 948 m and is ranked among the tallest waterfalls in the world. Tasmania.com names Montezuma Falls, at about 104 m, as Tasmania's highest waterfall. Even Tasmania's tallest falls are far shorter than Tugela, and Montezuma Falls is not at Butlers Gorge anyway. Butlers Gorge is known for Lake King William and Clark Dam, not for a record waterfall. Geoscience Australia also says that common claims about Australian waterfalls being the highest in the Southern Hemisphere ignore taller falls in South Africa and South America.

text: Cats have a unique Talent to Make themselves right-pawed or left-pawed when a brain function in a specific hemisphere begains to dominate.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say most individual cats favour one paw: in some studies about a third are right-pawed, a third left-pawed and a third have no preference. These sources tie paw preference to brain lateralization, since each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. Research has also linked paw dominance to hemisphere-related measures such as brain weight. The core claim, that a cat's right- or left-pawedness reflects which hemisphere dominates, is therefore supported. Two parts of the wording go beyond the evidence. Calling it a 'unique talent' is not backed up, because dogs and humans also show this kind of lateralization. And 'make themselves' is loose phrasing: cats don't choose a dominant paw, it develops from brain lateralization.

text: Malaria is a disease that affects over 228 million people worldwide each year.
label: supported
reason: WHO puts global malaria cases at 241 million in 2020, 263 million in 2023 and 282 million in 2024. Earlier WHO reports gave about 228 million for 2018. Every recent year is above 228 million, so 'over 228 million people worldwide each year' holds. One nuance: WHO counts cases, not people, but that is a fair reading of the claim.

text: The Fairy Spring located in Huaxi, China is the highest waterfall around the globe based on a non-direct plunge of 211 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because a 211 m waterfall can't be the tallest in the world. Encyclopaedia Britannica, Geology.com and Wikipedia all say Venezuela's Angel Falls is the world's tallest waterfall, at 979 m (3,212 ft). Even China's own tallest waterfalls, such as Baishui Fairy Waterfall in Guangzhou, aren't described as world record holders. My searches also found nothing reliable about a 'Fairy Spring' waterfall in Huaxi as the world's tallest.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range and that it is about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) long. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution calls it the planet's longest mountain range at nearly 65,000 km, and Guinness World Records lists it as the longest submarine range at 65,000 km. WorldAtlas gives the same figure. Some sources say 'nearly' or 'about' rather than 'over', and others commonly describe it as more than 65,000 km, so the small wording difference does not undermine the claim.

text: The screenWidth variable is a property of the screen that cannot be changed through code in CSS, but can be changed through XUL in Mozilla applications.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that describes a property actually named "screenWidth" in CSS or XUL, so it's unclear what the claim refers to. If it means window.screen.width, MDN says that property is read-only and reports the screen's width in CSS pixels, which fits the part about it not being changeable through code. But no source says the screen's width can be changed through XUL. XUL's window element has width and screenX/screenY attributes, and those set the window's size and position, not the screen's width. The XUL part can't be confirmed, and the claim names an unclear property, so the evidence doesn't settle it either way.

text: The universe is estimated to contain between 200 and 400 billion stars, although this number is constantly being refined as new discoveries are made.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA says the universe may contain up to one septillion (10^24) stars, and the Milky Way alone has more than 100 billion. Other sources put the observable universe at about 200 billion trillion stars. The claim's range of 200–400 billion stars is roughly the estimate for the Milky Way alone, not the whole universe, so it is wrong by many orders of magnitude.

text: There are approximately 37.5 trillion trees on Earth, with new forests being grown while others disappear due to human activities and natural causes.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate (Crowther et al., Nature, 2015) puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion, not 37.5 trillion. The 37.5 trillion figure is off by more than ten times. The same study says roughly 15 billion trees are cut down each year and that human activity is the biggest driver of tree numbers. That fits the general point about forest loss, but the specific number in the claim is wrong.

text: There are more particles in a single grain of sand than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.
label: supported
reason: Most estimates back this claim. The University of Hawaii figure, quoted by several sources, puts the number of sand grains on all of Earth's beaches at about 7.5 × 10^18. A typical ~1 mm quartz grain holds about 4×10^19 atoms (estimates run from about 10^19 to 10^20). The South African Institute of Physics, Quora answers and science explainer sites all say a single grain has more atoms than there are grains on Earth's beaches. If 'particles' includes subatomic particles like protons, neutrons and electrons, the count is about 30 times higher still. Two caveats: very fine grains (~0.1 mm) can hold fewer atoms than there are beach grains, and one site gives a lower atom estimate (~5×10^18). But for a typical grain, the claim holds.

text: There is enough DNA in the average human body to stretch from the Earth to the Moon and back about 100 times.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is off by roughly a factor of 1,000. Nature Scitable, a trustworthy source, says each person carries about 100 trillion meters (10^11 km) of DNA, enough to reach the Sun and back more than 300 times. Other estimates (about 2 m per cell × about 37 trillion cells ≈ 74 billion km) agree. A round trip to the Moon is about 769,000 km, so that much DNA would cover it roughly 100,000 times or more, not about 100 times. Some sites give other figures (about 1,500 times, or even 4), but no reliable source supports 'about 100 times'.

text: The vibrant flower, the infamous Opal Flower or the more popular known yuka flower,  is a rare snapdragons cultivar (yuka 'Snapdragon') from USA typically famous for having these Rainbow color variations of this flower on the flower by using the CRISPR breakthrough tech.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source for this claim. Nothing documents an 'Opal Flower' or 'yuka flower' as a snapdragon cultivar (yuka 'Snapdragon') from the USA, or any rainbow snapdragon made with CRISPR. The CRISPR flower-colour reports I found were about other plants, such as Japanese morning glory turned from violet to white in Japan, not rainbow snapdragons. Searches for 'yuka flower' only turned up unrelated results like an app, singers and anime characters. The claim looks like a viral or made-up story, but I found no fact-check that directly disproves it, so it can't be verified either way.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of the woven shape they can form together using their arms.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that calls a group of octopuses a "basket", and nothing supports the idea that they form a woven shape with their arms. Several sources say a group is usually called a "consortium" or, more playfully, a "tangle". Others point out that octopuses are mostly solitary, so there is no widely accepted collective noun for them at all. Either way, the claimed term and the explanation for it are not backed up.

text: Butler's Gorge in Australia is one of the deepest gorges in the world and is located in the grand tropic region of the Northern Territory.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality and gorge in Tasmania's Central Highlands, the site of Clark Dam on the Derwent River. It is not in the Northern Territory's tropical region. I found no reliable source calling it one of the world's deepest gorges.

text: Cactus flowers are typically only visible for about 24 hours before they bloom into fruit and subsequently wilt away.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe cactus flower lifespans as varying widely, from a few hours to one or two weeks. Plantin says most cactus flowers bloom for about 1 to 7 days. Succulent Alley notes that Discocactus, Coryphantha and Astrophytum flowers last longest, while Echinopsis and Lobivia flowers are the shortest-lived. The University of Arkansas Extension says Christmas cactus flowers last 4–5 days, and individual Easter cactus flowers keep opening and closing for 10–14 days. Some species do bloom for only a day, but that is not the typical case, so the claim of about 24 hours is contradicted. The claim also gets the order wrong: flowers wilt first, and the fruit develops afterward if the flower was pollinated.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique structure of their eyes, which force their eyelids to remain open.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say giraffes do close their eyes. They shut them during short naps while standing, and also when lying down in deeper sleep, and calves are seen sleeping with their eyes shut. Nothing I found says giraffes can't close their eyelids or that their eyelashes or eye structure keeps them open. These are safari and animal-information websites rather than scientific sources, but they agree with each other and nothing supports the claim.

text: HoneySpacing is unique because of its low viscosity which only occurs at a temperature around 89°F (31.7°C).
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing on a product, material or concept called "HoneySpacing." Searches for the name, including with "viscosity," only returned unrelated pages on honey dippers, honey rheology and beehive frame spacing. Since the claim's subject has no clear referent, I can't check whether it has low viscosity only at about 89°F (31.7°C).

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among all animals with big brains, typically living for just 1-5 years in the wild.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but the main point can't be confirmed. Several sources agree that octopuses are short-lived: most species live about 1–2 years, and the giant Pacific octopus lives about 3–5 years. That broadly fits the '1–5 years' range, though a few deep-sea species live longer. None of the sources says octopuses have the shortest lifespan of all big-brained animals; they only call it short compared with intelligent animals like dolphins, elephants and apes. Other cephalopods weaken that claim. MBARI says most squid, octopus and cuttlefish species live only about one year. Wikipedia says cuttlefish live about 1–2 years and have one of the largest brain-to-body size ratios. So squid and cuttlefish live as short or shorter lives. Because 'big brains' is vague, this falls short of a clear contradiction, but the evidence doesn't back the 'shortest' claim.

text: Riding a unicycle is considered a cognitive activity that can help improve balance and coordination in the brain.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed research supports the main point of the claim. A Scientific Reports study (Nature, also on PMC) found that learning to ride a unicycle reorganizes gray- and white-matter networks linked to motor and cognitive functions, which supports more automated postural (balance) control. A follow-up fMRI study on PMC found that functional brain changes after a unicycle intervention tracked riders' skill and supported more efficient balance coordination. Popular health sources, such as Dr Helena Popovic and NewsBytes, also describe unicycling as a demanding skill that needs concentration and builds balance and coordination. The research describes unicycling mainly as a complex balance or motor-learning task that also involves cognitive brain networks, rather than literally calling it a 'cognitive activity.' Still, nothing in the sources contradicts the claim.

text: Seahorses are one of the only species in the animal kingdom where the male becomes pregnant and gives birth to live young, a unique reproductive process called male pregnancy.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources (Science, Wikipedia's 'Male pregnancy' article, and ScienceABC) say male seahorses carry the young and give birth. They describe this male pregnancy as limited to seahorses and their close relatives in the family Syngnathidae, pipefish and seadragons. That fits the claim that seahorses are "one of the only" animals where this happens. The process is called male pregnancy.

text: Seahorses are one of the only species in the animal kingdom where the male becomes pregnant and gives birth to live young, a unique reproductive process known as male pregnancy.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Science.org calls seahorses the only group of animals in which males go through pregnancy and give birth. Wikipedia's article on male pregnancy says this is found in the family Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefish and seadragons. That fits the claim's wording 'one of the only' species, and the process is called male pregnancy.

text: The VOCABULARY COACH Gmail spam filter and search bot spam were eradicated from 2023 onwards as a result of Natural Language Processing and specific AI approach.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any 'VOCABULARY COACH' Gmail spam filter, so that part of the claim can't be verified. The main assertion, that Gmail spam and search bot spam were eradicated from 2023 onwards, is clearly false. A recent peer-reviewed paper (AIP Conference Proceedings) says email platforms like Gmail are still 'having the hardest time managing spam emails.' It describes NLP and machine learning as improving spam filtering, not eliminating it, and calls spam an 'escalating issue' that requires detection methods to keep evolving.

text: The VOCABULARY COACH Gmail spam filter program attained a substantial 99.9% precision in 2007.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a program called "VOCABULARY COACH" exists as a Gmail spam filter. The results only discuss Gmail's spam filtering in general, saying Google claims it blocks about 99.9% of spam. That is a block-rate figure, not a precision figure, and none of the sources I found ties it to 2007. Another filter, CRM114, reported 99.87% accuracy in 2002, but it is a different program. The name, the 99.9% precision figure and the 2007 date all remain unverified. I hit the search limit before I could look further.

text: The aforementioned Dover Street Market in London, is estimated to be around 40,000 square meters.
label: contradicted
reason: WWD says the London Dover Street Market's Haymarket store is 31,384 square feet, which is about 2,900 square meters. That makes it triple the size of the original Dover Street shop. The claimed size of around 40,000 square meters is more than ten times the actual figure.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, but it appears so bright in the sky because of an unusual alignment of its thick atmosphere and the way it reflects sunlight.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that Venus is the brightest planet in Earth's sky. They disagree with the claim's explanation, though. EarthSky and National Geographic say Venus looks so bright because it is close to Earth, fairly large, and covered by permanent, highly reflective clouds that give it a high albedo (bond albedo about 0.75). None of them mention an 'unusual alignment' of its atmosphere. Its brightness is a steady physical property, not the result of some unusual alignment, so that part of the claim is wrong.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on Venus is 243 Earth days.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that defines or even mentions a "Khayagan day." It looks like a made-up or unknown term, so the claim's main subject has no clear referent. Venus does take about 243 Earth days to rotate once relative to the stars (its sidereal day), but its solar day is about 116.75 Earth days. Because "Khayagan day" can't be matched to either measure, the claim can't be checked.

text: The longest an egg can remain incubated on land is around 9 to 10 days, without the need for fertilization or any external energy source.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the longest an egg can stay incubated on land is about 9–10 days, but that is far too short. Kiwi eggs take 63–92 days to incubate, and tuatara eggs generally take 11 to 16 months. Even a chicken egg takes about 21 days. The added idea that this happens 'without the need for fertilization or any external energy source' is also scientifically wrong: an unfertilized egg does not develop, and incubation needs outside heat.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is estimated to be the valley carving mountain range on Mars, which is over 4,000 kilometers long.
label: contradicted
reason: The 4,000-km feature on Mars is Valles Marineris, which Wikipedia lists as a fault system and Caltech calls a giant canyon, not a mountain range. It is known as the largest canyon in the solar system, not the longest mountain range. Wikipedia also says Earth's mid-ocean ridge forms a mountain system about 65,000 km long, which is far longer than any 4,000-km range. So the claim confuses a canyon with a mountain range and is wrong about it being the longest.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spanning over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. WHOI's Ocean Learning Hub calls the Mid-Ocean Ridge Earth's longest mountain range and says it is made up of 40,000 continuous miles (65,000 km) of underwater volcanoes that encircle the globe. WorldAtlas also describes it as the longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km. I didn't find a source that disputes this. One caveat: these sources give the length as about 65,000 km rather than spelling out 'over' that figure. That wording is a minor difference, and NOAA is commonly cited as saying the ridge is more than 65,000 km long, but I didn't open NOAA's page to confirm it.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," mainly due to its complex pronunciation.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. 'Stewardesses' has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be a one-syllable word. It is famous for something else: it's the longest common word you can type with only the left hand on a QWERTY keyboard. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable English words gives candidates such as 'strengths', 'scraunched' and 'strengthed'. 'Stewardesses' is not one of them.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived and fastest swimming shark species on record, capable of reaching speeds of up to 46 mph in the ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say the shortfin mako is the fastest shark, with top-speed estimates ranging from about 30 to 46 mph, but nothing shows it is the shortest-lived shark. It actually lives a fairly long time: about 29 years for males and 32 for females (EBSCO, Sharkwater, Oregon Sea Grant), and many smaller shark species have much shorter lifespans. The 'shortest-lived' part of the claim is false.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived shark specie with a maximum lifespan of around 10 to 13 years.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both points. A California Department of Fish and Wildlife report says shortfin makos are estimated to live up to about 29 years, and that females do not mature until about 19 to 21 years old. That is far more than 10 to 13 years. Other studies estimate ages of around 30 or more. The species is not the shortest-lived shark either: several small sharks live much shorter lives.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.1 x 10^8 times larger than the Earth's surface area.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Wikipedia's data on the Sun gives its surface area as about 6.09×10^12 km², which it says is roughly 12,000 times Earth's. That fits with the Sun's radius being about 109 times Earth's, since 109² ≈ 11,900. The figure 5.1×10^8 is actually Earth's own surface area in km², not the ratio between the two, so the claim mixes up the numbers.

text: The total surface area of the moon is approximately 34.4 million square kilometers, making it the fifth-largest moon in the solar system.
label: contradicted
reason: WorldAtlas puts the Moon's surface area at about 38 million km² (14.6 million sq mi), which matches the standard figure of roughly 37.9 million km². The claim's figure of 34.4 million km² is wrong. The same source does confirm that the Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the solar system, after Ganymede, Titan, Callisto and Io, but the surface-area number makes the claim as a whole contradicted.

text: The village ofuya in Nigeria has some residents that have ears that are shorter or absent because of a genetic condition.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source on a Nigerian village called "Ofuya" or on residents there with short or missing ears caused by a genetic condition. My searches turned up unrelated results: Ofu, a different place in Nigeria, a study of childhood hearing loss in the Yoruba population, and a person named Ofuya. My later searches failed because I hit the tool's usage limit. Without evidence for or against the claim, I can't judge it.

text: ThefadeIn of the AuroraBorealis (Northern Lights) can be caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with the Earth's magnetic field.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources, including PBS Nature and EarthSky, say the aurora borealis happens when charged particles from the sun interact with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere. That matches the core of the claim. The garbled word "fadeIn" doesn't change that main causal statement, and nothing in the sources contradicts it.

text: There are more neutrons in an atomic nucleus than there are protons and electrons in the entire known universe combined when considering the mass and energy present.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. The number of protons in the observable universe is estimated at about 10^79 to 10^80 (Eddington's figure is about 1.575 × 10^79). A single atomic nucleus holds at most a few hundred neutrons; the heaviest known nuclei have fewer than about 180. One nucleus cannot have more neutrons than all the protons and electrons in the universe combined, and the added condition about mass and energy doesn't change that.

text: There is a species of shellfish called the sea sponge that can be over 2,000 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The age part is right: some sea sponges live far longer than 2,000 years. The Max Planck Institute and peer-reviewed work on the glass sponge Monorhaphis chuni put one specimen at about 11,000 years old, and Rossella species are estimated at 1,500 to 23,000 years. The rest of the claim is wrong, though. A sea sponge is not shellfish. Sponges make up their own animal phylum, Porifera, while shellfish are molluscs and crustaceans. 'Sea sponge' is also the common name for the whole phylum, not a single species; Wikipedia's Sponge article describes sponges or sea sponges as marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera. Because the claim gets what kind of animal this is wrong, it is contradicted.

text: There is a species of shellfish called the sea sponge, although they're not actually that, they are known to have diversity of organisms flourishing within their structures.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is true: sponges are well known for hosting a wide variety of organisms, especially complex microbial communities. But the main premise is wrong. Sponges are not shellfish, and 'sea sponge' is not the name of a species. It covers a whole phylum, Porifera, which reliable sources describe as early-diverging animals. The phrase 'although they're not actually that' is ambiguous and does not fix the incorrect description of sea sponges as a species of shellfish.

text: Caterpillars have unique hairs on their bodies that contain a toxin to defend against predators, and some species can release a foul-smelling liquid to deter attackers.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim are backed by reliable sources, as long as the first part is read as describing some caterpillars rather than all of them. Clemson Extension and Northern Woodlands say many caterpillars have special defensive hairs (urticating setae) against predators, and some of these hairs are hollow or connected to poison sacs that release venom. A-Z Animals says swallowtail caterpillars push out an osmeterium gland that releases a foul-smelling chemical to ward off predators, which matches the claim that some species release a foul-smelling liquid.

text: The Vogel's starling, a bird species found in Australia, is known for its unique ability to change the color of its feathers to blend in with its surroundings.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a bird species called "Vogel's starling." Searches only turned up unrelated results, such as the Vogelkop bowerbird of New Guinea and German pages that use "Vogel" ("bird") and "Star" ("starling"). Several zoo sources (Philadelphia Zoo and others) say the metallic starling (Aplonis metallica) is Australia's only native starling. That conflicts with the claim that a native "Vogel's starling" lives in Australia, though it doesn't rule out a reference to an introduced species. The colour-changing claim also has no support. Sources on starling plumage describe fixed iridescence that only looks different depending on the angle of the light. Sources on birds changing colour describe seasonal moults, not a quick change to blend in with surroundings. The claim appears to be made up, and the sources contradict it.

text: Thekinetic energy generated by a speeding bullet can cause a crater of up to 2 centimeters deep in the surface of the Earth in ideal conditions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that sets a maximum of 2 cm for a bullet crater in the ground under ideal conditions. Lab studies, such as a Scientific Reports paper on bullets hitting building stone, show that crater size depends on the projectile's energy and the material it hits. That means there is no single figure for 'the surface of the Earth.' Bullets can also travel much deeper than 2 cm into soft soil, so the 2 cm limit can be neither confirmed nor ruled out. The claim is also too vague about the bullet, the surface material and what counts as ideal conditions to check.

text: The total surface area of the Moon is approximately 34.4 million square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Universe Today and other sources give the Moon's surface area as about 37.9 million km² (roughly 14.6 million square miles). That figure also checks out against the Moon's diameter of 3,474 km. The claim's 34.4 million km² is too low by about 3.5 million km².

text: CÃ NSFIS, the largest planet in our solar system, has a mass of approximately 2.25 x 10^26 kilograms.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no planet called "CÃ NSFIS". The largest planet in our solar system is Jupiter. The Canadian Space Agency gives Jupiter's mass as about 1.9 × 10^27 kg, roughly 318 Earth masses. That is about 8.4 times the 2.25 × 10^26 kg in the claim. Both the planet's name and its mass are wrong.

text: Did you know that honey is actually supersaturated with water, despite its thick and viscous texture, which is due to the unique properties of its molecular structure?
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is supersaturated with sugar, not with water. McGill's Office for Science and Society calls it a supersaturated sugar solution that is only about 17% water. A chemistry textbook resource agrees, explaining that honey holds more sugar than its water can dissolve at room temperature. Its low water content and high sugar concentration are what make it thick, so the claim gets the key fact backwards.

text: Did you know that honey is actually supersaturated with water, despite its thick and viscous texture, which is due to the unique properties of its sugar composition?
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the chemistry backwards. Honey is a supersaturated solution of sugar, not of water. It holds more dissolved sugar (mostly glucose and fructose) than its water could normally keep in solution at room temperature, and it is only about 17–20% water. Its thick texture comes from that high sugar concentration and low water content, not from being 'supersaturated with water.'

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be found in the stomachs of bees that have died up to 5,000 years ago?
label: contradicted
reason: What checks out: honey's low moisture and chemistry let it last for thousands of years, and archaeologists have found edible honey in sealed pots in ancient Egyptian tombs about 3,000 years old. What doesn't: no reliable source says ancient honey has been found in the stomachs of bees that died up to 5,000 years ago. The record points to honey stored in sealed jars and pots, so that part distorts the real finding. Also, 'never spoils' is too strong: honey lasts this long only if it is stored properly.

text: One in every 512 people on Earth has a rare genetic trait known as polydactyly, which results in having extra fingers or toes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the exact "1 in 512" figure, and part of the claim is shaky. Medical sources do confirm that polydactyly means extra fingers or toes, but they give a wide range of incidence estimates rather than one number. These include about 1.7 per 1,000 live births (roughly 1 in 590), 1 in 700 pregnancies, 0.3–3.6 per 1,000, and 8.4 per 10,000. Rates also vary a lot by ancestry, from 1 in 143 to 1 in 1,339. The 1-in-512 figure falls within that range, but no source supports it as a precise worldwide rate. The figures are also given per birth, not as a share of everyone alive. Calling it 'rare' is debatable, since it is one of the more common congenital limb differences.

text: Otters are able to drink saltwater because they have a special gland located above their eyes that filters out excess salt from the water they consume.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that sea otters can drink seawater, but they credit large, specialized kidneys for this, not a gland above the eyes. These kidneys can produce urine with sodium and chloride levels close to those of seawater (PubMed review on osmoregulation in marine mammals; Wikipedia's reniculate kidney article; floofmania). The salt glands above the eyes described in the claim are found in seabirds (cephalic/supraorbital salt glands), not otters. So the mechanism the claim gives is wrong.

text: Researchers have discovered that there are more trees on Earth now than there were 35 years ago, thanks to a global reforestation effort.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2018 Nature study (Song et al., University of Maryland/NASA) did find that global tree cover grew by about 2.24 million km² between 1982 and 2016, roughly the past 35 years. However, reports on the study don't credit a coordinated global reforestation effort. Tropical forest loss continued, and the gains came mostly from subtropical, temperate, boreal and polar regions. The drivers were a mix: climate warming that let trees grow in areas once too cold, abandoned farmland reverting to trees, and plantations in places like China. Coverage also notes that tree cover is not the same as forest cover. The claim's 'more trees' finding is accurate, but its stated cause is wrong.

text: The discharge of a blue whale can weigh as much as 40 pounds due to the massive amount of krill and saltwater it ingests.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The one search that worked found A-Z Animals and National Geographic pages saying blue whales eat about 4 tons (around 8,000 pounds) of krill a day. A-Z Animals also says their poop is pink and pebble-like because of the krill. Neither page gives a weight for one 'discharge,' so the 40-pound figure isn't confirmed or ruled out. Neither page backs up the claim that swallowed saltwater adds to the weight. My further searches failed with errors and then hit the tool's usage limit. Popular accounts often say one bowel movement can be around 200 liters, which would weigh far more than 40 pounds, but I couldn't confirm that with a source here.

text: The driest desert in the world is the Atacama Desert in Chile, accounting for only 0.01% of the world's freshwater resources.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part is roughly right. Many sources call the Atacama in Chile the driest non-polar desert, or the driest place where people live. But they also point out that parts of Antarctica, especially the McMurdo Dry Valleys, are drier, so calling the Atacama the driest desert overall is debatable. My searches found nothing to back the figure that the Atacama holds only 0.01% of the world's freshwater resources. That number looks made up and can't be checked, so the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: The length of the eye of the Argonaut octopus can be detached and used as an independent organ for vision.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as National Geographic and The Nature Conservancy say the part of the male argonaut that detaches is the hectocotylus. This is a modified, sperm-bearing arm used for mating, not for vision. It is kept in a pouch under the left eye, which is probably where the mix-up came from. None of the sources says the eye, or any part of it, can detach and work as an independent organ for seeing.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) long. WHOI also calls it the planet's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. One wording difference: NOAA says "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Other sources give lengths of 65,000 km or more, so this is a small difference. The main facts are correct: it is the longest range, and the figures of 65,000 km and 40,390 miles match.

text: The periodic table's element with the highest number of naturally occurring isotopes is Lead, which has a total of 24 known isotopes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the element wrong. Tin (Sn), not lead, has the most stable, naturally occurring isotopes, with 10. Guinness World Records and WebElements both say so. Lead has only 4 stable isotopes. The figure of 24 is also wrong: about 43 isotopes of lead are known.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. NOAA gives its length as "nearly 65,000 kilometers," and Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range. Wikipedia and New World Encyclopedia put the whole ridge system at about 80,000 km, and other sources say "over 65,000 km." So the length in the claim matches the accepted figures, even though NOAA's wording ("nearly") is slightly more cautious than "over."

text: There are approximately 1.3 billion unique species of organisms on Earth, according to estimates from taxonomists and scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The most widely cited scientific estimate, from Mora et al. (2011), puts the number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. That breaks down to about 6.5 million on land and 2.2 million in the oceans. Earlier expert guesses ranged from 3 million to 100 million. The claim's figure of 1.3 billion looks like the study's margin of error (±1.3 million) mistaken for the total, and it is not a recognised estimate from taxonomists.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some estimates suggesting as many as 100 sextillion stars exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim gets the logic backwards. Astronomers estimate the number of stars by multiplying the number of galaxies by the typical number of stars per galaxy. So the star count can't be larger than what the galaxies contain; it comes from what they contain. Yahoo/The Conversation multiplies about 100 billion stars per galaxy by about 2 trillion galaxies to get roughly 200 sextillion stars. Big Think says the newer, higher galaxy counts add little to the star total, which it puts at about 2 sextillion. Some estimates do reach the 100-sextillion range, but the second part of the claim doesn't fix the false premise in the first.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be approximately 3 trillion trees versus 200-400 billion stars.
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that Earth has about 3 trillion trees, based on Crowther et al.'s 2015 study in Nature. NASA puts the Milky Way at about 100–400 billion stars. The claim gives 200–400 billion, which sits inside NASA's range, and both ranges are far below 3 trillion. The main point holds: Earth has more trees than the Milky Way has stars. The only difference is that the claim's lower bound is narrower than NASA's.

text: There are over 320 million trees in London's urban area, which is roughly 21% of the city's residents.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say London has about 8.4 million trees, not over 320 million. That is roughly one tree for each of its approximately 8.6 million residents. The 21% figure is London's tree canopy cover, not a share of its residents, so the claim gets both the tree count and the meaning of the 21% figure wrong.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1993, is the world's oldest discovered boat, dating back over 8,000 years to the Stone Age era.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a "Janszoon boom log" exists. Searching for it only brought up unrelated pages, such as one on the explorer Willem Janszoon. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia and Live Science, say the world's oldest known boat is the Pesse canoe. It was found in 1955 near Pesse in the Netherlands, not in 1993, and dates to about 8040–7510 BC. The claim's age of over 8,000 years matches the Pesse canoe, but its name for the boat and its discovery date are wrong.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology, which allows it to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife) says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. It credits their unique wings, which can move in a figure-of-eight pattern. GardenBird also names hummingbirds as the only birds that fly backwards and links this to the figure-8 wing motion. One caveat: GardenBird notes that a few birds, such as herons, egrets and warblers, may briefly move backwards defensively. However, it says only hummingbirds can truly sustain backward flight, so the general claim stands.

text: Butler's Gorge Bridge, in Tasmania, Australia, holds the record for the longest single-span concrete arch bridge in the world, spanning 221 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: The record for the longest concrete arch span belongs to China's Tian'e Longtan Bridge, with a 600 m main span (ENR, Wikipedia). Earlier record holders were Krk Bridge at 390 m and Gladesville Bridge in Sydney at 305 m (ASCE). A 221 m span would therefore not be a world record. I found no sources describing a record-holding "Butler's Gorge Bridge": Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania known for its hydroelectric power station.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers and runs through all the world's oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources confirm the main parts of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km, and Wikipedia says the connected ridge system is part of every ocean. The length detail is not exact: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Other sources put it at or above that figure, though. Wikipedia gives about 65,000 km, and a NASA page gives 74,000 km. Because figures range from roughly 65,000 to 74,000 km, the difference is small, and nothing contradicts the main point of the claim.

text: Lemons are not naturally acidic and become sour due to a process that breaks down the fruit's natural sugars, which creates citric acid and ascorbic acid that gives them their distinctive flavor and high pH acidity.
label: contradicted
reason: WebMD says citric acid occurs naturally in citrus fruits and that lemon juice has a pH of about 2 to 3. That makes lemons naturally acidic, with a low pH rather than a high one. This contradicts the claim that lemons aren't naturally acidic and only become sour through sugar breakdown that leaves them with "high pH acidity."

text: There are over 8 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate by the Secretary-General of the International Institute for Species Exploration.
label: contradicted
reason: The details in the claim don't match the record. Wikipedia says the International Institute for Species Exploration (IISE) was founded in 2007 and shut down in 2018, so it couldn't have made an estimate in 2020. Its leader, Quentin Wheeler, was the executive director, not a Secretary-General. The well-known figure of about 8.7 million species came from a 2011 estimate that the institute helped with. So 'over 8 million species' is roughly right, but the 2020 date and the Secretary-General attribution are wrong.

text: The Taj Mahal in India is made up of over 28 types of precious and semiprecious stones, including jasper, jade, and diamonds.
label: supported
reason: Many sources say about 28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stones were inlaid in the Taj Mahal's white marble. They include jasper from Punjab, jade and crystal from China, and diamonds from Panna. One caveat: most sources give the number as exactly 28 or 'as many as 28', not 'over 28'. Wonders-of-the-world.net comes closest to the claim, saying there were no fewer than 28 kinds and that its list is not complete. The wording differs slightly, but the main points of the claim match the evidence.

text: There are more than 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2023 report by the World Wildlife Fund.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure did not come from a 2023 World Wildlife Fund report. It comes from a 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues, published in PLoS Biology and covered by Science and ScienceDaily, which estimated about 8.7 million (± 1.3 million) eukaryotic species, not 'more than' 8.7 million. WWF's own page gives a different range: 5 to 15 million species of plants, animals and micro-organisms. So both the source and the wording of the claim are wrong.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland (Mana) unique to a leveret is mostly composed of organisms that cannot be found anywhere else on Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. I found no island called "Mana" off Iceland, so it's unclear what place the claim means. A leveret is a young hare, and Iceland has no native hares; the Arctic fox is its only native land mammal. I found no record of a tick fauna tied to leverets in or around Iceland. A survey of ticks in Iceland lists eight species. Most are widespread species brought in by migratory birds, such as Ixodes ricinus. Only two seabird ticks, I. uriae and I. caledonicus, are considered native to Iceland, and neither is unique to it. That suggests Icelandic ticks are not mostly found nowhere else on Earth. Still, because the island and the host can't be identified, the claim can't be clearly confirmed or disproved.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to create a single glass of honey.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are wrong. A bee makes only about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life, so a 16-oz jar takes around 1,152 bees (Chowhound). A glass of honey cannot be made without bees. Honey is also not the only bee-made food people eat: royal jelly and bee pollen (bee bread) are commonly eaten too.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge system, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main point. NOAA Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at 40,389 miles (about 65,000 km). NOAA Ocean Exploration also calls it the longest and largest range. Wikipedia and WorldAtlas give about 65,000 km. Educational sources place parts of the system in the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Indian Ocean ridges) and Pacific (East Pacific Rise) Oceans. Two details are looser than the claim states. First, NOAA Ocean Exploration says 'nearly' 65,000 km, not 'over', so the figure is approximate either way. Second, the Pacific segment runs through the eastern Pacific, not the exact center. Neither detail changes the overall claim, so I rate it supported.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, just like fingerprints, which can be used to identify individuals.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed studies on tongue prints as a biometric, including a preliminary study in a dental/medical journal and a systematic review in forensic odontology, say each person's tongue has a unique shape and surface texture. They describe tongue prints as hard to forge and usable for identification, in the same way fingerprints are. The research calls this an emerging method that still needs more study, but that does not undercut the claim that tongue prints are unique and can be used to identify people.

text: ButDia'hismo, a unique new species of jellyfish, was discovered in 2020 off the coast of Australia.
label: not_verifiable

label: not_verifiable

text: Honeybee colonies make decisions through a form of democracy by voting with their dances.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Thomas Seeley's research, presented in his book "Honeybee Democracy", shows that when a swarm looks for a new home, scout bees advertise candidate nest sites with waggle dances. They follow a set of "voting" rules and gradually reach a consensus on the best site, with no single leader deciding. Betterbee, reviews of Seeley's book and an arXiv paper on nest-site selection all describe this dance-based collective decision. One caveat: the best-documented case is nest-site selection by scouts during swarming, but that is the standard example behind this claim.

text: Regions in Yellowstone National Park have areas where the ground can be so hot that it melts sneakers and scorch trees.
label: supported
reason: My searches clearly back up the tree part of the claim. The Bozeman Daily Chronicle reported that during the 2003 thermal disturbance at Norris Geyser Basin, ground temperatures reached about 200°F in places, which was hot enough to boil water and kill trees and other plants. A peer-reviewed Frontiers paper and USGS also say that trees in Yellowstone died from rising ground heat. National Parks Traveler, USGS and SFGate describe hot ground strong enough to soften or 'melt' asphalt roads, and the park closed about half of Norris to visitors for safety. However, none of the results I could read said directly that the ground melted sneakers. I hit the search limit before I could check that detail. The sneaker part is plausible given the heat described, but it is the weakest part of the claim. My verdict of supported rests mainly on the strong evidence for scorched trees and dangerously hot ground.

label: not_verifiable

The closest result was a PMC study of nose length during smiling, not flaring. It found an average increase of about 2.5% and a maximum of about 12%, and the 30% figure in that study refers to a drop in upper lip height. Nostril flaring mainly widens the nose rather than lengthening it, but no source directly confirms or rules out a 30% length change. I hit the search limit before I could check further, so there isn't enough evidence to decide either way.

Earth's diameter of about 12,742 km is correct, but the ratio is wrong.

text: The Nazi regime was responsible for the deaths of approximately 6 million Jews during the Holocaust.
label: supported

text: The cheese produced by the same process of fermentation, as with wine, is known as a type of cheese called "wine washed cheese."
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including ScienceDirect's overview of washed-rind cheese and a cheese guide from Striped Spatula, say wine-washed cheeses are washed-rind cheeses. During aging, their rind is bathed or brushed with brine or alcohol such as wine, beer, or brandy. The name comes from washing the surface with wine, not from making the cheese through the same fermentation process used for wine. Cheese is made by curdling milk and then ripening it with bacteria. Because the claim gets the defining process wrong, the evidence contradicts it.

text: The highest recorded speed reached by the bloodhound in a 100 yard dash was 45 miles per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Reliable sources say bloodhounds are scent hounds bred for stamina and tracking, not speed. In the AKC Fast CAT, the standard timed 100-yard dash for dogs, 45 mph is about the top speed of greyhounds, the fastest breed. Even greyhounds are often verified at roughly 41.8–43 mph. No credible source shows a bloodhound clocking 45 mph in a 100-yard dash. The only claim of 45 mph for bloodhounds came from a low-quality grooming blog, which did not mention any 100-yard dash record. Search results for 'Bloodhound' speed records instead point to the Bloodhound LSR car, which hit 628 mph and has nothing to do with a 100-yard dash. Overall, the evidence goes against the claim, though I didn't find a published official bloodhound Fast CAT record.

text: The highest recorded speed reached by the bloodhound in a 100-meter sprint is 35 miles per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: Taking 'the bloodhound' to mean the dog breed, the claim doesn't hold up. PetCalculator, which draws on American Kennel Club race data, says the fastest recorded speed for a bloodhound is 22.08 mph (35.5 km/h), with an average of about 19.7 mph. A-Z Animals gives a top speed of about 25 mph. The '35' figure seems to come from mixing up kilometres per hour with miles per hour. AKC sprints are run over 100 yards, not 100 meters, but the speed is the clear error. Whippets are the breed usually credited with 35 mph, not bloodhounds. If the claim meant the Bloodhound LSR car, its 628 mph top speed doesn't match either.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is located on the planet Venus, known as the Maxwell Montes mountain range.
label: contradicted
reason: Maxwell Montes is real, but the sources describe it as Venus's highest mountain range, not the longest range in the solar system. It is only about 850 km long from north to south (eSky). Other ranges are much longer: Earth's Andes run about 7,000 km, and the equatorial ridge on Saturn's moon Iapetus wraps around more than 75% of that moon's equator, roughly 1,300 km or more. So the claim that Maxwell Montes is the solar system's longest mountain range is false.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland has remained unchanged from over 20 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source saying that any island off Iceland has had the same ticks for more than 20 million years, and the evidence points the other way. Iceland is only about 16–20 million years old, and islands off its coast are younger still; Surtsey, for example, formed in 1963. That date comes from geological background knowledge, since a search to confirm it couldn't be completed. Research on the origins of Iceland's fauna supports colonization after the last Ice Age rather than long-term survival. Iceland's tick list has also changed over time: Icelandic Agricultural Sciences reports eight tick species, mostly brought in by migratory birds. Only Ixodes uriae and I. caledonicus are treated as native, and I. ricinus is increasingly being found. In the nearby Faroe Islands, new tick species have been recorded and I. ricinus is spreading. The claim doesn't name a specific island, but the evidence above rules out a tick fauna that has stayed the same for 20 million years.

text: The wavelength of light from a firefly's glow is so unique that scientists have discovered a species of Brazilian mosquitoes can use it to locate prey.
label: not_verifiable

The results covered unrelated topics: Aedes aegypti using infrared to find human hosts, mosquitoes being drawn to certain colours of light, bats learning to avoid fireflies, and Photuris fireflies using light to lure prey. None of this confirms the claim, and nothing directly disproves it, so it cannot be verified.

text: There are over 8 trillion tree seedlings grown every year, which is a significant percentage of the trees that currently exist on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no source for the figure of 8 trillion tree seedlings grown each year. Credible sources point to much lower numbers. The Yale-led study in Nature estimated that just over 3 trillion trees exist on Earth, so 8 trillion a year would be more than all existing trees, not a percentage of them. Estimates of trees planted worldwide each year are about 1.2 to 1.8 billion, and US nursery output peaked around 2.6 billion seedlings a year in the late 1980s. The '8' may come from a misreading of the Yale finding that the 3 trillion total is roughly eight times higher than earlier estimates. One caveat: I didn't find a figure for seeds that germinate naturally in the wild, but the claim doesn't fit what the sources say.

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the fastest ants in the world, capable of reaching speeds of up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no ant called the "Butterfly Pavement Ant." They only found the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium), and no source lists it among the fastest ants. Several reliable sources (Science/AAAS, EurekAlert, Guinness World Records, Wikipedia) name the Saharan silver ant (Cataglyphis bombycina) as the fastest ant in the world. Its record top speed is 855 mm/s, which is about 3.1 km/h or 1.9 mph. The claimed speed of up to 4 km/h (2.5 mph) is higher than the world-record ant speed, so the claim is contradicted.

text: Giraffes have a unique uneven heartbeat pattern, with a long heartbeat followed by a short heartbeat, known as "sinus arrhythmia," allowing them to pump blood efficiently throughout their long necks.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that giraffes have a unique heartbeat pattern of one long beat followed by one short beat. Reliable sources explain giraffe circulation differently: they credit very high blood pressure and a thick-walled left ventricle with pumping blood up the neck, not an irregular rhythm. The research on giraffe hearts I found also didn't describe this rhythm. The claim also misuses the term "sinus arrhythmia." The Cleveland Clinic describes it as a common, often normal change in heart rate that follows breathing, so it isn't unique to giraffes and isn't a long-short beat pattern. Because the term is defined wrongly and the giraffe research gives a different reason for pumping efficiency, the claim is contradicted. My search was cut off by a tool limit before I could run a direct search for "giraffe sinus arrhythmia," though.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish, which can be found in the oceans around the world, can bioluminesce and is often seen with an ethereal glowing appearance.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge, not a jellyfish. It also isn't found in oceans around the world: it lives in the deep waters of the Pacific Ocean, usually below about 500 m. Since the claim gets both what the animal is and where it lives wrong, it is contradicted, whatever the truth about its glowing.

text: There are over 5,000 languages spoken worldwide, with only about 2% of the population speaking the top 20 languages.

That means the top 20 or so languages are spoken by close to half of all people, not about 2%.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoral geothermal field.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to a 2021 research by the University of Oxford's Zoological Museum.

text: The discharge of a blue whale can weigh as much as 40 pounds due to the massive amount of dissolved gases mixed with water that are forced out of its blowhole.
label: not_verifiable

The blue whale's blow (spout) is warm exhaled air that turns into a visible cloud when it hits colder air, mixed with water and oil droplets from the airways or from water resting on the blowhole. They don't describe it as a heavy mass of dissolved gases mixed with water. That casts doubt on the stated cause, but nothing directly confirms or rules out the 40-pound weight. text: The remains of "The Great Blue Hole," a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, were once part of a land bridge that existed during the last ice age.

None of the sources I found says the site was part of a land bridge. They say it was once dry land, which is not the same as being a land bridge linking two landmasses. No source directly says it was not one either, so the land-bridge part can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The Gotland horse, a rare and ancient breed of horse, is primarily found in Sweden and is known for its unique physical appearance and ability to thrive in harsh environments.
label: supported
reason: Skansen, a Swedish zoo, says the Gotland pony (also called the Gotland horse) is Sweden's only remaining native pony breed. It dates back to the Iron Age on the island of Gotland and has lived there for thousands of years, which supports "ancient." Skansen puts the total at about 6,000 animals, all in Sweden, and around 50 still roam semi-wild on Lojsta Heath. That supports both "rare" and "primarily found in Sweden." Skansen calls the breed "extremely hardy" and resistant to disease, and Mad Barn's breed guide describes it living semi-feral for centuries, which supports its ability to thrive in harsh conditions. "Unique physical appearance" is vague, but it fits the breed's small, distinctive pony build, and nothing found contradicts it.

label: contradicted

The longest one-syllable words in common use have nine letters, such as "screeched," "strengths," "scratched" and "stretched." Rare ten-letter words like "scraunched" and "strengthed" are also cited. "Smiley" has two syllables, so it doesn't fit either; the old riddle about "smiles" (a "mile" between the s's) is a joke, not a syllable record.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, situated in the Great Hungarian Plain, where nightingales migrate to mate, making it a significant stop for these birds during their migration.
label: not_verifiable

Kiskunfélegyháza is a town in Bács-Kiskun county on the Great Hungarian Plain, and birding sites list the common nightingale as breeding in the wider Kiskunság region, including Kiskunság National Park. But I found no source that names the Kiskunfélegyháza area as a unique ecosystem or as a significant stop for migrating nightingales. The claim is also internally muddled: nightingales come to this region to breed, which is not the same as using it as a stopover on their migration. Because the specific claim about Kiskunfélegyháza can't be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with approximately 3 trillion trees and 200-400 billion stars in the Milky Way.
label: supported
reason: The 2015 Crowther et al. study in Nature, which is widely cited, estimates there are about 3 trillion trees on Earth. NASA puts the Milky Way at roughly 100–400 billion stars. Even at the high end of that range, there are still about seven times more trees than stars, so the main point of the claim holds. The claim's 200–400 billion range is narrower than NASA's 100–400 billion. It still falls inside a commonly cited range, though, and the comparison works either way.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to produce a whole gallon of honey.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false on both points. Making honey takes the work of very many bees: Omlet works out that a single 454 g jar needs about 22,700 nectar-collecting trips, shared among thousands of bees, so a gallon could never be made with no bees at all. Honey also isn't the only bee product people eat, since royal jelly and bee pollen are eaten too.

text: Honey is the only food that babies can digest perfectly well when they're born, due to its unique properties that make it easily absorbed by the human body without any enzymatic breakdown.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Babies are born able to digest breast milk or formula, and both rely on enzymes such as lactase, so honey is not the only food newborns can digest. Health authorities also say babies under 12 months should not be given honey at all. Healthline notes that the Mayo Clinic advises against it because Clostridium botulinum spores can germinate in an infant's gut and cause infant botulism. Honey also does not skip enzymatic breakdown: it contains sucrose and other carbohydrates that need digesting.

text: The darkest and coldest known natural place in the universe is a region in space known as BO trips (Background Oscillation, also called the Boomerang, supernova remnant) or SN 1006.
label: contradicted
reason: The coldest known natural place in the universe is the Boomerang Nebula, at about 1 K. It is a young planetary (pre-planetary) nebula in Centaurus, about 5,000 light-years away. It is not a supernova remnant, it is not called "BO trips" or "Background Oscillation", and it is not SN 1006, which is a separate supernova remnant. The claim gets the identity of the object wrong.

text: The color blue is actually not visible to the human eye under normal conditions, as the light waves that make up the color blue are shorter than those that the human eye can detect.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Blue light has wavelengths of roughly 400–500 nm, which falls inside the range the human eye can see (about 380/400–700 nm). Blue is part of the visible spectrum. The search results also say that the human eye perceives these wavelengths as blue, so its claim that blue is too short for the eye to detect is wrong.

label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are false. Honey is not the only bee-made food people eat. Royal jelly, which worker bees secrete, is sold as a dietary supplement (Healthline, MSKCC, NCBI), and people also eat bee pollen and honeycomb. Honey also can't be made without bees. Bees produce it, and sources say it takes about 12 worker bees their whole lives to make one teaspoon.

text: The pillow was invented around 7,000 years back by the Mesopotamians who filled buckwheat bags with lamb's wool for neck support during sleep.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the earliest recorded pillows come from Mesopotamia, around 7,000 BC. That is about 9,000 years ago, not 7,000. These pillows were not cloth bags of buckwheat filled with lamb's wool. They were hard headrests made of carved stone, and sometimes of marble, ceramic, ivory or wood. Their main use was to keep insects out of sleepers' ears, nose and mouth. Because the claim gets the materials wrong, and the timeframe too, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 8 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to scientists, but it's estimated that 80-90% of them remain undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: A 2011 study led by Camilo Mora, covered by National Geographic, ScienceDaily and the University of Hawaii, estimates about 8.7 million species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million). Of these, about 7.77 million are animals and about 298,000 are plants, so plants and animals together come to just over 8 million. The study found that about 86% of species are still undescribed (Nature News put it as more than 80%), which falls within the claim's 80–90% range. One caveat: 'undiscovered' in the claim means 'not yet formally described' in the study.

text: A honeybee colony can perform complex calculations and recognize patterns to gather up to 60 pounds of pollen and nectar in a single day.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put a colony's daily intake far below 60 pounds. USGS says that under good conditions a colony can collect "several pounds of nectar in a single day" and about 40 lb of pollen in a whole year. Wikipedia's Honey flow article says a hive may gain 4–10 kg (9–22 lb) in a day, and one beekeeping source gives a research-station record of 28 lb in a day, about half of it water lost overnight. Only one low-authority blog (beekeepercorner.com) says up to 60 lb of nectar per day, which is outweighed by USGS and the measured weight data. The 'complex calculations' wording is also an overstatement. Because the main number is contradicted, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 8.7 million bird species existing on Earth according to recent estimates, with scientists continuing to learn more about the vast diversity of avifauna worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Recent estimates put the number of bird species at about 9,000–11,000 on standard checklists, or roughly 18,000 to 20,000 under broader species definitions such as the PLoS ONE study by Barrowclough and colleagues. The 8.7 million figure is a well-known estimate for all eukaryotic species on Earth, not for birds.

text: Honey, when rendered under heat, can act as an adhesive and has been used in ancient times to repair pottery.

text: There are approximately 328 million trees in the city of Los Angeles.
