text: There are over 200 million triangles in a standard deck of 52 playing cards.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source saying that a standard 52-card deck contains a number of "triangles," let alone more than 200 million. The search results confirm only that a standard deck has 52 rectangular cards. They also turned up unrelated novelty decks shaped like triangles and the well-known fact about how many ways a deck can be ordered. The claim doesn't explain what counts as a triangle. By my own calculation, which no source states, choosing any 3 of the 52 cards gives only 22,100 combinations. That is far below 200 million, but because the claim's meaning is unclear and no source addresses it, it can't be either confirmed or refuted.

text: There is an estimated 250 billion trees on Earth, accounting for over 75% of the planet's biomass.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate, from a 2015 study in Nature led by Thomas Crowther, puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. That is more than ten times the 250 billion in the claim. Even the older estimate the study replaced was just over 400 billion. Because the tree count is clearly wrong, the claim is contradicted. The second part, that trees make up over 75% of Earth's biomass, may roughly fit published estimates that plants as a whole account for about 80%, but my search did not check this.

text: exceeds the total amount of water in all the Earth's rivers, lakes, and man-made reservoirs.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is a sentence fragment with no subject, so it never says what exceeds the water in Earth's rivers, lakes and man-made reservoirs. It could mean groundwater, glaciers or atmospheric moisture, and those would give different answers. The search results confirm that rivers and lakes hold only a tiny share of the world's water, but that does not tell us whether the missing subject holds more. Without knowing what the claim refers to, it can't be checked.

text: The Greenland shark is bioluminescent, emitting a blue-green light as a result of a chemical reaction within its body.
label: contradicted
reason: No trustworthy source describes the Greenland shark itself as bioluminescent. Wikipedia, the Florida Museum and elasmo-research.org link the only suggestion of light to the parasitic copepod Ommatokoita elongata, which attaches to the shark's eyes, not to the shark. Even that idea is described as an unverified hypothesis. ReefQuest (elasmo-research.org) reports that the copepod is not bioluminescent. The claim that the shark makes its own blue-green light through a chemical reaction in its body has no support and conflicts with these accounts.

text: The Arctic fox has one of the warmest fur colors in animals due to its thick double coat, which can retain up to 90% of its body heat in freezing temperatures.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Several sources (Animal Sake, Study.com) say Arctic fox fur is the warmest or best-insulating fur of any mammal, and that its thick coat keeps it warm. But the claim calls its fur "one of the warmest fur colors", which doesn't make sense: color isn't what makes fur warm. No source I found backs the figure that the coat "can retain up to 90% of its body heat." The only 90 I found was a 90–100 °C gap between outside air and the fox's core temperature, which is a different fact. The main idea that the fur insulates well holds up, but the 90% figure and the color wording can't be verified.

text: Researchers have discovered that there are more trees on Earth now than there were 35 years ago, with a 2.4 billion increase in the number of trees since 1980.
label: contradicted
reason: Researchers did find that Earth has more tree cover than it did about 35 years ago. That comes from the 2018 Nature study by Song et al., which was widely reported. The specific figures in the claim are wrong, though. The study measured land area, not tree numbers: it found that global tree canopy cover grew by 2.24 million square kilometers, about 7%, between 1982 and 2016. It did not count a '2.4 billion increase in the number of trees,' and its baseline year was 1982, not 1980. The claim appears to have turned '2.24 million km²' into '2.4 billion trees.'

text: The famous 'I love you' message in the famous Rosetta Stone is actually the Rosetta Stone tinha an inscription of a non-cooperation pact adopted by the Greek monarch Ptolemy V.
label: contradicted
reason: The Rosetta Stone has no famous "I love you" message, and its text is not a non-cooperation pact. It carries the Memphis Decree, which a council of priests issued in 196 BC to confirm the royal cult of Ptolemy V. The decree is written in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of the shape created when they are gathered together.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that list collective nouns for octopuses name 'consortium' as the most common term, with 'tangle' used more playfully. Some add that there is no formally accepted collective noun at all. None of the sources call a group of octopuses a 'basket', and none give a reason based on the shape they make when gathered. A search for 'basket of octopuses' only turned up baskets as containers, such as products and a basket of octopuses served as food.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to make a single pound of honey as the production is usually done by a large group of bees.
label: contradicted
reason: Beekeeping sources say a pound of honey takes the work of hundreds of bees: Ontario Beekeepers say about 556 worker bees, and American Agri-Women say about 768. That directly contradicts the claim that 'not a single bee is needed' to make a pound of honey. The same Ontario source lists five products from the hive, including pollen and royal jelly, which people also eat. So honey is not the only food bees make that humans eat.

text: Therypton, a rare and highly sought-after green diamond, contains an inclusion of a yellow diamond called a prehnite, which provides its distinctive green color.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of a green diamond called "Therypton." The claim's main factual statement is also wrong. Wikipedia and gem references describe prehnite as a calcium aluminium silicate mineral, Ca2Al2Si3O10(OH)2, and not as a kind of yellow diamond. Prehnite is a separate gemstone, so a 'yellow diamond called a prehnite' does not exist. Natural green diamonds get their color from radiation exposure, not from prehnite inclusions.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) around the globe and is not visible above the waterline.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim holds up. Sources such as WorldAtlas and NOAA describe the Mid-Ocean Ridge as Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,390 miles). The claim is wrong, though, to say the ridge cannot be seen above the waterline. In a few places it rises above the ocean surface. Iceland is the largest exposed section, and the ridge's crest also breaks the surface on Jan Mayen island. NOAA likewise says only about 90% of the ridge is underwater.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth and says it is "more than 65,000 kilometers long." WHOI and Wikipedia also call it the planet's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia adds that the full oceanic ridge system is about 80,000 km. Wikipedia also says the ridge is part of every ocean, so it does run through the Atlantic (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian and Arctic oceans. The claim leaves out the Pacific, where ridges such as the Juan de Fuca and Explorer ridges are found. Because the claim does not say the ridge runs only through those three oceans, the omission makes it incomplete but does not contradict it. One small difference: some NOAA pages say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," but other NOAA material and the 80,000 km total for the full system back up the claim's wording.

text: There are approximately 30 to 40 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone, but the estimated total number of stars in the observable universe is over 100 billion trillion.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim lowballs the Milky Way. Reliable sources estimate it holds about 100 billion to 400 billion stars (University of Arizona, WorldAtlas, Space.com), not 30 to 40 billion. The second part, that the observable universe has over 100 billion trillion stars, roughly matches common estimates, but the Milky Way figure is clearly wrong.

text: Butler's Gargoyle, a type of long-eared bat, is found only on the island of Rodrigues, a part of Mauritius, and is considered one of the rarest bats in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The 'Butler Gargoyle' is a cryptid, a Mothman-like creature reported in Butler County, Pennsylvania. It is not a long-eared bat. The bat found only on Rodrigues (Mauritius) is the Rodrigues flying fox (Pteropus rodricensis), a fruit bat, not a long-eared bat. So the claim confuses a folklore creature with a real bat.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to produce a single drop of honey since bees gather hundreds of thousands of nectar drops from flowers to make it.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are false. Bees make other foods that people eat. Royal jelly, which worker bees secrete, is sold as a dietary supplement and eaten by humans, so honey is not the only one. The idea that no bee is needed to make honey is also wrong. Sources say it takes the life's work of about 12 bees to make one teaspoon of honey, and thousands of worker bees collect the nectar and process it into honey.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," which is now often referred to as "flight attendant."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Dictionary.com names "squirrelled" (11 letters, as some Americans pronounce it) as the longest one-syllable English word, with "broughammed" also at 11 letters. "Stewardess" is better known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand on a keyboard. It's true that the job is now usually called "flight attendant," but that doesn't fix the main error.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, with a total length of over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) that runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the global mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range. NOAA Ocean Exploration says it is the 'most extensive chain of mountains on Earth,' stretching about 65,000 km (40,390 mi). WHOI likewise calls it the longest mountain range at about 65,000 km (40,000 mi). The sources do not agree exactly on the length: NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km,' while other sources give 'over 65,000 km' or up to 74,000 km. Taken together, that range is consistent with 'over 65,000 km.' The sources also show the ridge running through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Central and Southwest Indian Ridges) and Pacific (East Pacific Rise) Oceans. The East Pacific Rise is in the eastern Pacific rather than the exact center, but this is a loose description, not a factual error.

text: The butterfly is the only insect capable of preserving the memory of its habitat and migration patterns through generations by using complex internal navigation systems.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that butterflies are the "only" insects with multigenerational migration and navigation is false. Smithsonian Magazine reports that the green darner dragonfly (Anax junius) also makes a yearly migration that spans several generations, and says monarch butterflies "aren't the only migratory marathoners." Other sources, including the University of Florida's entomology department, describe the same thing. Separately, the claim that butterflies "preserve memory" across generations is misleading, since monarch navigation is generally explained as inherited instinct, not memory passed down.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 0.0011 gallons due to strict quality control regulations.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the basic facts wrong. A gallon is a unit of volume, not length. The US gallon is also defined as exactly 231 cubic inches, so it is a fixed definition rather than a physical product that 'quality control regulations' allow to vary within a tolerance. No source supports a 0.0011-gallon variation limit for the unit itself.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans approximately 65,000 kilometers across the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including WHOI and NOAA, call the Mid-Ocean Ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. WorldAtlas also says it stretches about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) across the ocean floor, which matches the claim.

text: The tongue of a chameleon is blue-colored due to the presence of small crystals that deflect light, giving it a blue appearance.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources describe chameleon tongues as usually pink, sometimes whitish-pink or dark depending on the species (Notre Dame biomechanics page, chameleon forums). None of them describe a blue tongue. The tiny light-reflecting guanine crystals the claim mentions do exist, but they sit in iridophore cells in chameleon skin and drive the animal's colour change (Nature Communications, Science). They have nothing to do with tongue colour. The claim seems to mix up chameleons with blue-tongued skinks and moves a skin feature onto the tongue.

text: The unique sound of a dripping faucet is often caused by a consistent change in air pressure as the water drops land in the sink.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2018 University of Cambridge Engineering study used high-speed cameras and sensitive microphones to work out where the 'plink' of a dripping tap comes from. It found the sound is driven by a small air bubble trapped under the water surface after the drop hits. The bubble oscillates and makes the water surface vibrate, and that vibration produces the airborne sound. The claim instead credits a consistent change in air pressure as drops land, which is not what the research found.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and is not located on land, but rather runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources back the main points of the claim, with two small caveats. NOAA's Ocean Service and Ocean Exploration pages call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,389–40,390 miles) long. WHOI and Wikipedia give the same figure of about 65,000 km (40,000 mi). These sources describe the ridge as winding across the seafloor of the world's oceans, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. The first caveat is that NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over.' The second is that about 90% of the ridge is underwater, not all of it: small parts rise above sea level, as in Iceland. These are minor wording issues and do not undercut the claim's main point.

text: The bear species that hibernates the longest is the black bear, which can have a hibernation period of up to 9 months.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no source that says any bear hibernates for 9 months, and none that names the black bear as the clear record-holder. The North American Bear Center (bear.org) says black bears and grizzlies can both hibernate for up to about 7½ months. Field & Stream and A-Z Animals put the top figure at 7–8 months in the far north. Other sources give black bears 3–7 months and northern brown bears or grizzlies 5–7 months. Pregnant polar bears can stay in maternity dens for 4–8 months. So the 9-month figure is contradicted, and the evidence suggests black bears are matched by grizzlies rather than being the longest hibernators.

text: The Draupnir, an ancient Norse mythical amulet, is said to have been created by the god Odin and is almost indestructible, immortal, with its power doubled with every eight days or nine night according to the legend.
label: contradicted
reason: Norse sources describe Draupnir as a gold ring, not an amulet. Odin owned it, but he did not make it: the dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri (also called Sindri) forged it, according to the Skáldskaparmál. Its power was also not 'doubled every eight days or nine nights'. Instead, eight new rings of the same weight dripped from it every ninth night. Nothing in the sources calls it 'almost indestructible' or 'immortal'.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) long, stretching across every ocean on Earth.
label: supported
reason: NOAA sources say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA Ocean Exploration puts its length at nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and NOAA Education calls it an underwater range "over 40,000 miles long." WorldAtlas and WHOI describe it as running through every major ocean basin and crisscrossing the world's oceans. The claim's 64,000 km figure is a slight rounding difference from these sources but does not contradict them, so all parts of the claim are supported.

text: There is an estimated 1.5 trillion now-dead trees on Earth, which is roughly 11 times more than the total number of living trees, emphasizing the vast and varied history of trees on our planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. The 2015 study led by Crowther and published in Nature estimates that Earth has about 3.04 trillion living trees. A figure of 1.5 trillion dead trees would therefore be about half the number of living trees, not 11 times more. The same study says the number of trees has dropped by about 46% since humans began farming. That points to roughly 3 trillion trees lost, not 1.5 trillion. The claim's numbers contradict each other and conflict with the well-established estimate.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of all the major ocean basins.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. NOAA and WHOI call the mid-ocean ridge the longest or most extensive mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, so "over 65,000 km" fits. WorldAtlas says the ridge runs "generally through the center point of all major oceans," and other sources say it is part of every ocean. One small caveat: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," but the larger total-system figure makes the claim reasonable.

text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total coastline of only around 25,148 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Geography of Norway article, citing Kartverket (Norway's mapping agency), gives the mainland coastline as 25,148 km. It counts 239,057 islands plus 81,192 islets along the coast, which is well over 18,000, so both numbers in the claim hold. HowStuffWorks gives the same island count. The claim technically holds, but '18,000' is a big understatement of the real figure, which is about 239,000.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring at the border between the demilitarized zone of South and North Korea, known as the DMZ, to ensure the best water quality for its highly unique ecosystem.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a "Lisburn hill spring" exists in or near the Korean DMZ. Searches for the name only turned up results about Lisburn in Northern Ireland, which have nothing to do with Korea. I also found nothing showing that North and South Korea jointly manage any spring there for water quality. The DMZ's unusual ecosystem is well documented, and the Joint Security Area is overseen by the UN Command and the Korean People's Army. But the claim's main subject can't be identified, so it can't be confirmed or directly disproven.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest recorded melting point among all the elements.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of any substance called "adidamite." Searches return only unrelated results, such as the mineral paradamite and studies of methane-explosion soot. Soot is a form of carbon, so it is not a separate element. Reliable sources name a different element: Wikipedia and Guinness World Records list tungsten (3,422 °C), and some sources say carbon is the highest. No source gives this record to "adidamite."

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of lines drawn at regular and equal intervals across a pull of gunpowder to measure time, firearms evolving from slow burn fuse to cap firing and ultimately to percussion cap firearms.
label: contradicted
reason: Merriam-Webster gives 1855 as the first known use of "time stamp" (mid-19th century, not early). Its original meaning was a stamping device that records the date and time on a document or envelope. No source mentions lines drawn on gunpowder, fuses or percussion-cap firearms, and the dictionary's account of where the word comes from contradicts that origin story.

text: The greatest waterfall in the world by volume is actually located underwater, being the Denmark Strait Cataract, which is a submarine waterfall where dense, cold water from the Arctic flows down a slope in the ocean.
label: supported
reason: Live Science calls the Denmark Strait cataract the world's largest waterfall. It is a submarine waterfall between Greenland and Iceland, where cold, dense water from the Nordic Seas flows down a slope in the seafloor into the Irminger Sea. Other widely cited sources (e.g., NOAA) say it carries about 3–5 million m³/s, far more water than any waterfall on land, which makes it the greatest by volume. Saying the water comes from 'the Arctic' is a loose but reasonable description, since the Nordic Seas sit at Arctic latitudes and feed this overflow.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.1 x 10^8 km², which is about 12 times larger than the surface area of the Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's data on the Sun puts its surface area at about 6.09×10^12 km², roughly 12,000 times Earth's. The claim gets both numbers wrong. 5.1×10^8 km² is Earth's own surface area, not the Sun's, and the ratio is about 12,000, not 12.

text: Honey, when freeze-dried, can last indefinitely because of its very hygroscopic water content being nearly removed, allowing the sugars present within to preserve its state.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found don't establish that freeze-dried honey lasts indefinitely. Several sources say ordinary honey keeps indefinitely when sealed and dry, because its natural low water content and high sugar stop microbes from growing. That stability doesn't come from freeze-drying. On freeze-drying itself, the evidence conflicts. Harvest Right, which makes home freeze dryers, and a homesteading site both say honey doesn't freeze-dry properly and turns into a sticky mess. Commercial freeze-dried honey does exist, but research describes it as needing carrier agents such as maltodextrin, and a promotional page only claims it keeps 'for years', not indefinitely. Sources also say honey is hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs moisture from the air, so a dried product would need to be protected from humidity. The claim's specific statement and its explanation could not be confirmed, and parts of it are disputed.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which runs for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, and that it stretches nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles) around the globe. That matches the claim's figure of about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). WorldAtlas also calls the Mid-Ocean Ridge the longest mountain range on Earth.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal and has the ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as EBSCO Research Starters and Britannica describe Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the 'immortal jellyfish.' When it is injured or starving, it can turn back into its juvenile (polyp) form and start its life cycle again. This happens through a process called transdifferentiation, in which specialized cells change into other cell types. The 'immortal' label is a common name for being biologically immortal in this sense, not a claim that the animal can never die.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting around 86 billion neurons.

reason: The figure of about 86 billion neurons is right; it comes from Azevedo et al. (2009). The comparison is wrong, though. The Nature Scitable article says the Milky Way has somewhere between 200 and 400 billion stars. text: serir's Danakil Depression is considered to be the lowest point on land in the world, with a depth of approximately 125 meters below sea level.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoralillo Geyser, which geysers have been observed for years undisturbed by other wind and sea erosion from bigger desert areas elsewhere on earth
label: not_verifiable

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range. One detail is loose: the ridge runs through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, but it isn't literally in the center of each. In the Pacific, its main section (the East Pacific Rise) lies toward the eastern side. This simplification doesn't contradict the claim's core facts.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,393 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: The core claim checks out. NOAA and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). The claim's 40,393 miles is a small conversion difference from the 40,390 miles NOAA gives. Since both versions put the length at roughly 65,000 km, the claim is substantially supported.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called the turbellarian flatworm that is both a parasite and a jellyfish, and it has no stinging cells, despite belonging to the phylum Cnidaria.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Turbellarian flatworms are not jellyfish and are not in the phylum Cnidaria. ScienceDirect explains that turbellarians, along with flukes and tapeworms, make up the phylum Platyhelminthes, a group of bilaterian flatworms. Most turbellarians are free-living, while the parasitic flatworms belong to other classes in that phylum. The claim's description of a parasitic jellyfish with no stinging cells puts this animal in the wrong phylum.

text: Butterfly Pavilion at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History has more than 7,000 live butterflies on display from 187species.
label: contradicted
reason: The Smithsonian's own press release about the opening of the Live Butterfly Pavilion at the National Museum of Natural History says the pavilion holds "more than 300 live butterflies." It also says new species are added every week, but it gives no fixed count of 187 species. A figure of more than 7,000 butterflies is far above the number the museum gives. My other searches failed (one hit the search limit), so I found nothing that supports the 7,000 or 187-species figures.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, situated in the Great Hungarian Plain, where nightingales migrate to mate, making it a significant stop for these birds.

The search results were mostly local business and tourism pages. Because the main nightingale part of the claim cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A platypus is one of the few venomous mammals known to science, with the male platypus having a venomous spur on its hind leg used in mating battles.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (a Springer review and WWF Australia) say the platypus is a venomous monotreme. Only males are venomous, and they deliver venom through spurs on their hind legs during the breeding season, likely to compete with other males. Venomous mammals are widely recognized as rare.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand nuclear attacks and other catastrophic events, with its creators using a mesh-like system to ensure that information could still be shared even if some nodes were destroyed.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'A Brief History of the Internet' calls the link between ARPANET and building a network that could survive nuclear war a 'false rumor'. It says this was never true of ARPANET: only the separate RAND study by Paul Baran considered nuclear war. ARPANET was built so researchers could share scarce computing resources. Its tolerance for failed nodes was mainly a response to unreliable switching equipment and links, not to nuclear attack. Later internetworking work did stress robustness, but the claim that the Internet was originally designed to withstand nuclear attacks is a well-known myth.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural hot spring in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest, remains a mystery as it does not appear to have a visible source or outlet for its hot water despite flowing 20 meters per second.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets basic facts about the river wrong. Wikipedia says the Shanay-Timpishka (Boiling River) has a known source, Mayantuyacu, and a known mouth: it flows into the Pachitea River, then the Ucayali, then the Amazon. Scholastic also says it flows into the Pachitea and is heated by geothermal water rising through cracks in the riverbed. It is also a 9 km river, not a hot spring. This disproves the claim that it has no visible source or outlet. No source supported the flow rate of 20 meters per second.

text: пергамент, первоначально создан в древней Персии, получил свое название от пергамонского острова в Малой Азии, где римляне впервые начали производить этот тип чёрного слоя из горной соломки для письма.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are false. Reliable sources describe parchment as specially treated animal skin, usually from calves, sheep or goats. It was not a black layer made from 'mountain straw', and the sheets were white or yellowish. Its name comes from Pergamon, which was a city in Asia Minor, not an island. Its invention is usually credited to the Greek-ruled Pergamene kingdom under King Eumenes II (197–159 BC), not to the Romans or to ancient Persia.

text: Butler's Penguins, a colony of Emperor Penguins, are found on the Antarctic coast, where they live in abnormally close synchrony with the British monarch's coronations.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions an emperor penguin colony called "Butler's Penguins", so the claim has no clear referent. The searches only turned up general information about emperor penguin colonies in Antarctica. The idea that a colony lives in close synchrony with British coronations also has no support. It doesn't make biological sense either: emperor penguins breed every year, while coronations are rare and irregular. Because the named colony can't be identified, the claim can't be properly checked.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1993, is the world's oldest discovered boat, dating back approximately 8,000 years to the Stone Age.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any record of a "Janszoon boom log". Searching for it only turns up the Dutch explorer Willem Janszoon and the surname itself. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Live Science, History.com) all name the Pesse canoe as the world's oldest known boat. It was found in 1955, not 1993, and is dated to about 8040–7510 BC, which makes it roughly 10,000 years old, not about 8,000. So the claim gets the boat's name, the discovery date and the age wrong.

text: There are approximately 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which is estimated to be around 3 trillion leaves and covers around 30% of the planet's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Nature study led by Thomas Crowther estimates about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth (roughly 422 per person), not 7.9 billion. About 7.9 billion is closer to the size of the human population. The claim also gets the 3 trillion figure wrong: that is the tree count, not a leaf count. And forests cover about 31% of Earth's land area, not 30% of the whole planet's surface.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, as evidenced by the discovery of the PARAM Bibliapt settlement site, dating to around 11,200 to 17,800 years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any record of a "PARAM Bibliapt" settlement site anywhere in the Catskills. The "oldest" find the Catskills are actually known for is the world's oldest fossil forest (about 385 million years old, found in a quarry in Cairo, NY), not an ancient human home. Reports on the oldest known dwelling in North America point elsewhere: a 13,800-year-old site in Alaska, Shég' Xdaltth'í', is described as the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere. Other sites put forward as the oldest homes or habitation sites are the Gault site in Texas and Paisley Cave in Oregon. So the claim is contradicted.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola being initially marketed as a "brain tonic and intellectual beverage" in the late 19th century.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part checks out. Pemberton was addicted to morphine and went looking for morphine-free alternatives, which led to French Wine Coca and then Coca-Cola, and he advertised it as a brain tonic. The Pepsi part is wrong. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893 as 'Brad's Drink' and sold it as a digestive aid for dyspepsia, not as a replacement for morphine. So saying both drinks were made as morphine alternatives is incorrect.

text: Greatereso volcanoes, found on the Galapagos Islands, have been erupting for over 20 years since 2000 and are some of the most active volcanoes on the planet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a volcano or volcano group called "Greatereso" in the Galápagos or anywhere else, so the claim doesn't point to anything that can be identified. Searches only turned up general news about real Galápagos volcanoes, such as the 2022 eruption of Wolf, the tallest volcano on the islands. Nothing confirms or rules out continuous eruptions since 2000 for any volcano with this name.

text: The彩虹nhond population of the world's language can approximate to around 7,097, according to ethnohistorians at Sydney University.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of 7,097 living languages comes from Ethnologue, the language catalog published by SIL International, not from ethnohistorians at Sydney University. I found no source that links this number to Sydney University researchers. The phrase "彩虹nhond population" is garbled and has no clear meaning, so that part can't be checked. The number itself is right, but the claim credits it to the wrong source.

text: The understandability of Orangutans' language has shown to be surprisingly similar to that of children, as research indicates they are able to master up to 400 words of sign language.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says orangutans can master up to 400 sign-language words, but reliable sources don't back that number. The best-known signing orangutan, Chantek, learned about 150 modified ASL signs over eight years, according to the Smithsonian, Wikipedia, AP/Review-Journal and Lyn Miles's own writing. Miles did describe his vocabulary as 'similar to that of a very young child,' which partly fits the comparison to children. No source supports anything close to 400 words, so the specific figure is contradicted.

text: The length of a ship's spider's web, or "spider silk-like" fiber netting, varies from 1/16-1/8 inch thick.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Searches turned up nothing about a ship's "spider's web" or "spider silk-like" fiber netting being 1/16 to 1/8 inch thick. The results were mostly climbing nets and replica ship mast nets made with 5/8" rope, which is a different product with no clear link to the claim. The claim is also unclear: it gives a "length" as a thickness, and it is not clear what "a ship's spider's web" refers to. With no evidence for or against the figure, the claim cannot be verified.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it can recover quickly from temporary outages and failures.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'Brief History of the Internet', written by Internet pioneers including Leiner and Cerf, says the idea that ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear war is a 'false rumor'. The rumor grew out of Paul Baran's separate RAND study on survivable networks. ARPANET itself was built for resource sharing between research computers, not to withstand nuclear attack. The claim's premise is a well-known myth, so its reasoning about why the Internet recovers from outages does not hold.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Australia, has the world's oldest known dam, with evidence suggesting it was built over 2,000 years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: Butler's Gorge is in Tasmania, Australia, so the location is correct. The dam there, Clark Dam, is a 20th-century hydro-electric dam. It was being built around the 1940s as part of the Hydro Electric Commission's Tarraleah Development. The University of Tasmania's Companion to Tasmanian History says Tasmania's earliest dams date only from about 1809, on the Hobart Rivulet. None of the sources suggest a dam at Butler's Gorge that is over 2,000 years old or the oldest in the world.

text: did you know that honey is the only food that bees make that humans eat, and not a single bee is needed to make a single drop of it.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is made by bees. Beekeeping sources say it takes about 12 bees their entire lifetimes to make one teaspoon of honey, so the idea that no bee is needed is false. The 'only food' part is also wrong, because people eat other bee products too, such as royal jelly and bee pollen.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, but when at its highest point in the sky (opposition), it can outshine the brightest planet, Jupiter, due to its proximity and reflective surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself and gets the astronomy wrong. Venus is the brightest planet as seen from Earth, so Jupiter is not 'the brightest planet.' Venus also orbits closer to the Sun than Earth does, which means it can never be at opposition (directly opposite the Sun in our sky). Only planets farther out, like Mars and Jupiter, can reach opposition. So the idea that Venus outshines Jupiter at opposition is wrong.

text: A platypus is one of the few venomous mammals known to science, with the male platypus having a venomous spur on its hind leg that it uses to defend itself.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources confirm the platypus is one of the few venomous mammals and that only males have venomous spurs on their hind legs. Scientists think the spurs evolved mainly so males can compete for mates during the breeding season, but they also confirm the spurs serve as a defense against predators. Because defense is a documented use, nothing in the claim is contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe and is not visible above water.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 mi). NOAA says "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over," but that difference is small. The claim is wrong to say the ridge is not visible above water. NOAA says only about 90% of it lies underwater, and other sources point to Iceland, including Thingvellir National Park, as a place where the ridge rises above sea level and can be seen on dry land.

text: The country of Saudi Arabia has over 22,000 artificial islands created using 262 million tons of reclaimed land that was worth over $1.5 billion during construction.
label: contradicted
reason: Saudipedia, a Saudi reference source, says the Kingdom has about 1,300 islands in total, mostly natural coral, sandy, continental or volcanic islands in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aqaba and Arabian Gulf. That total is far below the claimed 22,000 artificial islands. None of the search results supported the figures of 262 million tons of reclaimed land or $1.5 billion for Saudi Arabia.

text: Octopuses have nearly 400 million neurons in their brains, which is approximately 20-30% of the number found in the human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: Octopuses have about 500 million neurons in total, and roughly 180 million of those are in the central brain. Humans have about 86 billion neurons. So even 400–500 million octopus neurons would be well under 1% of the human count (around 200 times fewer), not 20–30%. The claim's 20–30% figure is clearly wrong.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it was built with redundancy and fail-safes at its core.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a common myth. The Internet Society's 'Brief History of the Internet' was written by Internet pioneers, including Vint Cerf, Barry Leiner and others. It says the idea that ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war is a 'false rumor' and 'was never true of the ARPANET.' Only Paul Baran's separate RAND study on secure voice communications looked at nuclear war. ARPANET was mainly built so researchers could share computing resources. Packet switching and redundancy were part of its design, but surviving a nuclear attack was not why ARPANET was built.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and able to quickly reroute around any disruptions.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources call this a common myth. Bob Taylor, who ran the ARPANET project at the Pentagon, and other people involved say the network was built so researchers could share computing resources, not to survive a nuclear attack. Paul Baran's earlier RAND research on survivable networks did influence packet switching, but that was not why ARPANET or the Internet was designed. So the claim's main premise is wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). It runs between the continents, including through the Atlantic, Indian and Arctic Oceans. There are two small differences. NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km where the claim says 'over,' and other sources give figures of 65,000 km or more. The claim also leaves out that the ridge extends into the Pacific. Neither difference contradicts the main point.

text: The Sundial Bridge in Redding, California, is the world's first self-supporting, single-span, arch bridge made from cable-stayed architecture, designed by architect Santiago Calatrava.
label: contradicted
reason: Santiago Calatrava did design the bridge in Redding, but the rest of the claim is wrong. Wikipedia and Architectuul describe the Sundial Bridge as a cantilever spar cable-stayed bridge, not an arch bridge. Its single cantilevered tower leans at 42 degrees and carries cable stays on one side only. It also wasn't the world's first of its type: both sources say it follows Calatrava's earlier Puente del Alamillo in Seville (1992). Calling it the 'world's first' arch bridge of this kind therefore conflicts with reliable sources.

text: The driest desert in the world, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is home to a unique archaeological site featuring the remnants of a 12,000-year-old forest petrified by the extreme dryness of the environment.
label: contradicted
reason: There is a real site like this, but the paper itself rules out the claim's 'petrified' wording. A 2024 PNAS study describes more than 150 preserved tree stumps from a grove about 11,600 to 11,200 years old. The stumps sit at Late Pleistocene/Early Holocene campsites, about 12,800 to 11,200 years old, in the Quebrada Maní and Guatacondo canyons of Chile's Atacama Desert. So the location, the roughly 12,000-year age and the link to archaeology all check out. However, the authors say the stumps survived because the extreme dryness 'prevents degradation and impedes fossilization.' That means the wood was preserved by dryness, not petrified (turned to stone by minerals). The claim gets this point backward.

text: There are over 8 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate by the Secretary-General of the United Nations.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the claim as worded. The figure of about 8 million plant and animal species comes from the 2019 IPBES Global Assessment, a scientific report produced under UN auspices (UN.org, UNEP, NPR, Wikipedia). It is not described as a 2020 estimate by the UN Secretary-General. In the 2020 speech by Secretary-General Guterres that I found ('State of the Planet', December 2020), he said one million species are at risk of extinction but gave no total of 8 million. The sources also give the number as an estimated 8 million, not 'over' 8 million. Only Popular Science says 'more than 8 million'. Since I found nothing tying the estimate to the Secretary-General in 2020, that part of the claim can't be verified.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1993, is the world's oldest discovered boat, dating back over 8,000 years.
label: contradicted
reason: No credible source mentions a "Janszoon boom log". Willem Janszoon was a Dutch navigator in the early 1600s, not an archaeological find. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, History.com and Live Science, name the Pesse canoe as the world's oldest known boat. It was found in the Netherlands in 1955 and dates to 8040–7510 BC, about 10,000 years ago. That conflicts with the claim's boat name and its 1993 discovery date.

text: A wombat's unique cube-shaped scat, which they use for communication, helps the wombat avoid being preyed upon by predators as it has a strong, unpleasant odor that is meant to deter them.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Credible sources (UGA, The Conversation, CNN, Lone Pine Koala Sanctuary) confirm that wombats leave cube-shaped scat on rocks, logs and near burrows. They say the scat is used to communicate with other wombats: it marks territory and carries information such as fertility. None of the sources found says the scat's odor deters or is meant to deter predators. The sources describe a function among wombats, not an anti-predator defense, but they also don't state that the scat has no anti-predator role. The predator-deterrence part can't be verified, but it isn't directly contradicted either.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Malahide Castle in Ireland, contains a doll that is said to be the oldest uniquely crafted doll in the world, dating back to 1628.
label: not_verifiable

None of them mention a "Butler's Grotto", a doll from 1628, or a claim about the world's oldest uniquely crafted doll. The search tool's usage limit was hit before I could try other queries, so I found no evidence either confirming or directly refuting the claim. text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar panels at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim says "the telescope" without saying which one, so there is no clear referent. I also couldn't find evidence that ALMA runs partly on a field of solar panels. The solar plant I did find, a 9 MW plant covering 7.2 hectares, powers ESO's Paranal Observatory (home of the Very Large Telescope), which is a different site from ALMA. Older sources say ALMA was powered by diesel or other conventional generators. Search limits stopped me before I could confirm or rule out a newer solar installation at ALMA.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals in the world, according to estimates from the Custodian of the World Register of Marine Species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the source wrong. The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 study by Camilo Mora, Boris Worm and colleagues, published in PLoS Biology and released through the Census of Marine Life. It did not come from a custodian of the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS). WoRMS was only one of the databases the researchers analysed, along with the Catalogue of Life. The claim also misstates the number. The study gave 8.7 million give or take 1.3 million, not 'over 8.7 million', and it counted all eukaryote species, not just plants and animals.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is home to several geysers, making it one of the few places on Earth where you can find geothermal activity in a desert.
label: supported
reason: Many sources place the El Tatio geyser field, with more than 80 geysers and fumaroles, in Chile's Atacama Desert, and describe the Atacama as the world's driest desert. One caveat: strictly speaking, it is the driest non-polar desert, since parts of Antarctica are drier, and one result calls it the driest place outside Antarctica. The claim that this is one of the few desert locations with geothermal activity is vague, but the sources fit it, describing El Tatio as the largest geothermal field in the Southern Hemisphere and among the highest in the world.

text: The vomitrocha frog, a species found in Papua New Guinea, can self-decapitate its head as a defense mechanism when it senses danger, releasing toxic chemicals from its skin.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no evidence that a frog called the "vomitrocha" exists, in Papua New Guinea or anywhere else. They returned real PNG frogs such as Paedophryne amauensis and unrelated pages about "vomit frogs," but nothing about this species. No source describes any frog cutting off its own head to defend itself or releasing toxins when it does. The only documented case of an animal shedding its body like this is in sea slugs (Elysia marginata and E. atroviridis), reported in 2021. In those slugs the head survives and regrows a new body, possibly to get rid of parasites; they are not frogs. The claim looks invented, but no source directly refutes it, so it can't be verified.

text: Antarctica is home to several large freshwater lakes, one of which, Lake Vostok, is the world's largest and deepest subsurface lake, covering an area of approximately 14,000 square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Guinness World Records names Subglacial Lake Vostok the largest subglacial lake and lists its area as 14,000 km², which matches the claim. Wikipedia gives a slightly smaller 12,500 km², so 14,000 km² is a fair approximation. Wikipedia also says Vostok is the largest of Antarctica's hundreds of known subglacial lakes, and Concordia Lake (900 km²) is another large one, which supports the part about Antarctica having several large lakes. No source I found states outright that Vostok is the deepest subglacial lake, though it is commonly described as having a maximum depth of about 900–1,000 m, and nothing contradicts that part. I treated the claim as supported overall, but that one detail was not directly confirmed.

text: Pineapples are not naturally sweet and will turn bitter if left to ripen on the plant, as they contain high amounts of an enzyme that breaks down their sugars.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on every point. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org) says pineapple does not ripen once it has been picked, so it has to ripen on the plant to get sweet. It also says a deeper yellow colour means more sugar, so pineapples are naturally sweet and get sweeter as they ripen, not bitter. The enzyme in pineapple, bromelain, breaks down proteins, which is why it is used to tenderise meat. It does not break down sugars.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it can recover quickly from errors and outages known as "packet loss" or "Internet hiccups".
label: contradicted
reason: The claim repeats a common myth. The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet" calls the idea that ARPANET was designed to survive nuclear war a "false rumor" that grew out of the unrelated RAND study. Internet history sources such as nethistory.info, the Internet Mythen project and AEI likewise say surviving a nuclear attack was not ARPANET's purpose. Packet switching was partly inspired by Paul Baran's RAND survivability work, but the Internet was not originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack. That also undercuts the claim's explanation for how the network recovers from packet loss.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources confirm the main claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the most extensive chain of mountains on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI calls mid-ocean ridges the planet's longest mountain range at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles), and says they crisscross the world's oceans. Wikipedia's list gives about 65,000 km (40,000 mi). Two details are slightly loose. The claim says 'over 65,000 km', while NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly'. It also says the ridge runs through the center of the Pacific, but the East Pacific Rise lies in the eastern Pacific. These differences don't change the core facts, so I rated the claim supported.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique trait where they can form long-lasting monogamous relationships, with some species staying with their mate for up to 30 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Butterflyfish do form long-lasting monogamous pairs, but the 30-year figure doesn't hold up. An aquarium source says most species stay with the same mate for 'several years' and some mate for life. Another source says pairs of coral-feeding species stay together 'for years.' Neither mentions anything close to 30 years. From my own background knowledge, not from these searches: the longest documented pair bonds are about 7 years, and butterflyfish usually live roughly 5–10 years in the wild, so a 30-year bond is implausible. Calling monogamy 'unique' is also wrong, since many other reef fish form pairs. My search tool hit its usage limit after a few results, so the evidence is thinner than I'd like.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and that it winds between the continents through the world's oceans. That matches the claim. Two small wording differences don't change this: NOAA's ocean exploration page says "nearly" 65,000 km where the claim says "over" (other NOAA pages say "more than"), and the claim's 40,400 miles is a rounded figure. The ridge does run through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, though in the Pacific it sits off-center (the East Pacific Rise) rather than in the middle.

text: There are over 8.4 million square miles of the Earth's surface covered in ice, which includes glaciers, ice shelves, and polar ice caps.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figure is too high for the ice types it lists. NSIDC says glacial ice, meaning glaciers, ice caps and the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, covers just over 15 million km², or about 5.8 million square miles (around 10% of land). USGS gives a similar figure of about 15.9 million km². Adding Antarctica's ice shelves, at roughly 1.5 million km² or 0.6 million square miles (my own background estimate, not from the search results), brings the total to about 6.4 million square miles. That is well short of 'over 8.4 million.' A figure that large is only reachable by counting sea ice, which the claim does not mention.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Nanay River," is a mysterious and unexplained natural geothermal hotspot in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest where the water appears to be boiling due to unknown geological reasons.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the river's name and its cause wrong. The Boiling River of the Amazon is the Shanay-Timpishka, a tributary of the Pachitea River (which flows into the Ucayali and then the Amazon). It is not called the "Boiling River of the Nanay River"; the Nanay is a different river near Iquitos. The heat isn't unexplained either. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and others say it comes from hydrothermal activity: groundwater heated deep underground rises along faults, with no volcano involved. That makes it a known geological anomaly, not a mystery with unknown causes. Its waters do get very hot, reaching about 210°F.

text: A honeybee in a honeybee colony typically produces and collects pollen for only 4-6 weeks out of its entire 6-week lifespan during the warmer months.
label: contradicted
reason: Several beekeeping sources say a summer worker bee lives about 6 weeks. She spends roughly the first 3 weeks doing jobs inside the hive and only starts foraging for pollen and nectar at around day 21. That leaves only about 2–3 weeks of foraging at the end of her life, and automated tracking suggests the foraging period may be as short as about 8 days. So the claim that a bee collects pollen for 4–6 weeks of a 6-week life is wrong; it would mean she forages for most or all of her life. Bees also collect pollen from flowers rather than produce it.

text: Honey is the only food that, when left untouched, will not spoil, as long as it has access to air and a decent moisture level, due to the acidity of hydrochloric acid within its composition.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are wrong. Honey's acidity comes from gluconic acid, which forms when bees add the enzyme glucose oxidase to nectar. It does not come from hydrochloric acid. Honey also keeps because it is low in moisture (about 17–18%) and has to be stored in a sealed container. Exposure to air and moisture can make it ferment, which is the opposite of what the claim says. It also isn't the only food that doesn't spoil: salt and pure sugar keep indefinitely too.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural wonder where river streams appear to boil, despite being over a mile away from the nearest waterfall or any visible source of water.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part is true. Wikipedia and other sources describe the Shanay-timpishka in Peru as the 'Boiling River of the Amazon,' a thermal river with water hot enough to kill anything that falls in. The second part gets the river's famous oddity wrong. Sources say what makes it remarkable is that it sits more than 700 km from the nearest active volcano, in an area with no known magma activity. They say nothing about it being over a mile from a waterfall or from any visible water. That part also can't be true: the river is itself water, it's heated by deep groundwater coming up through the ground, and it flows into the Pachitea River. So the distance claim is wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range and that it runs about 65,000 km (40,000 mi) around the globe. NOAA and WHOI describe it as "nearly 65,000 km." Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and about 80,000 km for the whole oceanic ridge system. A NASA page gives 74,000 km (46,000 mi). NOAA's "nearly" sits slightly under the claim's "over 65,000 km," but taken together the sources put the length at roughly 65,000 km or more, so the claim holds overall.

text: You can lead a cow upstairs, but not downstairs, as cows have a difficult time navigating steep or slippery surfaces due to their weight and unique foot structure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says a cow can't be led downstairs, and the more credible sources say that is false. BBC Science Focus calls it a widely held belief and says cows can go down stairs with some encouragement. All That's Interesting lists 'cows can't walk down stairs' among popular animal myths. Farmers and homesteading sources say cows can go downstairs but avoid it because their footing and balance on stairs is poor and it is hard for them to see the ground at their feet. That partly backs up the explanation in the claim, but not the 'not downstairs' part. A few low-quality pages (forum posts, Krishi Jagran) repeat the myth, but more reliable sources treat cows finding it difficult as different from cows being unable to do it.

text: The driest desert in the world is the Atacama Desert in Chile, which covers an area of over 105,000 square kilometers (41,000 square miles) and is also home to several islands in the Pacific Ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: Some of the claim checks out. Atlas.co says the Atacama Desert covers about 105,000 km² (it gives 40,500 sq mi, not 41,000) and calls it one of the driest places on Earth. Other parts are wrong or overstated. The Atacama is a mainland strip of desert between the Andes and the Coastal Range, along the Pacific coast of Chile and southern Peru. Being on the coast does not make it 'home to several islands in the Pacific Ocean.' Small coastal islands, such as those in the Humboldt Penguin reserve, belong to Chile's administrative Atacama Region, not to the desert. The claim also says the Atacama lies wholly in Chile, but it extends into southern Peru. Finally, the Atacama is usually called the driest non-polar desert, since Antarctica is drier. Because the island part is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is more than 1,300 times the size of the Earth and has a mass that is approximately 2.5 times the mass of all the other planets combined.
label: supported
reason: Caltech's Cool Cosmos (IPAC) page says Jupiter's volume is over 1,300 times Earth's and that it weighs two and a half times as much as all the other planets combined. CNES and Space.com say the same thing: Jupiter could hold more than 1,300 Earths (1,321 by volume) and is about 2.5 times as massive as all the other planets together. One note on wording: the claim says '1,300 times the size', but that figure is true only for volume, not diameter or mass. Read that way, which is how these sources present it, both parts of the claim check out.

text: Carpets of fluorescent algae were able to grow on the soil of the Danakil Desert, one of the hottest places on Earth, which challenges the long-held notion that only shaded areas can support life.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no source saying that carpets of fluorescent algae grew on Danakil Desert soil, and none describing a long-held idea that only shaded areas can support life. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia confirm that the Danakil is one of the hottest places on Earth. Microbiology studies of the Dallol area within the Danakil Depression (Nature Scientific Reports, bioRxiv, Europlanet) describe archaea, ultra-small microorganisms and the limits of life there, but say nothing about fluorescent algae carpets on the soil. The main claim can't be verified, though no source directly contradicts it.

text: Located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the small uninhabited Hawaiki island is only seen during low tide due to being almost completely submerged underwater at high tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Hawaiki isn't a real tidal island in the middle of the Pacific. Britannica and Wikipedia describe it as the legendary original homeland of the Polynesians from their folklore. It is sometimes linked to real places such as Raiatea or Tahiti, but those are inhabited islands that stay above water at high tide. No source describes an uninhabited island called Hawaiki that shows up only at low tide.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge System, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles) long, winding between the continents through the world's oceans, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. One wording difference: these sources say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" it. Other estimates, such as roughly 80,000 km when the full ridge network is counted, would put it above 65,000 km. Because the figure is approximate, this difference doesn't contradict the main claim.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world record for the highest waterfall in a canyon.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no source saying Butlers Gorge holds any waterfall record. Wikipedia and Wikidata describe it as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with a recorded population of nil. Its notable features are the Clark Dam at Lake King William and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, not a record waterfall. The world's highest waterfall is widely recognised as Angel Falls in Venezuela, which drops into Devil's Canyon. The record claimed for Butlers Gorge therefore appears to be false. One caveat: no source directly addresses 'highest waterfall in a canyon' as a category, so this verdict rests on the lack of any support and the fact that Angel Falls holds the record.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world record for the highest waterfall in a straight line, standing at over 157 meters tall.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, known for Lake King William and its dam. Nothing in the sources describes it as a record-holding waterfall. The world's highest waterfall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, at about 979 m, which is far taller than the 157 m in the claim. The world-record part of the claim is false.

text: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution and, when heated slowly, it remains stable due to the unique properties of the bonds in its molecules.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim checks out. Study.com and a BJCP document on honey crystallization both say honey is a supersaturated sugar solution. The rest doesn't hold up. The same sources call that supersaturated state unstable: over time, glucose separates out as crystals. They say heating turns crystallized honey back to liquid and that mild heat delays crystallization, but neither credits this to 'unique properties of the bonds in its molecules.' Neither source says honey is stable because of its molecular bonds. That part is vague and partly at odds with the evidence, so the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution that never spoils due to its unique combination of acidity and beeswax.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is indeed a supersaturated sugar solution and lasts a very long time, but the claim gives the wrong reasons. Sources say honey resists spoiling because it has very little water, a high sugar concentration that draws moisture away from microbes, natural acidity, and enzymes that produce small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Acidity is one of these factors, but beeswax is not. The claim's main explanation, acidity combined with beeswax, is therefore wrong. Calling it a substance that "never spoils" also overstates the case, since honey can ferment if it absorbs moisture.

text: New Zealand is home to a unique species of dolphin known as the bottlenose dolphin that has been known to form long-lasting friendships with humans.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim calls the bottlenose dolphin a species unique to New Zealand, and that is wrong. Bottlenose dolphins live in oceans all over the world. Wikipedia and NZ's Department of Conservation say Hector's dolphin (including the Māui subspecies) is the only cetacean endemic to New Zealand. Some bottlenose dolphins in New Zealand did become famously friendly with people, such as Opo and Moko, but the species is not unique to the country.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River', is a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains unexplained, as it appears to boil due to an unknown geological phenomenon.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is real: it is the Shanay-timpishka, popularly called the 'Boiling River of the Amazon', in the Peruvian Amazon. But the claim says it remains unexplained and is heated by an unknown phenomenon, and that is wrong. Studies by geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and his colleagues traced the heat to a fault-fed hydrothermal system. Rainwater seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, and rises back up through fault lines as hot springs. This happens even though no volcano is nearby. Sources including ScienceAlert, Slate and Discover Wildlife report this explanation. Slate says research on the river's thermal details is still going on, but the basic cause is known. None of the sources found call it the 'Hidden River', so that nickname is also unsupported.

text: The Boomerang effect, which was initially observed in physics and refers to the return of an object to its point of origin, has also been applied to sociological phenomena, such as changes in behavior after a specific action or event.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim that the boomerang effect was first observed in physics. Wikipedia's article on the boomerang effect (psychology), and a ResearchGate paper that agrees with it, say Hovland, Janis and Kelley first recorded and named it in 1953 in social psychology. There it means a persuasive message that produces the opposite attitude or behavior from the one intended. The disambiguation page lists only psychological and sociological meanings, not a physics one. The second half of the claim is partly true: the term is used in social science for behavior changes that backfire. However, I found no source saying the concept started in physics and was later applied to social phenomena. One caveat: the Wikipedia talk page questions whether the 1953 sourcing is strong enough.

text: The Cheesboro Canyon Natural Area in California, USA is one of the last remaining environments for the California grizzly bear that has not been significantly altered by humans.
label: contradicted
reason: The California grizzly bear has been extinct since about 1924. The Natural History Museum of LA and Wikipedia both say the last one was seen in the 1920s, so no remaining environment in California still supports it. The sources describe Cheeseboro Canyon as valley oak savanna and woodland in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. None of them calls it a remaining grizzly habitat or an unaltered refuge for the bear. My searches were cut short by a tool limit before I could check the canyon's Wikipedia article for a possible historical grizzly mention. Still, the claim's framing of a 'remaining environment for the California grizzly' conflicts with the bear's extinction.

text: The Cheesboro Canyon Natural Area in California, USA is one of the last remaining environments for the California grizzly bear that still exist today although there are no California grizzly bears.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the claim's main point, so it's inconclusive. The National Park Service page on Cheeseboro/Palo Comado Canyon covers the canyons' oaks, grazing history, raptors, deer, bobcats and coyotes, but says nothing about the area being one of the last remaining California grizzly habitats. Other sources only support the second part of the claim: the California grizzly is extinct, and the last one was killed in the 1920s. I hit the search limit before finding a reliable source that ties Cheeseboro Canyon to grizzly habitat in any way.

text: The Cheesboro Canyon Natural Area in California, USA is one of the last remaining environments for the California grizzly bear that still exists in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: The California grizzly bear is extinct. The last reliable sighting of one in the wild was near Yosemite in 1924, so it has no remaining wild habitat anywhere, including Cheeseboro Canyon. The Natural History Museum of LA County, Wikipedia (which lists its status as Extinct, 1924) and Backpacker magazine all confirm this.

text: The Human Brain contains over 100 billion neurons, with some estimates suggesting a total of 86 billion neurons, but each neuron can have up to 10,000 synaptic connections.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the brain has over 100 billion neurons, but current research puts the figure at about 86 billion. Scientific American, the Dana Foundation and Northwestern Medicine all give the 86 billion count, which is below 100 billion. The claim also contradicts itself by citing both figures. The synapse limit is also off: the Dana Foundation says Purkinje cells may have as many as 100,000 synapses, so 'up to 10,000' understates the maximum.

text: The Human Brain contains over 100 billion neurons, with some estimates suggesting a total of 86 billion neurons, but each neuron can make over 7,000 connections with other neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself. It says the brain has over 100 billion neurons, then gives 86 billion as one estimate, which is fewer than 100 billion. Reputable current sources, including Scientific American and Northwestern Medicine, put the figure at about 86 billion neurons, based on modern cell-counting research. The 100-billion figure is an older approximation that still shows up in some papers, but it is not accurate. The 7,000 connections per neuron figure is widely cited and plausible, since estimates range from a few up to 10,000 or more. Even so, the main 'over 100 billion' figure is contradicted by the better evidence.

text: The Tongue of the Ocean, located near the Bahamas, is the world's second-largest artificial harbor and was created by the US Navy in 1962.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Trustworthy sources, including the EU Space / Copernicus programme, describe the Tongue of the Ocean as a natural deep ocean trench in the Bahamas, set between shallow limestone banks near Andros Island. It is not an artificial harbour, and it was not built by the US Navy in 1962. The US Navy does run a testing range there (AUTEC), but that does not make the trench man-made.

text: The Tongue of the Ocean, located near the Bahamas, is the world's second-largest artificial harbor and was created by the United States Navy in the 1950s using dynamite to blast out a bay from a coral limestone ridge.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia and the EU Copernicus programme, describe the Tongue of the Ocean as a natural deep oceanic trench in the Bahamas between Andros and New Providence/Exuma, with shallow carbonate banks on either side. It is not an artificial harbour, and the US Navy did not blast it out with dynamite in the 1950s. The Navy runs a test range there (AUTEC), but it did not create the trench.

text: The ancient Egyptians are believed to have used a 365-day calendar, with an extra day added occasionally to account for the additional time it takes the Earth to orbit the Sun.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the ancient Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days: twelve 30-day months plus five extra (epagomenal) days at the end of the year. The claim is wrong about adding an extra day occasionally. The calendar had no leap years, so it drifted about one day every four years against the solar year, which is why it was called the 'wandering year' (annus vagus). The Ptolemaic rulers decreed a leap day in 238 BCE, but Egyptians did not accept it. A leap day only took hold under Augustus's Alexandrian calendar reform, with the first sixth epagomenal day added in 22 BCE.

text: The ancient Egyptians are believed to have used a 365-day calendar, with an extra day added occasionally to account for the solar year's duration.
label: contradicted
reason: The 365-day part of the claim is correct, but the leap-day part is wrong. The Egyptian civil calendar had twelve 30-day months plus five extra (epagomenal) days. The Coptic calendar article says it had only 365 days every year, with no extra day, so dates slipped against the seasons by about one day every four years (the 'wandering year'). A leap day every fourth year was first decreed in the Canopus reform of 238 BC under Ptolemy III. It was not adopted lasting until the later Alexandrian/Coptic reform. The traditional ancient Egyptian calendar did not occasionally add an extra day to keep up with the solar year.

text: The ancient Egyptians used a combination of mathematical concepts and astronomical observations to create their calendar system, with divisions for 365 days in a year and an extra five days for festivals and rituals.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the Egyptian civil calendar was built from astronomical observation (for example, the heliacal rising of Sirius) and simple arithmetic. However, it had 12 months of 30 days, which makes 360 days, plus 5 epagomenal days used for festivals, for a total of 365.
