The claim says there were 365 days and then an extra five days on top, which would make 370. That misstates the structure: the five festival days were part of the 365-day total, not added to it.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to Worm's Head, a unique natural limestone arch that becomes visible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Worm's Head is a tidal island, a headland about a mile long, at the southern end of Rhossili Bay. You can see it at all times. Low tide only matters because that is when the causeway from the mainland is uncovered and you can walk across. It is not itself a natural limestone arch. The arch on it is a separate feature called Devil's Bridge. So the claim gets wrong both what Worm's Head is and what happens at low tide.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to Worm's Head, a unique natural limestone arch that is completely submerged during high tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Worm's Head is a tidal island off Rhossili, not a natural limestone arch. It does have an arch on it, called Devil's Bridge. At high tide only the 700-yard causeway to the mainland goes under the waves, which cuts the island off. The island itself, with its grassy top where people have been stranded, stays above water, so the claim that it is completely submerged is false.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to a unique landlocked sandstone tombolo, also known as a land spit, that's over 1.5 kilometers long.
label: contradicted
reason: Rhossili Bay has no 'landlocked sandstone tombolo' over 1.5 km long. The feature the claim seems to mean is Worm's Head. According to Wikipedia and other sources, it is a tidal island and headland made of Carboniferous limestone, not sandstone. It is linked to the mainland by a rocky tidal causeway that floods at high tide, so it is not landlocked, and Atlas Obscura gives the causeway's length as about 650 m (700 yards). Sources describe Worm's Head and Burry Holms as limestone tidal islands. None of them mention a sandstone tombolo or land spit in the bay.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to a unique landlocked sandstone tombolo, also known as a spit, which is a rare geological formation.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source saying Rhossili Bay has a sandstone tombolo, landlocked or otherwise. Its well-known feature, Worm's Head, is described as a limestone (Carboniferous Limestone) headland and tidal island, reached by a rocky causeway at low tide. That is not a sandstone tombolo. Geography teaching material uses Rhossili Bay as an example of a swash-aligned beach, not a tombolo. The claim is also wrong on terms: a tombolo is a kind of spit that links an island to the mainland, not just another name for a spit, and a 'landlocked' tombolo makes no sense. The search results give the tombolo example as Chesil Beach in Dorset, not Rhossili.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales, UK, are home to a 400-meter-long natural rock arch called the Worm's Head that is only accessible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Worm's Head wrong. It is not a 400-meter-long natural rock arch. Wikipedia and other sources describe it as a limestone headland and tidal island about a mile (roughly 1.6 km) long, made up of the Inner, Middle and Outer Heads. The natural arch is a separate, much smaller feature on it called Devil's Bridge. Worm's Head is next to Rhossili Bay and can only be reached at low tide, but calling it a 400 m rock arch is wrong.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales, UK, are home to a 400-meter-long natural rock arch called the Worm's Head, which is visible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Worm's Head wrong. It isn't a 400-metre natural rock arch. Wikipedia describes it as a limestone headland and tidal island at Rhossili, about a mile long and made up of Inner, Middle and Outer Heads. The natural arch is a separate feature on it called the Devil's Bridge. What low tide does is uncover a causeway that lets people walk out to it; it doesn't make the headland visible, since it can be seen at any tide.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales, UK, are home to a 400-meter-long natural rock formation known as the Worm's Head that is only accessible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim checks out. Worm's Head is at Rhossili in Gower, Wales, and you can only walk out to it around low tide (about 2.5 hours either side). The length is wrong, though. Wikipedia says the headland, made up of the Inner, Middle and Outer Heads, is roughly one mile long (about 1.6 km), which is far longer than 400 metres. The claim also calls it part of 'the beaches' of the bay, but it is really a tidal headland made of islands joined to the mainland by a causeway.

text: The chemosynthetic bacteria that live near underwater volcanic vents can survive in temperatures ranging from slightly below freezing to as high as 110°F (43.3°C).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's upper limit is wrong. It says 110°F (43.3°C), but trustworthy sources give much higher temperatures. EBSCO Research Starters says some vent chemosynthetic bacteria can tolerate temperatures "up to 110 degrees Celsius or more," which is 230°F. WHOI's Dive & Discover says vent thermophiles grow best above 176°F (80°C) and that the high-temperature record for growth is 235°F (113°C). The claim seems to confuse 110°C with 110°F, and the evidence does not support a 43.3°C maximum.

text: The concept of the charitable trust dates back to ancient civilizations, with recorded evidence of such trusts in ancient Greece around 500 BCE.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The general idea is supported. Britannica says philanthropic groups and endowments existed in the ancient Middle East, Greece and Rome, and it cites the endowment for Plato's Academy (c. 387 BCE). I found no source that records a charitable trust in Greece around 500 BCE, though. Sources linked to that era (for example, Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound) tie it to the coinage of the word 'philanthropy,' not to evidence of trusts. Scholarship on Greek endowments also notes that they were not separate legal entities, so calling them 'trusts' is loose. Because the specific 500 BCE date can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The concept of the charitable trust dates back to ancient civilizations, with recorded evidence of such trusts in ancient Greece around 600 BC.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the specific date in this claim. Trustworthy sources such as Britannica and Encyclopedia.com support the general point that philanthropic foundations and endowments existed in ancient civilizations, including Greece. For example, Britannica says an endowment supported Plato's Academy, founded around 387 BCE. However, no source I found records a charitable trust in ancient Greece around 600 BC. The only 6th-century-BC reference was on an unreliable site, elpis.org.gr, and it was about a 'philanthropy' tax exemption, not a trust. It also wrongly ties that exemption to Byzantine emperors. The 'around 600 BC' detail is therefore unverified.

text: The darkest star in the universe, V616 Monocerotis, is a red giant star that is so dim and cool, it's darker than its surroundings in space.
label: contradicted
reason: V616 Monocerotis (also called A0620-00) is not a red giant. Wikipedia describes it as a binary system made up of a black hole and a K2 V star, which is an orange main-sequence star, not a giant. The black hole pulls matter off the star, so the system is an X-ray nova, not a star that is darker than the space around it. That makes the 'red giant' description wrong, and the claim that it is 'darker than its surroundings' has no support.

text: The highest mountain in the solar system, as of our current knowledge, is Olympus Mons on Mars, which stands at an impressive height of approximately 27 km above the Martian surface.
label: supported
reason: Several sources call Olympus Mons on Mars the tallest known mountain in the Solar System. Simple English Wikipedia gives its height as 27 km. Other sources give about 26 km above the surrounding plains (Big Think, Wikipedia) or about 25.75 km (EBSCO), so 'approximately 27 km' is a reasonable figure. One caveat: Wikipedia says Olympus Mons is roughly tied with Rheasilvia on the asteroid Vesta, and its height above Mars's datum is only about 21.9 km. Still, the sources mostly agree with the claim as worded.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is actually on Mars, known as the Arcadia Rupes, which stretches over 3,600 kilometers in length.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no Martian mountain range called 'Arcadia Rupes.' Searching for it only brings up Arcadia Planitia, which is a smooth lava plain on Mars, and the Arcadia quadrangle map region. The 3,600 km length also couldn't be the solar-system record. Wikipedia says Earth's mid-ocean ridge is a continuous mountain range about 65,000 km long, and even the Andes, about 7,000 km long, are nearly twice the claimed 3,600 km. So the claim is wrong about the feature's existence and about the record.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is found on Mars and is known as the Altai Range, also known as the Noctis Labyrinthus.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. NASA/JPL says Noctis Labyrinthus is a large system of intersecting valleys and canyons at the western end of Valles Marineris on Mars. It is not a mountain range. The Altai mountains are on Earth, in Central Asia, not on Mars, and they are not another name for Noctis Labyrinthus.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is on Mars, known as the Tartarus Dorsa.
label: contradicted
reason: Tartarus Dorsa isn't on Mars. It's a region of 'bladed' terrain on Pluto that NASA's New Horizons spacecraft imaged in 2015 (Nature; Astronomy Now). It also isn't described anywhere as the longest mountain range in the solar system. Its ridges are a few hundred metres high and spaced 3–5 km apart, so they look like penitentes, not a giant mountain range.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,389 miles long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Explorer says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest chain of mountains on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). That matches the claim's figure of about 40,389 miles. NOAA Ocean Service and WHOI also call it Earth's longest mountain range, and WHOI says it circles the globe. The search results did not explicitly name the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. That part rests on general knowledge, not quoted evidence: the ridge system runs through all three oceans, with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running down the center of the Atlantic. Saying it runs through the 'center' of the Pacific is loose, since the East Pacific Rise sits east of center, but I treat that as an approximation rather than a contradiction. No source contradicted any part of the claim.

text: The longest record of virginity in a woman is held by a Chinese woman named Feng Jiang, who waited until her wedding day at age 41 and remained a virgin for 41 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms this claim. My searches turned up no person named Feng Jiang tied to a virginity record. The results were about unrelated people: Luo Meizhen, who claimed to be extremely old, and the artist Fengzi, born Feng Jiren. There was also a Medium blog post titled 'The World's Oldest Virgin,' but it did not mention Feng Jiang. Guinness does not appear to keep a 'longest virginity' record, and the claim makes little sense: many people stay virgins well past 41, including lifelong celibates. My search limit ran out before I could find a source that clearly disproves it, so I can't verify or refute the claim.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "Strengths," but the officially longest one syllable is often considered to be "psych".
label: contradicted
reason: Sources commonly cite nine-letter words such as "strengths" among the longest one-syllable English words, and Guinness lists "strengths" as the longest English word with only one vowel. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable English words includes 10-letter candidates such as "scraunched" and "strengthed," and says there is no single correct answer. "Psych" has only five letters, so it is not considered the official longest one-syllable word, and no source suggests it is. That part of the claim is false.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Egyptian "Bi Brian" gold magnetic rings, at the British Museum, have shown a magnetic force as powerful as that of super-strong magnets used in modern magnetic confinement fusion devices.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of any Ancient Egyptian "Bi Brian" magnetic rings at the British Museum. Searches only turn up gift-shop fridge magnets and ordinary gold finger rings. The claim also conflicts with well-established facts. Gold is not magnetic; it is weakly diamagnetic. The strongest known magnets are modern laboratory magnets, such as the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory's 45.5-tesla magnet, the 100-tesla pulsed magnet at Los Alamos, and China's record-setting resistive and hybrid magnets. These sources directly contradict the idea that ancient gold rings are the strongest known magnet.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Egyptian 'magnets' at Visvakarma Temple in Kerala, India, still holds a magnetic charge after about 2600 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources name different record-holders for the strongest magnet. Among human-made magnets, Los Alamos' 100-tesla pulsed magnet holds the non-destructive field record, alongside laboratory hybrid magnets of about 45 tesla. Among natural objects, magnetars are the strongest known magnets. My searches found no reliable evidence that any Ancient Egyptian 'magnets' exist at a Visvakarma Temple in Kerala, or that they have kept a magnetic charge for about 2600 years. Results about Kerala's Vishwakarma metalworking traditions do not mention these objects. The claim appears to be fabricated and conflicts with the established record-holders.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Greek cities of Magnesia, was believed to have enough magnetic properties that they could pick up small iron objects from a distance.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the facts wrong. Magnesia was a place name, not a magnet. The word 'magnet' comes from the Greek for 'Magnesian stone' (lodestone), named after the city Magnesia ad Sipylum or the Greek region of Magnesia. Lodestone was never the strongest known magnet either. Today's records belong to lab magnets (for example, 45.5 T at the US National High Magnetic Field Laboratory and 100 T pulsed magnets at Los Alamos), and the strongest natural fields come from magnetars. Ancient lodestones were known to attract iron, but the claim's main point, that the cities of Magnesia were the strongest known magnet, is false.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient magnetite pieces called The M Manny Magnet, has a magnetic field that can hold 5000 pounds of weight, about the weight of a small car.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing about a "M Manny Magnet" or any ancient magnetite pieces holding a record. The search for that name only turned up unrelated results, like Manhattan School of Music souvenir magnets. Trusted sources say the strongest magnets are man-made laboratory magnets: the National High Magnetic Field Lab's 45.5 T hybrid and 100 T pulsed magnets, and China's 42 T resistive magnet. Natural magnetite is a weak magnet by comparison, so the claim that ancient magnetite is the strongest known magnet is false.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient ornamented Magnets found at a Neolithic site, have magnetic fields of up to 3000 Gauss and were discovered in Iraq around 2700 BC
label: contradicted
reason: The strongest known magnets are modern laboratory magnets. The US National High Magnetic Field Lab holds a record of 45.5 tesla (455,000 gauss), and China has built a 42-tesla resistive magnet. In nature, magnetars reach fields of billions of tesla. That makes a 3000-gauss magnet (0.3 T) far from the strongest. I found no credible source for 'two ancient ornamented magnets' from a Neolithic site in Iraq. The dating is also inconsistent: 2700 BC falls in the Bronze Age, not the Neolithic.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient piers on Cape Acre in Israel, has a magnetic field of approximately 8 times greater than Earth's field.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The strongest known magnets are lab magnets, not ancient piers in Israel. The MagLab hybrid magnet holds the record for the strongest continuous field at 45.5 tesla, and Los Alamos has a 100-tesla pulsed magnet. Earth's field is only about 25–65 microtesla, so these magnets are hundreds of thousands to millions of times stronger than Earth's field, not about 8 times. Magnetars in space are stronger still. No reliable source names any 'ancient piers on Cape Acre' as the strongest magnet.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient piers on Cape Acre in Israel, has a magnetic field of approximately 8,000 Teslas.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the strongest known magnets are magnetars, neutron stars with fields of roughly 10^10 to 10^11 tesla. A direct measurement found about 1.6 billion tesla. The strongest field made in a lab was about 1,200 T (Guinness World Records, Univ. of Tokyo 2018). The ancient piers at Acre (Akko) in Israel are a Hellenistic-era harbor structure. No source describes them as a magnet or links them to any 8,000 T field. Both the identity of the strongest magnet and its field strength are contradicted.

text: The vibrant blue-green bacteria known as "Glowing Mushrooms" also known as armillaria mellea is often not actually a fungus but a blue-green species of algae called leucocyclus.
label: contradicted
reason: Armillaria mellea (honey fungus) is a basidiomycete fungus in the kingdom Fungi, family Physalacriaceae. It is not a bacterium or a blue-green alga. Its mycelium glows while actively growing, but that doesn't make it an alga. I found no source for an alga called "leucocyclus". The claim that it is "not actually a fungus" is directly contradicted.

text: The world's longest mountain range, known as the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. Wikipedia calls the mid-ocean ridge the world's longest mountain range and says it is part of every ocean. It gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the full oceanic ridge system as about 80,000 km. A PMC/NCBI paper gives a total length of about 75,000 km. Several other sources describe the ridge as 'over 65,000 km' and say it runs through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), the Indian Ocean (Southwest and Central Indian Ridges) and the Pacific (East Pacific Rise). There is one small discrepancy: NOAA and WHOI describe the length as 'nearly 65,000 km' rather than over it. Because the larger total-system figures exceed 65,000 km, the claim is still broadly supported. The phrase 'through the middle' of the Pacific is loose, since the East Pacific Rise lies in the eastern Pacific.

text: TheSkills in opposites tasting - The combination of blue cheese and pears is an example of the flavor pairing known as "phenomenal opposites" in the world of food.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found agree that blue cheese and pears are a classic contrasting pairing. They describe the cheese as salty, sharp and creamy and the pear as sweet and juicy, and one calls them 'opposites that attract.' However, none of them use the term 'phenomenal opposites.' A direct search for that phrase in a food context only turned up unrelated antonym-dictionary pages. Nothing shows this is a recognised name for a type of flavour pairing. The contrast itself is supported, but the specific term in the claim can't be confirmed.

text: TheSkills in opposites tasting - The combination of blue cheese and pears is an example of the flavor pairing principle known as 'opposite taste'.
label: supported
reason: I found several sources that describe blue cheese and pear as a classic contrasting pairing, where sweet and salty or savoury flavours balance each other. St. James Cheese's pairing guide has a tip called "Opposites Attract" about contrasting pairs like sweet and salty, and gives blue cheese as an example. The Institute of Culinary Education uses the same "Opposites Attract" principle, and Cheese Scientist explains the pear–blue cheese match by sweet-vs-savoury contrast. The exact phrase 'opposite taste' isn't a standard term, but the principle the claim describes matches these sources, and none contradict it.

text: There are approximately 86 million species on Earth, but only about 1.3 million of them have been formally described and documented by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate is about 8.7 million species, not 86 million. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) and has a margin of ±1.3 million, with roughly 1.2–1.3 million species catalogued. The claim's figure of 86 million is off by about a factor of ten, likely a misreading of 8.6–8.7 million.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting around 86 billion neurons exist in the average adult human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain is correct. The comparison is wrong, though. Psychology Today calls the idea that the brain has more neurons than the Milky Way has stars a "widespread myth", and Nature Scitable also addresses it. Both put the galaxy at roughly 200–400 billion stars, which is well above 86 billion neurons. So the main comparison in the claim is contradicted.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called the Turkish sea nomad, also known as the 'Nomadic jellyfish', which has the unique characteristic of being immortal.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no jellyfish called the 'Turkish sea nomad.' The 'nomad' or 'nomadic' jellyfish is Rhopilema nomadica. It comes from the Indian and Pacific Oceans and has spread into the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal. It is known for painful stings, not for being immortal. The species known as the 'immortal jellyfish' is a different one, Turritopsis dohrnii (sometimes listed as T. nutricula), which can revert to an earlier life stage. The claim mixes up two different species.

text: пергамент, первоначально сделанный из кожи животных, был первым типом бумаги широко использованным цивилизациями.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Parchment was made from animal skins, but it was not the first widely used paper-like writing material. Papyrus came first: Egyptians were writing on it around 2800 BC, and it became the first standardized writing material in history. Parchment only began replacing papyrus as the main writing surface from about the 4th century AD. Strictly speaking, parchment isn't paper at all, since paper is made from plant fibers.

text: пергамент, первоначально считавшийся недосягаемым для人の использования, сегодня включает большинство современных бумаг.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim. Parchment is a writing material made from prepared animal skin. It was invented, or at least widely adopted, as a practical substitute for papyrus, so it was not originally thought to be beyond human use. In the later Middle Ages, cheaper milled paper largely replaced parchment. Modern papers are therefore not mostly made of parchment.

text: A group of kissing HUDS, which are also known as a cluster of greater flamingos, is estimated to be one of the largest known groups of individual birds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that "kissing HUDS" is a real name for a group of greater flamingos, or for any group of flamingos. Reliable bird sources say a group of flamingos is called a "flock," or archaically a "flamboyance." That doesn't strictly prove no such term exists, but the claim's main term has no clear referent and can't be verified. I also found no evidence that greater flamingo groups rank among the largest known bird gatherings; the huge flamingo flocks usually cited are of lesser flamingos. Because the key parts can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A group of kissing HUDs, also known as a "grouping," of octopuses can be named collectively as an 'octopus alignment.'
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found calls a group of octopuses an "octopus alignment." The term "kissing HUDs" also doesn't appear to have any real meaning. A Study.com explainer says there is no widely accepted collective noun for octopuses because they usually live alone. Where a collective noun is given, it is a different word: QuizzClub calls "consortium" the widely accepted term, and other informal lists use words like "tangle." These are low-authority trivia and educational sites. The claim's term is unsupported, and the sources I found give different names for a group of octopuses.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains a 25-meter-deep sinkhole that drops from a paved road and connects to an underground river.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that supports the claim. The sources I checked (Wikipedia, University of Tasmania archives, camping and rafting guides) describe Butlers Gorge only as a hydro-electric locality next to Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station on the Derwent River. None of them mention a sinkhole, karst features, or an underground river there. The Tasmanian sinkholes that did come up are in other places: Disappearing Falls in the Florentine Valley, Trowutta, Pyengana and Railton. No source directly rules out a sinkhole at Butlers Gorge either, so the claim can't be confirmed or refuted. My last search attempt also failed because I hit the tool-use limit.

text: Butler's Gorge, a major waterfall in Tasmania, Australia, drops water over 300 meters down into the sea.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's inland Central Highlands. It is home to Clark Dam on the River Derwent and the Butlers Gorge hydroelectric power station. None of them describe it as a waterfall, and nothing suggests it drops 300 m or more into the sea, which would be impossible from that inland location.

text: C manuscript, often called the oldest surviving actual map of the British Isles, on display at The British Museum.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm this claim. "C manuscript" doesn't point clearly to one document, and none of the sources I found use that term for a map. The likeliest candidates are Matthew Paris's map of Britain from about 1250 (Cotton MS Claudius D VI) and the Anglo-Saxon Cotton world map. Sources describe these as among the earliest fairly realistic maps of Britain, but both are held by the British Library, not The British Museum. The British Museum only appears as the publisher of a 1928 book reproducing the Paris maps; the manuscripts were then in its collections, before the British Library became separate. Because the manuscript can't be identified and its location doesn't match, the claim can't be judged true or false.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apoptosis, where they intentionally detach certain body parts to distract predators and increase their own chances of survival.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim uses the wrong term. Apoptosis is programmed cell death at the level of individual cells. In insects it happens during development and metamorphosis. It does not mean shedding body parts to escape predators. Dropping a body part to distract a predator is called autotomy, which is a different process. So the claim's key statement that caterpillars use apoptosis to detach body parts and distract predators is false.

text: Cutom made the first performance of the air jet machine, which is a precursor to modern vacuum cleaners, in 1901 in Chicago.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-documented 1901 demonstration of an American air-blowing (air jet) carpet-cleaning machine, which inspired the suction vacuum cleaner, happened in London, not Chicago. Wikipedia says it was at the Empire Music Hall, and other sources say St Pancras Station. Hubert Cecil Booth watched it. The machine's inventor isn't named, but it likely matches John S. Thurman's blown-air design. No source identifies anyone called 'Cutom' or places this first demonstration in Chicago.

text: Giraffes have a unique pulse pattern, with their heart rate dropping significantly when they run, allowing them to conserve energy and maintain their speed.
label: contradicted
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Experimental Biology, citing earlier field measurements from 1969, reports that a giraffe's heart rate goes up from about 40 beats per minute when it is standing quietly to as much as 175 beats per minute when it gallops. That is more than a fourfold rise. The claim says the heart rate drops significantly during running to save energy, which is the opposite of what was measured.

text: Our brains process visual information more efficiently than text-based information, which is why images can convey complex messages more quickly and effectively than words alone.
label: supported
reason: Many sources support the general idea that people take in images faster and remember them better than words. These include the documented picture superiority effect (Wikipedia), MIT research finding that an image can be processed in about 13 ms (cited by MedTech Intelligence), and design and psychology sources that explicitly say the brain processes visual information more efficiently than text. The popular "60,000 times faster" figure has been debunked as unsourced (Photutorial, Medium), but this claim doesn't use that number. Even the debunkers acknowledge that pictures can be processed faster than words in some contexts, so the claim's general direction holds. It is somewhat oversimplified, though: picture superiority mainly concerns memory, and it disappears when the pictures are very similar to each other.

text: Our brains process visual information more efficiently when we are exposed to bright surroundings, and in dim lighting situations, brain activity tends to increase significantly.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a reliable source that backs either part of the claim as stated, and the evidence I did find points in different directions. Bright light helps: a Michigan State University study found that dim lighting harmed brain function (the hippocampus in rats), which loosely fits the idea that bright surroundings are better. But brain activity does not reliably go up in dim light. A PNAS fMRI study found that activity in the visual cortex and visual thalamus rises as light gets brighter. The same study did report other light-dependent signals in the prefrontal cortex. Other studies only show that light changes brain-state dynamics. None of these sources clearly shows that brain activity 'increases significantly' in dim lighting or that visual processing is generally 'more efficient' in bright surroundings. My search was also cut short by a tool limit before I could look further.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a straight line, but rather zigzags through the Pacific Ocean to avoid several countries passing through it twice.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (Shaalaa, time.now, prepp.in) say the International Date Line is not straight. They say it zigzags through the Pacific so that countries and island groups such as the Aleutians are not split between two calendar days. The claim's wording, 'passing through it twice', is awkward, but it describes the same idea: the line bends to avoid cutting through countries. These sources are educational and reference sites rather than official authorities, but they all agree.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, with a total coastline of approximately 243,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, a government source, says Canada has the world's longest coastline at 243,042 km. Mental Floss agrees that Canada's lead is undisputed and cites Canada's national statistics office for the same 243,042 km figure. Some sources give a lower 202,080 km because of the coastline paradox, but the claim's figure of about 243,000 km matches the official Canadian number.

text: The driest desert on Earth is Antarctica, which is a frozen desert covering about 14 million square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Antarctica covers about 14.2 million km², and several sources call it the world's driest continent and largest desert. Its McMurdo Dry Valleys are described as the driest place on Earth. Some sources, such as WorldAtlas, popularly call the Atacama the driest desert, but History.com notes that the Atacama is technically wetter than parts of Antarctica. The Atacama is better described as the driest non-polar desert. The more authoritative evidence therefore supports the claim that Antarctica is the driest desert and covers about 14 million km².

text: The highest recorded number of piano notes played simultaneously is 376, achieved by Hong Kong pianist Yuja Wang in 2007.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Wikipedia, Classic FM and Interlude.hk all say Yuja Wang was born in Beijing, China (and is a US citizen), so calling her a Hong Kong pianist is wrong. I found no record of her playing 376 notes at once, in 2007 or any other year. The number also can't be right, because a standard piano has only 88 keys. The piano records that do exist are different kinds of feats: most key hits in a minute (824, by Domingos-Antonio Gomes) and most people playing one piano at the same time (20 students in Sarajevo).

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers).
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge is the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). NOAA's Ocean Service calls it the longest mountain range on Earth, and WHOI gives nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). These figures back the claim of 'over 40,000 miles' and roughly 64,000 km, and none of the sources contradicts it.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," regardless of the aftermath misconception that it is "smiles."
label: contradicted
reason: "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It is better known as the longest word you can type with only the left hand. A fact-check found that the longest one-syllable words in common use have nine letters, such as "screeched" and "strengths." Some rare ten-letter words like "scraunched" also exist. That evidence contradicts the claim.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strewn".
label: contradicted
reason: Dictionary.com names "squirrelled" (11 letters, said as one syllable by some speakers) as the longest one-syllable English word, with "broughammed" (also 11 letters) as another candidate. Other often-cited examples, like "strengths" and "scraunched", are also much longer than "strewn", which has only 6 letters, so it is not the longest.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to reverse its wing stroke.
label: supported
reason: Several trustworthy sources, including UC Davis's hummingbird research site, WorldAtlas, and Sciencing, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They explain this with the birds' special anatomy: a ball-and-socket shoulder joint, strong flight muscles, and the ability to invert or reverse the wing on the upstroke. That matches the claim about their physiology and reversed wing stroke. One caveat: Birdspot says some other birds, such as herons and flycatchers, can flutter backwards for a short distance. Even so, it agrees that hummingbirds are the only birds that can truly fly backwards for any length of time, so the claim still holds overall.

text: There are approximately 1.86 billion animals on the planet that migrate, which includes species such as elephants, caribou, and monarch butterflies.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for a global count of about 1.86 billion migratory animals, and reliable sources show the real number is far higher. Cornell's All About Birds says more than 1 billion birds can be migrating over the United States alone on a single autumn night. Estimates put the monarch butterfly migration alone at up to more than 1 billion. The Nature Conservancy notes that bogong moths were once estimated at about 4 billion. Scientific American reports that about 10 billion tons of marine animals migrate up and down the ocean every day, and NPR and Smithsonian describe 'billions of animals' migrating each year. Given these figures, a worldwide total of about 1.86 billion is a large undercount, even though elephants, caribou and monarchs are real migratory species.

text: There are approximately 3.8 million different species on Earth, which is a vast and still-unseen portion estimated to be around 8.7 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is right, but the 3.8 million figure is not. The 2011 census study reported by ScienceDaily estimates about 8.7 million species on Earth in total (give or take 1.3 million). Of those, only about 1.25 million had been described and catalogued, with roughly 700,000 more thought to be described but not yet in central databases. That puts the known total at about 2 million at most. My search found no source supporting a figure of about 3.8 million species, either as the number described or as the total, so this part of the claim conflicts with the sources.

text: There are more neutrons in the nucleus of an atom than protons, but the number of protons determines the chemical element.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim is right: the number of protons is what identifies the element. The first half is wrong as a general statement. Atoms do not always have more neutrons than protons. The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission says hydrogen-1 (protium) has 1 proton and no neutrons, and that a stable nucleus does not always have equal numbers of neutrons and protons. Light nuclei such as helium-4 and carbon-12 have equal numbers, and helium-3 has fewer neutrons than protons. Heavier elements do tend to have more neutrons than protons, but that is not true of every atom.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered on Earth, according to a 2021 estimate by biologists and naturalists.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says over 10 million species have been discovered, and that's wrong. According to Our World in Data, which draws on IUCN Red List tallies, only about 2.16 million species have actually been described, and some of those are probably duplicates. Estimates of more than 10 million (for example Chapman's 2009 estimate of 11 million) are projections of the total number of species on Earth, most of which haven't been discovered. The widely cited Mora et al. estimate is about 8.7 million species in total. So the claim mixes up projected totals with discovered species, and the evidence contradicts it.

text: There are over 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which is a significant portion of the approximately 3 trillion total plant and tree biomass.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Yale study led by Crowther, published in Nature, put the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. The claim confuses two figures. The roughly 3 trillion number counts trees, not 'total plant and tree biomass'. The 7.9 billion figure is about the world's human population, not a tree count. Even taken literally, 7.9 billion out of 3 trillion would be only about 0.26%, which is not 'a significant portion.'

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 86 billion stars and 86 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, but the Milky Way is usually estimated to hold 100 to 400 billion stars, not 86 billion. That means there are more stars than neurons, which is the opposite of what the claim says. The claim also contradicts itself: if both numbers were 86 billion, neurons could not outnumber stars. The older idea that the brain has 100 billion neurons has been revised down to 86 billion, which makes it even clearer that stars outnumber neurons.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) but is not visible above the ocean's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at roughly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). However, both describe that length as "nearly" 65,000 km, not over 65,000 km. The bigger problem is the claim that the ridge is not visible above the ocean's surface. NOAA says more than 90% of it lies underwater and WHOI says "nearly all" of it is beneath the sea. That means some of the ridge does rise above sea level; Iceland is the best-known example. The claim says the ridge is never visible, which these sources contradict.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stretch."
label: contradicted
reason: "Stretch" has only 7 letters, and several one-syllable words are longer. Dictionary.com names "squirrelled" (11 letters, in one common pronunciation) as the longest one-syllable English word and says "broughammed" is also 11 letters. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable words gives other candidates, such as "strengths" (9 letters) and 10-letter words like "scraunched" and "schmaltzed." No source names "stretch."

text: A ##### The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses"  when you pronounce it.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), not one. It is famous for a different reason: it is the longest common word you can type using only the left hand on a QWERTY keyboard. Wikipedia and Dictionary.com list much shorter words as the longest one-syllable words. These include "screeched" and "strengths" (9 letters) and ten-letter candidates such as "scraunched" and "schtroumpfed".

text: Butterfly fish have a unique way of eating: they have a specialized jaw structure that allows them to eat in tight spaces between coral and other structures.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back the claim. Encyclopedia.com says many butterflyfish species have the mouth at the end of a short, tubular snout that helps them poke into tiny crevices in coral reefs. The Waikiki Aquarium describes longnose butterflyfish probing coral branches and reef crevices using specialized jaw anatomy. EOL notes jaw specializations, with some jaws longer than 25% of body length, and ScienceDirect describes a 'specialized feeding apparatus' in Chaetodon. The National Marine Sanctuary Foundation and Scuba Diving also mention protruding jaws used to feed in small crevices. One caveat: snout and jaw shape varies by species, and some butterflyfish have short jaws for nipping coral polyps. Even so, the general claim holds.

text: Butterfly keys on pianos were developed to make playing harder for pianists with four fingers partially paralysed.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing about a piano keyboard called 'butterfly keys' that was developed for pianists with four partially paralysed fingers. The results were about other things: Apple's and IBM's 'butterfly' laptop keyboards, Wurlitzer's 'Butterfly' baby grand pianos, a teaching prop called the 'butterfly band', and unrelated pages about piano injuries. Some piano keyboard patents I found aim to make playing easier, so 'harder' seems an unlikely purpose for an adaptation like this. Still, no source confirms or contradicts what the claim says about the origin or purpose of 'butterfly keys'. My search tool hit its usage limit before I could check further.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique way of communicating with each other by initiating a complex courtship ritual involving color changes, posturing, and specific body positioning.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly back the claim. A-Z Animals says butterflyfish communicate mainly by sight, using colour patterns, lateral displays, fin erection and head-down or side-on postures. It adds that they actively change their colours depending on the situation and that courtship behaviours act as signals. Lamar University's Spotfin Butterflyfish page describes courtship with chasing, headstands and lateral displays. Reefs.com says courtship in banded butterflyfish is drawn out, with pairs circling each other head to tail. Encyclopedia.com notes that butterflyfish use display gestures that include colour changes. Two caveats apply. The colour-change evidence I found mostly concerns threat displays and general mood rather than courtship itself, and calling the behaviour 'unique' is an exaggeration. Still, posturing, body positioning, colour signalling and ritualised courtship are all documented, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: China is home to the world's largest singleiaplex of buddhist stupa complex, called theingga days site in sichuan.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is too garbled to check: "singleiaplex" and "theingga days site" don't clearly refer to any known place. Searches found no Buddhist stupa complex in Sichuan with a name like this, and no source calling any Sichuan site the world's largest stupa complex. Sources give that title to other places, such as the Great Peace Stupa in Dehradun, India, and Kesariya in Bihar, India. Sichuan's best-known large Buddhist site of this kind, the Songge (Gsumge) Mani Stone city in Sêrxü, is a structure built from carved prayer stones, not a stupa complex. It also has a different name. Because the claim's subject can't be clearly identified, it can be neither supported nor contradicted.

text: Despite being a predominantly aquatic animal, Octopuses can lose up to 30% of their body weight through dehydration while on land due to their bodies lacking a specialized kidney to conserve water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for the 30% figure. One search returned only processing and cooking studies on octopus weight change in water, and another returned only rat dehydration studies. My search limit ran out before I could find a source on octopus kidneys. From general zoology, octopuses do have kidney-like organs (renal sacs or appendages), so the claim that they lack a kidney is doubtful. However, the claim says a specialized kidney for conserving water, which I could not confirm or rule out. The specific number and the stated cause remain unverified.

text: Dolphins have been observed showing signs of empathy and compassion by helping other animals, including humans, in distress.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable news reports describe dolphins helping other animals and humans in trouble. NBC News and ABC News reported in 2008 that Moko, a bottlenose dolphin in New Zealand, guided two stranded pygmy sperm whales, a mother and her calf, back to safety. In 2004, a pod of dolphins off New Zealand reportedly circled a group of lifeguards for about 40 minutes and kept a great white shark away from them. Dolphins are also widely reported to hold up injured pod members so they can breathe. Whether this counts as true 'empathy and compassion' is still debated, but the claim only says the dolphins showed signs of it, and these accounts back that up.

text: Giraffes have a unique uneven heartbeat pattern, with a long heartbeat followed by a few short ones, allowing a 65- stunning 140 BPM average.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that giraffes have a unique uneven heartbeat, with one long beat followed by a few short ones. The heart-rate figures in the sources conflict. Africa Geographic and other sites give 40–90 bpm, and a measured average was about 56 bpm. A few less reliable sites say the heart beats 150 or up to 170 times a minute. The claim's garbled '65–140 BPM average' is neither clearly confirmed nor clearly ruled out, and its main point about the heartbeat pattern is unverified.

text: Rabella is the world's longest-living cat, confirmed to have lived to be 44 years and 283 days old.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. Guinness World Records names Creme Puff as the oldest cat ever. She was born on 3 August 1967 and died on 6 August 2005, aged 38 years and 3 days. Wikipedia's list of longest-living cats also gives Creme Puff as the oldest verified cat. No search turned up any cat called Rabella, and nothing confirms a cat living to 44 years and 283 days.

text: The Blar Speaker,  oldest known surviving working mech computer, was built in the 1910s by Canadian inventor Percy L. Spencer.
label: contradicted

text: The vinegar produced by the acetic acid fermentation of apple cider is a byproduct of the same microbial process that makes bread rise, known as yeast fermentation.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean.

It runs through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian, and Pacific (East Pacific Rise) oceans. One wording issue: these sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over.' Wikipedia gives a flat 65,000 km, and some estimates of the full ridge system are higher. The Pacific segment also lies to the east rather than in the middle of the ocean. These are small differences, so the main points of the claim hold.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Reello" or "Red River", is a mysterious river that appears to boil with bubbles, despite being located in the heart of the Amazon rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon is real, but its names are wrong in the claim. Wikipedia says its Quechua name is Shanay-timpishka, meaning 'boiled by the heat of the sun', and that its popular names are 'Boiling River' or 'Río Hirviente' in Spanish. Neither Wikipedia nor the other source found calls it the 'Reello' or 'Red River'. The rest of the claim is roughly right: the river is in the Peruvian Amazon, and hot underground springs make the water extremely hot.

text: The country of Singapore has the highest percentage of OPT (Optometrists, Pharmacists, Nurses, Doctors) professionals globally, making it a hub for medical care and research in Asia.

Wikipedia lists Singapore at about 26 doctors per 10,000 people, which is lower than many countries, and Cuba has the most doctors per capita. Also, 'OPT' is not a recognised abbreviation for these professions.

text: Honey is a super-conductor when it's heated above 2.5°C (36.5°F), and it's the only food item known to have this unique property.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is not a superconductor. A superconductor has zero electrical resistance, and that happens only in certain materials cooled to very low temperatures, not in food warmed above 2.5°C. Published research treats honey as having low, measurable electrical conductivity, which comes from its mineral and salt content and changes with viscosity. The Codex Standard for Honey even caps diluted honey's conductivity at 0.8 mS/cm and uses it as a quality measure. That is ordinary, finite conductivity, so both the superconductor claim and the 'only food with this property' claim are false.

text: The einzige weisse deutscher spitz, also known as the white German Spitz, has been a symbol of Russia since Peter the Great adopted the dog as the imperial breed in the 18th century.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that Peter the Great adopted the white German Spitz as an imperial breed, or that the breed is a symbol of Russia. Wikipedia, the VDH (the German Kennel Club) and other breed sources describe the German Spitz (Deutscher Spitz) as a German breed. Its history goes back to Central and Germany, with an early record from 1450 involving the German Count Eberhard zu Sayn. None of these sources mentions any link to Russia or Peter the Great. The German term in the claim, "einzige weisse deutscher spitz", means "only white German Spitz". No source uses it as a name for the breed. These sources do not directly say "this is not a Russian symbol", but their account of a German origin conflicts with the claim, and the claim appears to be made up.

text: The world's largest waterfall, when measured by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, where a submarine waterfall flows down a slope at the edge of the mid-Atlantic ridge.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is mostly right but gets the location wrong. Reliable sources (Live Science, HowStuffWorks, EarthSky, Wikipedia) agree that the Denmark Strait cataract is a huge underwater waterfall between Greenland and Iceland. They describe it as the world's largest, dropping about 3,500 m and carrying roughly 5 million m³ of water per second. However, those sources say the cold, dense water spills over an undersea ridge inside the Denmark Strait, which Wikipedia names as the Greenland–Iceland Rise, and then flows down into the Atlantic basin. None of them place it at the edge of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. That ridge runs through Iceland itself, east of the strait. The claim's location detail is therefore wrong.

text: The longest war in recorded history is the Roman-SССР л.atine Wars, but the conflict most often cited as the longest is the Hundred Years' War between England and Франция lasting 116 years from 1337 to 1453, but also the Roman-Sирий War or the Roman war against Pirates,

It is still being installed inside a mountain in West Texas, and the Long Now Foundation's site describes it as being built to need little maintenance, not as sealed. The search results do back up that the Long Now Foundation runs the project and that it is in Texas.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spanning over 65,000 kilometers in length, with most of it located underwater.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. NOAA Ocean Explorer calls the mid-ocean ridge the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km long, with more than 90% of it underwater. WHOI and Wikipedia also call it the world's longest mountain range, and WHOI adds that nearly all of it lies beneath the sea. NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," but other estimates are higher, such as about 74,000–75,000 km from NASA and a PMC study, which supports a length above 65,000 km.

text: Organisms in certain species of jellyfish are biologically immortal, meaning they can revert back into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation, essentially making them ageless.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and Britannica both describe Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the "immortal jellyfish," as biologically immortal. They say it can go back to an earlier, juvenile (polyp) stage through transdifferentiation, which restarts its life cycle and lets it avoid aging. Two small caveats don't contradict the claim: Britannica notes it is technically a hydrozoan rather than a true jellyfish, and individuals can still die from predators or disease.

text: Caterpillars have a natural defense mechanism where they secrete a toxic liquid from their bodies to deter predators, which is often harmless to humans but unpalatable and even toxic to animals.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed Scientific Reports (Nature) study confirms that many caterpillars use chemical defenses: secretions from exocrine glands such as the swallowtail osmeterium, regurgitated plant compounds, and toxins taken up from host plants. It also showed that the osmeterial secretion repels predators like ants and is toxic to some of them. The source doesn't directly address whether these secretions harm humans. Swallowtail osmeterial fluid is generally described as foul-smelling but not dangerous to people, so the 'often harmless to humans' part is plausible. Not every caterpillar has this defense, but the general claim is consistent with the evidence.

text: The glowworms in Waitomo, New Zealand, are actually a species of insect that produces a blue-green bioluminescent light through a chemical reaction within their bodies.
label: supported
reason: The Waitomo glowworm is Arachnocampa luminosa, a fungus gnat, which is an insect. Its larvae, and the adults too, give off blue-green light (peak around 487 nm). A peer-reviewed study in PMC shows the light comes from a chemical reaction inside the body: a luciferin–luciferase reaction that needs ATP and oxygen and takes place in a specialised light organ. Wikipedia gives the same account. All parts of the claim are backed up.

text: The continent of Antarctica is home to several active volcanoes, with the most recently discovered one being the Neumann Glacier volcanic complex, which erupted in 2015.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of a 'Neumann Glacier volcanic complex' in Antarctica. Searches turned up only unrelated places, such as Neumann Peak on Hansen Island. The Antarctic volcano reported to have erupted in 2015 is Mount Erebus, which has been known for a long time and has had an active lava lake since at least 1972. Erebus is not a recent discovery. The actual recent discoveries were a subglacial volcano in West Antarctica, found through earthquake data in 2013, and 91 new volcanoes identified under the ice in 2017. Neither has a Neumann name or a 2015 eruption, and ZME Science notes that no West Antarctic volcano has been seen erupting in the past century. Sources also say only a few Antarctic volcanoes are active; phys.org names just two, Erebus and Deception Island. The claim's main detail, a newly discovered volcano by that name erupting in 2015, appears to be made up, and the evidence assigns the 2015 eruption to Erebus.

text: There are over 8.3 million recognized species on Earth, according to the most recent estimates from the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) and the World Register of Marine Species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Only about 1.2–2 million species have actually been described, or recognized. The well-known figure of roughly 8.7 million comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is a projection of the total number of species, most of which haven't been described yet. It does not come from ITIS or WoRMS. WoRMS lists only about 250,000 accepted extant marine species, a milestone it passed in May 2026. So neither database backs the idea of over 8.3 million recognized species.

text: The Bactrian camels found in the Gobi Desert can go without water for several days due to their unique adaptations, including the ability to store water in their bloodstream by producing very concentrated urine.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back up each part of the claim. The Denver Zoo, Rosamond Gifford Zoo and Animal Diversity Web all say Bactrian camels live in the Gobi and can go days, sometimes weeks or months, without water. They put this down to adaptations like sweating very little and producing highly concentrated urine. Animal Diversity Web says the camel's kidneys return water to the bloodstream while getting rid of excess salt. Other sources say camels store water they drink in their bloodstream rather than in their humps, which hold fat. One caveat: the claim's wording, that concentrated urine is how camels 'store water in their bloodstream', is a loose description. Concentrated urine conserves water by recovering it in the kidneys and returning it to the blood. That is close to the mechanism the sources describe, so overall the claim holds up.

The phrase 'twilight planet' is just a descriptive label and doesn't change the facts being checked.

The study does say 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered, so the part about most species remaining unknown is correct. The claimed 8.7% share and the 'have existed' framing don't match the source.

text: The Bactrian camels found in the Gobi Desert can go without water for several days due to their unique adaptations, including the ability to store water in their bloodstream by producing a special type of red blood cell.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the main points of the claim. Camels, including Bactrian camels, can go days without drinking. Camels have unusual oval red blood cells that keep circulating when blood thickens and can swell a lot as the animal rehydrates (AskNature). A peer-reviewed PMC review of Bactrian camels says the oval red blood cells are 'conducive to water storage.' Other sources describe the water a camel drinks as being held in its bloodstream and body fluids rather than in the hump. One caveat: calling this 'storing water in the bloodstream' simplifies the biology somewhat. Still, no reliable source I found contradicts the claim.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola containing coca leaves and Pepsi containing "rare molasses" which would eventually be replaced with sugar, while Pepsi failed to cover the morphine production, but both were first introduced in the late 19th century.
label: contradicted
reason: Pepsi was not created as a morphine alternative. Caleb Bradham invented it in 1893 as "Brad's Drink," sold for its supposed digestive benefits (the name comes from "dyspepsia"). His recipe used kola nut extract, vanilla and "rare oils," not "rare molasses." The claim is right that Coca-Cola contained coca leaf, that Pemberton is often said to have sought a morphine substitute, and that both drinks date from the late 19th century. But the claims about Pepsi's purpose and ingredients are false.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual trees, which is roughly a billion times the number of trees in New York City.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 390 billion Amazon trees is correct. It comes from the ter Steege et al. study reported in Nature, and Mental Floss repeats it. The comparison is wrong, though. New York City has roughly 6 to 7 million trees (a Nature Scientific Data paper mapped over six million, and the USDA Forest Service urban forest report gives similar numbers). That makes the Amazon about 55,000 to 65,000 times larger than NYC, not a billion times. For the ratio to be a billion, NYC would need only about 390 trees.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, known as the Fertő-Hanság National Park, which supports an extremely diverse array of wildlife and plant species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts Fertő-Hanság National Park in the wrong part of Hungary. The park is in north-west Hungary, in Győr-Moson-Sopron county by Lake Fertő (Neusiedl), and its office is in Csorna. Kiskunfélegyháza is in Bács-Kiskun county on the Great Hungarian Plain, the area covered by Kiskunság National Park. So the Kiskunfélegyháza region's ecosystem is not known as Fertő-Hanság National Park.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it was built with redundancy and fail-safes.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'Brief History of the Internet', written by Internet pioneers including Leiner, Cerf and Kahn, says the idea that ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war is a "false rumor" that came from a separate RAND study by Paul Baran. ARPANET, the network the Internet grew out of, was built to let researchers share computing resources, not to withstand a nuclear attack. Packet switching did turn out to be robust, but that was not the original design purpose the claim gives.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the globe, primarily underwater.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas calls the global mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. It gives the length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) and says more than 90% of it is underwater. NOAA's Ocean Service says the same. The claim says "over" 65,000 km where the sources say "about", but that small difference doesn't change the substance, so every part of the claim is supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, spanning over 40,000 miles, is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a submarine mountain range that runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA confirms the main points. It calls the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,389 or 40,390 miles) long, with about 90% of it under the ocean. That fits 'over 40,000 miles' and 'submarine.' NOAA also says the ridge winds around the globe between the continents, through the major ocean basins. One detail is loosely worded: in the Pacific, the ridge (the East Pacific Rise) runs through the eastern part of the ocean, not its center. That is not enough to count as a contradiction.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees present worldwide compared to the Milky Way's estimated 200-400 billion stars.
label: supported
reason: The widely cited Crowther et al. (2015) study in Nature estimates there are about 3 trillion trees on Earth. Most estimates, including NASA's, put the Milky Way's stars at roughly 100 to 400 billion. That range covers the claim's 200–400 billion figure, and 3 trillion is still several times larger than the high end, so the comparison holds. Several sources, including WorldAtlas, reach the same conclusion.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point reached as high as 115.6 degrees Fahrenheit (46.1 degrees Celsius) in response to stepping into a parked car on a hot day.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records lists the highest recorded body temperature as 46.5°C (115.7°F). It belongs to Willie Jones, who was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta on 10 July 1980 with heatstroke. The search found no evidence that anyone named 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' exists or holds this record, and nothing supports the 115.6°F/46.1°C figure or the parked-car story. The claim gets the person, the temperature and the circumstances wrong.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," when it refers to the people, who work in the skies.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records names "scraunched" and "strengthed" (10 letters each) as the longest one-syllable English words. Nine-letter examples include "screeched" and "strengths". "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it isn't a one-syllable word at all. It's better known as one of the longest words you can type using only the left hand.

text: The bec kazakh steppe in Kazakhstan is home to the Saryarka National Park, which is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and contains over 200 species of birds, including the Demoiselle Crane.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no "Saryarka National Park" that is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Saryarka – Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, not a national park. It is made up of two State Nature Reserves, Korgalzhyn and Naurzum. Only Korgalzhyn was added to UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere network, in 2012. The site is home to many birds, but the claim gets both its name and its UNESCO status wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to the most recent estimates from the World Register of Marine Species and the International Institute for Species Exploration.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches show that the claim gets the source and the scope of the 8.7 million figure wrong. The figure comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, a study by Census of Marine Life researchers (Dalhousie University and the University of Hawaii). It was not an estimate from the World Register of Marine Species or the International Institute for Species Exploration. That study estimated about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species, not 'over' 8.7 million, and the total covers fungi, protozoa and chromists as well as plants and animals. Its own breakdown puts plants at about 298,000 and fungi at about 611,000. It is also a 2011 estimate, so calling it 'the most recent' is questionable.

text: The Butterflyfish, a species of marine fish, has been observed displaying a unique form of warning coloration, where they darken their bodies to warn potential predators that they taste unpleasant.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source saying that butterflyfish darken their bodies to warn predators that they taste bad. The research I found is about false eyespots. A Springer paper (Neudecker 1989) suggests daytime eyespots may misdirect attacks or advertise unpalatability. It says color changes at night, including nocturnal eyespots, probably intimidate predators and might also remind them that the fish are unpalatable. A 2024 study in Biological Journal of the Linnean Society tested the idea of eyespots as warning coloration and found no support for it. None of these sources describes body darkening as a warning signal or calls such behavior unique, but none clearly rules it out either. That leaves the specific claim unverified.

text: Did you know that honey, when stored properly in sealed containers, can last indefinitely due to its unique composition of sugars and acidity that prevent bacterial or fungal growth.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the same thing: honey kept in a sealed container that keeps moisture out can last indefinitely. They explain this by its high sugar concentration, low water content and acidity, which make it hostile to bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Some sources also credit naturally produced hydrogen peroxide. The claim leaves that out, but this doesn't contradict it. The sources also note that honey can ferment if it absorbs moisture, which fits the claim's condition of proper sealed storage. One caveat: the sources are blogs, honey sellers and a food magazine, not scientific or government references. Still, they agree with each other and with established food science.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1999, is a 4.2-meter-long Redwood tree trunk floating in the Bay of Fundy that establishes a possible link between Newfoundland and British Columbia about 15,000 years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Janszoon boom log" or a 4.2-meter redwood trunk found floating in the Bay of Fundy in 1999. Nothing I found suggests such a find linked Newfoundland and British Columbia about 15,000 years ago. Searches for "Janszoon" only turned up the Dutch name, the explorer Willem Janszoon, and Project Janszoon in New Zealand. Searches for the Bay of Fundy only turned up unrelated topics such as lobsters, tides and porpoises. The claim looks made up, but I found no source that directly says it is false, so I can't verify or refute it.

text: Pink mandate has been followed in the Ahwaz, Iran since 1963, to influence the women in that region from darkening their eyelids with Kohl.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing about a 'pink mandate' in Ahwaz (Ahvaz), Iran, whether from 1963 or in connection with kohl. The results about 1963 only covered Iranian women gaining the right to vote and run for office. The kohl sources describe kohl as widely used to darken the eyelids in Middle Eastern cultures, but none mention a mandate meant to discourage it. No source supports the claim, but none directly disproves it either, so the evidence is insufficient. My search limit ran out before I could check further.

text: The Draupnir, an ancient Norse mythical amulet, is said to have been created by the god Odin and is almost indestructible, immortal even, as it regenerates eight new golden armlets daily by reappearing and attenuating them.
label: contradicted
reason: In Norse mythology, Draupnir is a gold ring forged by the dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri (Sindri) and given to Odin. Odin did not create it. The ring also produces eight new gold rings of equal weight every ninth night, not every day. Both of these points contradict the claim.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests in Madagascar and Australia are believed to be the oldest living rainforests on Earth, estimated to be around 80 million years old.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results name Australia's Daintree Rainforest on its own as the oldest living rainforest, at about 180 million years old. None of them describe linked Madagascar–Australia rainforests as the oldest, and the 80-million-year figure doesn't match. WorldAtlas says the Daintree is about 180 million years old and roughly 100 million years older than the Amazon, which conflicts with the claim's estimate.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique angles, movements, and directions of their dances convey important information to the rest of the colony?
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Honeybees perform the waggle dance to tell other bees in the hive how far away food is and in which direction. The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the sun. The direction and length of the dance carry distance and direction information. Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize in 1973 for discovering this.

text: Butler's Gorge, a large gorge in Australia, contains a waterfall with a drop of 134 meters (440 feet) that is one of the highest and most powerful in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim. Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with a recorded population of zero. It is the site of Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. The dam is 67 m high and the power station has a hydraulic head of 49 m. None of the sources mention a 134 m waterfall there. Discover Tasmania and other sources name Montezuma Falls, at 104 m, as Tasmania's highest waterfall. A 134 m drop at Butlers Gorge would therefore be impossible, and there is no support for calling it one of the highest or most powerful waterfalls in the Southern Hemisphere.

text: The largest beehive ever recorded was found in a church in HAS Khan Saheb village, near Burdwan in West Bengal, India, and housed around 1 trillion bees.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source for any part of this claim. Searches turned up nothing about a record beehive in a church in a 'HAS Khan Saheb' village near Burdwan/Bardhaman, and no record body, including Guinness World Records, lists a 'largest beehive ever recorded' that matches it. Guinness lists related records, such as the largest honeycomb (10.4 kg, owned by Argirios Koskos), but none of them refers to this hive. The figure of about 1 trillion bees is wildly implausible, since a large honeybee colony usually holds about 30,000–50,000 bees. Still, no source directly refutes this specific claim, so it cannot be verified either way.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers (7,918 miles) at the equator due to its slightly oblate and not spherical shape.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts the wrong figure on the equator. 12,742 km (7,918 mi) is Earth's mean diameter, twice the mean radius of 6,371 km. Wikipedia gives an equatorial radius of 6,378.137 km, which makes the equatorial diameter about 12,756 km (about 7,926 mi). Earth is oblate, so it is wider at the equator than on average, and the polar diameter is about 12,714 km. The reasoning is also backwards: the oblate shape is why the equatorial diameter is larger than 12,742 km, not why it equals that number.

text: A comet that falls to the Sun's surface could leave behind a dust ring due to the cometary material disintegrating and distributing into an orbit about the Sun.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that directly addresses this scenario. Reliable sources (Space.com, EarthSky, LiveScience, and an arXiv paper on Comet Lovejoy) show that sungrazing comets break up near the Sun. They leave dust trails, and coarse debris can keep orbiting the Sun on elliptical paths close to the parent comet's orbit, much like meteoroid streams. However, none of them says that a comet hitting the Sun's surface would leave a dust ring around the Sun. ScienceAlert quotes an astronomer saying comet fragments 'don't slam into the Sun.' The dust rings that have been documented, such as the one along Earth's orbit, come from resonance trapping of interplanetary dust, not from a comet striking the Sun. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could check this specific mechanism further, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: A group of about 150-200 African elephants can be seen living together in a natural herd in the wild.
label: supported
reason: Sources say African elephant herds can sometimes reach 150–200 animals or more. Safari and travel sources mention 'super herds' of up to 350 elephants in Hwange National Park, herds of up to 300 at Tarangire's river in the dry season, and herds 'in the hundreds' at Chobe in Botswana. One source notes that typical family herds are smaller, usually 6–100 elephants, but these larger natural gatherings in the wild back up the claim that a group of about 150–200 can be seen together. The evidence mostly comes from safari operators rather than scientific sources, though it matches what is generally known about elephants forming large seasonal groups.

text: A honeybee colony can lose up to 40% of its bees over the winter due to factors such as disease, pests, and harsh weather conditions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources don't match what the claim measures. The claim is about a single colony losing up to 40% of its own bees. The evidence instead counts whole colonies lost. The Bee Informed Partnership estimated that U.S. beekeepers lost about 37.4% of their managed colonies in winter 2022–23 and 48% over the full year. It named varroa mites, other pests, disease, weather and starvation as causes. That fits the '40%' figure and the causes only if the claim is read as being about colonies. A colony that dies loses all of its bees, so these figures do not show that one colony loses up to 40% of its bees. My searches found no source giving that within-colony figure.
