text: A species of jellyfish found in the Sargasso Sea is biologically immortal, as it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The immortality and transdifferentiation part checks out. Britannica, Wikipedia and NOAA all describe Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish', as able to return to its polyp stage through transdifferentiation, which makes it potentially biologically immortal. The Sargasso Sea part does not. I found no source placing this jellyfish there. The sources say it is native to the Mediterranean and has spread to warm coastal waters such as California, Florida, Panama's Atlantic side, Spain and Japan. Wikipedia only says it is found 'worldwide in temperate to tropic waters'. The Sargasso Sea is open ocean in the middle of the North Atlantic, not a coastal area. Because the location can't be confirmed, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Butterfly fish can be found in large schools while migrating, sometimes numbering over 100 fish, allowing them to be visible during the journey.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that butterflyfish migrate, or that they gather in schools of more than 100 fish during a migration. The sources describe butterflyfish as reef fish that usually swim alone or in pairs, and some coral-feeding species defend territories. Britannica Kids says some types form small schools. A-Z Animals says some plankton-feeding species form groups or schools, and gives one example of schools of at least 10 fish. These sources do not support the claimed migrations, the specific number of more than 100, or the visibility described in the claim. They also do not directly rule them out, so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted.

text: Butterfly fish can be found in large schools while migrating, sometimes numbering over 100 fish, allowing them to be visible from great distances.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs up the specific details in this claim. The sources I checked (A-Z Animals, Britannica Kids, Study.com, Facts and Details, Wikipedia's pyramid butterflyfish page) say butterflyfish usually live alone or in pairs, often guarding reef territories, and that some species form small or large schools. None of them mentions butterflyfish migrating, schools of more than 100 fish during migration, or groups being visible from great distances. Wikipedia's schooling and fish migration pages describe huge migrating schools, but for other fish such as mullet and herring, not butterflyfish. Because the migration part of the claim can't be verified either way, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Buttering a piece of toast can help prevent it from becoming stale because the butter acts as a moisture barrier that inhibits the starchy carbohydrates in the toast from absorbing air.
label: contradicted
reason: The mechanism in the claim is wrong. Wikipedia and several baking patents say staling is not simply a matter of moisture moving in or out of the bread. Moisture moves from the starch granules into the spaces between them, and the starch molecules (amylose and amylopectin) recrystallize, a process called retrogradation. Starch does not go stale by 'absorbing air,' so a butter barrier blocking air cannot be the reason toast stays fresh. Fat in a dough recipe can slow staling, but that is a different effect from spreading butter on toast as a surface barrier. The explanation given in the claim conflicts with what these sources say about how staling works.

text: Cockroaches are able to survive for up to a week without their heads due to their open circulatory system and ability to breathe through their exoskeleton.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree with the main parts of the claim. Scientific American, citing physiologist Joseph Kunkel, says cockroaches can live without their heads. It credits this to their open circulatory system, which lets blood clot quickly at the wound, and to breathing through spiracles. Spiracles are openings in the body segments of the exoskeleton, so they don't need a head to breathe. ScienceABC and Atlas Obscura give the same explanation. One detail differs: these sources say headless roaches can live for 'weeks', which is longer than the claim's 'up to a week'. Since 'up to a week' falls within that range rather than going against it, this is an understatement, not a contradiction. 'Breathe through their exoskeleton' is loosely worded, but in substance it describes breathing through spiracles.

text: Dark matter makes up approximately 27% of the universe's total mass-energy density.
label: supported
reason: NASA Science says scientists estimate that dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe and ordinary matter about 5%, with dark energy making up the rest. That breakdown is the universe's mass-energy budget, so the claim matches.

text: Dry ice can sink in water due to its lower density compared to liquid water, despite being solid.
label: contradicted
reason: Dry ice does sink in water, but the claim gets the reason backwards. Science Notes says dry ice is denser than water, at about 1.55–1.7 g/cm³ compared with about 1.0 g/cm³ for water, and that is why it sinks. Lower density would make it float.

text: Lemedem, a chemical compound, is primarily responsible for the bacteria that cause the common cold to be the only phage treatment for those specific bacteria.
label: contradicted
reason: No chemical compound called "Lemedem" turned up in searches. The results were only unrelated items, such as a Stanisław Lem book review and a pharmacy. The claim also wrongly says the common cold is caused by bacteria. Reliable sources say colds are caused by viruses such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, coxsackievirus, RSV and echovirus. Phages target bacteria, so there are no cold-causing bacteria for Lemedem to be the only phage treatment for. Because this central premise is false, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Butterfly Garden, located in Petaluma, California, is one of the largest privately-owned butterfly aviaries in the United States.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a butterfly aviary called "The Butterfly Garden" exists in Petaluma, California. My searches only found unrelated results: a butterfly garden at the UC Santa Cruz Arboretum, a private Petaluma garden that helps migrating monarchs, the Petaluma Adobe (once the "largest privately owned adobe" in Northern California), and other U.S. butterfly houses. None of these confirm or rule out the facility, or its ranking as one of the largest privately owned butterfly aviaries. I hit the search limit before I could try more searches.

text: The Human Brain accounts for only about 2% of the body's total mass, but it consumes approximately 20% of the body's total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the human brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's energy. The Physics Factbook gathers a number of these references and puts the figure at about 20 W of a typical adult's 100 W. One caveat: the 20% figure usually refers to energy use at rest, which is consistent with the 'approximately' in the claim.

text: The Human Brain accounts for only about 2% of the total body weight but consumes around 20% of the total energy expenditure of the body.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the human brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy, at least at rest. The Physics Factbook, which cites encyclopedias and textbooks, says the brain is "only 2% of the weight of the body, but it consumes about 20% of the total energy in the body at rest." One caveat: the 20% figure usually refers to energy use at rest, not total daily energy expenditure, but the claim says "around 20%" and matches the standard scientific statement.

text: The Human Brain, which weighs around 3 pounds, contains approximately 86 billion neurons.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. Northwestern Medicine (nm.org) calls the brain "3 pounds of remarkable matter" and says it has about 86 billion neurons. Penn's NeuroKnow says the average adult brain weighs about 3 pounds. The University of Washington's Neuroscience for Kids page gives about 86 billion neurons, citing Azevedo et al. One lower-quality source gives older figures (10 or 100 billion neurons), but the more authoritative sources agree on 86 billion.

text: The agreement for the continental divide between the United States and Canada was finally settled in 2022.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of any US–Canada "continental divide" agreement settled in 2022. The Continental Divide is a watershed line running north to south, not the border between the two countries. Their land boundary was set mainly by 19th-century treaties (1818, 1846 and others), and some disputes, such as the Beaufort Sea, are still under negotiation. The well-known border settlement of 2022 was a different one: Canada and Denmark/Greenland split Hans Island in June 2022 (Washington Post, Wikipedia's Whisky War article). The claim seems to mix up that agreement and is contradicted.

text: The apциклоп parcersen dioxide is produced when gasoline and diesel fuel corrode.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled. "apциклоп parcersen dioxide" does not name any known substance, so there is nothing clear to check. It probably means carbon dioxide, but the evidence (an EIA-cited figure: about 19.64 lb of CO2 per gallon of gasoline and 22.38 lb per gallon of diesel) says it is produced by burning these fuels, not by their corroding. Because the substance can't be identified and the process described doesn't match the sources, the claim can't be verified either way.

text: The entirety of human DNA is contained within a space roughly equivalent to the size of a sugar cube.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that links human DNA to the size of a sugar cube. The well-known sugar-cube fact, reported by IFLScience, the Science Museum blog and ScienceABC, is about something else: if you removed the empty space from the atoms of every person on Earth, the whole human race would fit in the volume of a sugar cube. That is about compressed body matter, not DNA. The claim also has no clear meaning. If it means all the DNA in one body, estimates of about 200 g of DNA per person point to a volume far larger than a sugar cube. If it means one genome copy from every person, my rough calculation suggests it could fit, but no source says so. Because the claim is ambiguous and no source directly confirms or refutes it, the evidence is inconclusive.

text: The famous Goat Grotto, also known as the Goat Cave, is a specific type of cave found near the island of Hawaii in the United States.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that describes a famous "Goat Grotto" or "Goat Cave" in or near Hawaii. Searching for "Goat Cave" Hawaii only turned up Goat Island (Mokuauia), a seabird sanctuary islet off Oahu, which is not a cave. Searching for "Goat Grotto" turned up the "Grotto of the Goats" at Fontebello in Sicily, Italy, and Capri, whose name may come from the Latin word for goats. That suggests the name may belong to places outside Hawaii, but no source directly says the claim is false. Because the name doesn't clearly point to one place and the Hawaii link can't be checked, the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The fastest-living creature on Earth is the mayfly, with its lifespan ranging from a few minutes to up to 23 minutes, depending on the species.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claimed range. Wikipedia's Dolania page and the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy confirm the shortest case: adult female Dolania americana mayflies die within about 5 minutes. But they also show adult mayflies are not capped at about 23 minutes. Other species live as adults for about 24 hours (often 1–2 days), and the nymphs live underwater for 2–3 years. So the 'up to 23 minutes, depending on the species' upper limit is wrong.

text: The impressive-looking Gmelins snub-nosed monkey has a highly unique adaptation that sets it apart from other primates: it can only move its nose to the right.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no species called the "Gmelin's snub-nosed monkey," so the claim has no clear subject. The genus Rhinopithecus has five recognized snub-nosed species: golden (R. roxellana), black or Yunnan (R. bieti), gray or Brelich's (R. brelichi), Tonkin or Dollman's (R. avunculus), and Myanmar (R. strykeri). None is named after Gmelin. Sources do describe their noses as upturned because they lack nasal bones, with forward-facing nostrils and skin flaps. But no source mentions any snub-nosed monkey that can move its nose only to the right, or any such trait that sets it apart from other primates. Because the species isn't real and the nose claim has no evidence for or against it, the claim can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km. NOAA converts that to 40,390 miles, which matches the claim's 40,389 miles after rounding. One small difference: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Because some sources give a longer total for the full ridge system, I treated this as a minor wording difference rather than a contradiction. The main points of the claim are supported.

text: The understandability of Orangutans' language has shown to be surprisingly similar to that of children, as research indicates they are capable of learning and understanding hundreds of words.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly support the claim, though the word count is slightly overstated. Wikipedia says Chantek, an orangutan raised like a human child, learned about 150 modified ASL signs and understood spoken English. It also says he developed referential ability about as early as most human children and, like children, preferred names to pronouns. His researchers (White & Miles) say he reached language skills like those of a two- to three-year-old child and built a vocabulary similar to a very young child's. Other sources give 150–180 signs, and one says orangutans can learn hundreds of signs. That supports the claim's core point, but 150–180 is only loosely 'hundreds,' and that one source is low quality.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is not visible from space like many people believe is the case with mountain ranges.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (NOAA, WHOI, Smithsonian) back the first part: the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km, and roughly 90% of it is under water. No source supports the second part, that the ridge is 'not visible from space like many people believe is the case with mountain ranges.' The wording is vague and the evidence points both ways. Most of the ridge is submerged, so you can't see it by eye from orbit. But NOAA and Smithsonian show it mapped from satellite data, and some of it, such as Iceland, rises above sea level. There is also no evidence about what 'many people believe.' Because this part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the mid-ocean ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of every major ocean.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range. Wikipedia describes it as part of every ocean and lists it at about 65,000 km. A NASA page gives 74,000 km, and other sources say "over 65,000 km," which supports the length in the claim. NOAA and WHOI say "nearly 65,000 km," so the exact length depends on the source. The phrase "through the center" is loose wording: Wikipedia says the system is part of every ocean, and the ridges do not all sit exactly in the middle of each ocean. Overall, the main points of the claim are supported.

text: There are more chickens than humans in the world, with estimates suggesting that the global chicken population is over 19 billion, while the human population is approximately 8 billion.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out, though the chicken figure is out of date. Wikipedia says the world had more than 26.5 billion chickens in 2023. The Humane League, citing UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) data, puts the 2020 number at over 33 billion, compared with about 7.76 billion people, which is roughly four chickens per person. Those numbers are well above 19 billion, so "over 19 billion" is true but lowballs current estimates; 19 billion was an older figure. The world's human population is currently about 8 billion, so chickens clearly outnumber people.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting there are around 3 trillion trees on our planet.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the standard published estimates. A 2015 study in Nature (Crowther et al.) put the number of trees on Earth at about 3 trillion (3.04 trillion). NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Even at the top of that range, 3 trillion trees is more than seven times the star count. WorldAtlas, a fact-check site and several news and fact pages report the same comparison. Both figures are estimates with margins of error, but by mainstream estimates trees clearly outnumber the galaxy's stars.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon rainforest, which is estimated to account for about one-sixth of the world's total oxygen production.
label: contradicted
reason: The oxygen figure is wrong. Fact-checks, including Africa Check, say it is a myth that the Amazon produces about 20% of Earth's oxygen. Experts quoted there say the claim 'doesn't make any physical sense.' Scientists commonly estimate that the Amazon produces only about 6–9% of oxygen from land photosynthesis, and close to zero net oxygen, because the forest consumes most of what it produces. That does not support 'about one-sixth' (about 17%) of world oxygen production. The tree count is also misleading: the Amazon has an estimated 390 billion trees. 'Over 300 million' is technically true but understates this by about a thousandfold, so it may reflect a confusion with 300 billion.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon rainforest, which is estimated to account for about one-sixth of the world's total tree population.
label: contradicted
reason: The Amazon is estimated to have about 390 billion trees, not around 300 million. A count of 390 billion technically clears "over 300 million," but the claim's figure is off by roughly a factor of 1,000 and badly misstates the scale. With about 3 trillion trees worldwide, 390 billion is roughly 13%, or about one-eighth of the world's trees, not one-sixth.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon rainforest, which is estimated to account for about one-sixth of the world's tree cover.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count in the claim is off by about a thousand times. The Field Museum and other sources cite a peer-reviewed study in Science that estimated about 390 billion individual trees in the Amazon, not around 300 million. Strictly speaking, 390 billion is 'over 300 million,' but the claim is clearly giving the wrong estimate. The 'one-sixth' share is only a rough fit, and no source I found confirms it directly. Compared with about 3 trillion trees worldwide, 390 billion is roughly 13%, closer to one-eighth. Because the main number is wrong, I've labeled the claim contradicted.

text: There are over 845 million acres of rainforests around the world, which is equivalent to about 6% of Earth's land area.
label: contradicted
reason: The 6% figure is right: WWF, National Geographic and Rainforest Concern all say rainforests cover about 6% of Earth's land surface. The acreage is not. Earth has about 36.8 billion acres of land, so 6% would be roughly 2.2 billion acres. 845 million acres is only about 2.3% of land area, so the two numbers in the claim don't match. The figure is also far too small for the real extent of rainforest: one source says the Amazon alone covers over 1.2 billion acres. Earth.org gives 628 million hectares of Amazon tree cover in 2020, which is about 1.55 billion acres. 'Over 845 million acres' is technically true but badly understates the total, and it is not equivalent to 6% of Earth's land. I couldn't find any source for the 845 million figure.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crinan Canal, a 7-mile (11 km) long inland waterway that allows boats to travel from Ocean to Lochawe.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and Scottish Places both say the Crinan Canal is 9 miles (14 km) long, not 7 miles (11 km). It runs from Ardrishaig on Loch Fyne to Crinan, so it is not in the Vale of Awe and does not take boats to Lochawe.

text: The driest desert in the world, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is home to a unique archaeological site featuring the remnants of a 12,000-year-old long-abandoned lake.
label: not_verifiable
reason: There is good evidence that the Atacama is commonly called the driest (non-polar) desert on Earth. Studies also show it held freshwater lakes and wetlands roughly 9,000–25,000 years ago, and that early people camped beside lakebeds that are now dry. However, I could not find any specific "unique archaeological site" defined by the remains of a 12,000-year-old abandoned lake. The closest match is a PNAS Nexus/PMC study describing a "truly unique" record of tree stumps around campsites dated 12,800–11,200 cal BP in the Pampa del Tamarugal. That site is a grove and wetland setting, not the remains of a lake. The claim's central specific detail cannot be verified, so it is neither supported nor clearly contradicted.

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of letters or figures to identify a time, used on goods or documents in shipping and commerce.
label: contradicted
reason: Reputable dictionaries put the term's origin in the mid-to-late 19th century, not the early 19th century. Merriam-Webster gives 1855 as the first known use, and the OED dates its first sense to the 1850s. Etymonline gives 1888, and Collins gives 1890–95. They also define the original meaning as a mechanical stamping device that recorded the date or time of receipt on letters and documents. None of them describes it as a mark of letters or figures used on goods in shipping and commerce.

text: There are over 5 million different species of plants and animals that live on Earth, according to a 2020 scientific estimate.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The numbers back the "over 5 million" part. Mora et al. (PLOS Biology, 2011) estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, including about 7.77 million animals and 298,000 plants. Other summaries also put plants and animals at more than 7 million. But the claim says the figure comes from a 2020 scientific estimate, and I found no such estimate. The main estimate cited is from 2011, and a later PLOS Biology review appeared in 2023. Because the year can't be confirmed, the claim as a whole can't be fully verified.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to be constantly boiling, has been discovered in the Peruvian Amazon and is believed to be a result of a unique combination of geothermal activity and a vortex that mixes air and water.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is real. It is in the Peruvian Amazon, and geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo studied it starting in 2011. But what scientists say causes the heat contradicts the claim. Ruzo's research shows the water is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient: groundwater is warmed deep underground and comes back up through fault-fed hot springs, with no volcano involved. No source mentions a 'vortex that mixes air and water,' so that part appears to be made up. The claim is also wrong that the river is 'constantly boiling': it reaches about 86–94°C, which is hot but below boiling.

text: Antarctica is home to several unique species of penguins, but the Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo, and Emperor penguins can be found nowhere else on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Gentoo penguins (along with the others) live nowhere but Antarctica, which is wrong. A peer-reviewed Marine Ornithology study puts about 132,000 Gentoo breeding pairs in the Falkland Islands, roughly 34% of the world's population. Gentoos also breed on South Georgia and other sub-Antarctic islands, and Chinstraps breed on the South Sandwich Islands, South Georgia and Bouvet Island. So these species are not limited to Antarctica.

text: Octopuses have three hearts, with two working together to pump blood to their gills and a third being a branchial heart that pumps blood to the rest of the body.
label: contradicted
reason: Octopuses do have three hearts, but the claim gets the third one wrong. The two hearts that pump blood through the gills are the branchial (gill) hearts. The third heart, which sends blood to the rest of the body, is the systemic heart, not a branchial heart. Sources agree on this layout.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources confirm the main claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Wikipedia and WHOI also call it the longest mountain range in the world at about 65,000 km. One small caveat is the wording: NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', while some other sources say 'over 65,000 km'. The claim's 40,389-mile figure matches NOAA's 40,390 miles. Because all sources agree on roughly 65,000 km, the 'over' vs. 'nearly' difference is a minor rounding issue and does not contradict the claim.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar panels at the Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii, which helps the researchers maintain control over their equipment while minimizing their environmental impact.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim doesn't say which telescope it means, and at least two Mauna Kea observatories fit the general idea. Keck Observatory installed a rooftop solar PV system between its twin domes in 2020, and Gemini Observatory completed a solar panel installation in 2015. Without knowing which telescope is meant, the specific details can't be checked: that the panels fill a 'yard,' and that they help researchers 'maintain control over their equipment.' The general point that Mauna Kea telescopes use solar power to reduce environmental impact is plausible, but the claim as worded can't be fully verified.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although there is a debate about this, the actual longest is "interjection," or " psychologist" depending on the dictionary you consult.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. "Stewardess," "interjection" and "psychologist" all have more than one syllable (3, 4 and 4). Logically Facts, a fact-checking site, lists the longest one-syllable words still in common use as nine-letter words such as "screeched," "strengths" and "stretched." It also mentions rare ten-letter words like "scraunched" and "strengthed." None of the words in the claim are among them.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Malahide Castle in Ireland, houses the world's oldest known piece of graffiti, a 3600-year-old ancient Neolithic inscription discovered in 2019 that reads "Woman of Bunbo".
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence for this claim. Searches for Malahide Castle bring up its official site, Wikipedia and Discover Ireland, and none of them mention a 'Butler's Grotto', an ancient inscription found in 2019, or the words 'Woman of Bunbo'. Searches for the world's oldest graffiti point to other finds, such as the 6th-century BCE carvings on the Greek island of Astypalaia, not to anything in Ireland. The claim also contradicts itself: 3,600 years ago is the Bronze Age, not the Neolithic. It looks made up, but no reliable source directly says it's false, so it can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but scientists estimate that up to 80% of them remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The most widely cited estimate, from Mora et al. 2011 in PLoS Biology and reported by National Geographic and The Scientist, puts the number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million. That figure covers plants, animals, fungi and protists, and the study's range is 7.4–10 million, so it does not support 'over 10 million' plants and animals. The same study found that about 86% of species are still undescribed, which is more than the claim's 'up to 80%'. Some older guesses ranged from 3 to 100 million, so the total count is uncertain, but the study the claim appears to echo conflicts with both of its numbers.

text: The famous Goat Grotto, also known as the Goat Cave, is a specific type of cave found near the island of Formigas, but there is little information about it.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search tool hit its usage limit before it returned any results, so I couldn't check this claim against any evidence. I don't know of any well-documented 'Goat Grotto' or 'Goat Cave' connected to the Formigas islets near Santa Maria in the Azores. Nothing supports or contradicts the claim's details, including where the cave is, what type of cave it is, or that it is 'famous'.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that spans over 65,000 kilometers in length.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources such as NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI confirm that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest (most extensive) mountain range on Earth and that most of it lies underwater. They give its length as "nearly" or "about" 65,000 km (some estimates for the whole system run higher). That means "over 65,000 km" is slightly imprecise, but it matches the commonly cited figure. The main claim and the approximate length both hold up.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, are natural swimmers and can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to their large lungs and highly efficient gas exchange.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out. Reliable sources such as the Natural History Museum (London), the Rainforest Alliance and One Earth say capybaras are the world's largest rodents, swim well, and can hold their breath underwater for up to about five minutes. No authoritative source backs the stated cause, 'large lungs and highly efficient gas exchange.' Hobbyist blogs disagree on it: one (capybaraverse) credits large lungs, while another (capybaratalks) says their lungs 'aren't unusually large.' Because the explanation can't be verified and the available sources contradict each other, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: There are over 37 ultrahard and extremely rare naturally occurring diamonds found on Earth that have been classified as being greater in hardness than the Mohs scale of mineral hardness maximum value, diamond 10.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that mentions 37 or more natural 'ultrahard' diamonds rated above 10 on the Mohs scale, so that figure looks made up. Reliable sources say the opposite: the Mohs scale tops out at 10, and diamond, at 10, is the hardest naturally occurring material by scratch hardness. Some materials, such as lonsdaleite from meteorites and certain lab-made carbon forms, are reported to be harder than diamond in indentation tests. Even so, none is classified above 10 on the Mohs scale, and none matches a group of 37+ natural diamonds.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species palearctic short-faced elephant (Mammuthus galileus, Elephas falconeri and several others The Dwarf elephant is now introduced as the smallest yet or Land Elephant but a smaller related extinct species of the Dwarf Short-faced Elephant was found.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is muddled and most of it can't be checked. There is no species called simply the "short-eared elephant." The closest match is the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus), which Digimorph lists among the 15 living elephant shrews; it is not extinct and not on the IUCN endangered or vulnerable lists. That would contradict the first part, but only if that is the animal meant. "Mammuthus galileus" doesn't appear to be a real species, and the other statements about a "palearctic short-faced elephant," a dwarf elephant being "introduced as the smallest," and a "Dwarf Short-faced Elephant" don't point to any clear species or claim I could look up. Because the subjects are unclear and the rest can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot-water river, is a natural wonder found deep in the Peruvian Amazon region where the river's temperature remains at around 40°C (104°F) year-round despite its location in the tropics.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is real. The Shanay-timpishka, known as the Boiling River of the Amazon, is in the Peruvian Amazon. But the claim gets the temperature wrong. Wikipedia and BBC Discover Wildlife say the water along a stretch of about 6 km gets far hotter than 40°C, reaching up to about 94°C, which is hot enough to cook animals that fall in. Ruzo's TED talk describes the same thing. The river also starts out as a cold stream, so it is not a steady ~40°C all year.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, with a total length of over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles), and it runs through the center of the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range. They put its length at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles) and describe it winding through the world's oceans between the continents, which covers the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. One wording difference: both sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over.' Some other references give about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, so 'over 65,000 km' still fits. The 'center' of the Pacific is loose wording, since the Pacific ridge (the East Pacific Rise) lies in the eastern Pacific. Neither point contradicts the main claim.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments, such as the Antarctic ice, due to their ability to form cryptobiotic cells, which allow them to remain dormant and protected from harsh conditions.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's 'Antarctic microorganism' article says Antarctic microbes deal with harsh conditions by shutting down their metabolism and waiting in a cryptobiotic state, and that they can go dormant this way. Russian and NASA studies of the Vostok ice sheet report viable microorganisms that survived in deep anabiosis for thousands of years. Wikipedia's cryptobiosis article says anabiosis is the same thing as cryptobiosis. Together these back the claim that bacteria survive Antarctic ice by entering a protected, dormant cryptobiotic state. One caveat: the claim's wording 'cryptobiotic cells' is loose. The sources describe a cryptobiotic state rather than a special type of cell.

text: The Droxford ship burial, discovered in 1864, is a 5th-century Anglo-Saxon ship burial that is the only complete Anglo-Saxon ship discovered in the United Kingdom.
label: contradicted
reason: The trustworthy sources describe Droxford as a pagan Anglo-Saxon inhumation cemetery near Soberton, Hampshire. It was found in 1900 during railway construction, not in 1864, and they say nothing about a ship burial. The best-known Anglo-Saxon ship burial is Sutton Hoo. That alone undermines the claim that the only complete Anglo-Saxon ship in the UK came from Droxford.

text: There are over 388,000 languages in the world, although some sources estimate that almost 96% of the languages spoken worldwide are at risk of falling out of use due to globalization and urbanization trends.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's number is wrong. Ethnologue, the main reference catalog of languages, lists about 7,100 living languages, not over 388,000. Because the figure is off by roughly 50 times, the claim is contradicted, whatever the truth of the separate point about endangered languages.

text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total coastline that is only slightly over 25,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Both numbers in the claim hold up. Wikipedia's Geography of Norway page, citing Kartverket (Norway's official mapping agency), lists 239,057 islands and 81,192 islets along the coast. That is far more than 18,000, so 'more than 18,000' is technically true, though it greatly understates the real figure. The same page and the CIA World Factbook data on IndexMundi give the coastline as 25,148 km, which is slightly over 25,000 km. One caveat: 25,148 km is the commonly cited official figure, but the Factbook lists another 58,133 km of island coastlines separately, so other measurements give a much longer total.

text: The short-lived but highly notable element, Oganesson (Og), is the heaviest known natural element, having an atomic number of 118 and being identified in 2002.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica confirms that oganesson has atomic number 118 and was first synthesized in 2002. But it describes oganesson as a synthetic element that does not exist in nature and can only be made in a lab. The heaviest naturally occurring element is plutonium or uranium, depending on the definition. So calling oganesson the 'heaviest known natural element' is wrong.

text: You can lead a cow upstairs, but not downstairs, due to the structure of their joints, which make it difficult for them to walk down steep inclines.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches show that "cows can go up stairs but not down" is a widely repeated myth that has been debunked. AllThatsInteresting lists it among popular animal myths and says it's "not exactly true," because it depends on how steep the stairs are and cows can get used to stairs with practice. Enviroliteracy and FarmingFreak also call it a myth: descending is harder and cows are often afraid to do it, but they are not physically unable to. People on Straight Dope report seeing cows walk down steps easily. So the claim's point that steep descents are difficult has some support, but its main point, that you can't lead a cow downstairs because of its joints, is contradicted. Only informal social-media posts repeat it as fact.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Ira Springer of New York, who took a 10-minute sauna then took a 3-minute ice-water bath, experiencing a 75.6°F (43.7°C) drop in just a few minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing about an 'Ira Springer' or any record like this. My searches turned up only general articles on saunas and ice baths, and then hit the search limit. The numbers also can't be right. Starting from a normal 98.6°F, a 75.6°F drop would leave a body temperature of about 23°F, well below freezing. The widely reported survival records are about 115.7°F at the high end and about 56–57°F (roughly 13.7°C) at the low end, a gap of only about 59°F. A 10-minute sauna followed by a 3-minute ice bath cannot produce a drop larger than that whole range. The claim appears to be made up.

text: The Departed, a crime drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Matt Damon, holds the record for most Academy Awards won by a remake, having received a total of four Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards in 2007.
label: contradicted
reason: The Departed did win four Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards in 2007: Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay and Film Editing. But it does not hold the record for most Oscars won by a remake. Britannica says the 1959 Ben-Hur was a remake of the 1925 silent film, and it won 11 Academy Awards, far more than The Departed's four.

text: The Human Brain contains around 100 billion neurons and is estimated to be about 2% of the overall body weight but requires 20% of the total energy consumption.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a PMC/NIH-hosted paper by Herculano-Houzel, say the human brain makes up about 2% of body mass but uses about 20% of the body's energy budget. For neuron count, the most cited modern estimate is about 86 billion. That is close to the traditional figure of 'around 100 billion,' which is still widely used as an approximation, so the claim holds overall. The neuron figure is slightly rounded up.

text: The longest-reigning monarch in history was Queen Victoria's predecessor, Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother's although longer reigned it was queen reefha's of long died Malaysia queen relinquished but actually Queen Elizabeth 2 longer still reigned, however The longest was queen victoria's reign was largely spent by proxy as this
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled, and its main checkable statements are false. Louis XIV of France is the longest-reigning recognised monarch in history, at 72 years and 110 days. The record does not belong to Queen Victoria's predecessor, William IV, who reigned only about seven years. Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother was a queen consort and never a reigning monarch. Victoria also did not reign 'by proxy.' The 'queen reefha' of Malaysia has no clear referent, but the claim's core assertions are contradicted by reliable sources.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to gather in a communal area and their eight arms that resemble a wicker basket.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found calls a group of octopuses a "basket." Several say there is no standard collective noun. The terms they do mention are "consortium," "tangle" and "rally." The claim's explanation is also wrong. These sources describe octopuses as mostly solitary animals that rarely gather in groups in the wild, not animals that tend to gather in a shared area. The "wicker basket" origin story isn't backed by any source.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent bell-shaped body and is able to emit a purple glowing protein to lure in prey.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because the Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is not a jellyfish. Wikipedia describes it as a glass sponge from the deep Pacific. Its body is a tubular, basket- or vase-like lattice of silica spicules, not a transparent bell. Like other sponges, it filter-feeds on particles from the water. Nothing found supports it having a bell-shaped body or emitting a purple glowing protein to lure prey.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have found that longer ring fingers are associated with elevated levels of testosterone in the womb, which may increase the risk of heart disease later in life.
label: contradicted
reason: I found two problems with this claim. First, research by Manning and others says men with a relatively longer ring finger (a low 2D:4D ratio, which points to more testosterone before birth) may be protected against early heart attacks. A higher ratio, meaning a relatively shorter ring finger and less prenatal testosterone, has been linked to earlier heart attacks and to plaque in the coronary arteries. That is the opposite of what the claim says. Second, nothing I found shows that ring-finger length is often used to judge heart disease risk. It is only a research marker for prenatal hormone exposure, not a clinical test.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to estimates from the World Register of Marine Species and other scientific sources.
label: supported
reason: The figure comes from Mora et al. (2011), a study announced by the Census of Marine Life. It estimated about 8.74 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species on Earth. The researchers reached that number by analyzing the species listed in the Catalogue of Life and the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS), so the number and the WoRMS connection both hold up. There are two caveats. First, WoRMS supplied the data rather than producing the estimate itself. Second, the 8.74 million total covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not only plants and animals. Plants and animals alone come to about 8.1 million. The claim still matches how this estimate is widely reported in popular sources, so I rate it supported, with that loose wording as the main weakness.

text: Lemedem, a chemical compound, is primarily responsible for the bacteria that cause the common cold to be the only phage, which can attach to a red blood cell as well.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No search results identify any chemical compound called "Lemedem," and no source discusses it in relation to phages, the common cold, or red blood cells. The only hits for the term are unrelated (a video game location, similarly spelled names/drugs like "Lemed"). The claim also lacks a clear referent and rests on a premise not found in any source (the common cold is caused by viruses, not bacteria), but because there is no evidence directly addressing the alleged compound or its claimed role, the claim can be neither verified nor directly refuted from the search results.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range and give its length as about 65,000 km. Wikipedia's Mid-ocean ridge article states the same figures as the claim, 65,000 km (40,400 mi). It also says the total ridge system is 80,000 km long. NOAA and WHOI describe it as Earth's longest mountain range at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 to 40,390 miles). One small wording difference: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over." Since Wikipedia's figures match exactly and the total system is even longer, the claim is substantially supported.

text: The Draupnir, an ancient Norse mythical amulet, is said to have been created by the god Odin and is almost indestructible, immortal, just like the Norse gods.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Draupnir's origin wrong. In Norse mythology, Draupnir is a gold ring owned by Odin, but the dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri (or Sindri) forged it, not Odin. They made it as one of three gifts, along with Mjölnir and Gullinbursti, to win Loki's wager. It is also usually described as a ring that makes eight copies of itself every ninth night, not as an amulet. The sources don't support calling it almost indestructible or immortal. The source found is a fan wiki, but its account matches the Prose Edda tradition.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthen", however the correct word that holds this title is actually "smiles", because the word can also be spelled 'smyle's.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both counts. "Strengthen" has two syllables (streng-then), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Wikipedia's list of the longest English one-syllable words gives candidates like "scraunched" and "strengthed" (10 letters each), and Guinness lists "strengths" (9 letters) as the longest word with only one vowel. "Smiles" has just six letters, so it doesn't hold the title either. It only appears in an old riddle about the "longest word" (a "mile" between the two s's), and the 'smyle's spelling explanation has no basis.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has almost no fur, however, the animal with the most fur relative to its body size is thephasis opossum didelphimorphia and also typically known as Marsupials are the most furry based on
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources such as the Seattle Aquarium say the sea otter has the densest fur of any animal, at about 500,000 to 1,000,000 hairs per square inch. The chinchilla has the densest fur of any land mammal. No source names a 'comfortless waterhog' (water shrew) as the furriest animal. The claim also contradicts itself by calling that animal the furriest while saying it has almost no fur. Nothing supports opossums or marsupials being the furriest animals.

text: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with approximately 96.5% of that being seawater.
label: supported
reason: The USGS Water Science School says that about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water. This matches the claim's 71% figure and its statement that about 96.5% of that water is seawater.

text: The colony of Eskipoo is not found anywhere within the main group of Eskipoo Mix's but was introduced using European mantled as adults to stock a rubbish tip sewage works in Johannesburg South Africa in the 1960's.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable breed sources describe the Eskipoo (also called Eskapoo or Eskimopoo) as a designer dog, a cross between the American Eskimo Dog and the Poodle. They give its origin as the United States and say it was probably developed in the 1990s, when designer dogs became popular. No source mentions an Eskipoo 'colony' stocked with 'European mantled' adults at a rubbish tip or sewage works in Johannesburg in the 1960s. The claim's wording looks borrowed from a description of an introduced bird population and conflicts with what is known about where and when this dog breed arose.

text: The Human Brain contains around 100 billion neurons and is estimated to be about 2% of the overall body weight but consumes approximately 20% of the total body's energy.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the 2% of body weight and 20% of energy figures. Britannica says the brain is about 2% of adult body weight and uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest, and a PMC (NIH) paper gives the same 2% and 20% figures. The best current estimate for neuron count is about 86 billion (Britannica, PMC). That is a bit below 100 billion, but 'around 100 billion' is a widely used round figure that other sources also give, so the claim holds as an approximation.

text: The highest recorded speed of a jellyfish, the lion's mane jellyfish, was approximately 35 mph in a swimming experiment.
label: contradicted
reason: A peer-reviewed acoustic-telemetry study in Marine Ecology Progress Series (2012) tracked lion's mane jellyfish in the wild. Their fastest horizontal swimming came during flood tides, at about 5.24 cm/s, which is roughly 0.1 mph. Jellyfish swim slowly by pulsing their bells, and no reputable source reports a lion's mane jellyfish, or any jellyfish, reaching anything close to 35 mph.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the mid-ocean ridge system, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range and is about 65,000 km long. The exact wording is less settled. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km,' WorldAtlas says 'about 65,000 km,' and some other sources say 'more than 65,000 km.' Some estimates that count transform offsets put the length at around 80,000 km. Because the claim's main point matches these sources, I judged it supported. However, 'over' is somewhat imprecise next to NOAA's 'nearly.'

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and fault-tolerant.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'A Brief History of the Internet', quoted in the ARPANET article, calls it a "false rumor" that the ARPANET was built to withstand nuclear war. Only a separate RAND study on secure voice networks considered nuclear war. The network was built to survive failures mainly because its switching nodes and links were unreliable, not because of nuclear threats. The original motivation was sharing scarce computing resources. Later internetworking work did stress robustness, but the claim's main point, that the Internet was originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack, is a well-documented myth.

text: Carpets of fluorescent algae were able to grow on the soil of the Danakil Desert, one of the hottest places on Earth, which challenges the long-held notion that only specific types of organisms can survive in extreme environments.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source saying that carpets of fluorescent algae grew on Danakil Desert soil. The Danakil is confirmed as one of the hottest places on Earth (Wikipedia). However, the bright green colours seen at Dallol are attributed to sulphur and acidic hot springs, not algae. Research there found ultra-small microbes in some spots and, in the Dallol ponds, no life at all (EurekAlert/ScienceAlert). That does not confirm the algae discovery, and since it doesn't directly address it either, it doesn't clearly contradict it. Without any report of the algae finding, the claim cannot be verified.

text: The ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy have one of the highest concentrations of ice in the world, which is home to several permanently frozen waterfalls and a variety of unique subglacial organisms.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any specific place called the "ghiaccio stalactite caves" in Italy. "Ghiaccio" is simply the Italian word for ice, so the name doesn't point to a clear, identifiable location. My search turned up other Italian ice caves, such as Grotta del Gelo on Mount Etna and the Fellaria glacier caves, but no reliable source says that any Italian cave has one of the highest concentrations of ice in the world, several permanently frozen waterfalls, or unique subglacial organisms. Because the place can't be identified and none of these details can be confirmed, the claim can't be verified.

text: There are more than 100 known species of jellyfish that have been found to be immortal, possessing a unique ability called transdifferentiation, which allows them to transform their cells into different types.
label: contradicted
reason: Trusted sources such as the AMNH and Britannica point to a single species, Turritopsis dohrnii, as the known 'immortal jellyfish.' It uses transdifferentiation to revert from its adult medusa form back to a polyp. The AMNH says only one animal is known to have this ability. Some research suggests a few other hydrozoans may do something similar, but nothing comes close to more than 100 species, so the number in the claim is contradicted.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original recipe containing an extract from the coca leaf, which contained cocaine.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola half of the claim checks out. Sources say John Pemberton was a morphine addict who made the drink to wean himself off morphine, and the original recipe used coca leaf extract that contained cocaine. The Pepsi half is wrong. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893 as 'Brad's Drink', a digestive aid sold to treat dyspepsia (indigestion), which is where the name comes from. None of the sources say it was meant as a morphine alternative, so the claim that both drinks started that way is contradicted.

text: The largest beehive ever recorded was found in a church in HAS Khan Saheb village, near Burdwan in West Bengal, India, and housed around 468,000 individuals.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms this claim. Searches turned up no mention of a record beehive in a church in 'HAS Khan Saheb' village near Burdwan, and nothing on a colony of about 468,000 bees. Burdwan does have an old church, Christ Church Bardhaman, but no source I found links it to a beehive. Live Science notes that no official records are kept for the world's largest beehive, and Guinness World Records lists only unrelated bee-house records, so a 'largest ever recorded' title is doubtful. Still, no source directly contradicts the specific details. My searches were cut short by a tool usage limit before I could check further, so I can't verify the claim either way.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Tethys Enceladus český chasmata, which is located on the moon Tethys of the planet Saturn and stretches for approximately 1,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: No feature called the "Tethys Enceladus český chasmata" exists. The name mixes two Saturnian moons, Tethys and Enceladus, with a Czech word. A chasma is a canyon, not a mountain range. Tethys's large chasm, Ithaca Chasma, is a valley about 100 km wide and roughly 2,000 km long, so it is neither a mountain range nor about 1,000 km long. The Solar System feature usually cited as an enormously long mountain range is Iapetus's equatorial ridge, which runs along most of that moon's equator. The claim gets the feature, its type and its length wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Dorsa Argentea, which is a mountain range on Mars that stretches for over 1,500 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Dorsa Argentea isn't a mountain range. Peer-reviewed work (Icarus/ScienceDirect) describes it as a group of sinuous ridges near Mars's south pole, most likely eskers, which are deposits of sediment left by meltwater flowing under an ice sheet. Nothing I found calls it the longest mountain range in the solar system. That title would more plausibly go to Earth's mid-ocean ridge system, about 65,000 km long, or to another candidate such as Iapetus's equatorial ridge. The claim's '1,500 km' length did not appear in the search results, and the main assertion is false.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made of white Carrara marble, which is said to have been chosen by the architects to last longer due to its distinctive whiteness and resistance to atmospheric pollution.
label: contradicted
reason: San Miniato al Monte doesn't have marble steeples. It has one squat bell tower (campanile), which Baccio d'Agnolo began in 1523 after the earlier tower collapsed in 1499, and which was left unfinished. Sources describe it as brick ('realizzato in mattoni') and say it looks quite different from the marble church. The white Carrara marble, set against green serpentine/Prato marble, is on the façade, not the tower. I found nothing to support the idea that architects chose the marble for its whiteness or its resistance to air pollution.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, shines by reflecting about 60% of the sunlight that hits its thick atmosphere.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say Venus reflects much more than about 60% of the sunlight that reaches it. National Geographic quotes an astronomer who puts the figure at 75–90%. A University of Saskatchewan astronomy page says its thick atmosphere reflects about 75%, and it gives an albedo of 0.70. The usual published values (about 0.69 geometric albedo and about 0.76 Bond albedo) are also well above 60%. The claim is right that Venus is the brightest planet and that its clouds reflect sunlight, but the 60% figure is too low.

text: Buttress parsnip, also known as sand parsnip, is a type of plant that has seeds containing toxic properties called lignans, these can cause blisters on human skin.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source for a plant called "buttress parsnip" or for "sand parsnip" as another name for it. A search for "buttress parsnip" only brought up the Wikipedia parsnip disambiguation page and pages about unrelated uses of "buttress". The chemical part of the claim is contradicted. Government and extension sources (Oregon DOT, Wisconsin, Minnesota DNR and Illinois Extension) say parsnip blisters come from psoralens (furanocoumarins) in the plant's sap, not lignans. The sap causes phytophotodermatitis, a skin reaction that needs sunlight. They also blame the sap from stems, leaves and flowers, not the seeds specifically. My searches ran out before I could check the disambiguation page in full for "sand parsnip".

text: Aadhar is the world's largest biometric database, which includes fingerprints, iris scans, and facial recognition of over 1.3 billion Indians.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as ABC News call Aadhaar the world's largest biometric identity database, holding residents' iris scans and fingerprints. Aadhaar also collects a facial photograph, which is used for face authentication. Reported enrolment has been above 1.3 billion, given India's population of about 1.3 to 1.4 billion. Two details are a little loose: the system records a facial photo rather than doing 'facial recognition' as such, and it covers residents rather than only citizens. Neither point changes the main claim.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar panels powered at the Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii, by wind turbines, hydroelectric power, or mainly by solar panels.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is vague and garbled. It never says which telescope it means ("The telescope"), and it lists alternatives (wind turbines, hydroelectric power, or mainly solar panels) without committing to any one. Search results do show that W. M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea installed a rooftop solar array of 332 panels in 2020. However, that array covers only 10–15% of the observatory's electricity, and it sits on a roof rather than in "a yard full of solar panels." Nothing found confirms wind or hydroelectric power, or that any Maunakea telescope runs mainly on solar. Because the telescope has no clear referent and the claim doesn't say anything definite, it can't be verified.

text: The procession of the equinoxes is a phenomenon where the path of the Sun as seen from Earth appears to shift due to the procession of the Earth's rotational axis over a period of approximately 26,000 years.
label: supported
reason: The claim spells it 'procession', but it clearly means the precession of the equinoxes, and I'm reading it that way. Wikipedia's article on axial precession says Earth's axis slowly changes orientation in a cycle of about 26,000 years, and that this was historically called the 'precession of the equinoxes.' The article explains that as a result, the equinox points (where the Sun's path crosses the celestial equator) drift westward against the fixed stars by about 50 arcseconds a year. The claim's wording about the Sun's path appearing to shift is loose but broadly fits this. The main points, that axial precession causes it and the cycle is about 26,000 years, are supported.

text: There are over 6 million Species of plants and animals on our planet, according to the University of Edinburgh's School of Biological Sciences estimate.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a source that ties an estimate of over 6 million species to the University of Edinburgh's School of Biological Sciences. My first search found a different figure from different researchers: about 8.7 million species, from a study by Mora et al. at Dalhousie University and the University of Hawaii, reported by Nature. A total of 8.7 million is technically 'over 6 million', but it isn't the Edinburgh estimate the claim names. My follow-up searches failed because the search tool hit its usage limit. Without evidence for the specific attribution, I can't verify the claim.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, known for its distinctive bright red-orange color caused by the presence of high concentrations of salt and algae.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is a real lake in Tanzania, in Africa. Live Science says it can look red because of salt-loving microorganisms, including haloarchaea and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), which multiply in the lake's very salty water. This matches the claim that its red-orange color comes from high salt levels and algae. The color comes directly from the microbes' pigments, and the salt is what lets them thrive, but the claim's simplified explanation is still broadly accurate.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point rose to 115.5°F (46.4°C) in 2005.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records says the highest recorded human body temperature is 46.5°C (115.7°F). It belonged to Willie Jones, who was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta with heatstroke on 10 July 1980. A search for 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' found no such person tied to a body temperature record, and no record of 115.5°F (46.4°C) in 2005 turned up. The person, year and temperature in the claim all conflict with the documented record.

text: The ancient Egyptians were skilled astronomers who accurately calculated the circumference of the Earth to be approximately 40,000 kilometers, which is remarkably close to the actual circumference of about 40,075 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, World History Encyclopedia and StarDate (McDonald Observatory), credit the first known calculation of Earth's circumference to Eratosthenes, a Greek scholar working in Alexandria in Ptolemaic Egypt around 240 BC. They do not credit the ancient Egyptians with it. The claim gives the Egyptians credit for this calculation, which the sources contradict.

text: Aestvation, a type of heatstroke-like condition that occurs in animals, can be caused by a lack of rain in arid climates, and humans are the only vertebrates not affected by it.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets aestivation wrong. It isn't a heatstroke-like condition. It's an adaptive state of dormancy, a deep torpor with slowed metabolism, that some animals enter to survive hot, dry periods. Hot, dry conditions do trigger it, but it is a survival strategy, not an illness. The claim that humans are the only vertebrates 'not affected' also makes no sense. Most vertebrates never aestivate. Only certain species do, such as some frogs, lungfish, tortoises and a few mammals.

text: The famous painting "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh was sold at an auction in 1987 for $53.9 million, making it one of the most expensive paintings sold at that time.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The Starry Night was not sold at auction in 1987. MoMA acquired it in 1941 through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest, and it is still in the museum's collection. The $53.9 million sale on November 11, 1987 was for a different Van Gogh painting, Irises, which Alan Bond bought.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Inferno River," is a mysterious natural phenomenon in Peru where water is said to boil continuously, despite being in the middle of the Amazon rainforest.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, National Geographic, ScienceAlert, IFLScience) confirm that the Boiling River of the Amazon (Shanay-timpishka) is a real, unusual geothermal river in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest. Locals have long told legends about it, and it gets hot enough to kill animals that fall in. However, nothing I found supports the claim that it is also called the "Inferno River." Wikipedia lists its names as Shanay-timpishka, Boiling River, and Río Hirviente, and says "La Bomba" refers to one hot spring in the river. The only use of "inferno" I found was a YouTube Short describing it loosely as "Nature's Hidden Inferno," which is not evidence of an actual alternate name. The claim that the water "boils continuously" is also misleading. Measurements put the average temperature around 86°C, with readings ranging from about 45°C to nearly 100°C, so the water doesn't boil everywhere or all the time, though the claim does hedge with "is said to." Because a key part of the claim, the alternate name, can't be confirmed, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Over 70% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with approximately 96.5% of it being seawater and the remaining 3.5% being freshwater sources.
label: contradicted
reason: The 71% surface coverage and the figure of about 96.5% of Earth's water sitting in the oceans are both right. The problem is the last part: USGS-based sources say only about 2.5% of Earth's water is freshwater. The roughly 1% left over is mostly saline groundwater and salt lakes, so the remaining 3.5% is not all freshwater as the claim says.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual trees, which is roughly 10% of all the trees on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count is right, but the 10% share is not. The 2013 ter Steege study in Science, reported by ScienceDaily, Nature and the Field Museum, estimates that greater Amazonia has around 390 billion trees with trunks at least 10 cm across. The study gives about 390 billion, not more than that. The best global estimate (Crowther et al. 2015, Nature) is about 3.04 trillion trees. On those figures the Amazon holds about 12.8%, or roughly one-eighth of Earth's trees. No source gives a figure near 10%, so the claim understates the share and slightly overstates the count.

text: The vinegar produced by the acetic acid fermentation of apple cider is a byproduct of the same microbial process that makes bread rise.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because bread rising and vinegar-making are two different microbial processes. Bread rises because yeast carries out alcoholic fermentation, which releases carbon dioxide. Vinegar comes from a separate, later step: acetic acid bacteria (Acetobacter) oxidize the ethanol that yeast made earlier into acetic acid. The MDPI review says the bacteria convert ethanol generated by yeast during alcoholic fermentation, and the FAO source names Acetobacter as the vinegar producers. Bakery sources say dough rises from yeast-produced gas. So vinegar is not a byproduct of the process that makes bread rise.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal, called the turbellarian rotifer, due to its natural ability to revert back to a polyp stage after reaching adulthood.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal's name wrong. The 'immortal jellyfish' that can revert to a polyp stage after reaching sexual maturity is Turritopsis dohrnii, not a 'turbellarian rotifer.' That name is also biologically wrong: turbellarians are flatworms and rotifers belong to a separate phylum, so neither is a jellyfish. The part about reverting to a polyp is accurate, but only for Turritopsis dohrnii.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called the turbellarian that is biologically immortal, meaning it can cheat death by regenerating its body but the head dies before the body can fully mature.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal wrong. Turbellarians are free-living flatworms, such as planarians in the class Turbellaria, not jellyfish. Researchers call some planarians 'potentially immortal' because they can regenerate, but that is a flatworm trait. The jellyfish known as 'immortal' is Turritopsis dohrnii. No source supports the claim's detail that the head dies before the body can fully mature.

text: A cast-iron skillet can be a good heat distributor and can be preheated to high temperatures without losing its iron coating due to the presence of a layer called "scale," which provides some chemical protection to the iron beneath.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two key points wrong. First, cast iron spreads heat poorly. Cooking Issues says the idea that cast iron gives even heat is "misleading": a skillet develops distinct hot spots, and heat moves slowly toward the edge. Its strength is holding heat, not spreading it. Second, the protective layer on a cast-iron pan is seasoning, not "scale." Wikipedia describes seasoning as fat heated onto the surface to form a corrosion-resistant layer of polymerized fat, which protects the bare iron from rust. The phrase "losing its iron coating" also makes no sense, because the pan is solid iron rather than iron-coated.

text: The length of a cricket season, which varies by location, can be divided into two parts: an initial section where a bat is only used for scoring, called the "matcher itself" and then follows a second part in the season known as "over".
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica says an "over" in cricket is a set of six balls (sometimes eight) bowled by one bowler from one end of the pitch. It is not a part of a cricket season. Cricket also has no recognised season division called the "matcher itself" where the bat is only used for scoring. The claim gets basic cricket terms wrong.

text: Gibbs' phenomenon, a term coined by British mathematician James William Gibbs, involves oscillations or "ringing" of a function after a step change, similar to the vibrations that occur when a bell is struck.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the Gibbs phenomenon is named after Josiah Willard Gibbs, who was an American scientist. There is no British mathematician called "James William Gibbs" behind it. Gibbs also didn't coin the term: Maxime Bôcher did, in 1906. The claim is right that the phenomenon involves oscillation or overshoot near a jump, but it gets both the person and who coined the term wrong.

text: The length of a cricket season, which varies by location, can be divided into two parts: an initial section where a bat is only used for scoring, called the "matcher itself" and then follows the usage of a 'ball' by spin and throw/hit football just before the holiday.
label: contradicted
reason: Cricket seasons do run for different months in different places. In Australia, for example, the traditional season is October to March, and The Conversation article I found backs that part up. The rest of the claim doesn't hold up. I found nothing on any credible source suggesting a cricket season splits into an opening part called the "matcher itself", where the bat is used only for scoring, followed by a part where a ball is spun and a football is thrown or hit before a holiday. That doesn't match how cricket works: bat and ball are used together in every match all season, and football is a separate sport. In Australia, football is played in a different season from cricket, not inside it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the Earth.
label: supported
reason: NOAA sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA Ocean Service gives its length as 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km. NOAA Education calls it 'over 40,000 miles long', and WHOI puts it at 40,000 miles (65,000 km). NOAA Ocean Exploration uses the phrase 'nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)', so the claim's 'over 65,000 km' is a slight overstatement. Even so, it is within normal rounding of the cited figure, and the 'over 40,000 miles' part matches exactly. Overall, the evidence supports the claim.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and able to quickly adapt and route around damaged areas.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's "Brief History of the Internet", written by Internet pioneers including Cerf, Kahn, Kleinrock and others, says outright that the idea of ARPANET being built to survive nuclear war is a "false rumor" that came from an unrelated RAND study. It states this "was never true of the ARPANET." The same source does say that later internetworking work stressed robustness and survivability, so the network's ability to route around damage is real. But the claim's main point, that the Internet was originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack, is contradicted.

text: The이버thing, a periodic table element with the atomic number 118, is named after the German scientist Dmitry Mendeleyev who first proposed its existence, and the town of Omsk in Russia where the scientists who discovered it worked.
label: contradicted
reason: Element 118 is oganesson (Og). It is named only after Yuri Oganessian, the nuclear physicist at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. It is not named after Dmitri Mendeleev, who was Russian rather than German and has element 101, mendelevium, named after him. Oganesson's name has no link to Omsk either, and the scientists who discovered it worked in Dubna and at Lawrence Livermore, not Omsk.

text: A crucial protein named Myoglobin in muscles helps to store oxygen, enabling humans and other organisms to survive for extended periods of time without access to oxygen.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is accurate: myoglobin is a protein in muscle that stores oxygen. Research on diving mammals shows that high levels of muscle myoglobin help seals and whales hold their breath for long periods, up to about an hour in some species. The claim fails where it says this lets humans survive for extended periods without oxygen. The sources compare seals with humans and say seals can stay under longer because they have far more myoglobin. Humans have relatively little muscle myoglobin and rely mainly on hemoglobin in the blood. Even elite human breath-hold divers last only around 5 minutes. Because the long survival without oxygen applies to diving animals and not to humans, the claim is contradicted.

text: The darkest natural place on Earth is Lechuguilla Cave, located in New Mexico, United States, which remains in complete darkness due to its extreme depth and location.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that calls Lechuguilla Cave the darkest natural place on Earth. Wikipedia confirms the cave exists in Carlsbad Caverns National Park, New Mexico. However, none of the cave sources I found make a darkness claim. Pages about the darkest places on Earth instead name sites with the least light pollution for stargazing, such as Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, the Atacama Desert and Massacre Rim. Those rankings measure a different kind of darkness, so they don't clearly contradict the claim. One general answer notes that any sealed cave is completely dark, which means no single cave stands out as the darkest. The superlative can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon remains one of the world's greatest unsolved enigmas, and despite numerous investigations, the source of its heating water continues to be a mystery.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific research, mainly geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's studies, has explained what heats the river (Shanay-timpishka). Wikipedia says the predominant theory is a geothermal heat source. Slate reports that after testing hypotheses, Ruzo's team concluded the heat comes from a fault-led hydrothermal system, with no volcano or magma involved.
