A 2016 AccuWeather headline did call the river 'mysterious,' but that refers to its unusual nature, not to an unknown heat source. The claim that the heat source is still a mystery and one of the world's greatest unsolved enigmas therefore conflicts with the scientific findings.

text: There are over 8 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to scientists, but it's estimated that 80-90% of all species are still undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: The claim's main figures match the widely cited 2011 PLoS Biology study led by Camilo Mora, which estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. The study found that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described, so 'more than 80% undiscovered' fits the 80–90% range in the claim. Coverage of the study says less than 15% of the total has been catalogued. One small inaccuracy: the 8.7 million estimate covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. That detail does not change the core finding.

text: A group of octopuses is called a "склад" which translates to "squad" but can also be called a "commonwealth".​
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources, such as a Western Australian government marine education site, say the collective noun for a group of octopuses is a "consortium." Other common terms are "rally" and "tangle." None of the sources mention "склад" or "commonwealth" as a name for a group of octopuses. The translation in the claim is also wrong: in Russian, "склад" means "warehouse" or "composition," not "squad" (that would be "отряд"). The claim looks like a garbled version of "consortium."

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola being initially marketed as a "brain tonic and intellectual beverage."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Pepsi's origin wrong. Coca-Cola's inventor, John Pemberton, was a morphine-addicted Civil War veteran, and his coca-based drinks are often described as an attempt to find a substitute for morphine. Coke was also advertised as a brain or nerve tonic. Pepsi, however, was made in 1893 by pharmacist Caleb Bradham as 'Brad's Drink', a digestive aid for dyspepsia (indigestion). It was not created as an alternative to morphine. Because the Pepsi part is false, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The highest recorded speed of a human body propelled by Belgian dive bomber pilot and Stuka commander Hanna Reitsch reached 572 mph during a rocket-assisted glide, although this wouldn't be tested for many years following this claim of hers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets basic facts about Hanna Reitsch wrong. Sources say she was a German civilian test pilot for the Luftwaffe, born in Hirschberg, Silesia. She was not Belgian, and she was not a dive bomber pilot or a Stuka commander. She did fly the Me 163 Komet rocket plane in 1942 and crashed on her fifth flight. I found nothing to back up the claimed 572 mph 'human body' speed record or the idea that this was 'tested many years later'.

text: The ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy have one of the longest stalactites in the world, measuring over 8.8 meters in length.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches failed because the search tool hit its usage limit, so I found no web evidence for or against this claim. The claim also has no clear subject. "Ghiaccio stalactite caves" (ghiaccio is Italian for ice) does not name any known cave in the Italian mountains. From general knowledge, not from search results, the stalactites usually called the world's longest are in caves outside Italy, such as Jeita Grotto in Lebanon (about 8.2 m), so I know of no Italian ice cave with a stalactite over 8.8 m. However, I could not check this with sources, and because the cave is unidentified, the claim cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crinan Canal, a 7-mile (11 km) long man-made waterway that allowed ships to travel directly between the Atlantic Ocean and Loch Crinan.
label: contradicted
reason: Scottish Canals, the body that runs the canal, says the Crinan Canal is nine miles long, not 7 miles (11 km). It runs from Ardrishaig on Loch Fyne to Crinan on the Sound of Jura, giving boats a shortcut between the Clyde Estuary and the west coast so they avoid sailing around the Mull of Kintyre. That means it does not link the Atlantic Ocean directly with Loch Crinan. It is also not described as being in a 'Vale of Awe'.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to estimates by some biologists and naturalists.
label: supported
reason: The claim only says that some biologists estimate more than 10 million species exist, and published estimates back that. The Conversation reports that over the past quarter century, estimates of how many species exist have ranged from about 5 million to 100 million. It names Terry Erwin, whose canopy-insect work gave a well-known estimate of about 30 million species. A review on ResearchGate says estimates of species on Earth range from 2 million to 3 trillion. The widely cited 8.7 million figure from the 2011 PLoS Biology study is lower, but it doesn't contradict the claim, which is about what some experts estimate.

text: The mysterious Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Peruvian Amazon," is a meandering stream that seems to defy the laws of nature by emitting steam and flowing uphill due to its geothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The Shanay-timpishka, the "Boiling River of the Amazon" in Peru, is real. Sources confirm that it is a geothermal river, and its steaming hot water (about 86°C on average) is well documented. But the claim that it flows uphill is false. Wikipedia lists its source at Mayantuyacu at about 265 m elevation and its mouth at the Pachitea River at about 160 m, so it runs downhill like any normal tributary. Geothermal activity heats the water but does not make it flow uphill. No credible source supports the uphill claim, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Parà Boiling River," is a mysterious river in Peru where the water remains at a constant temperature of around 82°F (28°C), despite being located near the equator and surrounded by cold waterfalls.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon (Shanay-timpishka, in Peru) is famous for being extremely hot. Its water reaches up to about 94°C (around 200°F), hot enough to cook animals that fall in. That flatly contradicts the claim that it stays at a constant 82°F (28°C). Credible sources also don't call it the "Parà Boiling River"; its names are Shanay-timpishka and Río Hirviente. I found no support for the claim that it is surrounded by cold waterfalls either.

text: The-aligning of Haley's comet with planetary systems are consistent with the "Rare Earth Hypothesis", which suggests that certain planetary conditions must be met for life to form on another planet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No reliable source I found links Halley's comet, or any 'alignment' of it with planetary systems, to the Rare Earth Hypothesis. The claim's description of the hypothesis is roughly right: it holds that life, especially complex life, needs a rare combination of planetary and astronomical conditions. But the main assertion has no clear meaning or evidence behind it. My search turned up only general facts about Halley's comet, such as its roughly 76-year orbit and Edmond Halley's prediction of its return. It cannot be confirmed, and no source directly refutes it.

text: Penguins are able to drink saltwater due to a special gland located above their eyes that filters out excess salt, allowing them to stay hydrated.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Oceanwide Expeditions and Wikipedia's article on salt glands, say penguins have a supraorbital gland located above or near the eyes. This gland pulls excess salt out of the blood, and the salt leaves through the nasal passages. That lets penguins drink salty water and keep their salt balance in check while getting the water they need.

text: The platypus is one of the few venomous mammals in the world, with the male species having a spur on its hind leg that contains a venom strong enough to kill small animals.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back every part of the claim. Wikipedia says the platypus is one of the few living mammals that produce venom. The San Diego Zoo says only adult males produce venom, delivered through a spur on the hind leg. BBC Discover Wildlife and A-Z Animals say the venom is strong enough to kill smaller animals. One caveat: the Australian Platypus Conservancy calls the specific idea that the venom can kill a dog a myth. That challenges the dog example, not the broader claim about small animals.

text: Aestvation, a type of heatstroke-like condition that occurs in animals, can be caused by a lack of rain in arid climates and is most commonly found in ungulates, such as deer.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources describe aestivation as a state of dormancy. Animals enter it on purpose during hot, dry periods to save energy and avoid losing water. It is not a heatstroke-like condition. It is also best known in snails, lungfish, amphibians and some reptiles and insects, not in ungulates such as deer. The only part of the claim that holds up is that dry, arid conditions can trigger it.

text: A piece of silk production waste called a "lotus silk petal" is made from the cocoons of the Himalayan moon moth, and is typically worth more than its weight in gold due to its rare and luxurious properties.
label: contradicted
reason: Lotus silk comes from the lotus plant, not from moth cocoons. Wikipedia says it is a cellulose fiber pulled from lotus stems, and that the craft began at Inle Lake in Myanmar. Unlike true silk, which is a protein fiber made by insects, it has nothing to do with Himalayan or Indian moon moths. No source describes a 'lotus silk petal' as moth-cocoon production waste. Lotus silk is very expensive because the work is so labor-intensive, but the claim's origin story is wrong, and the 'worth more than its weight in gold' part is unsupported.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it can recover quickly from failures and disruptions.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim repeats a common myth. In its 'A Brief History of the Internet', the Internet Society calls the idea that ARPANET was built to withstand nuclear war a "false rumor". It says only an unrelated RAND study on secure voice considered nuclear war. Former ARPA Director Charles Herzfeld also said ARPANET was not started to build a command system that could survive a nuclear attack. ARPANET was designed to keep working when parts of the network failed, but mainly because its nodes and links were unreliable, not because of nuclear threats. The evidence here comes from a fandom wiki page, but it directly quotes those authoritative sources.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes to evade predators.
label: supported
reason: The Natural History Museum (London) calls capybaras the world's largest rodent. It also says they can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes, which helps them escape predators. That covers every part of the claim.

text: Mitosis, the process by which cells divide, is so precise that the DNA of the resulting cells is identical to that of the parent cell, with only slight variations in minor genetic details if any.
label: supported
reason: Biology education sources (Pearson, TutorChase) say mitosis makes two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell, unless a mutation happens. That matches the claim that the daughter cells' DNA is identical, with at most slight variations. Rare mutations, mostly from DNA replication errors, are the minor variations the claim allows for.

text: The ocena in the Great Blue Hole of Belize is so still and clear that visibility reaches as far as 485 feet horizontally and 75 meters below the surface due to the extremely low nitrogen levels and total absence of light.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources give much lower visibility figures for the Great Blue Hole. Ambergriscaye.com says the water is motionless and visibility "often approaches 200 feet," and another Belize site says visibility reaches up to about 150 feet in the dry season. No source supports 485 feet. The claim's explanation also fails: none of the sources link the clarity to low nitrogen levels or a "total absence of light," and the clear upper waters are lit by sunlight. The 485-foot figure is contradicted, and the stated causes are not supported.

text: The VOCAB (Vehicle Officers Capturing Drugs and Narcotics) sweeps across police jurisdictions often educate the community about outstanding issues by providing free substance abuse and health clinics at public gatherings to give out various confidential mailings that wipe out every sample case that occurs at public events.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no program called "VOCAB (Vehicle Officers Capturing Drugs and Narcotics)." The results only covered unrelated drug sweeps and vehicle interdiction in general. Nothing showed that any such program runs free substance abuse or health clinics, or sends out confidential mailings at public events. The claim is also too garbled to check as written, for example the part about mailings that "wipe out every sample case." text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, according to estimates from scientists, but it's estimated that as many as 80-90% of them remain undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: The claim is essentially supported, with two small inaccuracies. The 2011 Census of Marine Life / PLoS Biology study (Mora et al.) estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. It found that 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been discovered, and Nature News summarised this as 'more than 80% of species still undiscovered.' That fits the claim's 80–90% range. However, the figure is 'about' 8.7 million, not 'over' 8.7 million. It also covers all eukaryotic species, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. These imprecisions don't change the main point.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments such as deep-sea vents, where temperatures can reach as high as 221 degrees Fahrenheit, due to their simple and versatile cell structure.
label: contradicted
reason: Bacteria and other microbes do live around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, but the claim's numbers and explanation are wrong. Vents are much hotter than 221°F: vent water can reach about 400°C (750°F), and the NIH says black smokers reach 662°F. The Smithsonian says most bacteria and archaea cannot survive in the superheated vent fluid itself. They live in the cooler zones where vent water mixes with seawater. The known limit for microbial growth is about 122°C (252°F), and the organism that reaches it is an archaeon, not a bacterium. Microbes survive these conditions through specific heat-tolerance adaptations, which sources do not attribute to a 'simple and versatile cell structure.'

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as "El Estuerdo," is a river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains at a consistent temperature of 77°F (25°C) throughout the year, despite being located near a geothermal hotspot.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. The Boiling River's local name is Shanay-timpishka, also called Río Hirviente. It is not called "El Estuerdo." Sources also say the river is very hot, near 90–100°C (around 200°F) and hot enough to kill animals that fall in. That rules out a steady 77°F (25°C). Wikipedia also says it is not near any known active volcanoes or geothermal vents.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) and circles the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim's main point. NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge Earth's longest mountain range. They say it is nearly 65,000 km long (NOAA gives 40,390 miles) and winds around the globe through every major ocean basin. Guinness World Records and WorldAtlas give about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). One detail differs: the claim says 'over 65,000 km,' but NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly.' That gap is small, so the length figure, the 'longest' title and the globe-circling description all hold up.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which is closely related to African elephant.
label: contradicted
reason: No known animal is called the "short-eared elephant". The closest match is the short-eared (round-eared) elephant shrew, Macroscelides proboscideus, which still exists: the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Stegolophodon is not known as a "short-eared elephant", and it was not closely related to the African elephant. It is an extinct Asian genus in the family Stegodontidae, linked to Stegodon, while African elephants belong to the family Elephantidae.

text: The Bactrian camels found in the Gobi Desert can go without water for several days due to their unique adaptations, including the ability to store water in their bloodstream by producing highly concentrated urine.
label: supported
reason: Sources on camel physiology, including Bactrian camels, back up the main points: camels can go a long time without water, which comfortably covers 'several days'. Their adaptations include red blood cells that keep their blood working when water is scarce, and kidneys that make highly concentrated urine. One caveat: the claim's wording is loose. Concentrated urine saves water by cutting losses; it does not directly 'store' water in the bloodstream. Sources describe holding water in the blood and producing concentrated urine as separate adaptations. Because each element is backed by evidence, I've labelled the claim supported, though a stricter reading of that causal link could make it inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "ElSprites Hot River" is a natural wonder that remains a mystery as it appears to defy the laws of nature by existing in a strange other worldly liminal state below the river's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia and IFLScience, say the Boiling River is called Shanay-timpishka (also Río Hirviente or La Bomba). None of them mention the name "ElSprites Hot River." Its heat also isn't an unexplained mystery that defies nature: it comes from geothermal circulation, where hot water from deep faults rises to the surface, as Andrés Ruzo's research found. The idea of an "otherworldly liminal state below the river's surface" appears in no source and conflicts with the scientific explanation.

text: The tingling sensation people often experience in their fingers and toes while flying on an airplane is caused by a lack of air pressure at high altitudes, which leads to a decrease in oxygen levels and increased carbon dioxide in the bloodstream.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the carbon dioxide part backwards. The FAA handbook does list tingling in the fingers and toes as a symptom of hypoxia, which is a lack of oxygen at altitude. But it says the low-oxygen breathing pattern linked to tingling, hyperventilation, comes from too little carbon dioxide in the blood, not too much. Its treatment is to restore normal carbon dioxide levels. So the claim's statement that blood carbon dioxide goes up is wrong, even though the low-air-pressure and low-oxygen parts are roughly right.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Wikipedia also gives about 65,000 km (40,000 mi), and other sources say "over 65,000 km." NOAA's wording is "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," which is a small difference. The main claim and the approximate length match reliable sources.

text: The 길 Cheese is a type of Korean cheese made from a mixture of cow's, goat's, and sheep's milk that has gained popularity worldwide for its unique flavor and smooth texture.
label: not_verifiable

label: contradicted
reason: The only 2002 short called "Flicker" I could find is Conall Pendergast's Canadian horror short. That doesn't match the claim of a 79-second shot of TV static. It is black and white, which fits that one detail. I found nothing showing that this film, or any 2002 "Flicker," was accepted into Sundance or called its smallest film. The only Sundance-related "Flicker" in the results is an unrelated 2021 entry in a Sundance Collab challenge. Another 2002 "Flicker," by Chris Newby, runs 4 minutes 50 seconds and is about bonfire night in Lewes, so it doesn't fit either. Because the documented runtime and content conflict with the claim and the Sundance part has no support, I've marked it contradicted.

text: The only bird that can fly backward is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and wing movement, which allows it to hover and move in different directions.
label: supported
reason: Most sources I found back the claim. Wikipedia's 'Backward flying' article says hummingbirds (family Trochilidae) are the only birds that fly backward. Birdspot and Birds & Blooms say the same, and Birdspot puts it down to wing structure and wing movement, which also let hummingbirds hover and move in different directions. There is one caveat. A few lower-quality sources, such as a forum post, birdswave and earthofbirds, say birds like herons, sunbirds, kingfishers or kestrels can briefly flutter backward. More careful sources make a distinction here: hummingbirds are the only birds capable of true, sustained, controlled backward flight. That fits the claim as it is usually meant.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, the Lehigh Valley Mink Insula Prehistoric Earthen Enclosure also known as  Angel Mink Insula enclosure.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any record of a site called the "Lehigh Valley Mink Insula Prehistoric Earthen Enclosure" or "Angel Mink Insula enclosure" in the Catskills or anywhere else, so the name appears to be made up. Reliable sources also name other places as the oldest known dwellings in North America. Live Science reports a 13,800-year-old dwelling at the Shéyˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ site in Alaska, called the oldest in the Western Hemisphere. Other candidates are the Gault site in Texas and Paisley Cave in Oregon. None of these are in New York's Catskill Mountains.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it was built with redundancy and fail-safes to ensure maximum uptime.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a well-known myth. Bob Taylor, who started the ARPANET project in 1966, said its creation "was not motivated by considerations of war." The Internet Society's Brief History of the Internet calls the nuclear-war idea a false rumor. That rumor came from Paul Baran's separate RAND study on survivable communications. ARPANET was built so researchers could share computing resources, not to withstand a nuclear attack or to maximize uptime.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoralillo Geysers and the El Tatio Geysers, which are fueled by underground volcanic activity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some of the claim checks out. Reliable sources such as Chile Travel and Wikipedia say the Atacama Desert is in Chile and is often called the driest place on Earth, strictly the driest non-polar desert. They also confirm that the El Tatio geysers are a geothermal field in the Atacama region, and Wikipedia ties their heat to nearby volcanic calderas. However, I couldn't find any source for 'Totoralillo Geysers.' Searches turned up only Punta Totoralillo, a mining-export port on the Chilean coast, not a geyser field. Because part of the claim can't be verified and may refer to something that doesn't exist, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater in the Denmark Strait, where the Labrador Current meets the Irminger Current.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science and other sources confirm that the Denmark Strait cataract, an underwater waterfall between Iceland and Greenland, is the world's largest waterfall. That part of the claim is correct. The claim gets the cause wrong, though. The cataract forms when cold, dense water from the Nordic Seas (the Greenland, Norwegian and Iceland seas) flows over the strait's sill and plunges into the Irminger Sea. The Labrador Current is in the Labrador Sea, west of Greenland, and has nothing to do with it. So saying it is where the Labrador Current meets the Irminger Current is false.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible above water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about the ridge never showing above water. NOAA confirms the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain chain. It also says more than 90% of the ridge lies in the deep ocean, so not all of it is underwater. Several sources say the ridge rises above the sea surface in a few places, such as Iceland and Jan Mayen. The length is also slightly off: NOAA says "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km.

text: If you need to conduct a small research-based project and have time to dedicate up to 40 hours, it takes an average of 40 hours for a person to reach an appropriate level of expertise in their chosen subject.

Other sources give quite different figures for learning or mastery: Josh Kaufman says about 20 hours to learn a new skill, and Gladwell's well-known rule says about 10,000 hours to master one. None of them confirm or rule out the 40-hour average. My search limit ran out before I could check the exact wording further, so the claim can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and able to quickly recover from widespread disruptions.
label: contradicted

The Internet Society's "A Brief History of the Internet" says the idea that ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war is a "false rumor" that grew out of the separate RAND study by Paul Baran. ARPANET was actually built so researchers could share computing resources. The same history notes that later internetworking work did stress robustness and survivability, but that does not mean the Internet was originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack.

text: There is a species of jellyfish called the turbine jellyfish that can live forever due to its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The jellyfish this claim describes is real, but its name is wrong. Wikipedia, NOAA, AMNH and a PMC paper all identify it as Turritopsis dohrnii (sometimes given as T. nutricula), commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." Sources confirm that it can revert from its adult medusa form to the earlier polyp stage through transdifferentiation. However, "turbine jellyfish" is not a recognized name for this or any other species. An exact-phrase search turned up only wind-turbine designs. "Live forever" also overstates the case: the species is biologically immortal, but individuals can still die from predators or disease. Because the claim names a species that doesn't exist under that name, I rate it contradicted.

text: There is an underwater lake located beneath the surface of Visovac Island in Croatia, approximately 15 meters below ground level, also known as a lake or a subterranean water body.
label: not_verifiable

The sources I found, including Wikipedia, NP Krka, croatiatraveller and travel guides, describe Visovac as a small island inside Visovac Lake, a wide part of the Krka River. None of them mentions a lake beneath the island. They don't explicitly say there isn't one either, so the claim is unverified rather than directly contradicted. My search budget ran out before I could check depth figures for Visovac Lake.

text: The highest recorded human body temperature in space is of TessHB standing at 39°C (102.2°F), which occurred when an astronaut was in space without a suit from the hatch to the cabin.
label: not_verifiable

"TessHB" doesn't match any astronaut, mission or study I know of, so it has no clear referent. The scenario is also implausible: an astronaut moving through space without a suit would be exposed to vacuum, not just a raised body temperature. Research on astronauts has found that core body temperature can rise during spaceflight, but I found nothing showing a record of 39°C (102.2°F) tied to "TessHB" or to the event described.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, of which only about 1.3 million have been formally discovered and documented by scientists.
label: supported
reason: The figures come from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), which estimates about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species on Earth. ScienceDaily reports that about 1.25 million species have been described and catalogued, which rounds to the claim's "about 1.3 million." There are some imprecisions: the estimate is about 8.7 million, not "over" 8.7 million; it covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals; and the paper itself says about 1.2 million species are catalogued. These details don't contradict the main point of the claim.

text: The short-lived but highly notable element, Oganesson (Og), is the heaviest known natural element, having an atomic number of 118 and an atomic mass of 440 atomic mass units.
label: contradicted
reason: The atomic number of 118 is correct, but two other parts of the claim are wrong. Los Alamos National Laboratory describes oganesson as a synthetic element, made artificially with only a few atoms ever produced, so it is not a natural element. LANL also lists its atomic mass as 294, not 440.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into stone, preserving their bodies for centuries, a phenomenon known as "petrification".
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Natron is a real, highly alkaline soda lake in Tanzania, and dead animals there can end up calcified and preserved. But reliable sources say these animals do not actually turn to stone and are not 'petrified.' The Indian Defence Review notes that the animals in Nick Brandt's photographs 'are not petrified' and 'have not turned to stone at all.' Instead, they dry out and become coated with mineral deposits, which only makes them look like stone. Live Science puts 'stone' in quotation marks for the same reason. No source supports the claim that the bodies are preserved 'for centuries.'

text: There are approximately 500 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone, which is estimated to contain only about 2% of the total stars in the observable universe.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are wrong. Mainstream estimates put the Milky Way at about 100–400 billion stars (WorldAtlas cites about 100 billion), not 500 billion. The bigger error is the 2% figure. The observable universe holds hundreds of billions to trillions of galaxies, so the Milky Way's stars are a tiny fraction of the total. WorldAtlas multiplies 100 billion stars by 2 trillion galaxies, which gives about 2×10^23 stars. That makes the Milky Way's share roughly a billionth of a percent, not about 2%.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1993, is the oldest known example of a rainforest tree in the world, dated back approximately 126 million years to the Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a 'Janszoon boom log' exists. Searches turned up only unrelated things with similar names: the Dutch surname Janszoon, the explorer Willem Janszoon, Project Janszoon (a conservation trust in Abel Tasman National Park), Arent Janszoon Boom (a 16th-century Dutch dike warden), and the general term 'log boom.' Nothing describes a log found in 1993 or calls it the oldest known rainforest tree dated to about 126 million years ago in the Cretaceous. The claim's specific details can't be checked against any source, and the entity itself has no clear referent, so it is inconclusive. The search results also don't directly contradict it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible above the surface of the ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration agrees that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, but its details don't match the claim. NOAA says the ridge stretches "nearly 65,000 kilometers" (not over 65,000 km) and that more than 90 percent of it lies underwater. That means part of it does rise above the ocean surface, as in Iceland, so it is wrong to say it is not visible above the surface.

text: The planet Venus rotates in the opposite direction of its orbit around the sun, a phenomenon known as a retrograde rotation, which is relatively rare in the solar system.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on retrograde and prograde motion says Venus has an axial tilt of 177°, so it spins almost exactly opposite to the direction of its orbit. That is retrograde rotation. The same article says Venus probably started with a fast prograde spin like most planets in the Solar System. Since most planets spin prograde, retrograde rotation like Venus's is relatively rare, which supports the claim.

text: Butler's Elephant, a male African elephant, lived in the London Zoo from 1961 to 1978 and was said to have the longest-lived proboscis.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions an elephant called "Butler's Elephant" at London Zoo. Searches turned up general London Zoo elephant history, including Jumbo and the Elephant and Rhinoceros Pavilion built 1962–65, but nothing about a male African elephant kept there from 1961 to 1978. Nothing describes any elephant as having the "longest-lived proboscis" either. No source supports or contradicts the claim, so it can't be verified.

text: Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula is home to the world's second-largest spring system, known as the Sac Actun, which is approximately 347 kilometers long.
label: contradicted
reason: Sac Actun is real, it is in the Yucatán Peninsula, and its reported length in 2018 was about 347 km. However, it is an underwater cave system, not a spring system. Wikipedia calls it the world's second-longest underwater cave system (after Ox Bel Ha). The IUGS geoheritage site calls it the longest underwater cave system and the second-longest cave in the world. No source calls it the world's second-largest 'spring system,' so that part of the claim misdescribes it. Sources also disagree on whether it ranks first or second, so the ranking alone could not settle the verdict.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1991, is the oldest known piece of Australian timber and dates back approximately 6,500 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no reliable source that mentions a "Janszoon boom log" at all. Results about "Janszoon" covered Willem Janszoon's 1605–06 voyage to Australia, the Duyfken replica and Project Janszoon in New Zealand. None mentioned a log found in 1991 or one dated to about 6,500 years ago. Other results on ancient timber, such as Huon pine and subfossil wood, never mention this log either. Since the log itself, the 1991 discovery, the date and the 'oldest known' claim can't be checked, the claim can't be supported or ruled out.

text: The Andean condensed milk, a type of milk known to have originated in South America, can last for years without refrigeration due to the low water content and thanks to the addition of sugar, air-tight container, and functioning evaporation process.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any recognized product called "Andean condensed milk." A search for the exact phrase only returned general pages about condensed milk. Trustworthy sources say condensed milk comes from the United States, not South America. Wikipedia lists its place of origin as the United States, and Gail Borden patented it in 1856, with OUP's blog and Lancaster Farming saying the same. Sweetened condensed milk later became a staple in Latin American kitchens, but it didn't start there. The shelf-life part of the claim (sugar, low water content, sealed cans) is broadly true for sweetened condensed milk in general. However, the claim that it originated in South America is false.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of the Cannes Film Festival, consisting of only a 7-second clip of a burning match.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results contradict the claim. IMDb lists "Flicker" (2002) as a 5-minute horror video directed by Conall Pendergast about an old film reel that "holds deadly secrets." It is not a 7-second clip of a burning match. The other films called "Flicker" that turned up are a British documentary about the Lewes bonfire night, a Big Art Group stage work from 2002–2006, and a 2008 Canadian documentary. None of them matches the description, and no source mentions Cannes accepting such a film. Cannes also has no "canon" of accepted films, so the claim appears to be made up.

text: Butler's Panama, a part of Panama in the late 19th century, was an independent state that buffered the construction of the Panama Canal, from 1886 to 1901.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of an entity called "Butler's Panama". My one search on the name returned only unrelated business listings, and further searches failed when the tool limit ran out. The period claim is contradicted by well-documented history that I did not re-check with a search: under Colombia's 1886 constitution, the former Sovereign State of Panama became the Department of Panama, part of Colombia. It stayed part of Colombia until it declared independence in November 1903. So it was not an independent state from 1886 to 1901. Also, the US did not build the Panama Canal until 1904–1914, after independence.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is day and only see polarized light at night, which helps it navigate through murky or dark waters.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that danios see in full color by day but only polarized light at night. The evidence I did find points the other way. A ScienceDirect study on zebrafish (Danio rerio) found that the fish still told colors apart and showed color preferences at midnight (red > blue > green), with yellow preferred both day and night. That conflicts with the idea that they see only polarized light at night. Research on fish polarization vision ties it to UV and short-wavelength cones, which are cells used in daylight vision, not a night-only mode. The 'navigating murky waters' sources I found are about infrared vision in salmon and other freshwater fish, not polarized light in danios. My searches ran out before I could check a few more sources, so this rests on the evidence above.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the WR 104 horseshoe shaped binary star system's ring, but on Earth, the longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which extends over 65,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: WR 104 is not in our solar system and has no mountain range. It is a Wolf-Rayet star system about 8,400 light-years away in Sagittarius, surrounded by a spiral ("pinwheel") dust nebula. That nebula comes from colliding stellar winds, not from mountains. So the claim's main premise is false. The part about Earth's Mid-Ocean Ridge being over 65,000 km long is broadly accurate, but it doesn't save the claim.

text: The vibrant flower, the infamous Opal Flower or the more popular known yuka flower,  is a rare snapdragons cultivar (yuka 'Snapdragon Opal,').
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two unrelated plants. Yucca ("yuka") is a genus in the family Asparagaceae. Snapdragons are Antirrhinum majus, in the family Plantaginaceae. A yucca flower can't be a snapdragon cultivar, and the searches turned up no rare cultivar called "yuka 'Snapdragon Opal'". The plants that use "Opal" in their names are other things, such as Lachenalia aloides, Heuchera 'Opal' and Coreopsis 'Opal'.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have shown a correlation between long ring fingers and increased levels of testosterone in the womb, which is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.
label: contradicted
reason: The research says the opposite of the claim. A long ring finger compared with the index finger (low 2D:4D ratio) is taken as a sign of higher testosterone in the womb. In men, this is linked to protection against early heart attack or a later first heart attack. A high 2D:4D ratio (relatively short ring finger) is the one associated with early myocardial infarction. Finger length is also not a commonly used tool for assessing heart disease risk; it is a research proxy only.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the Earth's globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the most extensive mountain chain on Earth and puts its length at nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI also calls it the planet's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). Those figures match the claim of over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) around the globe.

text: A cast-iron skillet can be a good heat distributor and can be preheated to high temperatures without losing its iron coating due to the presence of carbon in the iron which makes it quite durable.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources, including Cooking Issues by food scientist Dave Arnold, say it's a myth that cast iron spreads heat well. It's actually a fairly poor heat conductor and develops hot and cold spots, though it holds heat well once hot. The claim's other parts are also off. Cast iron has no 'iron coating' to lose; its protective layer is polymerized oil seasoning. And the skillet doesn't keep that layer at high heat because of carbon in the iron. The searches found nothing supporting the claim that cast iron distributes heat well.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, where the cold, dense water from the North Atlantic flows downhill into the deeper waters of the North Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Live Science, EarthSky and Discover Wildlife, describe the Denmark Strait cataract between Greenland and Iceland as the world's largest waterfall. They say it is underwater and carries millions of cubic metres of water per second, far more than any waterfall on land. They also confirm that cold, dense water sinks and flows down a steep drop in the seafloor. One detail is imprecise: these sources say the cold water comes from the Nordic Seas or Greenland Sea and flows into the Irminger Sea, not 'from the North Atlantic.' The Nordic Seas are often counted as part of the wider North Atlantic, though, so this is loose wording rather than a real contradiction. The main claim holds up.

text: The fastest recorded speed of a projectile launched from a catapult was achieved in 2016 by a team from the University of Illinois, with a speed of 555 miles per hour.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No source I found mentions a University of Illinois team setting a catapult projectile speed record of 555 mph in 2016. Guinness's 'highest projectile velocity' record belongs to the Naval Research Laboratory and uses a laser, not a catapult. More recent reports describe engineer Tom Stanton's miniature trebuchet, a type of catapult, launching a 4 g projectile at about 716 mph. That suggests 555 mph is not the fastest catapult speed today, but it does not directly test the 2016 Illinois claim. Since the specific claim can be neither confirmed nor directly disproved, the result is inconclusive.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point rose to 115.5°F (46.4°C) during a severe case of heatstroke.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records gives the highest recorded human body temperature as 46.5°C (115.7°F). It belonged to Willie Jones, who was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta with heatstroke in 1980. Several other sources say the same. I found no source of any kind for a person named 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' or for a record of 115.5°F (46.4°C). The person and the figure in the claim both conflict with the documented record.

text: The world's largest planetarium, the Melville-Nathan Planetarium in Macau, China, covers over 11,000 square meters of space and features a massive dome that simulates celestial experiences for visitors.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any planetarium called the "Melville-Nathan Planetarium" in Macau. The planetarium there is part of the Macao Science Center. Reliable sources, including China Daily, Christie Digital and Blooloop, say the world's largest planetarium is the Shanghai Astronomy Museum (Shanghai Planetarium) in Pudong, Shanghai, with a total area of about 38,164 square meters. That contradicts both the name and the location given in the claim, as well as its size of over 11,000 square meters.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola containing coca leaves that had a small amount of the alkaloid cocaine.
label: contradicted
reason: Coca-Cola grew out of John Pemberton's search for a substitute for his morphine addiction, and his coca-leaf formula contained cocaine, so that part of the claim holds up. The Pepsi part does not. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893 as 'Brad's Drink,' a kola-nut beverage sold as a digestive aid and mild restorative, not as an alternative to morphine. Because the claim says both drinks were developed as morphine alternatives, it is contradicted.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and spans the globe, primarily underwater but also visible in some areas.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It says the ridge stretches nearly 65,000 km and that more than 90% of it is underwater. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, and some sources say 'over 65,000 km'. NOAA's 'nearly 65,000 km' is slightly lower than the claim's 'over 65,000', but the 80,000 km total for the full system covers the claim. The ridge circles the globe, and sources such as Wikipedia's Mid-Atlantic Ridge article and NASA's EPOD say parts of it rise above sea level, for example in Iceland.

text: Honey is the only food that babies can digest perfectly well when they're born, due to its unique properties that make it easily absorbed by the human body and liver.
label: contradicted
reason: Cleveland Clinic and other medical sources say babies under 1 year old should never be given honey, in any form, because it can cause infant botulism. Newborns cannot safely digest honey, so it is not a food they digest "perfectly well." Breast milk or formula is what newborns are fed. The claim is false.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and able to quickly recover from disruptions.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'Brief History of the Internet', written by Internet pioneers including Leiner, Cerf and Kahn, says outright that the idea that ARPANET was built to withstand nuclear war is a "false rumor". It says this "was never true of the ARPANET" and that only the separate RAND study on secure voice communications considered nuclear war. According to the same source, the main early reason for building ARPANET and the Internet was resource sharing. That contradicts the claim's main point about why the Internet was originally designed.

text: There are more bacteria cells in the human body than human cells, with estimates suggesting that for every cell in the human body, there are approximately 10 bacterial cells present, totaling around 39 trillion bacterial cells compared to 30 trillion human cells.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures of 39 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells come from Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016). That same study rejects the old 10:1 ratio. It puts the ratio at about 1.3:1, close to one-to-one, and Scientific American's coverage calls the 10:1 idea a myth. The claim's ratio of 10 bacterial cells per human cell is therefore contradicted, and it also clashes with the claim's own 39-to-30-trillion numbers. The part saying bacteria slightly outnumber human cells holds up, but the 10:1 figure is wrong.

text: Cats have a unique way of healing themselves, as they have a special type of collagen in their bones called "glucocorticoid-responsive collagen," which helps them recover from injuries more efficiently.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that mentions "glucocorticoid-responsive collagen" in cat bones or anywhere else, so the term looks made up. Searching for it only returns studies showing that glucocorticoids generally reduce collagen production, which doesn't fit the claim. When sources do talk about cats healing well, they credit purring vibrations, not a special collagen; Scientific American and Cats.com present this as a hypothesis or popular belief. Since nothing confirms the claimed mechanism, and no source directly rules it out either, the claim can't be verified.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some scientists estimating that there could be as many as 100 sextillion stars.
label: contradicted
reason: The 100 sextillion figure is roughly in line with published estimates, which range from about 10²² to a few times 10²³ stars. One example is about 200 sextillion. The main part of the claim, though, has the logic backwards. Astronomers get the number of stars in the universe by multiplying the number of galaxies by the typical number of stars in each galaxy, such as 100 billion for the Milky Way. Stars therefore don't exceed what galaxies can contain; they are counted as galaxy contents. Newer evidence also puts the number of galaxies at 2 trillion to 20 trillion, not 100 billion. Some galaxies hold far more than 100 billion stars, which easily accounts for star totals in the sextillions. The claim that there are more stars than the galaxies could possibly hold is not supported by the evidence and runs against how the estimates are made.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA, WHOI and WorldAtlas all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). NOAA Ocean Service gives 40,389 miles, which is about 65,000 km. One wording point is slightly off: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say 'nearly' 65,000 km, not 'over'. The figure is essentially right, though, so the claim holds overall.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the Monterey Bay in California that is immortal and has been estimated to be around 200 years old due to its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Parts of the claim check out. The Monterey Bay Aquarium has posted about the 'immortal jelly' (Turritopsis sp.), and other sources such as ScienceAlert and NOAA describe how Turritopsis can turn back into a younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation. However, no trustworthy source I found says this jellyfish has been estimated to be around 200 years old. Sources say these jellies can theoretically live forever but give no age estimates, and one site lists a typical lifespan of about 1.5 years. The '200 years old' detail cannot be verified, and the sources also do not clearly show that the species occurs in the wild in Monterey Bay.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history until the 16th century, when it was sometimes referred to as the " posterior."
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is garbled, and its checkable parts are wrong. It implies that people didn't wear pants until the 16th century, but trouser-history sources say trousers were worn as far back as the 6th century BC by Persians, Scythians and steppe peoples, with leggings-like garments even earlier. Etymonline also says the noun 'posterior' meaning 'buttocks' dates from the 1610s, which is the 17th century, not the 16th. The 1530s noun sense meant 'posterity,' not the backside. The word 'butt' for the buttocks dates from the mid-15th century, and 'buttocks' from about 1300. So the claimed timeline doesn't match the evidence.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have found that longer ring fingers are associated with elevated levels of testosterone in the womb.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up: a longer ring finger relative to the index finger (a low 2D:4D ratio) is widely treated as a proxy for higher testosterone exposure in the womb (e.g., the PMC/Melbourne cohort paper). The main claim does not hold up. Finger length is not 'often used to determine' heart disease risk. It is only a research biomarker, and the findings conflict. Some small studies report links with coronary artery disease or heart attack. Others find none: one 2021 study in the American Journal of Human Biology concluded that digit ratio 'is not related to cardiovascular diseases or their risk factors' in menopausal women, and another study found no 2D:4D difference between women with coronary heart disease and healthy controls. In several studies the direction is also the opposite of what the claim implies: men who had heart attacks had higher ratios, meaning relatively shorter ring fingers. Because the claim presents finger length as a common risk-assessment tool, which the evidence does not support, it is contradicted.

text: Antarctica is home to several long-lived species of jellyfish, with some reportedly being capable of surviving for up to 12,000 years in stasis, allowing them to revive when Environmental conditions become suitable.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that any Antarctic jellyfish can survive up to 12,000 years in stasis and then revive. The extreme ages reported for Antarctic animals belong to glass sponges such as Anoxycalyx (Scolymastra) joubini, estimated at up to 15,000 years. That figure is an estimated lifespan of a slow-growing sponge, not a jellyfish coming back from dormancy. The only Antarctic organism reported to revive after a long freeze is the moss Chorisodontium aciphyllum, after about 1,500 years. The so-called 'immortal jellyfish' (Turritopsis dohrnii) was discovered in the Mediterranean and is known for reverting to a juvenile stage, not for millennia of stasis in Antarctica. Antarctic jellyfish like Desmonema glaciale have no such reported ability. No source states outright that jellyfish cannot do this, but the claim appears to mix up facts about sponges and moss and give them to jellyfish.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Unexplained River" or "River of Lost Souls," is a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains unexplained despite extensive investigation.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the river is real, but they contradict the claim that it "remains unexplained." It is the Shanay-timpishka, also called Río Hirviente, in the Peruvian Amazon. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and his colleagues studied it and concluded it is heated by a fault-fed, non-volcanic hydrothermal system. In that system, rainwater sinks through cracks, is heated by the Earth's natural heat, and rises back up along fault lines. Atlas Obscura, an SMU geothermal researcher quoted on ScienceBlog, and other sources describe this as the accepted explanation. Wikipedia notes there are no active volcanoes nearby, but that does not mean the heat source is still a mystery. I also found no source using the nicknames "Unexplained River" or "River of Lost Souls" for it. Its documented names are Boiling River, Río Hirviente and Shanay-timpishka. "River of Lost Souls" turned up only as the title of an unrelated book about the Gold King Mine disaster.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect" that can make a candle flame inside a sealed glass jar appear to be able to "burn" in mid-air, despite there being no oxygen to fuel the fire.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions a "Kundsen effect" of CO2 that lets a flame burn without oxygen. The similar-sounding Knudsen effect is about gas flow and diffusion at very low density, and it has nothing to do with combustion. The ACS and Britannica explain that CO2 smothers a candle flame by keeping oxygen away from it. A candle in a sealed jar goes out once the oxygen is used up, so CO2 does not make a flame 'burn' in mid-air without oxygen.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon remains one of the world's most mysterious geographical formations, as its existence is confirmed by satellite images but the water source and method of staying warm despite being located 400 meters above sea level remain unknown.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim that the river's water source and heating mechanism are still unknown. Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo studied the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru. Chemical analysis shows the water started out as rain. The main explanation is that it is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient: the water sinks deep, warms up, and comes back up along faults. Wikipedia and ScienceAlert both describe this explanation, so the river is not a total unknown. The river's existence was confirmed by people going there and measuring the water (about 86 °C), not mainly by satellite images. The sources also say nothing to back the 400 m elevation figure. Some outlets still call parts of the river a mystery, but the core claim that both the source and the heating method are unknown goes against the research.

text: The Human Brain accounts for about 2% of the human body's mass, yet it uses approximately 20% of the body's total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the human brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy, at least at rest. The Physics Factbook gathers this figure from multiple published references, and it is widely accepted in physiology. The claim says "total energy expenditure" while the sources mostly specify energy use at rest, but this is a minor difference in wording and fits how the figure is usually stated.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly unstable nucleus that decays almost instantly.
label: contradicted
reason: Oganesson (Z=118) is the heaviest known element, meaning it has the highest atomic number and mass, and it is very unstable (half-life under 1 ms). That does not make it the largest atom by size. Its predicted covalent radius is about 157 pm, while caesium and francium have much larger atomic radii and are usually named as the largest atoms. Calling it a 'helium-like' species is also wrong. Oganesson sits in the same group as helium, the noble gases, but it has 118 electrons, not helium's two. The instability part is correct, but the claim that it is the largest atom ever discovered is not.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Guinness World Records and WorldAtlas, call the Mid-Ocean Ridge the world's longest mountain range and give its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Some sources say "nearly" or "about" 65,000 km rather than "over", but that is approximation wording, not a contradiction. The figure of 40,400 miles is a correct conversion of 65,000 km.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, where the cold, dense water of the East Greenland Current plunges into the Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources (EarthSky, Marine Insight, NOAA) describe the Denmark Strait cataract, between Greenland and Iceland, as the world's largest waterfall by volume of water flow. It is underwater: cold, dense Nordic and Greenland Sea water sinks below the warmer Irminger Sea water and drops into the Irminger Sea, which is part of the North Atlantic. Marine Insight ties this cold, dense flow to the East Greenland Current. Oceanographers more often call the sinking water 'Denmark Strait Overflow Water', so naming the East Greenland Current is a simplification, but popular sources commonly describe it this way and nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - notably The Weyerhaeuser Logging Company and more often now Tesla and companies like Google.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify every part of the claim. Several sources, citing the Crowther et al. study in Nature, estimate the U.S. has about 228 billion trees. That makes "over 300 million" technically true but a huge understatement. Weyerhaeuser is a long-running timber company with reforestation programs, but these searches didn't confirm how many trees it has planted. Tesla has paid for planting large numbers of trees, but around its factory near Berlin in Germany, not in U.S. forests, and only since about 2020. I found nothing showing that Google, or companies like it, plant trees in forests as described. Because of the misleading figure, the unconfirmed Weyerhaeuser and Google details, and the vague framing, the claim can't be fully supported.

text: There are more grains of sand on Earth than there are stars in the observable universe, with estimates suggesting approximately 7.5 x 10^18 grains of sand on our planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 7.5 x 10^18 figure for grains of sand on Earth is a commonly cited estimate. The comparison in the claim is the wrong way round, though. The usual estimates put the number of stars in the observable universe at about 10^22 to 10^24, far more than the sand grains. Sources such as Astronomy.com, Grunge and others say stars outnumber grains of sand on Earth, not the other way around.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoralillo Geyser in the region of El Loa.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out: the Atacama Desert is in northern Chile, is widely described as the driest non-polar desert, and has geysers. The best-known geyser field, El Tatio, is in El Loa Province in the Antofagasta Region. However, I found no source that mentions a 'Totoralillo Geyser.' The places called Totoralillo that I did find are a beach resort in Coquimbo and an industrial port (Punta Totoralillo), not geothermal sites in El Loa. The specific geyser named in the claim may not exist, but no source directly contradicts it, so the claim cannot be verified.

text: The colony of Eskipoo is not found anywhere within the main group of Eskipoo Mix's but was introduced using European mantled as adults to stock a fur farm.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches show the Eskipoo (also spelled Eskapoo) is a designer companion dog, a cross between the American Eskimo Dog and the Poodle. None of the sources mention a 'colony' of Eskipoo, adult animals called 'European mantled', or any link to a fur farm. The claim seems to borrow wording from some account of a fur-farm animal population, and its premise conflicts with what is documented about this dog's origin as a hybrid pet breed.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it can be liquefied at a relatively low temperature, around -56°C, when kept under pressure.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no CO2-specific "Kundsen effect." The closest real term, the Knudsen effect, describes gas transport (diffusion and thermal conductivity) in rarefied gases and tiny pores, and has nothing to do with liquefying CO2. The -56°C figure is CO2's triple point (-56.6°C at about 5.1 atm), which is ordinary phase behaviour, not a unique named effect. Liquid CO2 can also exist anywhere between the triple point and the critical point (31.1°C), not only at around -56°C.

text: The brightest planet in the sky, Venus, is extremely difficult to observe during the day due to its proximity to the Sun and extremely thick atmosphere, but it is visible with specialized techniques or early in the morning.
label: contradicted
reason: Sky & Telescope and Fourmilab both say Venus can be seen with the naked eye in broad daylight when the sky is clear and the planet is well away from the Sun. Sky & Telescope calls it "startlingly easy to see" once you find it. Venus's thick atmosphere is not what makes it hard to observe. Its cloud cover reflects sunlight, which is why Venus is so bright. The claim gets both the difficulty and its cause wrong, even though Venus is indeed the brightest planet and can be seen in the early morning.

text: There are more bacteria cells in the human body than human cells, with estimates suggesting that for every cell in the human body, there are around 10 bacterial cells.
label: contradicted
reason: The 10:1 figure is outdated. Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016) found that both numbers behind that ratio came from rough estimates made decades ago. Their revised estimate is about 3.9×10^13 bacteria and 3.7×10^13 human cells in a standard adult male. That puts the ratio at around 1.3:1, so the two counts are roughly equal. The claim says there are about 10 bacterial cells for every human cell, which this research contradicts. The first part, that bacteria slightly outnumber human cells, is still roughly true, but the 10:1 ratio is not.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point reached as high as 115.6 degrees Fahrenheit (46.4 degrees Celsius).
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records says the highest recorded human body temperature was 46.5°C (115.7°F). It belonged to Willie Jones, who was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta with heatstroke on 10 July 1980. A search for 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' found no person by that name with any temperature record. The claim gives the wrong person, and its figure of 115.6°F (46.4°C) also differs from the recorded value.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is so strong in some New Zealand caves that it mimics a starry night sky.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say that Arachnocampa luminosa glowworms in New Zealand caves such as Waitomo light up cave ceilings so that they look like a starry night sky. One source says they 'light up the cave ceiling like a starry night sky.' Another, drawing on KQED's Deep Look series, says the larvae 'create a starry night sky' deep inside the caves. Both are secondary sites rather than scientific sources, but they agree with each other and with how the caves are widely described.

text: Gravitational forces between objects too small to see can cause significant changes in the universe, such as the gravitational wave ripples that distort space-time, helping scientists understand the universe's earliest moments.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two separate topics. In 2021, physicists measured the tiny gravitational pull between two gold spheres about 2 mm across (ScienceDaily, Nature). Those reports present it as a precision lab measurement that may help study gravity at small scales and its link to quantum physics. They do not say such forces cause major changes in the universe or produce gravitational waves. LIGO explains the opposite: any accelerating object technically makes gravitational waves, but the masses of small, Earth-scale objects are far too small to make waves big enough to detect. Detectable waves come from huge, distant astronomical events. The waves linked to the early universe come from quantum fluctuations during inflation, not from gravity between tiny objects. So the claim's central link is contradicted.

text: Gallinules, a type of bird, have the unique characteristic of being able to tip their feet forward in the direction of movement as they walk.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms or disproves this claim. Trusted sources (Wikipedia, All About Birds, Audubon, NH PBS NatureWorks) describe gallinules' very long toes, which spread their weight so they can walk on floating plants like lily pads. They also mention a high-stepping, chicken-like walk, head-bobbing while swimming and tail-flicking. None of them says gallinules tip their feet forward in the direction they're moving, or that this trait is unique to them. Since the main part of the claim can't be verified, it is inconclusive.

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of letters or figures to identify a time, used on goods or documents.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the date wrong. The OED puts the earliest known use of the noun 'time stamp' in the 1850s, and Merriam-Webster gives 1855. Dictionary.com says it was first recorded in 1890–95. All of these are the mid-to-late 19th century, not the early 19th century. The original meaning is also off: Merriam-Webster's first sense, the one dated to 1855, is a stamping device for recording the date and time on a document, not a mark used on goods.

text: TheSusanooa deep sea creature can live up to 5,000 years in the ocean, making it one of the longest-lived animals on Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source describing a deep-sea creature called "Susanooa." Searches for the name, and for it alongside "5,000 years" and "deep sea creature," only returned pages about Susanoo, the Shinto god of the sea and storms, and fictional characters from games and anime. Because I couldn't identify the creature at all, I couldn't confirm or rule out the 5,000-year lifespan or the claim that it is one of the longest-lived animals.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some estimates suggesting as many as 2 trillion stars exist in the observable universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up the numbers. The 2016 Hubble-based estimate of about 2 trillion refers to galaxies in the observable universe, not stars. With the Milky Way alone holding hundreds of billions of stars, the estimated total for the observable universe is in the sextillions (around 10^22–10^24), far more than 2 trillion. The idea that there are more stars than galaxies "can possibly contain" is also unfounded, since all those stars are counted as being inside galaxies.

text: The highest recorded human body temperature in space is of TessHB who had a body temperature of 41.3°C (106.3°F) in August 2021 during a Virgin Galactic suborbital spaceflight.
label: contradicted
reason: No credible source records a person called "TessHB" or a 41.3°C body temperature during a spaceflight. The claim's key details also conflict with the known record. Virgin Galactic's only crewed spaceflight in 2021 was Unity 22 on 11 July 2021. Its crew were David Mackay, Michael Masucci, Sirisha Bandla, Colin Bennett, Beth Moses and Richard Branson, so there was no Virgin Galactic flight in August 2021 and no crew member named TessHB. Studies of astronaut body temperature (Stahn et al., reported by Space.com and ScienceDaily) found that core temperatures reached about 40°C (104°F) during exercise on the ISS, not a record of 41.3°C on a suborbital flight. The claim appears to be fabricated.

text: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with approximately 96.5% of that being ocean water.
label: supported
reason: The USGS Water Science School says about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water. The Canada WaterPortal gives the same figures, citing USGS. One nuance: 96.5% is the oceans' share of all Earth's water by volume, not a share of the water-covered surface area. Read as the oceans' share of Earth's water, the claim matches what the sources say.

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the most common household insects, found in many parts of the United States, and can be identified by their dark brown or black color and distinctive rectangular head shape.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that an insect called the "Butterfly Pavement Ant" exists. A search for that exact name returned only pages about the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium immigrans/caespitum), so the claim's subject has no clear referent. Some details would fit the ordinary pavement ant: it is a common household ant in many US regions and is dark brown to black. However, the sources identify it by the parallel grooves on its head and thorax, not by a "distinctive rectangular head shape." I couldn't confirm that detail, and the name itself doesn't match any known species.

text: The ancient Egyptians were skilled astronomers who accurately calculated the circumference of the Earth to be approximately 40,000 kilometers, which is remarkably close to the actual circumference of 40,075 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gives the credit to the wrong people. Reliable sources (EBSCO, CUNY Hunter, ABC) say the Earth's circumference was first estimated around 240 BC by Eratosthenes. He was a Greek scholar working as librarian in Alexandria, which was then Greek-ruled Ptolemaic Egypt. The calculation is not credited to native ancient Egyptian astronomers. The '40,000 km' figure is also uncertain, since it depends on how long a stadion was, which is unknown. Ancient Egyptians did practice astronomy, but the claim that they calculated the Earth's circumference is wrong.

text: The einzige weisse deutscher spitz, also known as the white German Spitz, has been a symbol of Russia since Peter the Great adopted it in 1705.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying the white German Spitz is a symbol of Russia or that Peter the Great adopted it in 1705. Sources on the breed, including Wikipedia, the AKC and breed histories, describe the German Spitz as an old Central European dog from Germany and don't mention Russia. The year 1705 does matter for Peter the Great, but for another reason: in 1705 he adopted the white, blue and red tricolour as the flag for Russian vessels. This suggests the claim mixes up the flag with the dog, but no source directly says the dog was never a Russian symbol. The key part of the claim therefore can't be confirmed or directly refuted.

text: The longest known storm on Earth is a tempest that has been raging in the Deer Island area of the North Atlantic Ocean for at least 120 years with no sign of abating.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of any storm that has lasted for over a century near Deer Island or anywhere else in the North Atlantic. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) recognizes Tropical Cyclone Freddy (2023) as the longest-lasting tropical cyclone on record, at 36 days. The previous record holder, Hurricane John (1994), lasted about 30–31 days. Earth's storm records are measured in days or weeks, not 120 years. The claim looks like a garbled version of the fact about Jupiter's Great Red Spot, a storm that has lasted for centuries.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history until the 16th century, an idea shared across the globe in Africa, Asia, the Americas, and in Europe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says people didn't wear pants until around the 16th century. Archaeologists found trousers in China's Yanghai Tombs dating to the 13th–10th century BCE, about 3,000 years ago. Trousers were also worn in antiquity by Persians, Scythians and Gauls, among others, so pants are far older than the 16th century. That date is wrong, and the rest of the claim, including the global framing, has no credible support.

text: The最高の人里.preference aspect of honeybees is communicated through complex dance movements, which help the colony determine the direction and distance of food sources.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify the claim as a whole. The garbled phrase "最高の人里.preference aspect" (Japanese for roughly "best village/human settlement", followed by ".preference") doesn't refer to any identifiable trait of honeybees. The rest of the claim is well supported: sources such as ScienceDirect and recent research papers confirm that the waggle dance tells other bees the distance and direction of food sources. But because the subject of the claim has no clear meaning, there is nothing to check it against.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to be permanently suspended in mid-air by NASA scientists through use of aerial photography because of very little to no water currents present in the center of the hole.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no record of anything called a "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole. They also found no NASA study using aerial photography that estimated an object to be permanently suspended there. Trustworthy sources such as Wikipedia, PADI and the Oceanic Society describe the Great Blue Hole as a large marine sinkhole off Belize, about 124 m (407 ft) deep. That supports only the background detail. None of these sources mentions the "Forever Float," the NASA estimate, or the idea that weak currents keep something suspended. The phrase "suspended in mid-air" is also self-contradictory for an underwater site. The claim looks fabricated, but no source directly refutes it, so it cannot be verified either way.
