text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees covering approximately 30% of the planet's land area.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up every part of the claim. The widely cited Crowther et al. (2015) study estimates about 3 trillion trees on Earth, and the Milky Way is estimated to hold roughly 100–400 billion stars, so there are more trees than stars. The FAO reports that forests cover 31% of the world's land area, which matches the claim's 'approximately 30%'. One caveat: that 31% figure is for forest area, which the claim loosely describes as the area 'covered' by trees.

text: The length of a cricket season, which varies by location, can be divided into two parts: an initial section where a bat is only used for scoring, called the "matcher itself" and then follows a run-off phase.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Only one part of the claim checks out. Wikipedia's 'Cricket season' article and cricket-season guides confirm that seasons vary by place. They are timed to each country's driest months, for example April–September in England and roughly October–March in Australia. However, no source I found describes a season split into an opening section 'where a bat is only used for scoring,' called the 'matcher itself,' followed by a 'run-off phase.' These terms don't appear to be real cricket terminology. I also found no source that directly refutes them, so the claim can't be verified either way.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the largest waterfall in the Asia-Pacific region, called Liwakun, but a better and more known fact is that the highest waterfall in the Asia-Pacific region is located in Kapuas Hulu Regency, and it's name is Kuming waterfall
label: contradicted
reason: This claim looks made up. 'Theona' is not an Indonesian province, and I found no evidence of a waterfall called 'Liwakun'. Searches for 'Kuming waterfall' in Kapuas Hulu Regency (West Kalimantan) also returned nothing. A post about Kapuas Hulu tourism names Sarai Biang as the regency's highest waterfall, not Kuming. Well-documented falls such as Tumpak Sewu are only about 120 m tall, while New Zealand's Sutherland Falls (about 580 m) is much taller. So neither waterfall could be the largest or highest in the Asia-Pacific region.

text: Sweden held the top spot in the UN's Human Development Index (HDI) from 1995 to 2001, and again from 2007 to the present day.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Sweden has not held the top spot in the UN Human Development Index for long periods. Norway was ranked first in 2016 (Nations Online, based on UNDP data), and in the 2021/22 UNDP report Switzerland was first. More generally, Canada and Norway led in the 1990s and early 2000s, Norway led for most years after that, and Switzerland has led recently. That rules out Sweden being first from 2007 to the present, and it was not first from 1995 to 2001 either.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious river that appears to bubble up from nowhere in the Peruvian jungle, with scientists still unable to determine the source of its unusual geology.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says scientists still can't explain where the river comes from or why it's so hot, and that part is wrong. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo ran the first scientific studies of the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru. He and his colleagues concluded that the heat comes from a fault-led hydrothermal system, not a volcano. Rainwater seeps deep underground through cracks, is heated by the Earth's natural heat, and rises back up along fault lines. The river's location in the Peruvian Amazon and its unusual, much-studied nature are accurate, but the part about scientists being unable to find its source is not.

text: There are over 100 million trees in New York City's Metropolis, and in Tokyo, they have many trees as well, including the Japanese metropolis, there were over 2 million trees within a city.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about New York City. A USDA Forest Service study of the city's urban forest puts the total at about 7.0 million trees (6,977,000), counting all woody plants. That is nowhere near 100 million. Since that part of the claim is false, the claim as a whole is contradicted, whatever the truth of the Tokyo figure.

text: The position of the constellation Orion changes over time due to the Earth's rotation and the procession of the equinoxes, but its appearance remains relatively consistent in the night sky.
label: supported
reason: My searches turned up only general material on precession, and I hit the search limit before finding a source about Orion itself. The verdict therefore rests on well-established astronomy. Earth's daily rotation makes Orion rise in the east and set in the west. Over thousands of years, precession of the equinoxes (spelled 'procession' in the claim) shifts the equinox points and changes where Orion sits in the sky. Wikipedia's Orion article and the partly loaded astronomers.fandom.com page both describe this. Because Orion's stars are very far away, their proper motions are tiny, so the constellation keeps its recognizable shape over human timescales. Nothing I found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The colorful and iconic bottle cap enamel company in the U.S, Anvil Brand, was originally a  non-profit division of the Child Welfare Association formed to fight tuberculosis.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe Anvil Brand in the U.S. as a work-clothing label, not a bottle-cap enamel company. A North Carolina State Historic Preservation Office document says Anvil Brand grew out of the High Point Overall Company, founded in 1899, which made sturdy work clothes. Trademark records also show that the High Point Overall Company of High Point, NC owned the 'Anvil Brand' mark, with first use dated 1910. The National Child Welfare Association did run anti-tuberculosis campaigns, but no source links it to Anvil Brand. A separate Anvil Brand Shoe Co. in Illinois makes horseshoes and is also unrelated. The claim's origin story conflicts with the documented history.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Lost River," is a mysterious river in the Amazon rainforest that remains unaccounted for by traditional maps and has been the subject of much scientific speculation.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Forbes and Discover Wildlife identify the Boiling River of the Amazon as the Shanay-timpishka in Peru. They give its other names as La Bomba and Río Hirviente, and none calls it the "Lost River." The river is also not unaccounted for. It has a known location: a roughly 6.4–9 km tributary of the Pachitea River in the Mayantuyacu area of central Peru. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo has studied it since 2011 and explained its heat as coming from fault-fed geothermal water. The claim that it is unmapped and still a mystery, and that it is called the "Lost River," is therefore not accurate.

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of 33 US RB-24 patrol planes flying on patrol intercepted 22 Japanese and laid mines near the Isle of Taiwan and sighting this, on 26 March 1940 Taiwanese guerrillas attacked the Japanese jail and had liberated over 4300 Chinese prisoners.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing in the searches mentions a 'Miracle March' of 1940, a guerrilla raid on a Japanese jail in Taiwan on 26 March 1940, or the release of 4,300 Chinese prisoners. Known facts also make the claim impossible. The B-24 Liberator first flew as a single prototype on 29 December 1939, so a squadron of 33 'RB-24' patrol planes could not have existed by March 1940. The US was also not at war with Japan until December 1941, so US patrol planes would not have been intercepting Japanese forces off Taiwan in 1940. The claim appears to be fabricated.

text: The baku is a type of fox found in East Asia, which is known for its unique ability to survive the extreme cold of its native regions by producing a thick layer of fur called "qiviut" that keeps it warm and acts as insulation.
label: contradicted
reason: The baku is not a fox. In Japanese and Chinese folklore it is a mythical creature that eats nightmares and is said to ward off evil, and 'baku' is also the Japanese word for the tapir. 'Qiviut' is the word for the soft underwool of the musk ox, not the fur of any fox or of the baku. So the claim gets the animal type and the fur term wrong.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some scientists estimating that there could be as many as 100 sextillion stars in total.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half is roughly right: published estimates of the total number of stars run from about 10^22 to 10^24, so '100 sextillion' (10^23) is within that range. The first half is wrong. Astronomers get the total star count by multiplying the number of galaxies by the average number of stars per galaxy, for example about 100 billion in the Milky Way. That method puts the stars inside galaxies, not beyond what galaxies can hold. Also, the latest galaxy estimates are far above 100 billion, at roughly 2 trillion or more (Astronomy.com, Big Think). No reliable source says the universe has more stars than its galaxies can contain.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting that the brain contains over 85 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 86 billion neurons in the human brain is right, so the 'over 85 billion' part checks out. The comparison is wrong, though. Nature Scitable's Brain Metrics blog (Bradley Voytek) gives the latest estimate for stars in the Milky Way as roughly 200 to 400 billion. That is far more than 86 billion, so the brain has fewer neurons than the galaxy has stars, not more. The popular comparison is a myth, and only synapses (about 100 trillion) outnumber the stars.

text: Gas giants like Jupiter have so many moons that the gravitational pull and collisions between them can sometimes cause a moon to break apart and re-form into new moonlets.
label: supported
reason: I'm calling this supported, though some of its wording is loose. A peer-reviewed paper by Nesvorný et al. (SwRI / the Astronomical Journal) proposes that collisions between Jupiter's irregular moons may have shattered parent bodies. It finds that the Ananke and Carme families could have formed this way. A Sky & Telescope article and a piece in The Conversation also say Jupiter's irregular moons come in families made of fragments from larger captured bodies, and that some of those bodies broke apart more recently. These fragments now orbit as smaller moons (moonlets). This backs the core idea that collisions between moons can break one apart and leave new moonlets. The sources don't directly say that having 'so many moons' causes these events, or that fragments 're-form' rather than simply staying separate. They also point to collisions, not gravitational pull, as the cause of the breakups.

text: Rongo is the only native Polynesian language whose original script has survived, consisting of 39 symbols and dating back to around the 13th century.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim seems to mix up rongorongo, the undeciphered glyph script of Easter Island (Rapa Nui), with a language called "Rongo". Rongorongo is a script, not a language. Reliable sources describe it as having more than 400 different glyphs across roughly 15,000 characters, not 39 symbols. The earliest radiocarbon date (wood from one tablet in Rome) points to the 15th century, not the 13th, and even that date is uncertain because the wood may have been old when it was carved. So the details about the symbol count and the date are contradicted.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the Sundance Film Festival, consisting only of a 79-second, black-and-white scene shot with a flip phone's camera.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any source saying a 2002 short called "Flicker" was accepted into Sundance, much less that it was the "smallest" film ever accepted. The only 2002 "Flicker" I found is a horror short by Canadian no-budget filmmaker Conall Pendergast. IMDb lists it as a direct-to-video release about 5 minutes long ("An old film reel holds deadly secrets"), not a 79-second scene. Other sources list it among his home-made shorts released on DVD and Blu-ray, with no mention of Sundance or of filming on a phone. A 2002 film shot with a flip phone's camera is also very unlikely, since camera phones that recorded video were barely available then. The phone-shot films linked to Sundance came much later, such as 'Tangerine' (2015, shot on iPhone 5s). The film's real length contradicts the claim, and nothing supports the rest of it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "River of Lost Souls," is a mysterious river in Peru where water is constantly boiling, but the exact cause remains unknown.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, it says the cause is unknown, but it has been explained. Wikipedia and other sources say the Shanay-timpishka is heated by geothermal water. Rainwater seeps underground, picks up heat as it goes deeper, and rises back up through fault zones. No volcano is involved. Second, it says the water is constantly boiling. Measured temperatures average about 86–95 °C, with a peak of 99.1 °C recorded in one hot spring, so the river is near boiling rather than boiling all the time. Also, the river's usual nickname is 'Boiling River of the Amazon'. No source here backs the name 'River of Lost Souls'.

text: The Andean condensed milk, a type of milk known to have originated in South America, can last for years without refrigeration due to the low water content and thanks to the addition of sugar, air, and packaging that causes a vacuum.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions an "Andean condensed milk" that originated in South America. Wikipedia lists the United States as condensed milk's place of origin, and other sources credit France (Nicolas Appert) and the US (Gail Borden). One source says condensed milk only became established in South America during colonization. Sweetened condensed milk does keep for a long time because of its low water content, added sugar and sealed canning, but the claim's South American origin is contradicted, and "adding air" is not part of how it is preserved.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, which occurs where the cold, dense water of the East Greenland Current flows down a slope in the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: My sources back every part of the claim. EarthSky says the world's largest waterfall is in the ocean beneath the Denmark Strait and calls it the Denmark Strait cataract. It describes cold, dense water dropping from about 600 m to about 3,000 m depth, with a flow 20 to 40 times that of the largest land waterfalls. Marine Insight also names it the Denmark Strait Cataract and says it is the largest waterfall by volume. It explains that the East Greenland Current carries cold, dense Arctic water south, and that this water sinks down the continental slope past warmer Irminger Sea water. One caveat: the sources trace the overflow water more broadly to the Nordic and Greenland Seas, but none of them conflicts with linking it to the East Greenland Current.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique mating system where they form monogamous pairs that can last for many years, and in some species, a pair can stay together throughout their entire lives.
label: supported
reason: I found several reliable sources that back the claim. Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan) and the Encyclopedia of Life both describe butterflyfishes as typically monogamous fish that form pairs. They say pairs in many species stay together for at least three years and that some butterflyfishes may pair for life. Wikipedia reports that some species, such as the longnose and oval butterflyfish, have stayed with the same partner for seven years or more. It also says the Hawaiian butterflyfish often pairs for life. Aquarium and animal-facts sites agree. Calling the system 'unique' is mild exaggeration, since other fish are monogamous too, but it doesn't contradict the facts.

text: 珠海塔 was the tallest structure in China during 1973 and before the Shanghai TV tower was completed in 1994.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is very unlikely to be true, but the search evidence only partly confirms that. My search for "Zhuhai Tower" returned a Skyscraper Center entry and a 330 m Zhuhai St. Regis Hotel & Office Tower completed in 2017. The results contained nothing about a Zhuhai tower existing in 1973, let alone being China's tallest structure. A source from my first search also says Shanghai's Oriental Pearl TV Tower was China's tallest structure when it was completed in 1994. Two further points come from my own knowledge and were not verified by search: Zhuhai was only a small county in 1973 and became a city in 1979, and the tallest structures in China just before 1994 were TV towers elsewhere, such as Tianjin's (415 m, 1991) and Beijing's (405 m, 1992). My searches hit a usage limit before I could directly confirm what "珠海塔" refers to.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is day and only see polarized light at night, which helps it detect the presence of other fish.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no source saying that danions see full color by day, see only polarized light at night, or use night-time polarization vision to detect other fish. The closest evidence is about zebrafish (Danio rerio). One study found zebrafish prefer different colors during the day and at night. Another (PNAS/PubMed) found that larval zebrafish become nearly blind at night. That casts doubt on the claim but doesn't directly test it, because it is about larvae and doesn't mention polarization. 'Danion' is also a loose name that can cover several genera (Danio, Devario, Danionella). With nothing directly confirming or refuting the claim, I can't verify it.

text: The entire human genome is encoded in a DNA molecule that is roughly 2 meters (6.6 feet) long when fully stretched out.
label: supported
reason: Biology textbook sources say that the DNA in a single human cell would be about 2 meters (roughly 6 feet) long if stretched end to end, which matches the claim's length. One detail is loose: a cell's DNA is not a single molecule but is split across 46 chromosomes, and the 2 m figure is their combined length in a diploid cell. That wording doesn't change the claim's main point, so the evidence supports it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and covers more than 40% of the Earth's circumference.
label: not_verifiable
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range. However, they put its length at "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Some other estimates of the full ridge system are larger (about 80,000 km), so the sources conflict on this detail. The claim that it "covers more than 40% of the Earth's circumference" is odd. Earth's circumference is about 40,075 km, so a ridge of about 65,000 km would be roughly 160% of it. That makes "more than 40%" technically true but misleading. No source makes this statement, so I couldn't verify it. The main claim is supported, but these details are disputed or unverified.

text: Olympic champion and amend 43rd U.S. President Jimmy Carter unwittingly grabbed onto and majoredly lifted Zbigniew Brzezinski while descending USS Nimitz Flight Deck, look: a life rings float maintenance steering cart ran away from him - though the action has been called "extremely
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is badly garbled, and parts of it are plainly false. Jimmy Carter was the 39th U.S. president (1977–1981), not the 43rd, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize, not an Olympic title. I found no reliable evidence that he lifted Zbigniew Brzezinski on the USS Nimitz flight deck to get out of the way of a runaway cart.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the Sundance Film Festival, consisting only of a 79-second, black-and-white shot of a light bulb turning on and off.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source for this claim. None of my searches turned up a 2002 short called "Flicker" that was accepted into Sundance, described as its "smallest" film, or made up of a 79-second black-and-white shot of a light bulb. The only 2002 "Flicker" I found is a 5-minute horror video directed by Conall Pendergast (IMDb), which doesn't match the description. Other films with that name are a 2008 Canadian documentary about the Dreamachine and a 2021 Sundance Collab challenge entry. A related film, Tony Conrad's "The Flicker" (1966), is made of flashing black and white frames, not a light bulb. I found nothing that confirms the claim, but nothing that clearly rules it out either.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate by biologists who assessed the global diversity of life.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is from Mora et al., published in PLOS Biology in August 2011, not a 2020 estimate. That study also estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species (give or take 1.3 million), not over 8.7 million plants and animals. It covered other eukaryotes such as fungi and protists as well. The date and the wording of the figure are both wrong.

text: The sentry plant, also known as the "pitcher plant," has a unique lower leaf that functions as a snap trap, quickly closing in just 0.1 seconds to capture insects for nutrition.
label: contradicted
reason: Pitcher plants catch insects with passive pitfall traps: prey slips on the slippery rim and walls and drowns in digestive fluid. They do not use a snap trap that closes in 0.1 seconds. That snap-trap description fits the Venus flytrap. Also, the name "sentry plant" or "sentry palm" refers to Howea belmoreana (the kentia palm), which isn't carnivorous at all.

text: Sweden has a bridge made from ice called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" that is built every winter and melts by spring, but there's also another Swedish unique ice road also known as "Ice Road" in the Abisko National Park in Lapland.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for either named attraction. Reliable sources describe the Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi as a hotel, not a bridge. It is rebuilt every winter from Torne River ice and melts back into the river. None of the sources mention an 'Ice Hotel Bridge.' Searches on Abisko National Park turned up hiking, skiing, frozen waterfalls and ice fishing, but no 'Ice Road.' Sweden's well-known ice roads are elsewhere, such as the Luleå archipelago. The claim looks garbled, but no source directly says these things don't exist, so I can't verify or refute it.

text: The colony of Eskipoo is not found anywhere within the main group of Eskipoos that are the result of a cross between an American Eskimo Dog and a Welsh Springer Spaniel.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Eskipoos come from crossing an American Eskimo Dog with a Welsh Springer Spaniel. PetGuide and other breed sources say the Eskipoo is a cross between an American Eskimo Dog and a Poodle, so that premise is wrong. The 'colony of Eskipoo' wording also makes no sense, because the Eskipoo is a designer dog breed, not a colony.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, as evidenced by the discovery of the PARAMARSO site in Ulster County which dates back to around 9,000 to 10,000 years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any record of a 'PARAMARSO site' in Ulster County or anywhere in the Catskills. Reliable sources also put the oldest known dwellings in North America far earlier and far from New York. Live Science reports a dwelling about 13,800 years old at Shéh' Xdaltth'í' in Alaska, and other reports point to a site in Texas about 14,000 years old. Both are much older than the 9,000 to 10,000 years the claim gives, so a New York site of that age could not be the oldest known dwelling.

text: The cheesiest pizza is made from Mozzarella and contains about 300 calories per slice with an 8-inch diameter pizza having a total of 32 slices making strength of 9600 calories.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Nutrition sources show an 8-inch pizza is usually cut into about 4 slices, not 32. One 8-inch pizza listing gives 4 slices at about 90 calories each, and an 8-inch cheese pizza from Mama Deluca's is listed at 390 calories for 3 slices. That puts a whole 8-inch pizza at a few hundred to roughly 1,000 calories, nowhere near 9,600. The 250–300 calories per slice figure applies to a slice of a large 14-inch pizza cut into 8, not to an 8-inch pizza. Nothing backs a 32-slice, 9,600-calorie 8-inch pizza, and the 'cheesiest pizza' part has no clear referent.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Tartarus Dorsa, located on Mars, which stretches for approximately 4,800 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts Tartarus Dorsa on Mars, but it is a region of bladed, penitente-like ridges on Pluto. NASA's New Horizons mission imaged it, as reported by NASA and the journal Nature. The search turned up nothing calling it the longest mountain range in the solar system or giving it a length of about 4,800 km.

text: Most frost is created through the nucleation of water vapor in the atmosphere, but black sand can actually lower the freezing point of water due to the high surface area of the tiny black particles, allowing frost to form more easily.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say frost forms by deposition: water vapor turns straight into ice on a surface that is colder than the dew point and below freezing. It does not come mainly from nucleation in the open atmosphere. I found no evidence that black sand lowers water's freezing point through its particles' surface area. The reasoning also fails on its own terms, because a lower freezing point would make ice and frost harder to form, not easier. Since the claim's description of how frost forms is contradicted and its causal mechanism is wrong, I've labeled it contradicted.

text: The ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy have one of the longest stalactites in the world, measuring over 100 feet in length.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any real place called the "ghiaccio stalactite caves" in Italy ("ghiaccio" is Italian for "ice"). Guinness World Records lists the longest free-hanging stalactite as 28 m (92 ft), in Gruta do Janelão in Minas Gerais, Brazil. Since that is the world record, no stalactite in Italy can be over 100 feet long, and the record isn't in Italy. Other sources name different contenders, such as Jeita Grotto in Lebanon at 8.2 m and Doolin Cave in Ireland at 7.3 m. All of these are far shorter than 100 feet, and none are in Italy.

text: The emotional support animal Sunny Boy, a Capybara, is often cited as the first emotional support animal in the United States, due to being certified by a New York psychologist in 2001.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions a capybara emotional support animal named Sunny Boy. Searches for "Sunny Boy" with capybara and emotional support animal only turned up plush toys, a three-legged dog, a Sesame Street dog, and a University of Washington mascot. None of the sources I found on emotional support animal history, such as EBSCO's overview and the Wikipedia article, mentions a first ESA certified by a New York psychologist in 2001. I also found nothing that directly disproves the story, so it can't be verified either way. It does look likely to be made up.

text: A flock of starlings is known for its unique ability to create the illusion of a single reflective surface, often referred to as a "mirage" or "boiling lake," by forming a flock in the shape of a hexagon and then flying in unison to create a cohesive visual effect.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe starling murmurations as fluid, constantly shifting formations, such as swirling blobs, teardrops, figure eights and columns. They explain the behaviour mainly as protection against predators through safety in numbers. None of the sources mention starlings forming hexagons or creating a single reflective surface, and none call the display a "mirage" or "boiling lake." The accepted name is "murmuration." Because these specific details conflict with how the phenomenon is documented, the claim appears to be invented.

text: A honeybee colony can perform complex calculations and make decisions as a single unit, often referred to as a "swarm intelligence," through distributed processing and communication within the colony.
label: supported
reason: Several trustworthy sources back the claim. Research on nest-site selection (arXiv papers, Physical Review E, Thomas Seeley's work at Cornell) shows that a honeybee swarm chooses a new home as a group. Scouts spread information through waggle dances, and stop signals add cross-inhibition, so the colony settles on one site without any single bee directing it. The literature calls this "swarm intelligence" and "swarm cognition" and describes the colony as a "superorganism" acting as one unit. The phrase "complex calculations" is a loose way to describe this distributed information processing, but none of the sources contradict it.

text: There are over 37,000 identified species of ants on Earth, but scientists estimate that the actual number could be as high as 20,000,000 different species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both numbers. Wikipedia says that more than 13,800 ant species have been described, out of an estimated total of about 22,000. That is far below 37,000 identified species, and nowhere near 20 million. The 20 million figure seems to be mixed up with estimates of how many individual ants exist (about 20 quadrillion), not how many species there are.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert, is located in Chile and is also home to several geysers, including the Totoralillo Geyser, the El Tatio Geyser, and the Kueu Kueu Geyser.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Parts of the claim check out. The Atacama in Chile is widely described as the driest non-polar desert, and El Tatio is a large geyser field in the Atacama region of northern Chile (Wikipedia; Wikidata). I found no reliable source that mentions a 'Totoralillo Geyser' or a 'Kueu Kueu Geyser'. Searches for both names turned up only unrelated pages about geysers in general. Chilean geyser sources name El Tatio, Puchuldiza and Alpehue, but not these two. Their absence suggests they may not exist, but it doesn't prove they don't. Because these parts can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A piece of quartz crystal, known as "Czech glass," discovered in 2008 in Denmark contains tiny bubbles that are completely free of nitrogen, even though the bubbles came from the air.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for a 2008 Danish find matching this description, and the evidence I did find conflicts with the claim. 'Czech glass' in this sense is moldavite, a tektite. Tektites are natural silica-rich glasses formed by impacts, not quartz crystals. A peer-reviewed review of gases in tektites (Žák et al., 2012, Meteoritics & Planetary Science) says their bubbles hold gas of terrestrial atmospheric composition. It reports that nitrogen-to-oxygen ratios in moldavite bubbles are roughly the same as in Earth's air, so the bubbles are not nitrogen-free. Nitrogen also turned up in the bubbles of other natural glasses it covers. I ran out of searches before I could look further, but these findings contradict the central claim.

text: The short-lived but highly notable element, Oganesson (Og), is the heaviest known element with an atomic number of 118 and hasDispose applications in Physical Studies within its field.
label: supported
reason: The sources confirm the main facts: oganesson (Og) is a short-lived synthetic element with atomic number 118 and is the heaviest known element. The last part of the claim is garbled ('hasDispose'). Read as 'it is used in physical studies within its field', it fits the sources, which say oganesson has no practical uses beyond basic scientific research. Because of the garbled wording, that last part is a judgment call.

text: There are over 388,000 languages in the world, although some sources estimate that almost 96% of the languages spoken worldwide are at risk of falling out of use.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about the number of languages. Ethnologue, the main authoritative catalogue, counts about 7,170 living languages, and other sources give around 7,100–7,159. That is nowhere near "over 388,000." Because this core figure is false, the claim is contradicted, whatever the accuracy of the endangerment percentage.

text: Over 70% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with approximately 96.5% of it being seawater and the remaining 3.5% being freshwater.
label: contradicted
reason: USGS says that about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water, so the first two figures are right. But the remaining 3.5% is not all freshwater. USGS and other sources put freshwater at only about 2.5% of Earth's water. The other roughly 1% is saline groundwater and saline lakes. That makes the claim's '3.5% freshwater' wrong.

text: The vibrant blue color of a butterfly's wings is not actually found in its body; instead, the butterflies produce pigments that create shimmering iridescence through microscopic crystals arranged on their wings.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets one part right: blue butterfly wings, such as the Blue Morpho's, contain no blue pigment. But it then says the butterflies "produce pigments" that create the iridescence, and that is wrong. Reliable sources (AskNature, Nature Scientific Reports, eLife) say the blue is structural color. It comes from nano-scale ridges and layers in the wing scales that reflect and diffract light, not from pigments.

text: The ocena in the Great Blue Hole of Belize is so clear that it can take divers up to 40 feet (12 meters) below the surface before they feel the slight pressure change from sea level, due to its remarkable visibility and slow water circulation.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources confirm the Great Blue Hole is very clear: ambergriscaye.com says the water is "motionless" and visibility often approaches 200 ft. But the idea that divers can descend up to 40 ft before feeling a pressure change is wrong. Diving sources say pressure is felt within the first few feet, and the change is proportionally strongest near the surface, so divers must equalize every 2–3 ft from the start. How clear the water is or how slowly it circulates has no effect on water pressure.

text: There is an underwater lake located beneath the surface of Visovac Island in Croatia, approximately 15 meters below ground level, also known as a lake or pool of land.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim, but nothing directly disproves it either. Reliable sources, including Krka National Park's official site, Croatian Wikipedia and travel guides, describe Visovac as a small island in Visovac Lake in Krka National Park. They mention its 15th-century Franciscan monastery and church. None of them mention an underwater or underground lake beneath the island, a depth of about 15 meters, or the name 'lake or pool of land.' Searches in English and Croatian ('podzemno jezero') turned up only underground lakes in other places. Since no source confirms or refutes the claimed lake, it cannot be verified.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious and inexplicable natural phenomenon where a river continuously boils and churns with no visible signs of volcanic activity or other geological forces.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka in Peru) has a known scientific explanation. Geothermal water rises along geologic fault zones and heats the stream, which makes it a non-volcanic hydrothermal feature. So it is not 'inexplicable,' and it is not free of 'other geological forces.' The river also doesn't boil continuously: its average temperature is about 86–95 °C, with a maximum of 99.1 °C measured in a hot spring that feeds it. Only the 'no volcanic activity' part is correct, since the nearest volcano is hundreds of kilometres away.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural geological phenomenon where a river appears to boil and foam, despite being thousands of miles from any known volcano.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources, including National Geographic, AccuWeather, Science Friday and Scholastic, put the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon about 700 km (roughly 400–430 miles) from the nearest volcano. That is hundreds of miles, not thousands. The sources do support the rest of the claim: it is a natural geothermal anomaly with near-boiling water and no nearby volcano. The 'thousands of miles' figure is wrong.

text: The characteristics of a solar eclipse, such as its path or frequency, can be predicted to the minute using mathematical calculations and observations of lunar and solar movements over several centuries.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Popular Science, Astronomy.com and Atlas Obscura, say solar eclipses can be predicted very precisely, often to the second. Their timing and paths can be mapped centuries ahead. These predictions rest on mathematical models (ephemerides that track lunar and solar positions, plus cycles like the Saros) built from long-term observations of how the Moon and Sun move. Being accurate to the second already covers the claim's 'to the minute,' and catalogs map eclipse paths and frequency over thousands of years.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater in the Denmark Strait, where the cold water from the Arctic Ocean sinks beneath the warmer water of the Norwegian Current.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including NOAA, agree that the world's largest waterfall by volume is the underwater Denmark Strait cataract. That part of the claim is correct. But NOAA says the frigid water comes from the Nordic Seas and sinks beneath warmer water from the Irminger Sea, which comes from the Irminger Current. It is not the Norwegian Current. Because the claim names the wrong warmer current, it is contradicted.

text: Cute: Penguins drink saltwater because they have a special gland above their eyes that filters out the salt, allowing them to stay hydrated.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back up the claim. Oceanwide Expeditions says penguins drink salty water and have a supraorbital gland near their eyes that takes salt out of the blood; the salt then drips out through the nose. Wikipedia explains that 'supraorbital' means the area just above the eye socket, and that this gland lets seabirds drink seawater. One detail: the gland removes salt from the blood after the bird drinks, not from the water itself. That is still consistent with the claim that the gland lets penguins drink saltwater and stay hydrated.

text: فيها شخص صيني Backpacker، يسمى ماو تسي تونغ، لديه سلسلة من المستشارين السياسيين في بانج كا هي تحت سلطته الكاملة.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I'm calling this inconclusive because the claim is garbled and can't be checked. "فيها" ("in it") doesn't say what it refers to. "Bang Ka He" isn't an identifiable place or body, and "Backpacker" doesn't fit anything known about Mao Zedong. The search results only give general facts about Mao and the people around him, such as Kang Sheng and Mao Yuanxin. None of them mention a backpacker, "Bang Ka He", or a group of political advisors there under his full authority.

text: The entire human genome is encoded in a DNA molecule that is roughly 2 meters (6.6 feet) long when fully stretched out, but it is condensed into the nucleus of a single cell.
label: supported
reason: A trusted biology textbook source (OpenOregon Pressbooks) says that the DNA molecules in one human cell, laid end to end, would be about 2 meters (roughly 6 feet) long. It also says this DNA has to be tightly packaged to fit inside the nucleus. That matches the claim's length and its point about condensation. One wording issue: the genome is spread across 46 chromosomes (separate DNA molecules), not one molecule. The figure the claim relies on is still correct, so this is supported.

text: пергамент, первоначально создан в древней Персии, получил свое название от пергамена, горной цоровыepergamon, возле города Эфес в современной Турции, которое было известно своим куском ткани сделанном из шкуры и
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up: reliable sources (Wikipedia, ABAA) confirm that the word "parchment" comes from the city of Pergamon (Latin pergamenum, French parchemin) in modern Turkey. The rest does not. Parchment was not created in ancient Persia. Ancient writers credit Pergamon, under Eumenes, with developing it as a papyrus substitute, and writing on skins was already in use in Egypt and elsewhere. Pergamon was also a city, not a "mountain" as the claim says. It lies near modern Bergama, well north of Ephesus rather than next to it (that distance is geographic knowledge, not something these sources state). The claim is also garbled and cut off at the end. Because the sources contradict key parts of it, the claim is contradicted.

text: The famous 'I love you' message in the famous Rosetta Stone is actually the Rosetta Stone's "Ptolemy loves" declaration on the Rosetta Stone isn't explicitly said as I love you however a stone from another site kindred native- Newport Symbols- more re correct all that was Rosetta actually
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is too garbled to check as a whole. It says the Rosetta Stone has a famous "I love you" message, but the stone is a priestly decree honouring Ptolemy V. The nearest wording in its translated Greek text is the royal title "Ptolemy... beloved of Ptah," not a declaration of love. The claim partly admits this ("isn't explicitly said as I love you"), but its other parts, such as "a stone from another site kindred native" and "Newport Symbols," don't point to anything identifiable. Because those parts can't be verified, the claim can't be called either supported or contradicted.

text: The�ước wich hypothesis suggests that life on Earth arose independently in multiple regions, which has sparked intense debate and research in the scientific community.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify this claim because it names a hypothesis whose name is garbled ("The�ước wich hypothesis"), so it's unclear which hypothesis is meant. Related ideas do exist. For example, a recent study reported on by ScienceAlert suggests that bacteria and archaea may have arisen separately. But I found no hypothesis by this name, and no source linking a named hypothesis to the idea that life began independently in multiple regions and sparked intense debate.

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of 33 US RB-24 patrol planes flying on patrol intercepted 269 enemy planes, downing 56 planes and destroying 5 industrial targets to help Burma defeat the Japanese.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of any "Miracle March of 1940" involving US RB-24 patrol planes in Burma. The timeline also rules it out. According to Wikipedia, Japan invaded Burma from 14 December 1941 to 28 May 1942 and won. So no Japanese forces were fighting in Burma in 1940, the US was not yet at war, and Burma did not defeat the Japanese. The claim's numbers (33 planes, 269 intercepted, 56 downed) appear to be made up.

text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space, although this is a common myth and has been largely debunked, with the wall being only about 30 feet wide and blending in with the surrounding terrain.
label: supported
reason: The sentence is awkwardly worded: it starts by saying the wall is visible from space, then calls that idea a myth. Read as a whole, it says the visibility claim is a debunked myth, and the sources back that. Travel China Guide says the myth was disproved by theoretical analysis and by what astronauts reported, including China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei. NBC News and Al Jazeera also cover the debunking. Sources say the wall is narrow: 15–30 feet wide, or about 13–16 feet on average. That makes 'about 30 feet' the upper end of the range rather than a typical width, but it is still roughly consistent. The sources also say the wall's materials blend in with the surrounding terrain. If the opening words were taken literally as saying the wall can be seen, that part would be contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs along the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: NOAA, WHOI, WorldAtlas and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as Earth's longest mountain range and say it runs along the seafloor, with about 90% of it underwater. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). One caveat on wording: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" it. The figure is still essentially the same, so the claim holds overall.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and bubble as if it's heated, has been studied and documented by scientists since its discovery in 2011.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up: geoscientist Andrés Ruzo first visited the river in 2011 and has studied it scientifically since then. The claim falls apart on the river's 'discovery in 2011.' ScienceAlert says plainly that Ruzo 'obviously wasn't the first to discover the river.' Its Indigenous name, Shanay-timpishka, and local communities who have revered it for centuries show it was already well known. National Geographic adds that oil companies in the area knew about the river earlier and played it down. One less reliable site does say Ruzo 'discovered' it, but more trustworthy sources contradict that. A smaller problem is the phrase 'as if it's heated': the water really is heated, by geothermal sources, to about 86°C on average.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly large atomic diameter of approximately 146 picometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia lists oganesson's predicted atomic radius as 152 pm and its covalent radius as 157 pm. So its diameter would be about 300 pm, not 146 pm. A radius is half a diameter, so the claim's figure is far too small whichever measure is meant. Oganesson is also a group-18 noble gas below radon, not a 'helium-like' species. It has the highest atomic number and mass of any known element, but that does not make it the atom with the largest size: alkali metals such as caesium and francium are usually cited as the largest atoms by radius. The key numerical and descriptive details are therefore contradicted.

text: Mitosis, the process by which cells divide, is so precise that the DNA of the resulting cells is identical to that of the parent cell, including the exact number of chromosomes.
label: supported
reason: Biology teaching sources say mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number and the same genetic information as the parent cell. During mitosis, sister chromatids separate and are divided equally between the two new cells. One caveat: the sources assume that no mutations or division errors occur. Errors such as aneuploidy, where a cell ends up with the wrong number of chromosomes, are rare but do happen. The claim matches the standard textbook description, so I rated it supported.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as "El Estero del Agua o del Diablo," is a mysterious and isolated river in Peru with a unique temperature that remains between 82°C and 88°C year-round, baffling scientists with its origin.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources agree the Shanay-Timpishka (Boiling River) is in the Peruvian Amazon and was considered mysterious because it is about 700 km from the nearest volcano. The temperature claim doesn't hold up. The water doesn't stay between 82°C and 88°C. Andrés Ruzo reported an average of about 86°C, but the temperature changes along the river: it starts as a cold stream, some stretches are around 80°C, and others reach about 94–97°C. Other sources give a range of roughly 45°C to nearly 100°C. The heat is also not an unexplained mystery anymore: it is attributed to geothermal (non-volcanic hydrothermal) water rising along a fault. I couldn't find any source for the name "El Estero del Agua o del Diablo"; the names that do appear are Río Hirviente, La Bomba and Shanay-Timpishka.

text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space, but this is a common myth: it is only about 30 feet wide and blends in with the surrounding terrain, making it barely perceptible from low Earth orbit.
label: supported
reason: Despite the awkward wording, the claim's point is that seeing the Great Wall from space is a myth, and reliable sources back this up. Scientific American says reports of astronauts seeing it are "wildly exaggerated." It explains that from low Earth orbit (about 400 km up) the wall would look extremely thin, roughly 0.1 arcminute wide. It also says the wall's stone doesn't contrast well with the terrain around it, so it is barely perceptible at best. The 'about 30 feet wide' figure fits commonly cited widths of roughly 15–30 ft (I didn't check this against a separate source). Note that this source says it is generally not visible, which is a bit stronger than 'barely perceptible.'

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point spiked to 116.7°F (46.5°C) without any apparent cause.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records credits the highest recorded human body temperature, 46.5°C (115.7°F), to Willie Jones. He was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta on 10 July 1980 with heatstroke. Several other sources say the same. The claim is wrong in three ways: it names 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' instead of Jones, it gives 116.7°F instead of 115.7°F, and it says there was no apparent cause when the cause was heatstroke. A search for 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' turned up no relevant results.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of Vilcabamba," is a mysterious river in Peru that boils due to the presence of geothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a real river in Peru, and sources say geothermal processes heat it. However, sources give its other name as Shanay-timpishka, not the "Boiling River of Vilcabamba." It is near Mayantuyacu and Santuario Huishtín in the Pachitea River basin (Huánuco region), not in Vilcabamba, which is in Cusco. No source uses the Vilcabamba name, so that part of the claim appears to be made up. Also, the water is near-boiling rather than literally boiling.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit that causes it to be closer to the sun at its perihelion (87.97 million kilometers) and farther away at its aphelion (46.00 million kilometers).
label: contradicted
reason: Mercury is the smallest planet and does have a highly eccentric orbit, but the distances in the claim are wrong. Its perihelion (closest point to the Sun) is about 46.00 million km, and its aphelion (farthest point) is about 69.82 million km. The claim puts perihelion at 87.97 million km and aphelion at 46.00 million km. That reverses the order, and 87.97 is actually Mercury's orbital period in days, not a distance. The claim also contradicts itself, since perihelion cannot be farther from the Sun than aphelion.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in the Australian state of Tasmania, is considered one of the deepest waterfalls in Australia, with a height of around 650 meters (2,133 feet) cascading through the Hartz Mountains National Park.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is not a waterfall. Wikipedia and Wikidata both describe it as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands Council area, with a population of nil in the 2016 census and an elevation of about 667 m above sea level. It is known as the site of the Clark Dam on the Derwent River. It is not in Hartz Mountains National Park, which is in southern Tasmania, and nothing describes it as a 650 m waterfall.

text: Cultural events and celebrations in Japan wouldn't be fully appreciated without their vibrant seasonal undertone because their lifecycle of festivals and events roughly parallels the climate; it pans out from the well-known and months-long cherry blossom 'Hanami,' in early spring.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim calls Hanami a "months-long" event, and that part is wrong. Wikipedia describes Hanami as enjoying the "transient beauty" of the blossoms and says they "only last a week or two" in any given place. The cherry blossom front does move across Japan from late March to early May (and January in Okinawa), so the national season covers several weeks. But Hanami is known for being brief, not for lasting months. The broader point, that Japan's festivals follow the seasons and that Hanami in early spring is well known, is reasonable but mostly subjective.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is underwater, but is unable to see colors above water due to its lack of cone cells necessary for processing long-wavelength light.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-studied danion, the zebrafish (Danio rerio), has four kinds of cone cells: red (long-wavelength), green, blue and UV. That makes it tetrachromatic. Because it does have red cones that respond to long-wavelength light, the claim's reason for why it couldn't see colour above water is false. I found no evidence that danios lose colour vision out of the water.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where the river's water not only remains warm year-round but also flows uphill, a mystery that scientists are still working to unravel.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as BBC Wildlife/Discover Wildlife and Atlas Obscura describe the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru as a stream whose water gets hot, up to about 94°C. Scientists, including geothermal researcher Andrés Ruzo, have explained the heat: water is warmed deep underground by the Earth's geothermal gradient and comes back up through hot springs fed by geological faults. None of the sources say the river flows uphill. That part of the claim is made up, and the claim's framing of the river as a mystery scientists are still trying to solve is also wrong, since the main explanation is already known.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the mid-ocean ridge system, spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through all the world's oceans.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia says the global mid-ocean ridge system is "part of every ocean" and is the longest mountain range in the world. It gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the whole ridge system as about 80,000 km, which fits the claim of "over 65,000 km." NOAA Ocean Exploration also calls it the longest mountain range on Earth and says it winds between the continents around the globe. One caveat: NOAA gives the length as "nearly 65,000 km," so whether it counts as "over" 65,000 km depends on which figure you use. Other sources put it at about 60,000 km. Even so, the main points of the claim match the sources.

text: Rivers account for approximately 20% of the Earth's surface despite only occupying a mere 0.08% of the Earth's volume.
label: contradicted
reason: Satellite mapping by Allen and Pavelsky (Science, 2018) found that rivers and streams cover about 773,000 km². That is just over half a percent of Earth's non-glaciated land surface, and far less of Earth's total surface. It is nowhere near 20%. No trustworthy source supports the 20% figure, so the claim is wrong.

text: The Human Deep Brain Stimulation has the ability to clump proteins that are associated with neurological diseases such as Parkinson's and has thus it been employed by scientists as an experimental therapy.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both what DBS does and why it is used wrong. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a surgical treatment that works by sending electrical signals to brain circuits. Reliable sources (PMC/NCBI, Nature Communications) describe it as an established, effective therapy for Parkinson's disease, not an experimental one. Nothing says it is used because it can clump disease-related proteins. One 2025 autopsy study did find abnormal tau and TDP-43 protein deposits near the tips of the electrodes. That was a side effect of the implant, not the reason DBS is used as a treatment.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the Earth's surface.
label: supported
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA's Ocean Service puts its length at 40,389 miles, which is more than 40,000 miles. NOAA Ocean Exploration gives the figure as "nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)." Wikipedia and WHOI say about 65,000 km, and other sources say more than 65,000 km. The wording differs slightly, since "over" versus "nearly" 65,000 km is a rounding difference. The claim's figures still match reliable sources: about 65,000 km and over 40,000 miles.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the world's largest living structure, the coral reef known as the Raja Ampat, which attracts over 1,500 species of fish and hundreds of other marine species.
label: contradicted
reason: Indonesia has no province called "Theona". Raja Ampat is an archipelago off the western end of New Guinea, in West Papua (now Southwest Papua province), according to the NCBI and bioRxiv papers and dive sources. Raja Ampat also isn't a single coral reef or the world's largest living structure. That title is widely given to Australia's Great Barrier Reef. Raja Ampat is known instead as the most species-rich reef area, with roughly 1,500+ reef fish species, so the fish figure is about right. But the province name and the 'largest living structure' claim are both wrong.

text: Approximately 71% of the world's surface is covered by water, with about 96.5% of it being the oceans.
label: supported
reason: The USGS says that about 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5 percent of all Earth's water. Several other sources repeat the same figures. The claim's phrase "96.5% of it" reads naturally as 96.5% of the world's water, which matches the USGS wording.

text: The planet Venus rotates in the opposite direction to its orbit around the sun, a phenomenon known as a retrograde rotation, which is unique among the eight planets in our solar system.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus does have retrograde rotation, meaning it spins in the opposite direction to its orbit. But it is not the only planet that does. Sources say Venus and Uranus both rotate retrograde, so the claim that this is unique to Venus among the eight planets is wrong.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that when animals die and fall into the water, their bodies are rapidly preserved and can take on a distinctive, long-lasting orange color.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out, but I found no support for the orange-color part. Lake Natron in Tanzania is a highly alkaline soda lake with a pH that can reach about 10.5. Animals that die there are preserved as calcified, stone-like mummies, and Nick Brandt's photographs made this widely known. However, the sources say the red or orange color belongs to the lake water, caused by salt-loving microorganisms and cyanobacteria. They describe the dead animals as calcified or turned to 'stone', not as turning orange. No source explicitly states the bodies' color either way, so the orange detail is unverified and appears to confuse the water's color with the remains.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature at one point spiked to 116.7°F (46.5°C), although treatments helped nurse her back to normal.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records lists the highest recorded human body temperature as 46.5°C, in Willie Jones (a man from the USA) during heatstroke in Atlanta in 1980. Other sources give the same figure as 115.7°F, not 116.7°F as the claim says. My searches found no record of anyone named 'Iwanowa-Danagumma,' so the claim gets both the person and the Fahrenheit figure wrong.

text: The Beehive mailbox, also known as the Pukekohe Post Office, located in Pukekohe, New Zealand, is considered the only example of a fully functioning post office built entirely out of airplanes.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence for any "Beehive mailbox" or for a post office anywhere built from airplanes. Library records describe the Pukekohe Post Office as an ordinary public building. It opened in King Street in 1909, and a new building in Hall Street opened on 30 September 1966. The records mention no aircraft. The name "Beehive" in New Zealand normally refers to the Parliament building in Wellington, not to anything in Pukekohe. The claim appears to be made up, and the records of a normal post office building contradict it. They don't explicitly rule out aircraft parts, but nothing supports the claim.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and isolated river in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest, is thought to be a result of a geothermal vent that heats the water, creating temperatures that are too hot for boats to navigate.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm part of the claim. The Shanay-Timpishka, known as the Boiling River, is in the Peruvian Amazon and is heated geothermally. Water rises along a fault system, with no volcano nearby. The river averages about 86°C and is hot enough to kill animals that fall in. However, no source I found says the river is 'too hot for boats to navigate.' Sources describe it in terms of the danger to animals and people, not boats, so that part of the claim cannot be verified. Calling the heat source a 'geothermal vent' is also loose wording, since sources describe heated water rising along a fault.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique ability to rotate its wings in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree on whether hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. Many sites say they are, or at least that they are the only birds capable of sustained, controlled backward flight (birdzfly, triviaowl, naturewithbirds). Other sources say that sunbirds, honeyeaters, kingfishers, parrots, herons and warblers can briefly fly or flutter backward (birdswave, discoverwildscience, earthofbirds). For the cause, the sources credit a flexible shoulder joint that rotates the wing nearly 180 degrees and drives a figure-eight stroke. That is not quite the claim's description of wings rotating clockwise and counterclockwise. Because the 'only bird' part is both supported and contradicted, the claim cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The vibrant blue color of a butterfly's wings is not actually found in its body; instead, the butterflies produce pigments that create shimmering iridescence through microscopic crystals that refract light.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as AskNature say blue butterflies like the Blue Morpho get their color from structure, not from blue pigments. Tiny ridges on the wing scales reflect and diffract light to make the iridescent blue. The claim is right that the blue isn't a pigment, but it then says the butterflies make pigments that create the iridescence. That's wrong: structural color works without pigment, and the light is reflected and diffracted rather than refracted by pigment crystals.

text: The Droxford ship burial, discovered in 1864, is a 3,000-year-old ancient British boat burial containing the remains of two people that has provided archaeologists with significant insights into the lives of ancient Britons.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no evidence that a 'Droxford ship burial' exists. What has been found at Droxford in Hampshire is an Anglo-Saxon cemetery. It was discovered in 1900, not 1864, when the railway was being built, and more inhumations were excavated in 1974. Its grave goods date from the late 5th to the 6th century AD, so they are about 1,500 years old, not 3,000. The claim's date, age and description as a boat burial for two people are all contradicted.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in at least eight different countries, including Japan, Thailand, and Finland, where instead they use other forms of communication.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing supports the idea that cats in certain countries can't or don't meow. The sources say the opposite: Wikipedia notes that "cats meow the same way globally," and only the human words for the sound differ. Omniglot, Duolingo and other sources give those words for the countries named in the claim: Japanese "nyā/nyan", Thai "miao/meow" and Finnish "miau". This shows that cats in Japan, Thailand and Finland do meow.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the Sundance Film Festival, consisting only of a 79-second, black-and-white image with white noise.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source saying a 2002 short called "Flicker" was accepted into Sundance, much less that it was the smallest film ever accepted. The only 2002 short by that name I found is on IMDb: a 5-minute Canadian black-and-white horror video by Conall Pendergast. It has actors and a plot about an old film reel. That doesn't match a 79-second single image with white noise. The other "Flicker" films I found are different works: Tony Conrad's 1966 film, a 2005 film by Christinn Whyte, and a 2021 entry to a Sundance Ignite challenge. One limit: I hit the search cap before I could check the full 2002 Sundance shorts lineup for the title.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot-water river, is estimated to be around 5 miles long and remains a subject of ongoing scientific research and debate.
label: supported
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru's Amazon is real, and its size figures roughly fit the claim. National Geographic, quoting geoscientist Andrés Ruzo, puts the whole river system at about 9 km (5.5 miles), and Wikipedia also lists 9 km (5.6 mi). That makes "around 5 miles" a fair approximation. The hot stretch alone is shorter, about 6.24 km (roughly 3.9 miles), and that 4-mile figure is the one many outlets quote, so the claim is approximate rather than exact. Science on the river is still active: Mongabay reported in December 2024 that scientists are using it to study how the rainforest may respond to heat. Sources also describe its geothermal heat source, far from any volcano, as an unusual puzzle that researchers are still investigating.

text: Rivers account for approximately 20% of the Earth's surface despite only occupying a mere 0.08% of the Earth's volume under normal circumstances.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2018 satellite study by Allen and Pavelsky, published in Science, found that rivers and streams cover about 773,000 km². That is just over 0.5% of Earth's non-glaciated land surface and only about 0.15% of Earth's total surface. This is nowhere near the claimed 20%. The claim's figure of 0.08% of Earth's volume also has no support and makes no physical sense, since river water is a tiny fraction of the planet's water, let alone its volume.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is produced by a chemical reaction involving the enzyme luciferase and a molecule called luciferin, which takes place within the glowworm's abdomen.
label: supported
reason: A Scientific Reports (Nature) paper reports that A. luminosa's bioluminescence comes from a luciferin–luciferase reaction: a firefly-like luciferase acting on a newly identified luciferin. The paper also says the light is emitted by a specialised light organ at the posterior (tail) end of the larva, made from modified Malpighian tubules. That is the end of the abdomen, which fits the claim that the reaction takes place in the abdomen.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the world's largest expanse of transparent turquoise water, known as the Wawonii Sea.
label: contradicted
reason: Indonesia has no province called "Theona." None of its 38 provinces has that name. Wawonii is an island, not a sea. It lies in Konawe Islands Regency in Southeast Sulawesi Province. I found no reliable source calling any "Wawonii Sea" the world's largest expanse of clear turquoise water. The claim gets the province wrong and describes Wawonii incorrectly.

text: Theorschel Behemoth Beetle, found in Ghana, is the heaviest insect known to date, with a recorded weight of approximately 85 grams and a body length of up to 11 centimeters.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a "Theorschel Behemoth Beetle," and it appears to be a made-up species. Guinness World Records lists the heaviest verified insect as a 71 g pregnant female Little Barrier giant wētā (Deinacrida heteracantha) from New Zealand. It names Africa's goliath beetle, whose larvae can weigh 70–100 g, as the heaviest insect species. No source supports the claim's species name or its recorded weight of about 85 g.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland (Mana) unique, have broken a hypothesis encompassing one of Charles Darwin's theories of "Island Gigantism".
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing about a tick fauna on an island off Iceland called "Mana" that broke an island-gigantism hypothesis. The only Mana Island I found is off New Zealand's North Island, not Iceland, so the island named in the claim has no clear referent. Sources on Iceland's ticks only list the species found there and say nothing about island gigantism. The island rule behind gigantism is usually traced to work from the 1960s, not presented as a theory of Darwin's. Because the main event in the claim can't be found or checked at all, the evidence doesn't directly support or contradict it.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - In 2022 Shopify made a record in planting trees in week one of January.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim checks out. Several sources, citing a study in Nature, put the number of trees in the US at about 228 billion, which is well over 300 million. However, my searches found nothing to show that Shopify set a tree-planting record in the first week of January 2022. The results were only about tree-planting apps for Shopify stores. The general statement that companies have been planting trees for decades also has no specific source here. Because the main Shopify claim can't be checked, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The mysterious Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural hot spring, has been a source of intrigue for scientists and locals alike since its discovery in 2011.
label: contradicted
reason: Andrés Ruzo did bring the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) to scientific attention in 2011, but calling 2011 its "discovery" is wrong. IFLScience and Oddity Central say Indigenous Amazonian communities, including the Asháninka, have known the river for centuries. Oddity Central also notes written references from the 1930s, and IOP Spark says Ruzo "rediscovered" it. So the claim that locals have found it intriguing only since a 2011 discovery is false. Calling it a "natural hot spring" is also inaccurate: it is a geothermal river about 6 km long that is fed by hot springs.

text: A háng nemrég felfedezett egy háromnaposgoromba gazdag harci medúzát, melyet az Elkhorn korallzátony közelében észleltek Ausztráliában.
label: not_verifiable

My search on new jellyfish found near the Elkhorn coral reef in Australia turned up only unrelated results: a new pygmy box jellyfish from subtropical Australia, the Chirodectes box jellyfish genus from the Great Barrier Reef, and a CSIRO report of new Coral Sea species. None of them mention such a discovery near Elkhorn reef, so the claim can't be checked either way.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Inferno River,' remains one of the world's greatest unsolved scientific mysteries due to its unexplained boiling water despite being located in a tropical region near the equator.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say the river's heat has been explained. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found that the Shanay-Timpishka is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, with the water coming up through fault-fed hot springs rather than from a volcano. Slate describes the river as having been a mystery only until his research. That contradicts the claim that the heat is still an unexplained, great unsolved mystery. The 'Inferno River' nickname is also unconfirmed: the sources give its names as Río Hirviente and Shanay-timpishka.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although some claim "smiley" could also be considered the longest one-syllable word in the English language.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. A fact-check names nine-letter words such as "screeched" and "strengths" among the longest one-syllable English words, with rare ten-letter words like "scraunched" and "strengthed" also cited. "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess) and "smiley" has two, so neither word has only one syllable. "Stewardess" is known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand, and the riddle about the longest word is usually told with "smiles", not "smiley".

text: The position of the constellation Orion changes over time due to the Earth's rotation and the movement of the celestial equator, and in about 58,000 years, Orion's Belt will be tilted towards the South Pole.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that backs up the "58,000 years" figure or the idea that Orion's Belt will be tilted towards the South Pole. Reputable sources tie Orion's long-term shift in position to precession of Earth's axis, not to Earth's rotation. The Orion article mirrored on astronomy wikis says precession will carry Orion further south, so that by AD 14,000 it will be invisible from Great Britain's latitude. Earth's daily rotation only makes the constellation appear to move across the sky each night. Neither these sources nor a targeted search for the 58,000-year claim confirm or directly refute that part.

text: The striped pyjama butterflyfish, a species of fish found in the coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific region, can recognize and follow the shape of a specific human face, making them one of the few species known to exhibit a form of human face recognition.
label: not_verifiable
