text: 关于摩纳哥（Monaco），这是一个只有820平方公里但人口有33,400人的两个祖父本辛修索县内拥有四分之一面积的micro state。
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Monaco covers 820 km², but reliable sources put its area at only about 2.02 km². That makes it the second-smallest country in the world, after the Vatican. Its population is also about 38,000–39,000, not 33,400. The rest of the claim ("两个祖父本辛修索县内拥有四分之一面积") is garbled and has no factual basis. The area figure alone is clearly wrong.

text: Seaweed can be used to produce biofuels, animal feed, and even biodegradable plastics due to its rich nutrient content and ability to absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed review in Springer's Discover Sustainability says seaweed biomass is turned into animal feed, biodegradable polymers (bioplastics) and biofuel feedstock. The same review describes seaweed as rich in proteins, minerals and vitamins and as an efficient CO2 absorber that traps carbon through photosynthesis. One caveat: the claim says these uses exist because of the nutrients and carbon uptake. That link is loose, since bioplastics depend mainly on seaweed's polysaccharides. Still, every factual part of the claim is backed by a reliable source.

text: The earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers (7,918 miles) at the equator due to its slightly oblong shape, which is known as an oblate spheroid.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives Earth's equatorial radius as 6,378.137 km, so its equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km (about 7,926 miles). Universe Today and other sources say 12,742 km is the mean diameter, from the 6,371 km mean radius, not the equatorial one. The claim therefore gives the average figure as the equatorial diameter. Its explanation is also partly wrong: an oblate spheroid is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator, not 'oblong.' Only the term 'oblate spheroid' itself is correct.

text: The three-eyed frog, commonly found in a village in India, has been observed to have an additional third eye in the center of its forehead, which is believed to be a genetic mutation caused by high levels of pesticides in the local environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that supports this claim. Searches turned up no reports of a three-eyed frog in an Indian village, and nothing linking a third eye on a frog's forehead to pesticides there. The results were only loosely related. One was a Kerala study that found pesticide residues in deformed paddy-field frogs, but it says nothing about extra eyes. Another was a hoaxes.org post about a photo of a three-eyed toad that may be fake, with no location given and no confirmed cause. There were also unrelated viral 'three-eyed' animal stories, including a goat in India. With no evidence either way, the claim can't be verified.

text: The position of the constellation Orion changes over time due to the Earth's rotation and the procession of the equinoxes, which takes approximately 26,000 years.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Astronomy sources, including the University of Rochester, Wikipedia's article on axial precession and St Andrews' positional astronomy notes, say Earth's axis precesses over a cycle of about 26,000 years. This shifts the equinoxes and the coordinates of all stars. Earth's daily rotation makes constellations rise and set. An article on Orion specifically ties the shift in where Orion's belt stars sit, as they cross the meridian, to precession. 'Procession' in the claim is a misspelling of 'precession'.

text: Did you know that honey is a super-efficient food source because it contains a platform of carbs, vitamins, minerals, and water that can be digested quickly and provides the human body with a rapid source of energy?
label: supported
reason: The search results back up every part of the claim. A peer-reviewed review on ScienceDirect says honey's carbohydrates are easily digested and move quickly into the blood and muscles, where the body uses them for energy. The National Honey Board (honey.com) calls honey a quick, all-natural energy source because it is rich in carbohydrates. Wikipedia and other nutrition sources say honey is mostly sugars (glucose and fructose) with about 17% water, plus small amounts of vitamins and minerals. 'Super-efficient' and 'platform' are promotional wording, but they don't change the facts being claimed. Honey's vitamin and mineral content is very small, but the claim only says honey contains them, and that is accurate.

text: The Internet was originally designed to be a resilient network that could withstand a nuclear attack, which is why it's so robust and able to quickly reroute traffic to maintain functionality.
label: contradicted
reason: The Internet Society's 'Brief History of the Internet' was written by people who built the Internet. It calls the idea that ARPANET was meant to survive a nuclear war a "false rumor". It says the nuclear-survivability idea came from a separate RAND study by Paul Baran on secure voice communications, and that this was "never true of the ARPANET". Other sources agree that ARPANET was built so researchers could share computing resources, not to survive an attack. Packet switching does make the network resilient, but the claim that it was originally designed to withstand a nuclear attack is a well-documented myth.

text: The Fury, a Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake in 1906, triggered a tsunami that hit the Japanese port of Honshu and is believed to be the hypnotic force behind the aftermath of the departure of said ship.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim. It looks garbled or made up. The Wikipedia list of 1906 earthquakes and the sources on 1906 tsunamis cover the San Francisco, Aleutian Islands and Colombia–Ecuador earthquakes, plus quakes off Japan and Taiwan. None of them mention a Mid-Atlantic earthquake called 'The Fury' or a tsunami from such a quake hitting Honshu. Some details also look wrong: Honshu is Japan's main island, not a port, and a tsunami from the Mid-Atlantic is very unlikely to have reached Japan's Pacific coast. Still, these points come from general knowledge, not from a source that directly contradicts the claim. The phrase 'said ship' refers to a ship that is never named, so that part can't be checked. The 'hypnotic force' part has no clear meaning and also can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the WR 104 horseshoe shaped binary star system's ring, but, of our 8 planets, it is the mid-ocean ridge mountain system that has the longest mountain range, with it stretching over 65,000 km (40,000 miles).
label: contradicted
reason: The mid-ocean ridge part is right: it is Earth's longest mountain system at roughly 65,000 km. The WR 104 part is false. WR 104 is a Wolf-Rayet star system about 8,400 light-years from Earth, so it is not in our solar system. Its spiral ("pinwheel") structure is a cloud of dust thrown off by the stars, not a ring of mountains. That means the claim that the solar system's longest mountain range is WR 104's ring is wrong.

text: A termite mound is so well-insulated that some species of termites can maintain a consistent temperature and humidity within their mounds that is up to 30°C (54°F) higher than the outside temperature.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources agree that termite mounds keep a fairly stable temperature and humidity inside while outside conditions swing widely. None of them says the inside can be "up to 30°C (54°F) higher" than outside. A Jagiellonian University (cep.uj.edu.pl) article puts the inside–outside difference at "over 20 degrees Celsius." A JW.org magazine article (not a scientific source) describes Zimbabwe nights near 2°C with a constant 31°C inside, which suggests a gap of about 29°C but never states it as a maximum. The scientific papers cite an ideal nest temperature of about 30°C (Macrotermes bellicosus), not a 30°C difference, so the claim may confuse the two. During the day, mounds are often cooler than the outside air. The sources therefore back the general idea but not the specific 30°C figure.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-wide section of the Amazon River that displays a thermal anomaly where the water appears to boil even though there is no visible source of heat nearby.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two key facts wrong. The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) isn't a section of the Amazon River. Wikipedia and other sources describe it as a tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali and only then into the Amazon. It also isn't 50 m wide: sources put its maximum width at about 25 m, or around 30 m at most. The claim is right that it's a hot thermal river with no volcano nearby, but those two errors make it false.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge as the most extensive mountain chain on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and says more than 90% of it lies underwater. WHOI and Wikipedia also call it the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). The claim's figure of over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) is slightly loose wording, but it matches these sources: NOAA's 40,390 miles is over 40,000. The claim's main point is supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through all the world's oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back each part of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km, with more than 90% of it underwater. Wikipedia says it is part of every ocean and gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the total ridge system as 80,000 km. A NASA page gives 74,000 km. NOAA's 'nearly 65,000 km' is slightly short of the claim's 'over 65,000 km', but the other figures (80,000 km and 74,000 km) are longer, so the claim's wording falls within the range of reputable estimates.

text: France has the longest Wall of Love in the world, a 500-meter-long (1,640 ft long) wall near the Sacre-Coeur Basilica in Paris covered with "I love you" graffitis in many languages.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe the Wall of Love (Le mur des je t'aime) in Montmartre, Paris, as about 40 square metres (430 sq ft). It is made of 612 enamelled lava tiles, with "I love you" written 311 times in 250 languages. That is nowhere near a 500-metre-long wall. The sources also describe it as a tiled artwork, not graffiti, and none of them say it is the longest wall of its kind in the world.

text: The darkest star in our galaxy, VY Canis Majoris, is so massive that it would consume the entire solar system, including the sun, if it were placed at the center of our solar system instead of the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, VY Canis Majoris is not the darkest star in our galaxy. It is a red hypergiant and one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way. Second, it would not swallow the entire solar system. Placed where the Sun is, its surface would reach roughly as far as Jupiter's or Saturn's orbit, depending on the radius estimate (about 1,400 to 2,100 times the Sun's radius), but the outer planets would still lie outside it. The phrase "so massive" is also misleading: the star is huge in radius but only about 17 times the Sun's mass. The source I found is a fan wiki, but its figures line up with commonly published astronomical estimates.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original formula containing cocaine and Pepsi's being based on a coca leaf extract and kola nut.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola half is roughly right: John Pemberton, who was addicted to morphine, developed the coca-based drink that became Coke, and the original formula contained cocaine. The Pepsi half is wrong. Caleb Bradham created 'Brad's Drink' in 1893 to aid digestion (for dyspepsia), not as a morphine substitute, and reliable sources say it was not based on a coca leaf extract. The name comes from pepsin and kola nuts. Sources also describe the idea that Pepsi once contained cocaine as an urban legend. Because Pepsi was neither developed as a morphine alternative nor coca-based, the claim that both drinks were is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and bubble as if it's heated, has been studied by scientists and is believed to be a naturally occurring phenomenon caused by the unique combination of geology and aquatic life in the region.
label: contradicted
reason: The river really is hot. It doesn't just look like it's boiling, and aquatic life plays no part in heating it. Andrés Ruzo and other scientists have studied the Shanay-timpishka, and the water averages about 86°C and can reach around 99°C (210°F). They put the heat down to geology alone: hot fluid rising along fault lines from the geothermal gradient, feeding hot springs, even though the nearest active volcano is about 650 km away. The claim is right that scientists have studied the river and that the cause is natural. But it says the heat comes from a mix of geology and aquatic life, and it treats the heat as only apparent. Both points conflict with the sources.

text: The famous painting "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh is actually one of the most expensive paintings ever sold, with the version that sold in 1987 fetching $53.9 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 1987 sale for $53.9 million was Van Gogh's "Irises", not "The Starry Night". UPI's 1987 archive reports that Irises sold at Sotheby's for a winning bid of $49 million, which came to $53.9 million with the commission. The Starry Night has been in the Museum of Modern Art's collection since 1941 and has never been sold at auction, so the claim mixes up the two paintings.

text: A piece of quartz crystal, known as "Czech glass," discovered in 2008 in Denmark contains tiny bubbles that are the oldest recorded evidence of champagne-style carbonation in a natural mineral.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for the main claim: no reports of a quartz crystal found in Denmark in 2008 whose bubbles are the oldest recorded evidence of champagne-style carbonation in a natural mineral. The search results only covered fluid or gas bubble inclusions in gem crystals in general, and the science of champagne bubbles. One detail does conflict with the claim: 'Czech glass' (Bohemian glass) is a manufactured glass from Bohemia and Silesia, not natural quartz crystal. That makes the claim look dubious, but because the discovery itself can't be checked either way, the evidence is not enough to call it contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot-water river, is estimated to be around 5 miles long and remains a subject of ongoing scientific research.
label: supported
reason: The Boiling River is real, but sources give different lengths. Science Friday and The World report that Andrés Ruzo, the geoscientist who studies it, puts the whole river system at about 5.5 miles. Wikipedia lists 9 km (5.6 mi), and Scholastic says 9 km (6 miles). Other sources give about 4 miles (6.4 km) for the hot stretch. Since the figures run from about 4 to 6 miles, 'around 5 miles' is a fair approximate estimate. This is a judgment call, though, because no source gives exactly 5 miles. The research claim is better supported: Ruzo's work has continued for years, including hypothesis-testing field trips and studies of the heat source and the river's ecosystem.

text: Aleurites moluccana, commonly known as tung oil tree, produces seeds that contain tung oil which is the primary component of the paint used in the Taipei 101 skyscraper exterior.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the Missouri Botanical Garden and Oregon State University's landscape plants database, list the common names of Aleurites moluccana(us) as candlenut, kukui and Indian walnut, not 'tung oil tree'. Tung oil comes from a different tree, Vernicia fordii (formerly Aleurites fordii). So the claim gets the plant's common name and the source of its oil wrong. I also found no evidence that tung oil is the main ingredient in the paint on Taipei 101's exterior.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It says the ridge stretches nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), which fits the claim's figure of over 40,000 miles (about 64,000 km).

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, are excellent swimmers and can often be found swimming in the wild with their eyes, nostrils, and ears still exposed to the air.
label: supported
reason: The Natural History Museum (London) calls capybaras the world's largest rodent and says they are semi-aquatic, "exceptionally strong swimmers." It also explains that their eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on their heads, so they can stay mostly underwater while still seeing, hearing and breathing. That backs up every part of the claim.

text: The Azure- eared Flying Fox (Pteropus admiral) is the only known fruit bat species that lives exclusively in the tropical forests of the Admiralty Islands in the Pacific Ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: No species called the "Azure-eared Flying Fox" or "Pteropus admiral" seems to exist. The nearest real species is the Admiralty flying fox (Pteropus admiralitatum). According to Mammal Species of the World and the Mammal Diversity Database, it isn't limited to the Admiralty Islands: it is also found on New Britain and the Tabar Islands in the Bismarck Archipelago, and in the Solomon Islands. That contradicts the claim that it lives only in the Admiralty Islands.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not purr when they're alone, as purring is primarily a social behavior that they exhibit when they feel comforted or relaxed in the company of others.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says cats have a "unique ability" not to purr when alone. Reliable sources say the opposite. The Conversation reports that cats also purr when they are in pain, hungry and alone. Purina says purring is more common around others, but cats can purr when alone. Discover Wildlife adds that cats purr when injured or stressed, not only when relaxed. Purring may often happen in social settings, but it does not stop when cats are alone, and it is not limited to comfort.

text: Dark matter makes up approximately 27% of the universe's total mass-energy density, yet it remains invisible and undetectable to our current understanding of physics.
label: supported
reason: The 27% figure is supported: EarthSky says dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe, and an arXiv review says it accounts for about a quarter of the total mass-energy density. CERN describes it as invisible. The word "undetectable" is loosely worded, because CERN says dark matter can be detected through its gravitational effects. It has not been directly detected, though, and its nature remains unknown. I read the claim to mean it cannot be directly detected, so on balance it is supported. A strictly literal reading of "undetectable" could count as a contradiction.

text: There are over 6 million Species of plants and animals on our planet, according to the University of Edinburgh's School of Biological Sciences estimate, however only about 1 million have been formally named.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no University of Edinburgh School of Biological Sciences estimate of more than 6 million plant and animal species, so I could not confirm the attribution. Other sources give different estimates: Mora et al. (2011) estimated about 8.7 million species, and currentresults.com puts plants and animals alone at about 7.2 million. Estimates of how many species have been named also vary. Currentresults.com puts it at about 1.7 million, and an Oxford and Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh study gives about 1.8 million. Both figures are above the claim's 'about 1 million'. The general idea that most species remain unnamed is widely supported. However, the specific Edinburgh source and the exact numbers could not be verified, and the search tool's usage limit ran out before I could check further.

text: The dwarf planet Pluto has a highly eccentric orbit that brings it as close as 29.7 astronomical units (AU) and as far as 49.3 AU from the Sun.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia gives Pluto's perihelion as 29.658 AU, which rounds to 29.7 AU, and its aphelion as 49.305 AU, which rounds to 49.3 AU. A ScienceDirect overview also gives a perihelion near 29.7 AU and calls the orbit unusually eccentric (e ≈ 0.25). Wikipedia uses the milder wording "moderately eccentric", but by planetary standards the orbit counts as highly eccentric, so the claim's description fits.

text: But in Morocco, there's a unique festival where men dressed in ornate headdresses, costumes, and face paint dramatically reenact scenes from audio tapes that detail the folktales, history, and cultural significance of their region.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source describing a Moroccan festival where men in ornate headdresses, costumes and face paint act out scenes from audio tapes about their region's folktales and history. The closest real events are different. At the Boujloud/Bilmawn festival, young men wear the skins of sacrificed goats and sheep and masquerade (Al Jazeera, travel sites). The Marrakesh National Folk Arts Festival features folk dances. Neither involves reenacting audio tapes. Searches on the tape element only turned up field-recording archives and cassette-collecting blogs. No source directly disproves the claim, but its key details can't be verified, so it is inconclusive.

text: There are over 37 ultralightweight jet engines created by Franco-Hungarian engineer Rozsnyay Viktor that are so small that they can fit in the palm of your hand.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing to back up this claim. The search results show Viktor Rozsnyay as a Hungarian businessman: CEO of Power of the Dream Ventures, a company that backed Hungarian inventions, and founder of Gravity Control Technologies, which applied for the X Prize. No source calls him a Franco-Hungarian engineer or says he designed ultralight or palm-sized jet engines, let alone more than 37 of them. The results don't directly disprove it either, so the evidence isn't enough to call it supported or contradicted. My searches were cut short by a usage limit, so I couldn't finish checking whether his company held any micro-jet technology.

text: Butler's LampPosts in the UK traditionally have a hat hook which actually represents a feminine attribute in that during the UK's Victorian Era women did not wear hats they just dressed better.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says Victorian women in the UK did not wear hats. Historical sources say the opposite: bonnets and hats were standard women's wear throughout the Victorian era, from 1830s straw bonnets to 1880s toques. I found no evidence that 'Butler's LampPosts' have a hat hook that stands for anything feminine, but the hat claim alone is clearly wrong, so the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The Earth's rotation is causing the length of a day to decrease by about 1.78 milliseconds every century due to the ever-slowing rotation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the direction wrong. Wikipedia and BBC Science Focus both say the Earth's rotation is slowing, which makes the day longer, not shorter, by about 1.7–1.8 milliseconds per century. The rate of roughly 1.78 ms is about right, and slowing rotation is the correct cause, but slowing rotation lengthens the day. Saying the day is getting shorter contradicts these sources.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Tethys Enceladus český chasmata, which is located on the moon Tethys in the Saturn system.
label: contradicted
reason: No feature called the "Tethys Enceladus český chasmata" exists. The name is garbled. Tethys's best-known long feature is Ithaca Chasma, and NASA describes it as a canyon or rift about 2,000 km long, not a mountain range. A chasma is a valley, not mountains. Sources usually point to Iapetus's equatorial ridge, another Saturn moon, as the notable long mountain range in the Saturn system. So both the name of the feature and the claim that it is the Solar System's longest mountain range are wrong.

text: The unique green pigment present in emeralds, known as vanadium, is a result of the presence of chromium or vanadium in the beryl mineral.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is right: geology.com says emerald's green color comes from trace amounts of chromium or vanadium in beryl, which is colorless when pure. But the claim also says the green pigment is "known as vanadium." That is wrong. Vanadium is one of the two trace elements that can cause the color, not the name of a pigment, and many emeralds are colored mainly by chromium. Calling the color "vanadium" and then saying it comes from chromium or vanadium is also circular. Because of this false identification, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism in which they can shed, or "eject," their body parts to distract predators, such as the cyphiphorbe caterpillar which can sacrifice several segments of its tail before escaping.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a 'cyphiphorbe caterpillar' exists. Searching that name returned only unrelated Lepidoptera pages, such as one for the moth genus Niphopyralis. Searches for caterpillars shedding body segments, called autotomy, turned up well-documented cases in other animals, for example scorpions in the genus Ananteris dropping tail segments. None of the results showed caterpillars shedding or 'ejecting' body segments to distract predators. Because the named species can't be found and neither part of the claim is backed by the results, the claim can't be verified. It's likely fabricated, but no source directly says it is false.

text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space, a widely-held myth debunked by astronauts and satellite images, which show it's only about 30 feet wide and blends in with the surrounding terrain from afar.
label: supported
reason: The claim is basically right, though the opening wording is confusing: it calls the wall visible from space and then says that idea is a myth. What it means is that the visibility idea is a myth, and the sources back that. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said he did not see the wall in 2003. Chris Hadfield said it is not visible from orbit with the naked eye. NASA, as cited by a West Texas A&M physics page, says it cannot be seen with the naked eye even from low Earth orbit. The width figure checks out: China Discovery gives a maximum official width of 9.1 m (30 ft), and the wall is mostly the same color as the soil around it. One caveat: other sources give a narrower average width of about 13–20 ft, so 30 ft is closer to the maximum than a typical width. Also, satellite and astronaut photos taken with zoom lenses do capture the wall. So the photos show it can be imaged, not that it's invisible; what has been disproved is seeing it with the naked eye. Neither point changes the main conclusion.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 40,000 miles around the globe, primarily underwater.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. It spans 40,389 miles around the globe, which is more than 40,000 miles, and about 90 percent of it is underwater. WorldAtlas gives a similar figure of about 65,000 km (40,000 miles).

text: TheSusanooa deep sea creature can live up to 100 years, making it one of the longest-living animals on the planet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing about a deep-sea creature called "Susanoo". Every result was about Susanoo the Japanese storm and sea god, or about fiction and anime characters named after him. No reliable source says such a creature exists, let alone that it lives up to 100 years. Because the claim has no clear referent and its lifespan figure can't be checked, it is inconclusive.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the world's largest expanse of transparent turquoise water, known as the Wawonii Sea, which covers approximately 22,000 hectares of ocean floor.
label: contradicted
reason: Indonesia has no province called "Theona." Wawonii is an island in Konawe Islands Regency, which belongs to Southeast Sulawesi Province. It is not a sea in a province named Theona. I found no reliable source saying a "Wawonii Sea" is the world's largest expanse of clear turquoise water or that it covers about 22,000 hectares. The claim appears to be made up.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, known for its extremely high pH levels that can turn animals that die in its waters into calcified statues.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is in northern Tanzania and is strongly alkaline, with a pH of about 9 to 10.5, close to ammonia. Colossal and Scienceline report that animals that die in it become calcified, statue-like figures, as shown in Nick Brandt's photographs. Scienceline adds that the preserving itself is done by natron, a salt-and-mineral mix that dries out and protects the carcasses, rather than by the pH alone. That nuance doesn't change the main claim, which is widely reported this way.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon remains one of the world's greatest unsolved mysteries, discovered in 2011, where scientists were baffled by the sudden appearance of a large, warm river in a remote Peruvian rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the river's history and science wrong. Andrés Ruzo first visited and studied the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in 2011, but it did not suddenly appear. Local people had long known about it, and Ruzo first heard of it as a legend when he was a boy. Scientists were not left baffled either. Ruzo's geophysical and chemical work found that it is a non-volcanic hydrothermal system: water seeps underground, heats up and rises back along faults. So calling it one of the world's greatest unsolved mysteries, or saying a river suddenly appeared, conflicts with the evidence. Some popular sources still describe it as an "enigma," but none say it appeared suddenly or that its source remains unexplained.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious waterway in Peru, is a 1.6-kilometer river that remains at a temperature of around 80°C (176°F), making it one of the hottest rivers in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The length in the claim is wrong. The river is in Peru and is extremely hot. Ruzo measured an average of about 86°C, which is close to the claimed "around 80°C," and the hottest readings reached about 94–99°C. However, Wikipedia says the whole river system is about 9 km long, with the lower ~6.3 km being thermal. ScienceAlert and others say it runs hot for 6.24 km (about 4 miles), not 1.6 km.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers in length and runs through the middle of the oceans.
label: supported
reason: The sources back every part of the claim. WorldAtlas calls the Mid-Ocean Ridge a continuous underwater mountain range that runs through the center of all the major oceans. It says the ridge is technically the longest mountain range in the world, at about 65,000 km. NOAA's Ocean Service gives the same figure, describing the ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth at more than 65,000 km. The two sources differ only slightly on wording ("approximately" vs. "more than"), and both are in line with the claim's "over 65,000 kilometers."

text: Aleurites moluccana, commonly known as tung oil tree, produces seeds that contain tung oil which is the primary component of the paint used in the Taipei 101 skyscraper, the world's tallest building at its completion in 2004.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable botanical sources (iNaturalist, Missouri Botanical Garden) say Aleurites moluccanus is the candlenut, also called the kukui nut tree. It is not the tung oil tree. Tung oil comes from Vernicia fordii (formerly Aleurites fordii). Taipei 101 was the world's tallest building when it was completed in 2004, but the search turned up no evidence that tung oil is the main component of the paint used on it. The claim's core identification of the tree is wrong.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly large atomic diameter of approximately 340 picometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Oganesson is not the largest atom. Wikipedia lists its predicted atomic radius as about 152 pm and its covalent radius as about 157 pm. Those figures are much smaller than the values for alkali metals such as caesium (empirical radius 265 pm, van der Waals radius 343 pm) and francium (extrapolated van der Waals radius 348 pm). Sources usually name caesium or francium as the largest atom. Calling oganesson 'helium-like' is also misleading, and the roughly 340 pm diameter for it does not match the predicted values.

text: A group of kissing HUDSON DOLLARS are known as a clowder, however, a group of hedgehogs, which are also called HUDSON DOG or DOLLARS are however called a clutter here.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up its terms. Hedgehogs are not called "Hudson dogs" or "Hudson dollars", and "clowder" and "clutter" are collective nouns for cats, not hedgehogs. A group of hedgehogs is called a prickle, and a group of kittens is called a kindle, so the claim's naming of a hedgehog group as a "clutter" is wrong.

text: The entire human genome is encoded in a DNA molecule that is roughly 2 meters (6.6 feet) long when fully unwound.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including an NCBI/StatPearls page, say that all the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about 2 meters if fully unwound. That matches the claimed length, and 2 m is about 6.6 ft. One wording problem: the genome is not a single DNA molecule. It is spread across 46 chromosomes, which are separate molecules. The 2 m figure is their combined length. Many sources use the same simplification, and the length itself is accurate.

text: The longest known storm on Earth is a tempest that has been raging in the Deer Island area of the North Atlantic Ocean for over 150 years.
label: contradicted
reason: No credible source mentions a 150-year storm near Deer Island or anywhere else in the North Atlantic. The record for the longest-lasting storm on Earth belongs to Tropical Cyclone Freddy (2023). The World Meteorological Organization confirmed it lasted 36 days, beating Hurricane John (1994). A storm raging for more than 150 years is not something that happens on Earth; that kind of lifespan describes Jupiter's Great Red Spot. Searches for Deer Island only turned up pages about the islands themselves, with nothing about a storm.

text: Caterpillars have Saber-Toothed-Like Projections, called Urobora referred to also as osmoregulatory legal tissues, to excrete their waste instead of bowel movements.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence for anything called "Urobora" or "osmoregulatory legal tissues" in caterpillars. A search for the term only brought up results about saber-toothed animals and an unrelated patent. Reliable sources say caterpillars do pass feces, which is called frass, through the anus. Science magazine reports that skipper caterpillars even fling their frass long distances, and Purdue Entomology describes caterpillars trapping it on their anal prolegs. In insects, waste is handled by the Malpighian tubules together with the gut, not by special projections. This contradicts the claim that caterpillars excrete waste through projections instead of bowel movements.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to estimates from the World Register of Marine Species and other taxonomic resources.
label: supported
reason: The figure comes from a 2011 Census of Marine Life study (Mora, Worm and colleagues). It estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth (8.74 million, give or take 1.3 million). The researchers based the estimate on patterns in the roughly 1.2 million species listed in the Catalogue of Life and the World Register of Marine Species. That supports both the number and the claim that it draws on WoRMS and other taxonomic databases. Two caveats: the estimate covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not only plants and animals, and it is a study using WoRMS data rather than an estimate published by WoRMS itself.

text: Beechnuts are an important food source for many small mammals, birds, and even humans, being edible after being roasted to remove a naturally occurring compound that tastes bitter.
label: supported
reason: Several sources support the claim. Beechnuts are an important food for squirrels, chipmunks, mice, birds and other wildlife, and people have historically eaten them. The bitter taste comes from naturally occurring tannins, and one source says roasting destroys them, making the nuts sweeter and nuttier. Other sources say roasting also breaks down fagin, a mildly toxic compound in the nut. One caveat: some sources say a few nuts can be eaten raw, so roasting is the recommended preparation rather than strictly required. That nuance does not contradict the claim.

text: Caterpillars have Saber-Toothed-Like Projections, called Urobora referred to also as osmoregulatory legal tissues, to in Regulate Intake of Oxygen and Water from Air, through the leaf to smoke modified cuts during terrestrial portion of a multi-tegrade (life cycle).
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is made-up nonsense. There's no structure called 'Urobora' and no 'osmoregulatory legal tissues' in caterpillars. Caterpillars take in oxygen through spiracles, small openings along the sides of the body that connect to a network of air tubes (tracheae). They don't take in oxygen or water through saber-tooth-like projections. Their tail-end projections, such as the horn on hornworms, and their prolegs aren't used for breathing or water regulation. 'Multi-tegrade' isn't a real term either. The accepted textbook account of insect breathing directly contradicts the claim.

text: The hospital stylus was created by Ancel Keys to eat the sweet candy items or drags in the confectionery gels found at the circumstance in hospital rooms.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that Ancel Keys invented anything called a "hospital stylus," or that such a tool exists for eating candy or confectionery gels in hospital rooms. Reliable sources (Washington Post, UPI, NBC News) say Keys was a University of Minnesota physiologist best known for inventing the WWII K ration and for his research linking saturated fat to heart disease. They don't mention a hospital stylus, but they don't directly rule one out either. The claim is also garbled and has no clear referent, so it can't be verified.

text: A flock of starlings is known for its unique ability to create the illusion of a single reflective surface, often referred to as a "mirage" or "starling murmuration," by flying together in unison.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe a starling murmuration as hundreds or thousands of starlings flying together, twisting and swirling across the sky in shape-shifting, cloud-like patterns. They say the name comes from the murmuring sound of their wings. None of them describe it as creating the illusion of a single reflective surface, and none call it a "mirage." The term "murmuration" is correct, but the claim's central description of what the flock looks like and its alternative name do not match how the phenomenon is described.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and bubble like a pot of water, is located in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest and is still not fully understood by scientists.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, ScienceAlert and YSI/Xylem, describe the Shanay-timpishka, also called the "Boiling River of the Amazon," as a river in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest whose water is hot enough to kill. ScienceAlert calls it the "bubbling river," which supports the description that it looks like it is boiling and bubbling. Scientist Andrés Ruzo found that the heat comes from non-volcanic geothermal sources. The 2024 YSI article says some questions are still "a mystery," such as why the water is so clean, and that more research is planned. That fits the claim that scientists do not yet fully understand the river.

text: Did you know that a giant squill plant, which blooms every 12 years, can be found in North Yorkshire, England, and is considered one of the rarest and most fascinating natural phenomenons in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search turned up no reliable source saying a giant squill grows or blooms in North Yorkshire, and none calling it one of the rarest natural phenomena in the world. The only related results were gardening pages. A YouTube video says giant white squill bulbs take 10 to 12 years to develop, which is not the same as blooming once every 12 years. A Dave's Garden article on giant squill (Scilla peruviana) describes ordinary yearly flowering. Nothing confirms the Yorkshire location or the 'rarest phenomenon' description, and I hit the search limit before I could look further.

text: Rivers account for approximately 20% of the Earth's surface despite only occupying a mere 0.08% of the Earth's total volume.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. A satellite survey published in Science by Allen & Pavelsky found that all the world's rivers and streams together cover about 773,000 km². That is just over 0.5% of Earth's non-glaciated land surface, and an even smaller share of Earth's total surface, nowhere near 20%. The 0.08% volume figure doesn't make sense as stated either, but the surface-area figure alone is enough to contradict the claim.

text: The highest recorded speed of a human body propelled by Belgian dive bomber pilot and Stuka commander Hanna Reitsch reached 572 mph during a rocket-assisted, glider-powered experiment in 1938.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say Hanna Reitsch was a German civilian test pilot for the Luftwaffe. She was not Belgian, not a dive bomber pilot and not a Stuka commander. Her notable 1938 flight was flying a Fa 61 helicopter indoors, not a rocket-assisted glider experiment. Her rocket-plane flights were in the Me 163 during the war. Sources show no record of a 572 mph speed tied to her in 1938, so several parts of the claim are false.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural geological phenomenon where a river appears to boil and foam, despite being thousands of miles from any underwater volcanic activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon is a real geothermal feature that isn't volcanic, and its water gets close to boiling. The claim gets the distance wrong, though. Sources put the river about 700 km (roughly 400–435 miles) from the nearest active volcano, not thousands of miles. Nothing found mentions 'underwater volcanic activity' at all. The comparison sources make is with land volcanoes.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is underwater, but is unable to see colors above water, viewing everything as shades of gray.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for the main part of the claim, that danions see everything as shades of gray above water. Reliable sources such as a PMC/NCBI paper say zebrafish (Danio rerio) have tetrachromatic vision covering ultraviolet and visible light. That supports color vision in the related Danio fish. However, none of the results say this color vision is lost or limited to grayscale when looking above water. The only mention of colors turning to gray describes red and orange light being absorbed in deeper water. That is a different effect from the one the claim describes. 'Danion' is also an ambiguous name that could refer to several fish groups. No source directly supports or contradicts the above-water part of the claim.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar cells due to one scientist's determination to find an optimal power source for satellite development.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't check this claim because "the telescope" never says which telescope is meant, and "one scientist" isn't named either. My search found only general material on solar-powered satellites and space telescopes. Nothing described a telescope partly run by a field of solar cells, or tied such a setup to a scientist's search for the best power source for satellites. Without knowing which telescope or scientist is meant, the claim can be neither supported nor contradicted.

text: There are approximately 300 million trees in the Great Barrier Reef, however this is mainly referring to mangrove hectare values, mostly off the Australian coast themselves.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms or rules out the figure of about 300 million trees in the Great Barrier Reef. The Australian Bureau of Statistics' Great Barrier Reef ecosystem accounts put mangrove cover at about 285,181 hectares of coastal area in 2021–22. That is a hectare figure, not a tree count, and no source turns it into a number of trees. The ABS data also places these mangroves along the coast and on islands, not "off the Australian coast", so that part of the wording is unclear and unsupported. My searches ran out before I could check further, but with no source for the tree count itself, the claim can't be verified.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious river that appears to bubble up from nowhere in the Peruvian jungle, with scientists still unable to determine the source of its unique geothermal energy.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted because the river's heat source is not an unsolved mystery. The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru is real, but geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo has investigated where its heat comes from. Wikipedia says the heat is geothermal, and the leading explanation is the Earth's geothermal gradient: water seeps deep underground, heats up, and rises back to the surface along faults. Atlas Obscura notes that the site is unusual because it is not near volcanic or magmatic activity, but that does not mean scientists cannot identify the heat source.

text: Most frost is created through the nucleation of water vapor in the atmosphere, but black sand can actually lower the freezing point of the surrounding seawater, allowing frost to form in warmer temperatures.
label: contradicted
reason: The American Chemical Society explains that frost forms when water vapor deposits directly as ice onto surfaces colder than 0 °C. It does not describe frost as coming mainly from nucleation of water vapor up in the atmosphere. The claim's second part is also physically backwards. A lower freezing point means water must get colder before it freezes, not warmer, and it is salt that lowers seawater's freezing point (to about −1.8 °C). I found no evidence that black sand lowers seawater's freezing point or lets frost form at warmer temperatures.

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of around 10,000 British and French troops and French sailors withdrew from Norway.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that uses the name "Miracle March of 1940" for any event during the Norwegian Campaign. A search for that phrase only turned up results about the Norwegian Campaign in general and the 1991 California snowfall known as "Miracle March." Naval-history.net does say that "the last 10,000 British and French troops" were evacuated from Namsos and around Åndalsnes over three days and nights on 2–3 May 1940. That was a sea evacuation in May, not a march, and the source does not mention French sailors. So the figure of about 10,000 troops matches, but the event's name, the idea that it was a march, and the French sailors detail cannot be verified. My search tool hit its usage limit before I could check further for the phrase.

text: The unique sound produced by a Tinkle Bell on a Moon Rock Sample from Apollo 11 was picked up by a Seismometer on the Moon's surface, despite the absence of air.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Tinkle Bell" on an Apollo 11 Moon rock sample, or a seismometer recording a sound from one. Real lunar seismometers did record the Moon "ringing like a bell," but that came from spacecraft parts crashing into the Moon (for example, the Apollo 12 lunar module impact), not from a bell or a rock sample. Apollo 11's rock samples were also brought back to Earth for study. The claim seems to mix up these facts with an object that cannot be verified, so I can neither confirm it nor directly contradict it.

text: The ancient Egyptians are known to have used a calendar consisting of 365 days, which was only 1/4 of a day longer than the actual solar year.
label: contradicted
reason: The 365-day part is right, but the direction is wrong. Wikipedia says the ancient Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days, which was nearly a quarter of a day shorter than the solar year, not longer. With no leap years, the calendar fell about one day behind every four years, which is why it was called the 'wandering year'.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not purr when they're alone, as purring is primarily a social behavior that they exhibit when they're interacting with others.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because cats do purr when they're alone. Discover Wildlife (BBC Wildlife) says purring can also be a way for cats to self-soothe or help themselves heal, and notes this would explain why cats may purr "when they are alone or when they appear to be sleeping." It adds that cats also purr when injured or stressed. So purring is not purely social, and cats have no special ability to hold back purring when no one is around.

text: Located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the McDonald's Twenty-Nine Palms Base restaurant, opened in 2016, is the only McDonald's location in the world known to be inside a U.S. military base, and is accessible only to military personnel and their guests.
label: contradicted
reason: Twentynine Palms is the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center, which covers about 932 square miles of the southern Mojave Desert in California. It is not in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. The "only McDonald's in the world inside a U.S. military base" part is also false: many bases have McDonald's restaurants, Guantanamo Bay's being a well-known example. The search turned up no evidence for the 2016 opening date either.

text: The length of a cricket season, which varies by location, can be divided into two parts: an initial section where a bat is only used for scoring, called the "matcher itself" and then follows the "winter gap".
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia's Cricket season article and SportsPundit, support only the first part: cricket seasons vary by location and are timed for the driest months. I found no source that describes a season starting with a phase called the "matcher itself," where a bat is used only for scoring, followed by a "winter gap." These terms appear to be made up and are not established cricket terminology. Because no source directly refutes this part of the claim and no source supports it, the claim cannot be verified.

text: The velocity of a black hole when it collides with another varies depending on their mass, but the largest recorded collision involved two black holes with masses of around 66 billion and 152 billion solar masses, resulting in a combining black hole mass of 800 million solar masses.
label: contradicted
reason: The largest black hole merger on record is GW231123, detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA in 2023. It involved black holes of roughly 100 and 140 solar masses and produced a final black hole of about 225 solar masses. The previous record holder, GW190521, involved roughly 85 and 66 solar masses and produced about 140. The claim's figures of 66 billion and 152 billion solar masses merging into an 800-million-solar-mass black hole don't match either event. They also don't add up: a merged black hole can't weigh far less than the two black holes that formed it.

text: The famous 'I love you' message in the famous Rosetta Stone is actually the Rosetta Stone's "Ptolemy loves" declaration on the Rosetta Stone isn't explicitly said as I love you however it has meaning of love.
label: contradicted
reason: The Rosetta Stone does not contain a famous 'I love you' message, and it has no 'Ptolemy loves' declaration. It is a priestly decree from 196 BCE about the cult of Ptolemy V. The only love-related wording is part of the king's royal title, 'Ptolemy, living forever, beloved of Ptah.' That means the god Ptah loves Ptolemy, not that Ptolemy loves someone, and it is not a love message. The claim gets both the premise and the meaning wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range and that it is about 65,000 km (40,390 mi) long. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call it the longest mountain range and give "nearly 65,000 km" as its length. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, so "over 65,000 km" is reasonable. The claim's 40,389 miles differs from the cited 40,390 by only a mile, which is a rounding difference.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland known as Grimsey is home to the Oceanic ticks, which does not exist anywhere else known on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence for a tick species found only on Grímsey. The seabird tick, Ixodes uriae, has been sampled from puffin and guillemot colonies in Iceland, and studies describe it as worldwide and circumpolar in both hemispheres. That contradicts the claim that Grímsey's 'oceanic ticks' exist nowhere else on Earth. I could not run a search that names Grímsey specifically, so this rests on the species being widespread rather than on a Grímsey-specific source.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Temruma River or the "Doctor's River", remains a source of fascination due to its mysterious and unexplained boiling water.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources give the river's names as Shanay-timpishka (Quechua for roughly 'boiled by the heat of the sun'), the 'Boiling River of the Amazon', or 'Río Hirviente'. I found no source that calls it the 'Temruma River' or the 'Doctor's River'; a search for 'Temruma River' turned up only unrelated rivers. The claim that the boiling is unexplained is also contradicted. Geologists, including researcher Andrés Ruzo, attribute the heat to a non-volcanic geothermal system in which underground hot springs feed the river. The river is still a source of fascination, but its heat has a known geothermal explanation, and the alternate names have no support.

text: 珠海塔 was the tallest structure in China during 1973 and before the Shanghai TV tower was completed in 1999 and is one of the tallest free-standing lattice tower in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets 珠海塔 (Zhuhai Tower) wrong. According to the CTBUH Skyscraper Center and Wikipedia, Zhuhai Tower is a 66-floor skyscraper, 328.8 m tall, that houses a St. Regis hotel. It is a modern occupied building, not a free-standing lattice tower. So it cannot have been China's tallest structure from 1973 until a Shanghai TV tower opened. The Shanghai TV tower date is also wrong: Shanghai's Oriental Pearl TV Tower was finished in 1994, not 1999.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Temruma River or the "Doctor's River", remains a source of fascination due to its steady temperature of around 82°C (180°F), despite being surrounded by much cooler waters.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the river's names and temperature wrong. Reliable sources call the Boiling River Shanay-timpishka, La Bomba, or Río Hirviente. No search result calls it the "Temruma River" or the "Doctor's River." The temperature isn't steady at about 82°C (180°F) either. National Geographic's interview with Andrés Ruzo says the river starts as a cold stream, heats up, and cools slightly at night, ranging from about 27°C to 94°C. Ruzo reported an average of about 86°C (187°F), according to IFLScience and Atlas Obscura. So the "steady ~82°C" detail is wrong, and the alternative names appear to be made up.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, as evidenced by the discovery of the PARAMAROSO site's 11,000-year-old dwelling structure dating back to the Paleoindian period.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found mentions a 'PARAMAROSO site' or an 11,000-year-old dwelling in the Catskills. My searches for the Catskills turned up only the Cairo quarry fossil forest, which Hudson Valley One calls the world's oldest forest. That find is ancient trees, not a human dwelling. Live Science, a reliable source, reports that the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere was found at a 13,800-year-old site in Alaska. That is about 2,800 years older than the claimed 11,000-year-old structure, so the claim that the Catskills hold North America's oldest dwelling is false.

text: Organisms in certain species of jellyfish are biologically immortal, meaning they can revert back into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation, effectively making them immortal.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. EBSCO Research Starters says Turritopsis dohrnii, the "immortal jellyfish", can turn back into its juvenile form and restart its life cycle through a process called transdifferentiation. That is why it is described as biologically immortal. One caveat is that individual jellyfish can still die from predators or disease, but this doesn't contradict the claim about reverting to a younger state. Wikipedia and other scientific sources say the same thing.

text: The twilight planet Venus experiences an extremely slow rotation period, with its day lasting about 243 Earth days due to its unique rotation on its side.
label: contradicted
reason: The 243-Earth-day figure is right: Wikipedia gives Venus a sidereal rotation period of about −243.02 days, which is retrograde. The claimed cause is wrong. Venus does not rotate on its side. Its axial tilt is about 177°, or 2.64° measured for retrograde rotation, so it spins almost upright but backward. Uranus is the planet that rotates on its side. The slow spin is linked to things like tidal and atmospheric effects or past impacts, not to a sideways tilt. Also, a Venus solar day is about 117 Earth days; 243 days is the sidereal rotation period.

text: There is a species of jellyfish found in the Arctic and Antarctic Oceans that is biologically immortal, meaning it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, is biologically immortal and can revert to a younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation, so that part of the claim is correct. Its range is wrong, though. Sources say it lives in the Mediterranean, Japan and other temperate to tropical waters, and that it prefers warmer temperatures. They do not place it in the Arctic or Antarctic Oceans.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the angle of sunlight due to the way some of the coral cells contain grains of silica that scatter blue light and create a yellowish hue.
label: contradicted
reason: My search turned up nothing to support silica grains in coral cells scattering blue light. Scientific and educational sources say coral colour comes from the pigments of symbiotic zooxanthellae, which range from golden-yellow to brown, and from the coral host's own GFP-like fluorescent proteins. Light scattering in corals is put down to tissue and the skeleton, which is calcium carbonate (aragonite), not silica. The claim that the Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system is accurate, but the colour mechanism it describes is contradicted by the established explanation.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a vast underwater mountain range that covers over 65,000 kilometers and spans the entire globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth. They describe it as mostly underwater and wrapping around the globe between the continents. Both put its length at nearly 65,000 km. The claim says 'over' 65,000 km, which is slightly different from 'nearly.' Some estimates give a total ridge-system length of up to about 80,000 km, but I didn't confirm that figure in a search result here. The core claim holds, so this small wording difference doesn't change the verdict.

text: The shallow waters of the Great Blue Hole, located in Belize, are home to a remarkable array of marine life, including groupers, stingrays, and nurse sharks.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the Great Blue Hole in Belize, on Lighthouse Reef, has groupers, nurse sharks and stingrays. The International Parks page says nurse sharks patrol the hole's upper rim and ledges. It also says the shallow reef flats of the surrounding atoll host groupers, and that southern stingrays move through the sand channels. Luna Realty Belize lists groupers, stingrays and nurse sharks among the Blue Hole's marine life. Marine Insight, Visit Centroamerica and Portofino Belize also mention nurse sharks and giant groupers. One caveat: the Blue Hole itself is deep, so this life is mainly on its shallow rim and the surrounding reef rather than throughout the hole. That fits the claim's reference to 'shallow waters', and no source contradicts the claim.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, are excellent swimmers and can often be found swimming in the wild and even in zoos for exercise and to escape heat.
label: supported
reason: The Jerusalem Zoo and World Land Trust both say capybaras are the world's largest rodents. The Jerusalem Zoo calls them excellent swimmers that can dive for up to 5 minutes. San Diego Zoo says they use water and mud to keep cool on hot days, and news footage shows capybaras at a British zoo swimming to cool off during a heatwave. No source says zoo capybaras swim specifically for exercise, but that small detail doesn't conflict with anything, and the rest of the claim is supported.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it is released at a rate of about 2.2 meters per second from a bubble, yet the exact origin of this property is still debated among scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: No source describes a CO2-specific "Kundsen effect." The real Knudsen effect, also called thermal transpiration, is a general gas phenomenon: a temperature difference in a narrow channel or at low pressure drives gas flow. It is not unique to carbon dioxide, has nothing to do with gas released from bubbles at about 2.2 m/s, and its physical origin is well understood rather than debated. Physics Today reports that bubbles in drinks grow at only tenths of a millimeter per second, and no source supports the 2.2 m/s figure. The claim appears to be invented.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which runs for approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) through the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI also says it is the planet's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). Neither snippet names the three oceans, but both describe the ridge as a global system that wraps around the planet between the continents, which includes the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

text: The/ng Ai Grotto located in China, also known as the "Glass Bridge," is a 272 meter (896 feet) long and 1,700 tons impressive architectural structure that was built to resemble a snake.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. The "Ah-ai Grotto" (阿艾石窟) in Xinjiang is a small Buddhist cave found in 1999. It is not a bridge, it has no "Glass Bridge" nickname, and it was not built to look like a snake. China's well-known glass bridges also don't fit the claim's figures. For example, the Zhangjiajie Glass Bridge is 430 m long, not 272 m (896 ft), and no source found describes a 1,700-ton, snake-shaped glass bridge by that name.

text: Three of the four Kennedy brothers who served in the US military during their lifetime (John F. Kennedy, Joe Kennedy Jr., and Robert F. Kennedy) served in World War II.
label: supported
reason: Joe Kennedy Jr. was a Navy aviator who was killed in 1944, and John F. Kennedy commanded PT-109. Both clearly served in World War II. Robert F. Kennedy enlisted in the U.S. Naval Reserve during the war (1943–44) and trained in the Navy's V-12 officer program from 1944 to 1946. Veteran records describe this as WWII Navy service. He then served as an apprentice seaman on the USS Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. in early 1946 and was discharged in May 1946. The fourth brother, Ted Kennedy, served in the Army in 1951–53, after the war. One caveat: RFK never saw combat, and his time aboard ship came after hostilities ended, so calling his service 'in World War II' is a looser description. Overall, the claim matches the evidence.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it contracts when it cools, which can lead to its density increasing as it sinks down in very cold dense fluids.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source describing a "Kundsen effect" as a property of carbon dioxide. The name looks like a misspelling of the Knudsen effect. That term refers to thermal transpiration: a temperature difference makes a gas flow or creates a pressure difference, mostly in rarefied gases or microchannels, as in the Knudsen pump. It applies to gases in general, is not unique to CO2, and has nothing to do with CO2 contracting and sinking in cold, dense fluids. Contracting when cooled is also normal behavior for almost every gas, not something special to CO2. The claim gets both the definition of the effect and its supposed uniqueness wrong.

text: Butler's Gorge, a remote region in Tasmania, Australia, is home to some of the oldest and most well-preserved pieces of Aboriginal rock art in the world, dating back over 40,000 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No source I found links Butlers Gorge to Aboriginal rock art, but none directly rules it out, so the claim can't be confirmed or disproved. Wikipedia and Hydro Tasmania-related pages describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in the Central Highlands. It is known for the Clark Dam, the Butlers Gorge hydroelectric power station and Lake King William, and the 2016 census recorded no residents. Reports on Tasmanian rock art point to other places, such as the Preminghana petroglyphs in the north-west, which are about 4,000 years old. Nothing I found shows rock art at Butlers Gorge, let alone art over 40,000 years old or among the oldest in the world. This makes the claim very doubtful.

text: The Bunny Hop, also known as the Bunny Hug or Single-Handed Bouquet, was a popular dance that originated in the late 19th century in the United States.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the bunny hop is a novelty dance created in 1952 at Balboa High School in San Francisco and made popular by Ray Anthony's song of the same year. It did not originate in the late 19th century. The Bunny Hug is a separate ragtime-era dance from the early 20th century, so it is not another name for the Bunny Hop. I found no source using the name 'Single-Handed Bouquet' for either dance.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, which occurs where the cold, dense water of the East Greenland Current flows down a slope in the ocean.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (EarthSky, Discover Wildlife, TheTravel and Marine Insight) describe the Denmark Strait Cataract, under the strait between Greenland and Iceland, as the world's largest waterfall. Marine Insight says it is the largest by volume of water flow. The sources say it forms when cold, dense water from the Nordic and Greenland Seas plunges down the slope of an underwater ridge into the warmer Irminger Sea, falling about 3,500 m. Marine Insight and Wikipedia say the cold East Greenland Current carries cold, dense water south through the strait. The claim simplifies the source of the overflow water, which comes from the wider Nordic Seas, but no source contradicts any part of it.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that when animals die and fall into the water, their bodies are rapidly preserved and can take on a distinctive, long-lasting, silver color.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The core of the claim checks out. Live Science and Smithsonian, among other reliable sources, confirm that Lake Natron in Tanzania is a highly alkaline soda lake (pH up to about 10.5). They also report that animals dying there are preserved as calcified, 'stone'-like mummies, as shown in Nick Brandt's 2013 photographs. However, none of the sources I found say the bodies turn a distinctive, long-lasting silver color. They describe the remains as calcified or 'stone' and petrified-looking, and Brandt's well-known photos are black and white, so they don't show the actual color. The sources also say the animals died on or near the shore and washed up, not that they fell into the water and were preserved quickly. Because the silver-color detail can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The이버thing, a periodic table element with the atomic number 118, is named after the German scientist Dmitry Mendeleyev's compiler of the periodic table, Glenn Theodore "Ted" Seaborg.
label: contradicted
reason: Element 118 is oganesson (symbol Og), and it is named after the nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian. It is not named after Glenn Seaborg, whose name went to element 106, seaborgium. The claim has other errors too. Mendeleev, who compiled the periodic table, was Russian, not German, and Seaborg had nothing to do with compiling it. The garbled element name at the start of the claim also doesn't refer to any real element.

text: The position of the constellation Orion changes over time due to the Earth's rotation and the movement of the stars, which is known as the process of precession.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the cause of precession wrong. Wikipedia and other sources define axial precession as a slow change in the direction of Earth's rotational axis, caused by gravity, with one full wobble taking about 26,000 years. Precession is not caused by Earth's daily rotation, and it is not the stars' own motion. Earth's spin only makes Orion appear to move across the sky each night, and the stars' slow real movement through space is called proper motion, which is a separate effect. So saying that Earth's rotation plus the movement of the stars is 'known as the process of precession' is incorrect.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that when animals die and fall into the water, their bodies are rapidly preserved and can take on a distinctive, long-lasting red or orange hue due to the water's high pH levels and the presence of algae.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Natron in Tanzania does exist. It is a highly alkaline soda lake, with a pH of up to about 10.5, and animals that die there are preserved as calcified, stone-like mummies. That part of the claim is supported. The red-orange colour is wrong, though. Sources say the lake's water is coloured red and orange by salt-loving haloarchaea and cyanobacteria. They do not say the animal bodies take on a long-lasting red or orange hue. The preserved remains are described as calcified, stone-like carcasses, sealed by sodium carbonate deposits. The claim moves the water's colour onto the carcasses and wrongly says the colouring comes from the high pH.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot-water river, is a natural wonder found deep in the Peruvian Amazon region where the river's temperature remains hot year-round despite being hundreds of miles from any known volcanic activity.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe the Shanay-timpishka, better known as the 'Boiling River of the Amazon', as a geothermally heated river in the Peruvian Amazon that stays hot even though no known active volcanoes are nearby. It also gives average temperatures above 186°F along a 4-mile stretch, and Wikipedia says the river 'maintains its high temperature'. Neither source explicitly says 'year-round', but the river is fed by a steady hydrothermal system, so constant heat is consistent with what they describe.

text: Seeds from a cactus called the "Prickly Pear" can be used to make a jelly, that's a popular dessert in the southern United States.
label: contradicted
reason: Prickly pear jelly is made from the juice of the cactus fruit (the tunas), not from its seeds. Recipe sources say the small, very hard seeds must be strained or filtered out before the juice is made into jelly. The jelly is a known Southwestern specialty, but the claim's statement that it is made from the seeds is wrong.

text: The Grover's cave in Mallorca, Spain, is the world's largest underwater cave system with approximately 230 kilometers of caverns and passageways.
label: contradicted

Guinness World Records and other reports list Mexico's Sistema Sac Actun on the Yucatán Peninsula as the world's longest underwater cave system, at about 347 km. Mallorca's underwater caves are described only as among Europe's largest, not the world's largest. I found no record of a "Grover's cave" in Mallorca at all.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it contracts when it cools, which can lead to its density increasing, allowing it to settle at the bottom of a container.
label: contradicted
reason: The "Knudsen" (misspelled "Kundsen" in the claim) effect has nothing to do with CO2 contracting as it cools. In reliable sources it refers to free-molecular flow and diffusion in rarefied gases or very small pores, where molecules hit the container walls more often than each other. It is not a property unique to CO2. All gases contract and become denser when cooled, and CO2 sinks mainly because its molar mass is higher than air's. The claim therefore misnames and misdescribes the effect.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,389 miles) around the Earth's surface.

One part of the wording is loose: the reaction does not literally turn oxygen into light. Oxygen is a reactant, and the light comes from the chemical energy released when luciferin is oxidized. text: Saltwater crocodiles can hold their breath underwater for up to 1.5 hours and remain at the surface with only their eyes, nostrils, and part of their nose exposed, allowing them to hunt and remain submerged for extended periods.
label: supported
reason: The claim is broadly supported, although its 1.5-hour figure is a conservative upper limit. It also says they can float with only their eyes and nostrils exposed, holding a 'minimum exposure' posture, so they can approach prey unseen. Other sources give 60–90 minutes at rest, and a tourism site says up to 2 hours in colder water. Australia Zoo reports longer dives of up to 8 hours, so 1.5 hours is not the true maximum. That conflict over the exact maximum is the main uncertainty in this verdict, but it does not undercut the core point. Saltwater crocodiles can stay submerged for well over an hour and hunt from a low-exposure posture at the surface.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish, also known as Chironex festivus, is the largest known jellyfish in the world, spanning up to 3 feet in diameter.

Only the Venus' flower basket point was confirmed in the search results; the other two points are based on well-established knowledge.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess,"  however, a more commonly accepted example is "bookkeeper" or "strengthen."

text: The Maasai people of East Africa have a unique tradition of removing their lower eyelid's outer portion, a practice known as "steatite," which is typically done during male initiation ceremonies for spiritual, aesthetic, and social reasons.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and covers a significant portion of the globe.

text: Located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the McDonald's Twenty-Nine Palms Base restaurant, opened in 2011, is the only McDonald's that serves breakfast year-round 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

text: The world's largest waterfall, when measured by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, which occurs where the cold, dense water from the Norwegian Sea flows down a slope in the ocean floor.
