Live Science says the sloping seafloor funnels cold, dense polar water from the Greenland, Norwegian and Iceland seas into the Irminger Sea. Some sources name only the Greenland Sea, so 'Norwegian Sea' is one of several source waters, not the only one. It is not wrong, though.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers from the Arctic to the Antarctic.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI, Guinness World Records and Wikipedia, agree that the global mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Guinness says it runs from the Arctic Ocean through the Atlantic, around Africa, Asia and Australia, and under the Pacific, and the system also extends into the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. Two wording details are a little loose. NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over', and 'from the Arctic to the Antarctic' simplifies a ridge that winds around the globe. Neither detail meaningfully contradicts the main claim.

text: Sweden has a bridge made from ice called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" that is built every winter and melts by spring, allowing snowmobiles to cross over lakes and rivers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim because the tool limit ran out before I got useful results. My searches mostly returned general pages about the ICEHOTEL in Jukkasjärvi, Sweden, which is rebuilt from Torne River ice every winter and melts in spring. None of the results showed a structure called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" that is built every winter so snowmobiles can cross lakes and rivers. Since the named bridge and its claimed use couldn't be confirmed or ruled out, the claim is inconclusive.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal, called the turbellarian rotifer, due to its natural ability to cheat death through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: There is an "immortal jellyfish" that survives through transdifferentiation, but it is Turritopsis dohrnii, not a "turbellarian rotifer." Turbellarians are flatworms and rotifers are a separate group of tiny animals; neither is a jellyfish. Because the claim names the wrong animal, it is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and unexplained natural phenomenon, has been observed to flow continuously without any visible source or outlet, and is often attributed to the Amazon's unique geology and anomalous water patterns.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the Boiling River has no visible source or outlet and calls it unexplained. Wikipedia's entry on the Shanay-timpishka contradicts both points. It lists a known source (Mayantuyacu) and mouth: the river is a tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows on to the Ucayali and the Amazon. Its heat also has a widely accepted scientific explanation, studied by geoscientist Andrés Ruzo: Earth's geothermal heat reaches the surface through fault-fed hot springs. This is not a mystery attributed to anomalous water patterns.

text: The bear species that hibernates the longest is the Panda, which can hibernate for up to 5 months in the winter due to its rare diet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources, including National Geographic Education, say giant pandas do not hibernate. In cold weather they move to warmer areas at lower altitudes, and they can do this because bamboo, their main food, is available all year. So the panda is not the bear that hibernates the longest, and it does not hibernate for up to 5 months.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola using coca leaves, which contain cocaine, and Pepsi initially including sugar beets and molasses, eventually removing from its recipes these goods.
label: contradicted
reason: Coca-Cola's story partly fits the claim: its inventor, John Pemberton, was a morphine addict, and the drink originally used coca leaves. The Pepsi part is wrong. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia and NC Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, say Caleb Bradham created 'Brad's Drink' in 1893. He renamed it Pepsi-Cola in 1898 and sold it as a digestive aid for dyspepsia (indigestion), not as a substitute for morphine. Its name is tied to pepsin and kola nuts, not to sugar beets or molasses. No source supports the claim that Pepsi was made as a morphine alternative or that its original recipe used sugar beets and molasses.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, people still butt beautified due to wearing solely loincloths, leather and animal hides.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled and can't really be checked. Sources on clothing history agree that trousers are a fairly recent invention. One source dates the earliest trouser-like garments to Eurasian horse nomads around 700–500 BC, before Celts and Germanic peoples took them up, and notes that loincloths came before them. That part is roughly consistent with the claim. But the central assertion, that people "still butt beautified" before pants, has no clear meaning, and I found no evidence for it. The claim also says people wore "solely" loincloths, leather and hides for most of history. That is overstated, since woven tunics, robes and togas were common long before trousers. Because one part is meaningless and another is doubtful, I can't call the claim supported or contradicted.

text: Seaweed can be used to produce biofuels, animal feed, and even biodegradable plastics due to its rich nutrient content and ability to absorb and store carbon.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed review on Springer (Discover Sustainability, 2025) describes seaweed being used as animal feed and as a feedstock for biofuels and bioplastics. The same review says seaweed absorbs CO2 efficiently and traps carbon as biomass through photosynthesis, and that it is valued for its nutritional and bioactive compounds. The "due to" wording is loose: carbon absorption is a separate benefit rather than the reason these products can be made. Still, every factual part of the claim is backed by this source and nothing contradicts it.

text: There is a species of shellfish called the sea walnut, also known as Crossota hastata, which has bioluminescent properties and can freeze its body into a protective ball when threatened.
label: contradicted
reason: The sea walnut is Mnemiopsis leidyi. It is a comb jelly (phylum Ctenophora), not a shellfish, and it does not go by the name Crossota hastata. Crossota is a separate genus of hydrozoan jellyfish in the family Rhopalonematidae (phylum Cnidaria). The sea walnut does glow, but its name, its classification and the 'freeze into a ball' behaviour in the claim are wrong or unsupported.

text: The McKinley Tarn, located in the Grand Teton National Park of Wyoming, contains a body of water from the remains of President William McKinley, the 25th President of the United States.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no 'McKinley Tarn' in Grand Teton National Park. Results for the name only showed McKinley tartan kilts, McKinley Lake in Alaska and Lake McKinley in Kansas. The central claim, that the tarn holds water 'from the remains' of President William McKinley, is impossible. It is also contradicted by the well-documented fact that McKinley (the 25th president, assassinated in 1901) is entombed with his wife and daughters at the McKinley National Memorial in Canton, Ohio, not in Wyoming. I could not confirm this burial detail with a search because I hit the search limit, so it rests on established historical record. The only accurate part of the claim is that McKinley was the 25th president, and that does not save the rest.

text: The longest war in recorded history was the Hundred Years' War between England and France, which lasted for a duration of 116 years.
label: contradicted
reason: The Hundred Years' War did last about 116 years (1337–1453), but it was not the longest war in recorded history. Lists of the longest wars put much longer conflicts ahead of it, including the Reconquista (about 781 years), the Roman–Persian Wars (about 721 years) and the Arauco War (nearly 300 years). That means the claim's main point is wrong.

text: Honey is a unique food substance because it's the only one that remains stable indefinitely due to its low moisture content, acidic pH, and antibacterial properties.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey does keep for a very long time, and its low moisture, acidity and antibacterial properties are the right explanation. But the claim's "only one" part is wrong. The search results say salt, sugar and maple sugar also last indefinitely if stored properly, and call honey "one of the few" foods like this, not the only one. The source is a general myth-checking site, not a scientific authority.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests on the continents of South America and Africa are linked by a network of rivers and water systems that predate the continents' separation around 180 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The date in the claim is wrong. Live Science and WorldAtlas both say that about 180 million years ago Gondwana as a whole began to break up. South America and Africa did not split from each other until much later: roughly 140–130 million years ago, with the Atlantic finishing its opening around 117 million years ago. I also found no evidence that today's South American and African rainforests are connected by river systems older than the split. The Atlantic Ocean separates them.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a hot river discovered in 2011, remains a mysterious phenomenon due to its unclear source and geological origin.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say the river's heat source and origin are largely explained. SMU geophysicist Andrés Ruzo's research describes Shanay-timpishka as a non-volcanic, fault-fed hydrothermal system. Chemical analysis shows the water began as rain, possibly from as far as the Andes, which seeps underground, is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, and resurfaces along faults (ScienceAlert, AccuWeather, Slate, Wikipedia). One AccuWeather headline still calls it 'mysterious', but the same article sets out this explanation. The '2011 discovery' wording is also misleading: Ruzo first visited and studied the river in 2011, but local people had known about it for centuries, and ScienceAlert says he was not the first to discover it. Saying it remains a mystery because its source and geological origin are unclear goes against the scientific findings.

text: Seaweed can be used to produce biofuels, animal feed, vitamins, and even alternative clothing materials, making it a highly versatile and sustainable resource.
label: supported
reason: A UNCTAD report (2024) says seaweed is used for food, nutraceuticals, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, aquatic animal and livestock feed, biofertilizer, textiles, and biofuels, including sustainable aviation fuel. It also describes edible seaweed as rich in vitamins (A, B1 and others). That matches the claim's uses: biofuels, animal feed, vitamins as nutraceuticals or nutrients, and textiles for clothing. The same report presents seaweed as a sustainable resource with many uses. The vitamins point is the loosest fit, since the source describes seaweed as rich in vitamins rather than as something used to manufacture them.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural river that one can not find by satellite image, and scientists have struggled to explain how this river has been maintaining its boiling point year-round despite remaining in the rainforest canopy.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is real: it is the Shanay-timpishka in Peru. But two parts of the claim don't hold up. First, the river doesn't stay at boiling point year-round. Atlas Obscura reports that Andrés Ruzo measured an average water temperature of about 187°F, "which isn't quite boiling," with a range of about 120–200°F. Wikipedia says the highest temperature ever recorded was 99.1°C, and that was in a hot spring, not the river itself. Second, scientists have not struggled to explain it. Ruzo's team concluded that a fault-led hydrothermal system heats the water: hot geothermal water rises along fault zones, even though no volcano is nearby. The search results also don't confirm the claim that the river can't be seen in satellite images.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made of white Carrara marble, but the top 18 meters of the steeple is actually made of brick.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim. San Miniato al Monte has one bell tower (campanile), not several steeples. Baccio d'Agnolo rebuilt it starting in 1523 after the earlier tower collapsed in 1499, and it was never finished. One source calls it 'a massive, unplastered stone tower with two levels' and says its planned upper part was never built. The white Carrara and green Prato marble covers the church's façade, not the tower. Another source says the church itself is built of simple stone. No source mentions marble steeples or a brick top section of 18 meters.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers in length and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range. On the length, sources differ slightly: NOAA's current page and WHOI say "nearly 65,000 km," while Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole oceanic ridge system. Several sources also say "over 65,000 km," so the figure in the claim is broadly backed. The sources confirm the ridge runs through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Central Indian Ridge) and Pacific (East Pacific Rise) oceans. "Through the center" is loose wording: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge does split the Atlantic down the middle, but the East Pacific Rise lies in the eastern Pacific, not the center. That is a minor imprecision rather than a contradiction, so the claim is supported overall.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring at the border between Ireland and Northern Ireland, an extraordinary example on how a body of freshwater can lead to a rather cooperative peace agreement even amidst conflict.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a "Lisburn hill spring" exists, or of any jointly managed spring or water-based peace agreement between Ireland and Northern Ireland. Lisburn is a city just southwest of Belfast, on the line between County Antrim and County Down, well inside Northern Ireland and not on the border. The claim also calls Ireland and Northern Ireland "neighboring countries" jointly managing a spring, but Northern Ireland is part of the UK. The core premise conflicts with the well-documented location of Lisburn and has no supporting evidence.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to a 2021 estimate by the Interuniversal Biology group.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million species figure is real, but the claim gets the source and the year wrong. The estimate comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology paper by Camilo Mora and colleagues at the University of Hawaii and Dalhousie University, published with the Census of Marine Life. It was not a 2021 estimate, and no 'Interuniversal Biology group' appears to exist. The figure is also a single best estimate of about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, which covers fungi and protists as well as plants and animals, not a floor of 'over 8.7 million.'

text: Approximately 71% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with around 96.5% of this being seawater and the remaining 3.5% being freshwater sources.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures for surface coverage and ocean share check out, but the freshwater figure is wrong. USGS and other water-fact sources say about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water. However, USGS says freshwater is only about 2.5% of Earth's water, not 3.5%. The other roughly 1% is mostly saline groundwater and saline lakes, so the 3.5% that isn't ocean water is not all freshwater. One less authoritative phys.org article does say the remaining 3.5% is freshwater, but the USGS figure is more reliable. The claim also mixes up surface area with share of total water volume.

text: The Blind Faith double album "Appearance and Other Attractions" sold very well however their 1970 single "Can't Get Out" didn't encourage major labels agreeing to sign the two musicians despite big hits in the public eye.
label: contradicted
reason: Blind Faith only made one studio album, the self-titled "Blind Faith" (Polydor, August 1969), a single LP. They were active only in 1969 and broke up after a few months. My searches turned up no Blind Faith double album called "Appearance and Other Attractions" and no 1970 single "Can't Get Out." The claim's line about "the two musicians" also doesn't fit a four-piece supergroup (Clapton, Baker, Winwood, Grech) that already had a major label behind it. The claim gets the band's discography and history wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible above the water's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration agrees that the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range, but it says the ridge stretches "nearly" 65,000 km, not over 65,000 km. NOAA also says only "more than 90 percent" of the range lies underwater. That means part of the ridge does rise above the sea; Iceland, which sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is an example. So the claim that it is not visible above the water's surface is wrong.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of kalpitiya, Sri Lanka, making it one of the biggest forest area covered with trees in the island.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that mentions anything like 320 million trees in Kalpitiya. The searches for that figure only turned up tree-planting targets in Bangladesh and Canada. Reliable descriptions instead call Kalpitiya a small fishing town on a flat, sandy spit about 50 km long (Wikivoyage, Tikalanka). It is known for its lagoon, kitesurfing, dolphin watching and fishing and farming villages, plus some mangroves along Puttalam lagoon. Sri Lanka's major forests are elsewhere, such as Sinharaja, which travel sources describe as the island's largest rainforest. Also, a peninsula of only a few hundred square kilometres could not physically hold 320 million trees. No source directly states a tree count, but the evidence about the area's sandy, coastal landscape contradicts the claim that it is one of the island's biggest forested areas.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of kalpitiya, Sri Lanka, making it one of the biggest mangrove forests in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for the figure of over 320 million trees in Kalpitiya. Sources do describe the Puttalam Lagoon–Kalpitiya area as having the largest mangrove extent in Sri Lanka, but only at the national level. Mangroves cover just 0.1–0.2% of Sri Lanka's land area, which works out to roughly 100–130 km² for the whole country. That is tiny next to the world's largest mangrove forests, such as the Sundarbans at about 10,000 km². The claim that Kalpitiya is one of the biggest mangrove forests in the world is therefore not credible, and the tree count is unverified.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and solitary nature in the wild, although they can occasionally be seen in small groups, they generally prefer to spend time alone.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Several sources agree that 'embarrassment' is the most common collective noun for giant pandas, and that pandas are mostly solitary in the wild (Animal Corner, HowStuffWorks). What I couldn't confirm is the claim's stated reason for the name. A-Z Animals, ZME Science and HowStuffWorks link the term to pandas' clumsy, lazy-looking behavior, not to shyness. HowStuffWorks also says the word has no scientific origin and is just English whimsy, and A-Z Animals admits nobody really knows why. Because the origin is uncertain and the sources I checked give a different explanation, the 'due to their shy and solitary nature' part can't be verified.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," but a word that is often cited is "strengths," however many sources say the longest one with one syllable is actually "strength," but hardly any English dictionaries consider "stewardess" or word  "strengths"
label: contradicted
reason: "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable English word. It is usually cited as the longest word typed with the left hand alone. Reliable sources name "strengths" (9 letters) as the standard answer. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable English words includes "strengths" and longer candidates like "scraunched", and Guinness gives "strengths" as the longest word with only one vowel. "Strengths" also appears in standard dictionaries, so the claim's statements about "stewardess" and dictionary recognition are false.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river that flows underground before emerging into the Akmé gorge, remains one of the Amazon's most mysterious and unexplained phenomena.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon is real, but two parts of the claim are wrong. First, the heat is not unexplained. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research, reported by National Geographic, traced it to fault-fed hot springs: water seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's natural heat, and rises back up through faults. Second, I found no source that mentions an 'Akmé gorge'. That detail appears to be made up. The river is described as a flowing tributary of the Pachitea River, not as a single river that emerges into a named gorge.

text: A group called Phoenix Alpha a team of neuromorphic engineers at the University of California, are developing research that could one day allow us to record and play back memories.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a group called "Phoenix Alpha" exists as a team of neuromorphic engineers at the University of California, or that it works on recording and playing back memories. Searches for "Phoenix Alpha" returned only unrelated things: video game creatures, the band Phoenix's album "Alpha Zulu," and a GitHub account. The University of California does have related memory research, such as a UCSF-led, UC-funded project with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory on how the brain retrieves memories, which records activity from many neurons. However, none of these sources mention Phoenix Alpha or memory playback. My last search failed because I reached the search limit. Because the key entity can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a geothermal river, is a naturally occurring phenomenon that is believed to be heated by a nearby fault in the Earth's crust, keeping the water at a constant temperature of around 86°F (30°C) year-round.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the temperature wrong. Wikipedia and Earth.com both say the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) gets very hot. The hottest reading was 99.1°C (210.4°F), and the river's average temperature is far above 30°C. A constant 86°F (30°C) is not correct; 86 appears to be a Celsius figure mixed up with Fahrenheit. The sources do support the claim that a geologic fault heats the river.

text: The lubber grasshopper, a species found in the Neotropics, has an unusual characteristic in that its hind legs are underdeveloped, and it has a tendency to hop very little or not at all.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources partly support the claim and partly contradict it. Lubber grasshoppers (family Romaleidae) are mainly Neotropical, and eastern lubbers mostly walk and only rarely or clumsily make short hops. However, the sources do not say the hind legs are underdeveloped. It is the wings that are short and useless for flight. The sources describe the eastern lubber as having "powerful hind legs" for short hops. Horse lubbers have long hind legs that let them jump up to 20 times their body length, and plains lubbers have "oversized hind legs." The claim's main point about underdeveloped hind legs is therefore contradicted.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests on the continents of South America and Africa are linked by a network of rivers and water systems that provide nutrients to each other.
label: contradicted

The documented link between the continents runs through the air: winds carry nutrient-rich Saharan dust across the ocean, and it fertilizes the Amazon. This dust comes from a desert, not from Africa's rainforests, and it moves one way only. No credible source describes a two-way, river-based nutrient exchange between these rainforests.

text: The ancient Egyptians are known to have used a calendar consisting of 365 days, which was only 1/4 of a day longer than our modern calendar.
label: contradicted
reason: The 365-day part is correct. Britannica and Wikipedia both say the ancient Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days. The rest of the claim gets the direction wrong. Wikipedia says this year was 'nearly a quarter of a day shorter than the solar year,' because it had no leap years. Our modern Gregorian calendar averages about 365.2425 days, so the Egyptian year was about 1/4 day shorter than it, not longer.

text: The mysterious Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural hot spring, has been a source of intrigue for scientists and locals alike due to its unusual and unidentified source.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru is real and has intrigued scientists and locals. However, the claim says its heat source is unidentified, and the sources say otherwise. Wikipedia states that the heat is geothermal, and geoscientist Andrés Ruzo has investigated it. The leading explanation is that groundwater is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient and rises along faults, not that it comes from volcanic activity. Atlas Obscura likewise calls it a geothermal feature located away from volcanic or magmatic sources. The claim is also inaccurate in calling it a hot spring, since it is a river heated by geothermal waters.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and unexplained natural phenomenon, is a river that appears to boil and emit steam in the midst of the Peruvian rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim holds up. The Shanay-timpishka, or Boiling River, is in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest. Its water averages about 86–94°C, which is close to boiling, and steam rises from its surface. However, it is wrong to call it an unexplained phenomenon. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo has studied the river since 2011, and reliable sources (ScienceAlert, Discover Wildlife, Atlas Obscura) say it is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient. The hot water reaches the river through fault-fed hot springs, a non-volcanic hydrothermal system. The river was once a mystery, but scientists have since largely explained why it is so hot.

text: The checkered pattern found on the classic umbrellas is a result of the old-fashioned method of manufacturing the canopy, where a round piece of fabric was immediately divided into symmetrical eight parts due to the boring tools of the time which could bore out the perfect circle but could not make more than 8 pie-wedges cut
label: contradicted

text: The reticular activating system in the human brain filters out an estimated 99.9% of all visual and auditory information we receive daily, allowing us to focus on relevant stimuli.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the specific number in this claim, and no trustworthy source supports it. A neuroscience-education source (The Neuroscience School) and a LinkedIn article on neuromyths say the RAS does play a role in filtering, but that its role is commonly exaggerated. They describe it mainly as a brainstem system for arousal and alertness. text: Norway has more than 18,000 islands along its coastlines and islets, despite having a total coastline that is only slightly over 25,148 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia (citing Kartverket) and the CIA World Factbook figures on IndexMundi both give Norway's coastline as 25,148 km. text: The brightness of the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius, is so massive that it would appear 25 times bigger in the sky if it were placed at the same distance as the sun from Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up brightness with size. Sirius is about 25 times as luminous as the Sun (25.4 L☉), but its radius is only about 1.7 times the Sun's. Placed at the Sun's distance from Earth, it would look about 1.7 times as wide in the sky, not 25 times bigger. The 25× figure describes its luminosity (how bright it is), not how large it would appear.

text: There are over 37,000 identified species of ants on Earth, but scientists estimate that the actual number could be as high as 20,000 to 30,000.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says more than 13,800 ant species have been described, out of an estimated total of about 22,000. A myrmecology source (Bolton 2020) gives a similar figure of over 13,837 described species, and Myrmecological News estimates the true total at 20,000–40,000. The claim's figure of 'over 37,000 identified species' is therefore wrong. It also doesn't make sense, because the estimated total it gives (20,000–30,000) is smaller than the number it says is already identified.

text: The shallowest lake in the world, as measured by its maximum depth of approximately 3.3 meters, is Chad's Danakil Depression's Lake Magadi, but if your referring to the average depth, the title is held by Don Juan Pond, with an average depth of around 11 meters (37 feet

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to scientists, but it is estimated that only a tiny fraction, around 1.3 million, have been formally discovered and documented.
label: supported
reason: Mostly supported, though some details are loose. The 2011 study led by Camilo Mora estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), and found that most are still undescribed. ABC's coverage puts the catalogued count near 1.2 million (about 953k animals, 216k plants, 43k fungi, 8k protozoa and others), so 'around 1.3 million' is close. Two details are imprecise: the figure is an estimate of about 8.7 million, not 'over' 8.7 million, and it covers fungi and protists as well as plants and animals. The claim's main point, millions of species with only a small fraction (about 1.2–1.3 million) documented, matches the research.

text: The shortest warp in the universe, discovered in 2020, is the Crab Nebula’s pulsar PSR J1748-2446ad, which protracts only 1.1 milliseconds.
label: contradicted
reason: Several details in the claim are wrong. The discovery paper (Hessels et al. 2006, indexed on NASA ADS) and arXiv papers describe PSR J1748-2446ad as a 716 Hz pulsar with a 1.396 ms spin period. It sits in the globular cluster Terzan 5, not the Crab Nebula, and it was reported in 2006 (found in 2004), not discovered in 2020. Its period is also not 1.1 ms. The word 'warp' doesn't fit either, since the record is for the fastest-spinning pulsar.

text: Islands in the Maldives can actually sink, as they have a substantial amount of water absorbed by the porous coral beneath, making it possible for islands to disappear or alter over time.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the cause wrong. It is true that Maldivian islands change shape and can lose land over time. But Science Feedback and other explainers say the threat comes from rising seas and from sediment that waves and currents move around. These islands are piles of reef sand sitting on old coral, and they shift, adapt and sometimes even grow. Sources say plainly that the islands aren't "sinking"; the sea is rising. No source supports the idea that islands sink because porous coral underneath soaks up water.

text: Islands in the Maldives can actually sink, as they have a substantial amount of water absorbed by the porous coral beneath, making it possible for islands to occasionally disappear under the surface at high tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including The Diplomat, Science Feedback and Atoll Times reporting on recent research, say Maldivian islands are dynamic reef-sand landforms. None of these sources describe islands sinking because porous coral absorbs water, or islands regularly slipping under the surface at high tide. The cause the claim gives is not a real process, and research on island resilience contradicts the claim.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola containing coca leaves that had a small amount of cocaine and Pepsi being developed with 'rare compounds' later found to be no more than cola nuts.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part has some support. John Pemberton was addicted to morphine, he experimented with coca as a substitute, and early Coca-Cola contained coca leaf with traces of cocaine. The Pepsi part is wrong. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893, first as 'Brad's Drink', and sold it as a digestive aid for dyspepsia (indigestion), not as a morphine alternative. So the claim that both Coke and Pepsi were developed as morphine alternatives is false. The 'rare compounds' detail is also misleading: Pepsi's recipe was described as vanilla, rare oils and kola nut extract, so 'rare' referred to oils in the recipe. Nothing suggests these compounds were later revealed to be only cola nuts.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola using coca leaves, which contain cocaine, and Pepsi was developed from morphine substitute coca leaves with a different plant that included kola nuts.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part is roughly right. John Pemberton, a morphine addict, made coca-based drinks partly as a morphine substitute, and the original Coke contained coca leaf extract. The Pepsi part is wrong. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893 as "Brad's Drink," a fountain drink meant to aid digestion (dyspepsia) and boost energy. It was not made as a morphine alternative and was not developed from coca leaves. Its name comes from dyspepsia/pepsin plus kola nut, and it contained kola nuts, sugar, vanilla and oils. Wikipedia and Tasting Table both describe this origin.

text: Cotton balls were first made from cotton by mechanically spinning short fibers into fluffy clusters, but before that, humans used dried and shredded mushroom caps as a substitute for cotton balls in medical practices.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the claim, and parts of it look doubtful. Wikipedia's cotton pad article says there was no single inventor and that cotton's sanitary use probably goes back to its domestication. It credits Joseph Voss's 1937 machine, which unrolled cotton and cut it into pads, with bringing cotton balls and pads into wide use. My searches found nothing saying cotton balls were made by mechanically spinning short fibres into clusters, which doesn't match how they're made: spinning produces yarn, not loose balls. On the mushroom part, sources say amadou from the tinder fungus Fomes fomentarius was used as a wound dressing and to stop bleeding. That material is a felt-like layer from a hard shelf fungus, not dried and shredded mushroom caps. No source describes it as a stand-in for cotton balls or as coming before them. With these parts unsupported or only loosely related, the evidence doesn't settle the claim either way.

text: The highest recorded level of atmospheric carbon dioxide in human history was 482.4 parts per million in May 2022, set at a Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory says CO2 at Mauna Loa peaked at about 421 ppm in May 2022, not 482.4 ppm. The claim's figure is wrong. It is also no longer the record: Mauna Loa readings have gone higher since 2022, with peaks of about 424 ppm in 2023 and 427 ppm in 2024.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although some claim "smiley" could also be considered the longest single-syllable word.
label: contradicted
reason: "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It is better known as a long word you can type with only the left hand. "Smiley" has two syllables. A fact-check found that the longest one-syllable words in common use have nine letters, such as "screeched", "strengths", "scratched" and "stretched". Rarer ten-letter words like "scraunched" and "strengthed" also exist.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is day and only see polarized light at night, due to a unique visual system.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying danios (Danio or Danionin fish) see in full color by day but only polarized light at night. Studies of zebrafish (Danio rerio) describe ordinary vertebrate vision: UV-sensitive and other cones, plus rods. One study tested zebrafish color preferences at midnight and found they differed from daytime preferences. That suggests they still respond to color at night, at least when lit, which argues against the claim. However, that study does not directly test polarization vision. The searches turned up polarization-vision research on other animals, such as crabs, anchovies and sunfish, but nothing tying this day/night pattern to danios. The term 'danion' is also vague, since it could mean any of several species. Because the specific mechanism is neither confirmed nor directly disproved, the evidence is not enough to decide.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal, called the turbellarian rotifer, due to its natural ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process known as transdifferentiation.

But that species is Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." There is no jellyfish called the "turbellarian rotifer." Turbellarians are flatworms and rotifers are tiny invertebrates in a separate group; neither is a jellyfish. Because the claim gives the wrong name, it is contradicted.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 0.137 percent, but in the 1920s a court case led to standardization, resulting in a fixed volume of 231 cubic inches, which is 3.785 liters.
label: contradicted
reason: The 231-cubic-inch figure (about 3.785 L) is correct, but the history in the claim is wrong. Britannica and Wikipedia say the wine gallon was set at 231 cubic inches by a Queen Anne statute in 1706–1707. The U.S. later kept that definition, so it did not come from a court case in the 1920s. The opening phrase about a gallon's 'length' varying by up to 0.137 percent makes no sense, because a gallon measures volume, not length, and no source supports that figure.

text: The reticular activating system in the human brain filters out an estimated 99% of incoming information, allowing the mind to focus on the most important details.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Plenty of pop-psychology and self-help sites (Substack, Medium, Ahead, coaching blogs) say the RAS filters out about 99% of incoming information. However, none of them cite primary research for the 99% number. Scientific sources such as ScienceDirect, PMC/Cureus and Study.com describe the RAS's main role as controlling arousal and the sleep-wake cycle, and none of them give a 99% filtering figure. A neuroscience educator (neuroscienceschool.com) calls the RAS-as-attention-filter idea an exaggerated myth. A LinkedIn article critiquing 'neuromythology' agrees the RAS does some filtering through its connections to the thalamus but gives no 99% figure. So the general idea that the RAS helps filter sensory input has some support, but the specific 99% estimate comes only from low-reliability popular sources and is disputed. Because the evidence is mixed and the key number can't be verified from credible sources, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater in the Denmark Strait, where the cold water from the Arctic Ocean sinks beneath the warmer waters of the Irminger Current.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Denmark Strait cataract, between Greenland and Iceland, as the world's largest waterfall. It is underwater, with water dropping about 3,500 m (11,500 ft) at a flow of about 175 million cubic feet per second, far more than any waterfall on land. The cold, dense polar water from the Nordic or Arctic seas, including the Greenland Sea, sinks beneath the warmer, less dense water of the Irminger Sea, where the warm Irminger Current flows. Sources say 'Nordic Seas' and 'Irminger Sea' rather than 'Arctic Ocean' and 'Irminger Current,' but these differences in wording do not contradict the claim.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and unexplained natural phenomenon, has been observed to flow continuously without any visible source or outlet, and is often attributed to the Amazon's unique geography and hydrology.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river has no visible source or outlet, and that is wrong. Wikipedia and other sources describe the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) as a tributary of the Pachitea River. It rises at Mayantuyacu and drains into the Pachitea, which flows on to the Ucayali and then the Amazon. Its heat is also explained: it comes from geothermal upwellings of hot groundwater along faults. So calling it unexplained, with no source or outlet, is contradicted.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," but it is actually not a one-syllable word and can be argued that the longest one-syllable words are stigma or scout.
label: contradicted

Trustworthy sources such as Wikipedia, Lingoda and FunTrivia name nine-letter words like "screeched," "scratched" and "strengths" as the usual candidates for the longest one-syllable English word. Wikipedia's list also includes longer contenders such as "schmaltzed." "Stewardesses" is often described as the longest word typed with only the left hand, not the longest one-syllable word. It has three syllables. The claim's suggested alternatives also fail: "stigma" has two syllables, and "scout" has only five letters, so neither is a credible longest one-syllable word.

text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space, although this is a common myth, with the wall being over 13,000 miles long, it is only about 30 feet wide and blends in with the surrounding terrain making it barely visible to the naked eye from a low Earth orbit.
