Vocal.media says the wall winds across more than 13,000 miles but is only about 20–30 feet wide. It also says the wall is extremely hard, if not impossible, to see with the naked eye from low Earth orbit. Grunge gives the same 13,000-mile length and a maximum width of 32 feet. It adds that the wall's colour doesn't contrast enough with the land around it. That fits 'about 30 feet wide' and 'blends in with the surrounding terrain'. 'Barely visible' is a slightly weaker phrase than the sources' 'difficult if not impossible', but it is broadly consistent. Both sources are popular-media sites rather than primary or scientific sources.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Delta Scuti, a mountain range on Jupiter's moon Io that stretches approximately 108 miles (174 kilometers) in length.
label: contradicted
reason: Delta Scuti is not a mountain range on Io. It is a variable star in the constellation Scutum, and also the name of a class of pulsating variable stars. The search results also point to Iapetus's equatorial ridge as the solar system's great mountain range: it is about 1,300 km long and runs around roughly 75% of the moon's equator. That makes the claim's 174 km range on Io wrong.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola using coca leaves, which contain cocaine, and Pepsi-Cola using pepsin, an enzyme found in the stomach.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part mostly checks out. Pemberton was addicted to morphine and tried coca/cocaine-based drinks as a substitute, and Coke did originally use coca leaves. The Pepsi part is wrong. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi ('Brad's Drink') as a digestive aid sold as a cure for indigestion (dyspepsia), not as a morphine alternative. Sources also tie the name to dyspepsia and only loosely to pepsin, so the claim that both drinks began as morphine alternatives is false.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have shown that women with a significantly shorter index finger compared to their ring finger have an increased risk of developing heart disease.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the direction of the finding backwards and overstates how the measure is used. Studies of the index-to-ring finger ratio (2D:4D) in women, such as Kumar et al. in North-West Indian women, link a HIGH right-hand 2D:4D to coronary artery disease. A high ratio means a relatively longer index finger, or shorter ring finger. The claim instead says a shorter index finger relative to the ring finger raises risk. Other studies found no link in women at all: a Chinese angiography study found no significant difference in 2D:4D between women with coronary artery disease and controls. The research also treats 2D:4D as a possible marker under investigation, not a tool that is 'often used' to assess heart disease risk.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of kalpitiya, Sri Lanka, making it one of the biggest forested areas in Asia.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that mentions 320 million trees in Kalpitiya or calls it one of Asia's biggest forested areas. Reliable travel sources describe it as a narrow, sandy coastal peninsula between the Indian Ocean and Puttalam Lagoon, known for beaches, dunes, salt pans, mangroves, kitesurfing and dolphin watching. The large forested area nearby is Wilpattu National Park, which lies across the bay and is not part of Kalpitiya. No source states the tree count directly, but the claim doesn't fit the documented geography of a small coastal town.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual trees, which is roughly 17% of all the trees on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The 390 billion figure is right: ter Steege et al. (2013) estimated about 390 billion trees in the Amazon, counting trunks at least 10 cm across, and Nature and the Field Museum both report it. The 17% figure is wrong. The Earth has about 3 trillion trees (Crowther et al. 2015, also cited by Amazon Aid), so 390 billion is only about 13% of the world's trees, not 17%. The claim also says "over" 390 billion, while the sources say "around" 390 billion.

text: The world's smallest particle, the neutrino, has a mass of less than 20 MeV, but its actual mass is yet to be precisely measured due to its weak interaction with matter.
label: supported
reason: The claim's main points hold up. The loosest direct upper limit on any neutrino mass comes from the ALEPH experiment, which put the tau neutrino below 18.2 MeV/c² at 95% confidence. That is under 20 MeV, and the limits for the other flavors are far tighter: KATRIN puts the electron neutrino below 0.8 eV. No experiment has yet measured the actual masses precisely, mainly because neutrinos interact so weakly with matter. Two caveats: the 20 MeV bound is very loose, and "world's smallest particle" is loose wording, since photons and gluons have no mass at all. Neutrinos are better described as the lightest known particles that have mass. Neither point contradicts the claim's numbers, so I judged it supported.

text: ктарое дерево живущее уже более 5 тысяч лет обнаружено в зелёном районе деревни Сайор, в Восточной Африке, и это дерево фикуса является старейшим деревом на Земле, согласно данным, полученным при помощи радиоуг
label: contradicted
reason: Я не нашёл ни одного источника о 5000-летнем фикусе в деревне «Сайор» в Восточной Африке, и в базе Methuselah такого дерева тоже нет. По надёжным данным старейшими деревьями на Земле считаются другие. EarthDate называет старейшим известным деревом сосну остистую Мафусаил (Great Basin bristlecone pine) в Калифорнии: в 2022 году ей было около 4854 лет. Есть и другой претендент: в найденном материале упоминается, что в Чили обнаружили самое старое дерево. Это чилийская фицройя («Прадедушка», Gran Abuelo), её возраст оценивают примерно в 5000 с лишним лет. Ни одно из этих деревьев не фикус и не растёт в Восточной Африке. Поэтому утверждение, что старейшее дерево на Земле — восточноафриканский фикус, противоречит найденным данным.

text: Saltwater crocodiles can hold their breath underwater for up to 1.5 hours and remain at the surface with only their eyes, nostrils, and part of their snout exposed.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The second half of the claim holds up. Animal Diversity Web, the NT Government's Be Crocwise site and a Journal of Experimental Biology paper all say saltwater crocodiles lie in the water with only their eyes and nostrils showing, and the nostrils sit on the snout. The 'up to 1.5 hours' figure is not confirmed. No source I found gives 1.5 hours. Be Crocwise and SLS Beachsafe say 'at least one hour' or 'more than an hour.' Other sources go further: Leo Zoo and another site say up to two hours, and Australia Zoo reports up to eight hours from its studies. These higher figures conflict with 1.5 hours as a maximum, while the 'more than an hour' sources fit it. Because the specific figure is neither directly confirmed nor consistently contradicted, I can't settle that part.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs down the center of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the global mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and the whole ridge system as 80,000 km, so "over 65,000 km" is fair, though some sources say "nearly" 65,000 km. The ridge does run down the middle of the Atlantic (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) and through the Indian Ocean. The claim leaves out other parts, such as the East Pacific Rise, but it doesn't say anything false.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although some claim "rhythm" can be longer if emphasizing the syllable stress.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), not one. It's actually known as the longest word you can type with only the left hand. A fact-check found that the longest one-syllable words in common use have nine letters: "screeched", "strengths", "scratched", "stretched" and "scrounged". Rarer ten-letter examples like "scraunched" and "strengthed" also exist. "Rhythm" is usually counted as two syllables and has only six letters, so it is not a candidate either.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which is now considered a prehistoric relative of the hippopotamus.
label: contradicted
reason: Stegolophodon is not a prehistoric relative of the hippopotamus. Wikipedia and Mindat both describe it as an extinct genus of proboscideans (order Proboscidea, family Stegodontidae), which makes it a relative of elephants that may have given rise to Stegodon. The claim that the short-eared elephant is extinct also appears false: the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus) is a living species. However, the one search I ran covered Stegolophodon, not the shrew.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, is often referred to as the narrowest place on Earth's land surface.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no source that calls Butlers Gorge the 'narrowest place on Earth.' Wikipedia describes it only as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with a population of nil in the 2016 census, near Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge hydroelectric power station. The nickname 'narrowest place on Earth' belongs to the Glass Window Bridge on Eleuthera in the Bahamas, according to The Weather Channel and Eleuthera sources. No result supports the claim.

text: The linguistic Diversity Tree is estimated to have more than 7,097 known languages, but it's believed that there may be as many as 10,000 to 15,000 total languages spoken worldwide.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything called the "linguistic Diversity Tree," so it's unclear what the claim refers to. The 7,097 figure is real: it is Ethnologue's 2016 count of known living languages, confirmed by Wikipedia and the W&M Libraries' database description. However, no reliable source I found says there may be 10,000 to 15,000 languages in total. Sources generally say there are "more than 7,000" languages, and note that experts don't agree on an exact number. One key part of the claim can't be verified, and the main subject is unclear.

text: Located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, Iceland's Vestmannaeyjar island volcanic eruption created the world's largest crack of ice, which split from a peninsula in 1991 into a small island.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources list Vestmannaeyjar's eruptions as 1637–38, 1896, Surtsey in 1963–67 (which formed a new island) and Heimaey/Eldfell in 1973. None occurred in 1991. The eruptions built volcanic islands and cones; none created a "world's largest crack of ice" or split a peninsula off into an island. The islands also sit just off Iceland's south coast, not in the middle of the Atlantic. The claim seems to be fabricated.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Yanachaga-Chemillén National Park", is a natural river that appears to boil due to a combination of geothermal activity and rainwater flowing underground, creating a warm and mysterious result.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up. Sources describe the Shanay-Timpishka ("Boiling River of the Amazon") as a natural, non-volcanic geothermal feature: rainwater soaks deep underground, is heated by the Earth's internal heat, and rises back to the surface. The claimed alias is wrong, though. The river is in the Honoria district of Puerto Inca Province, Huánuco region, near Mayantuyacu (about 8.81°S, 74.74°W). Yanachaga–Chemillén National Park is a separate protected area in the Pasco region (about 10.35°S, 75.45°W), roughly 190 km away. No source calls the river the "Boiling River of the Yanachaga-Chemillén National Park" or places it inside that park.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs along the floor of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). It winds across the seafloor between the continents, including through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. One small wording difference: NOAA says "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over." Other sources give figures as high as about 80,000 km when the whole ridge system is counted. That uncertainty is minor, and the main parts of the claim are supported.

text: The longest reigning monarch in recorded history is King Louis XIV of France, who ruled for an impressive 72 years and 110 days from 1643 to 1715.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia's list of longest-reigning monarchs, WorldAtlas and the Monarchies wiki, say Louis XIV reigned 72 years and 110 days (1643–1715). They call this the longest verified reign of any sovereign monarch in history. There is one caveat. Sobhuza II of Swaziland reigned longer, but most of his reign was as a non-sovereign ruler. Some legendary rulers, such as Pepi II, are claimed to have reigned longer, but their dates can't be verified. Under the usual sense of a verifiable sovereign monarch, the claim holds.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," mainly due to its complex spelling and multiple syllable pronunciations despite being commonly thought of as having a single syllable.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It's actually known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand. Fact-checkers name nine-letter words like "screeched," "strengths," "scratched" and "stretched" as the longest one-syllable words in common use. Rarer ten-letter words such as "scraunched" and "strengthed" are sometimes mentioned too.

text: Three of the four Kennedy brothers who served in the US military during their lifetime (John, Robert, and Joseph) were awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for their heroism.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Of the three brothers it names, only John F. Kennedy received the Navy and Marine Corps Medal, which he was given for rescuing his crew after PT-109 sank. The Naval History and Heritage Command says Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his drone bomber mission, a different and higher decoration. Robert Kennedy served briefly as a Navy seaman apprentice aboard the USS Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. near the end of WWII and did not receive a heroism medal. Ted Kennedy served in the Army.

text: The International Date Line (IDL) is an imaginary line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole and divides the world into two days, with dates changing at midnight when crossing from west to east.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that the International Date Line is an imaginary line running roughly from the North Pole to the South Pole. However, the date does not change at midnight because of the line. It changes the moment a traveler crosses it, at any time of day. Travelling east (from west to east) moves the calendar back one day, and travelling west moves it forward one day. For example, a two-hour flight from Tonga to Samoa arrives the day before it left. The claim misstates how the date changes.

text: A rare species of jellyfish found in the North Sea called the "Pelagia noctiluca" is bioluminescent, producing a blue glow in the dark.
label: contradicted
reason: Parts of the claim hold up. Pelagia noctiluca (the mauve stinger) is bioluminescent: it glows when disturbed, and its name means roughly "night light." It also does occur in the North Sea, where Ecomare lists it among the region's glowing organisms. But it is not a rare species. Sources describe it as widespread in warm and temperate waters, and it is known for large swarms, especially in the Mediterranean, where Meduseo calls it the jellyfish vacationers fear most. Northeast Atlantic surveys also recorded outbreaks in 2007–2008. Calling it a "rare species" is therefore wrong. The search results also never confirmed that its glow is specifically blue; the blue-light descriptions I found were about other organisms, such as Noctiluca scintillans and sea sparkle.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests on the continents of South America and Africa are linked by a network of rivers and water systems that predate the continents' present separation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Mongabay's worldrainforests.com says the Amazon River may once have flowed westward as part of a "proto-Congo" river system while South America and Africa were joined in Gondwana. That is only a hedged hypothesis ("perhaps"), and it describes an ancient drainage system. The same source says the Amazon reversed to flow eastward about 10 million years ago, when the Amazon rainforest formed, long after the continents split. No source I found shows that today's Amazon and Congo rainforests are "inter-dependent" or currently linked by a shared river network. The claim is partly backed by a speculative idea about the past, and its main present-tense claim is unverified and doubtful.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of organisms that have existed on Earth, but scientists have only formally identified and named around 8.7% of them, also known as 1% of species on the planet being described.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) estimates how many species are alive on Earth today. It does not count every species that has ever existed. The same work says about 1.2 million species have been catalogued, which is roughly 14% of the estimate. It also says 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undescribed. That means the claim's 8.7% described figure is wrong. Its line that this is 'also known as 1%' contradicts its own 8.7% and is also wrong.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that when animals die and fall into the water, their bodies are rapidly preserved and can take on a distinctive, long-lasting calcite or sodium carbonate coating, often turning them a calcified white color.
label: supported
reason: Live Science and National Geographic both describe Lake Natron in northern Tanzania as a highly alkaline soda lake with a pH of up to about 10.5. They say animals that die there, such as birds and bats, are preserved as 'calcified mummies' because of sodium carbonate in the water. Nick Brandt's well-known photos show these salt-encrusted, stone-like white bodies. The sources don't specifically measure how fast the preservation happens, but the claim's main points match their reporting.

text: The extremely rare meteorite known as the "A ValueEventListener" was found in Algeria in 2019, weighing approximately 160 kilograms and selling for over 1.2 million euros.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No meteorite called "A ValueEventListener" turns up in any search result. ValueEventListener is the name of a programming interface in Google's Firebase software for Android, not a meteorite. Because the claim's subject doesn't clearly refer to any real object, its details can't be checked. These are the find in Algeria in 2019, the weight of about 160 kg and the sale for over €1.2 million. The Algerian meteorites that do appear in the results are Erg Chech 002, NWA 13441 and Oued Sfayat, and none of them is linked to that name or those figures.

text: The ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy have one of the highest concentrations of ice in the world, which is home to unique species of life that exist nowhere else on earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any identifiable place called the "ghiaccio stalactite caves" in Italy. "Ghiaccio" just means "ice" in Italian, so the claim has no clear subject. Studies do describe ice caves in northeastern Italy with little-studied cold-adapted wildlife, some of it possibly endemic. However, no source says any Italian cave has one of the world's highest concentrations of ice, or that it holds species found nowhere else on Earth. The claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The linguistic Diversity Tree is estimated to have more than 7,097 known languages, but it is believed there could be over 10,000 languages spoken worldwide in remote communities.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything called a "linguistic Diversity Tree," so it's unclear what the claim is referring to. The 7,097 figure does exist: it's Ethnologue's 2016 count of known living languages (Wikipedia; W&M Libraries). But that number is an exact count, not "more than 7,097." I also found no trustworthy source saying there could be over 10,000 languages spoken in remote communities; mainstream estimates are about 7,000 to 7,500. Because the main subject has no clear referent and the 10,000 figure can't be checked, the claim can't be confirmed.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow when they're alone, as meowing is often a way for them to communicate with other cats.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the reverse of the claim's reasoning. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress both say adult cats seldom meow to each other. They talk to other cats mainly through scent, marking and body language, and they meow mostly to get attention from humans, a habit that grew out of domestication. The idea that cats have a "unique ability" not to meow when alone because meowing is for other cats is therefore not supported.

text: The Human Deep Brain Stimulation has the ability to clump proteins that are associated with neurological diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's to a block making disease progression much slower.
label: contradicted
reason: The available evidence points the other way. A preclinical study in Brain Stimulation found that electrical stimulation and deep brain stimulation (DBS) reduced toxic alpha-synuclein oligomers in rat models of Parkinson's, and suggested this might slow progression. So DBS was linked to reducing protein clumping, not to clumping proteins into a block. That finding came from rat models, not humans, and it did not show that DBS slows Parkinson's or Alzheimer's progression in people. Reviews note that DBS is established for managing Parkinson's motor symptoms, while its effect on disease progression is still unproven.

text: The highest recorded human body temperature in space is of TessHB standing at 39°C (102.2°F), which occurred when an astronaut was in space.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no astronaut or record called "TessHB." The name seems to be made up. The 39°C figure is also wrong. A Charité study of ISS astronauts, published in Scientific Reports in 2017, found that crew members' core body temperatures went above 40°C during exercise in space. Their resting temperatures rose to about 38°C. Since temperatures above 40°C were recorded, 39°C (102.2°F) cannot be the highest temperature recorded in space.

text: The Taj Mahal in India is made up of over 28 different types of precious and semi-precious stones, including jade, jasper, and turquoise.
label: supported
reason: Rock & Gem Magazine says that about 28 types of gemstones were inlaid in the Taj Mahal's white marble. It names jade from China, jasper from Punjab and turquoise from Tibet among them. Other common sources give the same count of 28 precious and semi-precious stones. Two caveats: sources say 28 or 'some 28', not 'over 28', and the stones are decorative inlay, so the building isn't literally 'made up of' them. I treated these as small wording differences rather than contradictions. The main points, roughly 28 stone types including jade, jasper and turquoise, are supported.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it contracts when it cools, which can lead to its density increasing with temperature when interacting with a container, unlike most other gases that expand with temperature.
label: contradicted
reason: No property called a "Kundsen" (Knudsen) effect belongs only to carbon dioxide. The Knudsen effect, also called thermal transpiration, is a general behavior of rarefied gases: a temperature difference in narrow channels drives gas flow or keeps a pressure difference in place. It applies to any gas, including hydrogen and gas mixtures, and is what Knudsen pumps rely on. It does not make CO2 denser as it gets hotter. Like other gases, CO2 expands and becomes less dense when heated at constant pressure, so the claim gets the effect's meaning wrong and wrongly says it is unique to CO2.

text: The sentry plant, also known as the "pitcher plant," has a unique lower leaf that functions as a snap trap, quickly closing in just 0.1 seconds to capture insects for nutrient digestion.
label: contradicted
reason: In reliable plant references, "sentry plant" is another name for Agave americana, the century plant. It is not a carnivorous plant and is not called a pitcher plant. Pitcher plants catch prey with pitfall traps: insects fall into tube-shaped leaves filled with fluid. The leaf that snaps shut in a fraction of a second belongs to the Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula), not to any sentry plant or pitcher plant. The claim mixes up separate plants and trap types.

text: The-colored planet in our solar system is Venus, which appears white to the human eye due to its thick atmosphere composed of sulfuric acid droplets and aerosols.
label: supported
reason: The garbled phrase "The-colored planet" probably means "the white-colored planet." Read that way, the claim is supported. Space.com says Venus looks like a brilliant white object in the sky. Astronomy Notes describes Venus as a yellow-white planet in visible light, and says its thick cloud layer of sulfuric acid droplets reflects about 70% of sunlight. Other sources also say Venus's white and yellowish clouds are mainly sulfuric acid droplets. Nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered on Earth, according to a 2021 estimate by the International Institute for Species Exploration.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on three counts. First, Wikipedia says the International Institute for Species Exploration disbanded in 2018, so it could not have issued a 2021 estimate. Second, its best-known figure is a 2011 estimate it contributed to, which put the total number of species thought to exist on Earth at about 8.7 million, not 'over 10 million discovered.' Third, only about 2 million species have actually been formally described; this last point comes from general knowledge of the institute's reports, not from the search result.

text: The highest recorded human body temperature in space is of TessHB who had a body temperature of 41.3°C (106.3°F) in August 2016 during a spacewalk on the International Space Station.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anyone called "TessHB" in any search result. I also found no record of a 41.3°C (106.3°F) body temperature during an August 2016 spacewalk on the ISS. Trustworthy sources do cover astronaut body temperature, mainly the 2017 Charité study in Scientific Reports. They report that core temperature in space rises about 1°C at rest and can reach about 40°C (104°F) during exercise, but they name no record holder. These sources don't confirm the claim and don't directly contradict it. The person named also has no clear referent, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers across the globe and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole ridge system. Other sources say "over 65,000 km." Sources also describe the system as running through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Pacific (East Pacific Rise) and Indian Oceans. One caveat: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly 65,000 km" rather than "over," but other sources back the higher figure, so this small difference doesn't contradict the claim.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which actually once lived in Asia.
label: contradicted
reason: No recognised species is called simply the "short-eared elephant." The closest match is the short-eared (round-eared) elephant shrew, Macroscelides proboscideus. That species still lives in southern Africa, and Wikipedia lists it as Least Concern under the IUCN, so it is not extinct. Stegolophodon is an extinct proboscidean genus that lived in Asia from the Miocene to the Pliocene, so that part of the claim is correct. However, I found no source that calls Stegolophodon a "short-eared elephant." Because the claim's main statements are false or unsupported, it is contradicted.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various animals and insects due to their durable, fibrous, and nutritious nature.
label: supported
reason: Coconuts are the fruit of the coconut palm, a tree. Search results show that animals use them for both shelter and food. The coconut octopus is known for using discarded coconut shells as shelter. Coconut crabs climb coconut palms and eat a range of foods, including coconuts, though Wikipedia says coconuts are not a major part of their diet. No result contradicted the claim. The specific mention of insects was not directly confirmed, but the claim is broad and nothing found argues against it, so it is labeled supported.

text: The periodic table's element with the highest atomic number is oxygen-118 (Og 118) but this has changed several times; briefly the highest number belonged to Moscovium which had a higher number however due to changes in revisions this is now held by oerk Guy Og-118 still basically unstable.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Element 118 is oganesson (symbol Og), not "oxygen-118"; oxygen is element 8. Oganesson has the highest atomic number of any known element. Moscovium is element 115, so it never had a higher atomic number than Og-118, and no revision has moved the top spot between them. The claim's only accurate point is that Og-118 is very unstable.

text: The Arctic fox has one of the warmest fur colors in animals due to its thick double coat, which can trap warm air and protect it from freezing temperatures as low as -58°F (-50°C).
label: supported
reason: WWF Canada says the Arctic fox has "the warmest fur of any mammal" and can survive Arctic temperatures as low as -50°C (-58°F). The fox's thick, dense, insulating double coat is widely documented. The claim's wording "warmest fur colors" is odd: fur colour doesn't make an animal warm. I read it as meaning "warmest fur," and on that reading every part of the claim is backed by the source and none of it is contradicted.

text: The country of Singapore has the highest percentage of OPT (Optometrists, Pharmacists, Nurses, Doctors) professionals globally, making it a hub for advanced healthcare.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results show that Singapore does not lead the world in health-worker density. Cuba has the most doctors per capita, at about 8.4 to 9.4 per 1,000 people. Monaco, Georgia, Greece and several European countries follow, and Singapore is not in the top 10. Singapore has roughly 2.5 doctors per 1,000 people, which is not among the highest. Also, 'OPT' is not a recognised acronym for optometrists, pharmacists, nurses and doctors. No reliable source says Singapore has the highest share of these professionals globally.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, is a notorious spot known for having the second-deepest gorge in the world with an estimated depth of approximately 2,500 feet (762 meters).
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is real, but the claim gets it wrong. Wikipedia and Wikidata describe it as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It was gazetted in 1971, had a population of zero in the 2016 census, and is known for a Hydro Tasmania dam and power station (Clark Dam / Butlers Gorge Power Station). Neither source mentions a famous gorge about 762 m deep, let alone the second-deepest in the world. The gorges usually ranked deepest are elsewhere, such as Yarlung Tsangpo, Kali Gandaki and Cotahuasi. The dam built across this gorge is a modest structure, roughly 67 m high, which doesn't fit a 2,500 ft gorge. The 'second-deepest gorge' claim appears to be made up.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river that flows underground before emerging into the Akmé gorge, remains one of the Amazon's greatest unsolved mysteries.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon is real. However, I found no source that mentions an 'Akmé gorge' or describes the river flowing underground and then emerging into such a gorge. Wikipedia gives its source as Mayantuyacu and its mouth as the Pachitea River. The claim that it 'remains one of the Amazon's greatest unsolved mysteries' is also contradicted. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo studied the river and found that its heat comes from geothermal sources, not volcanoes: groundwater is heated deep underground and rises back up through faults. Details such as the underground plumbing and fault geometry are still being studied, but the basic phenomenon has been explained.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Temruma River or the "Doctor's River", remains a source of fascination due to its steady temperature of around 100°F (38°C) which is over 10°F (5.6°C) higher than the temperature of the surrounding water and air
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River of the Amazon is Shanay-Timpishka in Peru. It is not known as the "Temruma River" or the "Doctor's River." Andrés Ruzo, the geoscientist who studied it, measured an average water temperature of about 86°C (around 187°F), and the hottest reading was 99.1°C (210°F). That is far hotter than the claimed steady 100°F (38°C), so the claim's temperature is wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as Earth's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). The ridge does run down the middle of the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), through the Indian Ocean, and into the Arctic (Gakkel Ridge). It also extends into the Pacific (East Pacific Rise), but there it is not in the middle of the ocean. The claim doesn't say the ridge is found only in those three oceans, so leaving out the Pacific doesn't make it wrong.

text: The vibrant flower, the infamous Opal Flower or the more popular known yuka bird flower(yuca), which is " Opal flower" actually belongs to the orchid family, that is scientifically known as  Zygopetalum.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats three different things as one plant. Zygopetalum is an orchid genus, which Gardenia.net confirms. But the yucca ("yuca"), New Mexico's state flower according to the New Mexico Secretary of State, is not an orchid or a Zygopetalum; it belongs to the asparagus family (Asparagaceae). That classification comes from general botanical knowledge, not from the search results. Yuca, or cassava, is also a different plant, in the spurge family. I found no reliable source that uses "Opal flower" or "yuka bird flower" as a name for Zygopetalum. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could check this further, so I may have missed a source. Still, the core claim that the yucca flower is the orchid Zygopetalum is false.

text: There are over 87 million stars in the Milky Way galaxy, but we can only see a few of them because most are invisible due to their vast distances and lack of light.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA and other astronomy sources put the Milky Way at about 100–400 billion stars. Strictly speaking, that is "over 87 million," but the claim's figure is off by more than a thousand times and badly misstates the scale. So the core number is misleading. The second part is roughly right: only a few thousand stars are visible to the naked eye, a tiny fraction of the galaxy. But distance and faintness aren't the only reasons. Interstellar dust also hides many stars. Because the main figure misrepresents the actual count, I've labeled the claim contradicted, though a strictly literal reading could call that part technically true.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1999, is a 4.2-meter-long Redwood tree trunk found in the 1920s that had been disturbed from its natural environment in Tasmania and is estimated to be between 2,000 and 9,000 years old, with its exact
label: not_verifiable

Searches only turned up unrelated results: the Dutch patronym Janszoon, Abel Janszoon Tasman, Jansz sparkling wine, and ancient Huon pine logs in Tasmania. The claim also doesn't hold together on its face. It says the log was "discovered in 1999" but also "found in the 1920s", and the sentence is cut off. Redwoods aren't native to Tasmania; an ABC report says they were planted there decades ago, which makes an ancient redwood log there implausible. Still, no reliable source addresses this specific log, so the claim can't be confirmed or directly disproved.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit that causes it to be closer to the sun at its perihelion (91 million kilometers) and farther away at its aphelion (70 million kilometers).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Mercury's perihelion wrong. Mercury's orbit is highly eccentric, but at its closest point it is only about 46 million km from the Sun, not 91 million km. The aphelion figure of about 70 million km is correct. The claim also contradicts itself: a perihelion of 91 million km would be farther from the Sun than the 70 million km aphelion.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the ocean that is immortal because it has the ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii, a marine hydrozoan known as the "immortal jellyfish," can revert to its juvenile polyp stage and restart its life cycle. EBSCO and Britannica both say it does this through transdifferentiation, which turns specialized cells into other cell types. These sources also note that "immortal" means biological immortality: the jellyfish can still die from predators or disease. That caveat fits the common meaning of the claim, so the claim is supported.

text: The three-eyed frog, commonly found in a village in India, has been observed to have an additional third eye in the center of its forehead, although this is extremely rare and thought to be caused by genetic mutations.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source describing a 'three-eyed frog' that is commonly found in an Indian village. The India search instead turned up a three-eyed calf born in Kolathur, India, which is a different animal. Other results cover unrelated topics: the frog's light-sensing pineal or parietal 'third eye', three-eyed tadpoles created by eye grafts in lab experiments, and viral mutant-frog photos discussed on hoax-debunking sites. None of these confirms the claimed frog, the village population, or a genetic-mutation explanation, and none clearly disproves them. The claim also contradicts itself by calling the frog 'commonly found' while saying the third eye is 'extremely rare'. The evidence isn't enough to support or refute it.

text: Volcanic eruptions are responsible for creating around 150 million years' worth of the Earth's ocean continents in approximately 20 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source for this claim. The closest evidence is about the mid-Cretaceous superplume. Larson's (1991) calculation of Earth's ocean crust budget covers the past 150 million years. It found that crust formed 50–75% faster between about 120 and 80 million years ago, a span of roughly 40 million years. That evidence does not say volcanism created "150 million years' worth" of crust in about 20 million years. The claim's term "ocean continents" is also unclear. Since the specific figures can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, as evidenced by the discovery of the PARAMARSO site which dates back approximately 13,000 years.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of a 'PARAMARSO site' in the Catskills or anywhere else. The Catskills' best-known 'oldest' claim is the world's oldest fossil forest, found in a quarry near Cairo, NY, not a human dwelling. Recent reports name a roughly 13,800-year-old shelter at Shég' Xdaltth'í' in interior Alaska as the oldest known dwelling in North America and the Western Hemisphere. A Texas report had earlier made a similar claim for a roughly 14,000-year-old site at Gault. Neither of these sites is in the Catskills, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit that takes it as close as 46 million kilometers and as far as 70 million kilometers from the Sun.
label: supported
reason: A phys.org explainer on Mercury says it is the smallest planet in the solar system and has the most eccentric orbit of any planet, with an eccentricity of 0.205. It gives Mercury's distance from the Sun as 46 to 70 million km, which matches every part of the claim.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar cells due to one scientist's determination to find an optimal power source for the instrument.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim says "the telescope" without naming it, so I couldn't tell which instrument it means. The search turned up several solar-powered telescopes and related projects: the James Webb Space Telescope has a fold-out solar array, the La Silla and Gemini observatories use solar PV, and a study proposed solar power for the planned Atacama Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (AtLAST). None of these sources says a telescope runs partly on a yard of solar cells because one scientist was determined to find the best power source. Without a clear telescope to check, that part can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The Fury, a Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake in 1906, triggered a tsunami that hit the Japanese port of Honshu and was among the earliest recorded modern tsunamis in the region.
label: contradicted
reason: No search result mentions a 1906 Mid-Atlantic earthquake called 'The Fury'. Wikipedia's list of earthquakes in 1906 has no Mid-Atlantic event that caused a tsunami. The 1906 Japan quakes it lists were off Honshu's own coast. The claim also gets basic facts wrong. Honshu is Japan's main island, not a port. Japan has recorded tsunamis for centuries before 1906, such as the 869 Jōgan and 1833 Shōnai events, so a 1906 tsunami would not be among the earliest recorded there. It is also physically implausible for a Mid-Atlantic quake to send a damaging tsunami to Japan's Pacific coast. The claim looks made up and conflicts with the available evidence.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring in county dado together and have utterly been unable to confirm whether i can find any specific lisburn springs with greater certainty
label: not_verifiable

Searches only turned up unrelated results, such as Lisburn in Northern Ireland, a Lisburn Road in Pennsylvania and several US places named Spring Hill. The claim doesn't say which "neighboring countries" it means. The second half ("unable to confirm whether i can find...") is a muddled first-person statement, not a fact that can be checked. Because the entities have no clear referent, the claim can't be confirmed or disproved.

text: Giraffe weeping, also known as the "giraffe's sad face," is a neurological condition often mistaken for crying due to swollen blood vessels in the white patches of their skin caused by extreme temperatures or stress.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim. None of the sources I searched describe a condition called "giraffe weeping" or "giraffe's sad face," and none mention a neurological condition that looks like crying. I also found nothing about swollen blood vessels in giraffes' white skin patches caused by heat or stress. The giraffe skin conditions that do appear in the literature, such as giraffe skin disease and lumpy skin disease, are not neurological and don't match this description. The claim appears to be made up, but no source directly refutes it, so I can't verify it either way.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as Shinbone, is a natural wonder located in the Peruvian Amazon where a river appears to be boiling despite being 30 miles upstream from any visible source of freshwater or boiling water.

Wikipedia and Earth.com both give its name as Shanay-Timpishka, which Earth.com translates as "boiled with the heat of the sun." No source I found supports the "30 miles upstream from any visible source" detail either. Because the alternate name is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: The desert town of Tal DESeret in Utah had a peculiar past, as it was a ""lost"" Mormon city that only existed on a map more than 50 years before the city was actually populated.
label: not_verifiable

Sources on Fort Deseret say settlers arrived there in 1860 and lived there until 1868. It was abandoned over water problems and resettled in 1874. That history doesn't match a lost city that existed only on a map for more than 50 years before anyone lived there. Search results about the proposed 'State of Deseret' (a 'state that never existed') are about a state, not a desert town. text: The famous painting "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh is actually one of the most expensive paintings ever sold, with a 1987 auction selling it for $53.9 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 1987 auction sale for $53.9 million (Sotheby's New York, November 11, 1987) was for Van Gogh's "Irises", not "The Starry Night". The Starry Night has been in the Museum of Modern Art's collection since 1941, and it has never been sold at auction.

text: The longest known storm on Earth is a tempest that has been raging in the Deer Island Baptist Church cemetery in Salem, Massachusetts, for over 100 years, creating a mysterious whirlpool of debris and leaves.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of any storm in a 'Deer Island Baptist Church cemetery' in Salem, Massachusetts, and a storm lasting more than 100 years is not physically plausible for Earth's weather. Reliable sources contradict the claim. The World Meteorological Organization officially recognizes Tropical Cyclone Freddy, which lasted about 36 days in 2023, as the longest-lasting tropical cyclone on record. The best-known persistent storm phenomenon on Earth is the Catatumbo lightning in Venezuela, which recurs on about 260 nights a year rather than raging continuously. The searches about the cemetery only turned up unrelated Salem Baptist Church cemeteries in other states. The claim appears to be made up.

text: There are around 8 million ants in every square kilometer in The Amazon rainforest of South America, making it one of the most densely populated areas on Earth by insect.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure is real, but the claim uses the wrong unit. Scientific sources (Hölldobler & Wilson's "The Ants" on AntWiki, and a SciELO paper citing Fittkau & Klinge 1973) say one hectare of Amazon terra firme forest can hold more than 8 million ants. A square kilometre is 100 hectares, so the density would be roughly 800 million ants per km², not about 8 million. BBC Science Focus gives a similar estimate of 3.5 million per acre, about 8.6 million per hectare. Stating 8 million per square kilometre understates the density by about 100 times.

text: A ball of twine can be used to reel in a fishing line without getting it all tangled.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs or disproves this claim. My searches turned up general information on fishing-line tangles, using twine as fishing line, and hand-line or survival setups. None of it says a ball of twine works as a tool for reeling in fishing line without tangling. The claim is also vague and reads like a made-up household tip, so the evidence doesn't settle it either way.

text: Europe's Rossel Creek Glacier in Antarctica is home to a vast iceberg that is over 6,000 years old.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a "Rossel Creek Glacier" exists, in Antarctica or anywhere else. Searches turned up only similarly named features, such as Rosselin Glacier, Mount Rossel and Ross Glacier, plus unrelated reports of 6-million-year-old ice in Antarctica. None of them mention a 6,000-year-old iceberg at a glacier with this name. The claim's wording is also confused, since Antarctica is not part of Europe. Because the glacier has no clear real-world match and nothing supports or refutes the iceberg's age, the claim can't be checked.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, similar to fingerprints, that can be used to identify individuals.
label: supported
reason: Forensic and biometric research, including a ResearchGate paper titled "Tongue Prints: An Emerging Biometric Forensic Tool", describes tongue prints as unique to each person. These studies say the tongue's shape, colour and surface texture differ between individuals and can be used for identification, much like fingerprints. One caveat: this is still an emerging field and is not yet as established as fingerprinting.

text: The domestic rabbit has a special sense in its paw called the plantaris, which helps it detect any potential predators and facilitates safe tunneling and burrowing.
label: contradicted
reason: The plantaris is not a sense organ in a rabbit's paw. Scientific papers, including one on PubMed and one in PLOS ONE, describe the rabbit plantaris (M. plantaris) as a multi-pennate calf muscle in the hind limb, studied alongside the gastrocnemius and soleus. A muscle is not a special sense, and I found no source saying it detects predators or helps with burrowing.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is Mount Olympus on Mars, with it being around 27 km long.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Olympus Mons (not "Mount Olympus") is a single shield volcano, not a mountain range. It is known as the tallest volcano, or tallest mountain, in the solar system. Its 22–26 km figure is its height. It is not 27 km long; it measures about 600 km across. So the claim confuses a single mountain with a mountain range and height with length.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting over 3 trillion trees cover our planet.
label: supported
reason: Crowther et al.'s 2015 study in Nature, which several sources cite, estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth. That is slightly more than 3 trillion. NASA estimates the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Even at the high end of 400 billion, trees outnumber stars by more than seven to one. Both parts of the claim hold up.

text: 珠海塔 was the tallest building  in the world from 1989 until 1998.
label: contradicted
reason: Zhuhai Tower (珠海塔) was built between 2013 and 2017 and opened in 2018, so it couldn't have been the world's tallest building from 1989 to 1998. In those years the title belonged to Chicago's Sears Tower, which held it from 1974 until the Petronas Towers overtook it in 1998.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river that flows from the Amazon rainforest, is a mysterious phenomenon that was only discovered in 2003.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say geoscientist Andrés Ruzo reached and began studying the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in 2011. Wikipedia calls him the first scientist allowed to study it, in 2011, and the Institute of Physics says he "rediscovered" it that year. Local and Indigenous people had known about the river and used it for centuries. None of the sources gives 2003 as the discovery date.

text: Butler's Gorge, a remote region in Tasmania, Australia is home to the world's highest waterfall, Slaty Moss Falls, which plunges 840m.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and geology.com name Angel Falls in Venezuela as the world's tallest waterfall, at 979 m. Some measurements instead rank Tugela Falls in South Africa, at 983 m, as the tallest. Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, best known for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. No source says it has a waterfall called 'Slaty Moss Falls', let alone the world's highest one.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original recipe containing an extract from the coca leaf and Pepsi's original recipe containing a unique formulation of vanilla and cola nuts.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part has some basis. John Pemberton was addicted to morphine, and his original formula contained coca leaf extract. The Pepsi part is wrong, though. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, North Carolina history pages and the NC Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, say Caleb Bradham created 'Brad's Drink' in 1893 as a digestive aid for dyspepsia (indigestion), not as a morphine alternative. The name 'Pepsi' itself comes from 'dyspepsia.' Its original recipe is also usually described as including pepsin and kola nuts, so 'vanilla and cola nuts' is not an accurate summary. Because the claim says both drinks were made as morphine alternatives, the Pepsi evidence contradicts it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans more than 65,000 kilometers across the globe.
label: supported
reason: I found agreement that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. Wikipedia, NOAA Ocean Exploration, WHOI and WorldAtlas all say so. Sources give different lengths, but most fit the claim. Several put it at over 65,000 km, and a NASA Ocean Planet page gives about 74,000 km. A peer-reviewed article on PMC says about 75,000 km. Some sources use the less exact wording "nearly 65,000 km" (NOAA, WHOI) or "about 65,000 km" (Wikipedia). That is a small difference in how the figure is estimated, not a real contradiction, so overall the claim is supported.

text: A VOLCANO ERUPTS ON MARS Every 700 years - No scientific evidence can confirm this though, The Olympus Mons on Mars has had less than 1 eruption in 1Mil and takes months to cool
label: not_verifiable
reason: There is partial support. I found no evidence that a Martian volcano erupts every 700 years, which fits the claim's own statement that no scientific evidence confirms it. The Olympus Mons part also roughly holds up: Space.com says its last eruption may have been as recently as 25 million years ago, and Astronomy.com reports that its youngest surface areas are about 2.4 million years old. That is consistent with less than one eruption per million years. However, I found nothing to confirm that Olympus Mons lava 'takes months to cool.' The claim is also internally muddled, since it states a 700-year eruption rate and then says there is no evidence for it. Because one part cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive overall.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original recipe containing an extract from the coca leaf.
label: contradicted
reason: Coca-Cola's part of the claim holds up: John Pemberton, a pharmacist who was addicted to morphine, created it in 1886 as a tonic, and the original recipe contained coca leaf extract. The Pepsi part is wrong. Reliable sources say pharmacist Caleb Bradham created Pepsi in 1893 as "Brad's Drink," a digestive aid for indigestion (dyspepsia), not as an alternative to morphine. Because the claim says both drinks were developed as morphine alternatives, it is contradicted.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit that causes it to be closer to the sun at its perihelion (about 46 million kilometers away) than to the Earth at its aphelion (about 222 million kilometers away is the closest that a planet gets to Earth,
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are correct. Mercury is the smallest planet, its orbit is highly eccentric, and its perihelion is about 46 million km from the Sun. The claim misuses the 222 million km figure, though. That number is Mercury's greatest distance from Earth, reached when the two planets are on opposite sides of the Sun. It is not the closest a planet gets to Earth. Mercury can come within about 77 million km of Earth, and Venus can come even closer. Calling 222 million km Mercury's 'aphelion' relative to Earth is also inaccurate, because aphelion is measured from the Sun.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique structure of their eyes, which allows them to blink mainly through lubricating tears.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Winks-and-Blinks, a specialist site on blinking in animals, lists the giraffe under mammals that blink by closing both the upper and lower eyelids. It explains that each blink sweeps tear fluid across the eye toward the tear ducts. Other sources describe giraffe eyelids flickering while they rest. So giraffes can close their eyelids and blink. Their long eyelashes protect their eyes from dust and help them sense thorny branches; they do not stop the eyelids from closing.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in at least eight different countries, including Japan, Thailand, and Finland, where instead they use other forms of vocalization and body language to communicate.
label: contradicted
reason: Cats meow in every country. Omniglot's list of cat sounds gives the local words for a meow in Japanese (nyā), Thai (miao, ngaew) and Finnish (miau, mau, nau), which shows cats in Japan, Thailand and Finland meow like cats anywhere else. Meowing is part of what a cat is, not something that depends on the country, and no reliable source says cats in some countries don't meow. The claim is a fabrication.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a rare and unexplained natural phenomenon, where a river of scorching hot water that is rich in sulfur flows through the Amazon rainforest in Peru.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is a real, rare, very hot river in the Peruvian Amazon, but two parts of the claim are wrong. First, it is not 'rich in sulfur.' Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo tested the water and said there was 'effectively nothing in the water.' He found its electrical conductivity was lower than Evian's, and it lacks the mineral signature of volcanic water. YSI and Xylem describe the water as unusually pure and safe to drink. Second, the heat is not 'unexplained.' Ruzo's research, reported by ScienceAlert, Slate and Atlas Obscura, points to a non-volcanic hydrothermal system: rainwater sinks deep underground, is heated, and comes back up through faults. Only the reason the water is so clean is still debated.

text: There are more trees on Earth covered in moss than you might think, with scientists estimating that as much as 3% of the Earth's land surface is covered by moss.
label: contradicted
reason: The main moss-coverage figure in the claim does not match the research. The 2022 UNSW study (Eldridge et al.) estimated that soil mosses alone cover at least 9.4 million km². Eos reports this as "at least," which makes it a minimum. That is about 6% of Earth's roughly 149 million km² of land, so "as much as 3%" understates it. EarthDate gives a different figure, 2% of Earth's total surface, which works out to about 6–7% of land. The 3% figure appears to come from peatlands, which several sources say cover about 3% of the land surface. Peatlands are dominated by Sphagnum moss, but that is not the same as total moss cover. No source addresses the vague first part about trees covered in moss.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their unique ability to fit together awkwardly, much like basket-weaved items.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources don't list "basket" as a collective noun for octopuses. Grammar Monster gives "consortium". A-Z Animals and Study.com say there is no widely accepted term, and "consortium" is the one usually suggested. Original Diving offers "consortium" or the more playful "tangle". Searching for "basket of octopuses" turned up only shopping listings and literal baskets of octopus. No source supports the term or the claimed reason that octopuses "fit together awkwardly" like woven baskets.

text: The characteristics of a solar eclipse, such as its path or frequency, can be determined using an unusual mathematical equation called Bessel functions, named after 19th-century mathematician Friedrich Bessel.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the mathematical tool wrong. Eclipse paths and circumstances are worked out with Besselian elements, a set of values describing the geometry of the Moon's shadow. Friedrich Bessel developed this method around 1842 (Wikipedia; IOP conference paper). Bessel functions are something else: solutions to Bessel's differential equation, and they are not how eclipses are predicted. Both are named after the 19th-century mathematician Bessel, but calling the eclipse method an 'unusual mathematical equation called Bessel functions' is incorrect. Besselian elements are also not one equation, and they describe the circumstances of a particular eclipse, not how often eclipses happen.

text: The 길 Cheese is a type of Korean cheese made from a mixture of cow's, goat's, and sheep's milk.
label: not_verifiable

Searches in both Korean and English turned up only unrelated pages: a dictionary entry for goat cheese, gilgeori (street) toast, which uses processed cheese slices, and Chuck E. Cheese. "길" means "road" or "way" in Korean, and the name doesn't seem to refer to any established cheese. Because nothing confirms that the cheese exists or what it's made from, the claim can't be checked either way.

label: not_verifiable
