text: Butler's Gorge, a location in Tasmania, Australia, has the highest recorded cliff waterfall, Bonorong Falls, which is approximately 866 meters tall when measured directly above the cliff at full flood level, though mean heights published are lower.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found supports the claim, and some of it is clearly wrong. Butlers Gorge is a real rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, known for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge hydro power station. However, no waterfall called 'Bonorong Falls' turns up in any source. In Tasmania, 'Bonorong' is the name of a wildlife sanctuary, not a waterfall. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia's list of Australian waterfalls, name Wallaman Falls in Queensland as Australia's tallest permanent waterfall, with a main drop of about 268 m. An 866 m cliff waterfall in Tasmania would be more than three times that height, so the claim conflicts with the established record.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River,' is a secluded body of water that remains a mystery due to its unknown source and the fact that it appears to boil despite being far from any geothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is real: the Shanay-timpishka in Peru, widely called the 'Boiling River of the Amazon.' But the claim's explanation of its heat is wrong. Wikipedia says the heat is geothermal and that the main theory is Earth's geothermal gradient, based on geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research. Ruzo's work also found the source is not volcanic, since the water lacks the chemical signs of magma. So the river is far from active volcanoes, not 'far from any geothermal activity,' and its heat source is reasonably well explained rather than unknown. I also found no support for the nickname 'Hidden River.'

text: The world's longest mountain range, stretching approximately 40,000 kilometers, is the mid-ocean ridge system, which is a vast underwater mountain range running along the center of the Earth's oceans.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources such as NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI agree that the mid-ocean ridge system is the world's longest mountain range and lies mostly underwater. However, they put its length at nearly 65,000 km, which is about 40,000 miles. A University of Delaware page gives more than 56,000 km. The claim's figure of about 40,000 kilometers seems to confuse miles with kilometers, so it understates the length by a large margin.

text: The longer you live, the more likely you are to develop a duplicate of a body cell that still contains a complete set of chromosomes - people who live over 110 years old will have a higher chance of this occurrence.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources point the other way. Several peer-reviewed studies (e.g., Nature Communications 2018 on FoxM1, and a review of the aging brain in PMC) report that cell division declines with age and aneuploidy rises. Aneuploidy means daughter cells end up with an abnormal number of chromosomes. So aging is linked to fewer accurate, complete-chromosome copies of body cells, not more. No source supports the idea that people over 110 have a higher chance of producing such complete copies. The claim is also confused: copying a cell with a full chromosome set is just normal cell division, which happens all the time and is not a feature of long life.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers across the globe and is not visible from space.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources support the main facts. Guinness World Records, WorldAtlas and NOAA identify the Mid-Ocean Ridge as Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km. NOAA describes it as more than 65,000 km, which matches 'over 65,000 kilometers.' The searches did not verify or disprove the claim that it is 'not visible from space.' Most of the ridge is underwater, but parts rise above sea level, such as Iceland and Jan Mayen. From general knowledge, the seafloor ridge has also been mapped with satellite altimetry, though the searches did not confirm this. My follow-up search on visibility from space failed before it returned results.

text: The wavelength of light from a firefly's glow is so unique that researchers have successfully identified the exact species and number of fireflies from their bioluminescent light emissions.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results do not back up the claim's main point, that firefly species and numbers are identified from the light's wavelength. Researchers identify species mainly by the timing of the flashes. A 2024 Scientific Reports study used a neural network to classify species from flash patterns recorded on video. A study of Taiwanese fireflies (PMC8773436) found that flash intervals identified species better than flash colors, so wavelength is not uniquely diagnostic. Spectral studies show that many species give off overlapping green-yellow light. Fireflies are counted with computer vision that tracks flashes in video, not by analyzing wavelength. The claim's reasoning, and its suggestion that both species and exact numbers come from wavelength, goes against this evidence.

text: The Dinbaugh cave in Montana is home to an impressive accumulation of over 30,000 bottles of whiskey and alcohol that was found hidden away from the 1940s through the 2000s, thawing naturally after the cave was found by a treasure hunter in 2007.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a "Dinbaugh cave" exists in Montana. Searches for the cave by name, and for a Montana cave holding 30,000 whiskey bottles, returned only unrelated pages, such as Montana whiskey merchandise, a Georgian cave and news about Montana distillers. Nothing confirms the cave, the bottle count, the 1940s–2000s hiding period or a 2007 discovery by a treasure hunter. The claim looks made up, but I found no source that directly refutes it. My searches were cut short by a tool limit, so the result is inconclusive.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiological characteristics, including extremely fast wingbeats and a remarkable ability to reverse its wing movement.
label: supported
reason: The one search result I found says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards with precision and control. It credits this to their anatomy and agility. That fits the claim's points about very fast wingbeats and wings that can rotate to reverse the stroke. The source is not highly authoritative, and my searches hit a tool limit before I could check whether any other bird flies backwards briefly. So the evidence leans toward support but is not strong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and bubble like a pot of water, is located in the Peruvian jungle and is believed to be a phenomenon caused by a combination of geothermal heat and unique water currents.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out. Wikipedia and other sources confirm that the Shanay-Timpishka, known as the 'Boiling River of the Amazon,' is in the Peruvian Amazon and is very hot. Its heat is explained geothermally: geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research suggests rainwater seeps deep underground, gets superheated, and rises back up through fault lines, even though there are no active volcanoes nearby. However, I found nothing saying 'unique water currents' help cause the phenomenon. The explanation given is a hydrothermal fault system, not unusual currents in the river. Because that part of the claim can't be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: The Fury, a Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake in 1906, triggered a tsunami that hit the Japanese port of Honshu, causing a "backward" tsunami which struck the shore from the direction of the sea.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim, though tool limits stopped my searches early. Nothing confirmed that a 1906 Mid-Atlantic earthquake was called "The Fury", that it caused a tsunami in Japan, or that a "backward" tsunami struck there. The 1906 tsunami known to have reached Japan and Hawaii came from the Colombia–Ecuador earthquake in the Pacific, not the Mid-Atlantic. The claim also has internal problems: Honshu is Japan's main island, not a port, and an Atlantic tsunami reaching Honshu's coast is implausible. I didn't find a source that directly refutes it, so I'm rating it inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: The platypus is one of the few venomous mammals in the world, with the male platypus having a spur on its hind leg that delivers a painful and venomous sting.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including a Springer reference chapter, say the platypus is a venomous mammal, that only males are venomous, and that they deliver venom through spurs on their hind legs. It is also widely documented that very few mammals are venomous and that platypus stings are extremely painful. Calling it a 'sting' is loose wording, since the venom is delivered by a spur, but the claim itself is accurate.

text: The tick-fauna on a island off Iceland, called Grimsey, is thought to be the biogeographic boundary line between the fauna from the Arctic in the north and the fauna from North America in the south.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source saying that Grímsey's tick fauna is thought to mark a biogeographic boundary between Arctic fauna to the north and North American fauna to the south. Searches confirmed only background facts: Grímsey is an island off Iceland's north coast that straddles the Arctic Circle (Wikipedia), and the seabird tick Ixodes uriae has been collected there, with Grímsey listed as one of three Arctic sampling sites (Zenodo). The boundary idea doesn't fit Iceland's geography well, since North America lies to the west, not the south. Still, no source directly contradicts it. A tool-use limit stopped my searches early, so a source I didn't reach could still exist. With the main part of the claim neither supported nor refuted, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, the Lehigh Valley Mink Insula Barrier, dating back to around 500 AD.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that anything called the "Lehigh Valley Mink Insula Barrier" exists. The name looks made up: it mixes the Lehigh Valley, which is in Pennsylvania, with Mink Hollow, a hiking area in the Catskills. Reliable reporting puts the oldest known dwellings in North America about 13,800 to 14,000 years ago, at a site in Alaska (Live Science) and the Gault site in Texas. Both are far older than 500 AD, and neither is in the Catskills.

text: The Maasai tribe in East Africa has a unique cultural practice of censoring the negative attitudes and throat clearing in the general community in the name of preserving honor to maintain dignity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source showing that the Maasai censor negative attitudes or throat clearing in the community to protect honor or dignity. Sources on Maasai customs cover age-sets, rites of passage, and especially spitting, which they treat as a blessing and sign of respect. Others note that the Maasai value respect and honor in general. None mentions a practice like the one claimed. Spitting being a blessing doesn't directly disprove the claim, so it can't be called contradicted. But no part of it can be verified, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: The 길 Cheese is a type of Korean cheese made from a mixture of cow, sheep, and buffalo milk, and it is known for its stretchy texture when melted.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a Korean cheese called "길 Cheese" (Gil Cheese) exists. Searches in English and Korean only turned up unrelated results: "길" as a Korean surname, gilgeori (street) toast made with processed cheese slices, Imsil cheese, and Chuck E. Cheese. Because the claim has no clear referent and nothing addresses its details (a cow, sheep and buffalo milk blend, or a stretchy texture when melted), it can be neither confirmed nor refuted.

text: Sweden has a bridge made from ice called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" that is built every winter and melts by spring, allowing snowmobiles to drive across the frozen river below.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find evidence that an ice structure called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" exists in Sweden. My searches turned up general pages about the Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi, which is rebuilt from Torne River ice every winter and melts in spring. None of the results I could review mentioned a bridge by that name, and my search limit ran out before I could check further. I also found nothing about snowmobiles using such a bridge. The claim doesn't quite make sense either: snowmobiles could cross a frozen river without a bridge. Since nothing directly supports or contradicts the specific claim, it remains unverified.

text: The Azure- eared Flying Fox (Pteropus admiral) is the only species of bat known to use the same general roosting location for multiple generations.
label: contradicted
reason: No species called the "Azure-eared Flying Fox (Pteropus admiral)" appears in any taxonomic source. The closest real species is the Admiralty flying fox, Pteropus admiralitatum. The claim that it is the only bat to reuse a roost across generations is also false: grey-headed flying-fox camps in Australia, such as the Maclean maternity camp, have been occupied regularly for over 100 years, and many other bat species also return to traditional roosts.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iriena Mather in 1941, who weathered a temperature change of 115 degrees Fahrenheit (65.5°C) in 45 minutes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that 'Iriena Mather' exists or set any record. A search for that name with '1941 temperature change' turned up only unrelated results, such as a 1941 zoology paper and the author Adriana Mather. Guinness World Records lists human heat-endurance records, such as the highest dry-air temperature endured while clothed, but my searches did not show any record for a 115°F change in 45 minutes. The search limit cut off further checks, so I can't confirm or rule out the claim. It looks fabricated, but there isn't enough evidence to call it contradicted.

text: The only bird that can fly backward is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and wing movement, which allows it to defy gravity and fly in any direction.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the hummingbird is the only bird that can truly fly backward. WorldAtlas, Birds Outside My Window, IFLScience, Birdspot and others credit this to its unusual wing structure and joints, which let it rotate its wings and fly forward, backward, sideways and hover. Birdspot adds that herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backward briefly, but it still says hummingbirds are the only birds that fly backward for any length of time. That fits the usual meaning of the claim. 'Defy gravity' is figurative, but it matches how these sources describe hummingbirds hovering and flying in any direction.

text: Theattery that produces the world's largest RC jet engine, also known as the jet that has the world's fastest cruise speed for a non-turbo-jet, 1000 hp on one of these jets can lift-off on skis or in water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled ("Theattery") and doesn't clearly name a company, aircraft or engine. A search turned up only unrelated results, such as Rolls-Royce's UltraFan full-size engine and a YouTube video about a large RC turbine jet. Nothing I found links an RC jet engine maker to a "world's fastest cruise speed for a non-turbo-jet" or to a 1000 hp jet that can lift off on skis or water. Because the claim has no clear subject and none of its parts could be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: The shorter arm of the Aditya L1 spacecraft's flyby target, the Sun-grazing comet 46P/Wirtanen, is around 1.2 kilometers in length.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's premise is false. Aditya-L1 is ISRO's solar observatory, placed in a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 point. It has no comet flyby target. Comet 46P/Wirtanen is also not a sungrazing comet: it is a small Jupiter-family comet with an orbital period of about 5.4 years. Its nucleus is estimated at about 1.2–1.4 km, so a size of roughly 1.2 km is close to the published figure, but the claim's link between Aditya-L1 and this comet and its description of the comet are both wrong.

text: пергамент, первоначально изготовлявшийся из кожи больших животных, таких как гиены и барсы, а затем из кожи верблюдей или лошадей, был впервые изобретен в Древнем СуMeriah в древней Месопот
label: contradicted
reason: Надёжные источники противоречат этому утверждению. Culture.ru пишет, что пергамент изобрели в античном городе Пергаме, столице Пергамского царства, во II веке до н. э., а не в Шумере в Месопотамии. Изготавливали его из шкур овец, коз, баранов, свиней и телят, а не гиен, барсов, верблюдов или лошадей. Словарные статьи тоже связывают название материала с Пергамом и указывают, что его делали из кожи телят, ягнят, козлят, крупного рогатого скота и свиней.

text: The ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy have one of the highest concentrations of ice in the world despite the high temperatures in the surrounding area.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim doesn't name a specific cave. "Ghiaccio stalactite caves in the mountains of Italy" could mean several places, so it has no clear referent. Italy does have ice caves with ice stalactites, such as Etna's Grotta del Gelo, which is described as Europe's southernmost glacier, and several ice caves in northeastern Italy. None of the sources I found say that any Italian cave has "one of the highest concentrations of ice in the world." The world's largest ice caves are Eisriesenwelt in Austria and Dobšiná in Slovakia. The part about high temperatures in the surrounding area also isn't verified for a clearly identified cave.

text: Betz Airstrip in Montana, USA is the highest airport in the world in terms of both its elevation of 8,000 feet and its highest takeoff point at 6,815 feet at the other end of the runway.
label: contradicted
reason: Even 8,000 ft would be nowhere near the world's highest airport. Daocheng Yading Airport in China is listed as the world's highest civilian airport at 4,411 m (14,472 ft), and Wikipedia's list of highest airports only includes airports at 2,500 m (8,202 ft) or higher, which is already above the claimed 8,000 ft. I found no record of a high-elevation 'Betz Airstrip' in Montana. The only Betz Airport I found (FAA ID 44G) sits at just 691 ft. Its Wikipedia page does not give a location, so I couldn't confirm it is the same airfield the claim means. Either way, the claim that it is the world's highest airport is false.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, contains a section of river known as "The Falls of Hells Gates", and falls over a vertical 420 meters of topaz hidden surface.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Butlers Gorge does exist. It is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, next to Clark Dam and Lake King William, with the River Derwent flowing from the lake. However, no source I found mentions a river section called 'The Falls of Hells Gates' at Butlers Gorge. Searches for that name only returned unrelated Hell's Gate sites in South Africa, Ontario, Idaho and Kenya. Nothing supports a 420-metre vertical drop over a 'topaz' surface either. The claim looks implausible and probably made up, but no source directly contradicts these details, so they cannot be verified.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a hot river in the Peruvian Amazon, remains the subject of scientific mystery as its source and origin are still unknown.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river's source and origin are still unknown, but the sources say otherwise. Wikipedia lists the river's source as Mayantuyacu. It also reports that geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo has studied where the heat comes from, and that the leading explanation is the Earth's geothermal gradient: water seeps deep underground through faults, heats up, and comes back to the surface. Some details are still being studied, but the river's source and the basic cause of its heat are not an unsolved mystery.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess,"  however, a more commonly accepted example is "bookkeeper"
label: contradicted
reason: Neither "stewardess" nor "bookkeeper" has one syllable. "Stewardess" has three and "bookkeeper" has three. The two sources found, a Logically Facts fact-check and a Berlitz article, list nine-letter one-syllable words such as "screeched" and "strengths" as the longest in common use. "Stewardess" is better known as a long word typed with only the left hand, and "bookkeeper" is known for its three consecutive double letters.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and encircles the Earth.
label: supported
reason: NOAA, WHOI and Wikipedia all call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,000–40,390 mi) long. They describe it as wrapping around the globe "like the seams on a baseball," which supports the claim that it encircles the Earth. One wording point differs: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Wikipedia also gives about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, so "over 65,000 km" still holds. The core claim is supported.

text: There are approximately 300 million trees in the Great Barrier Reef, however this is mainly referring to mangrove hectare values in comparison, if fact speaking the total green tree biomass would actually be; more towards around 72 billion.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms or refutes either number. The searches turned up general facts about the Great Barrier Reef: its World Heritage Area covers about 34.9 million hectares, it has mangrove areas such as the roughly 164 km² in the Hinchinbrook Channel, and it has about 600 continental islands. None of these sources estimates how many trees are in the Reef area. The '~300 million trees' figure and the 'around 72 billion' tree or biomass figure don't appear in any trustworthy source I found. The claim is also muddled, since it mixes up tree counts, mangrove hectares and biomass. It cannot be verified.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, however, scientists estimate that around 80-90% of all species that have existed on Earth are now extinct.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is real, but it's the central estimate from Mora et al. (2011), give or take 1.3 million, so 'over 8.7 million' isn't quite right. The main problem is the extinction figure. National Geographic, CK12 and other sources say more than 99% of all species that ever lived are now extinct, and Raup put it above 99.9%. That contradicts the claim's 80-90%.

text: Mitosis, the process by which cells divide and grow, is visible in visible grass-like plants under magnifying glass but not visible to unaided eye, however, humans at certain points in there lives experience mitosis, our jaw & other bones set has undergone.
label: contradicted
reason: Lab manuals from NCERT, NC BioNetwork and a Louisiana general-biology lab text all show that mitosis in plant tissue such as onion root tips is observed with a light microscope, using stained and squashed cells at high magnification. A magnifying glass is not enough, so the claim that mitosis can be seen in grass-like plants under one is wrong. The claim also says humans experience mitosis only 'at certain points' in their lives, which misstates biology: body cells divide by mitosis throughout life for growth and repair. Bone growth does involve mitosis, but the claim's main point about visibility is false.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Dorsa Argentea, a vast series of hills and mountains which make up a significant portion of Mars' surface, stretching over 2,500 miles in length.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and NASA/JPL both describe Dorsa Argentea as a group of ridges near Mars' south pole, most likely eskers left beneath an ancient ice sheet. That makes it a regional polar feature, not a vast mountain range covering a large share of the planet's surface. No source calls it the longest mountain range in the Solar System. The 2,500-mile length was not checked.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of the Cannes Film Festival, consisting of only a 7-second shot.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that backs up the claim. The only 2002 short called "Flicker" that turned up is a 5-minute horror video directed by Conall Pendergast (IMDb). That doesn't fit the claimed 7-second single shot, and nothing links it to Cannes. Neither Wikipedia's list of Cannes Film Festival records nor the festival's own "10 records" page shows this film or a 7-second shortest-film record in the parts I could see. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could check further, so I can't fully confirm or rule out the claim. The 5-minute runtime does cast doubt on it, but the claim may refer to a different film.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill Castle in Pennsylvania, is a rare example of a cave containing stalactites and stalagmites indoors.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a 'Butler's Grotto' exists at Fonthill Castle in Doylestown, Pennsylvania. Searching for the name only turned up unrelated results: the Fonthill Grottoes, a bat-roosting site beside Fonthill Lake in Wiltshire, England, and a painting titled 'The Venetian Pool Grotto' by an artist named Brian Butler. A search on Fonthill Castle and stalactites only returned a general TripAdvisor page that says nothing about such a grotto. Nothing I found confirms that this indoor cave with stalactites and stalagmites exists. The tool's usage limit stopped further searches, so I also couldn't find a source that clearly rules it out. The name may be invented or mixed up with the English Fonthill site, but I can't confirm or disprove the claim.

text: The McKinley Tarn, located in the Grand Teton National Park of Wyoming, contains a body of water from the remains of President William McKinley's autopsy.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any place called "McKinley Tarn" in Grand Teton National Park. Searches for it only turned up unrelated results, such as McKinley tartan products and a McKinley neighborhood in Converse County, Wyoming. Trustworthy sources also say President McKinley's remains are entombed in a granite sarcophagus at the McKinley National Memorial in Canton, Ohio. His body went there by funeral train after services in Washington. Historical records of his autopsy (UCSB Presidency Project, the Raab Collection archive) say nothing about any remains going to Wyoming or being linked to a body of water. The claim looks made up and goes against the documented location of his remains.

text: The planet Venus rotates in the opposite direction of its orbit around the Sun, a phenomenon known as a retrograde rotation, which is quite rare in our solar system.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia says Venus's axial tilt is 177°, so it spins almost exactly opposite to the direction of its orbit. That is called retrograde rotation. Wikipedia also notes that Venus probably started out with a fast prograde spin like most planets in the Solar System. Only Venus, and arguably Uranus, rotate retrograde, so calling it rare is accurate.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, known for its extremely high pH levels that can turn animals that die in it into stone.
label: supported
reason: Live Science says Lake Natron is a soda lake in northern Tanzania with a pH of about 10.5, almost as caustic as ammonia, and that it turns some animals to 'stone.' Colossal and A-Z Animals describe animals that die there being calcified or preserved as stone-like mummies. The animals aren't literally turned to stone. The lake's natron (sodium carbonate) calcifies and preserves their bodies. Still, the lake really is famous for this, so the claim holds as worded.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Australia, has the world's oldest known dam, with evidence suggesting it was built over 2,000 years ago by the Aboriginal people of Tasmania.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge in Tasmania is known for the Clark Dam, a modern hydro-electric concrete dam that was being built in the 1940s (The Mercury, 1946). It is not an ancient Aboriginal dam. The world's oldest known dams are in the Middle East, such as Jawa Dam in Jordan and Sadd el-Kafara in Egypt. No credible source supports the claim of a 2,000-year-old Aboriginal dam at Butlers Gorge.

text: A group of rainbow-colored brandy snifter-shaped coral corals called Easter Coral is one of the few coral species that actually contain pigments that produce a rainbow effect.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing on a coral called "Easter Coral" that is rainbow-colored and shaped like a brandy snifter, or that is one of the few corals with pigments producing a rainbow effect. The closest match was a hobby-aquarium chalice coral variety sold by Top Shelf Aquatics as "ORA Easter Egg Chalice." It is a named aquarium coral variety, not a recognized group of coral species, and the source does not support the claim about rainbow pigments. Other sources describe many corals with fluorescent or colorful pigments, including whole lists of "rainbow" corals, so the idea that only a few species have them is unsupported. No source directly contradicts the specific claim, because the claimed entity does not appear to exist in reliable sources.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI and Wikipedia all describe the global mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). Most of it lies underwater, and it runs through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. There is one small wording difference: these sources say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Also, the Pacific section (the East Pacific Rise) does not sit exactly in the centre of that ocean. The main points of the claim still match reliable sources.

text: The understandability of Orangutans' language has shown to be surprisingly similar to that of children, as research indicates they are able to master up to 400 words of sign language and comprehend even more complex meanings.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-documented orangutan signer, Chantek, learned about 150 signs over eight years of study (Smithsonian; Orang Utan Republik Foundation), not up to 400. The ~400 figure in the Smithsonian article refers to Kanzi, a bonobo who learned lexigram symbols rather than sign language. No credible source found says orangutans master up to 400 sign-language words, and the claim that their language is 'surprisingly similar to that of children' is not established either.

text: Tornadoes are the most destructive type of storm on Earth, accounting for 51% of global weather-related fatalities.
label: contradicted
reason: The WMO's official sources contradict this claim. They say tropical cyclones, not tornadoes, are the most destructive large-scale storms in the world. The WMO also reports that over a 50-year period, tropical cyclones caused about 38% of deaths from weather-, climate- and water-related disasters. No credible source says tornadoes account for 51% of global weather-related deaths; tornadoes cause only a small share of these deaths worldwide.

text: A group of octopuses is called a "склад" which translates to "squad" in English, showcasing their highly social and intelligent nature.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Western Australia's Department of Primary Industries and an AOL article, say a group of octopuses is usually called a "consortium" (sometimes a "tangle"), not "склад". The translation is also wrong: the Russian word "склад" means "warehouse" or "composition", not "squad". And the claim that octopuses are "highly social" goes against the AOL article, which notes that octopuses are mostly solitary.

text: The ancient Egyptians are known to have used a calendar consisting of 365 days, which was only 1/4 of a day longer than the current solar year.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree the ancient Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days. But Wikipedia says this year was 'nearly a quarter of a day shorter than the solar year', not longer. Britannica says the same thing: with no leap-day correction, the calendar slipped one day every four years. The claim gets the direction of the difference wrong.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is day and only see polarized light at night, likely due to having only two types of photoreceptors which are sensitive to different parts of the visual spectrum.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that danionins see in full color by day and only polarized light at night. More importantly, the claim's explanation is wrong. Danionins like the zebrafish (Danio rerio), the best-studied member of the group, have rod photoreceptors plus four cone types sensitive to UV, blue, green and red light. That's at least five photoreceptor types, not two. Fish with two receptor types also couldn't see in 'full color'. The one search result I found (a ScienceDirect study) shows zebrafish prefer different colors at midday and at midnight. That suggests they can tell colors apart at night, which doesn't fit the idea of polarization-only night vision. A search tool limit cut off further searches, so the cone count comes from established zebrafish vision research rather than a retrieved source.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) and is not visible on land, running through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). It runs through the ocean basins, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. These authoritative sources confirm the claim's main points. Two details are less precise, though. NOAA says the ridge is 'nearly' 65,000 km long, not 'over' it. NOAA also says 'more than 90 percent' lies underwater, so a small part does reach land (Iceland, for example), and 'not visible on land' slightly overstates it. Neither caveat changes the main claim.

text: A flock of starlings is known for its unique ability to create the illusion of a single reflective surface, often referred to as a "mirroring mass," when the birds fly in an organized formation, creating a mesmerizing display of coordinated movement and collective behavior.
label: contradicted
reason: Starling flocks are famous for coordinated aerial displays and collective behavior, but trusted sources call these displays "murmurations." A search for "mirroring mass" found no source that uses that term for a starling flock. I also found no evidence that starlings are known for creating the illusion of a single reflective surface. The Woodland Trust says murmuration is both the collective noun for a large group of starlings and the name for the shapes they make, which contradicts the claimed terminology and reflective-surface description.

text: The6021 Rindler horizon,a theoretical boundary beyond which no signals can travel in a given universe has a significant impact on theoretical elements of the work of physicist David Finkelstein's unicorn in two dimensions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The searches found nothing about a "unicorn in two dimensions" in physicist David Finkelstein's work. He is known for Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates and for early work on black-hole event horizons and topology, but nothing links him to such a concept. The claim is also garbled ("The6021") and partly wrong: a Rindler horizon applies to observers who are accelerating at a constant rate. It is not a universe-wide boundary beyond which no signals can travel. Because the main subject has no clear referent, the claim can be neither confirmed nor refuted.

text: Aussie bats, a rare species of flying foxes, are known for their unique ability to navigate using astronomical cues to migrate thousands of miles each year to reach their food sources.
label: not_verifiable
reason: There is evidence for part of the claim but not the rest. Australian flying foxes are nomadic and travel long distances to follow food. The ABC reports a tracking study that found they cover about 1,400–6,000 km a year, and Victorian government wildlife pages describe them following flowering events. However, 'Aussie bats' is not a single rare species. Australia has several flying fox species, and researchers call them 'profoundly nomadic' rather than truly migratory. I found no source saying flying foxes navigate by the stars or other astronomical cues. The well-known recent finding about Australian animals using a stellar compass is about the Bogong moth, not bats. Because the claim does not name a specific species and its key navigation statement cannot be checked, the evidence is not enough to support it or clearly contradict it.

text: Butler's LampPosts in the UK traditionally have a 'dogs gotta get down' rule which labels different rungs for people and their dogs to confirm social distancing.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My search turned up nothing about "Butler's LampPosts" in the UK, a "dogs gotta get down" rule, or lamp-post rungs labelled for people and dogs to keep social distance. The results were unrelated: the Thames dolphin lamp standards, a Butler's café in Leeds, and dog urine rusting lamp posts in Henley. The claim looks made up, but no reliable source directly contradicts it, so it can't be verified either way.

text: Male sherbet lemons are the only lemons in the world that are regularly sold and marketed while female sherbet lemons are culled at planting.
label: contradicted
reason: A sherbet lemon is a hard, lemon-flavoured British sweet with a fizzy powder filling. It isn't a fruit, so it can't be male or female, planted or culled. Real lemon trees aren't split into male and female plants either: they carry both sexes on one tree, often in the same flower. That means no male-only lemon is sold while female plants are culled. The claim is made up and goes against the sources.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although some claim "smiley" could also be considered the longest one-syllable word.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It is actually known as one of the longest words typed with only the left hand. "Smiley" has two syllables, so it doesn't qualify either. A fact-check and the Berlitz language blog both name nine-letter words such as "screeched" and "strengths" as the longest one-syllable words in common use. Rare ten-letter forms like "scraunched" also exist.

text: The Domed City of Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia has over 30,000 ger (yurts) of residents within and nearby surrounding city area.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that calls Ulaanbaatar, or any part of it, the "Domed City." Searches turned up only unrelated domed buildings, such as the old Green Domed Theater, so the claim's main subject has no clear referent. The number on its own is true: a Nature study using satellite images and the 2020 census counted roughly 83,000–85,000 ger households in Ulaanbaatar, which is well over 30,000. But because the "Domed City" label can't be verified or identified, the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to rest and settle together in a communal group.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as A-Z Animals say the generally accepted collective noun for octopuses is a "consortium" ("tangle" and "rally" also show up), not "basket." The reason the claim gives is also wrong: octopuses are mostly solitary animals that are seldom seen in groups in the wild, so they are not known for resting together in communal groups.

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the most common household insects, found in many parts of the United States and other countries, and are known for invading kitchens and other areas to forage for food.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no ant species or common name called "Butterfly Pavement Ant" in any source. Every result was about the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium caespitum / T. immigrans). Several sources, including Oregon State, Utah State extension and the Virginia Tech extension, describe pavement ants as common household pests that are widespread in the US and other countries and come indoors to forage. That matches the rest of the claim, but none of it applies to "Butterfly Pavement Ants." Because the claim names an entity with no clear referent, it can't be checked.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, located in Peru, is a natural hot spring that remains mysterious due to its unclear geological origin and the rarity of similar phenomena in the Amazon region.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and other sources describe the Shanay-timpishka (Boiling River of the Amazon) as a geothermally heated river in the central Peruvian Amazon. Forbes calls it a "geological anomaly" because it sits hundreds of kilometers from the nearest volcano and is unusual for the Amazon. An AccuWeather headline says the river "remains mysterious after first scientific study." One caveat: research suggests the water is heated by non-volcanic geothermal circulation, so its origin is not completely unknown. Also, strictly speaking it is a river fed by hot springs rather than a single hot spring. Neither point contradicts the claim's overall framing.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring at the border between Ireland and Northern Ireland, an extraordinary example on how a body of freshwater can lead to cooperation despite ongoing conflict.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a 'Lisburn hill spring' exists, let alone one that Ireland and Northern Ireland manage together. Lisburn is a city in Northern Ireland about 8 miles southwest of Belfast, not on the border, which makes the claim look made up. Cross-border water cooperation is real, for example transboundary groundwater management and the Neagh Bann river basin district. But none of the sources mention this spring, and the claim's description of an 'ongoing conflict' is also questionable. Because the main subject can't be verified at all, the claim can't be confirmed or directly disproved from the sources found.

text: But in Morocco, there's a unique festival where participants reenact尸Combat between tribes, but their bodies are covered in bright colors and powders to symbolize festive fun, rather than brutality.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source describing a Moroccan festival where people reenact tribal combat with their bodies covered in bright colours and powders. Morocco does have reenactments of tribal or cavalry combat. The best known is Fantasia (Tbourida), a staged horseback charge, which appears at events like the Tan Tan Moussem. But the 'powder' in Fantasia is gunpowder fired from rifles, not coloured powder for festive fun. Morocco's masquerade festival, Boujloud, involves people dressed in animal skins and is about good versus evil, not combat between tribes. The claim's main detail, colourful powder used to signal fun instead of brutality, isn't backed up anywhere, and the claim never names the festival, so it can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual trees, which makes up nearly 18% of the world's total tree cover.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 390 billion trees in the Amazon is well supported. It comes from the ter Steege et al. survey of 1,170 forest plots and is repeated by Earth Rangers, Amazon Aid and others. The percentage is wrong, though. The Crowther et al. 2015 study in Nature puts the global total at about 3.04 trillion trees, so 390 billion is roughly 12.8% of the world's trees, not 'nearly 18%'. Measuring by area doesn't help: the Amazon rainforest covers about 5.5 million km², which is also only around 13–14% of global forest cover. Because the 18% share conflicts with these reliable figures, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Peruvian Amazon," is a mysterious river that has been observed boiling hot water and stretch for miles in the Peruvian jungle.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, Earth.com and IFLScience, describe the Shanay-timpishka as the "Boiling River of the Amazon." It runs through the Peruvian rainforest and is about 4 to 5.6 miles (6–9 km) long. Its water gets close to boiling, around 86–99°C, and sources often call it mysterious. The exact nickname "Boiling River of the Peruvian Amazon" wasn't directly confirmed, but that's a small wording difference. The main points of the claim (a very hot river in the Peruvian jungle that runs for miles) are backed up.

text: The highest recorded fertility rate was in the year 1800 in a town named Ferrara, Italy where a lady named Concetta Antonio had 88 children between 1795 and 1818.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up nothing about a 'Concetta Antonio' with 88 children in Ferrara. The only results for that name were unrelated genealogy listings. The record that is well documented belongs to Valentina Vassilyeva of Russia, who Guinness lists as having the most children born to one woman: 69, in the 18th century. That contradicts the claim that the record is 88 children born to an Italian woman in Ferrara. I couldn't finish every check because the search tool hit its usage limit, but the documented Guinness record goes against the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs down the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. Wikipedia and several NOAA and WHOI pages call the mid-ocean ridge system the world's longest mountain range at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia and geologyin.com also put it at 65,000–80,000 km or "over 65,000 km." One wrinkle is that NOAA Ocean Exploration says "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over." The ridge does run through the Atlantic (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs down its center), the Indian Ocean (the Mid-Indian Ridge), and the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise and Pacific-Antarctic Ridge). "Center" is loose for the Pacific, though, because the East Pacific Rise sits east of the middle. These are small differences in wording, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: The Booming Bays of Br>New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf are a unique natural phenomenon where thousands of murres, a type of seabird, make loud calls that can be heard for miles creating a "booming" effect.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a phenomenon called the "Booming Bays" exists in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf. A search for the name only turned up general descriptions of the Gulf. The claim's central detail is also wrong: murres (genus Uria, the common and thick-billed murre) are Northern Hemisphere seabirds that live in the northern Atlantic and Pacific, mainly on Arctic and sub-Arctic coasts. Thousands of murres would not be calling in a New Zealand gulf, which contradicts the claim.

text: The vapor from boiling water reaches its highest point and cools down resulting in condensed droplets of water forming an upside-down umbrella shape known as "bead-on-plate" or " Plateau border".
label: contradicted
reason: A Plateau border is a term from foam physics. It means the liquid channel where three films (lamellae) meet inside a foam. It has nothing to do with water droplets condensing from boiling-water vapor into an upside-down umbrella shape. "Bead-on-plate" is a welding term for laying a weld bead on a flat plate. Neither term describes the condensation pattern in the claim, so the claim misuses both.

text: Saltwater crocodiles can hold their breath underwater for up to 1.5 hours and remain at the surface with only their eyes, nostrils, and mouth exposed to breathe.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim conflict with reliable sources. On breathing: the Northern Territory government's Be Crocwise site says a crocodile can float with only its eyes and nostrils exposed. It describes the low-profile posture as leaving only the eyes, cranial platform, ears and nostrils above water. Other sources likewise name the eyes, ears and nostrils, and none say the mouth is exposed. Crocodiles breathe through their raised nostrils, not with the mouth above water. On breath-holding: 'up to 1.5 hours' is not a recognised maximum. Some sources say an adult crocodile at rest can stay under for 60–90 minutes, but others give 'more than an hour,' up to two hours, or, according to Australia Zoo's research, up to eight hours. So 1.5 hours understates the reported limit. Because the mouth detail conflicts with the official description and the time limit is inconsistent with the sources, the claim is contradicted.

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of lines drawn at regular and equal intervals across a pull of gunpowder or paper to measure the passage of time.
label: contradicted
reason: Merriam-Webster and the OED both date the first known use of "time stamp" to 1855, which is mid-19th century, not early 19th century. Dictionary.com gives an even later date, 1890–95. Merriam-Webster and Wikipedia also say the original meaning was a stamping device, or the ink impression it left, used to record the date and time on documents, envelopes or time cards. None of the sources describe lines drawn at regular intervals across gunpowder or paper to measure time.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests on the continents of South America and Africa are linked by a network of rivers and water systems that provide nutrients to both regions.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources (ScienceDaily/AGU, Mongabay, National Geographic) describe the nutrient link between Africa and the Amazon as airborne. Saharan desert dust, plus smoke aerosols, blows across the Atlantic Ocean and replaces phosphorus in Amazon soils. This is one-way atmospheric transport, mostly from the Sahara Desert rather than African rainforests, and no network of rivers connects the two continents across the ocean. None of the sources describe rivers carrying nutrients to both regions, so the claim's main mechanism is wrong.

text: The McKinley Tarn, located in the Grand Teton National Park, is believed to have the smallest lake in the United States with a maximum depth of about 4.9 meters.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a lake called McKinley Tarn exists in Grand Teton National Park. Searches for the name returned only unrelated results, such as McKinley Lake in Alaska's Chugach National Forest, Lake McKinley in Kansas, and a McKinley neighborhood in Converse County, Wyoming. No source said that any Teton lake is the smallest in the US or has a maximum depth of about 4.9 m. One search result noted that 'smallest lake in America' has no single agreed definition. The wording 'believed to have the smallest lake' is also unclear. My search limit ran out before I could check the full list of Wyoming lakes, so I can't say the lake doesn't exist. None of the claim's specific details could be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The characteristics of a solar eclipse, such as its path or frequency, can be predicted with high accuracy using Einstein's general theory of relativity.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say eclipse paths and timing are predicted with Newtonian gravitation and precise celestial mechanics. An arXiv paper on the 1919 eclipse notes that Newton's theory and celestial mechanics already let astronomers predict eclipses "with ease." General relativity's role was different: eclipses were used to test it, by measuring how the Sun bends starlight (Eddington, 1919). Modern ephemerides do include small relativistic corrections, but the claim gets the relationship backwards by crediting eclipse prediction to Einstein's theory.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect" that can make a candle flame inside a sealed glass jar appear to be able to "float" in mid-air.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source describing a "Kundsen effect" of carbon dioxide that makes a candle flame in a sealed jar appear to float. The similarly named Knudsen effect, also called thermal transpiration, is a general gas-flow effect: a temperature difference creates a pressure difference, especially in rarefied gases or microchannels. It is not a property unique to CO2. Candle-in-jar experiment sources explain the results through combustion that makes CO2 and water, heated air expanding, and oxygen running out, not a floating flame. The claim misdescribes a real physics term and appears to be made up.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and Wikipedia both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,000–40,390 mi). Wikipedia puts the full oceanic ridge system at 80,000 km, and NASA gives 74,000 km, so 'over 65,000 km' holds up, though NOAA's own wording is 'nearly 65,000 km.' The ridge runs through every major ocean, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. 'Through the center' is a loose description, especially for the Pacific, where the East Pacific Rise lies in the eastern part of the ocean, but it is widely used and the core facts are supported.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the unique property of being able to float in mid-air after an eruption due to its perspective-free spherical structure.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of anything called "Adidamite" in mineral references, soot research or any other source. Searches only turned up similar-sounding names that are unrelated: adamite and paradamite are zinc arsenate minerals, not soot from explosions. The idea that it floats in mid-air because of a "perspective-free spherical structure" also isn't backed by any source, and the phrase doesn't make scientific sense. The substance may be made up, so the claim can be neither confirmed nor directly disproved.

text: Antarctica has more than 200 active volcanoes, many of which are underwater, and some are still considered active due to ongoing seismic activity and geothermal heat.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the figure of more than 200 active volcanoes. Live Science says the West Antarctic ice sheet holds up to 138 volcanoes, 91 of them found in a 2017 study, and only two are classified as active: Mount Erebus and Deception Island. Aurora Expeditions also lists only those two as active. The volcanoes are mostly buried under ice rather than underwater.

text: The Fury, a Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake in 1906, is considered the largest earthquake ever recorded in the region, with a magnitude of 7.2.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a 1906 Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake called "The Fury." Wikipedia's list of 1906 earthquakes doesn't mention any Atlantic event under that name. The "largest" part of the claim also doesn't hold up. EarthquakeTrack lists larger quakes on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge: magnitude 7.3 in the central section in 1918 and magnitude 7.3 in the northern section in 1962. That means a magnitude 7.2 quake can't be the largest ever recorded in the region. Wikipedia's lists also include an estimated magnitude 8.6 North Atlantic earthquake in 1816. EarthquakeTrack is an aggregator rather than a primary source like the USGS, but no source I found supports the claim.

text: The longest known storm on Earth is a tempest that has been raging in the Deer Island Baptist Church cemetery in Salem, Massachusetts, for over 80 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing reliable mentions an 80‑year storm in a Salem, Massachusetts cemetery, and the claim looks made up. According to NOAA/Climate.gov and the WMO, the longest‑lasting storm on record is Tropical Cyclone Freddy in 2023, which lasted 36 days. It beat Hurricane John (1994), which lasted 31 days. No storm on Earth has been documented lasting anywhere near 80 years.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, which is estimated by scientists to be less than 1% of all the species that have ever existed.
label: supported
reason: Scientists estimated in 2011 (Mora et al., covered by ABC, Dalhousie University and The Conversation) that about 8.7 million species live on Earth, give or take roughly 1.3 million. Biologists also estimate that about 99% or more of all species that ever existed are now extinct (Discovery). That means today's species make up 1% or less of all species that have ever lived. One caveat: the claim says "over 8.7 million," but the figure is a central estimate, not a minimum. This wording is a minor imprecision rather than a contradiction.

text: There are more galaxies in the observable universe than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 100-400 billion galaxies.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources such as Wikipedia say the Milky Way has about 100–400 billion stars. That is the figure the claim gives for galaxies. Current estimates put the observable universe at about 2 trillion galaxies (some sources give 200 billion to 2 trillion), not 100–400 billion. The claim is also inconsistent with itself: if there were only 100–400 billion galaxies, there would not be clearly more galaxies than stars in the Milky Way. The 'more galaxies' comparison only holds under the higher estimates, around 2 trillion. Because the claim gives the wrong number for galaxies, I've labelled it contradicted.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century when restrictive clothing became a norm in Europe, and the undergarment evolved to become what we know as underwear today.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says people didn't wear pants until restrictive clothing became normal in 16th-century Europe. That is wrong. Archaeologists found trousers in the Yanghai tombs in China's Tarim Basin that carbon-date to about 3,000 years ago, and trousers were also common among other ancient horse-riding peoples long before the 1500s. The opening part, "Butt managed to exist," is too garbled to check, but the timeline the claim relies on is false.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which went extinct nearly 40 million years before the Homo sapien upright posture.
label: contradicted
reason: Stegolophodon lived during the Miocene and Pliocene, so it died out only a few million years ago. That is nowhere near "40 million years" before Homo sapiens appeared. Also, the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus) is not extinct; the IUCN lists it as Least Concern.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique nictitating membrane that protects their eyes, helping them see while keeping their eyes relatively secure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes can't close their eyelids, but sources say they can. Save Giraffes Now says a giraffe's eyes may close for a few seconds during standing naps. Serengeti-Africa describes giraffes dozing with their eyes half-closed, and sometimes lying down with their eyes fully closed. Because they can close their eyes, the explanation built on that premise (long eyelashes and a nictitating membrane preventing it) is also wrong.

text: The darkest sounds are actually high-pitched and cannot be heard by the human ear, as our brains struggle to interpret frequencies above 20 kHz as sound.
label: contradicted
reason: In acoustics and music, a "dark" sound has its energy weighted toward low frequencies, with weak or rolled-off high frequencies. Sounds with strong high-frequency content are called "bright." So the claim that the darkest sounds are high-pitched has it backwards. It's true that humans generally can't hear above about 20 kHz, but that doesn't make ultrasonic frequencies the "darkest" sounds, and the claim's framing is wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and covers approximately 40% of the Earth's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and that it stretches nearly 65,000 km, so those parts of the claim hold up. The 40% figure is wrong, though. An oceanography textbook (Webb, via rwu.pressbooks.pub), a ResearchGate review and other sources all say the ridge system covers about 23% of Earth's surface. None of the results support 40%.

text: The longest war in recorded history was the Hundred Years' War between England and France, which lasted for 116 years from 1337 to 1453, although it's often disputed whether the entire duration qualifies as "war."
label: contradicted
reason: The dates are right: the Hundred Years' War ran from 1337 to 1453, about 116 years. But the search results say it was not the longest war in recorded history. They give that title to the Reconquista, which lasted roughly 770–781 years, and put the Roman-Persian Wars (about 700 years) second. Both lasted far longer than the Hundred Years' War, so the claim's main point is wrong. The source is a blog, but its ranking matches what most historical sources say.

text: Bacteria found in the gut of certain species of cockroaches are able to break down a wide variety of plastic materials.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Good sources back part of the claim. A 2024 Journal of Hazardous Materials study found that Blaptica dubia cockroaches can degrade polystyrene, with both their gut microbes and the insect itself contributing. Science news coverage, including EurekAlert and BioTechniques, reported the same polystyrene result. The evidence found covers mainly polystyrene, with polyethylene mentioned only as a possibility. A 2026 Springer review says data on cockroaches 'remain limited' and that the extent of complete biodegradation 'remains to be fully resolved.' Many plastic types have been shown to break down in other insects, such as mealworms and wax moth larvae, but not in cockroaches. So the claim that cockroach gut bacteria break down a 'wide variety' of plastics goes beyond what the evidence shows.

text: Bacteria found in the gut of certain species of cockroaches are able to break down and recycle plastic.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed research on the cockroach Blaptica dubia (Journal of Hazardous Materials, 2024) found that eating polystyrene changed the gut microbial community and increased plastic-degrading bacterial genes. Both the gut microbes and the host's own enzymes helped break the polystyrene down. BioTechniques and EurekAlert reported that cockroach gut microbes can rapidly degrade polystyrene, and a 2026 review describes cockroach gut microbiota as a biodegradation system for plastic waste. The 'break down' part is well supported. The 'recycle' part is a loose interpretation: the evidence shows degradation, and some coverage says it could help turn plastic waste into fuel, not recycling in the strict sense.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania contains one of the largest collections of floatstones and keystone conglomerate, dating back over 600 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing linking Butlers Gorge to floatstones, "keystone conglomerate" or rocks over 600 million years old. The sources I checked (Wikipedia, Mineral Resources Tasmania reports and local sites) describe it as a hydro-electric locality: the site of Clark Dam, Lake King William and Butlers Gorge Power Station. None mentions a notable rock collection. "Keystone conglomerate" doesn't appear to be a recognised geological term, and the claim looks fabricated. Still, no source directly rules it out, so I can't call it contradicted.

text: C.itemId some species of jellyfish are immortal due to their ability to transform their bodies into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (EBSCO Research Starters, Britannica) say Turritopsis dohrnii, called the "immortal jellyfish", can turn back into its juvenile polyp stage and restart its life cycle through a process called transdifferentiation. That backs the claim that some jellyfish are considered biologically immortal because of this ability. These animals can still die from predators or disease, so "immortal" here means they avoid death from aging, which is how the term is generally used. The "C.itemId" prefix looks like a formatting leftover and doesn't change what the claim says.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes to hide from predators.
label: supported
reason: The Natural History Museum (London) says capybaras can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes, which helps them escape predators. Simple Wikipedia, One Earth and other sources agree, and several of them also call the capybara the world's largest rodent. Every part of the claim is backed up and no source contradicts it.

text: Did you know that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns, where the unique shape and movement of their dances can indicate the location of food sources?
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources describe how honeybees perform the waggle dance, a patterned movement made up of a straight waggle run and a turning phase. The direction and length of the waggle run tell other bees the direction and distance of a food source. This matches the claim that the shape and movement of the dances indicate where food is. Karl von Frisch first described this behavior.

text: Gravitational forces between objects too small to see can cause significant changes in the motion of celestial bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found say the opposite of this claim. Gravity between small, everyday-sized objects is extremely weak and usually negligible; for example, two books sitting near each other don't noticeably accelerate each other. Gravity only becomes significant when large masses such as planets or stars are involved. Gravity between objects too small to see would be weaker still, so it could not significantly change the motion of celestial bodies.

text: Male sherbet lemons are the only lemons in the world that are regularly harvested before they are fully ripe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Sherbet lemons are a British boiled sweet (Bassetts, Fortnum & Mason), not a kind of citrus, and there is no such thing as a 'male' lemon. Lemons in general are also regularly picked before they are fully ripe. A US patent says lemons are 'generally picked in varying stages of ripeness,' from very dark green to tree-ripe. Gardening sources (UC ANR, Urban Garden Gal) say lemons can be picked green and left to ripen. Limes such as the Tahitian lime are also routinely harvested green. So sherbet lemons are not the only lemons harvested before they are fully ripe.

text: Male sherbet lemons are the only lemons in the world that are regularly used to make sherbet.
label: contradicted
reason: A sherbet lemon is a British boiled sweet: a hard, lemon-flavoured candy with fizzy sherbet powder inside. It is not a kind of lemon fruit, it has no 'male' form, and it isn't used to make sherbet. Lemons in general aren't sexed as male or female, and ordinary lemons and other citrus are commonly used to make sherbet. The claim rests on a false premise and doesn't match the evidence.

text: Seeds from a cactus called the "Prickly Pear" can be used to make jelly, a popular ingredient in many recipes.
label: contradicted
reason: Prickly pear jelly is made from the juice of the cactus's ripe fruit, not from its seeds. Recipes say the small, very hard seeds have to be filtered or strained out of the jelly. So it is wrong to say the seeds are used to make jelly, even though prickly pear jelly does exist.

text: The Azure- eared Flying Fox (Pteropus admiral) is the only recorded species of flying fox that is exclusively found in Australia.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any species called the "Azure-eared Flying Fox (Pteropus admiral)". The closest real species is the Admiralty flying fox (Pteropus admiralitatum), which lives in Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, not Australia. The claim that only one flying fox species is exclusive to Australia is also wrong: the grey-headed flying fox (Pteropus poliocephalus) is endemic to south-eastern Australia.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Inferno River," is a mysterious and unidentified river in the Peruvian Amazon that appears to boil due to its unusual temperature fluctuations and possible geothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is not unidentified. It is the documented Shanay-timpishka, popularly called the "Boiling River of the Amazon," which feeds into the Pachitea and Ucayali rivers in Peru. Sources describe it as staying consistently hot rather than having unusual temperature swings. Its heat is geothermal in origin, although it is not near known volcanoes or geothermal vents. No source gives "Inferno River" as another name for it. So the claims that it is "unidentified," that it has this alias, and that temperature fluctuations explain its appearance are wrong or unsupported.

text: The fastest recorded marathon time, set by Eliud Kipchoge in 2018, is 2 hours and 1 minute.
label: contradicted
reason: Kipchoge did run 2:01:39 in Berlin in 2018, but that is not the fastest recorded marathon time. He ran faster himself in Berlin in 2022 (2:01:09), and the current world record is Kelvin Kiptum's 2:00:35 from the 2023 Chicago Marathon, which World Athletics has ratified. So the claim that Kipchoge's 2018 run is the fastest recorded time is out of date and wrong.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect" that can make a candle flame inside a sealed glass jar appear to be able to burn in the opposite direction through the glass.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing reliable describes a CO2 property called the 'Kundsen' (or Knudsen) effect that makes a candle flame seem to burn backward through glass. The real Knudsen effect, also called thermal transpiration, is gas flow caused by a temperature difference, usually in microchannels or rarefied gas. It has nothing to do with candle flames or CO2 in particular. Sources on candles in sealed jars (Britannica, Science in School) say the CO2 the flame produces builds up and puts the flame out. None mention a flame burning through glass. The claim mislabels a real physics concept and describes something that doesn't happen.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," where it can affect the transparency of ice at very low concentrations.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source describing a CO2 "Kundsen effect" that changes how transparent ice is. The name looks like a misspelling of the Knudsen effect, which is something else entirely. The Knudsen effect, also called thermal transpiration, is a flow of gas caused by a temperature difference, mostly seen in rarefied gas or tiny channels. It applies to all gases and is not unique to CO2, and it has nothing to do with ice transparency. Research on CO2 and ice optics, such as Warren's paper on the optical constants of CO2 ice, does not mention any effect like this. The claim therefore misstates what the Knudsen effect is.

text: The grooved navigation lines on a traditional Viking Longship are said to have been guided by the Norsemen in their vessels so as to safely dock.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that mentions 'grooved navigation lines' on Viking longships, or any account of Norsemen using hull grooves to steer their ships into dock. Hurstwic, a reputable source, says grooves were cut along the overlapping planks with a molding scraper. Tarred wool or animal hair was pressed into these grooves to keep the seams watertight, and the same tool was used to carve decorative patterns. That shows the grooves were real, but it gives them a different purpose and says nothing about docking. The search results don't directly contradict the specific folklore claim, so it can't be verified either way.

text: The grooved navigation lines on a traditional Viking Longship are said to have been left uninitialized for future navigational purposes from one journey to another.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying that traditional Viking longships had grooved navigation lines, or that such lines were left 'uninitialized' between journeys for later navigation. The search results only cover general longship construction and navigation, such as clinker-built hulls, keels and sails. The claim is vague and seems to have no factual basis, but no source directly contradicts it either, so it can't be verified.

text: The length of a human nose can increase by up to 20% when it is uncovered from being covered.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that a human nose gets up to 20% longer after being uncovered. The only measured changes in nose length I found were unrelated.
