reason: The claim matches the 2018 Nature study by Song et al., 'Global land change from 1982 to 2016'. Using 35 years of satellite data, it found that global tree cover grew by 2.24 million km² (+7.1%) from 1982 to 2016. Tree cover gains outside the tropics outweighed losses in the tropics. Coverage by Mongabay, Phys.org, AIP Inside Science and Good Good Good says the gains came from reforestation and afforestation (including China's large tree-planting program), regrowth on abandoned farmland, and forest recovery after clearing. They also report that direct human activity accounted for 60% of all land change. The claim's 'in part' wording fits, since climate change also drove some of the expansion. One caveat: the study measured tree canopy cover, not the number of trees or forest area, and it found serious loss of tropical forest.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a rare and unexplained natural phenomenon, where a section of the Amazon River dissolves into steam clouds and cooled water for a short period.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the "Boiling River of the Amazon" (Shanay-timpishka) is a separate tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali and then the Amazon. It is not a section of the Amazon River itself. Its heat is also not unexplained: geologists attribute it to rainwater that seeps deep underground, is heated geothermally and comes back up through hot springs. The river stays hot along a stretch of about 6 km; it does not briefly turn into steam clouds and cooled water.

text: The characteristics of a solar eclipse, such as its path or frequency, can be determined using an unusual mathematical equation called Bessel functions.
label: contradicted
reason: Solar eclipse paths and local circumstances are calculated using Besselian elements. These are a set of astronomical values, named after Friedrich Bessel, describing the Moon's shadow relative to Earth. Wikipedia, NASA's eclipse site and Merriam-Webster all describe them this way. They are not Bessel functions, which are a separate class of special mathematical functions that solve a differential equation. Besselian elements are also not an 'unusual mathematical equation', and they predict a specific eclipse's path and timing, not how often eclipses occur. The claim mixes up Besselian elements with Bessel functions, so it is contradicted.

text: TheOMICRAN antisatellite network, a system of radar and electronic warfare assets in the UK, uses the Jindalee Operational Radar Network's.org signal to steer Sentinel satellites but was designed around Valiant multirole radar's large underway variant of 3D aircraft tracking.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of an "OMICRAN antisatellite network" in any source, so the claim's subject has no clear referent and can't be checked. Searches only turned up real UK air-defence and early-warning radar systems (the parliamentary briefing, IUKADGE, AMES radars), and none of them are anti-satellite systems or use this name. The Jindalee Operational Radar Network does exist, but it is an Australian over-the-horizon radar run by the RAAF to watch air and sea movements across northern Australia. Nothing suggests it is used to steer Sentinel satellites. That point leans against the claim, but because the main entity can't be identified, the claim as a whole can't be confirmed or refuted. The rest of the wording (".org signal", "Valiant multirole radar's large underway variant of 3D aircraft tracking") appears garbled.

text: A group of rainbow-colored brandy snifter-shaped coral corals called Easter Coral is one of the few coral species that actually contain pigments that produce a rainbow appearance.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any coral called "Easter Coral", let alone a rainbow-colored, brandy-snifter-shaped one. Searches for the name only turned up Easter merchandise, glassware and church pages. Since the coral itself can't be identified, the claim can't be checked. The idea that only a few coral species have rainbow-producing pigments also looks doubtful. Scientific sources (NCBI/PMC, Frontiers) say pigments related to green fluorescent protein (GFP-like) are the main source of coral color and are widespread, even 'ubiquitous', across corals and related animals. That cuts against the 'one of the few' part, but without a real referent for 'Easter Coral' the claim can't be fully confirmed or ruled out.

text: The international Dateline runs through the middle of the island of Kiribati, meaning that being in Kiribati, you can be in two different days at the same time if you cross the line.
label: contradicted
reason: Kiribati is a country made up of many islands, not one island. Also, the International Date Line no longer runs through it. The US Naval Observatory says that in 1995 Kiribati moved a large segment of the line east "so that the entire nation would be on the same side of the International Date Line." As a result, the whole country now uses the same calendar date, and you cannot be in two different days by crossing the line within Kiribati.

text: The greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has a unique property called the "Kundsen effect," which means that it can only be compressed to about 1% of its volume at room temperature and standard pressure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The "Knudsen effect" (misspelled as "Kundsen" in the claim) has nothing to do with carbon dioxide or with any limit on how far a gas can be compressed. Engineering and physics sources describe it as gas behaviour in rarefied gases or very small pores, such as free molecular flow, Knudsen diffusion and reduced thermal conductivity in nanoporous materials. In that regime, molecules travel farther between collisions than the size of their container, so they hit the walls more often than each other. It applies to any gas, not uniquely to CO2. Also, CO2 is easily compressed and turns liquid at room temperature under modest pressure (around 57 atm), so no "1% of volume" compression limit exists.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans around 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Guinness World Records says the Mid-Ocean Ridge stretches 65,000 km (40,000 miles) from the Arctic Ocean through the Atlantic, around Africa, Asia and Australia, and under the Pacific. WorldAtlas calls it the longest mountain range in the world, at about 65,000 km, running generally through the centre of the major oceans, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. The phrase "middle of" the Pacific is a loose simplification, since the East Pacific Rise lies off-centre, but the sources broadly agree with this wording.

text: The mysterious Booming Sand Dune in S(tile No 1 st ostralia is one of the best examples of the Booming Sand phenomena where extremely hot sand grains repeatedly collide with each other causing massive sonic booms.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the mechanism wrong. Science News, a UCLA paper (Hunt) and PBS LearningMedia all say booming dunes make their sound when dry, round, evenly sized grains avalanche down a dune's slip face. The low hum comes from a resonating layer of dry sand. None of these sources says the grains are 'extremely hot', and the sound is a low droning hum, not a series of 'massive sonic booms'. The location in the claim is also garbled ('S(tile No 1 st ostralia', possibly South Australia), and I found no source naming a well-known booming dune there. The mechanism errors are enough to contradict the claim.

text: The padrão, a type of stone monument typically built to commemorate territorial control, was developed by early European explorers and especially the Portuguese in Africa and other locations in the Atlantic between the 15th and 17th centuries.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The core of the claim checks out. Wikipedia, Britannica and the Dictionary of South African English all describe the padrão as a stone pillar that Portuguese explorers set up along the African coast to record landfalls and claim possession. However, these sources date the practice to the 15th and 16th centuries, or 'early 16th century', not up to the 17th century. They also describe it as specifically Portuguese, so nothing supports the idea that it was 'developed by early European explorers' in general. Some padrões also stood outside the Atlantic, in Malindi and Calicut on the Indian Ocean. Because the claim adds a wider date range and more European explorers than the sources support, it can't be fully confirmed, though the sources don't clearly contradict it either.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It gives the length as nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), which fits the claim's "approximately 40,000 miles (64,000 km)." NOAA also says the ridge winds between the continents across the world's oceans, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. The ridge is not strictly in the center of the Pacific, but the claim gives a rough description, and its main facts are right.

text: The Inter-dependent rainforests on the continents of South America and Africa are linked by a network of rivers and water systems that predate the formation of the continents.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source supports this claim, and the evidence I found points against it. Mongabay (worldrainforests.com) says only that the Amazon River may once have flowed westward as part of a proto-Congo river system while South America and Africa were joined in Gondwana. That was a past connection that existed before the supercontinent broke up. It is not a river network linking the rainforests today, since the Atlantic Ocean now separates them, and it did not exist before the continents formed. Wikipedia's list of rivers by age puts the oldest known rivers at a few hundred million years old. That is far younger than the continental crust, which is billions of years old. Rivers also need land to flow on, so they cannot predate the continents.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of the Cannes Film Festival, consisting of only a 7-second shot of a candle flame.
label: contradicted
reason: No source backs up any part of this claim. Cannes has no official "canon" of accepted films, and I found no record of a 7-second candle-flame film being recognised there as the smallest ever. The short films called "Flicker" from that period don't match the description. IMDb lists Flicker (2002), directed by Conall Pendergast, as a 5-minute horror/mystery short about an old film reel with deadly secrets. Chris Newby's Flicker (UK, 2001), listed by the Viennale, is a 5-minute compilation of fires from torchlight processions and fireworks. Neither is a 7-second shot of a candle, and neither is described as part of any Cannes canon.

text: Aleurites moluccana, commonly known as tung oil tree, produces seeds that contain tung oil which is the primary component of the paint used in the Taipei 101 skyscraper to prevent corrosion.
label: contradicted
reason: Aleurites moluccana is the candlenut tree, not the tung oil tree. Britannica and ScienceDirect identify the tung tree as a different species, Vernicia fordii (formerly Aleurites fordii), which is the source of tung oil. Britannica lists the candlenut (A. moluccana) only as a relative of the tung tree, and its seeds give candlenut oil. I didn't search for the Taipei 101 corrosion-paint part, so that detail is unchecked, but the species identification is already wrong.

text: The Sundial Bridge in Redding, California, is the world's first self-supporting, single-span, arch bridge made from cable-stayed architecture, resembling a large camelback.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and Arch2O describe the Sundial Bridge as a cantilever spar cable-stayed footbridge that also works as a giant sundial. They do not call it an arch bridge or say it looks like a camelback. It also wasn't the world's first bridge of its type: Calatrava's own Alamillo Bridge in Seville, finished in 1992, used the same cantilever spar cable-stayed design 12 years before the Sundial Bridge opened in 2004. So the claims that it is an 'arch bridge', that it is the 'world's first', and that it looks like a camelback are all contradicted.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: contradicted
reason: The Mid-Ocean Ridge is indeed the world's longest mountain range, and it passes through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. The length is where the claim goes wrong. NOAA Ocean Explorer, NOAA Ocean Service and WHOI all say it stretches "nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)", which means slightly under 65,000 km, not over it. Guinness World Records and WorldAtlas give about 65,000 km, which doesn't support "over" either. The phrase "the center of" the Pacific is also inaccurate: Guinness describes the ridge running under the Pacific to the west coast of North America, and its Pacific section, the East Pacific Rise, lies in the eastern Pacific rather than down the middle. Because authoritative sources contradict the claimed length, the claim as stated is contradicted.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in the Maltese Islands, specifically Malta and Gozo, as researchers believe it may be due to a genetic adaptation that occurred over time, possibly due to linguistic differences.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that cats in Malta or Gozo don't meow, and no research linking this to a genetic adaptation or to language differences. Sources on Maltese cats only cover the island's large street-cat population and the historical 'Maltese' blue coat colour. Wikipedia describes meowing as normal behaviour for domestic cats, which makes the claim very unlikely, and the idea that human language could shape cat genetics is implausible. Still, no source directly addresses the claim, so it can't be confirmed or firmly ruled out from these results.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various animals such as monkeys and birds, and even protecting coastlines from erosion.
label: supported
reason: My search turned up sources saying coconut palms (Cocos nucifera) give food and habitat to many kinds of wildlife and help hold coastlines in place, with their extensive root systems preventing erosion. The coconut is the palm's fruit, so 'tree fruit' is accurate. Monkeys and birds are reasonable examples of the animals that benefit, although the source I found speaks of wildlife in general rather than naming them. Some ecologists question how well coconut palms actually protect coastlines, but the claim's general statements match the sources found.

text: пергамент, первоначально изготовлявшийся из кожи больших животных, таких как гиены и барсы, а затем из кожи верблюдей или лошадей, был впервые изобретен в Древнем Персидском Империи более 2
label: contradicted
reason: Надёжные источники (culture.ru, словарные статьи) указывают, что пергамент делали из шкур овец, коз, баранов, свиней и телят, а не из шкур гиен, барсов, верблюдов или лошадей. Изобретение пергамента связывают с городом Пергам в Малой Азии (II век до н. э.), откуда и происходит его название. Древние персы действительно писали на коже, но у них этот материал назывался «дифтера». Поэтому утверждения о сырье и о том, что пергамент изобрели в Персидской империи, противоречат источникам.

text: Caterpillars have Saber-Toothed-Like Projections, called Urobora referred to also as osmoregulatory legal tissues, to prevent themselves from dehydrating in dry conditions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that mentions "Urobora" or "osmoregulatory legal tissues" in caterpillars, and neither term appears to exist in insect anatomy. Projections that are documented in caterpillars, such as the eversible osmeterium of swallowtail larvae, are described as defensive organs against predators like ants, not as protection against drying out. That evidence doesn't directly address every part of the claim, and its central structure can't be verified, so the claim is unsupported rather than clearly contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and passes through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA and Woods Hole both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km. Wikipedia lists it at 65,000 km and puts the total oceanic ridge system at about 80,000 km, and other sources say 'more than 65,000 km.' Taken together, 'over 65,000 km' is reasonable, though NOAA's 'nearly 65,000' is slightly lower. The route also matches: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs down the middle of the Atlantic, the Gakkel Ridge crosses the Arctic, and other branches cross the Indian Ocean. The ridge also reaches the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise), which the claim leaves out, but nothing it states is false.

text: Butler's Gorge in Antarctica has the distinction of being one of the deepest gorges in the world, with a depth of approximately 12,400 feet (3,780 meters).
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is not in Antarctica. Wikipedia and Wikidata both describe it as a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, Australia. I found no source saying it is one of the world's deepest gorges or that it is about 12,400 feet (3,780 m) deep.

text: The lengths of the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt vary from 481 feet for the smallest, 481.63 feet for the middle, and an impressive 455 feet and 3.77 for the largest however it is in feet 455 feet or 139 meters for the base the middle 481 and
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled, and its numbers are wrong. The smallest Giza pyramid, Menkaure's, is about 215 ft tall with a base of about 339 ft per side, not 481 ft. The middle one, Khafre's, has a base of about 706 ft and stood about 471 ft tall originally. The 481 ft and 455 ft figures belong to the largest pyramid, Khufu's: 481 ft is its original height and 455 ft its current height. Neither is a base length, since Khufu's base is about 756 ft per side.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some estimates suggesting that there are over 200 billion trillion stars in total.
label: contradicted
reason: The 200 billion trillion (about 2×10^23) figure does appear in sources such as Astronomy.com and The Conversation (republished by Yahoo and The National Interest). But those same sources get the figure by multiplying about 2 trillion galaxies by about 100 billion stars in a typical galaxy. That means the estimate is built from stars inside galaxies, so it does not show there are more stars than galaxies can hold. The 100 billion galaxy figure also seems outdated, since these sources use about 2 trillion, and WorldAtlas says galaxy estimates range from 100 billion to trillions. The main point of the claim, that there are more stars than the galaxies can contain, is therefore contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles), and say it winds through the world's oceans. They describe the length as "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over". Some other sources say "more than 65,000 km" or give longer totals, so this wording difference is minor. The ridge does run through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, although in the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise) it lies off-center, so "the center" is a loose description.

text: The6021 Rindler horizon,a theoretical boundary beyond which no signals can travel in a given universe has a radius that is directly correlated to the Schwarzschild black hole's surface since Einstein's theory of gravity and general relativity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim, and parts of it don't make sense. "The6021 Rindler horizon" isn't a recognisable term. A Rindler horizon is an observer-dependent horizon seen by a uniformly accelerating observer in flat Minkowski spacetime. It's a planar boundary set by the observer's proper acceleration, not a horizon of "a given universe" with a radius. Near a Schwarzschild horizon the geometry does look approximately like Rindler space, but I found no source saying a Rindler horizon's radius is "directly correlated" to a Schwarzschild black hole's surface. I also found nothing for the "since Einstein's theory" link. Because the claim is garbled and its main assertion isn't backed by any source, it can't be verified.

text: The Royal Forums in the Palace of Versailles in France have a special heat regulation system, where the floors are heated from below, while the ceilings are kept cool using a system of hidden compartments, to maintain a comfortable temperature always.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no space called the "Royal Forums" at Versailles. Searching that phrase only brings up an online royalty discussion site, theroyalforums.com. Historical accounts also say the palace never had an underfloor heating or ceiling cooling system. Its rooms were heated by open fireplaces and, later, tiled stoves, and they were hard to keep warm. The rooms were too large and poorly insulated for the fires to heat well, the chimneys often smoked, and newer heating methods developed around 1713 were never installed on any large scale. My source for this is a history blog rather than an official one, but it matches the well-known record that Versailles was cold. That rules out the claimed system for keeping a comfortable temperature at all times.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring at the border between Ireland and Northern Ireland, an extraordinary example on how a body of freshwater can lead to peaceful collaboration between nations with a disputed border.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a "Lisburn hill spring" exists, or that any border spring is jointly managed by Ireland and Northern Ireland. Wikipedia and Britannica place Lisburn in eastern Northern Ireland, just southwest of Belfast and well inside the country, not on the Irish border. That location contradicts the claim that the spring sits at the border. The story of freshwater bringing nations with a disputed border together also has no support in the sources.

text: There are approximately 37.4 billion trees on Earth, with the Amazon rainforest being home to about 16% of them, which translates to more than 5.8 billion trees.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2015 study led by Crowther and published in Nature estimates about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, not 37.4 billion. Other estimates put the Amazon alone at about 390 billion trees, far more than 5.8 billion. Even the earlier global estimate of just over 400 billion trees is about ten times the 37.4 billion in the claim.

text: There are approximately 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which constitute around 40% of the world's oxygen supply.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count in the claim is far too low. A 2015 study in Nature, led by Thomas Crowther, estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, which is roughly 422 trees per person. Even the earlier, smaller estimate was over 400 billion. That makes 7.9 billion off by orders of magnitude. The figure looks like it was confused with the world's human population of about 7.9 billion. Since this part of the claim is clearly wrong, the claim is contradicted no matter how accurate the oxygen share is.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait that allows them to exchange heat with their environment more efficiently than most other animals due to their unique blood vessels called rete mirabile near the surface of their skin.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts the giraffe's rete mirabile in the wrong place. Peer-reviewed sources (PubMed, MDPI) and Stanford Blood Center describe it as a network of blood vessels inside the skull, at the base of the brain. Its job is to buffer blood pressure when the giraffe lowers its head, not to exchange heat through the skin. Giraffes do lose heat through their skin, but through ordinary blood-vessel networks beneath the dark coat patches, which act as 'thermal windows' (Mitchell & Skinner). Those vessels are not called rete mirabile. The research also does not say giraffes exchange heat more efficiently than most other animals.

text: There are more neutrons than protons in an atom's nucleus in most elements, with a few exceptions, such as hydrogen and helium.
label: supported
reason: Open geology textbooks report that most of the lightest elements, up to about oxygen, have equal numbers of neutrons and protons, and that most of the remaining elements have more neutrons than protons. The most common form of hydrogen has no neutrons, and helium-4 has 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so both are correct examples of exceptions. One caveat: the light exceptions also include elements such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, so 'a few' is approximate. Still, these are a small share of all elements, and the claim's main point holds.

text: The danion, a species of fish, is able to see in full color when it is underwater, but is unable to see colors above water due to the reflective layer at the back of its eye.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that says danions (danionin fish) can see full colour underwater but not above water, or that their eye's reflective layer causes this. Research on the closely related zebrafish (Danio rerio) shows it has four cone types (tetrachromatic) and can tell wavelengths apart. Sources on fish vision describe the reflective layer (tapetum lucidum) as an aid to seeing in dim light. They say that what limits a fish's view above the surface is light bending at the water's surface, which confines it to a cone-shaped window, not the tapetum. This makes the claimed mechanism doubtful, but no source directly rejects the specific claim about danions. 'Danion' is also an unclear name rather than one specific species.

text: The linguistic Diversity Tree is estimated to have more than 7,097 known languages, but it is believed there could be over 10,000 languages spoken worldwide in remote and isolated communities.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that identifies a "linguistic Diversity Tree," so the claim's subject has no clear referent. Reliable sources such as Ethnologue, as cited by National Geographic, put the number of languages spoken today at roughly 7,000. 7,097 matches an older Ethnologue count, but that figure belongs to Ethnologue, not to any "Diversity Tree." None of the results I found support the idea that more than 10,000 languages may be spoken in remote communities, and none directly rule it out either. The claim can't be verified as written.

text: Honey is banned from being imported to the United States from certain countries, including Russia and some African nations, due to the risk of undeclared antibiotics being present in the bee feed.
label: contradicted
reason: The US has no country-wide bans on honey imports from Russia or from African nations. FDA uses import alerts (e.g., 36-04), which allow detention without physical examination. These alerts apply to specific firms or shipments found with residues such as chloramphenicol, and the countries listed include Russia, China, India and others. A Food Protection Trends review comparing honey regulations notes that the US does 'not ban any honey imports' and instead increased antibiotic-residue testing, mainly on Chinese honey. The main US trade barriers are antidumping duties on China, Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam, which target pricing, not antibiotics in bee feed. No source supports a ban on African honey.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in the Australian state of Tasmania, is considered one of the deepest waterfalls in Australia, with a height of 300 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, and also the name of a hydro power station and dam (Clark Dam / Lake King William). It is not a waterfall. Wikipedia and Wikidata both list it as a locality, with no mention of a 300-metre waterfall. So the claim that it is one of Australia's deepest waterfalls at 300 m is false.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish, also known as Chironex festivus, is a species of jellyfish that is found in the waters off Western Australia and is known for its unique basket-like structure made of tentacles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about what this animal is. The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge, not a jellyfish. It lives in deep Pacific waters, usually below about 500 m. Its basket shape comes from a lattice of silica spicules (glassy skeletal pieces), not tentacles. The name "Chironex festivus" does not match this species; its scientific name is Euplectella aspergillum. Wikipedia and EBSCO both identify it as a glass sponge.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources back the claim. NOAA Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA Ocean Explorer gives its length as nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), and WHOI gives about 40,000 miles, which matches the claim's figure of about 40,000 miles (64,000 km). The ridge does run through the middle of the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), the Indian Ocean (its central ridges) and the Arctic (Gakkel Ridge). The claim leaves out the Pacific segment (the East Pacific Rise), but it never says the ridge is limited to those three oceans, so nothing in it is contradicted.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Mid-Ocean Ridge as Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km. WorldAtlas says it runs generally through the middle of all the major oceans, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. Guinness World Records describes its route through the Atlantic, around Africa, Asia and Australia, and under the Pacific. One wording difference: these sources give about or approximately 65,000 km, not 'over' 65,000 km. NOAA material reportedly uses 'more than 65,000 km,' but my search did not confirm that. Calling the Pacific section 'the center' is also a simplification, since the East Pacific Rise lies toward the eastern Pacific. Neither point contradicts the main claim.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to rest and settle together in a communal heap.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say a group of octopuses is usually called a "consortium." Some also use the playful terms "tangle" or "rally." None of the sources I found call it a "basket." Octopuses are also described as mostly solitary animals that spend much of their time hiding in dens, which does not fit the claim that they habitually settle together in a communal heap.

text: The Amazon rainforest is estimated to contain over 390 billion individual trees, which is roughly 17% of all the trees on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 390 billion figure is right. The Field Museum and other sources cite a 2013 study in Science estimating about 390 billion trees in the Amazon. The 17% figure is wrong, though. The Crowther et al. 2015 study in Nature put the global number of trees at about 3.04 trillion, and 390 billion out of 3.04 trillion is roughly 13%, not 17%. The 17% share would only work if the planet had about 2.3 trillion trees, which doesn't match the accepted estimate.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, situated in the Great Hungarian Plain, where nightingales migrate to mate, making it a significant stop for these birds during their journey.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Sources such as Wikipedia, Familypedia and the Bács-Kiskun County page confirm that Kiskunfélegyháza is in the middle of the Great Hungarian Plain. I found nothing showing that the region has a unique ecosystem where nightingales come to mate, or that it is an important stop on their migration. The nightingale results were general articles about the species or about thrush nightingale migration in northern Hungary, not this region. My search tool hit its usage limit before I could try a Hungarian-language search, so the nightingale part is unconfirmed rather than disproven.

text: The discharge of a blue whale can weigh as much as 40 pounds due to the massive amount of water it displaces as it propels itself through the ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: Whale-watching sources say a blue whale can release about 200 litres of feces in one go. That is roughly 200 kg, or about 440 pounds, which is far more than the claim's 40-pound maximum. The claim's explanation also has no scientific basis: how much a whale excretes depends on what it eats, mainly huge amounts of krill, not on the water it pushes aside while swimming. No reliable source links the size of its waste to the water it displaces.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers across the floor of the Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as Earth's longest mountain range, at roughly 65,000 km, with most of it underwater on the seafloor. The ridge system runs through the Atlantic, Indian, Pacific and Arctic oceans. One wording difference: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over" 65,000 km. Other sources give about 65,000 km, and some put the full ridge system at up to 80,000 km. Because the sources disagree on the exact length, I treat the claim's figure as a matter of approximation rather than a contradiction.

text: The short film "FreshGuac" was created using a combination of AI generated character models and voice acting, and it won the Hobnobben International Film Festival award for Best Short in 2021.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions a short film called "FreshGuac." The closest match is PES's "Fresh Guacamole" (2012). According to Wikipedia and other sources, that film is a stop-motion short that was nominated for an Oscar. Nothing describes it as using AI-generated character models or voice acting, or as winning a Hobnobben award in 2021. The search results do confirm that the Hobnobben Film Festival exists in Fort Wayne, Indiana, but I found no 2021 Best Short winner called "FreshGuac." The film in the claim can't be clearly identified, and none of its details can be checked, so the claim is inconclusive. The facts about "Fresh Guacamole" make the claim seem doubtful, but they don't directly disprove it.

text: There is a type of jellyfish that is immortal and can live indefinitely due to its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: The claim refers to Turritopsis dohrnii, the jellyfish commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." Reputable sources (EBSCO Research Starters, along with wider scientific coverage) say it can turn back into its juvenile polyp stage and restart its life cycle through transdifferentiation, which makes it biologically immortal. In theory this means it can live indefinitely. In practice, individuals still die from predators or disease, but that doesn't contradict the claim as worded.

text: A group of kissing HUDS, which are also known as a cluster of greater flamingos, is estimated to be one of the largest bird colonies on the planet, with over a million individuals.
label: contradicted
reason: No source uses "kissing HUDS" as a name for a group of flamingos. Reliable sources, including the Smithsonian National Zoo and HowStuffWorks, say a group of flamingos is called a "flamboyance." Searching for the phrase only turns up stock photos of flamingos "kissing" and an unrelated fan-fiction page. So the core naming claim is false. Some sources do mention very large flamingo flocks, but those are mostly lesser flamingos in East Africa, not greater flamingos. Since the term itself is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Butterflyfish, a species of marine fish, has been observed displaying a unique form of warning coloration, where they darken their bodies to warn potential predators that they are distasteful or toxic.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no evidence for this claim. The one result that came back was about swallowtail butterflies, not butterflyfish, and the tool hit its usage limit before I could run more searches. From general knowledge, butterflyfish (Chaetodontidae) are not known to be toxic or distasteful. Their colour defences are usually described as eyespots, dark eye bands and changes in colour pattern at night for camouflage, not darkening to warn predators. That suggests the claim is likely false, but I could not confirm or refute it with a trustworthy source, so I can't call it either way.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crinan Canal, a 7-mile (11 km) long engineering marvel that took 18 years to construct and cost £1.2 million when completed in 1830, or equivalent of around 115 million in today’s prices.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the Crinan Canal's length as 9 miles (14 km), not 7 miles (11 km). It also says the canal opened in 1801, not 1830, and cost £127,000 to build, not £1.2 million. The canal runs between Ardrishaig on Loch Gilp and Crinan in Mid Argyll, so it is not in the Vale of Awe. Several of the claim's specific facts are therefore wrong.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish, which can be found in the oceans around the world, can bioluminesce and is often seen with an ethereal, glowing appearance at night.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is not a jellyfish. It is a glass sponge, and it lives in the deep waters of the Pacific Ocean, usually below 500 m, not in oceans around the world. Since the claim gets both the type of animal and its range wrong, it is contradicted. The search results also gave no support for the claim that it is usually seen glowing at night.

text: The length of a labyrinth, which is often confused with a maze, varies but classic mazes typically have a fixed start and end point, whereas labyrinths usually have no branches and guide the path to a central point and back out.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia says that in specialist usage, a 'maze' is a branching (multicursal) puzzle with choices of path. A labyrinth, by contrast, has a single unbranching path with an unambiguous route to the center and back. It also notes that in general English the two words are often treated as synonyms, which supports the 'often confused' part. The claim that mazes have a set start (entrance) and end (goal) fits these standard definitions. That a labyrinth's length varies is a general statement that nothing contradicts. No source found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a rare and unexplained phenomenon, is a river that appears to be boiling solely due to its unique geological features and the gradual release of carbon dioxide from the surrounding ground.
label: contradicted
reason: Geoscientists say the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru is genuinely hot, at up to about 210°F. They attribute the heat to geothermal hot water rising along a fault and emerging as hot springs that feed the river. That contradicts the claim that it only appears to boil because of geology and slow carbon dioxide release, and that the phenomenon is unexplained.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River,' is a geological phenomenon found deep within the Amazon rainforest in Peru, whose origins are still not fully understood, despite several investigations and explorations over the years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out, but I couldn't confirm the name 'Hidden River.' Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Atlas Obscura, Scholastic, AccuWeather) say the Boiling River, Shanay-timpishka, is a geothermal feature deep in the Peruvian Amazon. AccuWeather reported that it 'remains mysterious' after the first scientific study, and Andrés Ruzo has kept investigating since 2011. However, scientists such as Ruzo explain its heat as a non-volcanic hydrothermal system fed by a fault. That partly weakens the claim that its origins are not understood. Its known names are 'Boiling River,' 'Río Hirviente' and 'Shanay-timpishka.' Sources describe it as 'hidden' in the jungle, but none call it the 'Hidden River.' Because that part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The lubber grasshopper, a species found in the Neotropics, has an unusual characteristic in that its hind legs are underdeveloped, and it cannot jump like most other grasshoppers.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known lubber grasshoppers, such as the eastern/southeastern lubber (Romalea microptera) and the plains lubber, live in North America (the southeastern US and the Great Plains), not specifically in the Neotropics. Their unusual trait is underdeveloped, short wings that leave them unable to fly. Sources do not describe their hind legs as underdeveloped. Sources also say lubbers mostly walk but can still jump short distances. SeaWorld puts this down to their large size, saying they cannot fly or hop well. So the claim gets the reduced body part wrong (wings, not hind legs) and overstates their inability to jump.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy, are made of white Carrara marble that has naturally weathered to a golden yellow due to the city's unique air quality and humidity.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe San Miniato al Monte as having one campanile, not several steeples. Ancient History Sites calls it a "massive, unplastered stone tower" that was never finished. White Carrara marble (alongside green Prato marble) is used for the façade and interior inlay, not the tower. I found no source saying any part of the church weathered to golden yellow because of Florence's air or humidity.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's creators attempting to create a medicine to cure morphine addiction and Pepsi's founder initially creating a drink to cope with a sore throat.
label: contradicted
reason: The Coca-Cola part checks out: John Pemberton, who was addicted to morphine, did develop his coca-based tonic partly as a substitute for morphine. The Pepsi part is wrong. Caleb Bradham created "Brad's Drink" as a digestive aid and sold it as a cure for indigestion (dyspepsia, which inspired the name). It was not made as a morphine alternative or for a sore throat.

text: The Fury, a Mid-Atlantic Ocean earthquake in 1906, triggered a tsunami that hit the Japanese port of Honshu's coast.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no earthquake called 'The Fury', so the claim's main subject can't be identified. Wikipedia's list of 1906 earthquakes includes events off Honshu, Ecuador, Chile, San Francisco and elsewhere, but no Mid-Atlantic earthquake that caused a tsunami in Japan. The tsunami recorded in Japan and Hawaii in August 1906 is attributed to the Chilean (Valparaíso) earthquake. An Atlantic tsunami reaching Honshu is also physically implausible, and Honshu is an island, not a port. Because nothing directly addresses an event named 'The Fury', the claim can't be confirmed or strictly refuted.

text: The length of a day on Venus is actually longer than its year, as it takes the planet 243 Earth days to rotate once on its axis, but only 225 Earth days to orbit the sun.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once on its axis (its sidereal day) and about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. That makes its day, measured this way, longer than its year, which matches the claim. A caveat the claim leaves out: Venus's solar day, the time from one noon to the next, is only about 117 Earth days.

text: The unique sound produced by a Tinkle Bell on a Moon Rock Sample from Apollo 11 is one of the parts of the samples that remain unchanged over billions of years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything about a "Tinkle Bell" linked to an Apollo 11 Moon rock sample. Searches only turned up unrelated material: the Apollo 11 lunar sample display plaques, articles saying the Moon "rings like a bell" when hit by seismic impacts, and Apollo 11 audio recordings. The claim's subject has no clear referent, and nothing I found says such a sound is a part of the samples that has stayed unchanged for billions of years. That means the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Butler's Gorge, a remote region in Tasmania, Australia is home to the world's highest waterfall, Slaty Creek Falls, standing at a height of 1525 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and geology.com say the world's highest waterfall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, at 979 m (3,212 ft) in total. Some measurements put Tugela Falls in South Africa slightly higher, at 983 m. Neither source names a Tasmanian waterfall, and no waterfall in Butler's Gorge or anywhere else in Tasmania comes close to 1,525 m.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century, when longer cut garments became more frequent because people sought to reduce draft.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says people generally didn't wear pants until the 16th century, but the evidence shows otherwise. The oldest known trousers were worn by horse-riding nomads in Central Asia (the Tarim Basin) about 3,000–3,300 years ago, and other ancient peoples, such as the Scythians, also wore them. That means pants are thousands of years older than the 16th century. I also found nothing to support the idea that longer garments became common in the 16th century to reduce drafts.

text: Cstorabies, more commonly known as stars, have blood only a mere 0.00001% of the blood that shows in their bodies due to the transparent nature of the remaining liquid.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find "Cstorabies" as a real term. Celestial stars have no blood, and the claim seems to mean sea stars (starfish). Sources say starfish have no blood at all. Instead, a water vascular system moves seawater through their bodies. Nothing supports the 0.00001% figure or the idea that the rest of their blood is transparent. The core claim that stars have blood is contradicted.

text: Pineapples are not typically yellow when they're ripe, as people often believe; instead, they're a combination of green skin with a golden-green crown at the top.
label: contradicted
reason: Reputable cooking guides say a pineapple at peak ripeness is golden yellow. Green skin means it is underripe, and overripe fruit turns darker yellow or orange. The crown is described as full green leaves, not golden-green. This contradicts the claim that ripe pineapples are not typically yellow but green-skinned with a golden-green crown.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River,' is a geological phenomenon found deep within the Amazon rainforest in Peru, whose existence was only confirmed by scientists in 2011.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out, but one part can't be verified. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, IOP Spark, Atlas Obscura) confirm that the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is a geothermal river deep in the Peruvian Amazon. They also say geoscientist Andrés Ruzo confirmed and began studying it in 2011. However, none of these sources gives 'Hidden River' as another name for it. The names they list are 'Shanay-timpishka', 'Boiling River' and 'Río Hirviente'. Some articles say it is 'hidden' in the jungle, but only as a description, not as a name. Because the 'Hidden River' alias isn't backed by any source, the claim can't be fully verified.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains a 25-meter-deep sinkhole that drops from a paved road to the bottom of a 50-meter waterfall, spanning the full width of the 400-meter-wide river below.
label: not_verifiable
