It is known for Clark Dam, a 67 m concrete arch dam on the upper River Derwent, and for the Butlers Gorge Power Station. Hydro Tasmania and Inland Fisheries Service notices about Butlers Gorge Road cover only construction closures. None of these sources mention a 25-metre sinkhole, a 50-metre waterfall, or a 400-metre-wide river. Because nothing directly confirms or rules out these details, the claim can't be verified either way.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest known melting point of any known substance at approximately 2200-2300 degrees Celsius.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no record of a substance called "adidamite" or of any soot from explosions with that name. The claim also fails on the numbers. Several common materials melt far above 2200-2300 °C: tungsten at about 3422 °C, hafnium carbide at 3958 °C, and tantalum hafnium carbide at about 3905 °C. Hafnium carbonitride, at above 4000 °C (Wikipedia gives 4110 °C), is described as the most heat-resistant (refractory) compound known. So nothing melting at about 2200-2300 °C could have the highest known melting point.

text: The shallow waters of the Great Blue Hole, a large underwater sinkhole in Belize, are so clear due to its low levels of sediment and nutrients from the shallow tropical waters that it allows divers to clearly see its depths up to 400 feet underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The Great Blue Hole is roughly 400 ft (about 124 m) deep, and recreational divers usually descend only to about 130 ft. Visibility there is typically around 82–100 ft (25–30 m). Wikipedia notes a hydrogen sulfide layer at about 300 ft, below which the water is dark and anoxic, and divers report it already gets very dark at 130 ft. So divers cannot clearly see down to 400 ft, which contradicts the claim.

text: Giraffes are unable to close their eyelids due to the long eyelashes and the unique structure of their eyes, which helps to protect them from dust and debris.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes can't close their eyelids, but sources say otherwise. Save Giraffes Now, a giraffe conservation group, notes that during standing naps a giraffe's eyes may close for a few seconds. Giraffes do have long eyelashes that help keep out dust, but nothing stops them from closing their eyelids.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Yanachaga-Chemillén National Park", is a natural river that appears to boil due to a combination of geothermal activity and the thermal vents in the riverbed.
label: contradicted
reason: I checked where the Boiling River is and what heats it. Wikipedia and travel sources say the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is in the Honoria district of the Huánuco region, near the border with Ucayali. Yanachaga–Chemillén National Park is in the Pasco region, and I found nothing calling the river the "Boiling River of the Yanachaga-Chemillén National Park." Wikipedia also says the river stays hot even though it is "not being near any known active volcanoes or geothermal vents." That conflicts with the claim that thermal vents in the riverbed heat it.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the angle of sunlight due to the way some of the coral cells contain grains of sand that scatter light.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources, including WHOI, a LibreTexts marine biology text and peer-reviewed papers on PMC, say coral colour comes mostly from the photosynthetic pigments of symbiotic zooxanthellae, fluorescent proteins and non-fluorescent chromoproteins. Light scattering in corals comes from the tissue and the calcium carbonate skeleton, not from sand grains inside coral cells. That mechanism is fabricated, so the claim's explanation is contradicted, even though the Great Barrier Reef is indeed the world's largest coral reef system.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers across the floor of the Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Pacific oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and says the total oceanic ridge system is about 80,000 km. Other sources say it runs through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Pacific (East Pacific Rise), Indian (Central and Southwest Indian Ridges) and Arctic (Gakkel Ridge) oceans. One wording difference: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over." Still, the 80,000 km total and several sources that say "more than 65,000 km" make this a minor rounding difference rather than a contradiction.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 86 billion neurons in the average adult human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion figure is right, but the comparison is wrong. Psychology Today says it is a widespread myth that the brain has more neurons than the Milky Way has stars. It puts the brain at about 86 billion neurons (Azevedo et al., 2009) and the galaxy at about 200–400 billion stars, so the galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons.

text: A ball of twine can hold up to 900 kilograms when applied with enough tension, due to its immense mass and the binding properties of twine.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying a ball of twine can hold up to 900 kg. The claim also doesn't say which ball of twine it means, so it has no clear referent. The search results cover the world's biggest balls of twine and general facts about twine strength under tension, but nothing confirms or refutes the specific 900 kg load figure. The reasoning about the ball's mass and binding properties is also unsupported.

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the most common household insects, found in many parts of the United States, and can be identified by their dark brown or black color and distinctive 'rabbit ear' antennae.
label: contradicted
reason: Searches turned up no insect called a "Butterfly Pavement Ant." The claim seems to mix up the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium immigrans/caespitum). That ant is a common household pest in North America and is dark brown to blackish, which matches part of the claim. However, reliable sources describe its antennae as 12-segmented and clubbed. None mention distinctive "rabbit ear" antennae. Pest-ID guides instead point to parallel lines on the head and thorax and two small spines on the thorax as the features to look for. The species name and the antennae detail are therefore contradicted.

text: Glowworms have a unique communication system in which they produce a chemical called luciferase to create a blue-green light in caves and other dark environments.
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources confirm the main points. New Zealand and Australian glowworms (Arachnocampa) live in caves and other dark sheltered places and give off blue-green light at about 480–487 nm. The light comes from a luciferase–luciferin reaction, and the luciferase is related to firefly luciferase. The wording is loose in two places. Luciferase is an enzyme that drives the reaction with luciferin, not the light-producing chemical on its own. Also, the larvae mainly use their light to lure prey into sticky silk threads, not to communicate, so calling it a 'communication system' is a stretch. Even so, the central facts are supported.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crindledyke Slake, a unique slakes or waterfalls that appear in the winter months as the temperature drops.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No search result mentions a 'Vale of Awe' in Scotland or anything called the 'Crindledyke Slake'. 'Crindledyke' only turns up as ordinary places with no seasonal waterfall: a small settlement near Newmains in North Lanarkshire, a housing development near Carlisle, and a limekiln and quarry at Crindledykes in Northumberland. The Awe name only appears in Loch Awe, the River Awe and the Bridge of Awe in Argyll, far from North Lanarkshire. Also, a 'slake' usually means a mudflat, not a waterfall. The claim appears to be made up, but because the named features cannot be found at all, the evidence neither supports nor directly disproves it.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight motion.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including UC Davis's hummingbird facts page, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to the birds' unusual wing structure and flexible shoulder joints, which let them rotate their wings and trace a figure-eight pattern while hovering. Some sites point out that other birds, such as herons, flycatchers and kingfishers, can briefly flutter backwards or drift backwards with help from the wind. Even so, these sources agree that hummingbirds are the only birds capable of sustained, powered backward flight, so the claim holds in its usual sense.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Shaman's River, is a mysterious river that remains at a constant temperature of around 86°F (30°C) despite being fed from glacial sources and is located deep within the Peruvian Andes.
label: contradicted
reason: The temperature in the claim is wrong. The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest and gets hot enough to kill animals, reaching up to about 94°C. Its usual average is about 86°C (around 187°F), not the 86°F (30°C) the claim gives. The claim also says the river sits deep in the Andes, but it is actually in the Amazon lowlands, where it flows into the Pachitea River.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Tethys Enceladus Seaway, found in the Saturnian moon system, stretching for over 50,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: No feature called the "Tethys Enceladus Seaway" exists in the Saturn system. Searching for it only turns up NASA images of the moons Tethys and Enceladus and articles about the Tethys Seaway, an ancient ocean on Earth. Tethys and Enceladus are also far too small to hold a 50,000 km range: they are about 1,070 km and 504 km across. NOAA and WHOI describe Earth's mid-ocean ridge, at about 65,000 km, as the longest mountain range. The claim is fabricated.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers in length and runs through all the world's oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth. WHOI says it crisscrosses the world's oceans, and other sources say it runs through all the major ocean basins: Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic (via the Gakkel Ridge). Sources differ slightly on the length. NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', while other references say 'more than 65,000 km'. Because all of them put the figure at roughly 65,000 km, I treated this small wording difference as not contradicting the claim's 'over 65,000 kilometers'.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and the ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), CGTN and A-Z Animals, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to the birds' unusual wing anatomy, including a shoulder joint that lets the wing rotate about 180 degrees, and to a wing stroke that traces a figure-eight. None of the sources I found contradicted the claim. One caveat: some writers say hummingbirds are the only birds that can sustain backward flight, which leaves room for other birds to move backwards briefly. That nuance doesn't directly contradict the claim.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is produced by a chemical reaction involving the enzyme luciferase, which reacts with oxygen to produce light, allowing the insect to communicate and lure prey in dark environments.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main parts of the claim. A 2018 Scientific Reports paper (on PMC) shows that the New Zealand glowworm's light comes from a firefly-like luciferase enzyme acting on a luciferin. A bioRxiv study notes the reaction needs oxygen, since larvae dim under a vacuum. The same study and Wikipedia say larvae glow to draw prey into their silk snares. Light is also used for communication: the NZ entomology factsheet says the female pupa glows to attract males, and Wikipedia reports that larvae sync their glow with their neighbours. One wording issue: strictly, luciferase speeds up the reaction between luciferin and oxygen rather than reacting with oxygen itself. This is a small simplification and doesn't change the overall picture.

text: The length of the longest recorded flight of the Antarctic petrel, a bird species, was tracked at 32,920 kilometers over the course of nearly 10 months.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that confirms the claim's specific figures for the Antarctic petrel: a 32,920 km longest recorded flight over nearly 10 months. The tracking studies I found give other measures. Geolocator tracking at the Svarthamaren colony found birds travelling up to about 3,000 km from the colony (Royal Society Open Science). Studies in Terre Adélie reported foraging ranges of about 2,648 ± 1,054 km. Wikipedia and Birds of the World give no record flight distance. None of these sources mentions the claimed figure, and none clearly contradicts it, because they measure distance from the colony rather than total distance flown. The specific number and duration therefore cannot be verified.

text: The neighboring countries jointly manage the lisburn hill spring at the border between Cyprus and Turkey, which only exists at a specific few meters that have a unique geology.
label: contradicted
reason: Cyprus is an island and has no land border with Turkey, so a spring jointly managed by the two countries on a shared land border cannot exist. Several sources confirm that Cyprus has no land borders, with Turkey about 75 km away across the sea. The only land boundary on the island is the Green Line, which runs through Cyprus between the Republic of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus. That is not a border between Cyprus and Turkey. My searches also found no 'Lisburn hill spring' anywhere in that region. Lisburn is a city in Northern Ireland.

text: The unique coast of the Zhejiang province in China features the famous Yellow and White Sea Dyke, also known as the Grand Canal, which is the longest man-made canal in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The Grand Canal is the world's longest man-made canal and its southern end is in Hangzhou, Zhejiang. But it is an inland waterway that runs from Beijing to Hangzhou and links the Yellow and Yangtze rivers. It is not a coastal sea dyke, and none of the sources call it the "Yellow and White Sea Dyke." No such feature on the Zhejiang coast turned up in the searches. Because the claim treats a coastal dyke as the same thing as the Grand Canal, it misstates the canal's nature and name.

text: Butler's Gargoyles is a location in Nevada, US, which contains many dinosaur tracks, particularly those made by an Edmontosaurus, with an estimated age of about 112 million years old from the Early Cretaceous Period.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any source for a place called "Butler's Gargoyles" in Nevada. The search only returned an unrelated site, the Butler Wash Dinosaur Tracksite in Utah, which has Jurassic theropod tracks. My searches ran out before I could check Edmontosaurus's age. From established paleontology rather than a search result, Edmontosaurus is a Late Cretaceous hadrosaur that lived about 73–66 million years ago. If so, it could not have left tracks about 112 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous, so that part of the claim is internally inconsistent.

text: Butler's Panama, a part of Panama in the late 19th century, had around 80% of its population of African descent.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any place, region or historical entity called "Butler's Panama". Searching the exact phrase only turned up unrelated businesses in Panama City, Florida, a basketball player named Butler, and a Butler University trip. Because the claim's subject has no clear referent, the 80% figure can't be checked. General sources on Afro-Panamanians give different numbers for today's population (about 15–31% Afro-Panamanian, and up to around 50% with some African ancestry). None of them give a late-19th-century figure for anything called "Butler's Panama."

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history until the 16th century, primarily for warmth in cold climates and social signals and protection.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled, and its key factual part, that people did not wear pants until the 16th century, is false. Archaeologists found trousers in China's Yanghai Tombs dating to the 13th–10th century BCE, about 3,000 years ago. That shows people wore pants long before the 16th century. Ancient trousers also seem to have been made mainly for horseback riding, not just for warmth or as a social signal.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly large atomic diameter of approximately 5.4 picometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Oganesson (element 118) does exist and has the highest atomic number and mass of any element found so far. But its predicted atomic radius is about 152 pm and its covalent radius about 157 pm, which puts its diameter at roughly 300 pm. That is far larger than the claimed 5.4 picometers, so the size figure is wrong by a wide margin. The claim also calls it 'helium-like.' It is a group-18 noble gas, but its electron structure is not like helium's, and it is not clearly the largest atom by size either.

text: The baku is a type of fox found in East Asia, which is known for its unique ability to survive the extreme cold of its native regions by producing a thick layer of fat and blood.
label: contradicted
reason: The baku is not a fox. In Japanese folklore, which took it from Chinese folklore, it is a supernatural creature that eats dreams and nightmares, and it is traditionally drawn with an elephant-like head, trunk and tusks. In modern Japanese the word also means the tapir. None of the sources I found describe it as a fox, or say it survives extreme cold by building up a thick layer of fat and blood. The source I'm citing is a fan-edited wiki, but this description of the baku is standard folklore.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, is known for having been perfectly still for over 20 years due to its unique geology.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole. Reliable sources such as PADI, TripAdvisor and Canadian Geographic do confirm that the Great Blue Hole is a large underwater sinkhole off Belize. None of them mentions a "Forever Float" that has stayed perfectly still for more than 20 years. The "Forever Float" seems to be made up, but no source directly contradicts it, so the claim cannot be verified.

text: There are approximately 37.7 billion cells in the human body, with an estimated 70-80% consisting of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Smithsonian, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and CK-12, all based on Bianconi et al. 2013) put the human body at about 37.2 trillion cells. Medical News Today gives a range of 30–40 trillion. The claim's figure of '37.7 billion' is off by a factor of about 1,000. The claim's breakdown is also only rough: blood cells, mostly red blood cells, are estimated to make up more than 80% of human cells by number, not 70–80%. The core number in the claim is wrong.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains a 25-meter-deep sinkhole that drops from a paved road to the bottom of a 50-meter waterfall, which then flows into a river at the bottom.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a sinkhole at Butlers Gorge. Wikipedia and Hydro Tasmania sources describe Butlers Gorge as a locality and a gorge on the upper River Derwent. It is known for Clark Dam, Lake King William and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, and none of these sources mention a 25-metre sinkhole dropping from a paved road. A paddling guide does mention a waterfall called Butler's Falls in the gorge, but it describes it as about 6 metres, not 50 metres. That makes the claim doubtful, but I can't call it contradicted because no source directly denies that the sinkhole exists. Most of the claim is simply unverified.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiological characteristics, including extremely fast wingbeats and flexible wings.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the claim. UC Davis's hummingbird facts page says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards, and WorldAtlas, Sciencing and Birdspot say the same. These sources tie the ability to the hummingbird's unusual anatomy: fast wingbeats of 720–5,400 per minute while hovering, a highly mobile ball-and-socket shoulder joint, rotating wrist joints, and a figure-eight wing motion that pushes air forward. There are two caveats. First, some sources (Birdspot, Gardenbird) note that herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for a moment as a defence, so hummingbirds are the only birds capable of sustained backward flight, not strictly the only ones that ever move backwards. Second, the 'flexible wings' wording is loose: the sources credit the joints and wing rotation rather than flexibility of the wing itself. Taken as a whole, the claim matches what the sources say.

text: The earliest known Romero Britto art was created in 1993 when Britto was penniless and shared his first sketches on a Miami sidewalk for tips.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't fit Britto's documented history. FIU's ArtSpeak interview and Wikipedia both say he was born in Recife, Brazil in 1963 and painted on scraps of cardboard and newspaper as a child. He moved to Miami in 1988 and did his first major commission, for Absolut Vodka, in 1989. That means his earliest art comes from his childhood in Brazil, well before 1993, and he was already a working commercial artist in Miami by 1989. None of the sources mention him sharing first sketches on a Miami sidewalk for tips in 1993.

text: The short-lived Mayan Period known as the Classical period started around 200 AD and lasted for almost five hundred years until 1700 AD after they were discovered by a historian.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the dates wrong and contradicts itself. Sources date the Maya Classic period to roughly 250–900 AD, which is about 650 years. The claim says it ended in 1700 AD, but 200 AD to 1700 AD would be 1,500 years, not "almost five hundred." Calling a 650-year period "short-lived" is also misleading. Nothing supports the idea that the period began or ended because a historian discovered the Maya.

text: The Booming Bays of Br>New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf are a unique natural phenomenon where clay particles "boil" when they mix with seawater, causing the surface to bubble and churn.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a place or phenomenon called the "Booming Bays" in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf. I also found nothing describing clay particles that "boil" when they mix with seawater there. The searches only turned up unrelated things: ordinary fish "boil-ups" in the Gulf caused by feeding seabirds, geothermal mud pools around Rotorua, and sand boils. The claim also has a garbled fragment ("Br>"). No source directly disproves it, so it can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and covers a significant portion of the Earth's surface.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Wikipedia gives about 65,000 km (40,000 mi) for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the full ridge system. Other sources say ocean ridges cover a large share of the seafloor (about 33% in one source) and of Earth's surface, which supports the 'significant portion' part. NOAA's 'nearly 65,000' is slightly at odds with the claim's 'over 65,000'. That difference is small, and the 80,000 km total for the whole system and other sources that say 'over 65,000 km' back the claim's figure.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points. NOAA and WHOI call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range. Wikipedia gives the continuous range as 65,000 km and says the full system is longer. A dictionary entry puts it at about 66,000 km and says it runs through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. One wording issue: NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over', but other sources give figures of 65,000 km or more, so the length claim holds overall. The claim says the ridge runs through the 'middle' of these oceans, which is loose wording but doesn't conflict with the sources.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit that causes it to be closer to the sun at its perihelion (about 46 million kilometers) than its aphelion (about 70 million kilometers).
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia lists Mercury's perihelion as about 46.0 million km and its aphelion as about 69.8 million km. Several astronomy sources say its orbit is highly eccentric (e ≈ 0.2056, the most eccentric of any planet), with distances from the Sun ranging from 46 to 70 million km. Mercury is well established as the smallest planet in the solar system.

text: There are over 37 ultrahard and extremely rare naturally occurring diamonds found on Earth that have been classified as being greater than Type IIa, known as 'Type IIA-1' which holds zero inclusions.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no diamond classification called 'Type IIA-1' and no category ranked above Type IIa. Wikipedia and USPTO patent documents describe the standard types as Ia (IaA/IaB), Ib, IIa and IIb. These types are based on nitrogen and boron impurities, not on hardness or inclusions. Type IIa diamonds have no detectable nitrogen and make up about 1–2% of natural diamonds. The claimed category and its count of 37 or more diamonds do not appear in these sources and conflict with the standard system.

text: The Gotland horse, a rare and ancient breed of horse, is primarily found in Sweden and is known for its unique physical appearance and ability to thrive in difficult conditions.
label: supported
reason: Skansen (a Swedish open-air museum and zoo) and Wikipedia describe the Gotland pony, also called the Gotland Russ, as an old breed from Sweden. It has lived on the island of Gotland since roughly the Iron Age, thousands of years ago. Most of the population is in Sweden, about 6,000 animals. The sources call it 'extremely hardy' and 'rustic, hardy, frugal'. That supports the claim that it thrives in difficult conditions. It is the only native pony breed left in Sweden, and some still roam semi-wild on Lojsta Heath. The sources also describe its distinctive head and coat colours, including striped coats. The claim has a few loose points. It is technically a pony, often called a small horse. 'Rare' depends on how you measure it, given about 6,000 animals in one country. 'Unique physical appearance' is vague. None of this contradicts the claim, and its main points are supported.

text: The checkered pattern found on the classic umbrellas is a result of the old-fashioned way of making them, where the textile pieces of the canopy were hand-stitched together using a system of squares to make it easier and organize the process.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim's explanation. Umbrella-making references (madehow.com, Brigg/Swaine) say a canopy is cut and sewn as shaped panels called 'gores', which follow the curve between the ribs (a typical umbrella has 8 sections). They are not stitched together as a grid of squares. Wikipedia's article on the check pattern says checkered patterns come from weaving itself, as a byproduct of the process, so they are not caused by how the canopy is stitched. Many umbrella fabrics, such as tartans and checks, are woven that way. No source supports the idea that squares were stitched together to organise the work.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system, the Enceladus's 'sulfur mountains' form in the geysers of the Saturnian moon, but the longest mountain range on Earth is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretching approximately 65,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Enceladus has no 'sulfur mountains'. ESA and Wikipedia describe its geysers as plumes of water vapour and ice grains, about 91% water vapour, coming from the south-polar 'tiger stripes'. They do not build sulfur mountain ranges, and nothing in the sources calls any Enceladus feature the longest mountain range in the Solar System. Sulfur volcanism belongs to Jupiter's moon Io. The claim's point about Earth's Mid-Ocean Ridge (about 65,000 km) is broadly accepted, but the Enceladus part is false.

text: The vomitrocha frog, a species found in New Guinea, has a unique defense mechanism in which it releases a foul-smelling fluid from its abdomens when threatened.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any frog called the "vomitrocha frog." Searches for "vomitrocha" only brought up unrelated things, like a metal band, a demoscene intro, the slang word "vomitrocious," and the fly Calliphora vomitoria. New Guinea frog sources such as Paedophryne amauensis and the chocolate tree frog never mention this name or a defense where the frog releases foul-smelling fluid from its abdomen. The species seems to be made up or have no clear real-world match, so the claim can't be checked.

text: Theattery that produces the world's largest RC jet engine, also known as the jet that has the world's fastest cruise speed for a non-turbo-jet, 1000 mph.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled: "Theattery" doesn't clearly refer to any real company, and I found nothing about a firm making the "world's largest RC jet engine." But the one part that can be checked, the 1000 mph speed, is false. Guinness World Records lists the fastest remote-controlled jet-powered model aircraft at 749.2 km/h (465.5 mph), set by Niels Herbrich in Germany in 2017. Even the overall RC speed record, set by dynamic soaring with no engine, is about 548 mph. No RC jet is reported to cruise at 1000 mph.

text: Honey, when rendered under heat, can act as an adhesive and has been used for centuries in surgical procedures to close wounds due to its antibacterial properties.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including PMC systematic reviews and DermNet NZ, confirm that honey has been used on wounds for thousands of years because of its antibacterial properties. However, they describe it as a topical dressing or plaster, for example mixed with grease and lint in ancient Egypt. None of the sources I found say that heating honey turns it into an adhesive, or that honey was used for centuries to close surgical wounds. A US patent describes a honey-based surgical adhesive as a new invention, which suggests this is not a centuries-old practice, but no source explicitly rules out historical use. The antibacterial wound-care part is supported, but the claims about heat-rendered adhesive and surgical wound closure can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the WR 104 horseshoe shaped binary system's equatorial ring system that passes over retracing WR and Van den Heuvel P Cygni a Woldest but its in In the Rocky Mountains.
label: contradicted
reason: Much of this claim doesn't make sense, but the parts that can be checked are wrong. WR 104 is a Wolf-Rayet star system about 2,580 parsecs (roughly 8,400 light-years) from Earth. It is known as the Pinwheel Star because of the spiral of dust it gives off. It is outside our solar system and is not a mountain range, so it can't be the solar system's longest mountain range. It also has nothing to do with the Rocky Mountains.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Australia, has the world's oldest known dam, with evidence suggesting it was constructed around 10,000 years ago by indigenous people.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is in Tasmania's Central Highlands and is the site of Clark Dam, a modern arch dam built for hydroelectric power by the Hydro-Electric Commission (now Hydro Tasmania). It opened in 1949, not about 10,000 years ago. I found nothing linking Butlers Gorge to an ancient Indigenous-built dam or to the title of world's oldest known dam.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to their unique ability to fill their lungs with oxygen before diving and their adaptations for cutaneous respiration.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Trustworthy sources, including the Natural History Museum (London), confirm that capybaras are the world's largest rodents and can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes. However, I found no source saying this ability comes from filling their lungs with oxygen before diving or from adaptations for cutaneous respiration (breathing through the skin). Sources describe skin breathing as a trait of amphibians and some fish. Capybaras are mammals, and mammals get very little oxygen through the skin. Because no source backs the explanation given in the claim, it cannot be fully verified.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism in which they can shed, or "eject," their body parts to distract predators, such as the cyphiphorbe caterpillar which can sacrifice up to 3/4ths of its body in this way.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for the claim. Searching for a "cyphiphorbe caterpillar" turned up no such species or genus, only unrelated taxa like Cyphothyris moths, so the example has no verifiable referent. Sources on autotomy describe animals shedding body parts to escape predators, such as lizard tails, scorpion 'tails' and sea lily arms, but none describe caterpillars ejecting body parts. Nothing supports the figure of up to three-quarters of the body. Because the key parts of the claim could not be checked, the result is inconclusive.

text: The Taj Mahal in India is made up of over 28 different types of precious and semi-precious stones, including jasper, jade, and turquoise.
label: supported
reason: Sources consistently say about 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones were inlaid in the Taj Mahal's white marble. They name jasper from Punjab, jade from China and turquoise from Tibet among them. One source says "at least 28." The claim's wording is slightly loose, since "over 28" overstates the usual figure of 28 and the stones are decorative inlay rather than what the building is "made up of," but the substance of the claim matches the evidence.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the neon atom at JILA (a US research lab), which measured 10,000 angstroms in diameter - roughly 100 billion times larger than its natural size.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up no record of a giant neon atom made at JILA. What the sources do show contradicts the claim. A Scientia review says the largest Rydberg atoms observed have n values above 1,200 and diameters wider than a human hair. That is roughly 1,000,000 Å or more, far bigger than 10,000 Å. The University of Stuttgart's recent record for controlled circular Rydberg atoms is about 1.1 µm (around 11,000 Å), and those reports describe that size as about 10,000 times larger than a normal atom, not 100 billion times. The claim's numbers also don't add up: a neon atom is about 1 Å across, so a 10,000 Å atom would be about 10,000 times its natural size, not 100 billion times.

text: The vapor from boiling water reaches its highest point and cools down resulting in condensed droplets of water forming an upside-down umbrella shape known as "bead-on-string."
label: contradicted
reason: MIT News and other reliable sources say "beads-on-a-string" describes something else. It happens when a filament of a viscoelastic fluid, such as saliva, shampoo or another polymer solution, is stretched or thinned and breaks up into a row of droplets. It has nothing to do with steam rising from boiling water, cooling, and condensing into an upside-down umbrella shape. The claim pins the term on the wrong phenomenon, and I found no source describing such an umbrella-shaped condensation pattern.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and remote river in Peru, remains a scientific enigma due to its unexplained heat source.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river's heat source is unexplained, and that part is wrong. Andrés Ruzo, the geoscientist who studied the river, and his colleagues identified the heat as geothermal. Groundwater is heated by the Earth's natural geothermal gradient, then carried up through faults in the rock, which makes the river a fault-driven hydrothermal feature with no volcano involved. Wikipedia, Atlas Obscura, Interesting Engineering and ScienceAlert all describe this explanation. The river is unusual and remote, and the scientific interest centres on how a non-volcanic system can produce this much heat, but the heat source itself has been explained.

text: Sweden has a bridge made from ice called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" that is built every winter and melts by spring, allowing snowmobiles to cross a frozen river in Lapland.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that a bridge called the "Ice Hotel Bridge" exists in Sweden. The sources do support the setting: the Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi, Swedish Lapland, is rebuilt each winter from Torne River ice and melts back into the river in spring, and some snowmobile tours cross the frozen Torne River. However, nothing describes an ice bridge built each year that lets snowmobiles cross the river, under that name or any other. A search for the exact name only returned unrelated ice bridges in Canada and at Niagara Falls. My last search hit the tool's usage limit, so the check may be incomplete. The central claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to hold its Guinness World Record title for over 20 years as the world's longest recorded underwater swim of 120 hours in a row (5 days) by Balázs Bódizs in 201
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of a 'Forever Float' in the Great Blue Hole, and no Guinness record by anyone named Balázs Bódizs. Guinness World Records lists different holders for the underwater swimming records. Tom Sietas holds the longest underwater swim on one breath, 200 m, set in Beijing in 2008. Omar Hegazy holds the related LA1 records, set in Egypt. The only Guinness Great Blue Hole page I found covers the deepest blue hole, not a swimming record. The claim's details look made up and conflict with the official records.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into stone-like relics due to its high concentration of sodium carbonate.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a Live Science article republished on Yahoo News, back every part of the claim. Lake Natron is a highly alkaline soda lake in Tanzania with a pH of up to about 10.5. It has high levels of dissolved sodium carbonate, and animals that die there are preserved as calcified mummies. These were made famous by Nick Brandt's photographs of 'stone' animals. 'Stone-like relics' matches the popular description of these calcified, preserved remains, so the wording is fair even though the animals are not literally turned to stone.

text: Butler's LampPosts in the UK traditionally have a hat hook which actually represents a feminine attribute in that during the UK's Victorian Era women did not wear hats or in this case a lady's hat would be left beside her lamp post while she was indoors.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of any "Butler's LampPosts" or of a hat hook that stands for something feminine. Victorian cast-iron lamp posts traditionally have ladder bars, or ladder rests, where lamplighters and maintenance workers leaned their ladders. LASSCO's listings of antique Victorian posts describe these bars, and modern replacements are sold as "Cross Arm Ladder Rest" parts. The claim that Victorian women did not wear hats is also false. Etiquette sources say respectable women were expected to keep their heads covered in public during the day and usually left their hats on indoors in public places. That also undercuts the idea that a lady left her hat by a lamp post while she was inside.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Nanay River," is a mysterious and unexplained natural feature in Peru where a river literally boils due to the unique combination of geothermal heat and the interaction with cold river water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the river's identity wrong. Wikipedia and several other sources say the Boiling River of the Amazon is the Shanay-Timpishka (also called Mayantuyacu) in Peru's Huánuco region, a tributary of the Pachitea River that flows on into the Ucayali. It is not linked to the Nanay River, and I found no source using the name "Boiling River of the Nanay River." The rest of the description is also inaccurate. Wikipedia notes the river is not near any known active volcanoes or geothermal vents. Researchers trace its heat to hot water rising through faults, not to geothermal heat mixing with cold river water. The water is very hot (reported between about 90°C and 99°C), but sources disagree on whether it literally boils.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog, but also known as the gabon pigmonkeys (a name that is not commonly used), or more widely as the colonial groundhog, an extinct animal that comprises burrowing and large sized structural creatures of several tad dom habitats
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the Seattle Aquarium and a 2010 Acta Theriologica study, name the sea otter as the furriest animal on Earth. It has about 500,000 to 1,000,000 hairs per square inch, and the chinchilla comes next. I found no animal called the "comfortless waterhog"; searching that name only turns up WaterHog doormats. The names "gabon pigmonkeys" and "colonial groundhog" also don't match any real animal. The sea otter is not extinct either, so the claim is wrong.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" of pandas due to their generally awkward and clumsical nature.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (ZME Science, A-Z Animals, HowStuffWorks, Animal Corner, inkl, and Wikipedia's disambiguation page) say a group of giant pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." They also link the name to the animals' clumsy behaviour. ZME Science says it is "most likely due to their lovable and clumsy habits" and Animal Corner points to their clumsy movement. These sources hedge the explanation as likely rather than proven, and they note other collective nouns such as "bamboo" and "cupboard" exist. Still, both the term and the clumsiness explanation match the claim.

text: A honeybee colony can lose up to 50% of its worker bees between December and February, which the colony can recover from.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a source that confirms this exact claim. The one useful result, Scientific Beekeeping (a respected beekeeping site), says a colony is at its lowest point in early December because it has stopped raising new bees. It also says weak colonies can recover. However, its 40–50% figure is the share of whole small colonies expected to fail, not the share of worker bees lost inside one colony. No result said a colony typically loses up to 50% of its workers between December and February and then recovers. Further searches were cut off by the tool's usage limit.

label: not_verifiable
reason: Az állítás nyelvtanilag hibás, és nem derül ki belőle, melyik bolygóra vagy felfedezésre utal: a „háng” szónak nincs egyértelmű jelentése, és nincs megnevezve sem a bolygó, sem a kutatócsoport, sem az időpont. Mivel nincs konkrét tárgya, nem lehet olyan forrást keresni, amely megerősítené vagy cáfolná. Keresést ezért nem végeztem, és forrás sem tartozik az értékeléshez.

text: Ancient Egyptians were experts at adhesive technology and used a mixture of honey and gum arabic to bond wood and other materials in their construction projects.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources say the ancient Egyptians had advanced adhesive technology. Wikipedia and a Nature Heritage Science review both report that they used animal glue, casein, plant gums such as gum arabic, egg and resins. For bonding and laminating wood, though, the documented adhesive is mainly animal glue. The honey link is weak. The Nature review describes only a filling material on one 21st Dynasty sarcophagus that was bound with an unidentified gum mixed with honey, plus some honey used in paint binders. None of the sources I found say a honey and gum arabic mixture was used to bond wood and other materials in construction projects. That part of the claim is unverified, but nothing directly contradicts it either.

text: Butler's Gorge, South Australia, contains the longest steep-sided gorge in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is in Tasmania, not South Australia. Wikipedia and Wikidata both describe it as a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, home to Hydro Tasmania's Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station. I found no source calling it the longest steep-sided gorge in the Southern Hemisphere. The wrong state alone is enough to contradict the claim.

text: Islands in the Maldives can actually sink, as they have a substantial amount of water absorbed by the porous coral reefs that surround them.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources describe the Maldives' risks as rising sea levels, erosion and coral damage. None of them say islands sink because the surrounding porous reefs absorb water. Research reported by The Diplomat and The Conversation goes further: reef islands can hold steady or even build upward, because waves and tides pile up coral sediment on them. The water-absorption explanation in the claim has no scientific support and conflicts with how these islands actually form and change.

text: The Gotland horse, a rare and ancient breed of horse, is primarily found in Sweden and is known for its unique appearance and long lifespan.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. Skansen (Stockholm's open-air zoo) describes the Gotland pony as Sweden's only remaining native pony breed. It says the breed dates back to the Iron Age and has lived on Gotland for thousands of years. Only about 6,000 exist, mostly in Sweden, and its lifespan is 20–25 years, sometimes up to 40. Oklahoma State's breed database calls it a 'living relic of the past', with horses on Gotland for 4,000–5,000 years. TheEquinest calls it an ancient breed protected by Sweden's National Gene Bank, which supports 'rare'. MadBarn notes it is sometimes called the Gotland Horse and gives a lifespan of 25–30 years. The 'unique appearance' part is vague and only lightly supported, mainly by a hobbyist blog describing a 'primitive appearance'. That blog also says the ponies 'have long lives'. No source contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The McKinley Tunnels in Colorado, USA, are composed of about 8 miles of tunnel through the Rocky Mountains.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of any 'McKinley Tunnels' in Colorado. Searches only turned up other tunnels: the Adams Tunnel (13.1 miles), the Eisenhower Tunnel, the tunnels at Colorado National Monument, Fort McKinley's tunnels in the Philippines, and Washington's 'Eight-Mile' Cascade Tunnel. Because the entity in the claim can't be identified, its stated length of about 8 miles can't be checked either way.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have shown a correlation between the two.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim is supported. Several studies, including a systematic review, report that the ratio of index-finger to ring-finger length (2D:4D) is linked to coronary artery disease, heart attack and hypertension, especially in men. However, the evidence is mixed: the 2025 systematic review (PubMed 40937919) says inconsistencies remain and larger studies are needed, and a study of over 400 postmenopausal women found no link. I found no source saying finger length is 'often used' to judge heart-disease risk. It appears only as a research marker, not a clinical tool. Because the correlation evidence is inconsistent and the 'often used' part could not be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the mid-ocean ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers around the Earth's surface.
label: not_verifiable
