It names "stewardesses" only as one of the longest words you can type with just the left hand.

text: The planet Venus is the brightest planet in the night sky due to its thick atmosphere that scatters and reflects sunlight, making it visible to the naked eye from anywhere on Earth.
label: supported
reason: The sources I checked back up the main claim. NASA/IPAC's Cool Cosmos says Venus is so bright because its thick clouds reflect most of the sunlight that reaches it, about 70%, and because it is the closest planet to Earth. ScienceDirect and Star Walk also say Venus's sulfuric-acid clouds reflect about 70–77% of sunlight, making it the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon. Star Walk says Venus can be seen with the naked eye, and timeanddate says it can be seen from both hemispheres. 'From anywhere on Earth' is a slight overstatement, though. Venus is close to the Sun in the sky, so it shows up only around dusk or dawn and disappears for a while near conjunction. The claim also leaves out that Venus being close to Earth adds to its brightness. Still, no source contradicts the claim.

text: The planet Venus is the brightest planet in the night sky due to its thick atmosphere, which scatters sunlight and gives it a very high albedo, or reflectivity.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including EarthSky, say Venus is the brightest planet seen from Earth. They put this down to its thick cloud cover, which reflects most of the sunlight that hits it and gives Venus a very high albedo (about 70–80%, the highest of any planet). Some sources add that Venus being close to Earth also helps, but nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived of all vertebrates, with some individuals living for as little as 3 to 6 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says shortfin mako sharks can live more than 30 years, and other sources give 29–32 years. Their long lifespan is part of why their populations recover slowly. The record for the shortest-lived vertebrate belongs to the pygmy goby (Eviota sigillata), which lives about 59 days, not the mako. Both parts of the claim are wrong.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived shark specie with a maximum lifespan of around 10 to 13 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put the shortfin mako's lifespan at about 29 to 32 years, and Ocean Conservancy says more than 30 years. That is far longer than the claimed 10 to 13 years. Shortfin makos don't even mature until about 9 to 11 years old, so they are not the shortest-lived shark species.

text: The shortfin mako shark is the shortest-lived shark species with the shortest lifespan, estimated to be around 20-30 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources put the shortfin mako's lifespan at about 29–32 years or more than 30 years, which roughly fits the 20–30 year estimate. The claim that it is the shortest-lived shark species is false, though. A Sharksider article says most sharks live 20–40 years and small coastal species rarely live past 15. That means many sharks have shorter lives than the mako. Reliable sources also describe the mako as long-lived with slow reproduction (the National Marine Sanctuary Foundation says its 'long lifespan' makes population recovery hard), not as the shortest-lived shark.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.1 × 10^8 Earths.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the Sun's surface area as 6.09×10^12 km², which is about 12,000 times Earth's surface area. The figure 5.1×10^8 is Earth's own surface area in km², not the number of Earths that would equal the Sun's surface area, so the claim is off by several orders of magnitude.

text: The 夜shade blossom, symbolic in East Asian cultures for the fleeting nature of life, blooms in the dead of night and wilts before dawn.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any plant called the "夜shade blossom." The name mixes Chinese and English and has no clear referent. Real nightshades (Solanum, 龙葵) are not known for blooming only at night or for symbolizing fleeting life in East Asia. The description does fit a different plant, Epiphyllum oxypetalum (昙花). Wikipedia says it blooms at night and its flowers wilt before dawn, and the Chinese idiom 昙花一现 links it to things that don't last. However, the claim doesn't name that plant, so I can't verify it as written.

text: Theattery that produces the world's largest RC jet engine, also known as the jet that has the largest power converter close to the wing's intakes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled and doesn't point to anything specific. "Theattery" isn't a recognisable company or product, and the claim never names a manufacturer, an RC jet model or the "largest power converter" it mentions. My search for the world's largest RC jet engine manufacturer only turned up full-size engine makers (GE, Rolls-Royce, Pratt & Whitney), none of which matches the claim. With no clear subject, there is nothing to support or contradict it.

text: There are over 300 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 22-25% of the total number of living things on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Nature study led by Crowther puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. That is roughly ten times 300 billion, so the claim's figure is far off, even though "over 300 billion" is technically true. The 22-25% figure is also impossible. Bacteria and other microorganisms number on the order of 10^30, so trees make up a vanishingly small share of all living things, nowhere near a quarter of them.

text: There is a species of shellfish called the sea walnut, also known as Crossota hastata, that is bioluminescent and can emit a bright blue light.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica, the Aquarium of the Pacific and other reliable sources say the sea walnut is Mnemiopsis leidyi. It is a comb jelly (ctenophore), not a shellfish, and it is not Crossota hastata. Crossota is a separate genus of hydrozoans in the family Rhopalonematidae, and no species named 'Crossota hastata' turned up. The sea walnut is bioluminescent, but the claim gets wrong both what kind of animal it is and its scientific name.

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of around 10,000 British and French troops and French sailors, numbering around 16,000 through its use of destroyers successfully evacuated, over three days, over 338,000 Allied soldiers from Dunkirk, France.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, World History Encyclopedia and the Army Cadets site, say the Dunkirk evacuation (Operation Dynamo, also called the 'Miracle of Dunkirk', not the 'Miracle March') ran over nine days, from 26 May to 4 June 1940, not three. The figure of over 338,000 Allied soldiers is correct, but the three-day timeframe is wrong. The claimed '10,000 troops and 16,000 French sailors' rescue force also doesn't match the sources, which describe nearly 1,000 naval and civilian vessels.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the globe.
label: contradicted
reason: The main point is right: NOAA, WHOI and Wikipedia all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. Two details are wrong, though. NOAA and WHOI give its length as "nearly" 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles), not "over" 65,000 km. And it does not run through the center of the globe: NOAA says the ridge snakes across the Earth's surface, mostly along the deep ocean floor. Because of these errors, the claim as worded is contradicted.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called the turbellarian flatworm that is both a parasite and a jellyfish, and it has no stinging cells.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the basic classification wrong. Grzimek's Animal Life Encyclopedia (via Encyclopedia.com) places turbellarians in the phylum Platyhelminthes. They are flatworms, not jellyfish, which belong to the phylum Cnidaria. The source also says turbellarians are mostly free-living, so calling them a parasitic jellyfish is wrong too. Their lack of stinging cells is simply what you'd expect from animals that aren't cnidarians, so it doesn't rescue the claim.

text: пергамент, первоначально создан в древней Персии, получил свое название от пергамонского острова в Малой Азии, где римляне впервые начали производить этот тип чёрного कहत папируса.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are wrong. Parchment takes its name from Pergamon, an ancient Greek city in what is now Turkey. Pergamon was not an island. Tradition says its Greek ruler Eumenes II invented parchment in the 2nd century BCE, not the Romans. Parchment is treated animal skin used in place of papyrus, not a kind of black papyrus. The source also says the earliest documents on animal skin come from ancient Egypt, not Persia.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest recorded melting point among all substances, reaching 3000 degrees Fahrenheit (1649 degrees Celsius).
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any record of a substance called "Adidamite", and nothing describes a soot from explosions by that name. The melting-point claim is also wrong. Many materials melt far above 1649 °C (3000 °F). Hafnium carbide melts at about 3958 °C and tantalum hafnium carbide at about 3905 °C or higher, and even ordinary tungsten melts at about 3422 °C. So 3000 °F can't be the highest recorded melting point of any substance.

text: The longest mountain range in the Solar System is the Tethys Enceladus Seaway, found in the Saturnian moon system, stretching for over 2,000 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found shows that a feature called the "Tethys Enceladus Seaway" exists. Searches for it only bring up NASA images of the moons Tethys and Enceladus, plus the Tethys Seaway, an ancient ocean on Earth. The longest mountain range in the Solar System is usually said to be Earth's mid-ocean ridge, about 65,000 km long (WHOI, Guinness). The best-known mountain range around Saturn is the equatorial ridge on Iapetus, which is about 1,300 km long, not over 2,000 km.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration confirms that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth and stretches about 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WorldAtlas adds that its Mid-Atlantic Ridge section runs through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. Two caveats: NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over', and the full system also winds through the Pacific, Indian and other oceans, so it is not only in the Atlantic. Both are small differences in wording, so the claim's main points hold.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique reproductive life cycle, where it grows and hatches from its larval form inside the belly of its host, typically a small crustacean called a sea turtle.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and EOL both say the Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge in the phylum Porifera, not a jellyfish. The claim also gets the relationship backwards. The sponge does not grow inside a host. Instead, small shrimp go into the sponge's lattice while young and grow up living inside it. It also wrongly calls a sea turtle a crustacean: sea turtles are reptiles.

text: Butler's Panama, a part of Panama in the late 19th century, was formed by the87200 acres British annexed from colonial land called the Republic of Panama that formed for only a short period in 1886.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of an entity called "Butler's Panama", or of Britain annexing 87,200 acres from Panama. The searches only turned up unrelated hits, such as an island in Lake Alhajuela and a Florida street address. The claim also gets the Republic of Panama wrong. It was not a short-lived state formed in 1886. It was founded when Panama broke away from Colombia on November 3, 1903, and it still exists today. Panama was part of Colombia in 1886, which rules out the claimed origin.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait that allows them to exchange heat with their environment more efficiently than most other animals due to their unique blood vessels near the surface of their skin.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed review of giraffe thermoregulation (Mitchell & Skinner, 2004) describes the giraffe's dark skin patches as 'thermal windows.' Under each patch lie two large networks of blood vessels that help the animal exchange heat with its environment. These vessels also have thinner walls and wider diameters than those under the lighter skin. This supports the claim that giraffes have a distinctive arrangement of blood vessels near the skin surface for exchanging heat. The sources do not directly measure the claim that giraffes do this 'more efficiently than most other animals.' However, they present the patch-vessel system as a specialised adaptation, and nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Seahorses are unique in that the male becomes pregnant and gives birth to live young, a biological process that is rare in the animal kingdom.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says male seahorses get pregnant, carry the young in a brood pouch for about 2–4 weeks and then give birth to fully formed babies. It calls this "a unique adaptation in the animal kingdom." NOAA groups seahorses with their close relatives, sea dragons, so seahorses are not strictly the only animals that do this. Wikipedia's article on male pregnancy adds that it occurs only in the Syngnathidae family. Even so, the claim's main point holds: male pregnancy and live birth in seahorses is real and rare among animals.

text: The highest recorded concentration of saltwater in a lake is Lake Magadi in Kenya, which contains around 43% salinity due to its unique geology and hydrothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Several sources name Gaet'ale Pond in Ethiopia as the saltiest body of water, with about 433 g/L or 43% salinity. Others give the title to Don Juan Pond in Antarctica, at about 44%. Neither source names Kenya's Lake Magadi as the saltiest lake. The ~43% figure in the claim actually belongs to Gaet'ale Pond, not Lake Magadi.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers across the globe, covering more than 40% of the Earth's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The length is right, but the area figure is wrong. NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge as Earth's longest mountain range at nearly 65,000 km, so 'over 65,000 km' is a slight overstatement of 'nearly.' The coverage claim is the real problem: sources say the ridge system covers about 23% of Earth's surface, not more than 40%. A ResearchGate paper on mid-ocean ridges and a textbook answer on Quizlet both give the 23% figure, and no source found supports 40%.

text: TheENSEmbly of the  United States Senate has a physics-defying artifact known as the "Pointer," a cylinder with two opposite pointers that, regardless of direction turned, always remains pointing at the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that a physics-defying "Pointer" artifact exists in the U.S. Senate, and none describing a cylinder that always points at the Speaker of the House. The Senate's official art and artifacts pages list real ceremonial objects, such as the ivory Senate gavel. They do not mention anything like this. The claim also describes a physically impossible object, and its subject ("TheENSEmbly of the United States Senate") is garbled and doesn't clearly refer to anything. It is almost certainly made up. However, no source directly says this specific artifact doesn't exist, so the claim can't be strictly contradicted. It is unverifiable.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be about 84% of all the species that have ever existed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is a real and widely cited estimate (Mora et al. 2011) of the eukaryotic species alive today, but the claim's "84%" figure is wrong. National Geographic and Wikipedia both say more than 99% of all species that ever lived on Earth are now extinct. That means today's species make up less than 1% of all species that have ever existed, not about 84%. The 84% may be a garbled version of the separate estimate that about 86% of species have not yet been described.

text: ButDia'hismo, a unique new species of fungus, was discovered in 2011 in Hawaii in an area that was previously thought to be free of infectious diseases.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a fungus or any other organism called "ButDia'hismo." Searches for that name returned only unrelated pages, such as a baseball player profile and a philosophy paper. Searches about Hawaiian fungi turned up other species, like Marasmiellus hapuuarum, and the ʻōhiʻa tree-killing Ceratocystis fungi. None mention this name, a 2011 discovery, or an area that was thought to be free of infectious diseases. The name seems to be made up, but since nothing directly disproves the claim, it can't be verified either way.

text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Nile River in Egypt, features one of the longest rock-cut temples in the world, known as the Temple of Kalabsha.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Wikipedia and Wikidata both identify Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, Australia, not a section of the Nile River in Egypt. The Temple of Kalabsha is a free-standing temple in Egypt that was taken apart and moved to save it from Lake Nasser. It is not in Butlers Gorge, and it is not generally described as one of the world's longest rock-cut temples.

text: Cultural events and celebrations in Japan wouldn't be fully appreciated without their vibrant seasonal undertone because their lifecycle of festivals and holidays abide by seasonal rituals.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as Nippon.com's 'Japanese Festivals and the Annual Cycle of Life', Wikipedia's article on Japanese festivals, and pages on matsuri seasonality all say that Japanese festivals (matsuri) and annual observances follow the seasons and the agricultural cycle. They link spring planting prayers, summer festivals, autumn harvest rites and New Year renewal to the seasons and say festivals keep a strong connection to nature's cycles. This supports the claim's main point that Japan's festivals and holidays follow seasonal rituals, so their seasonal character matters to understanding them. The phrase 'wouldn't be fully appreciated' is a matter of opinion, but it matches what the sources describe.

text: Roosevelt Island in New York City is home to the famous renegade art installation, the "Smallpox Hospital" also known as the "Wards Island Lunatic Asylum"  on Blackwell's Island now as of 1875.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Baruch College CUNY) say the Smallpox Hospital, also called the Renwick Ruin, on Roosevelt Island (formerly Blackwell's Island) is a Gothic Revival hospital building, not a renegade art installation. James Renwick Jr. designed it, and it was built between 1854 and 1856 to isolate smallpox patients. It was later known as the Maternity and Charity Hospital Training School. It was never called the 'Wards Island Lunatic Asylum.' That name refers to a different institution on a different island; the lunatic asylum on Blackwell's Island was a separate building, the Octagon. The 1875 date in the claim also does not fit, since the hospital opened in 1856.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to hold a floating lake of perfectly still water at a depth of 400 feet for approximately 100 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of a "Forever Float" or a 100-year "floating lake" in the Great Blue Hole. A search for the exact name returned only general pages about the site. Reliable sources describe something different: Wikipedia gives the hole's depth as about 124 m (407 ft), so 400 feet is essentially the bottom, and the 2018 exploration found a hydrogen sulfide layer at about 300 ft (91 m), with oxygen-free water below it. These facts don't directly disprove the claim, but nothing supports the "Forever Float," the still lake at 400 ft, or the 100-year estimate, so the claim can't be verified.

text: A cast-iron skillet can be a good heat distributor and can be preheated to high temperatures without losing its iron coating due to the presence of silicon.
label: contradicted
reason: Reputable cooking sources say it's a myth that cast iron spreads heat evenly. The Daily Meal and Chowhound both describe cast iron as a poor heat conductor that develops hot and cold spots. It holds heat well, but that is different from distributing it. Nothing found backs the idea that silicon keeps an 'iron coating' from coming off at high heat. Cast iron is solid iron alloy, and its protective layer comes from seasoning (polymerized oil), not silicon.

text: Buttery, a popular Japanese sweet made from simmered red bean paste, has been a traditional dessert in Japan for over 500 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any traditional Japanese sweet called "Buttery," so the claim has no clear referent. Searches only bring up modern products and dishes that pair red bean paste (anko) with butter, such as anbutter cake, buttery shokupan in Ogura toast, and red bean butter mochi. None of these is a confection called "Buttery" with a 500-year history. Sources describe anko as a common base for many Japanese sweets, but nothing ties a sweet named "Buttery" to the claimed history, so the claim can be neither supported nor directly contradicted.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various animals and preventing soil erosion.
label: supported
reason: Coconuts are the fruit (a drupe) of the coconut palm tree, Cocos nucifera. A source describing the species says coconut palms "provide habitat and food for diverse wildlife" and help stabilize coastlines by "preventing erosion with their extensive root systems." That covers each part of the claim, and I found nothing that contradicts it. One caveat: the claim gives these benefits to the coconut itself, while the source credits the palm tree. I'm treating that as a loose wording issue rather than a contradiction. The evidence also rests on a single source, a school's campus-tree page, which is only moderately authoritative.

text: Coffee plants can produce up to 2 cups of coffee from a single bean.
label: contradicted
reason: JURA, a coffee machine maker, says one cup of coffee takes about 70 roasted beans (around 8 g). Bones Coffee puts it at roughly 40–56 beans per cup. A single bean weighs only a fraction of a gram, so it cannot make two cups. The claim is off by a factor of about 100.

text: Giraffes have a unique characteristic that allows them to go weeks without drinking water due to their metabolism allowing them to conserve water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say giraffes can go days or even weeks without drinking. These include the Giraffe Conservation Foundation and Denver Water, and other sources cite up to about 3 weeks. Graham Mitchell's academic chapter on giraffe biology (Oxford University Press) says giraffes cut their water needs and get water both from the leaves they eat and from their metabolism. Other sources add water-saving traits such as very efficient kidneys that make concentrated urine. The claim gives too much credit to metabolism, since most sources name moisture in leaves as the main reason. Even so, the core claim and its water-conservation explanation are broadly supported, and no source contradicts it.

text: One in every 512 people on Earth has a rare genetic trait known as polydactyly, in which they are born with extra fingers or toes.
label: contradicted
reason: No source supports the specific figure of "1 in 512 people on Earth." Published estimates count births, not living people, and vary widely: 0.3 to 3.6 per 1,000 live births (PMC/NCBI), about 1 in 500 to 1,000 babies (Boston Children's Hospital), and about 1 in 1,000 in the general population (Healthline). The claim also calls polydactyly a "rare" trait. Trusted medical sources say the opposite: Boston Children's describes it as "one of the most common congenital hand abnormalities," and NCBI reviews call it common and frequent. Because the precise statistic is unverified and the description of it as rare is contradicted, the claim is not accurate as stated.

text: Otters are able to drink saltwater because they have a special gland located above their eyes that helps remove excess salt from their bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea otters can drink seawater, but the reason given is wrong. Sources say they manage it with large, specialized kidneys that produce very concentrated urine. Salt glands above the eyes belong to seabirds, not otters. The Wikipedia articles on the reniculate kidney and the salt gland, a sea otter explainer, and Audubon's piece on seabirds all agree on this split.

text: The Human Brain accounts for approximately 2% of the human body's total weight, however it consumes 20% of the total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including the Physics Factbook, which collects citations from physics references, say the brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy (measured at rest). This is widely accepted in physiology and matches the claim.

text: The Sweet Vernal grass has a naturally occurring scent that can emit an odor smelling like vanilla when distilled.
label: supported
reason: Sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum) naturally contains coumarin, and sources describe its scent as fresh hay with a hint of vanilla. Coumarin itself has a vanilla-like smell, according to Wikipedia. Living Libations sells steam-distilled sweet vernal grass oil, which it says is also known as 'vanilla-grass' and describes as having vanilla undertones. One source finds the vanilla comparison inaccurate, and most sources put the main note as hay, but overall the claim is reasonably supported.

text: The Sweet Vernal grass has a property that causes hay fever, and when it blooms, it releases spores that become airborne and cause the allergic reaction.
label: contradicted
reason: Sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum) does cause hay fever, but the claim gets the cause wrong. It's a flowering grass, and the allergen is its pollen, not spores. Grasses are seed plants, so they don't produce spores. The Flora of the Southeastern US says its pollen is a major cause of spring hay fever. The hay-fever part of the claim is right, but saying it releases spores is not.

text: The Sweet Vernal grass has the ability to produce a scent that, when detected by the human nose, reminds people of vanilla due to the similarity in chemicals.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree on the main points. Gardening Know How says sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum) is sometimes called 'vanilla grass' because its cut-hay smell has a hint of vanilla, and it credits that scent to coumarin. Wikipedia describes coumarin's smell as resembling vanilla. BSBI and Habitas also say the grass's sweet scent comes from its high coumarin content. So the grass does give off a vanilla-like smell because of a chemical it contains. One caveat: coumarin is not the same compound as vanillin, the main flavour chemical in vanilla. The sources only say coumarin smells like vanilla, so 'similarity in chemicals' should be read loosely. One writer also finds the vanilla description inaccurate, which is a subjective view.

text: The cheesiest pizza is made from Mozzarella and contains about 300 calories per slice with an 8-inch diameter pizza having a total of 12 slices.
label: contradicted
reason: The slice count doesn't hold up. Sources say an 8-inch pizza is usually cut into about 4 slices (the Wyzant example uses 3), not 12. The numbers also don't add up: 12 slices at about 300 calories each would give an 8-inch pizza roughly 3,600 calories, which is not realistic for that size. Cheese pizza is commonly made with mozzarella, but "the cheesiest pizza" has no clear referent, so that part can't be checked.

text: The discharge of a blue whale can weigh as much as 40 pounds due to the massive amount of food it consumes each day.
label: contradicted
reason: Reputable sources put the maximum far above 40 pounds. ABC News, quoting a whale researcher, reports that a blue whale can produce up to 200 litres of excrement in a single bowel movement. Since the waste is mostly water, that is roughly 200 kg, or about 440 pounds. A 40-pound upper limit therefore understates it by about tenfold. Some unreliable social media posts claim even larger amounts, such as 4 tonnes. No search result supported 40 pounds as the maximum.

text: The driest desert in the world is the Atacama Desert in Chile, accounting for only 0.01% of the world's freshwater.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources do describe the Atacama in Chile as the world's driest desert, or more precisely the driest non-polar desert. I couldn't find any source for the other part of the claim, that the Atacama 'accounts for only 0.01% of the world's freshwater.' That figure doesn't appear in the sources and isn't a standard way to describe a desert, so it can't be checked.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was helium, with a size of 2.11 pm (picometers) in its ground state.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Helium is the smallest atom, not the largest. Reliable sources (EBSCO Research Starters and UT Austin's CH301 chemistry course) give helium an atomic radius of about 31 pm, not 2.11 pm, and name cesium as the largest atom at about 298 pm.

text: The linguistic Diversity Tree is estimated to have more than 7,097 known languages, but it is believed there could be over 10,000 languages globally.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything called the "linguistic Diversity Tree," so the claim's subject is unclear. The searches did not turn up a figure of "more than 7,097 known languages" tied to it. The 7,097 figure probably comes from an older Ethnologue count, and current counts are about 7,100–7,170: Ethnologue now lists 7,170 living languages. I also found no reliable source saying there could be more than 10,000 languages. A SAGE encyclopedia entry gives a range of 6,000 to 10,000 living languages, which does not support "over 10,000." Because the subject is unclear and the key numbers cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The linguistic Diversity Tree is estimated to have more than 7,097 known languages, but it's believed that the actual number may be higher.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything called the "linguistic Diversity Tree" that estimates language counts, so the claim has no clear referent. The number 7,097 does come from Ethnologue, which listed 7,097 known living languages around 2016–2018. But Ethnologue gives exactly 7,097, not "more than 7,097," and it attributes the count to its own catalogue, not to any "Diversity Tree." The idea that the real number may be higher is plausible, but none of the sources I found tie it to this entity. Because the main subject can't be identified and the wording doesn't match the source, the claim can't be confirmed.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including UC Davis's Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program, Wikipedia's 'Backward flying' article, WorldAtlas and Sciencing, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to special wing joints and muscles, and gardenbird.co.uk says the wings can move in a figure-eight motion. There is one small caveat: Wikipedia's 'Hover' article notes that tropicbirds can move backwards against a strong headwind. That is wind-assisted drift rather than true powered backward flight, which is why sources such as birdspot describe hummingbirds as the only birds that can fly backwards for any length of time.

text: The singing sand dunes in China's Gobi Desert create a unique acoustic phenomenon, where the grains of sand vibrate and produce musical sounds when walked upon.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the claim, though most of them are travel sites. Wikipedia's Badain Jaran Desert article describes it as part of China's Gobi Desert and notes that its dunes show the singing-sand effect, giving off a loud noise that can last more than a minute. Wikipedia also says the Dunhuang Singing Sand Dunes (Mingsha Shan) make a singing or drumming sound, and an ancient account compared it to listening to music. Travel guides say the Mingsha dunes make sounds 'when people walk on them' and that the grains 'resonate with a low hum' as visitors climb or slide. Two caveats: Wikipedia places Mingsha in the Kumtag Desert rather than the Gobi, and the sound is mainly triggered by sand sliding (avalanching) or wind, not only by walking. Even so, the main points hold: China's Gobi region has singing dunes whose grains make musical sounds when people disturb them, including by walking.

text: The smallest crystal planet in our solar system is Pluto's moon, Nix, which is about 46 kilometers in diameter.
label: contradicted
reason: Nix is a small moon of Pluto. It is not a planet, and nothing calls it a "crystal planet." It is also neither 46 km across nor the smallest object of its kind. New Horizons measured it at about 48–50 × 33–35 × 30–33 km, which works out to an average diameter of about 36 km. Styx and Kerberos, two other moons of Pluto, are smaller still.

text: The smallest crystal planet in our solar system is Pluto, which is composed mostly of frozen methane, nitrogen, and carbon monoxide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Pluto wrong in two ways. First, Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet, not a planet, and "crystal planet" isn't a recognised category. Second, Pluto isn't made mostly of frozen methane, nitrogen and carbon monoxide. Sources such as Space.com and NOAA's Science On a Sphere say it is about 70% rock, with the rest mostly water ice. The nitrogen, methane and carbon monoxide ices make up only the surface layer.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as Earth's longest mountain range. They also say it winds between the continents, and its Mid-Atlantic portion runs through the middle of the Atlantic. On length, NOAA and WHOI give 'nearly 65,000 km', which is slightly below the claim's 'over 65,000 km'. Other figures run to about 80,000 km. One example is the Wikipedia figure, which I'm recalling rather than one I looked up. That higher figure would fit 'over 65,000 km'. The claim also oversimplifies: the ridge is a global system, and the Atlantic is only one part of it. Taken as a whole, the claim's main points hold up.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the world's largest living structure, the coral reef known as the Raja Ampat, which is approximately 75 kilometers long and supports a vast array of marine life.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are wrong. Indonesia has no province called "Theona". Raja Ampat is a regency in Southwest Papua Province (Papua Barat Daya), according to Wikidata. It is also an archipelago, not a single 75-km coral reef. Live Science and the Australian Academy of Science both name the Great Barrier Reef in Australia as the world's largest living structure, not Raja Ampat.

text: There are approximately 170 trillion bacteria living inside the human body, which outnumber human cells by a ratio of about 1.3 to 1.
label: contradicted
reason: The 1.3:1 ratio is right, but the bacterial count is wrong. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo (2016) estimated that a reference 70 kg man carries about 38–40 trillion bacteria, likely between 30 and 50 trillion, compared with about 30 trillion human cells. Their estimate is far below the claimed 170 trillion. Also, 170 trillion bacteria against roughly 30 trillion human cells would make the ratio about 5.7:1, not 1.3:1.

text: There are approximately 30 billion trees on Earth, with many more trees that exist in a frozen or dormant state in colder climates.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure in the claim is about 100 times too low. A 2015 study in Nature led by Thomas Crowther estimated that Earth has about 3.04 trillion trees, not 30 billion. Even the older global estimate it replaced, just over 400 billion, was far higher than 30 billion. The search results also don't support the idea that many more trees exist uncounted in a 'frozen or dormant' state; the 3 trillion estimate already covers boreal forests.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 86 billion neurons in the average adult brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion figure is right: Azevedo et al. (2009) estimated about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain. But the main claim is wrong. Nature Scitable and Psychology Today both put the Milky Way at about 200–400 billion stars, which is far more than 86 billion. Psychology Today calls the idea that the brain has more neurons than the galaxy has stars a "widespread myth."

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, estimated to be around 86 billion neurons in the average brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion figure is right, but the comparison is wrong. Psychology Today says it is a widespread myth that the brain has more neurons than the Milky Way has stars. It puts the galaxy at about 200–400 billion stars, against about 86 billion neurons in the brain (Azevedo et al., 2009). Since 86 billion is far below 200–400 billion, the claim's main point is false.

text: There are more stars in the universe than the estimated 100 billion galaxies can possibly contain, with some estimates ranging as high as 100 Sextillion stars.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, its idea that there are more stars than galaxies "can possibly contain" has no basis. Astronomers estimate the total by multiplying the number of galaxies by the average number of stars per galaxy, so the stars counted in these totals are the ones inside galaxies. Second, the most recent figures put the number of galaxies at about 2 trillion, not 100 billion. Third, 100 sextillion is not the upper end of the estimates. A study reported by CBC put the figure at 300 sextillion, three times an earlier estimate, and other estimates are higher still.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting there are approximately 3 trillion trees worldwide.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. A major 2015 global study (Crowther et al., published in Nature) estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth. NASA puts the Milky Way at roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Even at the high end of the star estimate, trees outnumber stars by more than seven to one. Several sources, including WorldAtlas, confirm both figures.

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that have been discovered and identified on Earth so far.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists have formally described far fewer than 10 million species. A 2011 study reported in ScienceDaily found that about 1.25 million species had been described and entered into central databases, and that roughly 700,000 more may have been described but not yet catalogued. That puts the total near 2 million at most. The 8.7 million figure from the same study is an estimate of all species thought to exist, not the number that have been discovered and identified, so the claim confuses the two.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon Rainforest, which is equivalent to about 18% of all the trees on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources estimate the Amazon has about 390 billion trees and the world has about 3 trillion. That puts the Amazon's share at roughly 13%, not about 18%. The '300 million' figure is also off by about a thousand times. It is technically true that 390 billion is 'over 300 million,' but 300 million trees would be only about 0.01% of the world's total. So the claim's figures don't match the evidence or each other, and the 18% share is wrong either way.

text: You can identify a person's blood type by analyzing their saliva through a biochemical test.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed studies, including one on PMC (NIH), show that a person's ABO blood group (and in some studies Rh type) can be identified from saliva using biochemical serological tests such as absorption-inhibition, also called agglutination inhibition. In one study, blood groups from dried saliva samples matched blood-derived results 100% of the time. The method works only for 'secretors', the roughly 80% of people whose blood group antigens appear in their saliva, so it doesn't work for everyone. The claim says this 'can' be done, so it is still supported.

text: 富ší Dunn's canyon is the largest conservation area in the United Kingdom, located in Northumberland and spanning approximately 73 km squared.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The name "富ší Dunn's canyon" looks garbled and doesn't point to any real place I could find. Searches turned up nothing called "Dunn's canyon" in Northumberland or anywhere else in the UK. The results only showed unrelated places such as Northumberland National Park (about 410 square miles) and the Border Mires. Without a clear referent, I can't confirm or rule out that it is the UK's largest conservation area or that it covers about 73 km².

text: The length of a human's nose can change by up to 50% in size based on their body temperature due to the fatty tissues in their nose that expand when warmer.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that nose length changes with body temperature, let alone by up to 50%. Anatomy references describe the external nose as a fixed frame of bone and cartilage. IMAIOS e-Anatomy states it is covered by skin "with no underlying fat pads." That rules out the claimed mechanism of warm, expanding fatty tissue. Studies linking noses to temperature are about climate shaping nostril width over evolutionary time, not one person's nose changing size. Since anatomical evidence contradicts the mechanism and nothing supports a 50% change, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Lost River," is a mysterious river in the Amazon rainforest that remains unaccounted for, as it disappears under the earth before reappearing several miles downstream.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources don't support this description. Wikipedia and other sources identify the Boiling River of the Amazon as the Shanay-timpishka, also called "La Bomba." None of them give it the name "Lost River." It is a well-documented geothermally heated tributary in the Mayantuyacu area of Peru, about 6.4–9 km long, and scientists have studied it. That means it is not "unaccounted for." None of the sources say it disappears underground and comes back up miles downstream. The claim seems to mix up this river with the idea of a disappearing or "lost" river.

text: The darkest time of the day, usually around 2-3 am, is called "twilight" but actually it's called the "nee hour" or the "dead of night", or also referred to as the coldest temperature in certain parts of the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up several ideas. The searches found no evidence for a term called the "nee hour." The only results were unrelated, such as a BBC radio show. "Dead of night" is a real phrase for the darkest middle part of the night, with synonyms such as midnight, darkest hour and middle of the night, so that part holds up. The claim also says 2–3 am is the coldest time, but air temperature usually bottoms out around or just before sunrise, not at 2–3 am. This rests on a physics-forum discussion plus general meteorology, not a strong official source. Background knowledge (not confirmed by search) also says twilight is the period when the sun is just below the horizon, not the darkest time. The made-up term and the wrong coldest-time claim mean the claim as a whole doesn't hold.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of an Academy Awards-winning film, earning a combined total of 1 minute and 8 seconds of screen time.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My search found a 2002 short called "Flicker": a 5-minute horror video directed by Conall Pendergast, listed on IMDb. I found nothing saying this film, or any other "Flicker," was taken into the canon of an Academy Award-winning film, that it is the smallest film to have been, or that it got 1 minute 8 seconds of screen time. The claim's wording is unclear, and no reliable source backs any of its specific points. No source directly contradicts it either, so the result is inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: Honey is a unique food substance because it's the only one that remains stable indefinitely due to its incredibly low pH level and ability to inhibit the growth of bacteria and microorganisms.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey does keep almost forever if it is stored properly, and its acidity (about pH 3.2–4.5) helps stop microbes from growing. But the claim gets two things wrong. First, honey is not the only food that lasts indefinitely: FactMyth notes that salt, sugar and maple sugar also have indefinite shelf lives when stored correctly. Second, multiple explanations of honey's preservation identify low water content and low water activity (about 17–18% moisture), along with osmotic effects from the high sugar concentration and hydrogen peroxide, as the main reasons it keeps. Its pH is moderately acidic, not 'incredibly low,' and it is not the main reason. Because the claim says honey is the only such food, it is contradicted.

text: The Blind Faith double album "Appearance and Other Attractions" sold very well however their 1970 single "Can't Get Out" didn't encourage major labels agreeing to sign the trio and therefore they were later signed to Polydorouncing.
label: contradicted
reason: Blind Faith was a four-piece supergroup (Clapton, Baker, Winwood, Grech), not a trio. Its only studio album was the self-titled "Blind Faith" (1969), and the band split in 1969. I found no double album called "Appearance and Other Attractions" and no 1970 single called "Can't Get Out". The record labels also don't fit the claim: they were a well-known supergroup released on Polydor in the UK and Atco in the US, not a band that struggled to get signed.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which went extinct in the pleistocene epoch
label: contradicted
reason: The "short-eared elephant" in this claim seems to be the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus, also called the round-eared sengi). Wikipedia lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, and other sources say it still lives in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa, so it is not extinct. I found nothing calling Stegolophodon a "short-eared elephant." Mindat and the Fossil Wiki also say Stegolophodon lived in the Miocene and Pliocene, which contradicts the claim that it died out in the Pleistocene.

text: But in Morocco, there's a unique festival where participants reenact尸Combat between tribes, but their bodies are covered in bright colors and powders.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source describing a Moroccan festival in which people reenact fights between tribes with their bodies covered in bright colours and powders. Morocco does have Fantasia, also called Tbourida, a stylised reenactment of a cavalry charge, but the powder involved is gunpowder fired from rifles, not coloured powder on people's bodies. Boujloud is a Berber festival where participants wear sheep or goat skins, and the Tan-Tan Moussem brings Saharan tribes together. None of these matches the claim. The garbled characters ("尸") also make it unclear which festival is meant, so the claim can't be confirmed or clearly disproved.

text: Grapes are scientifically referred to as berries due to their structure, as they develop from a single ovary in a flower and adhere to a receptacle that eventually becomes the stem.
label: supported
reason: The main part of the claim checks out. Several sources say grapes are true berries in the botanical sense: fleshy simple fruits that grow from the single ovary of one flower, with seeds inside the pulp. The receptacle detail is loosely worded but broadly consistent with grape anatomy. A Frontiers in Plant Science study describes a receptacle/berry junction where the grape attaches to its pedicel (the individual grape stem). The receptacle is the tip of that stem, so it is more accurate to say it is part of the stem than that it 'becomes' the stem. Also, botanists classify grapes as berries because of the ovary and fleshy fruit wall, not because of the receptacle. These are wording problems, not contradictions, so the claim counts as supported.

text: Honey is a super-conductor when it's heated above 2.5°C (36.5°F), a property that's unique among all foods.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey isn't a superconductor. Research on honey shows it conducts electricity only weakly. Its conductivity is measured in milli-siemens per centimetre: the Codex Standard caps it at 0.8 mS/cm for a diluted solution, and samples ranged from about 0.08 upward. That is a weak conductor whose conductivity comes from its mineral and acid content, not something with zero resistance. Superconductivity requires zero resistance and has been seen only in particular materials, usually at very low temperatures, never in food warmed above 2.5°C. The idea that this property is unique among foods is also made up.

text: The mysterious Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Peruvian Amazon," is a meandering stream that flows through a remote area of Peru's Amazon rainforest, and its origin remains unknown despite numerous scientific investigations.
label: contradicted
reason: The river itself is real. The Shanay-timpishka, called the "Boiling River of the Amazon," runs through a remote part of Peru's Amazon rainforest. However, the claim says its origin "remains unknown despite numerous scientific investigations," and sources say otherwise. Wikipedia states that the heat is actually geothermal and that the main theory points to the Earth's geothermal gradient. Atlas Obscura and National Geographic describe geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo's research, which explains the heat as a non-volcanic geothermal feature. The water is thought to seep down through faults, get heated deep underground, and then come back to the surface. The heat source is therefore broadly explained, not a mystery that has resisted investigation. The alternative name "Boiling River of the Peruvian Amazon" also doesn't appear in the sources found.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, the Lehigh Valley Mink Insula's dating back to 10,000 years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trace of a "Lehigh Valley Mink Insula" dwelling in the Catskills. The name looks made up, and the Lehigh Valley is in Pennsylvania, not the Catskills. The search results also put the oldest known dwellings in North America elsewhere, and they are much older than 10,000 years. A roughly 13,800-year-old camp in Alaska (Shég' Xdaltth'í') has been reported as the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere. The Gault site in Texas, at about 14,000 years old, has also been called the oldest home in North America. Neither is in New York's Catskill Mountains.

text: The longest abrir flip has been recorded at 21.64 seconds by Croatian gymnast Ana Sabau in 2020, although typically abir flips are performed as part of gymnastic exercises, abir acrobatics derive from [traditional iranian circus arts].
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing about an "abrir" or "abir" flip. I also found no Croatian gymnast named Ana Sabau and no 21.64-second flip record from 2020. Guinness World Records lists flip records by distance, such as the longest sideflip and front flip, but none matches this claim. Nothing I found connects this move to traditional Iranian circus arts. A single flip lasting about 21 seconds also seems physically implausible, but no source directly contradicts the claim, so I can't verify or refute it.

text: Roosevelt Island in New York City is home to the only elevator in the United States that reaches and goes over a highway, allowing residents to travel directly from their homes to Manhattan.
label: contradicted
reason: Roosevelt Island's direct link to Manhattan is the Roosevelt Island Tramway, not an elevator. Wikipedia, NYC Tourism and other sources describe it as an aerial tramway with gondolas that cross the East River between Tramway Plaza on the island and 59th Street/Second Avenue in Manhattan. It is known for being the first commuter aerial tramway in the U.S. or North America, not the 'only elevator that reaches and goes over a highway.' Wikipedia says planners considered and rejected another option, 'an elevator extending directly from the Queensboro Bridge,' before choosing the tramway. Riders board at a station, so the tram does not take residents directly from their homes. None of the sources mention a unique elevator over a highway, so the claim misstates what this landmark is.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," mainly due to its complex spelling and multiple syllable pronunciations despite being commonly thought of as a one syllable word.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources say the longest one-syllable English words are nine-letter words such as "screeched" and "strengths", with rare ten-letter forms like "scraunched". "Stewardesses" (stew-ard-ess-es) has four syllables, and nothing suggests it is commonly thought of as one syllable. It is usually cited for a different reason: it is one of the longest words you can type using only the left hand.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a highly eccentric orbit, which causes its distance from the sun to vary by as much as 46% over the course of its nearly 88-day orbit.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim checks out. Mercury is the smallest planet, its orbit is highly eccentric (e ≈ 0.21), and it takes about 88 days to go around the Sun. The "46%" figure is wrong, though. Mercury is about 46 million km from the Sun at its closest and about 70 million km at its farthest, so the claim appears to confuse 46 million km with a percentage. A change of about 24 million km works out to roughly 34% of the farthest distance, 41% of the average distance (57.9 million km), or 52% of the closest distance. None of these is 46%.

text: The world's largest planetarium, the Melville-Nathan Planetarium in Macau, China, covers over 11,000 square meters of space and features a 60-meter-high dome with a seating capacity of approximately 900 people.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a "Melville-Nathan Planetarium" in Macau. Guinness World Records names the planetarium at Nagoya City Science Museum in Japan as the world's largest, with a dome 35 m across, and that dome seats about 350 people. If you measure by floor space, Shanghai's planetarium is the largest. Macau's real planetarium, at the Macao Science Center, has a tilted dome screen only about 15 m in diameter. Its Guinness record is for the highest-resolution 3D planetarium, not the largest. That rules out the claim's 60 m dome, its 900 seats, and its "world's largest" title.

text: The Fairy Spring located in Huaxi, China is the highest waterfall around the globe based on a non-direct, over 4km horizontal distance dropping.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for a waterfall called the "Fairy Spring" in Huaxi, China, and nothing describing a world-record drop spread over more than 4 km horizontally. The closest match was the Baishui Fairy Waterfall, which a travel source calls China's highest. But it is in Zengcheng District, Guangzhou, not Huaxi, and it drops about 428.5 m. That isn't a world record and doesn't match the claim. Angel Falls is widely recognized as the world's highest waterfall, but the claim's qualifier (a non-direct drop over 4 km horizontally) is too specific to rule out with what I found. My searches were cut short by a tool limit, so neither the waterfall's identity nor the record could be checked.

text: Roosevelt Island in New York City is home to the famous renegade art installation, the "Smallpox Hospital" also known as the "Wards Island Lunatic Asylum" or "Welfare Island Hospital," it was later renamed the Hart Island Pottery Barn and got destroyed before not being rebuilt.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources (CUNY Baruch history blog, NYC Correction History Society, Forgotten NY) describe the Smallpox Hospital as a hospital designed by James Renwick Jr. that opened in 1856 on Blackwell's Island, the island now called Roosevelt Island. Today it is a fenced-off Gothic Revival ruin known as the Renwick Ruin. It was never a renegade art installation, and it was not the Wards Island Lunatic Asylum, which was a separate institution. No source says it was renamed the 'Hart Island Pottery Barn'; Hart Island is a different island. The building also still stands as a stabilized ruin, so describing it as destroyed is misleading. Several parts of the claim are false.

text: The brightness of the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius, is so massive that it would be visible to the human eye even during the daylight hours due to its immense luminosity.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed work in Applied Optics (Können, Tinbergen & Stammes) reports that Sirius was seen with the naked eye in broad daylight from La Palma Observatory. It also concludes that Sirius could be visible in daytime even from sea level when it is high in the sky. So the main claim, that Sirius is bright enough to be seen in daylight, is backed by evidence. This holds only under good conditions: a clear sky with Sirius high overhead. Sirius is not routinely visible during the day. The claim also credits its 'immense luminosity', but much of its brightness comes from being close to us. It is about 25 times as luminous as the Sun, which is bright but not extreme. Even so, the central claim holds up.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 0.137 percent, but in the 1920s, when real temperature fluctuated, liquids in containers appeared to take up more or less space, due to expansion or contraction from the ambient temperatures.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found define the US gallon exactly as 231 cubic inches, or about 3.785 liters. That is a unit of volume, not length. None of them mention a permitted variation of 0.137 percent. I also found nothing about the 1920s or about temperature causing liquids in containers to seem to take up more or less space in that period. Liquids do expand and contract with temperature, but the specific figure and the historical claim could not be verified. The claim also mixes up length and volume, so it has to be judged inconclusive.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the Guinness World Record for being the deepest gorge in the Southern Hemisphere, stretching a depth of over 800 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Butlers Gorge is a small rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with no recorded population, and the name is mainly linked to Hydro Tasmania's Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station. No source says it holds a Guinness World Record or is especially deep. Peru's Cotahuasi Canyon is also in the Southern Hemisphere and is about 3,535 m deep, according to NASA JPL and several travel sources. That is far deeper than the claimed 800 m, so Butlers Gorge cannot be the deepest gorge in the Southern Hemisphere. The Guinness 'deepest gorge' record that sources do mention belongs to Vikos Gorge in Greece.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that have ever lived on Earth, but scientists estimate that around 80-90% of all species that have ever existed are now extinct.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim conflict with the sources. The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) estimates how many species are alive on Earth now. It is not a count of every species that has ever lived, and it covers more than plants and animals. Scientists also generally put the share of all species ever to have existed that are now extinct at about 99%, not 80–90%. That means the number of species that have ever lived is far larger than 8.7 million.

text: Therypton, a rare and highly sought-after green diamond, is only found in a number of locations around the world, including Russia, Australia, and South Africa.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trace of a gem called "Therypton". Searching for the exact name only turned up words that look similar, such as thiostrepton and Therocephalia. The name seems to be made up or have no clear referent. Trusted sources such as geology.com and Wikipedia do say natural green diamonds are rare and valuable. But none of them link a gem by this name to Russia, Australia or South Africa, so the claim can't be checked.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although it's often referred to as having two and a variant of that word is "steward"; another example is "strengths," this, however, can be seen as two but some people argue its the same root as strength
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about "stewardess". It is a three-syllable word (stew-ard-ess), not a one-syllable one. It is actually known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand. A NIEHS (NIH) trivia page says the longest one-syllable English words are "scraunched" and "strengthed", and that "stewardesses" is the longest word typed with the left hand alone. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable English words includes candidates like "strengths" but not "stewardess". "Strengths" is a fair example of a long one-syllable word, but the main claim is false.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill Castle in Pennsylvania, houses the world's largest collection of shells, totaling over 25,000 artifacts from around the world.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any 'Butler's Grotto' at Fonthill Castle, and nothing says the castle holds a shell collection. Wikipedia and several travel and heritage sites describe Fonthill Castle in Doylestown, Pennsylvania as the concrete home of Henry Chapman Mercer, built to show off his tiles and prints. None of them mention a shell grotto or a 25,000-piece shell collection. Searching 'Butler's Grotto' only turned up unrelated grottoes, such as St Giles House and Margate in England. The link to shells seems to come from mixing up this castle with Fonthill Abbey in Wiltshire, England, where grottoes and shell houses are recorded. I ran out of searches before I could check who actually holds the world's largest shell collection. No source directly states that the castle has no grotto, so this verdict rests on the reliable descriptions of what the castle contains.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly large atomic diameter of approximately 3.62 Å.
label: contradicted
reason: Oganesson (Z=118) is the heaviest known element, with the highest atomic number and mass, but it is not the largest atom. Wikipedia lists its predicted atomic radius as about 152 pm (covalent radius 157 pm). That gives a diameter of roughly 3.0–3.1 Å, not 3.62 Å. Alkali metals such as caesium (radius about 260 pm or more) and francium are much bigger, so the claim that oganesson is the largest atom ever discovered is false.

text: The short-lived but spectacular emerald rainbow, also known as "Moonbow," is a rare lunar phenomenon that occurs when the Moon is full and is shining brightly through water droplets in the air.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, the Old Farmer's Almanac and SKYbrary agree that a moonbow (also called a lunar or moon rainbow) is made when moonlight is refracted through water droplets, and that it is most likely near a bright full moon. However, none of them call it an "emerald rainbow." Wikipedia says a moonbow often looks white to the eye because it is so faint, and it is even listed under "White rainbow." The phrase "emerald rainbow" turns up only in a Bible verse (Revelation 4:3), with no link to moonbows. So the claim's name and green colouring are contradicted, even though its basic description of how moonbows form is correct.

text: There are approximately 37.7 million years between the largest known comet impact on Earth, which is believed to have caused a ~95% global extinction event, and the mass extinction event that wiped out the dinosaurs.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim don't match. The extinction that killed about 90–95% of species is the end-Permian event, about 250–252 million years ago. A NASA-funded study reported by SpaceNews suggested it may have been triggered by a comet or asteroid impact, though that idea is debated. It is not called an 'emerald rainbow' and is not described as spectacular. The phrase 'emerald rainbow' comes from Revelation 4:3 in the Bible, not from moonbows. So the claim's name and description are wrong, even though the parts about night and waterfalls are correct.

text: TheHistogram, a rare blood clotting disorder, is caused by a mutation that removes the entirety of the F8 gene, resulting in its near complete absence in people affected, thereby shutting down one of its two main clotting functions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No disorder called "TheHistogram" turned up in the search results, so it's unclear what the claim refers to. It might mean hemophilia A, which is caused by F8 gene defects. But hemophilia A comes from many kinds of F8 abnormalities, most often the intron 22 inversion. It is not usually caused by deletion of the whole gene. The "two main clotting functions" part is also unclear and can't be checked. Because the subject can't be identified, the claim can't be verified as written.

text: Cotton balls were first made from cotton by mechanically spinning short fibers into fluffy clusters, but before that, humans used dried and shredded mushroom caps as a substitute for cotton balls.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying people once used dried, shredded mushroom caps in place of cotton balls. None of the sources I checked mentions it, including the Wikipedia 'Cotton pad' history section and articles on cotton balls in pill bottles. The first part of the claim also conflicts with how cotton balls are described as being made. A process outline on Scribd says raw cotton is cleaned, scoured, bleached, opened and carded into a rope of fibres (sliver), and the sliver is then cut into balls. Spinning is the step that twists fibres into yarn, and no source says cotton balls were first made that way. Since the claim is partly unverifiable and partly at odds with only indirect, less authoritative evidence, it can't be judged supported or clearly contradicted.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to take centuries for a piece of paper to decompose in those conditions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing about a famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole. Reliable sources like Wikipedia, PADI and Newsweek confirm that the Great Blue Hole is a huge marine sinkhole off Belize. They also report that the first expeditions to the bottom found plastic bottles and the bodies of lost divers. None of them mentions a "Forever Float" or any estimate that paper would take centuries to decompose there. The item the claim refers to doesn't seem to exist, and its central claim can't be checked.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the observable universe, with an estimated 3 trillion trees covering the planet's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The 3 trillion tree estimate is right, but the comparison is wrong. Sources including Astronomy.com and WorldAtlas say Earth's roughly 3 trillion trees outnumber the stars in the Milky Way, which NASA puts at about 100 to 400 billion. That is not true of the observable universe. It holds hundreds of billions or more galaxies and an estimated 10^22 to 10^24 stars, far more than 3 trillion. The claim confuses the Milky Way with the whole observable universe.

text: serir's Danakil Depression is considered to be the lowest point on land in the world, with a depth of approximately 125 meters (410 feet) below sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that the Danakil Depression's lowest point is about 125 m (410 ft) below sea level, so that part of the claim holds. But it is not the lowest point on land in the world. Wikipedia describes the area only as "one of the lowest land points." The world's lowest exposed land is the Dead Sea shore, about 430 m below sea level. Even within Africa, Lake Assal in Djibouti is lower, at about 155 m below sea level. The "serir's" in the claim also has no clear meaning.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola containing coca leaves that had a small amount of morphine in them.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources show that Coca-Cola's inventor, John Pemberton, was addicted to morphine and created his coca-based drink partly as a substitute for it. However, coca leaves contain cocaine, not morphine. Morphine comes from the opium poppy. That part of the claim is false. The claim is also wrong about Pepsi, which was sold as a digestive aid rather than as a morphine alternative.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to rest and settle together in a communal gathering during the night.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources (A-Z Animals/AOL, QuizzClub, online-field-guide, nounmaster) agree that the generally accepted collective noun for octopuses is a "consortium," with "tangle" sometimes used as an alternative. None of them gives "basket." They also describe octopuses as mostly solitary animals. That undercuts the claim's explanation that they rest together in a communal group at night.

text: The color blue is invisible to some animals, specifically bees, due to their ability to see ultraviolet light, which allows them to perceive a wider range of colors and patterns.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees can see blue, so the claim is wrong. Bee-supply sources say honeybee colour vision is based on blue, green and ultraviolet light. The colour bees cannot see is red, not blue. Bees do see ultraviolet light, but that does not make blue invisible to them.

text: The Dinbaugh cave in Montana is home to an impressive accumulation of over 30,000 beaver dams, manifesting as a vast beaver landscape within the cave.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that mentions a "Dinbaugh cave" in Montana, so it's unclear what cave the claim refers to. I also found no evidence of 30,000 beaver dams inside any cave. Beavers build dams across streams, not inside caves. The closest result was Montana's Pictograph Cave, where excavations turned up about 30,000 artifacts, not beaver dams. That may be the source of the number, but it isn't enough to say the claim is about that cave.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, but it appears so bright in the sky because of an extremely rare phenomenon called a superior planetary conjunction where the Earth, sun, and Venus align.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is the brightest planet, but the explanation in the claim is wrong. Venus looks bright because thick clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits it (about 77%, more than any other planet) and because it comes close to Earth. A superior conjunction does not make it bright. At superior conjunction, Venus sits directly behind the Sun and is very hard to see for a few weeks either side of that date. It is also not an extremely rare event: it happens regularly as part of Venus's orbital cycle (e.g., 9 January 2018).

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to their unique ability to fill their lungs and stomach with air.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. The Natural History Museum and the Rainforest Alliance both describe capybaras as the world's largest rodent and say they can hold their breath underwater for up to about five minutes. However, I found no source that explains this with a 'unique ability to fill their lungs and stomach with air.' Credible sources link the ability to partially webbed feet, high-set eyes and nostrils, and escaping predators. Lower-quality blogs mention large lungs and a slower heart rate, but nothing about the stomach. Because the stated cause can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Delta Scuti, a mountain range on Jupiter's moon Io that stretches approximately 300 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. In Wikipedia's article, "Delta Scuti" is the name of a type of pulsating variable star, with Delta Scuti itself as the prototype and Altair and Denebola as other examples. It is not a mountain range, on Io or anywhere else. Io's mountains, such as Boösaule Montes, are also not considered the solar system's longest mountain range.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range, at roughly 65,000 km. NOAA and WHOI give the figure as "nearly" 65,000 km, which is slightly off from the claim's "over" wording. However, other sources (an NIH-hosted paper, New World Encyclopedia, ScienceDirect) put the whole system at about 75,000–80,000 km, so "over 65,000 km" holds up. The ridge does run through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), the Indian Ocean and the Arctic. It also reaches the Pacific (East Pacific Rise), but the claim doesn't say these are the only oceans, so leaving the Pacific out doesn't contradict it.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which is now a genus of extinct proboscideans.
label: contradicted
reason: No source calls any animal simply a "short-eared elephant." The closest match is the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus), also called the round-eared sengi. That small African mammal is still alive: it has current accounts on Animal Diversity Web, the US Fish and Wildlife Service site and Wikipedia, and none describe it as extinct. Stegolophodon is indeed an extinct genus of proboscideans from the Miocene and Pliocene, but no source refers to it as a "short-eared elephant." So the claim that the short-eared elephant is extinct is contradicted, and the link between that name and Stegolophodon is unsupported.

text: The Blackburn Buccaneer, a British Jet aircraft, holds the record for being the slowest jet-powered aircraft to fly across the Atlantic Ocean with a speed of about 217 knots (401 kilometers per hour).
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict this claim. The Buccaneer's real transatlantic record was being the first Fleet Air Arm aircraft to cross the Atlantic non-stop without refuelling. It flew from Goose Bay, Canada, to Lossiemouth, Scotland, a distance of about 3,138 km (1,950 miles), in 4 hours 16 minutes. That works out to roughly 735 km/h (about 397 knots), nowhere near the claimed 217 knots (401 km/h). None of the sources describe the Buccaneer as holding a record for the slowest jet crossing of the Atlantic.

text: The Azores Islands, an autonomous region of Portugal, are home to Goree's Algar do Carvão, a crater that is believed to have emitted steam from an underwater volcanic eruption for millions of years.
label: contradicted
reason: The Azores are an autonomous region of Portugal, and Algar do Carvão is there, on Terceira Island. The rest of the claim is wrong. Gorée is an island in Senegal and has nothing to do with this site. Algar do Carvão is not a steam-emitting crater from an underwater eruption active for millions of years. It is an old lava tube with a volcanic chimney about 90 m deep. The official Azores tourism site and an EGU blog both say it formed about 3,200 years ago, after magma drained back down to the magma chamber, and a second eruption about 1,200 years later created the chambers inside.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 40,000 miles long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. It gives the length as about 65,000 km (40,389–40,390 miles), which matches the claim of over 40,000 miles. NOAA describes the ridge as wrapping around the globe like the seam of a baseball, and it is widely documented to run through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. One detail is loose: the Pacific part (the East Pacific Rise) sits toward the east of that ocean rather than in its exact center. This is a common simplification, and the main points of the claim hold up.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the Moon appears in the opposite direction of its actual location in the sky, can sometimes be visible from locations in the Southern Hemisphere due to refraction through the Earth's atmosphere.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a phenomenon called "뒷문 (Hidden Moon)" exists. 뒷문 is Korean for "back door." Searches in English and Korean turned up only the far side of the Moon (달의 뒷면), lunar phases and the Moon illusion. None of these involves the Moon appearing in the opposite direction from where it really is. The claimed mechanism is also wrong.
