Trusted sources (USNO, RASC, and a Michigan Tech dissertation) put atmospheric refraction at only about 34 arcminutes even at the horizon. It makes objects look slightly higher than they are and cannot move the Moon's apparent position by about 180°. Because refraction is far too weak to do what the claim describes, the claim is contradicted.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism in which they can shed, or "eject," their body parts to distract predators, such as the cyphiphorbe caterpillar which can sacrifice its tail to escape capture.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no caterpillar or insect called "cyphiphorbe." The closest results were unrelated genera such as Cyphosticha and Cyphothyris, so the example in the claim has no clear referent and looks made up. The sources I found on autotomy, where an animal sheds a body part to escape, cover lizards, scorpions and sea lilies. None of them describe caterpillars shedding body parts or tails to distract predators. I also found nothing that directly disproves the claim, so the evidence is not enough to support or contradict it.

text: The oldest known piece of jewelry in the world is a 100,000-year-old piece known as the 'Floral Necklace' discovered in a cave in Morocco.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results show the oldest known jewelry is a set of 33 perforated sea snail shell beads from Bizmoune Cave in Morocco. They date to about 142,000–150,000 years ago, not 100,000 years, and nothing calls them a 'Floral Necklace.' Guinness World Records also lists the shell beads as the oldest jewelry. The claim gets the location right, but its age and name are wrong.

text: The short-lived but oxygenated Mars year of 687 was surprisingly the warmest year in the entire mission of the Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity Rover), with high temperatures recorded in the month of September.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up a fact: a Mars year lasts about 687 Earth days, but there is no 'Mars year 687.' Under the standard numbering, Mars Year 1 began in 1955. Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in 2012, during Mars Year 31, and its mission has continued through roughly Mars Years 31–38. A year 687, whether a Mars year or AD 687, cannot fall within Curiosity's mission, so it could not have been the mission's warmest year. Curiosity's REMS weather records and NASA's summaries of its seasonal cycles do not describe any 'short-lived but oxygenated' Mars year or a record-warm year with highs in September. September is also an Earth month and does not describe Martian seasons, which are tracked by solar longitude (Ls).

text: The Gotland horse, a rare and ancient breed of horse, is primarily found in Sweden and is known for its unique physical appearance and ability to thrive in cold climates.
label: supported
reason: My sources back the main points of the claim. Skansen, Sweden's national open-air museum and zoo, says the Gotland pony (Gotlandsruss) is a hardy breed that has lived on Gotland since the Iron Age and is Sweden's only remaining native pony breed, with about 6,000 in Sweden. ExploreNorth says the ponies are mostly in Sweden and nearly went extinct in the 1920s. Discover the Horse calls the breed rare, small and hardy. Mad Barn says its primitive markings reflect a link to ancient pony types and are a defining feature, which fits the 'unique appearance' part. No source says anything specifically about cold climates. However, the breed is described throughout as hardy, as having lived semi-wild in Scandinavia for thousands of years, and Mad Barn classes it as having cold-blooded influence. That fits the general description, and nothing I found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The length of a standard Khayagan day on the planet Venus, which is the period between two consecutive sunrises, is 116.75 Earth days due to its extremely slow rotation period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, such as Space Centre NZ, give Venus's solar day (sunrise to sunrise) as about 116.75 Earth days, which comes from its slow retrograde rotation. However, I found no source for the term "Khayagan day." It appears to be made up or to have no clear referent, so that part of the claim can't be verified.

text: Cotton balls were first made from cotton by mechanically spinning short fibers into fluffy clusters, but before this process existed, people used loose cotton fibers from quilts and clothing to create makeshift cotton balls for applications like applying nail polish.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for the story about makeshift cotton balls made from quilt or clothing fibers to apply nail polish. Cotton balls are mostly associated with removing nail polish, not applying it. The sources I found don't say cotton balls are made by spinning short fibers. Manufacturing guides describe carding the cotton into a web or sliver, then cutting and shaping it into balls. Spinning is the step that turns fiber into yarn. The history is vague in the results: Joseph A. Voss's 1937 machine, mass production possibly as early as 1816, and cotton used for wounds in earlier centuries. The spinning detail conflicts with the manufacturing descriptions, but the term is loose enough that it isn't clearly contradicted. Since the main historical claims can't be verified at all, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Octopuses have nearly 400 million neurons in their brains, which is more than the number found in the human brain but with less physical space.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. An octopus has about 500 million neurons in total, and only around 180 million of them, roughly a third, are in its central brain. The rest are spread through its arms. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons (estimates run from roughly 61 to 99 billion), which is hundreds of times more than an octopus has. So the octopus does not have more neurons than a human, and its brain count is not close to 400 million either.

text: The brightness of the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius, is so massive that it would appear 25 times bigger in the sky if it were placed at the same distance as the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives Sirius A a radius of about 1.71 times the Sun's and a luminosity of about 25 times the Sun's. The claim mixes these up. Placed at the Sun's distance, Sirius would look about 25 times brighter, but only about 1.7 times wider (roughly 3 times the area), not 25 times bigger. Brightness also isn't 'massive': Sirius A has about twice the Sun's mass.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait that allows them to close their valves in their ears when their long neck is bending, which helps to prevent their brain from getting an excessive amount of blood at such altitudes.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources, including an NCBI/PMC paper on giraffe hemodynamics and other wildlife sources, say the valves that control blood flow to the brain when a giraffe lowers its head are one-way valves in the jugular veins of the neck, working together with the rete mirabile. None of them mention valves in the ears. The claim puts the valves in the wrong place, and the phrase 'at such altitudes' is also misleading.

text: The extremely rare meteorite known as the "A ValueEventListener" was found in Algeria in 2010, which is the oldest known extraterrestrial material discovered with an age of approximately 4.57 billion years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no meteorite called "A ValueEventListener". That name is a programming interface in Google's Firebase software, not a space rock, so the claim has no clear subject. The closest real match is Erg Chech 002, an ancient meteorite found in Algeria. But it was found in May 2020, not 2010, and it is dated to about 4.566 billion years. It is described as one of the oldest stony meteorites, not the oldest known extraterrestrial material. Since the named meteorite can't be identified, the claim can't be properly checked.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Australia, has the world's oldest known dam, with evidence suggesting it was built over 2,000 years ago by the Indigenous people of Tasmania.
label: contradicted
reason: The dam at Butler's Gorge, Tasmania, is the Clark Dam. The Hydro-Electric Commission built it in the 1940s; a Mercury article from 1946 describes the construction under way. It is not an Indigenous structure more than 2,000 years old. The University of Tasmania's Companion to Tasmanian History says the earliest dams in Tasmania were built along the Hobart Rivulet from about 1809. Nothing I found supports the claim that Butler's Gorge has the world's oldest known dam.

text: The finish on the Lincoln Memorial in Washington D.C. was actually created using a technique called "fox and subs" where a woman named Kelsie Benson applied the finish by hand using linen to buff it.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a "fox and subs" finishing technique or a person named Kelsie Benson in connection with the Lincoln Memorial. Official and reference sources, including the National Park Service and Wikipedia, say the memorial was designed by Henry Bacon. The statue was sculpted by Daniel Chester French and carved from Georgia marble by the Piccirilli Brothers. None of them mention hand-buffing with linen or anyone named Kelsie Benson. The claim looks fabricated, but no source directly contradicts it, so it cannot be verified either way.

text: Researchers have discovered that there are more trees on Earth now than there were 35 years ago, thanks in part to massive reforestation efforts and the natural regrowth of forests.
label: supported
reason: A 2018 study in Nature, led by Song and Hansen at the University of Maryland, used satellite data from 1982 to 2016. It found that global tree cover grew by about 2.24 million km² over those 35 years, and Mongabay's headline puts it as 'Earth has more trees now than 35 years ago.' According to coverage of the study, the gains came from human activity, such as afforestation and plantations in places like China and Europe, and from trees growing back naturally on abandoned land and in areas affected by climate change. The researchers point out that tree cover is not the same as forest cover, but that caveat doesn't contradict the claim.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the neon atom at JILA (a US research lab), which had a much larger-than-normal electron cloud that contained 2,600 atoms.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no record of a giant neon atom made at JILA whose electron cloud held 2,600 atoms. Reliable reports describe the real 'atoms inside an atom' experiments, called Rydberg polarons, differently. They were done in 2018 by Rice University and TU Wien using strontium atoms in a Bose-Einstein condensate. Up to about 170 strontium atoms fit inside the excited electron's orbit, not 2,600 (phys.org, Wikipedia). Rice researchers say the largest atoms observed so far are Rydberg atoms with n above 1200, not a neon atom at JILA. The element, the lab and the atom count in the claim all conflict with these sources.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait that allows them to close their valves in their ears when their long neck is bending, which helps to prevent water and debris from entering their ears.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the valves that close when a giraffe lowers its neck are in the jugular veins, not the ears. Sources include EarthDate and a peer-reviewed study of giraffe jugular vein valves. These valves close when the head drops below heart level, holding back blood so it doesn't flood the brain. They have nothing to do with keeping water or debris out of the ears. I found no evidence that giraffes have ear valves, so the claim appears to confuse the jugular valves with something else.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 0.137 percent, but in the 1920s a court case resulted in the U.S standard gallon, used for measuring liquids, becoming a fixed unit.
label: contradicted
reason: A gallon measures volume, so it has no "length." The U.S. liquid gallon is fixed by definition at exactly 231 cubic inches (about 3.785411784 L). That figure comes from the Queen Anne wine gallon of 1706, which the U.S. adopted as its standard in the early 1800s. It did not become a fixed unit through a 1920s court case. I found no source for the "0.137 percent" variation figure or for any such court case, and the documented history conflicts with the claim.

text: The lingering scent of certain foods, such as asparagus and garlic, persists on clothes and breath due to a protein called allyl methyl sulfide that is released when the foods are broken down in the body.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong in two ways. First, allyl methyl sulfide is not a protein. Wikipedia and NPR describe it as a volatile sulfur compound, one of the organosulfur molecules behind garlic breath. Second, the claim credits it for the asparagus smell too. Asparagus odor actually comes from the breakdown of asparagusic acid into other sulfur compounds, not from allyl methyl sulfide. So calling it a protein that explains both foods contradicts the evidence.

text: The mysterious Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural hot spring, has been a source of intrigue for scientists and explorers due to its unexplained origins and location deep within the Amazon rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is real, lies in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest, and has drawn scientists' interest. However, the claim gets two things wrong. First, its origins are not unexplained: geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo's research found that the water is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, not by a volcano, and comes back up into the riverbed through fault-fed hot springs. Second, it is a river about 9 km long that is fed by hot springs, not a single natural hot spring.

text: The6021 Rindler horizon,a theoretical boundary beyond which no signals can travel in a given universe has a radius that is directly correlated to the Schwarzschild black hole's surface since Einstein's theory of relativity.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the Rindler horizon wrong. It is not a boundary 'in a given universe' that no signal can cross. It is an observer-dependent horizon in flat Minkowski spacetime that appears in the rest frame of a uniformly accelerated observer, and it sits at a distance of about c²/a from that observer, where a is the observer's acceleration. It is a plane, so it has no 'radius' tied to the surface of a Schwarzschild black hole. The two are related only in that the region just outside a Schwarzschild event horizon locally looks like Rindler space, which is not the 'direct correlation' the claim describes. The 'since Einstein's theory of relativity' wording also misplaces the history: Rindler coordinates were introduced by Wolfgang Rindler decades after general relativity was published. Note that the claim's text is partly garbled ('The6021').

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in at least eight different countries, including Japan, Thailand, and Finland, where instead they use other forms of communication such as purring, hissing, or making other sounds like birds or animals.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results show that cats meow in Japan, Thailand and Finland just as they do elsewhere. Each language simply has its own word for the sound: "nyā" or "nyan" in Japanese, "miao" or "ngaew" in Thai, and "miau" or "nau" in Finnish. One source says the basic meow is consistent across regions and countries, with only slight differences in frequency, tone and intensity. No source suggests that cats in any country don't meow.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crindledyke Slake, a unique slakes or plunge pool in a waterfall over 1.8 meters drop that can freeze solid in winter.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Vale of Awe" or a "Crindledyke Slake". Searches turned up the River Awe, Loch Awe and the Bridge of Awe in Argyll. Crindledyke is a small settlement in North Lanarkshire, and Crindledykes is a limekiln site in Northumberland. Nothing describes a plunge pool or waterfall with a drop of over 1.8 meters that freezes solid in winter. Because no source supports or contradicts the claim, it can't be verified, and it looks like it may be made up.

text: The6021 Rindler horizon,a theoretical boundary beyond which no signals can travel in a given universe has a radius that is directly correlated to the Schwarzschild black hole's surface since Einstein's theory of general relativity.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. arXiv papers (gr-qc/0010055 and gr-qc/0508095) describe the Rindler horizon as the horizon seen by an observer accelerating at a constant rate in flat Minkowski spacetime, where no gravity is present. It depends on the observer. It is not a fixed boundary of a given universe beyond which no signals can travel; that description fits a cosmological event horizon. A Rindler horizon is also a plane, so it has no radius, and its distance from the observer (c²/a) depends only on the observer's acceleration, not on the size of a Schwarzschild black hole. The only real link to black holes is that the region just outside a Schwarzschild horizon looks like Rindler space locally. The garbled wording ("The6021") also makes the claim's subject unclear.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon remains one of the world's greatest unsolved enigmas, and despite numerous investigations, its origins and the source of its heat remain unclear.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific sources disagree with the claim that the river's heat source is still unclear. Wikipedia says the Shanay-timpishka's heat "is actually geothermal." It adds that the main theory, based on geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo's research, is that rainwater seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, and rises back up through fault lines; no volcano is involved. Some sources still call the river mysterious, but its heat source is reasonably well explained rather than an unsolved enigma.

text: The cheese produced by the same process of fermentation, as with wine, is called a "washed-rind cheese," such as Limburger, which requires an extremely controlled environment to develop its distinctive pungent smell and savor.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results back the claim that Limburger is a washed-rind (smear-ripened) cheese with a strong smell. Wikipedia says that smell comes from Brevibacterium linens. However, the claim gets the definition wrong. A washed-rind cheese is not named for being made by the same fermentation process as wine. Cabot's explainer says the name comes from repeatedly washing the rind during aging, usually with salty brine or alcohol such as brandy or beer. That washing encourages bacteria like B. linens to grow on the surface. Since the central definition in the claim is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, approximately 86 billion neurons and 100-400 billion stars.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the brain has more neurons than the Milky Way has stars, but its own numbers show the opposite: 86 billion neurons is fewer than 100–400 billion stars. Nature Scitable (Bradley Voytek's blog) gives about 86 billion neurons in the human brain and 200–400 billion stars in the Milky Way, so the galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons. The numbers in the claim are roughly right, but the comparison is backwards.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the WR 104 horseshoe shaped binary system's equatorial ring system, but in terms of a solid body, it's actually the mid-ocean ridge system on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says WR 104's "equatorial ring system" is the longest mountain range in the solar system, and that is false. WR 104 is a Wolf–Rayet star system about 2,580 parsecs (roughly 8,400 light-years) from Earth, so it is not in the solar system. It is also not described as horseshoe-shaped: it is a triple system known for its spiral dust "pinwheel nebula." A cloud of dust around a star is not a mountain range. The second part of the claim, that Earth's mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on a solid body, is widely cited, but the first part makes the claim false overall.

text: The unique sound produced by a Tinkle Bell on a Moon Rock Sample from Apollo 11 is one of the parts of the samples that remain unchanged over billions of years on Earth due to being in a vacuum.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that anything called a "Tinkle Bell" exists on an Apollo 11 Moon rock sample, or that such a sample makes a unique sound. Searches only turned up general pages about the Apollo 11 lunar sample displays, such as dust particles set in acrylic buttons. Since the claim's main subject has no clear referent and can't be checked, it can't be verified. The rest of the claim also makes little sense: Apollo 11 samples have only been on Earth since 1969, not billions of years, and NASA generally keeps them in dry-nitrogen cabinets rather than a vacuum. That last point comes from general knowledge, not from the search results.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural river that one can not find by satellite image, and scientists have struggled to explain how this river has been flowing continuously for so long without being visible.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, National Geographic, Atlas Obscura, Discover Wildlife) say the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru is a known, mapped river about 6 km long that people visit and study. Scientists haven't been puzzled by how it could flow for so long without being visible. What they asked was where its heat comes from, since there is no volcano nearby. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found that the water is heated by the Earth's natural geothermal gradient, with hot water moving up through faults. None of these sources says the river cannot be seen in satellite images. The claim's description of an invisible river that scientists cannot explain contradicts the evidence.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers, running through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km long. It winds between the continents through the major ocean basins, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. One small mismatch: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Some other estimates that count the whole ridge network run longer. The claim also simplifies things by saying the ridge runs through the "center" of each ocean, since the ridge in the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise) sits off to the east. Overall, the claim matches what these reliable sources say.

text: The vomitrocha frog, a species found in Papua New Guinea, can self-decapitate its head as a defense mechanism to distract a predator, a biological process known as autotomy.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a frog called the "vomitrocha frog" in Papua New Guinea or anywhere else. Searches only turned up real PNG frogs such as Paedophryne amauensis, and none of them self-decapitates. Self-decapitation as autotomy is documented in two sea slugs, Elysia cf. marginata and Elysia atroviridis, which shed the body from the head and regrow it. No frog is reported to do this. The claim seems to give a real sea-slug behaviour to a frog that may not exist. No source says outright that frogs cannot do this, but the evidence points against the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main parts of the claim. Wikipedia and WHOI call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range in the world, at about 65,000 km. A NOAA Ocean Exploration lesson says it is "more than 65,000 kilometers long," which supports "over 65,000 km." NOAA's main fact page and WHOI say "nearly 65,000 km," so the "over" wording is borderline. The ridge does run down the middle of the Atlantic (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) and through the Indian and Arctic oceans (the Arctic section is the Gakkel Ridge). It also extends into the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise), but the claim never says it is limited to those three oceans, so leaving out the Pacific doesn't contradict it.

text: The vomitrocha frog, a species found in Papua New Guinea, can self-decapitate its head as a defense mechanism to distract a predator, a biological process known as "autotomy."
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a 'vomitrocha frog' exists. Searches turned up only real Papua New Guinea frogs, such as Paedophryne and Oreophryne, and none of them self-decapitate. The well-documented case of self-decapitation by autotomy involves two Japanese sea slugs, Elysia cf. marginata and Elysia atroviridis, not a frog. In those slugs, the head lives on and regrows a new body after shedding the old one. The claim assigns this behavior to a frog that appears to be made up and gets the process wrong, since the shed head would not be left as a decoy for a predator.

text: Centaury flowers, which are used in herbal medicine, have the unique ability to bloom only at night in a color change from white to pink.
label: contradicted
reason: Centaury is used in herbal medicine, but the claim gets its flowering wrong. Reliable sources say the flowers are pink to pinkish-lavender and bloom in the daytime. Like other members of the gentian family, they close in the afternoon, at midday on sunny days, or in dull weather. None of the sources mention night-only blooming or a change from white to pink.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlyweds symbolically cross the rippling waters to begin their life together.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nairs (Nayars) are a community from Kerala in southwestern India, so that part holds up. The description of the ceremony is wrong, though. Wikipedia describes Thalikettu (Thalikettu Kalyanam) as the "tāli-tying ceremony": a ritual or mock marriage in which a tali, a wedding necklace or string, is tied around the girl's neck before puberty. Sources describing Kerala Hindu weddings likewise say Thalikettu means the groom tying the thali around the bride's neck. No source supports calling it a "boat bridge ceremony" in which newlyweds symbolically cross water.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made from white Carrara marble that is stained yellow by the environmental conditions in the area, giving them a distinctive golden hue.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't match what reliable sources say about the church. San Miniato al Monte has no white-marble 'steeples.' It has a single bell tower, rebuilt from 1523 to a design by Baccio d'Agnolo and never finished. One source describes it as a massive, unplastered stone tower. The white Carrara marble, set against green Prato (serpentine) marble, belongs to the façade. No source mentions marble turned yellow by local conditions or a golden hue on the tower.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, but it appears so bright in the sky because of an extremely rare phenomenon called a superior planetary conjunction where the Earth, sun, and Venus line up together.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is indeed the brightest planet. But it doesn't look bright because of a rare superior conjunction. Caltech's Cool Cosmos, EarthSky and Live Science all say it's bright because its thick, highly reflective clouds bounce back about 70% of the sunlight that hits them, and because it's the planet closest to Earth. At superior conjunction, Venus sits on the far side of the Sun, where the Sun's glare hides it, so that alignment can't explain its brightness. These conjunctions are also not extremely rare; they come roughly every 584 days.

text: The humans have a unique genetic trait, known as the ability to smell as infants, which is a rapidly fading learned sense that starts to fade from around 6 to 12 months of age.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy pediatric sources (CHOP, Cincinnati Children's, Pathways.org) say smell is an innate sense that forms early in fetal development. Newborns are born with a keen sense of smell and keep it, using it for bonding, learning and memory. Smell is not a unique genetic trait, not a learned sense, and does not start fading at 6–12 months. The 6–12-month timeframe likely comes from a mix-up with 'perceptual narrowing' (for example, infants losing the ability to tell apart foreign speech sounds), which has nothing to do with smell.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge system, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main parts of this claim. NOAA and WHOI describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and about 80,000 km for the whole ridge system, so 'over 65,000 km' fits. Wikipedia also notes the system reaches every ocean: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge splits the Atlantic, and there are ridges in the Indian Ocean and in the Arctic (the Gakkel Ridge). The claim leaves out the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise), but that omission doesn't contradict anything. The one soft spot is the length: NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over'. That is only supported if you count the full system.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill, Connecticut, is a natural limestone cavern that features the longest underwater body of water in the world, known as the Stepping Stones.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of a place called 'Butler's Grotto', and no trace of a place called 'Fonthill, Connecticut'. Searches for 'Fonthill' turned up only places in other locations: the Fonthill Grottoes in Wiltshire, England; Fonthill Castle in Doylestown, Pennsylvania; and Fonthill Castle in the Bronx, New York. 'Butler' searches turned up only Butler Cave in Virginia, which is unrelated. Nothing mentioned a limestone cavern or a 'Stepping Stones' underwater feature in Connecticut. The claim looks made up. From my own knowledge (not checked by search), the world's longest underwater caves are in Mexico, not Connecticut. Still, my searches can't positively rule out the place existing, and my search limit ran out before I could try more queries, so the claim can't be confirmed or directly disproven.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iwanowa-Danagumma, whose body temperature rose to 114 degrees Fahrenheit (45.6 degrees Celsius) as a result of a severe heat stroke.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records lists Willie Jones as holding the record for the highest body temperature. He was admitted to Grady Memorial Hospital in Atlanta in July 1980 with heatstroke and reached 46.5°C (115.7°F). The claim instead names someone called 'Iwanowa-Danagumma' with 114°F (45.6°C), but I found no evidence that this person or record exists. Both the name and the figure conflict with the documented record.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and is not visible from space.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including NOAA and Guinness World Records, say the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Guinness specifically calls it the longest submarine mountain range. The ridge lies almost entirely underwater, so it can't be seen directly from space, which fits the claim's last part. One caveat: the searches found no source that directly addresses visibility from space. Also, satellite measurements of sea-surface height can map the ridge indirectly, and a small part of it rises above water in Iceland.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the world's largest living structure, the coral reef known as the Raja Ampat, also considered one of the most biodiverse marine ecosystems on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: Indonesia has no province called "Theona". Raja Ampat is a regency and archipelago in Southwest Papua Province. Raja Ampat is known for very high marine biodiversity, but it is not the world's largest living structure. That title belongs to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, according to sources such as Live Science and the Australian Academy of Science.

text: Coconuts are a type of tree fruit that can help the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for various animals and insects due to their durable, insulated husks and abundant supplies of nutrient-rich seeds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Parts of the claim check out. Coconuts are fruits of the coconut palm: the Library of Congress calls them a fibrous one-seeded drupe. Animals such as coconut crabs and rhinoceros beetles feed on coconuts, and coconut crabs line their burrows with husk fibres. Other parts are shaky. The coconut palm is a palm rather than a typical tree. Each coconut holds only one seed, so the phrase 'abundant supplies of nutrient-rich seeds' is only true if it means a palm produces many coconuts. If it means each coconut has many seeds, it is wrong. I also found no reliable source showing that 'durable, insulated husks' give animals and insects meaningful shelter in the wider ecosystem. The general idea is plausible, but the specific details are not clearly supported, so I can't call the whole claim supported.

text: Cultural events and celebrations in Japan wouldn't be fully appreciated without their vibrant seasonal undertone because their lifecycle of festivals and dances, called the 'seasonal idea', fills their holistic thought mechanisms from its dynamics.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources such as nippon.com and Go Tokyo confirm that Japanese festivals (matsuri) are closely tied to the seasons and the yearly cycle of life. However, I found no source that calls this cycle the 'seasonal idea.' Nothing supports the claim's vague assertions that this idea 'fills their holistic thought mechanisms' or that cultural events wouldn't be fully appreciated without it. The core of the claim is too vague to verify.

text: Butt holes  are actually a bright red color; however, our eyes see them as BLACK due to the way they appear with our limited human vision.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Medical and dermatology sources say the skin around the anus is naturally pink, brown or darker. When it looks darker than nearby skin, the reason is extra melanin (hyperpigmentation), often from friction or irritation. Wikipedia's anal bleaching article describes darker anal skin as localized hyperpigmentation, and Statcare's article on anal darkening gives the same explanation. No credible source says the anus is really bright red and only looks black because of limited human vision. Human eyes see red clearly, so any darkness people notice comes from pigment and shadow, not a trick of perception.

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the only ant species able to be able to swim and are known for being found in large numbers both indoors in homes and outdoors near pavement streets.
label: contradicted
reason: No ant species called the "Butterfly Pavement Ant" turned up in my searches. The only matches were the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium caespitum / T. immigrans). The swimming part of the claim is clearly wrong anyway: Aptive Pest Control's "Can Ants Swim?" page says "Most ant species can swim to some degree." It also notes that carpenter ants are good swimmers, army ants form rafts, and pavement ants can only swim short distances before tiring. So pavement ants are not "one of the only" species that can swim. Pavement ants are indeed common around pavement and in homes, but the claim that they are uniquely able to swim is false.

text: The desert town of Tal DESeret in Utah had a peculiar past, as it was a ""lost"" Mormon city that only existed on a map more than 160 miles away, when it disappeared anytime before 1900.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any place called "Tal Deseret" in Utah. My searches turned up only related subjects: the proposed State of Deseret (1849–51), Fort Deseret (an adobe fort built in 1865 in Millard County, now in ruins), and the real community of Deseret in Millard County. None of the sources describes a "lost" Mormon city that existed only on a map more than 160 miles away, or one that disappeared before 1900. Because the place has no clear referent and none of the specific details can be checked, the claim can be neither confirmed nor refuted.

text: The padrão, a type of stone monument typically built to serve as a territorial marker, was known for playing a significant role in many exploration and trade missions led by Europe and particularly Portugal in the 16th century.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the claim. Wikipedia defines a padrão as a stone pillar that Portuguese maritime explorers left in the 15th and 16th centuries to record significant landfalls and establish primacy and possession. That matches the claim's description of a territorial marker. A Sri Lankan heritage source describes a 16th-century padrão in Colombo that Portuguese explorers erected as a territorial marker to claim land in newly explored regions. Padrões were set up on many voyages, including those of Diogo Cão, Bartolomeu Dias and Vasco da Gama, and on a 1522 treaty mission. The claim slightly overstates things in two ways: padrões were almost entirely a Portuguese practice rather than a wider European one, and many date from the late 15th century rather than the 16th. Still, nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: The classification of species according to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature changed from one example per species to the selection of the type specimen for further identification and naming in 1895.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found don't support this claim, and they contradict its central point. The ICZN was set up in 1895, when the 3rd International Zoological Congress in Leiden appointed a five-member commission. Nothing I found says that this changed species classification from "one example per species" to choosing a type specimen. The Code's own text and the ICZN FAQs say that fixing a name-bearing type (a holotype or syntypes) has been required only for new species names published after 1999 (Article 16.4). Many 19th-century species were described from several equal type specimens called syntypes, not from one designated type. The claim therefore attaches the wrong rule change to the date the commission was founded.

text: The/ng Ai Grotto located in China, also known as the "Glass Bridge," is a 272 meter (896 feet) long and 1.7 meter (5.6 feet) wide glass-bottom bridge.
label: contradicted
reason: The closest real match for the garbled name "Ai Grotto" is the Ah-ai (A-ai) Grotto in Kucha County, Xinjiang. According to Wikipedia and Wikidata, it is a small, standalone Buddhist cave that a local shepherd discovered in 1999, not a bridge. My searches found no glass bridge in China called "Ai Grotto" or matching 272 m × 1.7 m. The well-known glass bridges have different measurements: Zhangjiajie is 430 m long and 6 m wide, Haohan Qiao is about 300 m, and Huangchuan is 526 m. The name in the claim is mangled, so this verdict assumes it means the Ah-ai Grotto. If it refers to some other site, the claim would be inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: The humans have a unique genetic trait, known as the ability to smell as infants, which is a rapidly fading learned sense that virtually all humans start with, and is partially seen in up to 70% of people in some parts of Europe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim seems to mix up smell with lactase persistence, the inherited trait that lets some adults keep digesting milk. The evidence goes against the smell version. Sources on infant development say the sense of smell starts forming in the womb and keeps getting stronger for the first several years of life. It is not a learned sense that quickly fades, and it is not a trait seen only in part of the population. The real 'fading' trait is lactase production, which drops off after weaning in most people (about 70% worldwide). That trait is common in northwestern Europe, where more than 95% of Swedes and Danes keep it, so even the Europe percentage in the claim does not match.

text: Did you know that honey is a super-efficient food source because it contains a platform of carbs, vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and antioxidants that can be digested by the human body with almost 100% efficiency?
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. Honey.com (the National Honey Board) and GloryBee say honey contains carbohydrates plus trace amounts of vitamins, minerals, amino acids and antioxidants. I found no reliable source for the central point, though: that all of these are digested with "almost 100% efficiency," making honey a "super-efficient" food. Research gives a mixed picture. A PMC study notes that honey's main sugars, glucose and fructose, are absorbed without modification. But a ScienceDirect review of honey digestion found that digestion can cut honey's antioxidant activity by up to 80%, while some phenolic compounds showed bioaccessibility above 100%. Digestion efficiency varies by component, so a blanket near-100% figure isn't supported, and it isn't clearly disproved either.

text: TheOMICRAN antisatellite network, a system of radar and electronic warfare assets in the UK, uses the Jindalee Operational Radar Network's.org signal to steer and track Incoming active ballistic missiles , Origins for systems initially starting as full surface coverage.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of an 'OMICRAN antisatellite network' in the UK or anywhere else. Searches on UK air and missile defence returned only real systems such as the UK early warning radar network and IUKADGE, so the main subject of the claim has no clear referent. The Jindalee Operational Radar Network (JORN) does exist: it is a set of three over-the-horizon radars run by the Royal Australian Air Force that watches air and sea movements across northern Australia. No source says a UK network uses a JORN signal to steer or track ballistic missiles. The claim is also garbled ('.org signal', 'Origins for systems initially starting as full surface coverage'), so it can't be checked as written.

text: Shark Bay in Australia is home to an incredible phenomenon called Hampden Creek, where the unique Zhars of Shark Bay seaweed, through symbiotic processes, form 90% of a bacteria to nitrogen conversion process.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms either "Hampden Creek" in Shark Bay or a seaweed called the "Zhars of Shark Bay." I also found no source for the idea that seaweed forms "90% of a bacteria to nitrogen conversion process." Shark Bay's real, well-documented phenomenon is the stromatolites at Hamelin Pool. These are rock-like structures built by microbial communities that include cyanobacteria, not a symbiosis with seaweed. The claim seems to garble or invent its key terms, so the entities have no clear referent and the main assertions can't be checked. The searches turned up nothing that directly disproves the claim, so I've labelled it inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers around the globe and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the global mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth. They give its length as about 65,000 km and say it winds around the globe through the world's oceans, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. Two small details are looser than these sources: NOAA says 'nearly' rather than 'over' 65,000 km, though other sources give figures of 65,000–80,000 km, and the Pacific section (the East Pacific Rise) lies in the eastern Pacific rather than its exact middle. Neither difference changes the main point, so the claim is substantially supported.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although this is often disputed with other one-syllable words.
label: contradicted
reason: "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be a one-syllable word. The usual candidates for the longest one-syllable English words are nine-letter words like "screeched," "strengths" and "scratched." Rarer or archaic ten-letter words such as "scraunched" and "strengthed" are also cited. "Stewardess" is better known as the longest common word typed with only the left hand on a standard keyboard.

text: The unique coast of the Zhejiang province in China features the famous Yellow and White Sea Dyke, also known as the Grand Canal, that stretches over 1,100 miles long, making it the world's longest man-made waterway.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim checks out. The Grand Canal (Beijing–Hangzhou) is about 1,794 km (1,115 miles) long, is widely called the world's longest man-made waterway, and ends in Hangzhou, Zhejiang. But the rest is wrong. No source calls it the "Yellow and White Sea Dyke"; that name doesn't seem to exist. It is also an inland canal running from Beijing to Hangzhou, not a dyke and not a feature of Zhejiang's coast. Because the claim links the Grand Canal to a made-up coastal dyke, it is contradicted.

text: Roosevelt Island in New York City is home to the famous renegade art installation, the Smallpox Hospital, also known as the Old Smallpox Hospital, designed in 1854 but was never actually used for that purpose.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the hospital's history wrong. A Roosevelt Island Historical Society marker and a CUNY history-of-medicine page both say the Smallpox Hospital was a Gothic Revival building designed by James Renwick Jr. It opened on December 18, 1856, as the first hospital in the US dedicated to treating smallpox, and it did treat smallpox patients. So the statement that it was "never actually used for that purpose" is false. The building is also a historic ruin and a city landmark, not a "renegade art installation."

text: Cstorabies, more commonly known as stars, have blood only a mere 0.00001% of the blood that shows in their bodies due to the transparent nature of the plasma in their circulatory system.
label: contradicted
reason: The term "Cstorabies" doesn't appear in any source I found. Searching for it only returns results about scabies. If the claim means starfish (sea stars), reliable sources say they have no blood. Instead, a water vascular system moves seawater through their bodies. That directly contradicts the idea that they have a tiny amount of blood that is hard to see because their plasma is transparent.

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to hold its Guinness World Record title for over 20 years as the longest recorded underwater permanent float lasting from April 1983 to 2004.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any record of a "Forever Float" at the Great Blue Hole, or of a Guinness World Record for the "longest underwater permanent float" held from 1983 to 2004. Reliable sources, including Guinness World Records, Wikipedia and Atlas Obscura, confirm only that the Great Blue Hole is a large underwater sinkhole in Belize, about 124 m deep. Nothing I found speaks to the record, its dates or how long it was held. The claim may well be made up, but because no source directly contradicts it, I can't verify it or rule it out.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not purr when they're alone, as purring is primarily a social behavior that they exhibit when they're feeling content or calm in the presence of others.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say cats do purr when they're alone. The Conversation reports that cats purr when in pain, hungry and alone, not only around humans. Wikipedia says cats also purr to soothe themselves and manage pain. Discover Wildlife notes that cats purr when injured or stressed. So there is no special inability to purr alone, and purring is not mainly a social signal of contentment. No reliable source supported the claim.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river that flows underground for several hours before resurfacing, remains one of the greatest unexplained mysteries in science.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Atlas Obscura, Discover Wildlife) show that the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru has a scientific explanation. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found that rainwater sinks deep underground, gets heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, and comes back up through fault-fed hot springs, making it a non-volcanic hydrothermal system. Some details, like the exact path the water takes, are still being studied. But nothing describes it as a river that runs underground for several hours before resurfacing, and it is not 'one of the greatest unexplained mysteries in science.'

text: The Elephant Seal species can hold its breath underwater for up to 2 hours in some cases, but typically for about 1 minute, although the continuous period of sleep while underwater, or "unihemispheric slow-wave sleep," typically lasts up to 2 hours.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources agree that elephant seals can hold their breath for up to about 2 hours, but their usual dive lasts about 20 minutes, with only 2–3 minutes at the surface in between. That rules out the claim's "about 1 minute." The sleep part is also wrong: research (e.g., Kendall-Bar et al., 2023) found that elephant seals sleep in short naps of up to about 20 minutes during dives, totaling about 2 hours a day. Their deep sleep at sea is not described as unihemispheric, and it doesn't come in continuous 2-hour stretches.

text: The Maasai people of East Africa have a unique tradition of removing their lower eyelid's outer portion, a practice known as "steatite," which is typically done by young men as a rite of passage to signify manhood.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that the Maasai remove part of the lower eyelid, and the claim's details conflict with what is documented. UNESCO describes the Maasai male rites of passage as Enkipaata, Eunoto and Olngesherr, with circumcision as the rite that turns boys into warriors (morans). The Maasai body modifications that sources do record are earlobe piercing and stretching, plus canine tooth removal in early childhood. "Steatite" is not a name for any rite: it is another word for soapstone, a soft rock made mostly of talc (Wikipedia, MFA CAMEO).

text: The Cat's Pyjamaas, a species of moth, has a unique characteristic of having fur-like eye spots on its caterpillars that resemble the eyes of a feline predator, serving as a defense mechanism to deter its natural predators.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence of a moth species called "The Cat's Pyjamas" (or "Cat's Pajamas"). Wiktionary and phrases.org.uk describe "the cat's pyjamas" as a dated idiom meaning something excellent. Other searches turned up only a fabric pattern, a catmint plant variety ('Cat's Pajamas' Nepeta) and real moths with eyespots, such as the eyed hawk-moth. Because the claim names something that doesn't appear to exist as a moth, its description of caterpillar eyespots can't be checked.

text: The McKinley Tunnels in Colorado, USA, hold the record for the most railroad tunnels in the world, with a total of 48 separate tunnels on the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any railroad tunnel group called the "McKinley Tunnels" in Colorado. The nearest real match is the Moffat Road (Denver & Salt Lake, later part of the D&RGW), which a historical source says needed 33 small tunnels along South Boulder Creek. Photo collections number its tunnels up to 48. Even so, the world-record claim is false: India's Kalka–Shimla Railway alone runs through 102 tunnels (107 were originally built), far more than 48.

text: The nucleus of an atom, which consists of protons and neutrons, makes up approximately 99.9% of the atom's total mass, but occupies only about 1/100,000th the volume of the atom.
label: contradicted
reason: The mass part checks out: sources say the nucleus holds about 99.9% (or more) of an atom's mass. The volume part is wrong. Encyclopedia.com says the nucleus's radius is about 1/100,000 of the atom's size. Volume scales with the cube of the radius, so the nucleus takes up only about 1/10^15 of the atom's volume, not 1/100,000. The claim mixes up the radius (or diameter) ratio with the volume ratio.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their tendency to gather in groups.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found uses "basket" as a collective noun for octopuses. Several sources say the generally accepted term is "consortium." They also describe octopuses as mostly solitary animals that are rarely found in groups in the wild, which contradicts the claim's reasoning that they tend to gather in groups. When I searched for "basket of octopuses," the only results were about baskets of octopus for food or octopus-themed products.

text: A group of octopuses is referred to as a "basket" because of their unique shape when they gather together.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources, including a Western Australian government marine site, Grammar Monster and A-Z Animals, say a group of octopuses is commonly called a "consortium." A few other lists give alternatives such as "memory" or "tangle." None of the sources I found uses "basket," and nothing supports the idea that the name comes from the shape octopuses form when they gather. The supposed origin appears to be made up.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apolysis, where they release their body parts in the form of silk threads, only to reattach and rebuild new body parts in a process called ecdysis.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both terms wrong. Apolysis is when the old cuticle separates from the underlying epidermis during molting, and molting fluid helps break down the old cuticle. Ecdysis is the shedding of that old cuticle, after which the new exoskeleton expands and hardens. Caterpillars do not release body parts as silk threads and then reattach them.

text: The einzige weisse deutscher spitz, also known as the white German Spitz, has an unusual characteristic: it can turn predominantly or fully white during the winter season to reflect sunlight and warmer its skin.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that the white German Spitz turns white in winter. Breed sources describe white as a fixed coat colour that the dog has all year. The colour changes they mention happen as a puppy grows into an adult, not with the seasons. The seasonal change they do describe is shedding the thick winter undercoat in warmer months. The claim also undercuts itself: a dog that is already white cannot 'turn white' in winter, and a white coat reflecting sunlight would not warm the skin. Seasonal whitening is a trait of some wild animals, such as the arctic fox, not of this breed. The sources don't directly say 'this dog does not turn white in winter', but what they say about the breed conflicts with the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the northeastern portion of the mountain range on Mars, commonly known as the 'Terra Cimmeria', with elevations reaching up to 15 kilometers above the Martian surface.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and ESA both describe Terra Cimmeria as a large, heavily cratered region of Mars's southern highlands. It is not a mountain range, and nothing calls it the longest mountain range in the solar system. The figure of about 15 km fits Olympus Mons, a volcano, not Terra Cimmeria. Elsewhere, the title of longest mountain range in the solar system is usually given to other features, such as Earth's mid-ocean ridge or the equatorial ridge on Saturn's moon Iapetus.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,389 miles long.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's National Ocean Service names the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth and says it spans 40,389 miles around the globe. That is exactly the figure in the claim. WHOI gives a similar number, nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). One other source estimates a lower length (about 35,000 miles), but the authoritative NOAA source directly matches the claim.

text: The only bird species capable of flying backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and rapid wing movement.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including UC Davis's hummingbird facts page, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to special wing joints that let the wing rotate, strong flight muscles and very fast wingbeats, which matches the claim's 'unique physiology and rapid wing movement.' There are two caveats. Some sources say birds like herons, flycatchers and sunbirds can briefly flutter backwards, though only hummingbirds can sustain controlled backward flight. Also, 'Hummingbird' is a family of many species, not a single species. The core claim is still broadly supported.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique wing structure and rapid wing movement.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including UC Davis's hummingbird facts page, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. WorldAtlas and BirdSpot link this ability to the hummingbird's unusual wing structure, and UC Davis notes its very fast wingbeats (720–5,400 per minute while hovering). One caveat: BirdSpot says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards "for any length of time," which suggests other birds might manage it briefly. Still, no source found contradicts the claim.

text: There are over 259 billion bushels of corn produced globally every year.
label: contradicted
reason: USDA FAS reports global corn production of about 1.2 to 1.3 billion metric tons a year: a 10-year average of 1.18 billion, 1.23 billion in 2024/25 and about 1.33 billion forecast for 2025/26. A metric ton of corn is about 39.37 bushels, so that works out to roughly 46 to 52 billion bushels a year. The claimed 259 billion bushels is about five times too high.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century when undergarments became prevalent.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts the spread of pants and undergarments in the 16th century, but the sources show both are much older. Science News reports that the world's oldest known pants were made in the Yanghai graveyard in the Tarim Basin about 3,200–3,000 years ago. National Geographic notes that ancient Egyptians wore schenti, Greeks the perizoma and Romans their own undergarments, and that 15th-century male underpants were found at Lengberg Castle. The basic idea that buttocks existed before clothing is trivially true, but the timeline in the claim is wrong.

text: The shallow waters of the Great Blue Hole, a large underwater sinkhole in Belize, are so clear due to its low levels of sediment and nutrients from the surrounding environment that divers can reportedly view down to depths of over 400 feet.
label: contradicted
reason: Dive sources describe good visibility at the Great Blue Hole, but nowhere near 400 feet. Dive the World puts it at about 82–100 ft (25–30 m). Thoroughly Travel says about 100–130 ft. Even the most generous source, Ambergris Caye and Belize Treasure Diving, says visibility 'often approaches 200 feet.' The hole itself is only about 406–407 ft (124 m) deep, so seeing 'over 400 feet' would mean seeing past the bottom. Sources also say little light reaches the deeper parts, and a hydrogen sulfide layer sits around 90 m (295 ft). This contradicts the visibility figure in the claim.

text: A group of pandas known as a "beverage" or more commonly an "embarrassment" of pandas can usually consist of 16 pandas in total but sometimes housed units have larger pandas populations.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources (ZME Science, A-Z Animals, Animal Corner) agree that a group of pandas is usually called an "embarrassment." The other names they list are "cupboard" and "bamboo." None of them mention "beverage." The claim that a group usually has 16 pandas is also wrong. Giant pandas are solitary and live alone in their own territories. A-Z Animals says an "embarrassment" just means two or more pandas, with no typical size. A ZME Science source says there may be no true scientific name for a group because pandas live alone.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains a 25-meter-deep sinkhole that drops from a paved road to the bottom of a 50-meter waterfall, making it a unique and breathtaking natural wonder.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing a 25-metre sinkhole at Butlers Gorge that drops from a paved road to the base of a 50-metre waterfall. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Wikidata and the University of Tasmania archive describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. They link it to the Clark Dam, Lake King William and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, and Paddle Tasmania covers a whitewater stretch of the Derwent River there. None of them mentions a sinkhole or a 50-metre waterfall. The only Tasmanian sinkhole waterfall that came up is Vanishing Falls, which is a different place in South West Tasmania. The details look made up, but no source directly says they are false, so the claim cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of an Academy Awards-winning film, earning a combined total of 7 minutes 31 seconds playing at 72 frames per second.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source saying a 2002 short called "Flicker" was accepted into the "canon" of an Academy Award-winning film. I also found no record of it running at 72 frames per second or being the "smallest" such film. The only 2002 short by that name I found is a horror video directed by Conall Pendergast. IMDb lists its runtime as 5 minutes, which contradicts the claim's 7 minutes 31 seconds. The claim looks made up, and the runtime it gives conflicts with the source.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the Moon appears in the opposite direction of its actual location in the sky, can sometimes be seen with the naked eye during lunar eclipses.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source describing a phenomenon called "뒷문" or "Hidden Moon" in which the Moon appears in the opposite direction from where it actually is. In Korean, 뒷문 means "back door," not "Hidden Moon." Searches only turned up unrelated topics: the Moon's far side, transient lunar phenomena, quasi-moons, and selenelions (when the Sun and an eclipsed Moon are visible at the same time because of atmospheric refraction). None of these match the claim. Since nothing confirms or directly addresses this phenomenon, and it may be made up, the claim can't be verified.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that inhabit the Earth, which is estimated to be less than 10% of the total number of species that may exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. It is not a count of known species that makes up less than 10% of some larger total. The study found that only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued, which is under 15% of the 8.7 million estimate, and that 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered. The claim treats a total estimate as a known count and misstates what it is a share of.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apolysis, where they release their body parts in the form of a yellowish liquid called haemolymph to be regrown again into their adult butterfly or moth form.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets apolysis wrong. Apolysis is the first step of insect molting, when the old cuticle separates from the epidermis and molting fluid is secreted. It does not involve releasing body parts as a liquid to be regrown into the adult form. Haemolymph is the insect's circulating blood-like fluid, not dissolved body parts. The breakdown of larval tissue during metamorphosis happens in the pupa (histolysis), not through apolysis.

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of lines drawn at regular and equal intervals across a pull of gunpowder.
label: contradicted
reason: Merriam-Webster gives the first known use of "time stamp" as 1855, which is mid-19th century rather than early 19th century. Its original meaning was a stamping device that records the date and time on a document or envelope. No source describes it as lines drawn at regular intervals across a pull of gunpowder; that definition appears to be made up.

text: There are over 3 trillion trees on Earth, with the Amazon rainforest alone accounting for an estimated 17% of all the trees in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part holds up. Several sources repeat the widely cited estimate of about 3 trillion trees on Earth (Crowther et al., 2015). The 17% figure does not. The Amazon is estimated to hold about 390 billion trees (Field Museum and Amazon Aid). Out of about 3.04 trillion, that works out to roughly 13%. One source puts it at about 14%, using a world total of 2.7 trillion. No source I found says the Amazon has 17% of the world's trees. The 17% figure seems to be mixed up with a different statistic: the Amazon has lost about 17% of its original forest cover (WWF, Arbor Day Foundation).

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Rio del Gado, is a mysterious river that flows through the Peruvian Amazon Rainforest at a steady boil despite being far from any known volcanic activity.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are right: the Boiling River is in the Peruvian Amazon and is far from active volcanoes. But the alternate name is wrong. Wikipedia and IFLScience give its names as Shanay-timpishka, La Bomba, or Río Hirviente/Boiling River. No source calls it "Rio del Gado." A similar name, Rio do Gado (Do Gado River), belongs to a different river in Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil. The claim that it flows "at a steady boil" is also overstated: sources put its water temperature at about 45°C to nearly 100°C, so it is not boiling all along its length.

text: The classification of species according to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature changed from one example per species to the selection of the type specimen for a species, starting in 1842.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up nothing showing that the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN) brought in type-specimen selection in 1842, and the date doesn't fit the record. The 1842 rules were the Strickland Code, written by a British Association committee. The ICZN's own FAQ and other sources describe that code as a forerunner that later grew into the international rules, so the Commission didn't exist yet in 1842. Under the ICZN Code itself, new species names only have to come with an explicitly fixed name-bearing type (such as a holotype) if they were published after 1999 (Article 16.4). A study of reference specimens also says the type concept came in gradually during the 19th century, starting with genera, not through a single change in 1842. Nothing found supports the claimed shift from 'one example per species'.

text: The highest recorded human temperature variation is attributed to Iriena Mather in 1941, who weathered a temperature change of 115 degrees Fahrenheit (65.5°C) in her dedication to a Japanese Appalachian evening guide in Colorado where it reached an extremely high 115 degrees followed by a cool down of about -
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a person named "Iriena Mather" existed or set a temperature record in 1941. Searches turned up no "Japanese Appalachian evening guide" in Colorado and no 115°F human temperature change. Trusted sources on temperature extremes cover changes at weather stations, not people. For example, the U.S. record for a change at one place within 24 hours occurred in Montana in January 1972, which doesn't match the claim. Because the claim cannot be verified and is cut off mid-sentence, the evidence neither supports nor directly contradicts it.

text: But in Morocco, there's a unique festival where participants reenact尸Combat between tribes, but their bodies are covered in bright colors and powders resulting in a spectacular scene to watch.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a Moroccan festival that matches the claim. Morocco does have staged battle traditions: Tbourida, or Fantasia, reenacts a cavalry charge, and the Tan Tan Moussem holds inter-tribal competitions. But no source I found says participants cover their bodies in bright colors and powders. The claim also never names the festival, so there is no clear event to check. The combat part is loosely plausible, while the colored-powder part has no support.

text: A piece of silk production waste called a "lotus silk petal" is made from the cocoons of the Himalayan moon moth, and is typically worth more than its weight in gold due to its rarity.
label: contradicted
reason: Lotus silk is not made from moth cocoons. According to Wikipedia, it is a cellulose fibre pulled from lotus plant stems, a craft that began at Inle Lake in Myanmar, and unlike real silk it is not a protein fibre. That contradicts the claim that a "lotus silk petal" comes from the cocoons of the Himalayan moon moth. I found no source describing any "lotus silk petal" waste product from moon moth cocoons, and nothing supports the claim that it is worth more than its weight in gold. Lotus silk is expensive because it takes so much labour to make, but that is a different product from the one the claim describes.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has the densest fur of any mammal in the world, with up to 1 million hairs per square centimeter.
label: contradicted
reason: The National Park Service and the Marine Mammal Center both say the sea otter, not a water shrew, has the thickest fur of any mammal. They give its density as 850,000 to 1 million hairs per square inch, which is about 155,000 per square centimeter, not 1 million per square centimeter. No reliable source supports a 'comfortless waterhog' or a water shrew as the animal with the densest fur.

text: The nucleus of an atom, which consists of protons and neutrons, makes up approximately 99.9% of the atom's total mass, but occupies only about 1/10,000th of its volume due to the positive charge repulsion between protons.
label: contradicted
reason: The 99.9% mass figure is correct. The rest of the claim is wrong. Encyclopedia.com says the nucleus's radius is about 1/100,000 of the atom's radius, so its volume is about 10^-15 of the atom's volume (10^-12 even using the 1/10,000 diameter figure), not 1/10,000. The reason given is also backwards: the strong nuclear force holds protons and neutrons in that tiny space. Repulsion between the positively charged protons pushes the nucleus apart rather than making it small.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Inferno River,' remains one of the world's greatest unsolved scientific mysteries due to its unexplained boiling water that flows in the midst of the tropical rainforest.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river's heat is unexplained and that it is one of the world's greatest unsolved scientific mysteries. That part is wrong. Wikipedia, citing National Geographic, describes the Shanay-timpishka as an entirely natural, non-volcanic geothermal feature. Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo's studies found that rainwater seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's normal increase in temperature with depth, and rises back up through fault lines. It is unusual because no volcano is nearby, but the cause is understood. I found no reliable source that uses the name 'Inferno River,' and the water reaches near-boiling temperatures (up to about 99–100 °C) rather than actually boiling throughout.

text: Cactus flowers are typically only visible for about 24 hours before they bloom into fruit and subsequently wilt, as they need to focus all of their energy on producing and dispersing seeds.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say cactus flowers usually last much longer than 24 hours. Bloom time ranges from a few hours to several days, and most species keep their flowers for about 5–7 days. Examples include Mammillaria at 7–14 days, Gymnocalycium at 5–10 days and Rebutia at 5–7 days. Only some night-blooming species, such as Epiphyllum oxypetalum, last about a day. The claim's wording is also off: flowers don't 'bloom into fruit'. After pollination, the flower wilts and the fruit develops afterward.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crinan canal and the Knapdale Peninsula where a considered number of European wildcats are found.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any recognised place called the "Vale of Awe" in Scotland. Searches only turn up Loch Awe, the River Awe and the Bridge of Awe. Loch Awe drains north through the Pass of Brander. The Crinan Canal runs from Ardrishaig on Loch Fyne to Crinan in Knapdale/Mid Argyll, so it's unclear what area the claim means or whether the canal belongs to it. Knapdale is best known for the Scottish Beaver Trial. Only one lower-quality travel site mentions the rare Scottish wildcat there, and no reliable source backs the idea of a sizeable wildcat population. Because the main place has no clear referent and the wildcat part can't be confirmed, the claim can't be verified.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees covering about 30% of the planet's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree and star numbers check out. The Crowther et al. global estimate puts Earth at about 3 trillion trees, and NASA estimates 100–400 billion stars in the Milky Way, so there are more trees than stars. The coverage figure is wrong, though. FAO says forests cover about 31% of Earth's land area, not 30% of the planet's surface. Land is only about 29% of Earth's surface, so forests cover roughly 9% of the planet as a whole.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only 15% of the total number of species that are believed to exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2011 Mora et al. study (PLoS Biology) put the estimated total number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million species have been identified, which is less than 15% of that total; an estimated 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undescribed. The claim gets this backwards: it treats 8.7 million as the number of species that exist, then says that figure is only 15% of the true total. In fact, 8.7 million is the estimated total, and the roughly 15% refers to the 1.2 million species already catalogued.

text: Did you know that honey never expires, as it is hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs and retains moisture from the air, which helps preserve it and prevent bacterial growth?
label: supported
reason: Popular sources like ScienceABC and HelloFresh say honey essentially doesn't spoil, and they name its hygroscopic nature, together with low moisture content and low pH, as a main reason microbes can't grow in it. The claim's wording is a bit loose, though. What keeps honey safe is that it has very little water and pulls moisture out of microbes. Taking in water from the air is actually what can make honey ferment and spoil if it isn't sealed. The claim's main point still matches these sources, but they are general-interest sites, not scientific ones.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs down the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources back the main point. NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest, most extensive mountain chain on Earth, at about 65,000 km. Wikipedia gives 65,000 km for the continuous range and 80,000 km for the whole oceanic ridge system, and a peer-reviewed paper gives about 75,000 km, so 'over 65,000 km' is reasonable. NOAA's wording is 'nearly 65,000 km', though, so the 'over' part depends on which measure is used. The ridge does run through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian and Arctic (Gakkel Ridge) Oceans. It also reaches the Pacific (East Pacific Rise), which the claim leaves out, but leaving it out doesn't make anything in the claim wrong.

text: A ball of twine can hold up to 900 kilograms when applied with enough tension, due to its immense mass and tensile strength when properly wrapped and pulled.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that a ball of twine can hold 900 kg. The claim doesn't say which twine it means, how thick it is, what it's made of or how it's wound, and the breaking strength of twine depends heavily on all of these. Its reasoning is also confused: a ball's mass doesn't add to how much load it can bear. The search results were mostly about record-sized twine balls, like the roughly 7,900 kg ball in Darwin, Minnesota. They describe how much the balls weigh, not how much load twine can hold. So the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest known ignition temperature of any element at approximately 4400 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no record of a substance called "Adidamite" anywhere. The closest match was Paradamite, a zinc arsenate mineral that has nothing to do with explosion soot. Because the substance can't be identified, its ignition temperature (~4400 °F) and the claim that it is the highest of any element can't be checked. The claim also doesn't hold together: soot is mostly carbon, not an element of its own. Since the subject has no clear referent and no source backs the figures, the claim is inconclusive.
