text: Roosevelt Island in New York City is home to the famous renegade art installation, the Smallpox Hospital, also known as the Old Smallpox Hospital, which was originally built in the 19th century.
label: contradicted
reason: Some of the claim checks out. The Smallpox Hospital, also called the Renwick Ruin, is on Roosevelt Island, and it was built in the 19th century: construction began in 1854 and it opened in 1856. But it is not a "renegade art installation." Sources describe it as a former hospital for smallpox patients, designed by architect James Renwick Jr. It is now an abandoned Gothic Revival ruin and is called New York City's only landmarked ruin. That makes the main description in the claim wrong.

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of 8,000 Finnish soldiers successfully defended against a massive Soviet attack with around 400,000 soldiers during the Winter War.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a 'Miracle March of 1940' in any source, and the figures in the claim don't match the record. Wikipedia and other histories say Finland fielded about 300,000–340,000 soldiers, not 8,000, against an initial Soviet force of roughly 425,000. The claim also gets the outcome wrong: in February–March 1940 Soviet forces broke through the Mannerheim Line, and Finland signed the Moscow Peace Treaty on 13 March 1940, giving up territory. The 'miracle' accounts describe smaller battles such as Suomussalmi or Kollaa, not 8,000 troops holding off 400,000 in March 1940.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlywed couples participate in a risky boat ride across calm waters by jumping from one boat to another carrying a variety of offerings to the local deity.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the Nairs are a Kerala community, which matches the claim. But it describes Thalikettu (Kettu Kalyanam) as a 'tāli-tying ceremony': a ritual mock marriage held for girls before puberty, in which a groom ties a gold tāli ornament around the bride's neck. It was not a 'boat bridge' ceremony, and there is no risky boat ride with newlyweds jumping between boats carrying offerings to a deity. The claim misdescribes the ceremony.

text: There are approximately 6.2 million languages worldwide, with English being the most widely spoken andeasy to use for many people however when we consider spoken languages there are over more than 7200 spoken languages in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about the number of languages. Ethnologue, the standard catalog of world languages, counts about 7,170 living languages, not about 6.2 million. Other sources also put the total at roughly 7,100. The claim also contradicts itself: it says there are millions of languages but only 7,200 or so spoken ones. Since the main figure is off by several orders of magnitude, the claim is contradicted.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into stone, preserving their bodies for centuries, a phenomenon known as " Fade to Light".
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found strong support for the main idea. Lake Natron in Tanzania is highly alkaline, with a pH of about 9 to 10.5. Smithsonian and Live Science describe it as calcifying or mummifying dead animals into stone-like forms, though not literally turning them to stone, and Nick Brandt photographed these remains. I found nothing calling this phenomenon "Fade to Light." The name doesn't appear in any trustworthy source, and Brandt's photos were published in his book "Across the Ravaged Land." I also found no source saying the bodies are preserved for centuries. Because these parts can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: There is an island in Japan called Okinoshima, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site and home to the tranquil Chikugo-taisha Shrine, a Shinto sacred space with over 1,000 years of history.
label: contradicted
reason: Okinoshima is a real Japanese island and has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since July 2017, as part of the Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region. But the shrine on the island is Okitsu-gū, one of the three shrines that make up Munakata Taisha. It is not called 'Chikugo-taisha Shrine'. The claim names the wrong shrine.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthened" when sounding out its length in syllables however the word 'strengths' makes a very close match.
label: contradicted
reason: "Strengthened" has two syllables (strength-ened), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Wikipedia's list of candidates for the longest one-syllable English words, along with other sources, points to words like "scraunched" and "strengthed" (10 letters). Guinness lists "strengths" as the longest word with only one vowel, not one syllable. The claim's main assertion is wrong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a hot river in the Peruvian Amazon, remains the subject of scientific debate due to its rare properties of forming a flow of boiling water that runs along a riverbed for miles.
label: contradicted
reason: The river exists and is in the Peruvian Amazon, but two parts of the claim don't hold up. First, the water is not actually boiling. Discover Wildlife reports that along the roughly 6.2 km (about 4 mile) hot stretch, the water reaches up to about 94°C, which is near boiling but below it. Second, the heating has a known scientific explanation. Researcher Andrés Ruzo concluded the river is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient: rainwater sinks deep underground, warms up, and comes back to the surface. That is not a volcano, and there is no ongoing scientific debate about it. Wikipedia does call the river unusual because it is not near any active volcano, but that does not mean it is boiling or that scientists are still arguing over the cause. The claim that it 'remains the subject of scientific debate' over 'boiling water' is therefore contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Apocalypse," is a mysterious and seemingly inaccessible river in the Peruvian Amazon where a stream of hot water flows uphill into a natural lake, which was unknown to the local people and was discovered in 2011.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several key facts wrong. Reliable sources say the Shanay-timpishka, or Boiling River, was well known to local people long before 2011. Communities such as Mayantuyacu and Santuario Huishtín treat it as sacred, and local shamans link it to the spirit Yacumama. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo only went there in 2011 after hearing stories about it from locals, so it was not unknown to them. The river is a tributary of the Pachitea River in the Amazon basin. It does not flow uphill into a natural lake; its water is heated by underground geothermal sources. The search results also don't support the nickname "Boiling River of the Apocalypse."

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the ocean called the turquoise jellyfish, also known as the nomadic jellyfish, that is biologically immortal.
label: contradicted
reason: The jellyfish known as biologically immortal is Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." No reliable source calls it the "turquoise jellyfish" or the "nomadic jellyfish." The name "nomad jellyfish" belongs to a different species, Rhopilema nomadica, a large light-blue jellyfish that is not described as immortal. The claim therefore mixes up the names and pins the immortality trait on the wrong species.

text: The	length of a human nose can change by as much as 30% when its tip is depressed and the nostrils flare, due to the elasticity of its skin and underlying cartilage tissue.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for a 30% change in nose length. NIH-hosted studies that measured nasal length during dynamic tip depression (smiling with depressor septi nasi activity) found much smaller changes. One reported an average change of 4.7% ± 5.9% (maximum 9.4 mm). Another found a maximum increase of 12.07% and a maximum decrease of 6.16%. In that second study, the roughly 30% figure (30.37%) was the average decrease in upper lip height, not nose length. So the claim's 'as much as 30%' figure is far above the measured values. Neither study tested manual pressing of the tip, so this contradiction comes from the closest available measurements rather than a direct test.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Inferno River,' remains one of the world's greatest unsolved scientific mysteries due to its unexplained boiling water within the Amazon River.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources say the river's heat is not a mystery. Andrés Ruzo's fieldwork, later confirmed by a 2022 University of Miami study, traced it to deep hydrothermal circulation along geological faults, with no volcano involved. Wikipedia also shows the claim gets the location wrong: the Shanay-timpishka is not in the Amazon River itself. It flows into the Pachitea, then the Ucayali, and only then reaches the Amazon. It also isn't boiling; its average temperature is about 86°C. No search result calls it the 'Inferno River.'

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made of white Carrara marble, but the top 18 meters (59 feet) are actually made of black slate to create a striking visual effect, balancing the light-colored stone below.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't match how sources describe the church. San Miniato al Monte has no 'steeples.' It has one bell tower (campanile), begun by Baccio d'Agnolo around 1523 after the earlier tower collapsed in 1499, and sources including Wikipedia and churchesofflorence.com say it was never finished. An unfinished tower doesn't fit the claim's 18 m (59 ft) black slate top. The polychrome marble that sources mention is on the façade, and none of them describe a slate top or a white Carrara marble tower.

text: Honey is a super-conductor when it's heated above 2.5°C (36.5°F), a property that's unique among all foods and a few other materials.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is not a superconductor at any temperature. It's a supersaturated sugar solution. Its small electrical conductivity comes from dissolved minerals and acids, and that conductivity is used as a quality indicator for honey (botanical origin, ash content). Superconductivity requires zero electrical resistance and is found only in certain metals, alloys and ceramics, usually at cryogenic temperatures far below 0°C. No food becomes a superconductor when heated above 2.5°C. The claim goes against basic physics and the established scientific literature on honey's properties, so I didn't need to run a search.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River,' is a geological phenomenon found deep within the Amazon rainforest in Peru, whose source and drainage system remain a mystery despite extensive scientific investigation.
label: contradicted
reason: The river does exist: Shanay-Timpishka, popularly called the Boiling River of the Amazon, is in Peru's Amazon rainforest. But the claim that its source and drainage remain a mystery is wrong. Wikipedia says it flows into the Pachitea River, then the Ucayali and the Amazon, so its drainage is documented. Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo has studied where the heat comes from, and the leading explanation is the Earth's geothermal gradient, not an unexplained source. I also found no evidence that it is widely called the 'Hidden River.'

text: The famous "Forever Float" in the Great Blue Hole, a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, was estimated to take centuries for a piece of paper to decompose in those conditions due to various factors.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything about a famous "Forever Float" in Belize's Great Blue Hole. I also found no estimate that a piece of paper would take centuries to decompose there. The searches did confirm that the Great Blue Hole is a large underwater sinkhole in Belize. They also showed that its deep water holds a layer of low-oxygen, hydrogen-sulfide-rich water, which could slow decay. Still, no trustworthy source mentions the named "Forever Float" or the paper-decomposition claim, so the main part of the claim can't be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs down the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, about 40,389 miles (roughly 65,000 km) long, and that it snakes across the globe between the continents. That includes the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. Other sources put the length at 'about', 'some' or 'over' 65,000 km. The claim's core points are supported. Two details are imprecise: NOAA Ocean Exploration says 'nearly 65,000 km' rather than 'over', and in the Pacific the ridge (the East Pacific Rise) runs along the eastern side rather than down the center.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth according to a 2020 estimate by the World Register of Marine Species, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and other taxonomic authorities.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues, published in PLoS Biology. It was not a 2020 estimate by the World Register of Marine Species, the IUCN and other authorities. The study also put the total at about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species, which includes fungi and protists as well as plants and animals, so it is not "over 8.7 million plants and animals." The claim gets the date, the source and the scope wrong.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in New York's Letchworth State Park, contains a unique natural limestone cave system that is one of the longest in the Eastern United States.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no record of a place called "Butler's Grotto" in Letchworth State Park, or anywhere else. Descriptions of the park's geology say the Genesee River gorge cuts through layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone. Nothing describes a major limestone cave system there, let alone one of the longest in the Eastern U.S., so the claim looks doubtful. I hit the search limit before I could run a direct search for the name, so I can't prove the site doesn't exist, only that nothing confirms it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a waterfall that appears to boil due to the natural geothermal activity in the Amazon rainforest, has been a topic of research and debate since it was first described in 1900.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on its central point. The Boiling River of the Amazon, Shanay-timpishka in Peru, is a river and not a waterfall. Wikipedia lists it as part of the Pachitea, Ucayali and Amazon river system, and other accounts say it is a hot stretch of river about four miles long. It is a natural, non-volcanic geothermal feature, but the 'waterfall' description is false. I also found nothing to support the claim that it was first described in 1900. Accounts link its modern study to geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's work around 2011–2016, while local legends about it are much older.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengths," but most linguists agree that "stochastic" is longer and the longest one-syllable word.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because "stochastic" has three syllables (sto-chas-tic), so it can't be a one-syllable word, and nothing suggests linguists treat it as one. Guinness lists "strengths" (9 letters) as the longest English word with only one vowel, not specifically the longest with one syllable. Wikipedia says there is no single agreed answer for the longest one-syllable word and lists longer candidates such as "scraunched" (10 letters). So the first part is also off.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the globe.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). The length is described inconsistently: NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, and the claim says "over." The clear error is the claim that the ridge "runs through the center of the globe." The sources say it lies on the seafloor and wraps around the Earth's surface like the seams on a baseball, winding between the continents. It does not pass through the planet's center.

text: A large portion of the world's fresh water, approximately 68.7%, is trapped in the Polar Ice Caps.
label: supported
reason: USGS says about 68.7% of Earth's freshwater is held in ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow. USGS also says this ice is mostly in Greenland and Antarctica, the polar ice sheets. The claim is a little loose because the 68.7% includes all glaciers and permanent snow, not only the polar ice caps. Still, nearly all of that ice is polar, so the figure and the main point of the claim hold up.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's creators attempting to create a medicine to cure morphine addiction.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up: John Pemberton, Coca-Cola's creator, was addicted to morphine and wanted to make a substitute for it. The Pepsi part does not. Caleb Bradham created Pepsi-Cola in 1893 as "Brad's Drink", a digestive aid named after "dyspepsia" and sold as a cure for indigestion, not as a replacement for morphine. That makes the claim that both drinks began as morphine alternatives false.

text: Grapes are scientifically referred to as berries due to their structure, as they develop from a flower's ovary and contain seeds.
label: supported
reason: Botanical sources say grapes count as berries because each grape grows from a single flower's ovary and holds its seeds inside fleshy fruit layers. That matches the claim, and no source contradicts it. The supporting page is hosted on a Colorado State University domain, though its 'Web Monitor' subdomain looks more like a content site than an academic publication.

text: The Andrade effect is the phenomenon where certain materials exhibit an unusual increase in electrical resistance when subjected to high pressure.
label: contradicted
reason: The term "Andrade effect" usually refers to Andrade creep. In 1910, Andrade observed that metal wires held under constant stress slowly stretch over time, with strain growing roughly as t^(1/3). This is about time-dependent mechanical deformation. It is not about electrical resistance rising under high pressure. Several sources (arXiv, ResearchGate) describe the phenomenon this way, so the claim's definition is wrong.

text: The Andrade effect is the phenomenon where certain salts can become spontaneously superconducting at low temperatures when an electric field is applied.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Physics sources use the name Andrade for a materials-deformation effect, not for superconductivity. What they describe is Andrade creep: E.N. da C. Andrade reported in 1910 that soft metals under a constant load keep deforming slowly over time, at a rate that follows a power law in time (strain growing roughly as t^1/3). It is about how metals and other materials flow plastically under stress. My search found no source linking the name to salts turning superconducting at low temperature when an electric field is applied.

text: The country of Singapore has the highest percentage of OPT (Optometrists, Pharmacists, and Physicians) per capita in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no standard "OPT" health-workforce measure that groups optometrists, pharmacists and physicians, and nothing I found ranks Singapore first in the world for these professions. On physicians specifically, Singapore's Ministry of Health reported about 2.4 doctors per 1,000 people in 2018, which it called comparable to Japan, the US and the UK. That is well below the leaders: a WorldAtlas summary of World Bank data puts Sweden first at over 5 per 1,000, and other countries such as Cuba and Monaco also report much higher ratios. Since Singapore's physician density is moderate rather than the world's highest, the claim is contradicted.

text: The famous painting "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh was sold at an auction in 1987 for $53.9 million to the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
label: contradicted
reason: MoMA says it got The Starry Night in 1941 by exchange through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest, so the museum did not buy it at a 1987 auction. The $53.9 million sale in 1987 was a different Van Gogh, "Irises," which went to a private buyer, not MoMA. That detail is well known but comes from my own knowledge; this search didn't check it. The claim mixes up the two paintings.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans approximately 65,000 kilometers across the globe.
label: supported
reason: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and WorldAtlas both describe the Mid-Ocean Ridge as Earth's longest mountain range and give its length as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). No result I found contradicted the claim.

text: The total surface area of the Sun is approximately 5.10 x 10^8 square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The Sun's surface area is about 6.09 × 10^12 km², which is roughly 12,000 times Earth's surface area. The claimed 5.10 × 10^8 km² is Earth's surface area, not the Sun's. You can check this from the Sun's radius of about 696,000 km: 4π × (6.96 × 10^5 km)² ≈ 6.1 × 10^12 km². The Australian Bureau of Meteorology's Space Weather Services page lists a radius of about 700,000 km and a surface area of '6.1 billion billion square kilometres.' That wording overstates the value (it should be about 6.1 million million km²), but it still shows the Sun's surface area is far larger than 5.10 × 10^8 km².

text: Butterfly Pavement Ants are one of the only ant species able to be able to swim and are known to be adept at holding their breath underwater for approximately 100 minutes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no species called the "Butterfly Pavement Ant". Searches for that name only return the ordinary pavement ant (Tetramorium immigrans/caespitum), so the claim has no clear referent. Nothing I found mentions any ant species holding its breath for about 100 minutes. Pest-control sources say that most ant species can swim to some degree, which undercuts the idea that this is one of the only swimming ants. Even so, because the species can't be identified and the 100-minute figure can't be checked, the claim can't be confirmed or firmly ruled out.

text: Cotton balls were first made from cotton by mechanically spinning short fibers into fluffy clusters, but before that, humans used dried and shredded mushroom caps as a substitute for cotton balls in ancient Europe and Asia.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying that people in ancient Europe and Asia used dried, shredded mushroom caps in place of cotton balls. The closest real practice I know of is amadou, a felt-like material made from bracket fungi (not mushroom caps) and used for tinder and to dress wounds, but no search result linked it to cotton balls. The first part of the claim also looks doubtful. Spinning turns cotton into yarn, while cotton balls are made from loose fibers that are cleaned, carded and bleached. Even so, no source directly describes how the first cotton balls were made, and Wikipedia's cotton pad article only gives patchy 20th-century history. Since neither part can be confirmed or clearly disproved, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A giant squishy jellyfish-like creature called the Uluben Leafy Seadragon is one of the most venomous animals on the planet: it has a sting potent enough to kill an adult human in about 20 seconds.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions an "Uluben Leafy Seadragon." The real leafy seadragon (Phycodurus eques) is a small bony fish related to seahorses, not a giant jellyfish-like animal. It has no venomous sting. Wikipedia, the Australian Museum and SeaWorld all describe it as a marine fish, and other sources say plainly that leafy seadragons are not venomous or poisonous. I found nothing to support the claim that it can kill an adult in about 20 seconds.

text: A háng nemrég felfedezett egy háromnaposgoromba gazdag harci medúzát, melyet azóta fokozatosan kedvenc támadóink sorát növelet fazsámították,hogyha számontart
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim can't be checked because it's garbled Hungarian with no clear meaning. Its subject, "A háng", has no identifiable referent, and the rest is nonsensical (it mentions a "three-day rude rich battle jellyfish" and "our favourite attackers"). My search turned up only unrelated jellyfish articles, such as Telex's piece on the immortal Turritopsis dohrnii. Nothing confirms or refutes the claim.

text: The greatest waterfall in the world by volume is actually located underwater, being the Denmark Strait Cataract, which is a submarine waterfall that forms when cold, dense water from the East Greenland Current flows down a slope in the ocean.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Denmark Strait cataract as a submarine waterfall between Greenland and Iceland and call it the world's largest waterfall by volume of flow. According to these sources, it forms when cold, dense water from the Nordic Seas and Greenland Sea sinks beneath warmer Irminger Sea water and flows down a slope in the seafloor. Marine Insight links this cold, dense water to the southward-flowing East Greenland Current. Most sources describe the water as coming from the Nordic or Greenland Seas rather than naming the East Greenland Current, but this broadly fits the claim's description.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Antarctic oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the most extensive and longest mountain chain on Earth, at about 65,000 km (~40,000 miles). Wikipedia gives the same length, and other estimates run as high as about 75,000 km. NOAA's exact wording is "nearly" 65,000 km rather than "over," but other figures support the claimed scale, so the difference is minor. The ridge does run through the Atlantic, Indian and Southern (Antarctic) oceans. It also extends into the Pacific (the East Pacific Rise). The claim leaves the Pacific out but does not say the ridge is limited to the three oceans it names, so this omission doesn't contradict it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious natural wonder, was discovered by scientists in 2007 and is thought to be a rare geological feature that remains unexplained despite numerous studies.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, scientists didn't discover the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in 2007. Local people have long known about it, and geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo first went there in 2011 after hearing about it from his grandfather. Second, it isn't unexplained. Ruzo's research showed the water is heated by geothermal fluids rising through faults, not by a volcano (the nearest is about 700 km away), so it's a non-volcanic geothermal feature. Calling it a rare natural wonder is fair, but the discovery date and the 'unexplained' part are false.

text: There is a type of jellyfish called Turbojellyfish, which is biologically immortal, meaning it can revert to a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Britannica and NOAA describe a biologically immortal jellyfish that can return to its younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation. However, that species is Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly called the 'immortal jellyfish.' None of the search results mention a jellyfish called 'Turbojellyfish.' The biology in the claim is correct, but the name is wrong, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The Lion King, an Animated film, was the highest-grossing film of 1994 with a worldwide box office collection of over 968 million dollars.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia confirms that The Lion King (1994) is an animated film and that it ended its theatrical run as the highest-grossing film of 1994. The over-$968 million figure is its lifetime worldwide total including re-releases, recorded as $968.5 million and now listed as about $979 million. Its gross from the original 1994 run alone was about $763 million. Read as a total gross, the claim is accurate.

text: The short-lived but brightest supernova ever recorded, SN 1006, was visible in the sky for over 8 months in the year 1006 and could be seen during the day for at least 14 months.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim's daytime-visibility figure. NASA's Chandra page says SN 1006 was far brighter than Venus and visible during the daytime "for weeks," not for at least 14 months. Other historical accounts describe roughly three months of visibility in the south, and Yemeni records point to at least two months. The claim also contradicts itself: the star could not have been visible in daylight for 14 months if it was visible in the sky for only about 8 months.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy, are made of white Carrara marble that has naturally weathered to a darker color over time due to exposure to the elements.
label: contradicted
reason: The basilica has one bell tower (campanile), not several steeples. Baccio d'Agnolo started building it in 1523 to replace an earlier tower that collapsed in 1499, and it was never finished. An Italian source describes it as squat, made of brick ("realizzato in mattoni"), and looking quite different from the rest of the church. The white Carrara and green marble is on the basilica's facade. No source says the tower is built of white Carrara marble that has darkened with age, so the claim mixes up the facade with the bell tower.

text: The VOCAB (Vehicle Officers Capturing Drugs and Narcotics) sweeps across police jurisdictions often result in thousands of drug charges being recorded within a matter of months.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that mentions a "VOCAB (Vehicle Officers Capturing Drugs and Narcotics)" program or sweep. Searches for the full name and the acronym only turned up unrelated drug operations, such as Operation Pipeline and several "Clean Sweep" operations. Since there's no evidence the program exists, I can't check the claim that it often produces thousands of drug charges within months.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, changes slightly depending on the angle of sunlight due to the way some of the coral cells contain grains of the pigmentatyrial protein called scleraxanthin.
label: contradicted
reason: No pigment or protein called "scleraxanthin" turned up in any source, and "pigmentatyrial" isn't a real term. Coral research says something different: GFP-like fluorescent proteins in the coral host are "the key color determinants in reef-building corals." Symbiont pigments such as peridinin, diadinoxanthin and chlorophyll also add to coral colour. No source supports the claimed mechanism of colour changing with the sun's angle because of scleraxanthin grains. The claim appears to be made up and conflicts with the established explanation of coral colour.

text: The highest recorded fertility rate in human history was observed in 1796 in Sweden, with an average birth rate of approximately 55 births per 1,000 people per year.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. A peer-reviewed article in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (also on PMC) says the highest recorded fertility of any population in human history belongs to the Hutterites, a North American Anabaptist group, in the early 20th century. It does not credit Sweden in 1796. I couldn't find a sourced figure for Sweden's 1796 birth rate. For context, Sweden's pre-industrial total fertility rate was about 4–4.5 children per woman according to Wikipedia's Demographics of Sweden page, and crude birth rates in that era were generally in the 30s per 1,000, not about 55. That 30s range is general knowledge and wasn't confirmed in these search results.

text: The sensation ofeidet hand in the mouth can elicit a survival response in humans, which is called "conditioned taste aversion."
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and NCBI/PMC sources define conditioned taste aversion as a learned aversion to a taste that has been paired with illness, such as gastric malaise or poisoning. It is a survival mechanism, but it is triggered by that taste–illness pairing, not by the feeling of a hand (or any object) in the mouth. The garbled phrase 'eidet hand' does not refer to anything known, and that sensation is not what conditioned taste aversion means. So the claim mislabels the phenomenon.

text: The classification of species according to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature changed from one example per species to the selection of the type specimen for further identification and naming in 1842.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable sources say the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature was set up in 1895, so it could not have changed any classification rules in 1842. The 1842 rules were the Strickland Code, drafted by Hugh Edwin Strickland for the British Association, not by the ICZN. That code was mainly about priority and making names consistent. It did not set up the type-specimen practice the claim describes. Formal type rules came much later.

text: The shortest warp in the universe, discovered in 2020, is the Crab Nebula’s pulsar PSR J1748-2446ad (also known as the "pulsar of pulses") which makes one rotation every 0.00137 seconds.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several key facts wrong. Discovery papers (Hessels et al., 2006) place PSR J1748-2446ad in the globular cluster Terzan 5, not the Crab Nebula. The Crab pulsar is a different object, PSR B0531+21. Its rotation period is 1.396 ms (716 Hz), not 0.00137 s. It was found with the Green Bank Telescope in 2004 and reported in 2005–2006, so the 2020 date is also wrong. The 'pulsar of pulses' nickname and the 'shortest warp in the universe' label have no supporting source.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar panels powered at the Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii, accommodating about 13% of its power.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the claim because it never says which telescope it means, and Mauna Kea has several observatories. The sources describe two solar installations there. Gemini North added rooftop panels in 2015, which supply about 10–12% of its power. Keck put 332 panels on its roof in 2020, expected to cover 10–15% of its electricity needs. In both cases the panels are on roofs, not in a 'yard full of solar panels,' and no source gives the exact 13% figure. Keck's 10–15% range includes 13%, but the unclear telescope, the different setup and the unconfirmed number leave the claim unverified.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the heaviest known crystal structure due to its manufacturing occurring in meteorites millions of years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a substance called "Adidamite" exists. Searches only turned up minerals with similar names, such as adamite (a zinc arsenate), paradamite and adelite. None of them is a soot from explosions or comes from meteorites. Explosion soot is a real thing: research describes nanodiamonds and graphite forming in detonation soot. However, no trustworthy source connects that to "Adidamite" or to the "heaviest known crystal structure" or to formation in meteorites. The claim may be mixing up detonation nanodiamonds with lonsdaleite, a meteorite-associated form of carbon. Because the named entity has no clear referent and none of the specific details can be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The 길 Cheese is a type of Korean cheese made from a mixture of cow, goat, and sheep's milk, and is often served as a side dish or used in various traditional Korean recipes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a Korean cheese called "길 Cheese." "길" means "road" in Korean, and the name looks made up or unclear. Reliable sources say Korea had no traditional cheese. Milk was historically little used, and the first domestic cheese came from Imsil in the 1960s. It was made first from goat's milk and later from cow's milk. That makes the claim's link to traditional recipes doubtful, but nothing confirms or directly disproves the specific cheese, its mix of cow, goat and sheep's milk, or how it is served. With no clear entity to check, the claim cannot be verified.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the Moon seems to change its phase by 12 hours behind its actual phase, can be observed from Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a lunar phenomenon called "뒷문" or "Hidden Moon" exists. In Korean, 뒷문 means "back door" or "back gate," not "Hidden Moon," so the name in the claim is a mistranslation. The claim's description also conflicts with how lunar phases work. A phase comes from the Sun–Earth–Moon geometry, and the same phase is seen everywhere on Earth at the same moment. Nothing makes the Moon appear 12 hours behind its actual phase. Sites that discuss a "hidden phase" are describing the period around the new moon when the Moon can't be seen, which is a different thing. Overall, the claim appears to be made up.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be about 8.7% of all possible species that could exist, given the planet's variety of environments and conditions.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011). It is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million, and includes fungi and protists, not only plants and animals. The claim treats 8.7 million as a minimum count and adds that this is only 8.7% of all possible species. The study says nothing like that. Its actual finding is that about 86% of these estimated species have not yet been described. Reliable sources (University of Hawaii, National Geographic, EurekAlert) present 8.7 million as the estimated total of existing species, not as a share of some larger number of possible species.

text: The largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is more than 1,300 times the size of the Earth and has a mass that is approximately 2.5 times that of all the other planets combined.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found back up both parts of the claim. Jupiter is the largest planet, and its volume is about 1,321 times Earth's, which is more than 1,300. Universe Today and the Wikipedia data both say this. Universe Today also says Jupiter has about 2.5 times the mass of all the other planets combined. One caveat: "size" in the claim only works if it means volume. By diameter, Jupiter is only about 11 times wider than Earth. Volume is the usual meaning in comparisons like this, so the claim holds.

text: The lengths of the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt vary from 481 feet for the smallest, 481.63 feet for the middle one, and a length of 455.65 feet and a height of 481 feet were scratched off and the tallest great pyramid measures exactly 481 feet or an extremely accurate
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled, but its main measurements are wrong. 481 feet is the original height of the largest pyramid, Khufu's Great Pyramid (146.6 m). Its base is about 756 feet (230.3 m) per side, and it now stands about 454–455 feet tall. 481 feet is not the length of the smallest pyramid: Menkaure's is only about 213 feet tall, with a base of about 102–105 m (roughly 335–345 ft). Khafre's is about 471 feet tall, with a base of about 706 feet. The figures given for the pyramids' lengths are therefore incorrect.

text: The word " timestamp" dates back to the early 19th century and originally referred to a mark or sign consisting of lines drawn at regular and equal intervals across a pull of gunpowder to determine its accuracy.
label: contradicted
reason: Merriam-Webster and the OED both date the first known use of "time stamp" to 1855. That is the mid-19th century, not the early 19th century. Neither source mentions anything about lines drawn across gunpowder. Merriam-Webster's original meaning is a stamping device that records the date and time on a document or envelope, and Wikipedia says the term comes from office rubber stamps used to mark when a document was received. Both the dating and the claimed original meaning are wrong.

text: The world's largest planetarium, the Melville-Nathan Planetarium, is located in Glendale, California, and is capable of accommodating over 1,000 people at a time.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no evidence that a 'Melville-Nathan Planetarium' exists. The only planetarium that turned up in Glendale, California is the small digital dome theater at Glendale Community College. According to Guinness World Records, the world's largest planetarium is at the Nagoya City Science Museum in Japan, which has a 35 m dome. A Glendale planetarium is not the world's largest.

text: Butler's Panama, a part of Panama in the late 19th century, had around 80% of its population infected with hookworm at the end of the 19th century.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. Searches for "Butler's Panama" found no historical region, territory or period by that name, only unrelated businesses and people. Without a clear referent, the 80% figure can't be checked. I also found no reliable source giving a hookworm infection rate of about 80% for Panama, or any part of it, in the late 19th century. The results were mostly about modern hookworm studies in Panama and figures for other countries.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high pH levels that it can turn animals that die in it into stone statues due to its ability to preserve their bodies through alkaptonization.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Natron in Tanzania is real, and its pH can reach about 10.5. However, the claim gets the process wrong. Live Science says the animals do not actually turn to stone. Sodium carbonate deposits, the same compound once used in Egyptian mummification, preserve and calcify the dead animals so they look stone-like when they dry. Fact-checks (The Star, DismissLab) also say they are not truly petrified. 'Alkaptonization' is not a term used for this process; the closest real term, 'alkaptonuria', names a human metabolic disease. The stated mechanism and the literal 'stone statues' claim are therefore contradicted.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1999, is a 4.2-meter-long Redwood tree trunk in Western Australia, which may be over 2,000 years old, making it a significant example of a living fossil.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No reliable source mentions a 'Janszoon boom log'. Searches for the name, the 1999 discovery, a 4.2 m redwood trunk in Western Australia and a 2,000+ year age only returned unrelated pages, such as ones about the explorer Willem Janszoon, the 1999 Duyfken replica and log booms in general. The claim also has problems on its face. Redwoods are not native to Australia, and a dead tree trunk would not normally be called a 'living fossil'. With no evidence for or against the specific claim, it can't be verified.

text: The McKinley Tunnels in Colorado, USA, hold the record for the most railroad tunnels in the world, with a total of 48 separate tunnels.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any railroad tunnel group called the "McKinley Tunnels" in Colorado. Searches for that name only turned up unrelated places: the Fort McKinley tunnels in the Philippines, the McKinley Mine, and several towns and roads named McKinley. Reliable sources on Colorado rail tunnels cover others, such as the Moffat Tunnel and its line, the Alpine Tunnel and the Hagerman Tunnel, but none mention a McKinley tunnel set, a count of 48 tunnels, or a world record. The "48 tunnels, world record" part also looks doubtful, since lines elsewhere, such as India's Kalka–Shimla Railway, are generally said to have about 100 tunnels. Because the claim's main subject can't be found and nothing confirms it, it can't be verified.

text: There are over 100 million trees in New York City's Metropolis, and in Tokyo, they have many trees as well, however the greatest number can be found in those that densely cultivate in Jinan the city that has in China more than 860 million trees around this metropolis.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says New York City has more than 100 million trees. A USDA Forest Service study of NYC's urban forest estimates about 7 million trees, and Wikipedia gives roughly 5.2 million as of 2020. No source supports a figure anywhere near 100 million. This contradiction is enough to make the claim false. The figure of more than 860 million trees in Jinan was not checked or confirmed.

text: Atrafenate, a compound found in some types of mushrooms, has been shown to have potential as an anticancer agent due to its ability to selectively target and induce autophagy in cancer cells.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a compound called "atrafenate" in any reliable source. Searches for the name only turned up similar-sounding but unrelated substances: atrasentan (a drug), antrafenine (a drug), arhalofenate (a drug) and Atrafen (a diet pill). There is real research showing that some mushroom compounds, such as astrakurkurol, cordycepin and Latcripin 1, trigger autophagy in cancer cells. None of it mentions atrafenate. Because the compound itself can't be identified, the claims that it occurs in mushrooms and acts as an anticancer agent by selectively inducing autophagy can't be checked.

text: Dolphins have been observed showing signs of empathy and compassion by helping other animals, including humans, in distress and even sometimes working together to rescue each other from nets or other entanglements.
label: supported
reason: The sources back most of the claim. A peer-reviewed field study, written up on Atlas of Science, recorded several wild bottlenose dolphins working together to hold up a distressed companion. A Baleines en Direct review treats rescue and caregiving behavior as expressions of empathy. It also cites Pacific white-sided dolphins helping a newborn porpoise, a case of helping another species. Ocean Conservation and ScienceABC give credible accounts of dolphins protecting people, such as circling a hypothermic swimmer until researchers arrived and guarding swimmers from sharks. National Geographic describes a group of male dolphins helping a mother and calf escape. The weakest part is nets: no source I found clearly shows dolphins working together to free each other from nets or entanglements. I couldn't run a final search on this point. Because the claim says 'nets or other entanglements' and the rescue reports are consistent with it, I judged it supported, but that detail is not directly confirmed.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species palearctic short-faced elephant (Mammuthus galileus, Elephas falconeri, and Mammuthus Cretacicous skeleton fossils remain intact.
label: contradicted
reason: The only real animal called the "short-eared elephant" is the short-eared (round-eared) elephant shrew, Macroscelides proboscideus. It is not extinct. Wikipedia lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The rest of the claim is also inaccurate. Elephas (Palaeoloxodon) falconeri is a real extinct dwarf elephant from Sicily and Malta, but it is not a "short-faced elephant," and it lived in the Middle Pleistocene, not the Cretaceous. "Mammuthus galileus" and "Mammuthus Cretacicous" do not appear to be recognized species, and mammoths did not exist in the Cretaceous.

text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Nile River in Uganda, is home to the mighty Murchison Falls, which is the world's most powerful waterfall measured by volume of water.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality and hydroelectric site in Tasmania's Central Highlands, on the River Derwent scheme in Australia. It is not part of the Nile in Uganda. Murchison Falls is on the Victoria Nile, where the river squeezes through a narrow gorge, but that gorge is not called Butler's Gorge. Murchison Falls is also usually described as one of the most powerful waterfalls, not the world's most powerful by volume of water. Much larger falls, such as Inga or Boyoma in Congo, carry far more water. A few promotional sites do call Murchison 'the most powerful waterfall in the world', but more reliable sources describe it as 'one of' the most powerful. The location claim is clearly wrong either way.

text: The Booming Bays of Br>New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf are a unique natural phenomenon where thousands of murres (a type of seabird) take off from the water in unison, creating massive booms or thunder-like sounds.
label: contradicted
reason: Murres are auks that live only in the Northern Hemisphere. The common murre is found in low-Arctic and boreal waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific. They do not occur in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf, so thousands of murres could not be taking off there. I also found no trustworthy source describing a phenomenon called the 'Booming Bays' in the Hauraki Gulf.

text: Lemedem, a chemical compound, is primarily responsible for the bacteria that cause the common cold to be the only phagerowable (the only kind of the bacteria can be infected so that ceases to exist) of Cold causing organism.
label: contradicted
reason:
Searches turn up no evidence that any chemical compound called "Lemedem" exists, nor any concept of being "phagerowable." More importantly, the claim's core premise
i.e., that the common cold is caused by bacteria
is directly contradicted by medical sources, which state that the common cold is initiated by viral infections (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, coxsackieviruses, RSV, echoviruses, etc.), not bacteria. Since the cold is not a bacterial disease, there can be no compound responsible for making 'the bacteria that cause the common cold' uniquely susceptible to being eliminated.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and surrounds the globe.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including NOAA Ocean Service, NOAA Ocean Explorer, WHOI and Wikipedia, agree that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. They describe it as about 65,000 km (40,389–40,390 miles) long and say it wraps around the globe like the seam of a baseball. One wording difference: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km,' while the claim says 'over.' Other sources give about 65,000 km or more, so this is a rounding difference and not a real contradiction.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescence to light up their habitats, but they do this by having a symbiotic relationship with themselves where some females only emit light to entice mates, while others react with a defensive flash when threatened.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say glowworm light is used to signal, not to light up their habitats. Females glow to attract males, and the glow may also warn predators that the insects taste bad. That warning is part of the general glow, including in males and larvae, and is not described as a separate 'defensive flash' given by a different group of females. The light comes from the insect's own chemistry (luciferin and luciferase), not from any 'symbiotic relationship,' and an organism can't have one with itself anyway. So the mate-attraction part is right, but the claim's explanation of how and why glowworms glow is wrong.

text: The darkest time of the day, usually around 2-3 am, is called "twilight" but actually it's called the "nee hour" or the "dead of night", but the earliest and the darkest time in the 24-hour cycle of time is also known as the 'eternal darkness'; more
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up several terms. Twilight is the period around dawn or dusk when the Sun is below the horizon but still lights the sky. It is not the darkest time of night. Folklore names for the 2–4 am stretch are the "witching hour" or "devil's hour", sometimes linked to the "dead of night". I found no recognized term called the "nee hour" or "eternal darkness" for the darkest time of the 24-hour cycle. Some of these points rest on the absence of evidence, but the core claim about twilight is plainly wrong.

text: The hakkebushi mushroom, found in Japan, has a unique property that allows it to glow in the dark after being exposed to sunlight during the day.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source showing that a mushroom called "hakkebushi" exists, in Japan or anywhere else. Searches for the name returned only unrelated Japanese terms. Because the claim's subject can't be identified, its properties can't be checked. Japan does have glow-in-the-dark mushrooms (Japan Times, 2008), but their light comes from a chemical reaction involving the enzyme luciferase and oxygen. They don't need to absorb sunlight first. That casts doubt on the claim's "exposed to sunlight" mechanism, but the claim still can't be tested without an identifiable mushroom.

text: The Blind Faith double album "Appearance and Other Attractions" sold very well however their 1970 single "Can't Get Out" didn't encourage major labels agreeing to sign the act.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says Blind Faith (Clapton, Winwood, Baker, Grech) made only one studio album, the self-titled single LP 'Blind Faith' from 1969. The band was already signed to Polydor and Atco, so it was not looking for a major label. My searches found no Blind Faith double album called 'Appearance and Other Attractions' and no 1970 single 'Can't Get Out'. The closest results were real tracks like 'Can't Find My Way Home'. Both titles in the claim look made up, and they conflict with the documented discography.

text: The Boomerang effect, which was initially observed in physics and refers to the return of an object to its point of origin after being projected, also holds true for the long-term effects of international trade sanctions, which can sometimes paradoxically strengthen the targeted country's economy.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the boomerang effect was "initially observed in physics," but that's wrong. Hovland, Janis and Kelley first recorded and named it in social psychology in 1953, where it means a persuasion attempt backfiring so the audience adopts the opposite position. So the stated origin of the term is false. The claim's point about sanctions sometimes backfiring or strengthening a targeted economy wasn't checked. It doesn't change the verdict, because the origin claim alone is enough to contradict the statement.

text: The Katherine Wheel, a large, medieval defensive stone catapult, was used in the Middle Ages, specifically during the 13th century, and is considered one of the earliest known types of siege engines.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe the Catherine (Katherine) Wheel as the breaking wheel, a device used for torture and public execution. It also names a firework and a decorative motif. None of these sources describe it as a defensive stone catapult or a siege engine. Searches for a 'Katherine Wheel' catapult turned up only general pages on catapults and trebuchets. The claim gets the basic identity of the object wrong, and the siege-engine details have nothing to support them.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest known ignition temperature of any element at approximately 4,562 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no source mentioning "Adidamite" at all, so there is no evidence about it either way. The name has no clear referent and may be made up. The claim also doesn't hold together: soot is a form of carbon, not a separate element, so a "type of soot" can't be the element with the highest ignition temperature. The 4,562°F figure doesn't match any element data I'm aware of. I couldn't find a reliable source to confirm or refute the claim directly. The only result returned was an unrelated article about lowering the ignition temperature of diesel soot.

text: Plants are capable of producing up to 20% of their daily growth through a process known as twigs photoperiodism, in which the duration of daylight drives the increase in stem elongation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for a process called "twigs photoperiodism" or for the figure of up to 20% of daily growth. The term appears only by coincidence, in studies that used cut twigs to test photoperiod effects on budburst. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, ScienceDirect and Encyclopedia.com, describe photoperiodism as a plant's response to day length. Encyclopedia.com notes it can influence stem length, but that matches only the general idea. None of the sources mention the specific term or the 20% figure, and none clearly contradicts them either, so the claim can't be verified.

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, often extend beyond the support line, act as monumental gateways, or become free-standing structures, like the famous Gateway of India in Mumbai.
label: contradicted
reason: The Gateway of India is a free-standing triumphal or memorial arch made of basalt and concrete, completed in 1924. It is not a buttress or a structure built to support another building. Reliable sources describe buttresses as elements that reinforce walls, including flying buttresses that carry sideways forces from a wall to a separate pier. None of them describe buttresses as monumental gateways. So the claim's example is wrong, and so is its suggestion that buttresses commonly act as gateways.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil in the middle of the dense Amazon rainforest, is still not fully understood and its origins remain a subject of ongoing research.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon is still being studied, and none say its origin is settled. Wikipedia calls a geothermal-gradient explanation the 'predominant theory', which suggests the question is not fully closed. Atlas Obscura says Ruzo and his colleagues 'believe' a fault-led hydrothermal system heats the river. Forbes calls the river a 'geological anomaly' and says the heat 'likely' reaches the surface through fault-fed hot springs. IFLScience notes that its scale and temperatures are unmatched by any other non-volcanic geothermal system. Research is ongoing through the Boiling River Project and Feeley's lab (Earth.com, Frontiers for Young Minds). One caveat: the main mechanism (fault-fed, non-volcanic geothermal heating) is broadly accepted, so 'mysterious' overstates things a little. Still, the claim that the river is not fully understood and remains under active research is consistent with the sources.

text: The Tongue of the Giant Leveret, a type of turtle, can live up to 252 years in the wild, making it one of the longest living animals on Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no turtle species, or any animal, called the "Tongue of the Giant Leveret." A leveret is a young hare, so the name doesn't fit a turtle anyway. Searches only brought up "Giant Turtle Tongue," a World of Warcraft crafting item, and general sources on giant tortoises. Those sources say some Aldabra giant tortoises may live past 200 years, though that's hard to verify, and Jonathan, the oldest known land animal, is estimated at about 192 years. Since the animal in the claim doesn't clearly exist, the 252-year lifespan can't be checked, and no source supports it.

text: A.shortcuts, in some specific contexts, such as flight or horse riding, the term "Ground Control" can also refer to an Aerodrome Control Tower (ATC) directly managing aircraft or help manage and input instructions for handling specific aircraft, so the term is perekhana to both the cab and the ground control
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled and can't be checked as a whole. It includes stray text ("A.shortcuts"), an undefined word ("perekhana") and an unsupported reference to "horse riding." Reliable sources describe Ground Control as an ATC position, usually in the aerodrome tower, that handles aircraft movement on taxiways and aprons but not on the runway. Takeoffs and landings are handled by Tower (aerodrome) control. That partly fits the claim's idea that Ground Control is linked to the tower cab, but it conflicts with the claim that the term means the Aerodrome Control Tower itself. No source supports the horse-riding usage or the claim's final conclusion.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world's longest saltwater waterfall, despite it being non-visible in certain conditions due to the tidal nature of the falls.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia describes Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, about 667 m above sea level. The River Derwent flows from there, and the Lake King William (Clark) Dam is in the area. Because it is a high inland freshwater area, it cannot have a tidal saltwater waterfall. None of the search results link Butlers Gorge to a saltwater or tidal waterfall, much less the world's longest one.

text: Cocateo, a type of Almond tree that also grows bitter, fragrant fruit,  is a popular fruit in Culao people diet in the Valencia area of Spain.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched for "Cocateo" as an almond variety and for a "Culao" people in Valencia and found nothing on either. The results only cover ordinary Valencia almonds, Valencian people in general, and unrelated words like "coca" (a Catalan pastry). Since no source shows that either name exists, the claim can't be checked, but nothing directly disproves it either.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "River of Lost Souls," is a mysterious river in Peru where water is constantly boiling, but the surrounding area is peaceful, calm, and contains an abundance of aquatic life.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru is real, but sources say its water gets close to 100°C. They also say it has no fish or other typical river life, and that animals that fall in die almost instantly. That contradicts the claim that it holds plenty of aquatic life. It is also not literally boiling all the time, and the nickname "River of Lost Souls" isn't backed up by any source.

text: There is an estimated 1.5 trillion now-dead trees on Earth, which is roughly 11 times more than the total number of living trees, emphasizing the vast and varied history of trees on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. A 2015 Nature study puts the number of living trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. So 1.5 trillion dead trees would be about half the number of living trees, not 11 times more. The study does say tree numbers have fallen by about 46% since agriculture began, which means about 2.6–2.8 trillion trees have been lost. That is still far less than 11 times the living count and doesn't match the 1.5 trillion figure either.

text: The short-lived Mayan Period known as the Classical period started around 200 AD and lasted for almost five hundred years until 1700 AD after they were brewed with beer.
label: contradicted
reason: Historians date the Maya Classic period to about AD 250–900, not 200–1700 AD. The source divides Maya history into Pre-Classic (2000 BC–AD 250), Classic (AD 250–900) and Post-Classic (900–1519). The claim also contradicts itself: 200 AD to 1700 AD is about 1,500 years, not "almost five hundred." Calling a period of more than 600 years "short-lived" is wrong too, and the part about the Maya being "brewed with beer" is nonsensical and has no basis.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique reproductive life cycle, where it grows and hatches from its larval form inside the belly of its host, typically a small crustacean called a sea snail.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge in the phylum Porifera, not a jellyfish. It does not grow inside a host. Instead, small shrimp live inside the sponge's lattice and often grow too large to get out. A sea snail is also a mollusk, not a crustacean. The claim gets the animal's type, its relationship to its host, and the host's classification wrong.

text: The bear species that hibernates the longest is the Panda, which can hibernate for up to 5 months in the winter due to a low rate of metabolism.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say giant pandas do not hibernate at all. National Geographic Education says that, unlike many bears, pandas do not hibernate and instead move to warmer areas in the cold season. The Chengdu panda base's knowledge database (panda.org.cn) says giant pandas "never hibernate." So pandas cannot be the bear that hibernates the longest or hibernate for up to 5 months. Bears known for long hibernation are species such as American black bears and grizzly bears.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible from space.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm the first part of the claim. NOAA, WHOI and Wikipedia all name the mid-ocean ridge as Earth's longest mountain range, at roughly 65,000 km. The length wording is less clear. NOAA says the ridge stretches "nearly" 65,000 km, while other sources estimate the whole ridge system at about 80,000 km, so "over 65,000 km" fits some sources but not others. The "not visible from space" part can't be confirmed and is partly undercut. More than 90% of the ridge is underwater, but some of it, such as Iceland, is above sea level. NOAA and the Smithsonian also show the ridge in maps made from satellite data. Because the evidence on this part is mixed and unclear, the claim as a whole can't be clearly supported or contradicted.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which is now referred to as genus Diceros due to Stegolophodon being mis classified  its original name was a different genus.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up unrelated animals and gets them wrong. The 'short-eared elephant shrew' (Macroscelides proboscideus, the round-eared sengi) is not extinct; the IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Stegolophodon is still a valid genus. It is an extinct proboscidean in the family Stegodontidae, and its type species was first named Mastodon latidens. It has not been moved into Diceros, which is the genus of the black rhinoceros and not a proboscidean.

text: The world's largest planetarium, the Melville-Nathan Planetarium, is located in Glendale, California, and is capable of accommodating over 1,000 people.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any planetarium called the 'Melville-Nathan Planetarium.' The only planetarium that turns up in Glendale, CA is the small digital one at Glendale Community College. Guinness World Records and the museum's own site say the world's largest planetarium is at the Nagoya City Science Museum in Japan. Its dome is 35 m across and it seats about 350 people, not over 1,000. The claim is wrong about the name, the location and the capacity.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments such as deep-sea vents, where temperatures can reach as high as 221 degrees Fahrenheit, due to their adaptable physiology.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is true: microbes do live around deep-sea hydrothermal vents. Kenyon's MicrobeWiki says thermophilic microorganisms can live at up to about 115°C (239°F). The claimed vent temperature is wrong, though. The claim says vent temperatures can reach 'as high as 221°F' (about 105°C), but NOAA, WHOI and EBSCO all report that vent fluids reach about 400°C (750°F), or over 700°F. That means 221°F greatly understates how hot vents get. If the claim was meant to give the highest temperature microbes can survive, 221°F would also be too low. Because the claim gives the wrong maximum temperature, it is contradicted.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built parts for various iconic aircraft including the famous Supermarine Spitfire and both versions of the Bristol Beaufighter.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing on a British aerospace engineering company called "Arotech Limited". The only Arotech that came up is Arotech Corporation, an American defense and security company (with operations in Alabama and Lod, Israel). It makes vehicle armor, training simulators and batteries, and has no link to wartime British aircraft. No trustworthy source said that any "Arotech Limited" built parts for the Supermarine Spitfire or the Bristol Beaufighter. A similarly named firm, Aero Research Limited, a British adhesives maker, showed up, but nothing I found tied it to these claims. The company in the claim can't be clearly identified and its details can't be checked, so the claim is inconclusive. Arotech Corporation doesn't match it, but that alone doesn't prove the claim false.

text: The extremely rare meteorite known as the "A ValueEventListener" was found in Algeria in 2010, which is the oldest known extraterrestrial material discovered, dating back approximately 4.56 billion years.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no meteorite called "A ValueEventListener." That name belongs to a Firebase Android software interface used to listen for database changes. The real Algerian meteorite matching the rest of the description is Erg Chech 002, an achondrite about 4.565 billion years old. According to Wikipedia and several news reports, it was found in May 2020, not 2010. It is also described as the oldest achondrite or volcanic meteorite, not the oldest extraterrestrial material ever found. The name and the 2010 date are therefore wrong.

text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Nile River in Uganda, is home to the mighty Murchison Falls, which is the world's most powerful waterfall in terms of volume.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, Australia, on the River Derwent, home to the Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station. It is not a stretch of the Nile in Uganda. Murchison Falls is on the Victoria Nile, where the river forces its way through a gorge about 7 m wide. Some sources call it the 'most powerful' waterfall because of how hard the water is squeezed, but it is not the world's largest by volume. Falls such as Inga and Iguazu carry far more water.

text: Honey, when rendered under heat, can act as an adhesive and has been used historically to attach beads and even bones in jewelry due to its great bonding capabilities.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source showing that heated honey was historically used to attach beads or bones in jewelry. The searches only turned up loosely related uses of honey. One heritage-conservation source says honey was added to fish glue to make it more flexible in Russian icon restoration, so it was an additive rather than the glue itself. A patent describes heating honey to make an adhesive, but it is a modern invention. The documented ancient jewelry and hafting adhesives are beeswax, pine resin and birch tar, not honey. The claim's specific historical statement and its point about honey's bonding strength can't be verified, though no source directly contradicts them either.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 86 billion neurons and over 100 billion stars in the Milky Way.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures are right, but the comparison is backwards. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, and the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars (Nature Scitable puts it at 200 to 400 billion). That means the galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons. Psychology Today says this directly: the Milky Way has more stars than the brain has neurons. The claim's own numbers (86 billion is less than over 100 billion) also contradict its statement that neurons outnumber stars.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is home to several geysers, making it one of the few places on Earth where you can find geothermal activity in the middle of a desert environment.
label: supported
reason: Several travel sources say the Atacama Desert in northern Chile contains the El Tatio geyser field. It is described as the highest geyser field in the world and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere, with dozens of geysers and fumaroles. The sources also call the Atacama the driest place on Earth. One caveat: strictly speaking, it is the driest non-polar desert, because parts of Antarctica are drier. Even so, the claim's main points hold up: the Atacama is a hyper-arid desert, and it has several geysers that are rare examples of geothermal activity in a desert setting.

text: The finish on the Lincoln Memorial in Washington D.C. was actually created using a technique called "fox and subs" where a woman named Kelsie Benson applied the finish by hand.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim. My searches turned up nothing about a finishing technique called "fox and subs" or anyone named Kelsie Benson working on the Lincoln Memorial. Reliable sources say Henry Bacon designed the memorial, Daniel Chester French designed the statue, and the Piccirilli Brothers carved it from Georgia marble. None of them mention this technique or person. No source directly says otherwise, so the claim can't be shown false, but it can't be verified either. It looks made up.

text: The extremely rare meteorite known as the "A ValueEventListener" was found in Algeria in 2010, which is the oldest known extraterrestrial material discovered to date.
label: contradicted
reason: No meteorite called "A ValueEventListener" shows up anywhere. That phrase is a software term (a Firebase class name), not a meteorite name. The best-known record-setting meteorite from Algeria is Erg Chech 002, but it was found in May 2020, not 2010. Its record is also narrower: it is the oldest known igneous (volcanic) rock, not the oldest extraterrestrial material. The oldest material ever found on Earth is presolar silicon carbide grains inside the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969. Some of those grains are up to about 7 billion years old. So the name, the year and the 'oldest material' part of the claim are all wrong.

text: The length of a labyrinth, which is often confused with a maze, can vary, but a traditional Greek labyrinth is typically around 600 to 800 feet in circumference.
label: contradicted
reason: No source backs the claim that a traditional Greek labyrinth is typically 600–800 feet around. Examples of the classical seven-circuit ("Greek") design are much smaller. The Druid's Garden describes building one about 36 ft across, and a church installation (fccmorehead.org) is about 40 ft in diameter. The Labyrinth Society's building guide works from 36–88 ft diameters. That puts the circumference at roughly 110–280 ft, well below 600–800 ft. Even the large medieval Chartres labyrinth is only about 42 ft across, which is roughly 133 ft around. The figure of about 860 ft found in sources is the length of the winding path at Chartres, not a circumference. The claim's numbers therefore don't match typical sizes. One caveat: no source sets an official standard size for a 'traditional Greek labyrinth', so this verdict rests on representative examples rather than a defined norm.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made from white Carrara marble that is stained yellow by the environmental conditions and moss, giving them a unique golden appearance over time.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe San Miniato al Monte as having a single campanile, not multiple steeples. Baccio d'Agnolo built it in 1523 to replace an earlier tower that collapsed in 1499, and it was never finished. Ancient-history-sites.com calls it a massive, unplastered stone tower. It is not described as white Carrara marble turned golden by moss. White Carrara marble, set against green serpentine/Prato marble, appears on the church's façade, not the bell tower. No source mentions marble stained yellow by the environment or moss.

text: The world's longest mountain range, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) long, stretching across every ocean and covering nearly 23% of the Earth's surface.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the claim. NOAA Ocean Explorer calls the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth and puts its length at nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), which is over 40,000 miles. WHOI also gives about 40,000 miles (65,000 km) and says the ridge circles the globe. A Roger Williams University oceanography textbook (Pressbooks) and other sources state that it covers about 23% of Earth's surface. The claim's 64,000 km figure is a little lower than the cited 65,000 km, but this rounding gap is minor. 'Stretching across every ocean' fits these sources' description of a near-continuous system winding through the world's ocean basins, though none of the results states it word for word.

text: If we were to place all the stars in the observable universe shoulder to shoulder, they would stretch over 250 billion light-years in length, approximately 4.25 billion times larger than the size of our own Milky Way galaxy.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim don't hold up. NASA puts the Milky Way at about 100,000 light-years across, and 250 billion ÷ 100,000 is about 2.5 million, not 4.25 billion. Read the other way, 250 billion ÷ 4.25 billion would make the Milky Way only about 59 light-years wide, which is clearly wrong. The total length is also off by orders of magnitude. Space.com cites about 2 trillion galaxies with roughly 100 million stars each, which comes to about 2×10^20 stars at minimum, and common estimates run as high as 10^22–10^24. Even at 2×10^20 stars of the Sun's diameter (about 1.39 million km), a side-by-side line would be about 2.8×10^26 km, or roughly 3×10^13 light-years. That is tens of trillions of light-years, far more than 250 billion. So both numbers in the claim are contradicted.
