text: The short-lived Mayan Period known as the Classical period started around 200 AD and lasted for almost five hundred years until 1700 AD after they were at their peak with a highly developed civilization.
label: contradicted
reason: Scholars date the Maya Classic period to about AD 250–900, so it did not last until 1700 AD. It came after the Pre-Classic period and was itself the peak of Maya civilization. The claim also contradicts itself: 200 to 1700 AD is about 1,500 years, not "almost five hundred," and an era of roughly 650 years is not "short-lived."

text: The Gallah birds of Australia's Galapagos-like Cocos (Keeling) Islands are the only birds in the world with blue feet, which turn bright pink or red during courtship.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different birds. The galah (Eolophus roseicapilla) is a pink-and-grey Australian cockatoo, not a blue-footed bird. Blue feet used in courtship belong to the blue-footed booby (Sula nebouxii), which breeds on tropical and subtropical Pacific islands such as the Galápagos, not the Cocos (Keeling) Islands. Male boobies show off their blue feet in a high-stepping courtship walk, and the sources describe no change to bright pink or red. So galahs are not 'the only birds in the world with blue feet,' and the colour-change detail is unsupported.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which lives in Northern Africa though Old world short-faced rhinoceros existed.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. The short-eared (round-eared) elephant shrew, Macroscelides proboscideus, is not extinct. It is a living species listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Stegolophodon is extinct, but it lived mainly in Asia from the Middle Miocene to the Pliocene, not in Northern Africa. It also died out long ago, so it does not 'live' anywhere today. The sources found do not call it a 'short-eared elephant' either.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest recorded melting point among all substances, reaching 5,740 Kelvin or 4,470 degrees Celsius.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions a substance called "Adidamite", whether as soot from explosions or anything else. Trustworthy sources name refractory carbides and carbonitrides as the record holders instead. Wikipedia gives hafnium carbide's melting point as about 4,231 K (3,958 °C) and says it beats tantalum hafnium carbide (about 4,178 K). Recent research on hafnium carbonitride, reported by phys.org, predicts at most about 4,400 K. None of these sources mention a substance melting at 5,740 K. The figures in the claim also don't agree with each other: 4,470 °C is about 4,743 K, not 5,740 K.

text: The nucleus of an atom, which consists of protons and neutrons, makes up approximately 99.9% of the atom's total mass, but occupies only about 1/1,000,000th the volume of the atom itself.
label: contradicted
reason: The mass part of the claim is correct: the sources agree that more than 99.9% of an atom's mass is in its nucleus. The volume figure is wrong. A nucleus has a radius of about 10^-15 to 10^-14 m, while an atom's radius is about 10^-10 m. That makes the nucleus roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller across, so its volume is only about 10^-12 to 10^-15 of the atom's. The claim's figure of 1/1,000,000 (10^-6) overstates the nucleus's share of the volume by about a million times or more.

text: The-colored planet in our solar system is Venus, which appears white to the human eye due to its thick atmosphere composed of sulfuric acid clouds and other gases that reflect sunlight.
label: supported
reason: Space.com confirms what the claim says about Venus. Venus looks like a brilliant white object in the sky because of its reflective clouds. Its thick atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide with sulfuric acid clouds, which make the planet look white or very pale yellow to the human eye. The opening phrase 'The-colored planet' seems to be a typo for 'white-colored planet', but the facts in the claim are correct.

text: The Andrade effect is the phenomenon where certain materials exhibit an unusual increase in electrical resistance when they are subjected to high compressive stress, rather than the expected decrease in resistance.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe the Andrade effect (Andrade creep) as a creep behaviour, not an electrical one. In 1910 Andrade found that metal wires under constant stress keep stretching over time, with strain growing roughly as t^(1/3). This is transient creep in materials. None of the sources link the term to electrical resistance rising under high compressive stress, so the claim gets the phenomenon wrong.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will actually " sacrifice" its own mycelium to feed the embryos of the previous year's offspring.
label: not_verifiable

Since the organism can't be identified, its life cycle can't be checked. The claim's idea of mycelium sacrificing itself to feed "embryos" of last year's offspring also doesn't match anything I found, and fungi don't produce embryos. text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will actually " sacrifice" its own mycelium to help facilitate the growth of other organisms in a mutualistic relationship.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any fungus called "chantinggorias" in the search results. The search only turned up unrelated taxa such as Cantharellus (chanterelles), which are mycorrhizal fungi that form symbiotic associations with plants. Since the claim's subject doesn't seem to exist, there is no way to check the described life cycle, in which the mycelium "sacrifices" itself to help other organisms grow.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the claim overall, with two caveats. UC Davis's hummingbird facts page says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards, and WorldAtlas, BirdSpot and others say the same. Some sources, such as BirdSpot and NatureWithBirds, qualify this: hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards in a sustained, controlled way, while herons or warblers may flutter backwards for a moment. The physiology part is also supported. Several sources explain that a flexible ball-and-socket shoulder joint lets hummingbirds rotate their wings almost 180 degrees, or in a 'full circle', in a figure-eight stroke. No source used the exact wording 'clockwise and counterclockwise', so that detail is only loosely confirmed. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Aona Costa Rica is the world's first and onlycipally BREW-tiful SURF school in the world that's certified for generating 40% of cast-off energy from an Albertson generator.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of a surf school called "Aona" in Costa Rica. I also found no certification for producing "40% of cast-off energy from an Albertson generator". Phrases like "onlycipally BREW-tiful" are garbled and make no sense. The closest real claim I found is that Safari Surf School in Costa Rica calls itself the "world's first STOKE-certified sustainable surf school." That is a sustainability certification for a different school, not anything about energy generation. Because the subject can't be identified and nothing in the claim can be checked, there isn't enough evidence to support it or rule it out.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-wide section of the Amazon River in Peru that maintains a temperature of around 40 degrees Celsius throughout the year, despite being surrounded by much colder water.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and Scholastic Science World describe the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) as a tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali and then the Amazon. It is not a section of the Amazon River itself. Its temperature also changes along its course: it starts at about 21°C, and its hottest parts are widely reported to reach close to boiling (around 86°C or more). A steady 40°C year-round is therefore wrong. Commonly cited figures put the river at about 25 m wide at most, not 50 m.

text: A honeybee in a honeybee colony typically produces and collects only about 1/12th of a teaspoon of honey in its entire lifespan, which is a remarkable example of industrial efficiency among these creatures.
label: supported
reason: Beekeeping sources say a single worker honeybee makes about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her lifetime, which matches the claim's main factual point. Carolina Honeybees adds that this is only an estimate, because no one can measure what a single bee makes. The claim says 'a honeybee', but strictly speaking it is the worker bees that make honey. Calling this 'industrial efficiency' is a matter of opinion and can't be checked; the sources treat the small amount as a sign that honey-making is a group effort. Since nothing contradicts the factual part, the claim counts as supported.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains the highest vertical distance of a sedimentary river gorge in the world, dropping approximately 725 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, about 667 m above sea level, where the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station sit on the River Derwent. None of them mention any world record for gorge depth, and nothing supports the figure of about 725 m. The record claim is also false on its face. Gorges cut mostly through sedimentary rock go far deeper than 725 m. The Grand Canyon, for example, is about 1,800 m deep, and Greece's Vikos Gorge, which Guinness lists as the deepest relative to its width, is up to about 1,350 m deep. So Butlers Gorge cannot hold the world's greatest vertical drop for a sedimentary river gorge.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism in which they can shed, or "eject," their body parts to distract predators, such as the cyphiphorbe caterpillar which can sacrifice part of its body to escape danger.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched for a "cyphiphorbe caterpillar" and found nothing. The results only returned unrelated Lepidoptera genera such as Cethosia, Cyphosticha and Cyphothyris, so the example species may not exist or may be misnamed. The sources I found describe autotomy, meaning shedding a body part to escape, in lizards, scorpions, crinoids and arthropods in general. None of them document caterpillars shedding body parts to distract predators. Nothing directly contradicts the claim, but its key parts can't be verified.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent bell-shaped body and is able to swim upright using its bioluminescent bells that resemble flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is not a jellyfish. Wikipedia and NOAA both describe it as a deep-sea glass sponge. It is a sessile animal with a silica skeleton that lives fixed to the seafloor. It does not have a transparent bell-shaped body, and it does not swim upright using bioluminescent bells.

text: The biosphere, which is the global sum of all ecosystems on Earth, contains approximately 30% of all known plant and animal species in under 2% of its surface area.
label: contradicted
reason: Encyclopedic sources define the biosphere as the global sum of all ecosystems, the zone that holds all life on Earth. By that definition it contains essentially all known species, not about 30% packed into less than 2% of its area. The "large share of species in a tiny area" idea actually describes other things. Wikipedia's Biodiversity article says tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land and hold about 50% of species. Biodiversity hotspots are often described as holding about half of plant species in roughly 2.3% of the land surface. The claim seems to confuse the biosphere with hotspots or tropical forests, so its figures conflict with what the biosphere is.

text: Aleurites moluccana, commonly known as tung oil tree, produces seeds that contain tung oil which is the primary component of the paint used in the Taipei 101 skyscraper's facade due to its water and UV resistant properties.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim misidentifies the species. Aleurites moluccana is the candlenut, also called kukui or the candlenut oil tree. The tung oil tree is a different species, Vernicia fordii (formerly Aleurites fordii), and tung oil comes from its seeds. I also found no evidence that tung oil is the main component of paint on Taipei 101's facade; that skyscraper is clad mainly in glass curtain walls.

text: The	length of a human nose can change by as much as 30% when a person blows their nose due to the leverage and pressure applied to the nasal cartilage.
label: not_verifiable

The search did turn up nasal-length research, but it measured length changes during smiling, not nose-blowing. Other results covered nose-blowing technique and nasal patency. In Q&A answers, doctors said blowing the nose does not permanently enlarge or reshape it. Those answers address lasting change, not a momentary change in length, so they do not directly contradict the claim. Because the claim's specific figure and mechanism cannot be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: فيها شخص صيني Backpacker، يسمى ماو تسي تونج عندما كان شاباً، هبط على جبل EVEREST في سن 18عامًا وتخطى يقربًا الي 8000 متر.
label: contradicted

It doesn't say he was a backpacker on Everest. The nearest thing to backpacking in his youth was a walking tour of Hunan with a classmate, where they begged for food. Also, mountaineering on Everest's north side came decades later: the first Chinese expedition to succeed via the North Ridge was in 1960. text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a naturally occurring phenomenon where a river in the Amazon rainforest appears to be boiling due to a combination of geothermal heat and water conditions.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and several science outlets describe the Shanay-timpishka, or "Boiling River of the Amazon," as a natural river in the Peruvian Amazon. It stays very hot, near 100°C in places, because geothermal water rises along a fault rather than because of any nearby volcano. Its water is hot enough to steam and seem to boil. This matches the claim that geothermal heat and water conditions make it appear to boil.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Hidden Hot Springs," is a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains unexplained by scientists, listed as having a persistent boil level of unknown origin and energy source.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the river's heat has an unknown origin and energy source and that scientists can't explain it. Reliable sources say otherwise. Atlas Obscura reports that geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and his colleagues tested several hypotheses and concluded that a fault-led hydrothermal system heats the river. In this system, groundwater is warmed deep underground by the Earth's natural heat and rises back up through fault lines. ScienceAlert and YSI describe the same explanation, and YSI calls the river's sources fault-fed hot springs. Some details of the water's path are still being studied, but the heat source is understood. The claim also says the river has a persistent boil, yet the water averages about 86°C (187°F), which is not quite boiling. Finally, no source supports the alternative name "Hidden Hot Springs." The river's names are Shanay-timpishka and the Boiling River of the Amazon.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, as evidenced by the discovery of the PARAMAROS site which dates back over 11,000 years.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trace of a 'PARAMAROS site' in the Catskills. Searches turn up nothing about it, so the site appears to be made up. Reliable reports also place North America's oldest known dwellings elsewhere and make them older than the claim says. Live Science reports a dwelling about 13,800 years old at Shég' Xdaltth'í' in Alaska. Texas news covered a roughly 14,000-year-old site in Texas, and Paisley Cave in Oregon is about 14,000 years old as well. Both of those were reported as the oldest homes or habitation sites. The Catskills are known for the Gilboa/Cairo fossil forests, which are ancient forests, not dwellings. The claim that the Catskills hold North America's oldest known dwelling is therefore contradicted.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a perfect straight line and it is actually 172°East longitude by a slightly curved/smoothly curved route that reduces instances of date discontinuity.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica says the International Date Line follows the 180th meridian for most of its length. It only bends away from that meridian in places, for example through the Bering Strait and around the Aleutian Islands, so that it doesn't split closely linked areas. Britannica describes its course as zigzagging, not a smooth curve. The claim gets one thing right: the line is not perfectly straight. But saying it is "actually 172°East longitude" on a smoothly curved route contradicts the source.

text: The victim of the infamous murder that inspired H.G. Wells to write the novel "The Invisible Man," was the Count Alvise individual's servant.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's article on The Invisible Man says Wells named W. S. Gilbert's Bab Ballad "The Perils of Invisibility" as his inspiration. The claim's premise appears to be made up and conflicts with the documented inspiration.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 86 billion neurons in the average human brain.

reason: The 86 billion figure is right. It comes from Azevedo et al. (2009), as cited by Psychology Today and Nature Scitable. But the main claim is wrong. text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengths," but most linguists agree that "stochastic" is longer and the 'longest monosyllabic word' is the word "Strengths" is not true - The longest one syllable word mondegreen most linguists, "

text: Cotton balls were first made from cotton by mechanically spinning short fibers into fluffy clusters, but before that, humans used dried and shredded mushroom caps as a substitute for cotton balls in pre-industrial times.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source saying people used dried, shredded mushroom caps instead of cotton balls before industrialisation. But that comes from the fungus's inner tissue, not mushroom caps, and no source I found links it to cotton balls. The first part of the claim also looks shaky. Cotton balls are made by cleaning, carding and rolling fibres, not by spinning them, which turns fibres into yarn. Their mass production is credited to a machine Joseph A. Voss invented in 1937. Even so, no source directly says the spinning description is wrong. Because the key mushroom-cap claim can't be checked at all, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River,' is a geological phenomenon found deep within the Amazon rainforest in Peru, whose origin remains unexplained despite extensive research and exploration.
label: contradicted
reason: The river is real: Shanay-Timpishka, the Boiling River of the Amazon in the Peruvian Amazon. But the claim that its origin remains unexplained is contradicted. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo, the first geoscientist to study the river, found that it is a non-volcanic hydrothermal system fed by a fault. Rainwater seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's natural heat, and rises back up through faults and cracks. Some popular articles (e.g., AccuWeather) still call it 'mysterious,' but that refers to details still being studied, not to the basic heat source. I also found no evidence that it is known as the 'Hidden River.'

text: Butler's Gorge, located in a remote area of Tasmania, Australia, is one of the world's highest and longest bridled waterfalls, pouring over the landscape for over 800 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It has a population of nil and is where Butlers Gorge Road ends at the Lake King William (Clark) Dam. It is not a waterfall, and no source calls it one of the world's highest or longest waterfalls, let alone one falling over 800 m. "Bridled waterfall" is also not a recognised type of waterfall.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high pH levels that it can turn animals that die in it into stone statues due to its ability to preserve their bodies through alkaptoniq reaction.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Natron is a real, highly alkaline soda lake in Tanzania, with a pH of about 10.5. Reliable sources say that animals dying there can become calcified, stone-like mummies. However, the claim gets the mechanism wrong. Sources credit the preservation to the lake's sodium carbonate (natron) and salts, which encrust and mummify the bodies. There is no such thing as an "alkaptoniq reaction." The animals also do not literally turn into stone statues. They are salt-encrusted, calcified remains, and the photographer Nick Brandt posed them as if they were alive.

text: Centaury flowers, which are used in herbal medicine, have the unique ability to slowly increase their own height by lengthening their stems as they grow, often over time allowing them to reach above higher plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (Grieve's Modern Herbal at botanical.com, Ceres Heilmittel, Naturescape) confirm that centaury is used in herbal medicine. However, none of them describe a 'unique ability' to slowly lengthen its stems so it can grow above taller plants. All plants grow taller by lengthening their stems, so this would not be unique. The sources describe centaury as a small, unassuming plant, usually 5–50 cm tall (about 3–12 inches in Grieve), found in open, nutrient-poor habitats where other plants struggle to grow. That makes the claim unlikely, but no source directly addresses or refutes it. The plant's medicinal use is supported, but the main growth claim cannot be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is found on Mars and is known as the Altai Range, also referred to by some as the "Tartarus Dorsa", however most refer to the highly disputed claim; more likely the "Dorsa Argentea".
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Tartarus Dorsa is a mountainous region on Pluto, not Mars. NASA, Nature and the Planetary Society all describe it as Plutonian terrain that New Horizons imaged, spreading about 530 km. I found no source that names a Martian mountain range the "Altai Range" (the Altai Mountains are on Earth). I also found no source saying the solar system's longest mountain range is on Mars. Dorsa Argentea is a set of ridges near Mars's south pole, not a recognized longest mountain range.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 65,000 kilometers around the Earth's surface.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. WorldAtlas describes it as an underwater range about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) long that runs through all the major oceans. NOAA Ocean Exploration also describes the ridge system as the most extensive mountain chain on Earth and gives its length as more than 65,000 km. Together, these sources support both the 'longest' claim and the 'over 65,000 km' figure.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made of white Carrara marble, but the top 18 meters are made of green Prato marble, contrasting with the white stone below.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources (Wikipedia, ancient-history-sites.com, Frommers, florentapartments) say the white Carrara and green Prato marble is used on the church's facade and interior, not on any steeple. The basilica has no steeples, only one campanile (bell tower). That tower collapsed in 1499, was rebuilt from 1523 and was never finished. Sources describe it as a massive, unplastered stone tower with two levels whose planned upper section was never built. So no source mentions a green Prato marble top of about 18 m, and the tower descriptions conflict with that detail.

text: Antarctica is home to several active volcanoes, including Mount Belinda, which is a 3,447-meter-tall volcano found in East Antarctica.
label: contradicted
reason: Mount Belinda is not in East Antarctica and is not 3,447 m tall. NASA describes it as a stratovolcano on Montagu Island in the South Sandwich Islands, in the Scotia Sea between South America and mainland Antarctica. NASA gives its height as 1,370 m above sea level.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlyweds cross a thin wooden plank suspended between two boats, ensuring they will have children in future marriages.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nair community of Kerala is real, but the claim gets the Thalikettu ceremony wrong. Wikipedia describes Thalikettu (Kettu Kalyanam) as a 'tāli-tying ceremony': a ceremonial mock marriage performed for girls before puberty, in which a tāli (wedding pendant) is tied. It is not a 'boat bridge' ritual where newlyweds cross a plank between two boats to ensure they will have children. Nothing in the sources supports that description.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and is a vast underwater mountain range that runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth and say about 90% of it is underwater. They give its length as about 65,000 km (NOAA: 40,389 miles), and NOAA says it winds between the continents across the world's ocean basins, including the Atlantic. The only wording difference is that NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over." Other sources give figures of 65,000 km or more, so this is a small difference, and the main points of the claim hold up.

text: Coffee plants naturally lose most of their flowers and produce fruits because it's extremely rare for the coffee plant to fruit and set seed at the same time.
label: contradicted
reason: Research on coffee pollination contradicts the claim. Coffea arabica pollinates itself and usually sets fruit from about 48–60% of its flowers, and up to 95% in Colombian studies, so it does not naturally lose most of its flowers. The reason given also makes no sense: coffee fruits (cherries) contain the seeds (beans), so fruiting and setting seed happen together routinely, not 'extremely rarely'. Low fruit set (10% or less) is reported only for the self-sterile C. canephora when it isn't cross-pollinated, which doesn't match the reason the claim gives.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will actually " sacrifice" its own mycelium to degrade the surrounding plant material, in order to fuel the reproduction of new fungi.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any fungus called "chantinggorias" in my searches. The only results were about chanterelles (Cantharellus), and those are mycorrhizal fungi that live in partnership with plants rather than breaking down plant material. Because the name doesn't point to any real species, I can't check the claimed life cycle where the fungus "sacrifices" its own mycelium.

text: The Vogel's starling, a bird species found in Australia, is known for its unique ability to change the color of its feathers to match its environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a bird called "Vogel's starling". Searches turned up only unrelated birds, such as the common starling and the Vogelkop bowerbird. Australian sources list the common starling (Sturnus vulgaris) as an introduced pest, and none mention a 'Vogel's starling'. Because the bird the claim refers to doesn't seem to exist, it can't be properly checked. Separately, birds change feather colour through moulting and wear, not by deliberately matching their surroundings, so the claimed ability is highly doubtful. Still, no source deals with this species directly, so I can't confirm or refute the claim.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be about 84% of all the species that have ever existed on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is real. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) and is an estimate of all eukaryotic species, not just plants and animals. The 84% part is wrong, though. Scientists commonly estimate that about 99% (some say 99.9%) of all species that have ever lived are now extinct. That would make today's species roughly 0.1–1% of all species ever, nowhere near 84%. The 84% figure looks like a confusion with Mora et al.'s finding that about 86% of land species have not yet been described.

text: The "Gravity Hills" in Leeson Street, Dublin, Ireland, is one of the most famous examples of a "gravity hill," where the apparent direction of gravity is inverted, making it seem as though objects roll uphill.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing a gravity hill on Leeson Street in Dublin, much less a famous one. Wikipedia describes Leeson Street as a city-centre street divided by the Grand Canal and does not mention any such feature. Wikipedia's list of gravity hills names the Irish examples as the Cooley Peninsula/Jenkinstown in Co. Louth, Ballintrillick in Co. Sligo, Slievenamon in Co. Tipperary and the road to the Mahon Falls in the Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford. Euronews and the Irish Examiner also point to rural sites such as the Magic Hill in the Mourne Mountains, Co. Down. This evidence comes from leaving Leeson Street out rather than from a source that directly rules it out, but the claim that it is one of the most famous examples is clearly at odds with the sources.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, situated in the Great Hungarian Plain, where nightingales migrate to mate, making it a significant stop for these birds globally.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Kiskunfélegyháza is a real town on the Great Hungarian Plain. The nearby Kiskunság National Park is known as an important bird breeding and migration area, especially for the great bustard. However, I found no source that names Kiskunfélegyháza as a place where nightingales come to mate, or that calls it a globally significant stop for them. Nightingales do breed widely across Europe, Hungary included, but nothing I found backs the claim that this region has a unique ecosystem with global importance for nightingales. That part can't be verified, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: The largest atom ever discovered was the helium-like superheavy species with atomic number 118, oganesson (Og), which has an incredibly large atomic diameter of approximately 13.3 picometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Wikipedia and American Elements give oganesson's predicted atomic radius as about 152 pm and its covalent radius as about 157 pm. That works out to a diameter of roughly 300 pm, not 13.3 pm. Oganesson also isn't the largest atom: caesium's empirical atomic radius is 265 pm, and francium or caesium usually has the largest atomic radius. Finally, oganesson is a group 18 element with configuration [Rn]5f14 6d10 7s2 7p6, so calling it 'helium-like' is misleading.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built parts for various iconic aircraft including the famous Supermarine Spitfire and both versions of the Bristol Blenheim Bomber.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that a British aerospace company called "Arotech Limited" existed, or that it built parts for the Spitfire or the Bristol Blenheim. The name Arotech is best known as an American defence and power-systems company. Searches only turned up similarly named British firms: Aero Research Limited, an adhesives maker, and Airtech Ltd, set up at Haddenham in 1947. Neither result tied either firm to these aircraft. The search limit stopped me before I could check further. With no clear match for the company and no evidence for the parts claim, I can neither confirm nor rule out the claim.

text: The padrão, a type of stone monument typically built to serve as a territorial marker, was known for playing a significant role in many exploration and colonial endeavors of European empires.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia, the Dictionary of South African English and Wiktionary all describe a padrão as a stone pillar, usually topped with a cross and the Portuguese coat of arms. Portuguese explorers set them up in the 15th and 16th centuries to mark important landfalls and claim possession. Diogo Cão, Bartolomeu Dias and Vasco da Gama left about 11 of them along the African coast, and others stood elsewhere, such as in Sri Lanka. That supports the claim that they were territorial markers that played a major role in exploration and colonial claims. One caveat: the sources tie padrões specifically to Portugal. 'European empires' in the plural overstates this, since the Portuguese Empire is the only one documented using them. I treated that as loose wording rather than a contradiction.

text: Butler's Grotto in Carlsbad, California, was built by James Gamble	bg and John McEnery in 1906, and is one of the oldest and largest commercial caverns in the United States.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a place called "Butler's Grotto" exists in Carlsbad, California. Searches turned up only unrelated results: a Carlsbad massage spa named "Grotto" and Butler Cave in Virginia. Nothing I found links James Gamble or John McEnery to building a cavern in 1906, and nothing lists this site among the oldest or largest commercial caverns in the US. The claim looks doubtful. Carlsbad Caverns is in New Mexico, not California, and the well-known James Gamble, co-founder of Procter & Gamble, died in 1891. Still, no source directly contradicts the claim, so it can't be verified either way. The search limit stopped me from running further searches.

text: Butler's Grotto in Carlsbad, California, was built by James Gamble	bg and John McEnery in 1906, and is one of the largest artificial grottos in the USA.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing about a "Butler's Grotto" in Carlsbad, California. The results were mostly for an unrelated massage business called Grotto Massage, plus a page on the Southern California Grotto caving club. None of them mention James Gamble or John McEnery, a 1906 construction date, or any claim that this is one of the largest artificial grottos in the USA. Because no part of the claim could be checked against a reliable source, there isn't enough evidence to call it supported or contradicted. The stray text "bg" in the claim also hints that it may be garbled or made up.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where the river's water not only appears to be boiling but remains liquid, with a mystery surrounding the source of its heat that has puzzled scientists for decades.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Sources confirm that the Shanay-timpishka in Peru is called the Boiling River of the Amazon. They also confirm that it is very hot, around 86–99°C, and that its heat seemed puzzling because the nearest volcanic system is about 700 km away. However, no source shows that scientists were puzzled about it for decades. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo began studying it in 2011, and colleagues and experts had doubted such a river could exist at all. The heat is now mainly explained by geothermal heating, with Ruzo's work pointing to fault-fed hot water rather than an unsolved mystery. The "decades" part is unverified and partly at odds with the sources.

text: The Catskill Mountains in New York are home to the oldest known dwelling in North America, the Lehigh Valley Mink Insula at Dell tree,  visited from pre-historic tribe Scorrier, which further dated back over thousands of years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a place called the "Lehigh Valley Mink Insula at Dell tree" or a prehistoric tribe called "Scorrier" exists. Neither name turns up in any search result, and both look made up. My searches did find that the Catskills (in Cairo, NY) are home to the world's oldest known fossil forest, about 386 million years old. That forest is a fossil site, not an ancient human home. Lehigh Valley is in Pennsylvania, not the Catskills. Because the people and places in the claim have no clear referent and none of its specific details can be checked, the claim can't be rated supported or contradicted.

text: Located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the McDonald's Twenty-Nine Palms Base restaurant, opened in 2016, is the only McDonald's location in the world that has a drive-thru.
label: contradicted
reason: Twentynine Palms is a Marine Corps base in California's Mojave Desert, not in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, so the claim gets the location wrong. It is also widely known that thousands of McDonald's restaurants around the world have drive-thrus, so this one cannot be the only location with one.

text: The Venus Flower Basket jellyfish, a species of jellyfish found in the Indo-Pacific region, can bioluminesce and change its color to communicate with other jellyfish.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about what the Venus flower basket is. Wikipedia describes it (Euplectella aspergillum) as a glass sponge, not a jellyfish, living in the deep Pacific usually below 500 m. A sponge cannot change colour to communicate with other jellyfish, so the claim's basic premise is false.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 0.137 percent, but in the 1920s a court case found that a gallon in a New York State dairy had 2829.54 cubic centimeters instead of 3786 cubic centimeters.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing to support this claim. Searches turned up no 1920s court case about a New York dairy gallon measuring 2829.54 cm³, and no official 0.137 percent tolerance on a standard gallon. The claim also gets details wrong: a gallon is a unit of volume, not length, and the US liquid gallon is defined as exactly 3,785.411784 cm³, not 3,786. The only 1920s/1930s New York milk litigation that came up was Nebbia v. New York (1934), a case about milk price controls, not measurement. Because the main event can't be checked and other details look wrong or made up, the claim can't be supported.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says people didn't wear pants until the 16th century, and that's wrong. Science News reports that the oldest known trousers, found in the Yanghai graveyard in the Tarim Basin, are about 3,000 years old. It also says herders and horse riders there were making pants roughly 3,200–3,000 years ago, and that pants spread across Eurasia within a few hundred years. So people were wearing pants more than two thousand years before the 16th century.

text: The McKinley Tarn, located in the Grand Teton National Park, is believed to have the smallest lake in the United States, covering about 100 square centimeters of surface area.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that mentions a "McKinley Tarn" in Grand Teton National Park. Searches for that name only returned McKinley tartan kilts, and lists of the park's lakes don't include it. I also found no source saying the smallest lake in the US is in Grand Teton or that it covers about 100 square centimeters. A Quora answer points out that there is no agreed definition of the "smallest lake." The claim is very likely made up, but no source directly contradicts it, so I couldn't confirm or disprove it.

text: The6021 Rindler horizon,a theoretical boundary beyond which no signals can travel in a given universe has a radius that is directly correlated to the Schwarzschild black hole's surface since Einstein's theory works similarly.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the Rindler horizon wrong. It is not a boundary of signal travel "in a given universe" (that describes a cosmological horizon). It is an observer-dependent horizon seen by a uniformly accelerated observer in flat Minkowski spacetime. It is a plane, not a sphere, and sits at a distance of about c²/a set by the observer's acceleration, so it has no radius tied to a Schwarzschild black hole's surface. Sources note only that Rindler spacetime's diagram looks like the Kruskal diagram of Schwarzschild spacetime and shares some physical properties, such as Unruh/Hawking-like radiation. They do not say the Rindler horizon's size depends on the Schwarzschild radius. (The '6021' in the claim also appears to be a typo.)

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of organisms on Earth, as estimated by scientists based on DNA samples collected from remote areas and other sources.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011). Scientists got that number from a statistical pattern in how taxonomic levels relate to each other, extrapolated from groups that are already well catalogued, not from DNA samples collected in remote areas. The study also gave about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as a central estimate, not a floor, so 'over 8.7 million' misstates it too.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to their unique ability to fill their lungs and nostrils with air before submerging.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but part could not be verified. Trustworthy sources, including the Natural History Museum (London), One Earth and IFLScience, confirm that capybaras are the world's largest rodents and can hold their breath underwater for up to about five minutes. However, none of the sources I found give the stated reason, a 'unique ability to fill their lungs and nostrils with air before submerging.' What they describe instead is partially webbed feet, a streamlined face and using water to escape predators. Filling the nostrils with air is not a recognised way of holding breath, and nothing I found backs it up. My later searches on this point returned no results, and I then hit the search limit. Because the explanation in the claim can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has the most dense and coarse fur of any mammal, sometimes weighing down the animal's limbs and reducing its swimming speed.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records says the sea otter (Enhydra lutris) has the densest fur of any mammal, at about 100,000–160,000 hairs per square centimetre. Other sources also call the sea otter the furriest animal on Earth. No real animal goes by the name "comfortless waterhog," and nothing supports the claim that a water shrew has the densest fur or that its fur weighs down its limbs and slows its swimming.

text: The padrão, a type of stone monument typically built to commemorate territorial control, was developed by early European explorers and especially the Portuguese in Africa from the 15th century onward.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and the Dictionary of South African English both describe the padrão as a stone pillar that Portuguese maritime explorers set up in the 15th and 16th centuries. The pillars recorded important landfalls and asserted possession and sovereignty, which matches the claim's 'commemorate territorial control'. Diogo Cão placed the first stone padrões along the African coast in 1482–84, and Bartolomeu Dias and Vasco da Gama later erected others in Africa. One caveat: the sources tie padrões specifically to the Portuguese, so 'early European explorers' in general is broader than the evidence. Because the claim names the Portuguese as the main group, I don't treat this as a contradiction.

text: The padrão, a type of stone monument typically built to serve as a territorial marker, was known for playing a significant role in many exploration and colonizing feats.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia, Wiktionary and Wikimedia Commons all describe the padrão as a stone pillar that Portuguese explorers set up in the 15th and 16th centuries. They used these pillars to record important landfalls and claim the land for Portugal along the coasts of Africa and Asia. This supports describing the padrão as a territorial-marker monument. The sources also say that "numerous Portuguese explorers" used padrões during the Age of Discovery to establish possession, which fits the somewhat vague claim that they played a significant role in many exploration and colonizing feats.

text: Butterflyfish were one of the only species to thrive in and around the bleached coral of the Great Barrier Reef, showing its adaptability even within catastrophe.
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows butterflyfish are among the fish hit hardest by coral bleaching, not among the few species that thrive. Many of them depend on coral for food, and their numbers have fallen as bleaching has killed coral, including on the Great Barrier Reef. Studies of the 2016 bleaching event report that butterflyfish became less aggressive and their populations dropped. Some species did change their diets, but that was a way of coping, not thriving.

text: The Gallah birds of Australia's Galapagos-like Cocos (Keeling) Islands are the only birds in the world with blue feet, which turn bright pink or red during breeding season.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Galahs (Eolophus roseicapilla) are pink-and-grey cockatoos found across mainland Australia. Their feet are greyish or bone-coloured, not blue, and their feet do not change to pink or red when they breed. Galahs are not a special bird of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands either. Also, other birds have blue feet, most famously the blue-footed booby, so galahs could not be the only ones.

text: The Lucerne Lion Monument in Switzerland is a famous stone sculpture carved by Danish philosopher and artist Bertel Thorvaldsen in 1824.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say Bertel Thorvaldsen designed the Lion Monument, but Lukas Ahorn carved it into the rock in 1820–21. So three parts of the claim are wrong: Thorvaldsen did not carve it, it was not made in 1824, and Thorvaldsen was a Danish sculptor, not a philosopher.

text: The longest war in recorded history is the Roman-SССР л.atine Wars, but the conflict most often cited as the longest war in history is the Hundred Year's War that lasted for 116 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The second half of the claim checks out. Sources such as Factinate describe the Hundred Years' War as lasting 116 years, and one site notes that many people assume it was the longest war ever. The first half can't be verified because "Roman-SССР л.atine Wars" is garbled and has no clear referent. If it was meant to say the Roman-Latin Wars, those were short conflicts and not the longest war. The wars usually named as the longest are the Roman-Persian Wars (about 681–721 years), the Roman-Germanic wars (about 708 years, per WorldAtlas) or the Reconquista (about 780 years). Because the main entity in the claim is unclear, it can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: The remains of "The Great Blue Hole," a massive underwater sinkhole in Belize, were once part of a land bridge that existed during the last ice age before it collapsed and became submerged underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: My search found that the Great Blue Hole began as a limestone cave system. It formed during the last glacial period, when sea level was about 400–500 feet lower and the area was dry land. As the ice age ended and the sea rose, the caves flooded and the cave roof collapsed. The sinkhole is a flooded, collapsed cave (a 'sea hole'), not the remains of a land bridge, so the claim gets its origin wrong. One caveat: the source is a Belize tourism site rather than a scientific one, but its account matches the commonly cited explanation of how the Blue Hole formed.

text: The total distance covered by the Milky Way galaxy in its entirety, from one end of the galaxy to the other, is estimated to be about 100,000 light-years.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources give the Milky Way's diameter as roughly 100,000 light-years. Universe Today says the visible galaxy is at least 100,000 light-years across, or about 100,000–120,000 when more of the disk is counted. Britannica reports Shapley's estimate of about 100,000 light-years, and many educational references use the same figure. Some estimates are larger: Britannica's summary says about 150,000, and the halo extends further still. Because the claim says 'in its entirety,' a full-halo reading would make it inaccurate. Still, about 100,000 light-years is the standard estimate for the galaxy's diameter, so the claim is supported.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world's longest saltwater waterfall, despite it being non-visible in certain conditions due to its freshwater cascades being covered.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a real place, but nothing in the sources fits the claim. It is an inland rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, next to Clark Dam on the River Derwent and Lake King William, and none of the sources mention a saltwater waterfall there. The waterfall usually described as the world's largest is the Denmark Strait cataract. It is underwater, deep beneath the North Atlantic between Greenland and Iceland, not in Tasmania. The claim's idea of a saltwater fall hidden because its freshwater cascades are covered also has no support in any source.

text: There are approximately 37.7 million years between the largest known comet impact on Earth, which is believed to have caused a ~95% global extinction event and formed the Chicxulub crater, and a key mass extinction event after it, such as ones that may have wiped out the dinosaurs like in 1.
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are wrong. The Chicxulub impact happened about 66 million years ago and wiped out about 75% of species, not about 95%. It is generally described as an asteroid impact, not a comet, and Vredefort, not Chicxulub, is usually cited as the largest known impact structure. Chicxulub itself is linked to the dinosaur extinction (the K–Pg event), so it makes no sense to describe a separate dinosaur-killing extinction coming after it. The ~95% figure fits the Permian–Triassic extinction, which was not caused by Chicxulub. Neither the ScienceDaily article nor the PMC paper on the impact's timing supports a 37.7-million-year gap.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Australia, has the world's oldest known dam, with evidence suggesting it was constructed around 10,000 years ago by the indigenous people of Australia.
label: contradicted
reason: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania is where the Clark Dam was built. It is a modern concrete hydro-electric dam that was under construction in the 1940s, as a 1946 report in The Mercury describes. The University of Tasmania's Companion to Tasmanian History says Tasmania's earliest dams date from about 1809. No source suggests there is a 10,000-year-old Indigenous dam at Butler's Gorge or that it holds the world's oldest dam. (Very old Aboriginal water structures, such as the Budj Bim eel traps, are in Victoria, not at Butler's Gorge.)

text: Pineapples are not typically yellow when they're ripe, as people often believe; instead, they're a combination of green skin with a brown or reddish tint near the fruit's base.
label: contradicted
reason: Dole's communications director, quoted by Food Republic, says a ripe pineapple's skin should be golden yellow, with the colour getting stronger from the bottom up. He says fully green fruit is underripe, while dark yellow or orange fruit is overripe. That contradicts the claim that ripe pineapples are not typically yellow. Fresh Del Monte does note that some varieties stay green when ripe, but that is an exception, not the norm. No reliable source found describes green skin with a brown or reddish tint at the base as the typical sign of ripeness.

text: The short film "Flicker" (2002) is the smallest film to have been accepted into the canon of the Cannes Film Festival, consisting of only a 7-second 5x5mm scan of a single frame.
label: contradicted
reason: I found the 2002 short film "Flicker": it was directed by Conall Pendergast and released straight to video. IMDb lists it as a 5-minute black-and-white horror short about an old film reel, made on a budget of about CA$180. A 5-minute runtime contradicts the claim that it is only a 7-second, 5x5mm scan of a single frame. I found nothing linking the film to Cannes, and the festival does not have a "canon" that films are accepted into. The claim appears to be made up.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and gentle nature, which makes them blush or appear embarrassed when they are together in a group.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up. Several sources, including HowStuffWorks and IFAW (as cited by inkl), confirm that a group of pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." The claim's explanation does not hold up. Sources describe the term as a whimsical label with no scientific basis and an unclear origin. Where they do offer reasons, they point to pandas' clumsy antics and slow pace, to the fact that pandas are solitary and rarely seen together in the wild, or to a link with the French word "embarras" (obstacle). No source says pandas blush or look embarrassed when they gather, and saying they are often together in groups goes against their known solitary nature. Because the stated reason for the name conflicts with the evidence, I judged the claim contradicted, even though no source directly rules out the blushing story.

text: ButDia'hismo, a unique new species of jellyfish, was spotted in 2021 in the waters off the coast of Australia, only existing for a single day in its adult form.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trace of a jellyfish called "ButDia'hismo" in my searches, and the name looks made up. The closest real case is a jellyfish filmed by a scuba diver off Australia in December 2021. It may be a new species, possibly in the genus Chirodectes, but it has no such name and nothing says its adult form lives for only one day. Because no source either confirms or directly disproves the claim, it can't be verified.

text: Butler's Gorge, a series of waterfalls on the Whanganui River in New Zealand, are one of the country's least visited and most beautiful waterfall attractions.
label: contradicted
reason: My search found no waterfall called Butler's Gorge on the Whanganui River. Butlers Gorge is a locality in Tasmania, Australia, named after surveyor John Leslie Butler. It is also home to the Butlers Gorge Power Station, a hydroelectric station in Tasmania's Central Highlands. That contradicts the claim that it is a series of waterfalls on New Zealand's Whanganui River.

text: Centaury flowers, which are used in herbal medicine, have the unique ability to slowly increase their own height by lengthening their stems after they have bloomed.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that mentions centaury stems slowly lengthening after the plant blooms, let alone calls this a unique ability. The botanical sources I checked (BSBI Fermanagh, Wikipedia, Wild Flower Finder, Ceres Heilmittel) describe common centaury (Centaurium erythraea) as a rosette-forming biennial or winter-annual. In spring it sends up an upright flowering stem, usually 5–50 cm tall, and growth is said to resume in spring rather than after flowering. Wikipedia does confirm that centaury is used in herbal medicine. Still, nothing I found either supports or directly rules out the claim that stems lengthen after blooming, so the key part of the claim can't be verified.

text: The Blue Fairy Tern, also known as Arenaria interpres, is a rare and endangered tern species that lays its eggs on the ground in dense vegetation, rather than on rocks or nests like many other terns.
label: contradicted
reason: Arenaria interpres is the ruddy turnstone, a sandpiper-family shorebird, not a tern. No species is called the "Blue Fairy Tern." The ruddy turnstone is a widespread migratory shorebird, not a rare or endangered tern, so the claim misidentifies the species.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Lost River of Zenith," is a mysterious river that appears to be a thermal spring with elevated temperature and high water level in the midst of the dense Amazon rainforest.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no support for the name "Lost River of Zenith." Trusted sources (Wikipedia, National Geographic, IFLScience, Science Friday) call the river Shanay-timpishka, La Bomba, or Río Hirviente. They confirm it is a geothermally heated river in the Peruvian Amazon rainforest, with water ranging from about 45°C to nearly 100°C. However, none of my searches turned up the "Lost River of Zenith" alias, and none mention it having a high water level. The legend linked to the river is about a lost city of gold, not "Zenith." Because these parts of the claim can't be checked, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Cstorabies, more commonly known as stars, have blood only a mere 0.00001% of the blood that shows in their bodies due to the transparent nature of the rest of their body tissues.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no organism or term called "Cstorabies." The searches for that word only returned pages about scabies. The claim names it as another word for "stars." Stars in space are not living things and have no blood. If "stars" means starfish (sea stars), the sources say they have no blood or circulatory system like ours. Instead, they move seawater through their bodies with a water vascular system. So the claim that stars have a tiny amount of blood that shows because the rest of their tissue is transparent is wrong. The 0.00001% figure and the transparency explanation also have no support.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in the Maltese Islands, specifically Malta and Gozo, as researchers believe it may be due to a genetic adaptation that occurred over time on these islands.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source saying that cats in Malta and Gozo don't meow, or that researchers have linked this to a genetic adaptation. Research on Maltese cats, such as the 'Blue Cats of Malta' article, covers coat colour and where the cats came from, not meowing. General coverage of Malta's well-known street cat colonies describes ordinary cats and never mentions silent cats. The claim looks made up, but no source directly refutes it, so it can't be verified either way.

text: The color blue is a rare color in nature, with only a few examples existing such as blueberries, blue butterflies, and blue-colored geodes, making it a highly sought-after pigment in art and design throughout history.
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that blue is fairly rare among plants and animals. They say blueberries get their colour from anthocyanin pigments and blue butterflies like the morpho get theirs from structural colouring. A UCSD article also notes that people have long coveted blue, using expensive ultramarine from lapis lazuli during the Renaissance, which backs the claim that the pigment was highly sought after. Two caveats: 'only a few examples' overstates how rare blue is, and I found no specific source for blue geodes. Neither point is contradicted, though.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is created by a result of a chemical reaction in the insect's abdomen that involves the oxidation of a molecule called luciferin, producing a blue-green light.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports (Nature) describes the New Zealand glowworm's blue-green bioluminescence. It says the light comes from a specialised light organ at the posterior end of the larva's body, which is derived from modified Malpighian tubules, so it sits at the tail end of the abdomen. The study also says the light is produced by a firefly-like luciferase acting on a luciferin. Luciferase reactions of this kind work by oxidising luciferin; the search result does not spell out the word 'oxidation', but this is the standard firefly-type mechanism. Each part of the claim (reaction in the abdomen, luciferin, blue-green light) matches the source.

text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Nile River in Uganda, is home to the mighty Murchison Falls, which is the world's most powerful waterfall in terms of water volume, with an average water flow of 54 million liters per second.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets three key facts wrong. First, Butlers Gorge is a locality and the site of a hydroelectric power station on the River Derwent in Tasmania, Australia, not a section of the Nile in Uganda. Second, Murchison Falls carries about 300 cubic metres (roughly 300,000 litres) of water per second through a 7-metre gap, not 54 million litres per second. Third, at that flow it is nowhere near the world's most powerful waterfall by water volume.

text: The vomitrocha frog, a species found in Papua New Guinea, can self-decapitate its head as a defense mechanism: when threatened, the frog can release a powerful toxin and separate its head from its body, allowing the rest to escape.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no species called the "vomitrocha" frog, from Papua New Guinea or anywhere else. My search turned up only unrelated results: an Instagram account named "Vomit Frog," a Smithsonian video about a different frog nicknamed the "vomit frog" (known for playing dead and raising tadpoles in its vocal sac), and an article about ordinary frog vomiting. Nothing describes a frog that releases a toxin and separates its head from its body. Self-decapitation is documented only in certain sea slugs, and in those it is the head that survives, not the body. Biologically, the claim looks impossible for a vertebrate. Because the entity has no clear referent and no source addresses the claim, it can't be verified either way.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting around 86 billion neurons in the average human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion neuron figure is correct, but the comparison is backwards. Nature Scitable says recent estimates put the Milky Way at about 200–400 billion stars, and the 86 billion neurons in a human brain fall well short of that. Even the lowest common estimate of roughly 100 billion stars (Bell Museum) is higher than 86 billion. So the brain has fewer neurons than the galaxy has stars, not more.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will actually " sacrifice" its own mycelium in order to give its connected mycelium and a fungal species across a "fixed distance nitrogen link".
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no fungus called "chantinggorias" in my searches. The closest results were unrelated: Cantharellus (chanterelles) and a Portuguese verb form. I also found no source describing mycelium that "sacrifices" itself across a "fixed distance nitrogen link." Because the organism has no clear referent and the claimed life cycle appears in no source, the claim can't be verified either way.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will actually " sacrifice" its own mycelium to stimulate the reproduction of its own kind, essentially making them a selfless organism.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no fungus called "chantinggorias" in any search result. Searching that name only brought up pages about chanterelles (Cantharellus), and none of those sources mention mycelium sacrificing itself to trigger reproduction. Because the organism the claim refers to can't be identified and the life-cycle claim isn't backed by any source, the evidence doesn't settle the claim either way.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only 15% of the total number of species that existed in the past.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is real. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, though it counts all eukaryotic species, not just plants and animals. The 15% part is wrong, though. Scientists estimate that more than 99% (AMNH says at least 99.9%) of all species that ever lived are now extinct, so today's species make up roughly 1% or less of the historical total, not 15%. The 15% probably comes from mixing up a different finding in the same paper: about 86% of existing species have not been described yet.

text: The surface area of the Earth is 510 million square kilometers, but scientists estimate there are around 750,000 square miles of underground tunnels and caverns beneath it.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only confirm the first part of the claim. Universe Today and Space.com both put Earth's surface area at about 510 million km² (about 197 million square miles). I found no scientific source estimating that there are around 750,000 square miles of underground tunnels and caverns. Searches turned up figures for single cave systems, such as Mammoth Cave's roughly 426 miles of passages, and for unrelated things like fungal networks. None gave a global estimate of underground void area. The second part of the claim can't be verified.

text: TheOMICRAN antisatellite network, a system of radar and electronic warfare assets in the UK, uses the Jodrell Bank telescope to track objects in space.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trace of an 'OMICRAN antisatellite network' in the search results, so the system seems not to exist or at least has no reliable record. Sources such as Britannica, the ICE and Universe Today confirm that the Jodrell Bank telescope has tracked spacecraft and space debris. That includes Sputnik's carrier rocket, early lunar probes and a bistatic radar setup. But nothing links Jodrell Bank to a UK antisatellite or electronic warfare network called OMICRAN. The main part of the claim can't be checked.

text: The Blind Faith double album "Appearance and Other Attractions" sold very well however their 1970 single "Can't Get Out" didn't encourage major labels agreeing to sign the group.
label: contradicted
reason: Blind Faith never made a double album called "Appearance and Other Attractions." Wikipedia says the band's only studio album was the self-titled "Blind Faith," released in August 1969 on major labels, including Atco in the US. I found no Blind Faith album by that name and no 1970 single called "Can't Get Out." The claim that major labels were reluctant to sign the band also conflicts with the documented record, since they were already on a major label.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the WR 104 horseshoe shaped binary system's equatorial ring system, but in terms of Earth, the longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which surrounds the globe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's first part is false. WR 104 is a Wolf-Rayet star system about 8,000–8,400 light-years away in Sagittarius, and it is known for its pinwheel-shaped dust nebula. It lies outside the solar system and is not a mountain range of any kind. The second part, that Earth's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, is accurate. Because the WR 104 part is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). It winds through all the major ocean basins. One detail is slightly off: these sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over'. Some broader estimates that count every ridge segment give larger figures. Saying it runs 'through the middle' of the Pacific is also loose, since the East Pacific Rise lies toward the eastern side. Neither point contradicts the main claim.

text: Butterflyfish have one of the most unique reproductive strategies among fish, where the parents do not produce eggs or sperm, but instead give live birth to miniature versions of themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say butterflyfish are oviparous pelagic spawners. They release eggs and sperm into the water column, fertilization happens outside the body, and the eggs hatch into larvae. That contradicts the claim that they produce no eggs or sperm and give live birth.

text: Located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, Iceland is home to the world's oldest and most northernmost "post glacial lake" which is located at the highest point and has some evidences of human habitation a long, long, long time ago.
label: contradicted
reason: Iceland is in the North Atlantic, but the evidence does not support the rest of the claim. Studies identify lowland Lake Torfdalsvatn on the Skagi peninsula as Iceland's oldest known post-glacial lake record. That contradicts the claim that the lake is at the highest point. Torfdalsvatn is only called Iceland's oldest, not the world's oldest or most northerly. Iceland was also settled by people only about 1,100 years ago (Landnám), which does not fit evidence of human habitation 'a long, long, long time ago.'

text: The Azores Islands, an autonomous region of Portugal, are home to Goree's Algar do Carvão, a crater that is believed to have been formed over 4 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The Azores are an autonomous region of Portugal, and Algar do Carvão is there, but it is on Terceira island. It has nothing to do with Gorée, which is an island in Senegal. Algar do Carvão is also not a crater that formed over 4 million years ago. Sources describe it as a volcanic chimney about 90–100 m deep that formed roughly 3,200 years ago.

text: The enabling of specialized light behaviors in certain sharks and other marine animals are known as counter-illumination, which allows them to blend into their environment more effectively by producing light to match the surrounding light conditions.
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources describe counterillumination as a common camouflage strategy in the open ocean. Animals give off light from their undersides to hide their silhouette when seen from below. This has been documented in sharks such as the kitefin shark and the velvet belly lanternshark (Etmopterus spinax), whose ventral light matches the intensity and color of the daylight filtering down from above. The source also says the strategy is widespread among other marine animals, which supports every part of the claim.

text: Therypton, a rare and highly sought-after green diamond, is only found in a number of locations around the world, including Russia, Australia, and South Africa, due to its unique geology.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trace of "Therypton" as a green diamond, a gemstone, or anything else. A search for the exact term only turned up unrelated words like thiostrepton and Therocephalia. Searching for green diamonds brings up general sources (geology.com, Wikipedia's Dresden Green page, jewelers), but none of them mention "Therypton" or connect it to Russia, Australia, or South Africa. Because the claim's subject has no identifiable referent, it can't be checked.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless water hog's closest relative, the paw-mandibular hair furred  mangabey some observations however say its cousin which is known as a hog isn't the closest match.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the Seattle Aquarium, say the sea otter has the densest fur of any animal on Earth. The chinchilla is the land mammal with the densest fur. No source names a mangabey as the furriest animal. Mangabeys are Old World monkeys, so they are not close relatives of any 'water hog' such as the capybara. The rest of the claim is not coherent enough to check.

text: The impressive-looking Gmelins snub-nosed monkey has a highly unique adaptation that sets it apart from other primates: it can sleep standing upright, leaning against a tree to save Energy.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no snub-nosed monkey species called "Gmelin's." The five known Rhinopithecus species are the golden/Sichuan, black-and-white, gray, Tonkin (Dollman's) and black/Myanmar snub-nosed monkeys, so the claim's subject has no clear referent. I also found no evidence that any snub-nosed monkey sleeps standing upright against a tree to save energy. Studies of their sleeping sites and sleeping clusters describe groups that sleep huddled together in tall trees, which doesn't back up the claimed unique adaptation. That fits a made-up claim, but no source directly disproves it either.

text: The Greenland Shark is bioluminescent, meaning it can produce its own light due to a chemical reaction within its body that occurs in its liver and muscle tissues.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found don't describe the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) as bioluminescent. The only glow linked to it comes from the parasitic copepod Ommatokoita elongata, which attaches to the shark's eyes. Shark Guardian says some researchers think these parasites may be bioluminescent, but that this 'has never been proven.' No source says the shark makes its own light, in its liver, muscles or anywhere else. Unlike the closely related bioluminescent lantern sharks and kitefin sharks, the Greenland shark is not listed among light-producing species.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique flight characteristics and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), CGTN and A-Z Animals all say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They link this to the birds' unusual wings, which move in a figure-eight pattern and can rotate at the shoulder. Some sources add a caveat: a few other birds, such as herons or kingfishers, can flutter backwards for a second or two, but only hummingbirds can sustain controlled backward flight. The claim matches the general consensus in these sources.

label: contradicted
reason: Надёжные источники (culture.ru, словари) пишут, что пергамент делали из шкур телят, овец, коз, баранов и свиней. О гиенах, барсах, верблюдах или лошадях они не упоминают. Но это не меняет вывода: остальные части утверждения прямо опровергаются источниками.

text: A honeybee in a honeybee colony typically produces and collects pollen for only 4-6 weeks out of its entire 6-week lifespan during the warmer months of spring and summer.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable beekeeping sources say a summer worker bee lives about 6 weeks. It works inside the hive for roughly the first 3 weeks and only forages, which includes collecting pollen, during the last 3 weeks or so. The claim that a bee collects pollen for 4-6 weeks out of a 6-week life conflicts with this, because it would mean the bee forages for most or all of its life. Bees also don't produce pollen; they gather it from flowers.

text: The highest recorded speed of a human body propelled by Belgian dive bomber pilot, Andy Pickering on a rocket-powered steamboat, '100 mph' is not accurate. The highest recorded speed in a human was achieved by Andy Green, who reached 754 mph on October 15, 1997.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts this claim in two ways. On 15 October 1997, Andy Green drove ThrustSSC to a land speed record of 763.035 mph, not 754 mph. That was also only a land speed record. The highest speed any human has reached is about 24,791 mph, set by the Apollo 10 crew on 26 May 1969 while returning from the Moon. So it is wrong to call Green's run 'the highest recorded speed in a human.' No search results support the claim's figures.

text: A VOLCANO ERUPTS ON MARS Every 700 years - No scientific evidence can confirm this though, The Olympus Mons on Mars has had less than a 1% chance to erupt any time in the last 2 million years of Martian staleness though.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source saying a Martian volcano erupts every 700 years, and the claim itself admits there's no evidence for it. I also found nothing behind the figure of 'less than a 1% chance' of Olympus Mons erupting in the last 2 million years. Space.com, Wikipedia, LPI and Sky at Night say its last large eruption was about 25 million years ago, and ESA's Mars Express crater counts date some lava flows on its flanks to as recently as about 2 million years ago. That suggests it may have been active within that window, which loosely cuts against the low-probability claim. Scientists describe the volcano as dormant rather than extinct. Because the main parts of the claim can't be checked and the evidence that does exist doesn't clearly support or refute them, the result is inconclusive.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the heaviest known crystal structure due to its manufacturing occurring within extremely high hot temperatures, contributing to iron, copper, and zinc bonding under immense pressure making it the heaviest mineral known to scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no mineral called "Adidamite." The closest real mineral is adamite, a zinc arsenate, Zn2(AsO4)(OH). It forms as a secondary mineral in the oxidised parts of ore deposits, so it is not explosion soot, it is not formed from iron, copper and zinc bonding under extreme heat and pressure, and it is not especially dense. The densest naturally occurring substances are platinum-group metals such as osmium (about 22.59 g/cm³) and iridium. That contradicts the claim that this "Adidamite" is the heaviest mineral known. My search limit ran out before I could run a search aimed specifically at the densest mineral, so that last point comes from a source on the densest metals.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait called "tachyglossy," which means that the retinas of their eyes are made up of more than one layer, allowing them to see the world in a wider field of color and detail.
label: contradicted
reason: No source describes a giraffe eye trait called "tachyglossy." The root "tachyglossus" means "fast tongue" or "swift tongue." It's the genus name of the echidna, so it has nothing to do with retinas or giraffes.
