Scientific studies of giraffe vision, covering retinal ganglion cell topography and eye morphometrics, never mention this term or a giraffe-specific multilayer retina that widens color perception. (All mammal retinas are layered, so that wouldn't be unique to giraffes anyway.) The claim appears to be made up.

text: The European robin's distinctive red breast is actually more blue-black than red due to its coloration appearing red to the human eye because of the way that light scatters and interacts with the microscopic structure of the feathers.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the European robin's orange-red breast comes from carotenoid pigments the bird gets from its diet, not from light scattering off the feather structure. Its true colour is orange-red, not blue-black. A PLOS ONE study of plumage colour lists the robin among species with carotenoid- or melanin-based colouring, and Songbird Survival and Britannica both describe the breast as orange or red. I found no source supporting the claim that it is blue-black with a structural colour.

text: A rainbow can appear circular when viewed from an airplane because the observer is within the cloud, and the rainbow is formed by the water droplets in the cloud, as well as the position of the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources explain that from an airplane you can see the whole circle because the observer is high above the water droplets, so the ground or horizon no longer hides the lower half of the rainbow. That is the opposite of the claim's reason, which is that the observer is inside the cloud. A rainbow also needs the sun behind the observer shining on droplets in front of them. When you are inside a cloud the light is usually scattered, and you would not see a clear circular bow. The claim gets the role of the droplets and the sun right, but its key explanation is wrong.

text: Butterflyfish were one of the only species to thrive in and around the bleached coral of the Great Barrier Reef, showing its adaptability even within harsh environments.
label: contradicted
reason: Butterflyfish did not thrive around bleached coral. Many of them feed on coral, and the research shows they do worse after bleaching events. Carbon Brief reports that butterflyfish numbers fell in parts of the Great Barrier Reef, and that after coral die-off they ate less often and were up to two-thirds less aggressive in guarding their territories. Practical Fishkeeping reports research finding that coral loss from bleaching can severely reduce butterflyfish numbers. No source I found backs the idea that they were one of the few species to thrive.

text: Shark Bay in Australia is home to an incredible phenomenon called Hampden Pool, where sharks gather to mate in a saltwater lake, a place known for being the only tidal amphitheater in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Shark Bay has no place called 'Hampden Pool'. The name appears to be a garbled version of Hamelin Pool. Hamelin Pool is a hypersaline marine basin within Shark Bay, not a saltwater lake where sharks gather to mate. It is famous for holding the world's largest known living marine stromatolite system, not for shark mating, and no source describes it as 'the only tidal amphitheater in the world.' These details of the claim conflict with reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Britannica and an AGU abstract.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century when pants (popularized in Turkey first)  became more prevalent.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts the claim's timeline and origin story for pants. Archaeologists found wool trousers in the Yanghai Tombs in China's Tarim Basin dating to between the 13th and 10th centuries BCE, about 3,000 to 3,300 years ago. These are the oldest known pants, made for horseback riding, and they are not linked to Turkey. Researchers think horse riders probably wore pants even earlier. So pants did not first become common in the 16th century after being popularized in Turkey. The point that buttocks existed before pants is trivially true, but the claim's main historical point is false.

text: If you need to conduct a small research-based project and have time to dedicate up to 40 hours, it can be more effective to start it than putting it off or scheduling it for a longer, but indefinite, period of time. There's actually a real life phenomenon called 'The Zeigarnik Effect.
label: supported
reason: The Zeigarnik Effect is real. It is named after the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik, whose 1927 experiments found that people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. PsyBlog and similar sources say it is a simple way to beat procrastination: once you start a task, the unfinished work stays on your mind and pushes you to keep going. That backs the claim that starting a project now works better than putting it off. The '40 hours' detail is a framing example, not a factual statement, and no source contradicts it.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent bell-shaped body and is able to swim upright using its bioluminescent bells to float upwards through the water column.
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is not a jellyfish. It is a deep-sea glass sponge from the Pacific with a tubular, basket- or vase-shaped skeleton made of silica spicules, and it lives anchored to the seafloor. It has no transparent bell-shaped body, no bioluminescent bells, and it does not swim upright through the water column.

text: A giant squishy jellyfish-like creature called the Uluben Leafy Seadragon is one of the most venomous animals on the planet: it emits a stinging toxin.
label: contradicted
reason: No creature called the "Uluben Leafy Seadragon" turns up in any search. The real leafy seadragon (Phycodurus eques) is a small bony fish in the seahorse and pipefish family (Syngnathidae), not a giant squishy jellyfish-like animal. None of the reliable sources (Wikipedia, the Australian Museum, Aquarium of the Pacific) describe it as venomous or say it produces a stinging toxin. It is known for its leaf-like camouflage and for males carrying the eggs.

text: Located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, Iceland is home to the world's oldest and most northernmost "post glacial lake" which is located at the highest point and is in fact a glacial lake because of the overflow of a glacial lake known as Öskjuvatn.
label: contradicted
reason: Öskjuvatn is not a glacial lake. It is a volcanic caldera lake that filled the caldera left by the 1875 Askja eruption, which makes it one of Iceland's youngest lakes rather than the world's oldest. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and a Limnology and Oceanography paper both describe it as a caldera lake that formed after the 1875 eruption. That contradicts the claim's central points that the lake is glacial in origin and is the oldest in the world.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as phytoplankton, which are microscopic plants that can produce a blue-green glow in the darkness.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim is supported. Reliable sources, including National Geographic and KQED, say some phytoplankton, such as dinoflagellates, are microscopic and give off a sparkling blue-green glow in the dark. However, I found no source calling phytoplankton "Floating Islands"; the nickname seems to be made up. Not all phytoplankton glow, either. Since no source confirms the nickname and none directly rules it out, the claim can't be fully verified.

text: A VOLCANO ERUPTS ON MARS Every 700 years - No scientific evidence can confirm this though, The Olympus Mons on Mars has had less than that (in last 250 million years) Some volcanic activity can last less than 700 years
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that says a Martian volcano erupts every 700 years. The search results do show that Mars had long-lasting volcanism: Nature reports Alba Mons has been continuously active for about 500 million years, and EarthSky reports ancient super-eruptions spread over 500 million years. They also say Mars's volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, now appear dormant. The claim itself is confusing and partly contradicts itself, since it states a 700-year rate and then says no evidence confirms it. Its other parts, about Olympus Mons having 'less than that' in the last 250 million years and activity lasting under 700 years, are too vague to check. No source confirms or directly refutes these points.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, boasts one of the highest childbirth rates in the world, with over 40 births occurring within the gorge since 1995.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a real rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, but the 2016 census recorded its population as nil. It is a former hydro-dam site with no resident community, so it cannot have one of the world's highest birth rates or have recorded over 40 births since 1995. No source supports the birth-rate claim.

text: ButDia'hismo, a unique new species of jellyfish, was spotted in 2021 in the waters off the coast of Australia, only existing for a matter of hours after its reproductive cells release and dies shortly after.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched and found nothing about a jellyfish called "ButDia'hismo". The name looks made up or garbled, so it has no clear referent. Reports from 2021–2022 do describe possible new jellyfish species near Australia, such as a box jellyfish filmed off Sydney in December 2021 (genus Chirodectes). None of them uses this name or says the animal lives only hours and dies after releasing its reproductive cells. No source directly contradicts the claim either, so it can't be verified.

text: Coke and Pepsi were originally developed as alternatives to morphine, with Coca-Cola's original recipe containing an extract from the coca leaf and Pepsi's containing an extract from the kola nut.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Pepsi's origin wrong. Coca-Cola's part is broadly accurate: John Pemberton, a morphine addict, is widely reported to have been looking for an alternative to morphine, and the original recipe did contain coca leaf extract. Pepsi, however, was not created as a morphine alternative. Pharmacist Caleb Bradham made it in 1893 as a digestive aid called 'Brad's Drink,' sold as a remedy for indigestion (dyspepsia). Several sources agree on this. Since the claim says both drinks were developed as morphine alternatives, it is contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, "stretching nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)". That matches the claim's figure of about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). The ridge does run through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian and Arctic Oceans. The claim leaves out the Pacific, where the system continues as the East Pacific Rise, but it does not say the ridge is limited to the three oceans it names, so this omission does not contradict it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the main claim. NOAA Ocean Service and NOAA Ocean Exploration both call the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) long. WHOI and Wikipedia give about 65,000 km (40,000 mi), and the ridge system does run through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. There is one small wording difference: NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km rather than 'over'. I treated that as a rounding difference, not a contradiction. Also, the Pacific segment, the East Pacific Rise, lies in the eastern Pacific rather than its center, so the 'center' wording is loose for that ocean.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as Vellela Vellela, which are colonies of tiny marine animals that can light up the surrounding waters.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some parts check out, but key details cannot be confirmed. Velella velella, the by-the-wind sailor, is a small floating hydrozoan that is often described as colonial. A Beachcombing Magazine blog says it can glow blue at night through bioluminescence, but more authoritative sources found in the search (Wikipedia, National Geographic, Animal Diversity Web) do not confirm this. Animal Diversity Web also notes that describing it as a colony reflects an older scientific view. No source calls these animals 'Floating Islands' of life, and the claim misspells the name as 'Vellela Vellela'. Because the nickname and the light-producing ability are unverified or only weakly sourced, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The	length of a human nose can change by as much as 30% when a person blows their nose due to the leverage and pressure applied to the nasal passages.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that backs the claim that nose length can change by up to 30% during nose-blowing, or that leverage and pressure would cause such a change. The nearest data I found is a clinical study of nasal length during smiling, where the average change was about 2.5% and the largest increase was about 12%. Surgeon Q&A pages (RealSelf, Quora) say frequent blowing may cause swelling but does not change the nose's size or shape. Those answers are about lasting change, though, not a temporary change while blowing. Because no reliable source directly measures or rules out a temporary change in length during blowing, the claim cannot be confirmed or clearly disproven. It looks unfounded, but that is not proof it is false.

text: The Fangshan Cooked Treasures, a 2,000-year-old collection of over 2,000 well-preserved ancient Chinese meals, was discovered in an archaeological site in China in 1975.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that anything called the "Fangshan Cooked Treasures" exists. I couldn't confirm a 1975 discovery of more than 2,000 preserved 2,000-year-old meals in China. Searches for "Fangshan" only bring up Fangshan Restaurant and Fangshan imperial cuisine, a Qing-court style of cooking served in Beijing, and Fangshan District in Beijing. Ancient Chinese food finds that do appear in the results are different, such as a 2,400-year-old soup found in a tomb near Xi'an and a recreated Western Han rice recipe. The claim seems to be made up, but I found no source that directly disproves it.

text: The Droxford ship burial, discovered in 1864, is a 3,000-year-old ancient British boat burial containing the remains of two people that has been found almost completely intact.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a "Droxford ship burial." The known archaeological site at Droxford, Hampshire, is a pagan Anglo-Saxon inhumation cemetery. Reliable sources, including the Hampshire Field Club proceedings (Aldsworth & Welch, 1978) and the Archaeology Data Service, say it was found in 1900 during construction of the Meon Valley railway, not in 1864. It held many graves, including 41 more excavated in 1974, rather than a single boat burial of two people. Being Anglo-Saxon, it dates to roughly the 5th–7th centuries AD, not 3,000 years ago. The date, the age, the description as a boat burial and the 'two people' detail all conflict with the evidence.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescence to light up their habitats, but they do this by having a symbiotic relationship with themselves where some females capture and store the larvae of other glowworms and use them as a food source, but the adult glowworms will normally eat one of the males.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. Glowworms do not glow to light up their habitats. In the New Zealand and Australian species (Arachnocampa), the larvae glow to lure insect prey into sticky threads. In European glow-worm beetles, the females glow to attract mates. The claim that adults normally eat males is also wrong: Zealandia and Woodland Trust both say adult glowworms have no mouthparts and can't feed. Woodland Trust adds that glow-worm larvae eat slugs and snails, not other glowworm larvae. No source supports the idea of a 'symbiotic relationship with themselves' or females storing other glowworms' larvae as food.

text: The/ng Ai Grotto located in China, also known as the "Glass Bridge," is a 272-meter long footbridge made of glass that is over 300 feet above the ground.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing called "The/ng Ai Grotto" or any "Ai Grotto" in China. The name looks garbled and doesn't clearly point to any real place. The glass bridges I did find have different sizes from the claim. The Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon bridge is about 430 m long and roughly 300 m high. The Brave Men's Bridge in Shiniuzhai is 300 m long and 180 m above the ground. The Yalong Bay Forest Park bridge is 400 m long. None of them is 272 m long or goes by the name in the claim. Because the claim doesn't refer to anything I can identify, I can't check its details either way.

text: There is an island in Japan called Okinoshima, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site and home to the tranquil Chikugo-taisha Shrine, known for its serene and peaceful atmosphere.
label: contradicted
reason: Okinoshima is a real island in Japan and a UNESCO World Heritage Site: it is part of the "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region," inscribed in 2017. But the shrine on the island is Okitsu-miya (also called Okitsu-gu), which belongs to Munakata Taisha. It is not a "Chikugo-taisha Shrine." No shrine by that name exists on Okinoshima. The claim gets the shrine wrong, so that part of it is contradicted.

text: Located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the McDonald's Twenty-Nine Palms Base restaurant, opened in 2016, is the only McDonald's location in the world that has no marked price for food items due to the military base exchange system.
label: contradicted
reason: Twentynine Palms is a Marine Corps base (MCAGCC) in the Mojave Desert in San Bernardino County, California. It is not in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, so the claim's location is wrong. I also found nothing to support the other details: a 2016 opening date, the 'only McDonald's with no marked prices' claim, or the tie to the military exchange system.

text: The length of a person's ring finger is often used to determine their risk of heart disease, as studies have shown that those with a longer ring finger tend to have lower levels of cortisol, a hormone often associated with heart health.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the index-to-ring finger ratio (2D:4D) is studied as a rough sign of how much testosterone and other sex hormones a person was exposed to before birth, not cortisol. A longer ring finger points to more testosterone in the womb, and sources call these links suggestive but not definitive. I found nothing showing that ring finger length is often used to judge heart disease risk, or that a longer ring finger means lower cortisol. The claim gets the hormone wrong and overstates how the measure is used.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers in length and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). They describe it winding through every major ocean basin between the continents, which includes the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. Wikipedia also gives about 65,000 km. One wording differs: NOAA says 'nearly' 65,000 km where the claim says 'over'. The claim also oversimplifies by saying the ridge runs through the 'middle' of the oceans, since the East Pacific Rise is not centered in the Pacific. These are small points of wording, and the main facts hold.

text: The Booming Bays of Br>New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf are a unique natural phenomenon where clay particles "booming" from sediment, produces loud sounds in the water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My search turned up no credible source describing any place or phenomenon called the "Booming Bays" in the Hauraki Gulf, or any account of clay particles in sediment making loud underwater sounds. Acoustic studies of the Gulf, including research by Rosalyn Putland reported by the NZ Herald and RNZ, link its underwater sounds to animals and human activity, such as snapping shrimp, fish, sea urchins, whales, dolphins and boat noise. None of them mention booming clay. The claim also contains a garbled fragment ("Br>"). Because there is no evidence for the claim and no source directly rules it out, I can't verify it, though it looks likely to be made up.

text: Octopuses possess the unique ability to lose a limb as a defense mechanism, and then regrow it in a process that can take several weeks to a year.
label: supported
reason: The sources support the main parts of the claim. A UC Berkeley study (SICB abstract) describes arm autotomy, the deliberate shedding of an arm, as an octopus defense that helps it escape predators. Other sources say octopuses regrow lost arms. Regrowth begins within days, and Discover Magazine reports that a giant Pacific octopus can regrow a third of an arm in six weeks. A study of the common octopus found a fully regrown arm after about 130 days (roughly four months), and other sources give 2–4 months or 6 weeks to several months. These times fall inside the claimed range of several weeks to a year. One caveat: calling the ability "unique" overstates it, since other animals such as lizards and sea stars also shed and regrow body parts. Because the factual details hold up, I still judge the claim supported.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest known ignition temperature of any element at approximately 5,366 °C.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of any substance called "Adidamite". The term appears to be made up. The claim also calls it a type of soot, but soot is a mixture of mostly carbon, not an element. My sources put the ignition temperature of soot far below 5,366 °C: about 300–400 °C for boiler soot deposits, and diesel soot is burned off at a few hundred degrees. No element has an "ignition temperature" anywhere near 5,366 °C. The claim conflicts with the available evidence.

text: The Greenland shark is bioluminescent, emitting a blue-green light as a result of a chemical reaction within its body that helps it communicate and attract prey in the dimly lit waters of the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions.
label: contradicted
reason: The Greenland shark is not known to produce its own light. The only glow linked to it is a speculative idea about the parasitic copepods attached to its eyes. Shark Guardian notes these parasites may be bioluminescent, but that this 'has never been proven.' The sources describe the shark as finding prey by senses other than sight, not by emitting light. Nothing supports the claim that the shark gives off blue-green light through a chemical reaction to communicate or attract prey.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains the Oldest Natural Bridge in the world, dated to 300-400 million years ago, discovered in 1968.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything that backs up this claim. Wikipedia and other sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality with no population, best known as the site of Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station on the River Derwent. None of them mention a natural bridge, the "oldest natural bridge in the world," an age of 300–400 million years, or a discovery in 1968. Searches for the oldest bridges in Tasmania only turned up man-made ones, such as Richmond Bridge (1825). The claim is probably wrong, but I didn't find a reliable source that directly disproves it, so it can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Butler's Gorge, a remote region in Tasmania, Australia, boasts an impressive array of layer-caked tree species, including living examples of dolerite weathered gorge trees, a natural wonder formed over 2 million years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources confirm only that Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, near Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge hydro power station. No source mentions 'layer-caked tree species' or 'dolerite weathered gorge trees', or anything at Butlers Gorge formed over 2 million years ago. Dolerite is a rock, not a tree, and the searches turned up only geology articles about dolerite weathering, none linked to trees at this site. The key parts of the claim appear to be made up, but no source directly addresses or rules them out, so the claim cannot be verified.

text: Butler's extract of honeybee venom, apitoxin, has been used to treat arthritis and now is being tested to reverse the effects of multiple sclerosis in patients.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Parts of the claim check out. Bee venom (apitoxin) has been used for arthritis, and it has been tested in people with multiple sclerosis, including a 2005 phase I safety study and a 2005 randomized trial. But nothing I found identifies a 'Butler' who made a honeybee venom extract. The only Butler that came up was actor Gerard Butler, who tried bee venom therapy himself, so 'Butler's extract' has no clear referent. The rest of the claim is also overstated. The trials were done years ago and are not 'now' under way. They also did not show the treatment reversing MS: the randomized trial in Neurology found no reduction in disease activity, disability or fatigue. Because the claim's main subject can't be identified, the overall verdict is inconclusive.

text: Caterpillars go through a process called apoptosis, where they intentionally detach certain body parts to distract predators and increase their chances of survival during the metamorphosis process.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different things. Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a genetically controlled way of removing unwanted cells. In metamorphosis it breaks down larval tissues inside the body. It is not a behaviour where the animal deliberately drops body parts to distract predators. That defensive behaviour is called autotomy, and it is a separate process. So the claim's definition of apoptosis is wrong, and the claim is contradicted.

text: Butt managed to exist before people wore pants, i.e., throughout the majority of human history, until the 16th century AD, when trousers fully became fashionable throughout Europe, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent over the course of time.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says trousers only became widespread in Europe, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent in the 16th century AD. The sources say otherwise. The oldest known trousers are about 3,000 years old (13th–10th century BC) and come from the Tarim Basin. Encyclopedia.com says Persians, Scythians, Phrygians and others wore trousers in ancient times, and that Lydians and Sarmatians took them up from the Persians after 700 BCE. Wikipedia notes that Germanic men generally wore long trousers, and Gauls were known for wearing them too. Trousers were already common in parts of Europe and the Middle East more than 2,000 years before the date the claim gives. It is true that people went without trousers for most of human prehistory, but the 16th-century timeline is wrong.

text: Honey is banned from being imported in the United Kingdom due to a species of bee that is found nowhere else in the world: the Norfolk Island bee, however that import ban has recently been relaxed.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two places. Norfolk Island is an Australian external territory, not part of the UK. It does restrict honey imports, but that rule covers imports into Norfolk Island itself. The aim is to protect its honey bees (Apis mellifera), which are unusually free of pests and diseases; they are not a species found nowhere else. Australian government documents describe the island's restrictions and recommend allowing only certified irradiated honey to be imported commercially. Neither the UK nor any 'Norfolk Island bee' species is involved. The UK routinely imports honey, and there is no UK ban that was recently relaxed.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where the river's water not only remains warm year-round but also flows uphill, defying the laws of gravity and conventional hydrology.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, National Geographic and Forbes describe the Shanay-timpishka (the "Boiling River of the Amazon") as a hot river heated by geothermal processes. It is a normal tributary that flows downstream into the Pachitea, then the Ucayali, the Amazon and finally the Atlantic. None of these sources say it flows uphill or breaks the laws of gravity or hydrology. The geothermal explanation for its heat directly contradicts the claim that it defies conventional science. The heat part of the claim is supported, but the uphill-flow part is false.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the Moon seems to change its phase by 12 hours behind its actual phase, can be observed when you are at 180 degrees to its position relative to the Earth and Sun.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of a lunar phenomenon called '뒷문' or 'Hidden Moon'. In Korean, 뒷문 means 'back door'. Trustworthy sources, such as Wikipedia's Lunar phase article, say the Moon's phase depends on the angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon. Observers on Earth all see essentially the same phase, though it may appear rotated in different hemispheres. No observing position on Earth makes the phase appear 12 hours behind. The 'Hidden Phase' that search results describe is the ordinary new-moon period when the Moon can't be seen, not this phenomenon. The claim appears to be made up and conflicts with established lunar science.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a perfect straight line and it is actually 172°East longitude by a slightly curved/smoothly curved route that reduces instances of date and time differences in places like Samoa.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is right that the International Date Line isn't straight, but the rest of it is wrong. The line roughly follows the 180° meridian, not 172°E. Wikipedia says it follows the 180° meridian exactly in many places and swerves east or west elsewhere for political and economic reasons. Those swerves are sharp zigzags, not a gentle curve. The US Naval Observatory adds that, because of Kiribati, the line now reaches as far east as about 150°W. Samoa's position came from a deliberate 2011 change that moved it to the western side of the line, not from a curved route along 172°E.

text: The Cheeky Parrotfish, a species of marine fish, can make a loud bruiting sound by grinding its teeth, a unique ability known as "bruiting" that is often compared to the grating of shells on rocks.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no fish species called the "Cheeky Parrotfish". The only results for that name were a swimsuit product and unrelated species like the red-cheeked parrot, so the claim has no clear subject. I also found no source that calls any fish sound "bruiting". Reliable sources do say parrotfish in general make loud scraping and crunching sounds when they bite coral and grind it with their throat teeth. However, none of them describes a unique ability called "bruiting" or compares it to shells grating on rocks. The specific details of the claim can't be verified.

text: Theona, a province located in eastern Indonesia, is home to the active Kawah Ijen volcano, also known as the "Blue Fire," which is one of the few places on Earth where lava is visible burning with a bright blue flame due to its high sulfur content.
label: contradicted
reason: Indonesia has no province called "Theona." According to Wikipedia and other sources, Kawah Ijen (the Ijen volcano complex) sits on the border between Banyuwangi and Bondowoso Regencies in East Java province. So the claim gets the volcano's location wrong, even though Kawah Ijen really is famous for its sulfur-driven blue fire. The claim is also inaccurate about the flame itself: sources say the blue light comes from burning sulfur gases, not from lava.

text: The Maasai tribe in East Africa has a unique cultural practice of censoring the negative attitudes and throat clearing in the morning by performing what they call their morning "greeting songs".
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source describing a Maasai custom of morning "greeting songs" used to censor negative attitudes or throat clearing. The sources I checked cover Maasai spoken greetings (for example, "Supa" and the morning greeting "Kasserian Ingera?", meaning "Are the children well?"), the adumu jumping dance, war songs and blessing ceremonies. None mention a morning song practice like the one in the claim. Nothing directly contradicts it either, so it can't be verified.

text: The darkest star in our galaxy, VY Canis Majoris, is so massive that it would consume our Sun and all of its planets if it were placed at the center of our solar system.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets three things wrong. VY Canis Majoris is not the "darkest" star in our galaxy. It is a very luminous red hypergiant, roughly 178,000 to 270,000 times as bright as the Sun. It is also famous for its size, not its mass: its radius is about 1,420 times the Sun's. Most importantly, placed at the centre of our solar system it would reach past Jupiter's orbit but not as far as Saturn's (Wikipedia and star-facts.com), so it would not swallow all the planets.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill, Connecticut, is a natural limestone cavern that features the longest underwater body of water in the world through its caves.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing showing that a "Butler's Grotto" exists in Connecticut, and the claim's main superlative is wrong. Reliable sources (Earth Magazine and National Geographic, with Wikipedia agreeing) say the world's longest underwater or flooded cave system is in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula: Sistema Sac Actun, or Sistema Ox Bel Ha near Tulum. Searches for "Fonthill" grottoes only turn up 18th-century artificial grotto follies at Fonthill in Wiltshire, England. Sources on Connecticut caves also note that it is not a major limestone-cave state.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, which is roughly estimated to be around 7-75 million, but only about 1.3 million have been formally described and documented by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is built on the 2011 Mora et al. study (PLoS Biology), but it gets the study's figures wrong. The study estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, give or take 1.3 million. That is a central estimate, not "over 8.7 million." The uncertainty works out to roughly 7.4 to 10 million species (about 7.5 to 10.1 million in press coverage), not "7-75 million"; experts' earlier estimates spanned 3 to 100 million. The study also counted about 1.2 to 1.25 million species already catalogued, not 1.3 million. The 1.3 million figure is the study's margin of error, apparently mixed up with the count of described species. The estimate also covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not only plants and animals. The range and figures in the claim conflict with the original sources.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill, Connecticut, is a natural limestone cavern that features the longest underwater body of water in the world without significant artificial human conduct, covering approximately 10,234 feet.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trace of a 'Butler's Grotto' cavern in Fonthill, Connecticut. The search only turned up unrelated places: Fonthill Grottoes in Wiltshire, England, and Butler Cave in Virginia. The world-record part of the claim is clearly wrong. The longest known underwater caves are in Mexico, such as Sistema Ox Bel Ha and Sistema Sac Actun, and they run for hundreds of kilometers. The Sac Actun figure cited is about 524 km, far more than about 10,234 feet (roughly 3.1 km). Even Orda Cave in Russia has about 4.8 km of underwater passage. So the claimed record is contradicted, and the cave itself appears to be made up.

text: Pineapples are not naturally occurring fruits, and they were once considered a symbol of wealth due to the rare and long process of manual cultivation involved in their production.
label: contradicted
reason: Pineapples do occur naturally. Reliable botanical sources, including ScienceDirect, ITFNet and Wikipedia, say Ananas comosus is native to South America (Brazil, Paraguay, northern Argentina and Uruguay). It was domesticated from wild Ananas plants such as var. ananassoides, so it is not an artificial or non-natural fruit. The second part, that pineapples were once a symbol of wealth in Europe because hothouse growing was rare and costly, is well documented. Even so, the first part of the claim is false.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-wide section of the Amazon River that maintains a constant temperature of 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit), despite being located near the equator and with the surrounding water temperatures varying.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River, called Shanay-Timpishka, is not part of the Amazon River's main channel. It is a tributary in central Peru, about 6.4 km (4 miles) long and up to about 6 m (20 feet) wide, so it is nowhere near 50 meters across. Its water is also far hotter than a steady 38°C. Sources give a range of roughly 30–99°C (86–211°F), often above 80°C, and say it can reach 210°F.

text: The Kiskunfélegyháza region in Hungary has a unique ecosystem, known as the Fertő-Hanság National Park, which is the largest protected wetland in Europe.
label: contradicted
reason: Fertő-Hanság National Park is in Győr-Moson-Sopron county in northwestern Hungary, near the Austrian border and Lake Fertő (Neusiedl). It is not in the Kiskunfélegyháza region, which is part of the Kiskunság area of the Great Hungarian Plain and falls under Kiskunság National Park. The claim's description of the park as Europe's largest protected wetland is also not supported by any source found.

text: The McKinley Tarn, located in the Grand Teton National Park of Wyoming, contains a body of water from the remains of President William McKinley's mistress who was there on vacation when the mistakenly misdirected particles from a USA atomic bomb spewed upon her then now remains at the tarn out where today one could
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that supports any of the claim's specific details. Searches for a "McKinley Tarn" in Grand Teton National Park turned up only general park pages and unrelated McKinley tartan products. I found nothing about a mistress of President McKinley, or about fallout from a U.S. atomic bomb landing in Grand Teton and leaving remains in a tarn. Reliable sources confirm only that McKinley was shot in 1901 and died later that year. The first atomic bombs came decades later, in 1945, which makes the story very implausible. Still, no source directly disproves each detail, and the claim cuts off mid-sentence. Because none of its core assertions can be checked, the verdict is inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: The short-lived but spectacular emerald rainbow, also known as "Moonbow," occurs when the Moon is full and is shining brightly, creating a rare and breathtaking rainbow effect.
label: contradicted
reason: A moonbow is real, and it does usually form when the Moon is full or nearly full. However, Wikipedia says its other names are "moon rainbow" or "lunar rainbow", not "emerald rainbow". Wikipedia also says a moonbow is "often white" to the naked eye, with its colors showing up mainly in long-exposure photos. That goes against calling it a green, "emerald" rainbow. Moonbows are also much fainter than daytime rainbows, according to The Old Farmer's Almanac, which doesn't match "spectacular". The searches found no reliable source that uses "emerald rainbow" as another name for a moonbow.

text: The 길 Cheese is a type of Korean cheese made from a mixture of cow, sheep, and buffalo milk, and it's often melted as a stringy, gooey ingredient in Korean dishes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a cheese called "길 Cheese" (Gil cheese) exists. "길" is Korean for "road" and is also a surname. Searches turned up only general Korean dairy vocabulary, gilgeori (street) toast, and unrelated people named Gil. Nothing describes a Korean cheese made from a mix of cow, sheep and buffalo milk or used as a melted, stringy ingredient. The claim's subject has no clear referent and none of it could be verified.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,389 miles long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says the longest mountain range on Earth is the mid-ocean ridge, at about 65,000 km (about 40,390 miles). Encyclopaedia Britannica's verified X account gives a length of 40,389 miles. The ridge system winds through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, as the claim says. The claim's "through the middle" wording is loose, because in the Pacific the ridge (the East Pacific Rise) sits toward the east rather than the centre, but this doesn't change the main points.

text: The process of crackling that occurs when you walk across a carpet in cold weather is known as "static discharge" and happens because the dry air strips away electrons from the surface of the carpet.
label: contradicted
reason: Calling the shock or crackling a "static discharge" is correct, but the claim gets the cause wrong. According to The Conversation, the charge builds up through friction between your shoes and the carpet, which moves electrons from the carpet's surface onto the shoe sole (triboelectric charging). Dry air doesn't strip electrons from the carpet; it just makes static shocks more likely.

text: Pink mandate has been followed in the Ahwaz, Iran since 1963, to influence the women and maintain their honor and due to this most women there don't have nipples.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a 'pink mandate' in Ahwaz (Ahvaz) or anywhere else in Iran. My searches only turned up unrelated news about pink-painted weapons used in regime propaganda. The history of 1963 points the other way: the Foundation for Iranian Studies records that the Shah's reform program that year, the White Revolution, included voting rights for women, and the first women entered parliament and the Senate in 1963. The idea that most women in a region lack nipples because of a decree is biologically impossible and has no documentation at all. The claim appears to be made up.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent bell-shaped body and is able to float upwards in the water column due to gas-filled "statoblasts."
label: contradicted
reason: The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) isn't a jellyfish. It is a deep-sea glass sponge. It stays fixed to the seafloor, held in place by a lattice skeleton made of silica. It has no transparent bell-shaped body and doesn't float up through the water using gas-filled structures. Statoblasts are a different thing entirely: they are the dormant reproductive buds of freshwater bryozoans, not flotation organs in sponges or jellyfish.

text: Buttress, a remarkable plant from the Amazon rainforest, can lift up heavy objects with its powerful roots that anchor deep in the soil, allowing it to potentially raise a car or a book off the ground.
label: contradicted
reason: No plant species is called "Buttress." Buttress roots are wide, above-ground roots that some tall rainforest trees grow at the base of the trunk. Sources say these trees grow in thin soil where roots often don't reach far down, so the buttresses keep the tree stable and upright. That contradicts the claim's 'roots that anchor deep in the soil.' The search found no evidence that these roots can lift heavy objects such as a car or a book.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," which was originally coined as a two-word title, "steward" and "ess", but later became a single word.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Lingoda and FunTrivia name nine-letter words like "screeched," "strengths" and "scratched" as the longest one-syllable words in English. "Stewardess" is better known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand.

text: There are approximately 13 billion trees on the planet Mars, but this number is based on images taken by satellites and should be used with caution as it is an estimate.
label: contradicted
reason: Mars has no trees and no known life of any kind. Its surface is a cold, dry desert with a very thin CO2 atmosphere, and no satellite or rover has ever seen vegetation there. The figure of about 13 billion is probably a garbled version of real Earth tree counts: roughly 3 trillion trees worldwide (Crowther et al., Nature 2015), or national figures such as Canada's. NASA's Mars exploration pages confirm that no life, let alone trees, has been found on Mars.

text: The country of Singapore has the highest percentage of OPT (Optometrists, Pharmacists, Nurses, Doctors) professionals globally in its population due to government incentives and policies.
label: contradicted
reason: Singapore does not have the highest share of health professionals in the world. WHO figures listed on Wikipedia put Singapore at about 26 doctors per 10,000 people (2021). That is far below Cuba (about 83 per 10,000, or 8.3–8.4 per 1,000), Monaco and Georgia, which IndexMundi/CIA and other compilations rank at the top for physician density. Comparisons of nurses and other health staff likewise put other countries, such as Cuba and the Nordic states, ahead of Singapore. Also, 'OPT' is not a standard grouping for these professions. Since the claim that Singapore ranks first globally is false, the part about government incentives being the cause doesn't matter.

text: A honeybee in a honeybee colony typically produces and collects only about 1/12th of a teaspoon of honey in its entire lifespan, which is remarkably efficient considering the entire colony can produce up to 60 pounds of honey per year.
label: supported
reason: Several bee and honey sources, including PBS NOVA, Golden Blossom Honey and the Loudoun beekeepers' association, say a worker bee makes only about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in her lifetime. That supports the main claim. Golden Blossom Honey also says one colony can produce 60 to 100 pounds of honey a year, which backs the claim that a colony can produce 60 pounds. The 'up to' wording is the weak point: it sets 60 pounds as the maximum, but sources give higher figures. Golden Blossom's range goes to 100 pounds, and one honey seller says a hive can make up to 400 pounds. Read strictly as a ceiling, that part is contradicted. Read as 'as much as 60 pounds', it fits the evidence, and I chose that reading. 'Remarkably efficient' is a subjective description and cannot be checked.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments such as deep-sea vents, where temperatures can reach as high as 221 degrees Fahrenheit, due to their highly adaptable and resilient nature.
label: contradicted
reason: Bacteria do live at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, but the claim's temperature is wrong. Calling 221°F (105°C) the most vents can reach is far too low. WHOI and NOAA say vent fluids reach about 400°C, or more than 750°F, and WHOI says temperatures well above 662°F (350°C) are common. WHOI also gives the record for life growing at high temperature as 235°F (113°C), which is above 221°F, so that figure does not match the known limit for microbes either.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to their unique ability to fill their lungs and nostrils with air before fully submerging into the water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Several sources (One Earth, IFLScience, FactAnimal, and capybara fact sites) agree that capybaras are the world's largest rodents and can hold their breath underwater for up to about 5 minutes. None of them back the stated reason, a 'unique ability to fill their lungs and nostrils with air' before diving. Instead, they credit adaptations such as closing the nostrils and ears to keep water out, and eyes, ears and nostrils set high on the head. Since the causal explanation can't be verified and doesn't match what the sources describe, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and gentle nature, which makes them blush or appear embarrassed when they are together in large groups.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is right: many sources say a group of pandas is often called an "embarrassment" (HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals, Animal Corner, ZME Science). The explanation is wrong, though. These sources link the name to pandas' clumsy, lazy-looking behavior or to plain English whimsy. HowStuffWorks says the word has no scientific origin. None of them mention shyness, and none say pandas blush or look embarrassed in large groups. Pandas are also solitary animals and are rarely seen together in the wild, so the idea that they blush when gathered in large groups is false.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology, which includes extremely fast wing-beat rates and reversible wings.
label: supported
reason: UC Davis's hummingbird facts page, a trustworthy academic source, says hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. It also puts their wingbeats at 720 to 5,400 per minute when hovering, which backs the claim about very fast wing-beat rates. WorldAtlas, Vedantu, Birdspot and A-Z Animals also say hummingbirds are the only birds that fly backwards. They credit this to the hummingbird's shoulder: a ball-and-socket joint lets the bird rotate its wings about 180 degrees, so the wingtips trace a figure-eight and produce lift on both the forward and backward stroke. That matches the claim's 'reversible wings.' One caveat: Birdspot says herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for a short distance, but only hummingbirds do it for any length of time. Mainstream sources still describe hummingbirds as the only birds capable of true backward flight, so the claim is generally supported.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe hummingbirds as the only birds that can fly backwards. Wikipedia's 'Backward flying' article says that among birds, only one family (Trochilidae, the hummingbirds) shows backward flight. WorldAtlas and BirdSpot say the same and link it to the hummingbird's unusual wing structure and muscles. A-Z Animals and Animal Corner describe a rotating shoulder joint that lets the wing twist about 180 degrees and beat in a figure-eight motion. Some less authoritative sites say a few other birds can move backward briefly, but they still say hummingbirds are the only birds capable of sustained, controlled backward flight. That fits the claim rather than contradicting it.

text: A giant protein in the Venus flower basket jellyfish is incredibly strong and can lift 125,000 times its own weight.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal wrong. Wikipedia and other sources describe the Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) as a glass sponge (phylum Porifera, class Hexactinellida), not a jellyfish. Its strength comes from its lattice skeleton of silica spicules, not from a 'giant protein.' I found no source saying any protein from this animal can lift 125,000 times its own weight. Searching for that figure only turned up reports on artificial muscles, which lift about 1,000 to 12,600 times their weight.

text: A honeybee colony can lose up to 50% of its adult population during the winter months, yet still maintain its overall strength due to the age structure of its social hierarchy.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources partly support the claim and partly cut against it. Scientificbeekeeping.com says larger colonies lost about half their strength going into winter cluster. Another source says a typical hive loses only 5–10% in an average winter, or 15–20% in a harsh one, and that losses of 30–50% make it hard for a colony to recover. The Nature study finds that the age structure of the winter population matters for survival. But it also says colonies made up mostly of older workers can dwindle and fail. None of the sources confirms that a colony keeps its overall strength after losing up to 50% of its adults because of its age structure. That central causal part of the claim can't be verified.

text: Able-seaman Samuel Platford set a record for the first solo non-stop circumnavigation of the globe by a British sailor in 1785-87 but went unrecognised as the extensive records of his voyage were lost at sea.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record anywhere of an able seaman called Samuel Platford making a solo circumnavigation in 1785–87. The searches turned up only unrelated genealogy pages. Reliable sources contradict the claim's central point instead. Guinness World Records, Wikipedia and Knox-Johnston's official site all say Robin Knox-Johnston, a British sailor, was the first person to sail solo and non-stop around the world, from 14 June 1968 to 22 April 1969. Even the first solo circumnavigation with stops was Joshua Slocum's, in 1895–98. A solo non-stop voyage in the 1780s is therefore not supported and is contradicted by the recognised record.

text: Antarctica has more species of exitiple and possibly living organisms (extremophiles) than any other place on Earth due to its unique subglacial lakes and aquifers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm that Antarctic subglacial lakes contain extremophile microbes. National Geographic reports that Lake Whillans holds nearly 4,000 operational taxonomic units of chemoautotrophs. However, I found no evidence that Antarctica has more extremophile species than any other place on Earth, or that its subglacial lakes and aquifers are the reason. Deep-sea vents, hot springs and the deep subsurface also host large extremophile communities. The claim also uses a nonsense term, 'exitiple'. The core comparison can't be verified.

text: Bacteria are actually more abundant in the human body than human cells themselves.
label: supported
reason: The most-cited current estimate, from Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016), puts a 'reference man' at about 39 trillion bacteria and about 30 trillion human cells. That is roughly 1.3 bacteria per human cell, so bacteria still slightly outnumber human cells. However, this research overturned the old 10:1 figure and showed the two counts are about the same size. Some headlines describe it as busting the 'more bacteria' myth, and the authors note the balance can shift, for example after a bowel movement. The claim is technically supported, but only by a small margin.

text: Bacteria are actually more closely related to humans than plants and are both capable of surviving in extreme environments.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the relationships wrong. Humans and plants both belong to the domain Eukarya, so they are more closely related to each other than either is to bacteria, which sit in a separate domain. Molecular evidence links eukaryotes most closely to a group of archaea, not to bacteria. The well-known 'closer to humans than plants' fact is about fungi, not bacteria. Some bacteria do survive in extreme environments, but the main point about relatedness is false.

text: Butler's Gorge, a major waterfall in Tasmania, Australia, drops water over 300 meters down into the sea due to its varied geological formation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about what Butlers Gorge is. According to Wikipedia and Wikidata, it is a rural locality in Tasmania's inland Central Highlands, at about 667 m above sea level. It is home to the Clark Dam / Lake King William and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. It is not a major waterfall, and it does not drop water 300 m into the sea.

text: Butler's Gorge, a series of waterfalls on the Whanganui River in New Zealand, are one of the most unique waterfall groups in the world, featuring around 27 waterfalls along a 5km stretch.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is in Tasmania, Australia, not on New Zealand's Whanganui River. It is a locality in the Central Highlands next to Clark Dam on the Derwent River, where the Butlers Gorge Power Station sits. No source describes it as a group of about 27 waterfalls along a 5 km stretch.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, holds the world record for the highest waterfall in a straight line, reaching a height of 167 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge really is in Tasmania, but it is a rural locality in the Central Highlands with a dam and power station. It does not hold any waterfall record. The world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, at 979 m total height with a longest single drop of 807 m. That is far more than the 167 m in the claim, so the claim is false.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, is the deepest gorge in the Southern Hemisphere, with a depth of approximately 669 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It is known for the Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station. No source calls it the deepest gorge in the Southern Hemisphere. The roughly 667–669 m figure is the weather station's elevation above sea level (Wikipedia gives 667 m AMSL in the Bureau of Meteorology climate data), not the depth of a gorge. The claim treats an elevation figure as a gorge depth and makes a superlative that no source supports.

text: Buttering a muffin or a piece of toast browning in the toaster helps it stick and gives it a satisfying crunch.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a source that directly supports or contradicts this claim. Food sites say buttering bread before toasting can work in a toaster oven, letting the butter melt into the bread. But Mashed warns against putting buttered bread in a regular pop-up toaster, because the butter melts off onto the electrical parts and could start a fire. None of the results say that butter 'helps it stick,' and the claim never says what is supposed to stick. Because the claim is unclear and only partly addressed by the evidence, it can't be verified.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes due to a unique adaptation that allows them to store oxygen.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Several sources agree that capybaras are the world's largest rodents and can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes. These include One Earth, Rainforest Alliance-type fact pages and capybara information sites. However, I found no reliable source that credits this ability to a 'unique adaptation that allows them to store oxygen.' One informal site says it comes from a drop in heart rate (bradycardia) that makes their oxygen last longer, not from a special way of storing oxygen. Because the cause given in the claim can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils because of its unique properties, which include a low water content, acidity, and the presence of hydrogen peroxide produced by enzymes in the bees' bodies, making it virtually immortal in the food world?
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back every part of the claim. Smithsonian Magazine's explainer on honey's 'eternal shelf life' says honey can stay unspoiled for millennia. It credits this to honey's very low moisture, its acidity, and glucose oxidase, an enzyme from the bee's stomach that produces hydrogen peroxide. Other beekeeping and honey sources say the same thing: about 17–18% water, a pH of roughly 3.2–4.5, and glucose oxidase producing small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. One caveat is that honey can ferment if it soaks up moisture, but the claim's word 'virtually' allows for that. One online commenter disputes the reports that 2,000-year-old honey is still edible, but the claim does not depend on those reports.

text: Did you know that humans and dinosaurs coexisted on Earth for about 150 million years until the mass extinction event that occurred 65 million years ago?
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Discover Magazine says humans and dinosaurs coexisted only "in our imaginations." Modern humans appeared about 300,000 years ago, more than 65 million years after the non-avian dinosaurs died out. Only early mammal ancestors of humans lived alongside dinosaurs. So the two could not have shared the Earth for 150 million years.

text: Giraffes have a unique reproductive strategy, with females often giving birth to twins, which is relatively rare in the animal kingdom and is only common in about 4-5% of mammals.
label: contradicted
reason: Female giraffes normally have a single calf. Twins are extremely rare, not common: Auckland Zoo said only about 30 cases of giraffe twins have been documented worldwide. That contradicts the claim that females often give birth to twins.

text: Glowworms produce their own cold light through a chemical reaction involving a compound called luciferin, which reacts with oxygen to create a glowing effect.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back this claim. A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports (also on PMC) found that New Zealand glowworm light comes from a luciferin–luciferase reaction, which uses oxygen like the firefly system. A glowworm site in Tamborine says glow worms make light by bioluminescence, a chemical reaction that involves luciferin and the enzyme luciferase. This light is well known as 'cold light' because the reaction gives off very little heat. The claim leaves out the enzyme luciferase (and ATP), but that omission doesn't make anything it says wrong.

text: Mitosis, a type of cell division, occurs not only in living organisms but also in plants when they grow new cells to develop flowers or grow leaves from flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats plants as if they were separate from living organisms, but plants are living organisms. It also says leaves grow from flowers, which gets plant development backwards. Mitosis does happen in plant meristems, but botanical sources say these meristems produce leaves and shoots early in the plant's life cycle, and flowers only later, from floral meristems. Leaves do not grow out of flowers. So although mitosis in plants is real, the way the claim describes it is wrong.

text: Mitosis, a type of cell division, occurs not only in living organisms but also in plants when they grow, repairing injuries, or when regenerating damaged tissues.
label: supported
reason: Sources such as BYJU'S say that mitosis drives growth, vegetative propagation in plants, and the repair and regeneration of damaged tissues. Other results also describe plant cells dividing by mitosis to grow, heal wounds and regenerate tissue. The wording "not only in living organisms but also in plants" is odd, since plants are living organisms, but nothing in the claim's substance is contradicted.

text: New Zealand is home to a unique species of dolphin known as the bottlenose dolphin that has been known to form long-lasting social bonds with humans and can be seen swimming alongside boats and interacting with people in a playful manner.
label: contradicted
reason: The bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) does live in New Zealand, but the species is not unique to the country. The Whale and Dolphin Trust says bottlenose dolphins live in most of the world's coastal areas, and research describes the Fiordland population as being at the southern limit of the species' worldwide range. New Zealand's endemic dolphin is Hector's dolphin, including its Māui subspecies, not the bottlenose. The claim's central point, that the bottlenose is a unique New Zealand species, is false.

text: Olympic synchronized swimmers use a technique called "dna" (delayed start of movement) to ensure a synchronized entrance into the water from the springboard.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a technique called "DNA" (delayed start of movement) exists in synchronized/artistic swimming. The claim's premise also looks wrong. Under the World Aquatics artistic swimming rules, routines begin with a walk-on and deck movements, and they may start on the deck or in the water. Swimmers enter from the pool deck, not from a springboard, which is used in synchronized diving. Still, no reliable source directly states that the "DNA" technique doesn't exist, so the specific claim can't be confirmed or firmly disproved.

text: Our brains process visual information more efficiently than text-based information, which is why images can convey complex messages more quickly and effectively than written descriptions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed. Some sources, such as a Medium article on the picture superiority effect, state almost exactly that 'our brains process visual information more efficiently than textual information.' However, the well-established picture superiority effect (see Wikipedia) concerns memory: people remember pictures better than words. It does not show that images convey complex messages faster or better than written descriptions. Fact-checks by Photutorial, PolicyViz and Learnlets debunk the related claim that images are processed '60,000 times faster' than text. Photutorial adds that this 'does not prove a general superiority of images over text' and calls the comparison a false dichotomy. Because the general claim that images communicate complex messages more efficiently is backed by some sources and disputed by others, the evidence does not settle it.

text: Pink mandate has been followed in the Ahwaz, Iran since 1963, to influence the women and maintain their honor and due to this most women wear these blocking burka clothing in public.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a "pink mandate" has ever existed in Ahwaz/Ahvaz or anywhere in Iran. A search for the exact phrase only turned up pages about the US activist group Code Pink. The claim's history is also wrong. In 1963 Iran was under the Shah, whose White Revolution gave women the vote and pushed modernisation and unveiling, not veiling. Compulsory hijab (headscarf) came after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and it does not require burqas. Burqas are not the usual public dress for most women in Ahvaz. The LSE blog on Iran's veiling policy tells this history (the Pahlavi era's unveiling first, mandatory hijab only after 1979), which contradicts the claimed 1963 mandate.

text: Pluto has a highly eccentric orbit that brings it as close as 29.7 astronomical units (AU) from the sun and as far as 49.3 AU from the sun.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia gives Pluto's perihelion as 29.658 AU and its aphelion as 49.305 AU. Rounded, those match the claim's 29.7 AU and 49.3 AU. With an eccentricity of about 0.25, Pluto's orbit is highly eccentric by planetary standards.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious and unexplained natural phenomenon, is a river in the Peruvian Amazon that appears to boil due to unknown geological processes.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is a real river in the Peruvian Amazon, but the claim is wrong to say its heat comes from unknown or unexplained geological processes. Wikipedia says the heat is geothermal and has been studied by geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo, with the main theory pointing to the Earth's geothermal gradient. Other sources say rainwater seeps down through faults, gets heated deep underground, and rises back to the surface without any volcano involved. Some details, such as the exact fault layout, are still being studied, but the basic mechanism is known.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River', is a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that appears to originate from nowhere and flow underground, only to resurface in a different location.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River is real. Its proper name is Shanay-timpishka, and it lies in the Peruvian Amazon. I found no reliable source that calls it the "Hidden River." Wikipedia and geological accounts describe it as an ordinary surface tributary of the Pachitea River. Underground hot springs along its course heat the water: rainwater seeps deep underground, warms, and rises back to the surface as hot springs that feed the river. These sources do not say the river comes from nowhere, flows underground, or resurfaces somewhere else. The underground-river idea seems to mix the Boiling River up with something else, so the claim misdescribes it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the 'Hidden River', is a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains unsolved as to its origins, despite scientists studying it extensively.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources (Wikipedia, YSI, Slate/Atlas Obscura, Geoscopy) say the river's heat source is known. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research and other work on fault-controlled circulation (Taillefer et al.) show that it is geothermal: a non-volcanic hydrothermal system in which water sinks deep underground, heats up, and rises along fault zones. Slate describes the river as a mystery only until Ruzo studied it. This contradicts the claim that its origins remain unsolved. The sources also give its names as Shanay-timpishka, Río Hirviente and Boiling River. None calls it the 'Hidden River'.

text: The Boomerang effect, which was initially observed in physics and refers to the return of an object to its point of origin, also applies to sound waves, where a bird's echo can help it locate its own screech.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and Wiktionary say the 'boomerang effect' comes from social psychology, not physics. It describes persuasion backfiring, so that people move toward the opposite position. It also has related senses in sociology (the 'imperial boomerang') and in unintended consequences generally. None of the sources say the term began in physics as an object returning to its origin. None mention it applying to sound waves or birds using echoes to locate their own screech; that idea is closer to echolocation, a different concept. The claim's account of where the term came from conflicts with these sources.

text: The Debol Mars, a volcano on Mars, has a caldera that is one of the largest on the planet, measuring approximately 80 km wide.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a Martian volcano called "Debol Mars" (or "Debol") exists. Searches for the name turned up only unrelated pages: people named Debol and lists of Mars and lunar craters with different names. Because the claim's subject can't be identified, there's no way to check the caldera size or its ranking. The large calderas the searches did find belong to other volcanoes, such as Olympus Mons and Apollinaris Patera.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a perfect straight line and it is actually 172°East longitude by a slightly longer distance of 180°.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is right: the International Date Line is not a straight line, because it bends east and west around some territories and island groups. The second part is wrong. Wikipedia and NOAA both say the line roughly follows the 180° meridian, and in many places follows it exactly. Neither says it actually runs along 172°E or that 180° is only a 'slightly longer distance' away. The claim's wording is garbled, but its core statement that the line is really at 172°E conflicts with these sources.

text: The Earth's international date line is not a straight line, but rather zigzags through the Pacific Ocean to avoid several island nations.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree on this, including Wikipedia and CBC News. The International Date Line roughly follows the 180° meridian but isn't straight. It bends through the Pacific around Kiribati, Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, Russia and the Aleutian Islands so that a country's islands aren't split across two calendar dates. CBC notes that one of the biggest zigs is around the island nation of Kiribati.

text: The Human Brain contains over 100 billion neurons, with some estimates suggesting a total of 86 billion neurons, and nearly 100 trillion synaptic connections.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the brain has "over 100 billion neurons", but that figure is an outdated estimate. Suzana Herculano-Houzel counted neurons by dissolving brain tissue and counting cell nuclei, and found about 86 billion, which is now the accepted number. BrainFacts.org (from the Society for Neuroscience) and LiveScience describe the 100 billion figure as a myth that doesn't hold up to measurement. The claim also contradicts itself, since 86 billion is less than 100 billion. The figure of roughly 100 trillion synapses is commonly cited, but because the main neuron figure is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: The Human Brain contains over 100 billion neurons, with some estimates suggesting a total of 86 billion neurons, but each neuron is connected to an average of 7,000 other neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself. It says the brain has over 100 billion neurons, then gives 86 billion as an estimate, which is less than 100 billion. Herculano-Houzel's direct cell counts put the figure at about 86 billion, and the reporting describes the old 100 billion figure as a decades-long overestimate. So the 'over 100 billion' part is contradicted. The figure of roughly 7,000 synaptic connections per neuron is commonly cited, but the false neuron count is enough to make the claim contradicted overall.

text: The Human Brain processes and stores vast amounts of information throughout a person's lifetime, and it's estimated that it contains over 70 billion neurons.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as PMC/NIH and Nature Scitable give the widely accepted estimate of about 86 billion neurons in the human brain, which is more than 70 billion. A 2025 PMC article questions how precise that figure is and gives a possible range starting at about 61 billion. Even so, the standard estimate is still 86 billion, so the claim of "over 70 billion" holds. The claim's other point, that the brain processes and stores vast amounts of information over a lifetime, is uncontroversial.

text: The Tongue of the Ocean, located near the Bahamas, is the world's second-largest artificial harbor and was created by the US Navy in the 1950s and 1960s.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The EU Space Programme (Copernicus) describes the Tongue of the Ocean as a natural deep oceanic trench between shallow limestone banks, running between Andros Island and the Exuma Cays. It is not an artificial harbor, and the US Navy did not build it. The Navy does run the AUTEC test range there, but that does not mean it created the feature.

text: The Tongue of the Ocean, located off the coast of the Bahamas, is the world's second-largest navy tank dumping area, where equipment and waste were historically disposed of.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources confirm that the Tongue of the Ocean is a deep oceanic trench in the Bahamas, between Andros and New Providence. It is used by the US Navy for the test ranges of the Atlantic Undersea Test and Evaluation Center (AUTEC). None of the sources I found, including Wikipedia, Copernicus and Gizmodo, describe it as a navy tank dumping area, let alone the world's second-largest, or say that equipment and waste were dumped there. No source directly disproves the claim either, so the dumping claim can't be verified. My search was cut short by the search limit before I finished looking for dumping-specific sources.

text: The ancient Egyptians used a combination of mathematical concepts and astronomical observations to create their calendar system, with divisions for 365 days in a year and an extra 5.25 days to account for the leap year.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days in total: twelve 30-day months (360 days) plus 5 extra 'epagomenal' days. It did not add 5.25 days, and it had no leap year. EBSCO says the Egyptians 'did not incorporate leap years,' so the calendar drifted by a quarter-day each year, and PlanetCalc lists 'Leap year: none.' The part about astronomical observation, such as tracking the rising of Sothis (Sirius), is accurate. But the claim of an extra 5.25 days to account for a leap year is wrong.

text: The ancient Egyptians were known to use a device called the "atmospheric water generator" to collect and purify water from the air as early as 2500 BCE.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources describe the atmospheric water generator as a modern machine. One source says AWG history is "relatively recent": American engineers developed it in the late 1990s, and the first commercial units went on sale in 2000. Wikipedia and HowStuffWorks also present AWGs as modern machines that pull water from the air. Studies of ancient Egyptian water management mention the Nile, canals, wells, the shadouf, rainwater tanks and drainage systems. None of them mentions Egyptians collecting water from the air around 2500 BCE. The claim is anachronistic and conflicts with the documented history of the technology.

text: The ancient Egyptians were known to use a device called the "atmospheric water generator" to collect and purify water from the air in their habitats, primarily in their temples and homes.
label: contradicted
reason: There's no evidence that ancient Egyptians used an "atmospheric water generator." Wikipedia and HowStuffWorks describe the AWG as a modern machine that pulls water from humid air by refrigeration-style condensation or desiccants, much like an air conditioner. Neither credits Egypt with collecting water from the air. Wikipedia credits the Incas with collecting dew into cisterns, and HowStuffWorks says passive air wells are widely believed to have been used by the ancient Greeks.
