Wikipedia's history of water filters says Egyptian depictions at Thebes show water being treated with substances such as alum, not drawn from the air. The claim is therefore anachronistic and conflicts with the documented history.

text: The ancient Egyptians were known to use a device called the "atmospheric water generator" to collect and purify water from the air.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found says the ancient Egyptians used an "atmospheric water generator." The term refers to a modern machine that cools air below its dew point with a refrigerant compressor, or uses chemical desiccants, to condense drinking water out of humid air. Moses West is one modern inventor who developed such a device. Wikipedia's history of water collection from air mentions the Incas collecting dew, fog fences, and air wells in Middle Eastern deserts going back at least 2,000 years, but not Egyptian atmospheric water generators. Sources on ancient Egyptian water treatment describe methods for treating water they already had, such as filtering it, not drawing water from the air. Because the device is modern technology, the claim is false.

text: The baku is a type of fox found in East Asia, which is known for its unique ability to survive the extreme cold of its native regions by producing a thick layer of heat-generating fat.
label: contradicted
reason: The baku is not a real fox or any real animal. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia's "Baku (mythology)" article describe it as a mythical creature from Chinese and Japanese folklore that eats dreams and nightmares. It is usually shown as a mix of animals, with an elephant's trunk, a tiger's paws and an ox's tail. Nothing links it to foxes, to surviving extreme cold, or to heat-generating fat.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to Worm's Head, a unique natural limestone arch that is completely submerged at high tide and only visible at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Worm's Head is a tidal island off the end of Rhossili Bay. It is not itself a limestone arch, although it does have a natural rock arch on it called Devil's Bridge. It is also not completely submerged at high tide. Only the causeway linking it to the mainland goes underwater, which cuts the island off, but the island stays visible.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to Worm's Head, a unique natural limestone arch that is completely submerged at high tide.
label: contradicted
reason: Worm's Head is not a natural arch, and it is not completely submerged at high tide. Wikipedia and Coflein describe it as a limestone tidal headland made up of three islands (Inner, Middle and Outer Head). Only the rocky causeway to the mainland goes under water, so high tide cuts the headland off without covering it. The natural arch, Devil's Bridge, is just one feature on Worm's Head. The claim is right that Worm's Head is limestone and sits at Rhossili Bay in Wales.

text: The brightest planet in our night sky, Venus, is often difficult to spot due to its extreme brightness because its thick atmosphere scatters and reflects sunlight in all directions.
label: contradicted
reason: Several trustworthy sources say Venus is easy to see because it is so bright. National Geographic calls it an 'extraordinarily bright, steady point of light' that 'should be easy to spot, even during dusk', and LoveTheNightSky says finding it 'is not hard'. Caltech's Cool Cosmos does back the claim that Venus's thick clouds reflect most sunlight (about 70%), which is why it is so bright. But that brightness makes Venus easy to spot, not difficult. Venus can be hard to see at times, but that happens when it sits close to the Sun in the sky, not because it is too bright. So the claim that its extreme brightness makes it hard to spot is contradicted.

text: The brightest planet in our night sky, Venus, is often difficult to spot due to its extreme brightness because its thick atmosphere scatters and reflects sunlight.
label: contradicted
reason: National Geographic says Venus is the brightest planet in our sky and that its reflective cloud cover is what makes it so bright. It also says Venus appears as a bright, steady point of light that "should be easy to spot, even during dusk." That contradicts the claim's main point: Venus's brightness makes it easy to see, not hard to spot. The difficulty in seeing Venus comes from it sitting close to the Sun and low on the horizon, not from its brightness.

text: The crystal-clear waters of the Great Blue Hole in Belize are home to a vast array of marine life, including sharks, stingrays, and colorful tropical fish.
label: supported
reason: Several dive and travel sources describe the Great Blue Hole and its rim as having clear water and plenty of marine life. Belizehub lists tropical fish such as angelfish, butterflyfish, groupers and parrotfish, along with Caribbean reef, nurse and blacktip sharks. Marine Insight mentions the 'crystal clear water' and several shark species. Scubago's species list for the Great Blue Hole site includes stingray sightings. One caveat: Scubago says the dive is more about the rock formations than the wildlife, and the deep interior has little life, so 'vast array' is a bit generous. Still, the reef around the rim supports the main parts of the claim: sharks, stingrays and colorful tropical fish.

text: The driest desert in the world is Antarctica, which contains over 70% of the Earth's freshwater in the form of ice.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The freshwater part checks out. Britannica, Wikipedia and WorldAtlas say Antarctica holds about 70% of the world's fresh water, and Wikipedia's 'Climate of Antarctica' page says 'more than 70%'. The 'driest desert' part is disputed. Antarctica is often called the driest continent, and History.com notes parts of it are drier than the Atacama. But NASA Astrobiology says the Atacama is 'probably also the driest desert in the world', and Discovery and WorldAtlas call the Atacama the driest place on Earth. EarthDate names both the Atacama and Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys as the driest deserts. Because reliable sources disagree, the claim that Antarctica is the driest desert can't be confirmed.

text: The highest mountain in the solar system, as of our current knowledge, is Olympus Mons on Mars, which stands at a height of approximately 27 km.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the claim overall, though the 27 km figure is at the high end. Guinness World Records names Olympus Mons on Mars the highest mountain in the solar system. Current sources measure it at about 21.9 km above the Martian datum and about 25–26 km from base to summit. Older references often give about 27 km, so 'approximately 27 km' is close to the base-to-summit figure. One caveat: Wikipedia says Olympus Mons is roughly tied with the central peak of Rheasilvia on the asteroid Vesta (about 19–22 km), but it is still widely called the tallest known mountain.

text: The highest mountain in the solar system, as of our current knowledge, is Olympus Mons on Mars, which stands at an impressive 27 km high.
label: contradicted
reason: Olympus Mons is often called the tallest mountain in the solar system, but the 27 km height is wrong. Wikipedia gives about 21.9 km above the Martian datum, or about 26 km of local relief above the surrounding plains. Other sources give 21.9 km (Science Focus, Study.com) or 24 km (Caltech's Cool Cosmos). Wikipedia and Science Focus also say Olympus Mons is roughly tied with, or slightly shorter than, the central peak of the Rheasilvia crater on the asteroid Vesta (about 22.5 km), so it is not clearly the single highest mountain either.

text: The lengths of the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt are so precisely aligned with the four cardinal directions (north, south, east, and west) that their shadows align on an inner chamber's floor at the summer solstice.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm the first part of the claim. The Giza pyramids line up with north, south, east and west with great precision. The Great Pyramid is off by only about 0.067°, or a few arcminutes, according to Newsweek, an arXiv paper and Astronomy.com. However, I found no reliable source saying their shadows line up on an inner chamber's floor at the summer solstice. The solstice alignment that is documented is different: seen from the Sphinx, the sun sets over the pyramids at the winter solstice. The shadow claim also seems physically unlikely, because the inner chambers are enclosed and sunlight does not reach their floors. Still, I found no source that directly rules it out. Since part of the claim cannot be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: The lengths of the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt match the unusual mathematical ratio of Phi (1.618) with remarkable precision.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including a Springer (Nexus Network Journal) article, give the Great Pyramid of Khufu as about 146.5 m tall with a base of about 230.4 m. With those measurements, its slant height (186.37 m) divided by half its base (115.18 m) is about 1.618, which matches Phi to several decimal places. Other sources, such as goldennumber.net, report the same match. The claim fits the Great Pyramid; the other Giza pyramids have different slopes. Whether the builders chose this ratio on purpose is still debated, but the claim is only about the numerical match, and the measurements support it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge System, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible above sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part checks out. Sources agree the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and stretches about 65,000 km or more. The claim that it is "not visible above sea level" is wrong, though. WorldAtlas says the Mid-Atlantic Ridge crest rises above the water at Jan Mayen island, and other sources say Iceland is the largest part of the ridge exposed above sea level. The ridge is mostly underwater, but not completely.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the center of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) and say it winds through the world's oceans between the continents. Two details are slightly off: these sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, not 'over', though other NOAA pages say 'more than 65,000 km', and the ridge does not run exactly through the center of the Pacific. These are minor differences, so the claim is broadly correct.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers across the oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and is about 65,000 km long. NOAA Ocean Service puts it at 40,389 miles (about 65,000 km), and Wikipedia gives about 65,000 km. One caveat on wording: NOAA Ocean Explorer and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km', not 'over'. Since this is only a small rounding difference around the same widely cited figure, the claim is supported overall.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for approximately 40,389 miles (65,000 kilometers).
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth and says it stretches nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI and Wikipedia give the same figure of about 65,000 km. The claim's 40,389 miles is just a slightly different conversion of 65,000 km and matches these sources.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, "stretching nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 miles)." WorldAtlas gives a similar length of about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Both sources back the claim that the ridge is the longest mountain range and runs more than 40,000 miles (about 64,000 km) around the globe. The figures differ only slightly: NOAA's 40,390 miles is just over 40,000 miles, which fits the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which surrounds the globe and is approximately 65,000 kilometers long.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration, a reliable government source, says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It says the ridge "wraps around the globe like seams on a baseball" and stretches nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). That matches every part of the claim.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). Guinness World Records and WHOI give about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). That fits the claim of more than 40,000 miles (about 64,000 km). The figures differ only slightly from source to source, and none of them contradicts the claim.

text: The longest planet in our solar system, Neptune, has a diameter of approximately 49,528 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The diameter is right: NASA gives Neptune's equatorial diameter as 49,528 km. But the claim calls Neptune the largest ("longest") planet in the solar system, and that is wrong. Jupiter is the largest planet, at about 142,984 km across, and Neptune ranks fourth by diameter, after Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus.

text: The longest planet in our solar system, Neptune, is approximately 49,528 kilometers (30,777 miles) in diameter, making it slightly smaller than Uranus.
label: contradicted
reason: The diameter is right: Neptune is about 49,528 km across, slightly smaller than Uranus at 51,118 km. But the claim calls Neptune the longest, or largest, planet in the solar system, and that is wrong. NASA and WorldAtlas say Jupiter is the largest planet, at about 142,984 km across, and that Neptune is the fourth largest. The claim also contradicts itself by calling Neptune the largest planet while saying it is smaller than Uranus.

text: The longest planet in our solar system, Neptune, is approximately 49,528 kilometers (30,777 miles) in diameter.
label: contradicted
reason: The diameter is right but the main premise is wrong. Neptune's diameter is about 49,528 km, but Neptune is not the biggest planet in the solar system. Jupiter is the largest, at about 142,800 km across. Neptune is fourth-largest, behind Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus (51,118 km). Because the claim calls Neptune the largest ('longest') planet, it is contradicted.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "strengthen"
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Strengthen" has two syllables (strength-en), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. Wikipedia's list of the longest English words with one syllable names 10-letter candidates such as "scraunched", and notes that the answer is somewhat subjective. Guinness World Records cites "strengths" (9 letters), not "strengthen", as a related record holder: the longest word with only one vowel.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable, according to the Oxford English Dictionary, is 'stewardess', but often the word "scuba" is mentioned as the word with one syllable in many contexts.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. 'Stewardess' has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It is usually cited as the longest word you can type with only the left hand. Wikipedia's list of the longest one-syllable English words names candidates like 'strengthed' (10 letters, found in the OED) and 'scraunched', which Guinness lists alongside 'strengthed'. 'Scuba' (scu-ba) has two syllables, so it isn't a one-syllable word either.

text: The oldest known piece of wooden furniture is the Sorghum wooden boat dating to around 820 BCE found in China's Xi'an city.
label: contradicted
reason: No source mentions a "Sorghum wooden boat" from Xi'an dating to about 820 BCE. The only wooden boat found at Xi'an is "Silk Road No.1", which dates from the Han Dynasty (202 BC–220 AD), not 820 BCE. A boat is also not furniture. Wooden furniture much older than 820 BCE is well documented, for example beds, chairs and chests from Egyptian tombs dated to around 3100 BC.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. These include UC Davis's hummingbird health program, WorldAtlas, Sciencing, A-Z Animals and CGTN. The same sources tie this to the bird's unusual anatomy. Hummingbirds have a ball-and-socket or rotator-cuff-like shoulder joint that lets them pivot and rotate their wings about 180 degrees, so they move the wings back and forth in a figure-eight instead of just up and down. One caveat: WorldAtlas and BirdSpot note that herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for short distances. Hummingbirds are the only birds that can truly fly backwards under their own power and keep it up, which is how the claim is generally meant, so the core claim holds.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), CGTN and A-Z Animals, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. CGTN and other sources link this to the bird's figure-eight wing movement, which comes from its ability to rotate its wings (about 180 degrees, according to A-Z Animals). One caveat: some sites, such as Birdspot and Gardenbird, say other birds can flutter backwards for a second or two. However, they agree that only hummingbirds can sustain controlled backward flight, so the claim holds in its usual sense.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the hummingbird, due to its unique wing movement and the ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards, including the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine's Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program, WorldAtlas, CGTN and Sciencing. They put this down to the birds' unusual wing anatomy: wings that rotate about 180 degrees at the shoulder and move in a figure-eight pattern, which lets them push air forward. That matches both the 'only bird' part of the claim and the reason it gives. One caveat: some sources (BirdSpot, WorldAtlas) note that herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for short distances. However, they still describe hummingbirds as the only birds capable of true, sustained backward flight, so the claim holds overall.

text: The polarity-reversal event that occurred around 41,000 years ago is one reason why the Earth's magnetic field has been steadily weakening over time.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources confirm a reversal around 41,000 years ago, called the Laschamp(s) excursion, but they describe it as temporary. It lasted about 2,000 years, and the field was flipped for roughly 440 years. During that time, field strength fell to about 5–10% of today's value and then recovered. The sources give it no lasting role in how the field behaves today, and the field has not weakened steadily since then. It is much stronger now than it was during the excursion. The claim's cause-and-effect link (that the 41,000-year-old event is a reason for steady weakening) is therefore contradicted.

text: The shallowest lake in the world, as measured by its maximum depth of approximately 3.3 meters, is Chad's Lake Assal.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Assal is in Djibouti, not Chad. Its maximum depth is more than 40 m, with an average depth of about 7.4 m, so it does not have a maximum depth of about 3.3 m. It is known as Africa's lowest point and one of the world's saltiest lakes, not as the world's shallowest lake.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Egyptian "Bi Brian" gold magnetic rings, at the British Museum, have shown a magnetic field strength of 2,200 years old that is capable of lifting a paper clip.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that Ancient Egyptian "Bi Brian" gold magnetic rings exist at the British Museum. The claim also doesn't hold together: gold isn't magnetic, and "2,200 years old" is an age, not a measure of field strength. Reliable sources name the strongest known magnets as man-made lab magnets, such as MagLab's superconducting and resistive magnets and the 100-tesla pulsed magnet at Los Alamos. The strongest naturally occurring magnet is magnetite, and the strongest fields in the universe come from magnetars. None of these are ancient rings, so the claim that the rings are the strongest known magnet is contradicted.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Greek Magnets from Magnesia, is estimated to have a magnetic field strength of over 17 times that of any other known magnet.
label: contradicted
reason: The record-holding magnets are modern lab electromagnets, not ancient Greek lodestones from Magnesia. One example is the 45.22-tesla hybrid magnet built in China in 2022, and another is a 42-tesla resistive magnet from Hefei. Natural lodestones like those linked to Magnesia are weak, so the claim that they are the strongest known magnets, with fields over 17 times those of any other magnet, is false.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Greek cities of Magnesia, was believed to have enough magnetic properties that they could magnetize any iron object.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different things. The cities of Magnesia were not magnets. According to Wiktionary and a UT Austin physics lecture, the word "magnet" comes from lodestone, or "Magnesian stone," which was named after Magnesia, a city in Asia Minor or a Greek region. That makes Magnesia the source of the name, not a magnet. Lodestone, a natural form of magnetite, was the first known permanent magnet, but it is not the strongest one. Modern rare-earth (neodymium) magnets and astrophysical magnetars are far stronger. The sources also say nothing about the cities being able to magnetize any iron object.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) around the Earth.
label: supported
reason: The claim checks out. Guinness World Records and WorldAtlas both name the mid-ocean ridge as the longest mountain range on Earth. Guinness puts its length at 65,000 km (40,000 miles), and WorldAtlas says it runs about 65,000 km (40,000 miles), more than 1.5 times Earth's circumference, winding through every major ocean basin. Some sources say 'about' or 'nearly' 65,000 km instead of 'over', but that is a minor wording difference. Estimates that count the whole ridge system go higher still, so the main point of the claim holds.

text: There are approximately 200 billion trees on Earth, with the Amazon rainforest alone being home to around 390 billion individual tree trunks.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Nature study led by Thomas Crowther (Yale) puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. That is far more than the 200 billion in the claim; even the older global estimate was over 400 billion. The Amazon figure of about 390 billion trees matches widely cited research, but it also exposes a problem with the claim: one region cannot have more trees than the whole planet. Because the global total is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are approximately 7.9 billion people living on Earth, which is roughly one-sixth of the total number of all humans who have ever existed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 7.9–8 billion population figure is roughly right, but the 'one-sixth' part is wrong. The Population Reference Bureau (PRB) estimates that about 109–117 billion people have ever been born, so people alive today make up only about 7% of that total, or roughly one-fourteenth to one-fifteenth. One-sixth would be about 16.7%. The World Economic Forum and Visual Capitalist cite the same figure of about 7%.

text: There are more atoms in a single grain of sand than there are grains of sand in all the deserts on Earth.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the claim as it is usually stated. The most widely cited estimate, credited to University of Hawaii researchers, puts all sand on Earth's beaches and deserts at about 7.5 quintillion (7.5×10^18) grains. Several sources estimate that one typical sand grain holds about 4×10^19 to 1×10^20 atoms: Lancelhoff gives 4.17×10^19 for a 1 mm quartz grain, Quora and FunFactz give similar figures, and Conceptual Academy gives about 1.25×10^20. That is more than the estimated number of desert grains. There are caveats. Atom counts depend on grain size: a fine 0.1 mm grain has only about 4×10^16 atoms. Sand-count estimates are also very uncertain, and one South African Institute of Physics post reached the opposite conclusion. Still, most sources support the claim for a typical grain.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with approximately 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 86 billion neurons is right, but the comparison is backwards. Nature Scitable (Bradley Voytek) gives current estimates of 200 to 400 billion stars in the Milky Way, which is more than 86 billion. Even the low estimate of about 100 billion stars cited by the Bell Museum is higher than the neuron count. The galaxy has more stars than the brain has neurons, not the other way around.

text: There are more than 1.3 million species of animals, plants, and fungi that have been identified and classified on Earth, which is estimated to be a very small fraction of the total number of species that exist.
label: supported
reason: The sources mostly back both parts of the claim. Our World in Data says the IUCN Red List counted about 2.16–2.17 million described species in 2025, or about 1.7 million after allowing for duplicate names. A PMC review gives about 1.5 million, and another PMC paper gives about 1.7 million multicellular species. All of these are above 1.3 million. The older Mora et al. (2011) estimate counted only 1.2 million described species, but newer counts put the figure higher. On the second part, Mora et al. estimate that about 86% of species are still undescribed (8.7 million in total), and other estimates run into the billions or trillions. That makes the described species a small fraction of the total. Calling it a 'very small' fraction is somewhat subjective, but it fits the scientific consensus.

text: There are more than 300 million trees along the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, but also in the Amazon rainforest in Brazil, South America.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The Amazon part holds up: several sources estimate the Amazon rainforest has about 390 billion trees, which is far more than 300 million. The Great Barrier Reef part could not be checked. The reef is a marine coral system. Its islands support plant species and mangroves, but no source gives a tree count for the reef or says there are more than 300 million trees along it. Because one part of the claim can't be verified, the overall claim is inconclusive.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the observable universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because it mixes up the Milky Way with the whole observable universe. Earth has about 3 trillion trees (3×10^12), going by the 2015 global tree count published in Nature. That is more than the roughly 100–400 billion stars in our own galaxy, which is where the popular fact comes from. Sources such as WorldAtlas say this outright. The observable universe, though, holds hundreds of billions to trillions of galaxies, for a total of about 10^22–10^24 stars. That is billions of times more than the number of trees. One search result also says directly that Earth does not have more trees than the universe has stars, and that 'the gap there is not close.'

text: There are over 10 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but scientists estimate that up to 80 percent of them remain undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: My searches mostly back the claim, though its numbers are loosely worded. In a New York Times piece reposted by the E.O. Wilson Foundation, Wilson says a widely accepted estimate puts the number of living species at about 10 million, with only about 20% known and 80% undiscovered. Other estimates support the general point: the Mora et al. figure reported by Nature is 8.7 million species with more than 80% undiscovered, and some estimates run much higher, up to a trillion species if microbes are counted. The figures don't line up exactly with the claim. The best-known estimate (8.7 million) is below 10 million, and the undiscovered share is often given as 80–90%, so 'up to 80%' may understate it. Still, the claim matches Wilson's mainstream estimate closely enough to count as supported.

text: There are over 100 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone, with the estimated number of stars in the observable universe being significantly higher.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and WorldAtlas give the Milky Way 100 to 400 billion stars, and NASA and the University of Arizona put it at roughly 100 billion. That fits the claim of "over 100 billion," with the caveat that the low-end estimates are about 100 billion rather than clearly above it. The University of Arizona also says there are at least 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, so the total number of stars there is far higher.

text: There are over 64 million species of plants and animals estimated to exist on Earth, yet only about 1.3 million have been formally described by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no support for the claim's "over 64 million" figure. The best-known estimate, from Mora et al. in 2011 and reported by ScienceDaily and the California Academy of Sciences, puts the total at about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million. That 1.3 million is the margin of error, not the number of described species, so the claim may have mixed the two up. Wikipedia also notes that most estimates are around 11 million species or fewer. Some figures run much higher (up to 1 trillion), but those count microbes and are not estimates of "plants and animals." Current counts of described species are about 1.2–2.2 million, depending on the source. Because the claim's central number is far above mainstream estimates, I judged it contradicted.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high pH levels that it can turn animals that die in it into stone statues due to its ability to preserve their bodies through alkaptonemia.

reason: Lake Natron in Tanzania is real. It is a very alkaline soda lake (pH up to about 10.5), and animals that die on its shores end up looking like stone. Alkaptonemia (properly called alkaptonuria) is a genetic disorder that affects how the body breaks down certain amino acids, and it has nothing to do with preserving carcasses. The preservation comes from natron, a mix of sodium carbonate salts, which calcifies and mummifies the bodies.

Wikipedia's article on the check pattern says the design has no single definitive origin and appears in weaving as a byproduct of the process, which doesn't confirm the claim. text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has the most dense and coarse fur of any mammal, sometimes weighing down the animal's limbs and tails by as much as 70% of their body weight.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Guinness World Records says the sea otter (Enhydra lutris) has the densest fur of any mammal, at about 100,000–160,000 hairs per square centimetre. Other sources also call the sea otter the furriest animal on Earth. No reliable source mentions a "comfortless waterhog," and none says a water shrew holds this record. I also found nothing supporting the claim that fur can make up 70% of an animal's body weight.

text: The longest anaphase ever recorded in a cell lasted 34.5 minutes in a type of Mustard plant cell.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms or refutes this claim. Searches turned up no record of a "longest anaphase ever recorded," no 34.5-minute figure, and no link to mustard plant cells. The sources I did find only give typical stage lengths, such as anaphase lasting about 5 minutes in pea root cells. That makes the specific record and number impossible to verify, and the claim may be made up.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is actually the mid-ocean ridge system that runs around the entire globe on Earth and total length is about 65,000 kilometers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources back up the Earth part of the claim. NOAA, WHOI and AMNH all say the global mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,390 miles). However, every one of these sources limits the record to Earth ("the longest mountain range on Earth" or "in the world"). None of the trustworthy sources I found calls it the longest mountain range in the solar system. The solar system lists I found rank mountains by height, such as Olympus Mons, not ranges by length. Because the 'solar system' part could not be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is actually the mid-ocean ridge system that runs around the entire globe on Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: NOAA, WHOI and AMNH all say the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA puts its length at about 40,389 miles and describes it as wrapping around the globe like the seam of a baseball, so the Earth part of the claim is well supported. The claim goes further and calls it the longest range in the whole solar system. None of the results I found says that, and none compares it with mountain ranges on other planets or moons. The solar-system results I found cover only the tallest mountains, such as Olympus Mons, not the longest ranges. A follow-up search aimed at this point was cut off by the search tool's usage limit. The solar-system claim may well be true, but these sources don't verify it.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) and is not visible above the ocean surface.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, at roughly 65,000 km (about 40,389 miles). It describes the length as "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over" 65,000 km. The claim is still wrong to say the ridge isn't visible above the ocean surface. NOAA says only about 90% of the ridge system is underwater, so part of it rises above sea level. Iceland is the best-known example, since it sits on the exposed Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs along the floor of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, about 40,389 miles (roughly 65,000 km) long. NOAA Ocean Explorer, WorldAtlas and Wikipedia also give about 65,000 km and describe a system running through all the major ocean basins, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific. One wording difference: NOAA Ocean Explorer says 'nearly 65,000 km', while the claim says 'over 65,000 km'. Because other sources give the length as about 65,000 km, this is a small rounding difference rather than a real contradiction.

text: The plankton in the Sargasso Sea are a midnight blue color due to a combination of bioluminescent dinoflagellates and the high concentration of a substance called water fleas.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe the Sargasso Sea's water, not its plankton, as deep blue. The colour comes from the water's exceptional clarity (visibility up to about 61 m), which reflects how few plankton there are. Bioluminescent dinoflagellates and 'water fleas' play no part in it. The claim is also wrong that water fleas are a 'substance': they are small crustaceans such as Daphnia, found mostly in fresh water. No source supports the claimed explanation.

text: The short-lived but spectacular emerald rainbow, also known as "Moonbow," occurs when the Moon is full and is shining brightly in the sky but at a very low angle.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, Almanac.com and Farmers' Almanac back the conditions in the claim. A moonbow forms from moonlight, most likely near a full Moon, when the Moon is low in the sky (below 42°) and the night is dark. But they describe it as a lunar or moon rainbow: faint, and usually looking whitish to the human eye because the light is dim. None of them call it an "emerald rainbow" or say it is green. Calling a moonbow an "emerald rainbow" is a false description, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The sugar ants do not eat sugar, their name comes from their propensity to battle over sweet substances.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Wikipedia and iNaturalist both say the banded sugar ant (Camponotus consobrinus), also called the sugar ant, gets its common name from its liking for sugar and sweet food, plus the orange-brown band around its gaster. So these ants do eat sugar, and the name has nothing to do with fighting over sweet substances.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km. The system runs through all the major ocean basins, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. That fits the claim, although "middle of the oceans" is a loose way to put it, since the East Pacific Rise is not in the centre of the Pacific.

text: The 粉алом SERVER forest in Ecuador is home to a species of orchid that is found nowhere else, and is called the Coelia cuprea.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't identify the place the claim is about. "粉алом SERVER forest" is garbled text that mixes Chinese, Cyrillic and English, and it doesn't match any known forest in Ecuador. I also found no record of an orchid called "Coelia cuprea." Searching for that name only turned up Coelogyne cuprea, a Southeast Asian (Bornean) orchid. Separately, the genus Coelia is generally known from Central America and the Caribbean rather than Ecuador, though that comes from background knowledge and not the search. Because the location can't be identified and the species can't be verified, the claim can't be judged.

text: There are approximately 170 million trees in the streets of Paris, France, known as the "Green Lung" which account for nearly 40% of the city's total green space.
label: contradicted
reason: Paris does not have anywhere near 170 million street trees. FUSAC counts about 484,000 public trees in the whole city, and only around 96,500 of them line streets. The rest are in parks, cemeteries and the Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes. The figure of 170,000 that shows up in sources is the city's planting target for 2026, not 170 million street trees. The claim is off by about three orders of magnitude.

text: There are currently more neurons in the brain of an octopus than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. An octopus has about 500 million neurons across its whole body, and only about a third of them are in its central brain. The Milky Way, by widely accepted estimates, has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. That means the Milky Way has hundreds of times more stars than an octopus has neurons, and even more compared with the neurons in its brain alone.

text: There is an estimated 1.5 trillion now-dead trees on Earth, which is roughly 11 times the number of trees currently existing.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's numbers don't work. The widely cited 2015 Nature study led by Crowther, as reported by EarthSky and Phys.org, estimates about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth today. A figure of 1.5 trillion is about half that number, not "roughly 11 times" it. The same study says tree numbers have fallen by about 46% since farming began, which would mean roughly 2.6–3 trillion trees lost, not 1.5 trillion that equal 11 times today's total. The claimed ratio is contradicted by these sources.

text: There is an estimated 1.5 trillion now-dead trees on Earth, which is roughly 11 times the number of trees that are currently alive.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Crowther et al. study in Nature puts the number of living trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. That means 1.5 trillion dead trees would be about half the number of living trees, not about 11 times as many, so the claim contradicts itself on the arithmetic. The same study says tree numbers have fallen about 46% since the start of human civilization. That suggests a loss of roughly 2.6 trillion trees, not 1.5 trillion, and the search turned up no source for the 1.5 trillion or 11-times figures.

text: Vesta, the second smallest planet in our solar system, has a highly eccentric elliptical orbit that causes its distance from the Sun to vary significantly throughout the year.
label: contradicted
reason: Vesta (4 Vesta) isn't a planet. It's a main-belt asteroid, the second-largest one after the dwarf planet Ceres. Its orbital eccentricity is about 0.089, which is only moderate, not highly eccentric. Its orbital period is also about 3.6 years, so any change in its distance from the Sun doesn't happen 'throughout the year'. Mars, not Vesta, is the second smallest planet.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly after eating tend to be less hungry sooner, potentially due to increased insulin sensitivity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a study showing that people who walk more quickly after eating are less hungry sooner, or that insulin sensitivity is the reason. The evidence I found is mixed. Some studies and articles say brisk walking can curb cravings or appetite, including a 15-minute brisk-walk craving study and BYU work on how the brain responds to food. But King et al. found an acute bout of brisk walking did not change appetite, energy intake or acylated ghrelin. A trial in people with type 2 diabetes also found no appetite or energy-intake differences after walking. Research on walking after meals mostly shows lower blood sugar spikes and better insulin response, not lower hunger. The specific comparison and mechanism in the claim remain unverified.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly after eating tend to be more satisfied with their meal.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no study showing that people who walk faster after eating feel more satisfied with their meal, which is the specific evidence the claim relies on. The closest research I found is mixed or unrelated. Brisk walking can lower brain responses to food cues and craving for chocolate (Dummies/BYU). A 60-minute brisk walk did not change subjective appetite (hunger, fullness, satisfaction) or energy intake (King et al., 2010, MSSE). A randomized trial of moderate walking after meals found that satiety depended on the type of meal, not on walking (Nutrients 2019). Without evidence for the cited link between post-meal walking speed and meal satisfaction, the claim can't be confirmed.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly after eating tend to eat smaller portions and feel fuller longer due to increased blood flow and digestive movement.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no study showing what the claim describes: that people who walk faster after eating eat smaller portions and stay full longer because of increased blood flow and digestive movement. The closest controlled study (King et al., 2010, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise) found that 60 minutes of brisk walking did not change hunger, later food intake or levels of ghrelin, a hormone that stimulates appetite. In other words, brisk walking did not make people hungrier, but it also did not reduce how much they ate or make them feel fuller. Other sources say only that walking after meals may help digestion, bloating and blood sugar (National Geographic mentions more blood flow to digestive organs), or that walking may reduce cravings (a Dummies article citing a BYU study). None of them show the portion-size or longer-fullness effect. The general idea is loosely related to some evidence, but the specific causal claim is not verified, and the King study points partly against it.

text: Walking quickly can help reduce extreme hunger, as studies have shown that people who walk more quickly have a lower frequency of eating.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no study showing that people who walk faster eat less often, which is the main evidence the claim relies on. The evidence on brisk walking and hunger is mixed. Small experiments (Ledochowski et al.; the Appetite 2012 workplace study) found that a 15-minute brisk walk reduced sugary-snack cravings and chocolate snacking. Other trials (MSSE 2010; McIver et al. 2018) found brisk walking did not change appetite, food intake or hunger hormones. None of these studies looked at walking speed in relation to how often people eat, and none addressed 'extreme hunger.' The claim may have mixed up walking speed with eating speed, since studies on slow eating do link it to less hunger.

text: Butler's Gorge, a major waterfall in Tasmania, Australia, drops water over 300 meters down into the sea, making it one of the largest waterfalls of its type in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Butlers Gorge is not a waterfall. Wikipedia and Wikidata describe it as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It sits about 667 m above sea level, well inland, and is known for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. It does not drop water 300 m into the sea, and it is not one of the world's largest waterfalls.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and bubble like a pot of water, is located in the depths of the Amazon rainforest in Peru.

Other reports, including one from earth.com, describe it as a very hot river in the Amazon rainforest of Peru. The water does not reach a true boil, but the claim only says it "appears" to boil, so that wording is fair.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life called "Werthamia" found in only one place on Earth, specific to the Lake Qarun, Lake Manzala and lake Timsha in certain arid regions.

text: The strongest known magnet, the two Ancient Greek Magnets from Magnesia, is estimated to have a magnetic field strength of 17 gauss, or approximately 1.7 tesla, which is capable of lifting around 3 kilograms of iron nails.

The National High Magnetic Field Laboratory holds world records for the strongest magnets, including a 45.5 tesla field, and China has reported resistive and hybrid magnets above 40 tesla. The units in the claim are also wrong: 17 gauss is 0.0017 tesla, not 1.7 tesla.

text: Coffee plants naturally lose most of their flowers and produce fruits because it's extremely rare for the coffee plant to fruit and set seeds, known as coffee cherries, at the same time.

Dallmayr says coffee plants commonly carry flowers, unripe fruit and ripe fruit at the same time, and that one branch may hold both ripe and unripe cherries. Perfect Daily Grind explains that flowers on the same tree are pollinated at different times, so fruits mature at different rates. It also describes falling petals as a normal step: each flower leaves behind a small nub that grows into a cherry. The claim's reason for flower loss therefore doesn't hold.

text: Butler's Panorama, located in Hobart, Tasmania, is the world's longest and oldest surviving panorama painting, created by H.P. Gill in 1860.

A minor point: the river is near boiling rather than literally boiling throughout, and its location is documented, not just 'said to be.'

text: A honey bee in a single trip will only collect and store about half a milligram of nectar.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique mating ritual in which some species perform a synchronized "dance" of vertical jumps, often for several minutes, to attract a mate and maintain their pair bond.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source describing butterflyfish doing a synchronized dance of repeated vertical jumps that lasts several minutes. Animal Diversity Web says butterflyfish reproduction has been studied in only a few species. In the documented cases, pairs ascend into the water column to release eggs and sperm, and Chaetodon aculeatus pairs have been seen chasing each other around a sponge. MarineBio describes bank butterflyfish courtship in hedged terms ("thought to", "likely"): the pair swims closely together, circles, and makes synchronized movements. None of these sources mentions repeated vertical jumps lasting minutes, and calling this ritual unique is not supported. A 'signal jump' courtship display is documented, but in damselfish, a different family. Some general parts of the claim are plausible, such as pair bonding and synchronized courtship movements. text: Buttering can help to prevent sweat and smell when you're working out, due to its antibacterial properties which kill odor-causing bacteria on your skin.
label: not_verifiable

A few commercial sites say shea butter in deodorants helps with odour, but they don't say it reduces sweating or has proven antibacterial effects. text: The Bend in the Grand Coulee in Washington state, USA, is the largest retention dam in the world and is a vital source of hydroelectric power for the region.
label: contradicted
reason: No dam is called "the Bend in the Grand Coulee." The Grand Coulee is a canyon cut by Ice Age megafloods, and the nearby "Big Bend" is a region along the Columbia River. If the claim means Grand Coulee Dam, the hydroelectric part holds up: ASCE and other sources call it the largest hydroelectric facility and largest concrete structure in the US. But the claim that it is the largest retention dam in the world is wrong. Sources describe it as the largest in the United States, and Study.com says outright that it is not the largest dam in the world. So the claim mislabels the structure and overstates its rank.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a mysterious river in Peru whose existence was only confirmed in 2007, and its cause of boiling water remains unexplained.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru was not confirmed in 2007. Local people had always known about it, and geoscientist Andrés Ruzo first visited and studied it scientifically in 2011, according to IOP Spark, ScienceAlert, AccuWeather and Atlas Obscura. Second, its heat has been explained. Ruzo's research found a fault-fed hydrothermal system that has nothing to do with volcanoes. Rainwater, possibly including Andean meltwater, seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's natural geothermal gradient, and rises back up along fault lines. Some sources still call the river mysterious, but the stated cause directly contradicts the claim that the heating is unexplained. Only its location in the Peruvian Amazon is correct.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where a river in the Amazon rainforest appears to boil, due to a natural mixture of cold water and hot water from underground volcanic activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru is real, but its heat does not come from volcanic activity. National Geographic, as cited by Wikipedia, calls it a non-volcanic geothermal feature. The main explanation is that water is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient, not by volcanic activity. That contradicts the claim that underground volcanic activity causes the heat.

text: The Djallonke sheep, a breed of West African sheep, can weigh as much as 100 kg (220 pounds).
label: contradicted
reason: ILRI's breed profile describes the Djallonké as a small, dwarf breed with a body weight of 20–30 kg. It cites mature ewes at about 21 kg and mature rams at about 26 kg. No source suggests the breed can reach anywhere near 100 kg, so the claim is contradicted.

text: The Sirroco Wind, which is a type of strong, dry and hot wind, is primarily found in the Mediterranean area and originated in the Sahara Desert.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe the sirocco (spelled "Sirroco" in the claim) as a hot, dry, often dusty wind. It starts over the Sahara and other North African deserts and blows north across the Mediterranean, reaching places such as Italy, Malta and Sicily. Merriam-Webster says it can reach hurricane speeds, which supports "strong." One caveat: the wind picks up moisture as it crosses the sea, so it can arrive humid in southern Europe. It is still described as hot and dry where it begins, so the claim holds overall.

text: The cheese produced by the world's largest cheese producer, Fonterra Cooperative Group in New Zealand, accounts for approximately one-third of the world's total cheese production each year.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. USDA FAS data shows the EU makes about 47% of the world's cheese and the US about 29%. New Zealand isn't even among the leading cheese-producing countries listed, so Fonterra can't make about a third of global cheese. Industry rankings also don't name Fonterra as the single largest cheese producer: Lactalis and Leprino are listed among the biggest, with Fonterra as just one of several major players.

text: The cheese produced by the world's largest cheese producer, Fonterra Cooperative Group in New Zealand, accounts for around 25% of the world's total cheese output.
label: contradicted
reason: Fonterra is usually described as the world's largest dairy exporter, not the world's largest cheese producer. Cheese makers such as Lactalis rank above it. An IMARC market report says Lactalis, Kraft Heinz, Arla and Fonterra together account for only about 25–30% of global processed cheese revenues. That means Fonterra alone cannot produce around 25% of the world's cheese. Its yearly cheese output is a few hundred thousand tonnes, a small fraction of the roughly 20+ million tonnes made worldwide.

text: The cheese produced by the world's largest cheese producer, Fonterra Cooperative Group in New Zealand, accounts for over 30% of global cheese production.
label: contradicted
reason: Fonterra is not the world's largest cheese producer. Lactalis is widely described as the world's largest dairy company and makes about 1.9 million tons of cheese a year. TechSci lists Fonterra only sixth among the top cheese companies. Global cheese output is over 20 million tonnes, so even Lactalis's volume is under 10% of it, and Fonterra's share is much smaller. One market report says Lactalis, Kraft Heinz, Arla and Fonterra together make up only about 25–30% of global processed-cheese revenue. That rules out Fonterra alone producing more than 30% of the world's cheese.

text: The cheese produced by the world's largest cheese producer, Fonterra Cooperative Group in New Zealand, equates to about 160,000 wheels of cheese every day.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim calls Fonterra the world's largest cheese producer, and the sources I found say otherwise. Zippia states that "Lactalis is the largest cheese manufacturer in the world," and IMARC also ranks Lactalis first, with Fonterra second. Wikipedia describes Fonterra as the world's largest dairy exporter and the sixth-largest dairy company, not the largest cheese producer. No source I found backed the figure of about 160,000 wheels of cheese a day. Because the core premise is contradicted, the claim is contradicted.

text: The fastest recorded speed of a golf ball was achieved by a golf ball launched by a whirlwind generates and reached over 430 mph.

Wikipedia says Kyle Berkshire set the ball speed record at 241.6 mph in October 2023. I found nothing about a whirlwind launching a golf ball or about any golf ball going over 430 mph. text: The fastest recorded speed of a golf ball was achieved by a golf ball launched by a whirlwind tornado in 1971, hitting 232 miles per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any source for a golf ball being launched to 232 mph by a tornado in 1971. The fastest recorded golf ball speeds come from long-drive hitters. Kyle Berkshire set a ball-speed world record of 241.6 mph in October 2023, after earlier marks of 233.4 mph and 236 mph. Both the claimed record-holder and the speed conflict with these records.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless water weasel also known as a binturong also known as a bearcat.
label: contradicted
reason: The binturong is indeed sometimes called a bearcat, but it is not the furriest animal on Earth, and it is not known as a "comfortless water weasel." Several sources name the sea otter as the furriest animal: it has the densest fur of any mammal, at about 140,000 hairs per square centimetre, according to a 2010 study published in Acta Theriologica.
