text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog (water shrew), which has nearly 4000 hairs per square centimeter of skin.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources name the sea otter as the furriest animal on Earth, with about 140,000 hairs per square centimetre and up to roughly 165,000 on some parts of the body. That is far more than 4,000, and Eurasian otters, Arctic foxes and chinchillas also have much denser fur than the claim's figure. The 'comfortless waterhog' doesn't appear to be a real animal name, and no source calls the water shrew the furriest animal.

text: The highest recorded number of premature births occurred during the Great Flood of 1931 in China, where more than 3 million premature births occurred.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The 1931 China floods were real and are among the deadliest disasters on record: they hit the Yangtze and Huai river regions, including Wuhan and Nanjing, from about June to August 1931. But none of the sources I found mention premature births or any figure of 3 million. These include Wikipedia's articles on the floods and on 1931 in China, Britannica, FloodList and Great Disasters. I also found nothing to show that this was the highest number of premature births ever recorded. No source directly says the claim is false either, so the evidence is not enough to support or contradict it.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the Macedonian Mountain Range, which is a massive 6,800 km long on the planet Mars.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no 'Macedonian Mountain Range' on Mars. The Macedonian Mountains are on Earth, in North Macedonia on the Balkan Peninsula, and their highest peak is Bakardan at 2,700 m. The 6,800 km Martian range does not exist. Earth's mid-ocean ridge system is about 65,000 km long, far longer than the 6,800 km claimed. Both the location and the length in the claim are wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the mountain range on Mars, which is known as the Olympia Mons and is around 27 km high.
label: contradicted
reason: The height in the claim is roughly correct: NASA JPL says Olympus Mons rises about 27 km (17 miles). The rest of the claim is wrong. Olympus Mons (not "Olympia Mons") is a single shield volcano, not a mountain range, and the sources describe it as the tallest mountain in the solar system, not the longest mountain range. Calling it the longest mountain range misstates what it is.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) long and runs through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration calls the mid-ocean ridge system the longest and largest mountain range on Earth. It says the ridge stretches nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles), which fits the claim of over 40,000 miles (about 64,000 km). NOAA also says it winds between the continents across the world's ocean basins, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. One caveat: the East Pacific Rise runs through the eastern Pacific rather than its exact middle, but that is a loose description, not a factual error.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and is not visible above water.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration confirms that the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain chain on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,390 mi). That supports the main part of the claim, although the claim says "over" 65,000 km, while NOAA says "nearly." The claim's statement that the ridge is not visible above water is false. NOAA says more than 90% of it lies in the deep ocean, which means some of it does not. Other sources, including WorldAtlas and Amusing Planet, note that the ridge rises above the ocean surface in a few places, most notably Iceland.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers and is home to many active volcanoes.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the Mid-Ocean Ridge Earth's longest mountain range. WHOI describes it as about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) of continuous underwater volcanoes and says most of Earth's volcanic activity happens along mid-ocean ridges, which supports the part about many active volcanoes. One small mismatch: NOAA and WHOI say 'nearly 65,000 km,' not 'over' that figure. Other sources give lengths ranging from more than 56,000 km to around 80,000 km depending on how the ridge is measured. Since 65,000 km is the standard figure, the claim is essentially correct.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardesses," although its usage is often varied and not always as a monosyllable.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Reliable sources name 9-letter words such as "screeched" and "strengths" as the longest one-syllable words in common use, with rare 10-letter ones like "scraunched" and "strengthed". "Stewardesses" has four syllables (stew-ard-ess-es), so it can't be a one-syllable word. It's actually known as one of the longest words you can type with only the left hand.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life called "Werth Bridge"
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing about bioluminescent "Floating Islands" in the ocean called "Werth Bridge." The only real Werth Bridge I found is a steel tied-arch road bridge built in 1903 in Wuppertal, Germany, which has nothing to do with ocean life. Floating islands do exist, but they are mats of vegetation and are not known by this name. The claim looks made up, but no source directly says the phenomenon doesn't exist, so it can't be confirmed or disproven.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as phytoplankton, which can be seen glowing in the darkness.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is true: some phytoplankton, especially dinoflagellates, are bioluminescent and can be seen glowing in dark water (National Geographic, CPAWS). But I found no source that calls phytoplankton "Floating Islands." Phytoplankton are microscopic drifting organisms. "Floating island" normally means a mass of floating plants, peat or pumice, so the nickname appears to be made up. The claim also suggests all phytoplankton glow, when only certain species do.

text: The total surface area of the glaciers in Antarctica is approximately 5.5 million square miles, covering about 98% of the continent.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Antarctic ice sheet article says the ice sheet, a continental glacier, covers 98% of the continent over about 14 million km², or 5.4 million sq mi. Other sources give the continent's total area as about 5.5 million sq mi, and say that figure includes the ice sheet covering 98% of the land. So the claim's '~5.5 million sq mi' is a close round-up of 5.4 million, and the 98% figure matches. One caveat: 5.5 million sq mi is really the area of the whole continent, and Encyclopedia.com gives a lower ice figure of 5.1 million sq mi. The claim is still broadly right within the 'approximately' it allows.

text: Theaffe, a commonly consumed type of tea in Germany, is served with a generous helping of sugar and is traditionally enjoyed with a variety of sweet pastries or cakes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a German tea called "Theaffe" exists. Searches for the name only turned up unrelated pages: a family foundation and OCR typos for "Theatre" in old newspapers. Sources on German tea culture talk about Ostfriesentee and the Kaffee und Kuchen tradition, but none mention "Theaffe." Because the claim has no clear referent, nothing about how it is served (with lots of sugar) or eaten (with pastries or cakes) can be checked.

text: There are more hairs on the average human head than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the comparison badly wrong. NASA estimates the Milky Way has about 100 billion stars, and other estimates go as high as 400 billion. Hair-research sources put the average human head at only about 100,000 hairs, roughly a million times fewer than the number of stars.

text: There are more neutrons in an atomic nucleus than there are protons, with a typical atom having around 50 neutrons for every 20 protons.
label: contradicted
reason: A University of Texas chemistry source says the stable neutron-to-proton ratio is about 1:1 for light nuclei (up to roughly Z = 20) and rises to only about 1.5:1 for the heaviest elements. So a nucleus with 20 protons, such as calcium-40, typically has about 20 neutrons, not 50. A 2.5:1 ratio is far outside the band of stability. The claim that nuclei always have more neutrons than protons is also wrong: hydrogen-1 has no neutrons, and many light nuclei have equal numbers of each.

text: There are over 2 million species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to recent estimates from the World Register of Marine Species and the International Institute for Species Exploration.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The number is plausible, but the claim's source attribution doesn't hold up. More than 2 million species do exist: about 2 million have been described, and a widely publicized 2011 estimate, to which IISE contributed, puts the total at about 8.7 million. However, the World Register of Marine Species covers only marine species. It lists about 242,000 known valid marine species, and estimates of total marine species range from 0.3 to 2.2 million. I found no evidence that WoRMS has estimated more than 2 million plant and animal species on Earth. Also, IISE disbanded in 2018, so calling its figures 'recent estimates' is questionable. Because the attribution can't be verified, and the WoRMS part is doubtful, the claim as worded is inconclusive.

text: There are over 328 million trees in California's Yosemite National Park.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that gives a total tree count for Yosemite. Reliable sources such as the NPS and the SF Chronicle report about 2.4 million dead trees across roughly 131,000 acres of the park. They also report 102 million dead trees across the Sierra Nevada and 142 million trees lost statewide in California. None of them mention a total number of trees in the park, so the figure of over 328 million can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on our planet, but an estimated 80-90% of them remain undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources covering the 2011 PLoS Biology study by Mora et al., including EurekAlert, ScienceDaily, the University of Hawaii and Nature News via BioEd Online, report about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. They say more than 80% of species are still undiscovered: about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species. That matches the claim's 80–90% figure. The claim has two small inaccuracies. It says 'over' 8.7 million, but 8.7 million is a central estimate. It also refers to 'plants and animals', but the estimate covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists. Neither point changes the claim's main point, which matches the study.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to estimates from the best available data, however, around 86% of them remain undiscovered.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology. That study estimates about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth (8.74 million in its Table 2, ± 1.3 million SE), and says about 86% of species on Earth still await description. The claim's wording is a little loose in two places. "Over 8.7 million" fits the 8.74 million point estimate, but the paper presents ~8.7 million as an estimate with a wide error range. "Undiscovered" stands in for the paper's "still await description." Neither difference contradicts the source.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity levels that it can calcify and preserve dead animals, creating unique and striking forms and structures.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is a real soda lake in northern Tanzania. Its water is strongly alkaline, at about pH 9 to 10.5. Colossal's coverage of Nick Brandt's photographs describes birds and bats that died in the lake becoming calcified and preserved as striking, statue-like forms. An Africa Check fact-check also confirms the bodies are calcified, while correcting the myth that they are 'turned to stone.' One caveat: the striking poses in Brandt's widely shared photos were arranged by the photographer, but the calcification itself is real.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into stone, through a process called calcification.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Explorersweb and Colossal, describe Lake Natron in northern Tanzania as a highly alkaline lake, with a pH of about 9 to 10.5. They say animals that die in it become calcified and look like stone statues. Both outlets use the 'turn to stone' wording that the claim relies on. One caveat: the animals are really preserved or mummified by the lake's mineral deposits rather than literally turned into stone. Still, the claim matches how these reports describe it.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, which has such high alkalinity that it can turn animals that die in it into stone.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is a real lake in northern Tanzania. Live Science and Colossal both report that it is highly alkaline, with a pH up to about 10.5, and that animals dying in or around it become calcified, which these sources describe as turning them to 'stone'. Strictly speaking, the bodies are preserved as calcified mummies rather than literally turned to stone, but the claim matches how reliable sources describe it.

text: You can fit the entire Great Wall of China inside the Grand Canyon, as the Great Wall stretches approximately 13,170 miles and the Grand Canyon is about 277 miles long.
label: contradicted
reason: Both figures in the claim are correct. Britannica and other sources give the Great Wall's total length as about 21,196 km (13,171 miles), and Wikipedia gives the Grand Canyon's length as 277 miles (446 km). But those numbers disprove the conclusion. The wall is nearly 48 times longer than the canyon, so it could not fit inside it laid end to end. The comparison the claim uses to support its point actually contradicts it.

text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Southwest Wilderness in Tasmania, Australia, holds one of the world's longest stretches of uninterrupted wilderness along the Franklin River with nearly 750 miles preserved since its protection in 1983.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a hydro settlement in Tasmania's Central Highlands, next to the Clark Dam on the River Derwent. It is not a section of Southwest wilderness along the Franklin River. The Franklin River is only about 129 km (80 mi) long, so it cannot have nearly 750 miles of river preserved.

text: Honey is a super-conductor when it's heated above 2.5°C (36.5°F), and it's the only food item known to retain this property.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is not a superconductor. Studies of honey's electrical conductivity report very low values, roughly 0.08 to over 0.8 mS/cm. That makes it a poor ionic conductor that still has electrical resistance. Superconductivity means zero resistance, and it is known only in certain materials kept at very low temperatures, such as layered nitrides and cuprates at tens of kelvin. No credible source says honey superconducts above 2.5°C or that any food does.

text: The Royal Forums in the Palace of Versailles in France have a special heat regulation system, where the underfloor heating is warmed by pipes that tap into the hot water from a boiler powered by coal and ash, however this is not fully operational today.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no record of a place called the "Royal Forums" at the Palace of Versailles, so the claim has no clear referent. I also found nothing describing an underfloor heating system there fed by pipes from a coal- and ash-fired boiler, or saying such a system is only partly working today. The sources I found say Versailles was historically heated mainly by fireplaces and stoves, and that its large rooms were hard to keep warm. That doesn't directly disprove the claim, but nothing supports it either.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious natural wonder, was discovered by scientists in 2007 and is thought to be a rare geological feature that holds significant clues about the Amazon River's geological history.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2007 date is wrong. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, say geoscientist Andrés Ruzo became the first scientist allowed to study the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in 2011. Local Indigenous communities had known about the river long before that. The search found nothing showing scientists discovered it in 2007.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent bell-shaped body and is able to swim upright using its bioluminescent bells to confuse predators.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal wrong. The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a deep-sea glass sponge, not a jellyfish. As a sessile sponge, it stays fixed in place and has a lattice-like silica skeleton. It does not have a transparent bell-shaped body, it does not swim upright, and it does not use bioluminescent bells to confuse predators.

text: The Blue Fairy Tern, also known as Arenaria interpres, is a rare and endangered tern species that lays its eggs on the intertidal zone and is found primarily in the Red Sea and India.
label: contradicted
reason: Arenaria interpres is the ruddy turnstone, not a tern and not a "Blue Fairy Tern". It is a widespread migratory sandpiper that breeds in the far north (Arctic), not a rare, endangered tern found mainly in the Red Sea and India. The claim gets the species' identity and range wrong.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlywed couples walk over a rope bridge suspended high above the water as a rite of passage to ensure safe passage into married life.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nayars (Nairs) are a community in Kerala, but Thalikettu has nothing to do with a boat or rope bridge. Wikipedia describes Thalikettu (Kettu Kalyanam) as an elaborate ceremonial mock marriage, a pre-pubertal ritual in which a tali was tied for girls of the Nair and related communities. It was not a rite where newlywed couples walked over a rope bridge above water. That part of the claim is made up, and no source supports it.

text: Plants are capable of producing up to 20% of their daily growth through a process known as twigs photoperiod, which occurs during the dark periods of their day-night cycle.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no scientific source for a process called "twigs photoperiod." Where that wording appears, it refers to experiments on cut twigs placed under different day lengths to study when buds open, not to growth happening in the dark. I also found nothing saying plants make up to 20% of their daily growth through any such process. Photoperiod is the length of day and night. Some research does show plants keep growing at night, for example seedlings stretching most at the end of the night (PIF1 study), using sugars stored during the day. But that is not the specific process or the 20% figure the claim describes. The claim looks made up, yet no source directly refutes it, so I can't verify its central parts.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a Peruvian river that appears to boil with steam, yet its source and reason behind this phenomenon remain unknown.
label: contradicted
reason: The river does exist: the Shanay-Timpishka in the Peruvian Amazon is very hot and steams. But the claim that its source and the reason for the heat are unknown is wrong. Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo has studied the river, and sources including Wikipedia, National Geographic and Forbes say the heat is geothermal. The leading explanation is that the Earth's geothermal gradient heats water underground, which then rises back to the surface along faults. Since the cause has been studied and explained, the 'unknown' part is contradicted.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, contains the Oldest Natural Bridge in the World, estimated to be approximately 30 million years old.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no evidence that Butlers Gorge has a natural bridge, let alone the world's oldest one, and nothing supports the 30-million-year age. Wikipedia and other sources describe Butlers Gorge as a Central Highlands locality with no recorded population. It is known for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, part of Hydro Tasmania's hydroelectric scheme. The only 'oldest bridge' results for Tasmania were about the man-made Richmond Bridge (1823–25), not a natural bridge at Butlers Gorge. No source I found directly says the claim is false, so I can't label it contradicted, but it is unsupported and probably made up.

text: Giraffes, despite their tall stature, are actually able to developگه hypertrophic cardiomyopathy which a weakened heart, leading to a higher risk of death due to their defective heart valve.
label: contradicted
reason: Giraffes do have a naturally thick left ventricular wall, but the research describes this as a healthy adaptation to their very high blood pressure, not a disease. Studies found that giraffe hearts stay healthy and working well because the thickened wall has little fibrosis (stiff scar-like tissue). Giraffes appear to avoid the heart failure that this kind of thickening causes in humans. None of the sources link giraffes to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that weakens the heart, or to a higher risk of death from a faulty heart valve. The evidence points the other way: giraffe hearts are seen as protected from these problems.

text: The infamous avalanches that occur every year in the Langjökull glacier in Iceland are believed to be caused by the melting of which released massive amounts of methane, estimated to weigh as much as 200 elephants.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of yearly 'infamous avalanches' at Langjökull caused by methane release. The real research reported in the Newsweek article is about a different glacier, Sólheimajökull, which flows from the Katla volcano. Up to 41 tonnes of methane a day leaves it in summer meltwater, produced by microbes on the glacier bed. That study does not mention avalanches. The claim gets the glacier wrong, and the 'avalanche' cause and the '200 elephants' comparison appear to be made up.

text: If we were to place all the stars in the observable universe shoulder to shoulder, they would stretch over 250 billion light-years in length, approximately 4 times the age of the universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figure is off by many orders of magnitude, and its own comparison doesn't hold up. Sources estimate roughly 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe, with commonly cited figures of about 2×10^23 or 3×10^23. The Sun is about 1.39 million km across. Even assuming 10^22 stars that are each only one-third the Sun's width, a shoulder-to-shoulder line would be about 4×10^27 km, or roughly 4×10^14 light-years. With about 2×10^23 stars, it would be on the order of 10^15 to 10^16 light-years. That is millions of times longer than 250 billion light-years. The claim is also inconsistent with itself: 250 billion divided by the universe's age of about 13.8 billion years is about 18, not 4. Comparing a length to an age is also not meaningful.

text: The einzige weisse deutscher spitz, also known as the white German Spitz, has been a symbol of Russia since Peter the Great adopted one in the early 18th century and since then they were used as royal pets in the imperial family of Russia.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a white German Spitz was ever a symbol of Russia, or that Peter the Great adopted one. Sources on German Spitz history say the breed comes from Germany/Pomerania and mention no link to Russia or the Russian imperial family. Peter the Great's documented dogs were different breeds: his small dog Lisette was a smooth-haired terrier, which is preserved and exhibited as such, and Tiran was a Bullenbeisser. Sources on Russian national symbols list the flag, the coat of arms and the Bronze Horseman statue, not any dog. Since the documented record of Peter's dogs conflicts with the claim, it is contradicted.

text: Centaury flowers, which are used in herbal medicine, have the unique ability to slowly increase their own height by lengthening their stems after being injured.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Centaury (Centaurium erythraea) is well documented as a medicinal herb, so that part of the claim holds up. I found nothing showing that it grows taller by lengthening its stems after injury, and nothing describing that as a unique ability. The research on how centaury responds to wounding (PMC6963686) covers a chemical response: changes in secoiridoid glucoside metabolism in damaged leaves. It does not mention stem growth. Botanical descriptions give its height as 2–50 cm with straight stems and describe no regrowth trait like this. Because I found no evidence either way on the main part of the claim, I can't verify it, though it does not appear to be true.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as Vellela Vellela, which are colonies of tiny marine animals that can light up the surrounding water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. Wikipedia describes Velella velella (correctly spelled "Velella," not "Vellela") as a free-floating colonial hydrozoan that drifts on the ocean surface, and it is commonly called the "by-the-wind sailor." The rest is unverified or weakly sourced. I found no source that calls Velella "Floating Islands"; Wikipedia's ocean surface ecosystem page uses "living islands" only for neuston in general. The bioluminescence claim also rests on weak sources: a beachcombing blog and a nature website say Velella glows blue, while authoritative pages (Wikipedia, Scripps' zooplankton guide, Oregon Sea Grant) don't say this species is bioluminescent. Oregon Sea Grant mentions bioluminescence only for a different jellyfish, Aequorea. Because the nickname is unsupported and the light-producing claim isn't reliably confirmed, the claim can't be fully verified.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique wing movement and ability to rotate its wings in a figure-eight pattern.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the hummingbird is the only bird that can fly backwards, and explain it by its unusual wing motion: the wings rotate at the shoulder and sweep in a figure-eight pattern that produces lift on both strokes. These include WorldAtlas, Birds & Blooms and Garden Bird. The same sources add a caveat: herons, egrets, flycatchers and warblers can flutter backwards for a second or two. They still describe the hummingbird as the only bird that can truly fly backwards for any length of time. This supports the claim as it is normally meant, though it is a simplification.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is created by a chemical reaction that converts oxygen into light, allowing the worm to lure prey in the dark.
label: supported
reason: A bioRxiv study of Arachnocampa larvae says their light needs oxygen and ATP, and that the larvae glow through the night to lure arthropods into silk snares. Other sources describe it as a luciferin–luciferase reaction that uses oxygen. Strictly speaking, the reaction oxidizes luciferin rather than turning oxygen itself into light, so 'converts oxygen into light' is a loose simplification. Still, the core of the claim matches the evidence: light comes from an oxygen-dependent chemical reaction and is used to attract prey in the dark.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans approximately 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the center of the Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). One part of it, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, runs down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. The full system also winds through the other oceans, but the claim doesn't say it is only in the Atlantic, so that part is still accurate.

text: Researchers have discovered that there are more trees on Earth now than there were 35 years ago, thanks in part to massive reforestation efforts and the natural regrowth of forests after being cleared for agriculture and other purposes.
label: supported
reason: A 2018 Nature study led by Xiao-Peng Song and Matthew Hansen at the University of Maryland analyzed satellite data from 1982 to 2016, about 35 years. It found that global tree cover grew by 2.24 million km², roughly 7%. The authors linked about 60% of all land change to human activity. The gains came mainly from tree planting and forest management, for example in China and Europe, and from forests growing back on abandoned farmland, with warming at high latitudes also contributing. Coverage in Mongabay, Eco-Business and UMD's Maryland Today reports these findings. One caveat: the study measured tree cover, which is not necessarily forest cover, but the claim's core points hold up.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life in the Sargasso Sea, which are actually vast clusters of algae-covered seaweed and dead marine organisms that defy complete explanation.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (National Geographic, Britannica) describe the Sargasso Sea's floating mats as living masses of free-floating brown algae, Sargassum natans and S. fluitans. Gas-filled floats keep the algae up, and the mats reproduce by breaking into pieces that keep growing. They are not clusters of algae-covered seaweed and dead marine organisms. Neither source describes them as bioluminescent or as something science can't fully explain. Their biology and role as habitat are well understood, so the key parts of the claim are wrong.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made of white Carrara marble, but the top 18 meters is actually covered with a smooth, unglazed, white glazed terracotta known as 'majolica'.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. San Miniato al Monte has one campanile, not several steeples. Baccio d'Agnolo began building it in about 1523 to replace a tower that collapsed in 1499, and it was never finished. During the 1529–30 siege, it was used as an artillery tower. None of the sources say the tower is made of white Carrara marble or that its top 18 meters is covered in majolica. The only marble they describe is the white-and-green facade, and the only glazed terracotta is in Luca della Robbia's ceiling decoration inside the chapel. The claim also contradicts itself by calling the terracotta both 'unglazed' and 'glazed', even though majolica is a glazed ware. These sources do not directly say what stone the tower is built from.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is created by a result of a chemical reaction in the glowworm's body involving a compound called luciferin and oxygen.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports (2018) found that the New Zealand glowworm's bioluminescence comes from a luciferin–luciferase reaction that needs ATP-Mg2+ and oxygen. That means the light is produced by a chemical reaction in the glowworm's body involving luciferin and oxygen, which matches the claim. A related study adds that the reaction happens in a specialised light organ. The claim does not mention the luciferase enzyme or ATP, but leaving them out does not make it wrong.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan in the animal kingdom with some species living only 1-3 years in the wild, while others in captivity can live for up to 5 years.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says octopuses have the shortest lifespan in the animal kingdom, and that is false. Several sources, including CK-12, say mayflies are generally considered the shortest-lived animals: adults live about a day on average, and in some species only about 5 minutes. Many other animals, such as some insects and gastrotrichs, also live far less than 1–3 years. The figure of 1–3 years for some octopus species is roughly accurate, but the main claim is contradicted.

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, were used as early as ancient Egyptian architecture around 2500 BC.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources confirm that buttresses are supporting structures and that they are very old. Wikipedia says early examples appear on Mesopotamia's Eanna Temple at Uruk as early as the 4th millennium BC, though it flags that date as needing a citation. text: Pineapples are not naturally occurring fruits, and they are the result of a accidental mutation of a different plant species.

text: The Beehive dome in Utah, USA, is the largest free-standing museum in the world and is part of the Dinosaur National Monument.

Wikipedia, citing Forbes and National Geographic, describes it as a hot river with no nearby active volcanoes or geothermal vents. text: The ME-361 AC-10 is the world's oldest flyable aircraft, with its first flight taking place in 1922.

text: The Sundial Bridge in Redding, California, is the longest single-span, self-supporting, pedestrian cable-stayed bridge in the world.
label: not_verifiable

text: The Sundial Bridge in Redding, California, is the world's largest metal arch bridge made of a cable-stayed truss design.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources describe the Sundial Bridge as a cantilever spar cable-stayed footbridge, not a metal arch bridge or a cable-stayed truss. text: The cheese in the iconic grilled cheese sandwich, the American cheese, has a formula that's owned by the company that makes Velveeta.
label: contradicted
reason: Kraft is the company behind Velveeta. Its founder, James L. Kraft, patented a process for making processed cheese in 1916, and Kraft bought Velveeta in 1927. But that patent was granted for a process more than a century ago and does not mean Kraft owns 'the formula' for American cheese today. Processed cheese was first invented in Switzerland in 1911 by Gerber and Stettler. American cheese is now a generic, legally standardized type of processed cheese sold by Kraft, Borden and other companies. Kraft's later American-cheese patents are listed as expired. So the claim that the formula is owned by Velveeta's maker misstates the facts.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, with a total coastline length of approximately 243,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: The claim checks out. Fisheries and Oceans Canada, a government source, says Canada has the longest coastline in the world, at 243,042 km across its Atlantic, Arctic and Pacific coasts. That rounds to about 243,000 km. Mental Floss also says experts agree Canada's coastline is the longest, though the exact length varies depending on the source.

text: The highest recorded human body temperature in space is of TessHB standing at 39 degrees Celsius by an active highly skilled unidentified space swimmer.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and powerful wing movement.

GardenBird does add that a few other species can flutter backwards for a second or two. text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique wing movement and powerful muscles.

text: There are more Plastic bags than stars in the Milky Way galaxy.

Related figures point the same way: UN News says there are about 51 trillion microplastic particles in the ocean, 500 times the number of stars in our galaxy.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with estimates suggesting that over 3 trillion trees cover the planet.
label: supported
reason: A 2015 global study in Nature (Crowther et al.) estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth. NASA puts the number of stars in the Milky Way at roughly 100–400 billion, so trees outnumber the galaxy's stars by more than seven to one even at the high star estimate. Several sources, including WorldAtlas, repeat the fact that Earth's roughly 3 trillion trees outnumber the stars in the Milky Way. One detail: the estimate is about 3 trillion (3.04 trillion), so the claim's 'over 3 trillion' wording is only slightly loose.

text: There are over 320 million trees in the city of New York State, with forests covering nearly 60% of the state's total area.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count in the claim is wrong. The "city of New York State" wording is muddled, but the number fails either way. USDA Forest Service inventory data puts New York State at about 11.5–12 billion live trees on forest land, and a Forest Service analysis estimates about 7 million trees in New York City, so 320 million matches neither. The forest figure is roughly right: NYSDEC says forests cover 61–62% of the state (about 18.6 million of 30.2 million acres), though that is a bit over 60%, not "nearly 60%." Because the core tree count is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built parts for various iconic aircraft including the famous Supermarine Spitfire and both versions of the Bristol Blenheim.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source saying a British company called "Arotech Limited" ever existed, or that it made parts for the Spitfire or either version of the Bristol Blenheim. text: Butler's Gorge, a section of the Nile River in Egypt, features one of the longest rock-cut temples in the world, known as the Temple of Isis on Philae Island.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-long (164-foot-long) stretch of river that remains at a boiling temperature despite being in the middle of the rainforest, surrounded by cooler water.
label: contradicted

Wikipedia lists the Shanay-timpishka (the 'Boiling River of the Amazon') at about 9 km long, and other reports put the hot stretch at about 6.24 km. That is far longer than 50 m. text: The lubber grasshopper, a species found in the Neotropics, has an unusual characteristic in that its hind legs are underdeveloped, and it cannot jump or fly, making it one of the few grasshoppers in the world that cannot jump.
label: contradicted
reason: Lubber grasshoppers do not fly, but they can jump. The LSU AgCenter says the eastern lubber jumps clumsily and is a poor jumper, and other sources say lubbers can make short jumps. The University of Wyoming describes the plains lubber's hind legs as large, not underdeveloped, and reports that males were seen jumping about 9 feet in one leap. These grasshoppers are also North American (for example, the southeastern U.S. and the Great Plains), not Neotropical. So the claims that they cannot jump, have underdeveloped hind legs and live in the Neotropics are all contradicted.

text: The short and rare Icelandic burst of light known as the "Northern Lights" or Aurora Borealis can be seen in the night sky at latitudes north of 30.5°.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several things wrong. The aurora borealis isn't specifically Icelandic. It occurs right around the polar regions. Near the auroral oval it isn't rare either: NOAA/NWS says it can be seen on more than half of nights there. Reliable sources (NWS, National Geographic) put the main viewing zone at about 60–75° latitude, not anywhere north of 30.5°. It can occasionally reach much lower latitudes during extreme geomagnetic storms, but the claim's description and latitude are inaccurate.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the northeastern portion of the mountain range on Mars, commonly known as the 'Terra overlook', with its height being roughly 3.4 kilometers.

text: Did you know that honey is a super-efficient food source because it contains a platform of carbs, vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and antioxidants that can be digested quickly by bees but takes a human's body hours to break down?
label: contradicted

Because of that, the human body absorbs these sugars quickly in the small intestine, with little further digestion needed. This goes against the claim that honey takes the human body hours to break down. The claim's other parts, about the nutrients in honey and how bees digest it, don't change the fact that the part about human digestion is wrong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a naturally occurring phenomenon where a river in the Peruvian Amazon appears to boil, but there is no known geological explanation for this occurrence.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim is accurate. The Shanay-Timpishka, known as the Boiling River of the Amazon, is a naturally hot river in the Peruvian Amazon. The claim is wrong, though, that there is no known geological explanation. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research found that the heat comes from a hydrothermal system fed by deep faults. Rainwater and groundwater sink deep underground, are heated by the Earth's natural heat, and rise back along faults as hot springs that feed the river. Geochemical testing ruled out volcanic heat. Sources note that the river is unusual because it is far from any volcano, but that is not the same as having no explanation.

text: The Boomerang effect, which was first discovered in the 14th century by an English traveler, occurs when a slingshot's trajectory changes direction as it returns to its starting point, often due to air resistance and the curvature of the Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the meaning, the origin and the physics wrong. In reliable sources (Wikipedia, Oxford Reference and an arXiv paper), the boomerang effect is a psychology and persuasion idea: an attempt to persuade someone pushes them toward the opposite position. Wikipedia says Hovland, Janis and Kelley first recorded and named it in 1953. It was not discovered by a 14th-century English traveler, and it is not about a slingshot's path curving back because of air resistance or the Earth's curvature.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a naturally occurring phenomenon where a river in the Amazon rainforest inexplicably remains at a high temperature throughout the year, with some locations reaching boiling point despite being 6,000 feet above sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's article on Shanay-timpishka, the 'Boiling River of the Amazon,' gives its elevation as about 265 m (869 ft) at the source and 160 m (520 ft) at the mouth. That is nowhere near 6,000 feet. The heat also isn't unexplained: geothermal water rises along geologic fault zones and heats the river. The claim does get some things right: the river is very hot, with a spot reaching 99.1 °C. But the 6,000-foot elevation is wrong, and calling the heat 'inexplicable' isn't accurate.

No source confirms or rules out the 107-foot entrance or the 60-foot waterfall inside the cave, so the claim can't be verified either way.

text: The entire human genome is encoded in a DNA molecule that is roughly 2 meters (6.6 feet) long when fully stretched, but it is tightly packed into the cell nucleus of a single human cell.
label: supported
reason: I labelled this supported because reliable sources back the main point. A biology textbook (OpenOregon) says the DNA in a single human cell would be about 2 meters (roughly 6 feet) long if stretched end to end, and that it must be packaged in a very ordered way to fit inside the cell. Physics papers on arXiv likewise describe about two meters of DNA stored in a nucleus only microns across. One detail is imprecise: that 2 meters is not one molecule. It is 46 separate DNA molecules (chromosomes), making up two copies of the genome. A single copy is roughly 1 meter. These details refine the wording but don't change the core claim about length and packing.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 40,389 miles (65,000 kilometers) long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported

text: There are more trees on Earth covered in moss than you might think, with scientists estimating that as much as 10% of the world's tree population has visible moss growth.

Local surveys, like one in British Columbia that found mosses and liverworts on about 54% of the trees sampled, can't be extended to the world. text: The Andean condensed milk, a type of milk known to have originated in South America, can last for six months unopened and still potently retain its original taste at room temperature due to its high sugar content.

text: The rate at which Paper Money deteriorates can increase over 30 years if exposed to high humidity and temperature fluctuations up to four times its original weight due to Moisture retention.

text: Adidamite, a type of soot found from explosions, has the highest recorded melting point among all substances, reaching 3,200 degrees Celsius.
label: contradicted

Tungsten (3,422 °C) also melts above 3,200 °C. So the claim that something melting at 3,200 °C has the highest melting point of any substance is false.

text: The short film "FreshGuac" was created using a combination of AI generated character models and voice acting, and it won the Best Narrative Short Film award at the 2023 Artificial Intelligence Film Festival.

text: The Greenland Shark is bioluminescent, meaning it can produce its own light due to a chemical reaction within its body that occurs when oxygen levels are low.
label: contradicted

Even that guess is about the parasite, not the shark. Among sharks, bioluminescence is documented in groups like lanternsharks (Etmopterus). The claim's explanation, a chemical reaction triggered by low oxygen, has no support either; bioluminescence is generally an oxygen-dependent reaction.

text: The surface of Venus has volcanoes, but it's home to the largest volcano in our solar system, called Maat Mons, a shield volcano estimated to be about 5 kilometers high.
label: contradicted
reason: Maat Mons is not the largest volcano in the solar system. It is the tallest volcano on Venus. That title belongs to Olympus Mons on Mars, a shield volcano that rises about 21–26 km. Trusted sources, including Sky at Night Magazine and Lowell Observatory, describe Olympus Mons as the largest volcano in the solar system, which directly contradicts the claim's main point.

text: The highest recorded number of premature births occurred during the Great Flood of 1931 in China, where more than 4 million infants were reportedly born with premature conditions due to their mothers' stress and body changes caused by the disaster.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim. Sources on the 1931 Central China flood cover the flooding, deaths from starvation and disease, and relief work. One missionary account says infants and young children were the first to die. None of them mention premature births, a figure of 4 million premature infants, or a record for premature births. The number also seems unlikely. Tens of millions of people were affected, and that population would have had only a few million births in total in a year. Still, no source directly refutes the figure, so the claim cannot be verified either way.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and runs through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

Sources also say the ridge runs through every ocean basin, which includes the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where the river's water not only appears to be boiling but remains liquid, with scientists still unsure about the exact cause, although most believe it's due to a unique combination of geological and ecosystem factors.
label: contradicted

Andrés Ruzo, the geoscientist who studied the river, is the source of this explanation. So the cause is largely understood, even though researchers are still studying the details.
