That makes both 'scientists still unsure' and 'geological and ecosystem factors' misleading or wrong.

text: The steeples of the Basilica di San Miniato al Monte in Florence, Italy are made from white Carrara marble and contain a range of 416 steps that lead to the ngang frieze.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs up the specific details in this claim. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, churchesofflorence.com, aviewoncities) say San Miniato al Monte has one campanile, not several steeples. The original tower fell down in 1499, and Baccio d'Agnolo started a replacement around 1520–1523 that was never finished. The church is known for its white and green marble facing. None of the sources say the tower is built of white Carrara marble, none mention 416 steps, and none describe anything called a 'ngang frieze', which doesn't appear to be a real feature. The steps that are mentioned (for example, 273 steps) are the stairway up the hill to the church, not steps inside a tower. The claim has factual problems (one tower, not steeples), but most of its details simply can't be checked, and part of it doesn't seem to refer to anything real.

text: The beaches of Rhossili Bay in Wales are home to a unique landlocked sandstone tombolo, also known as a 'tombolo with a tidal chasm', that connects a small rocky island, known as 'Burry Strand', to the mainland.
label: contradicted
reason: Rhossili Bay has no sandstone tombolo connecting an island called 'Burry Strand'. Its islands are Worm's Head, which is joined to the mainland by a rocky causeway that is exposed at low tide, and Burry Holms at the north end of the bay. Both are tidal islands made of carboniferous limestone, not sandstone. The softer Old Red Sandstone is found along the bay itself, between the two islands. The island the claim names is actually Burry Holms; Burry Strand is not an island.

text: The extremely rare meteorite known as the "A ValueEventListener" was found in Algeria in 2010, which is the oldest known extraterrestrial material discovered and dates back over 4.55 billion years.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no meteorite called "A ValueEventListener." That name belongs to a Firebase software interface used to listen for changes in database data. The real ancient meteorite from Algeria is Erg Chech 002. It was found in May 2020, not 2010, and is about 4.565 billion years old. Guinness and Phys.org call it the oldest known volcanic (achondrite) meteorite, not the oldest extraterrestrial material ever found. The claim gets the name wrong, the year wrong and overstates the record.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life, also known as Vellela Vellela, which are colonies of tiny marine animals that can light up the water around them.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Velella velella (the by-the-wind sailor, also called sea raft or purple sail) is real, and Wikipedia and Animal Diversity Web describe it as a floating hydrozoan, each apparent individual being a hydroid colony. So part of the claim holds. But no source uses the nickname "Floating Islands"; the known common names are by-the-wind sailor, sea raft, purple sail and little sail. The bioluminescence part is also shaky. A beachcombing blog says Velella glows at night, but it seems to have mixed it up with the water jelly Aequorea, which Oregon Sea Grant's Velella page names as the glowing animal. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, National Geographic and Oregon Sea Grant do not describe Velella as bioluminescent. Because the nickname and the light-producing claim can't be verified and the evidence on glowing conflicts, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, often extend beyond the support line, act as monumental gateways, or become free-standing structures.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Britannica and Wikipedia back up the basic definition: a buttress is a structure built against or projecting from a wall to support it. Britannica also describes 'hanging buttresses' as freestanding piers connected to a wall by corbels, and flying buttresses do reach away from the wall. That gives partial, loose support to the 'free-standing' and 'extend beyond' parts. However, I found no reliable source saying buttresses often act as monumental gateways, and nothing explaining what 'extend beyond the support line' means. I couldn't confirm the claim's 'often' wording either. My searches were cut short by a tool usage limit, so there may be sources I didn't reach. With key parts unverified, the claim can't be judged supported or contradicted.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescence to light up their habitats, but they do this by having a symbiotic relationship with themselves where some females excrete a protein that acts as a chemical reactant to produce light.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific sources show that glowworms make light inside their own light organs. A luciferase enzyme acts on a luciferin, using ATP, Mg2+ and oxygen. The claim says the light comes from a 'symbiotic relationship with themselves' in which some females excrete a reactant protein, which does not match this mechanism. The glow is also mainly used to lure prey or attract mates, not to light up the habitat. In Arachnocampa, the larvae of both sexes glow.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious natural wonder, is located in the Peruvian Amazon and remains a source of scientific fascination due to its extremely hot water and unclear origins.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and other sources say the Shanay-timpishka, known as the 'Boiling River of the Amazon,' is in the Peruvian Amazon. Its water reaches about 86°C, hot enough to kill. Wikipedia notes that it stays this hot even though there are no known active volcanoes or geothermal vents nearby. Researchers such as Andrés Ruzo study it, and sources often call it a mystery that fascinates scientists. Many explain the heat as non-volcanic geothermal circulation along faults, so 'unclear origins' overstates things a little. Still, the claim matches how reliable sources describe the river.

text: The water in the Great Barrier Reef is so clear that visible from space; however, in reality, the visible color is a result of an extremely shallow area called the "cloud" from the bottom of the ocean causing the image made by clouds overhead.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources say the Great Barrier Reef shows up in astronaut and satellite images because of its huge physical structure: a system of more than 2,900 individual reefs and about 900 islands. Its visibility has nothing to do with unusually clear water. No source mentions a shallow area called the "cloud," and none says the colour seen from space comes from clouds overhead creating an image. That explanation looks made up and goes against the accepted reason the reef can be seen from orbit.

text: Buttress, a remarkable plant from the Amazon rainforest, can lift up heavy objects with its powerful roots that anchor deep in the soil, allowing it to potentially raise a car or a large branch that uproots it.
label: contradicted
reason: "Buttress" isn't the name of a plant. Buttresses are wide roots that grow on many different kinds of rainforest trees. The sources also say these roots spread out sideways along shallow soil and reach down only a few metres at most, so they don't anchor deep in the ground. Their job is to brace tall trees against the wind and keep them from falling over. No source says they can lift heavy things like a car.

text: The length of the longest recorded flight of the Antarctic petrel, a bird species, was tracked at 32 days, 16 hours, and 52 minutes without stopping or sleeping.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't check this claim because my searches failed: the first returned unreadable output, and later ones hit the tool usage limit. Nothing I found confirms or refutes a 32-day, 16-hour, 52-minute nonstop flight by an Antarctic petrel. From background knowledge, I know of no reputable source reporting this record for the species. The best-known nonstop flight records are for other birds, such as bar-tailed godwits (about 11 days) and common swifts (months spent airborne). The claim that the bird went without sleeping is also doubtful, since some seabirds and swifts are thought to sleep while flying. The claim looks unlikely, but without supporting or contradicting evidence it cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: The McKinley Tunnels in Colorado, USA, are composed of about 8 miles of tunnel through the rock face, which was accomplished using a method called the "Great Tunnelling Machine," making it one of the most impressive tunneling feats in history.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that anything called the "McKinley Tunnels" exists in Colorado. Searches turned up the state's real tunnels instead, including the Eisenhower, Moffat (6.2 mi), Adams, and Gunnison tunnels and the Colorado National Monument tunnels. None of them is an 8-mile tunnel built with a so-called "Great Tunnelling Machine." The only "Fort McKinley Tunnels" I found are in the Philippines. The 8-mile railroad tunnel I found, through the Cascade Mountains, has no link to McKinley or Colorado. The entity in the claim seems to have no clear real-world match, but no source directly contradicts it either, so the claim can't be verified.

text: The Taj Mahal in India is made up of over 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones, including jasper, jade, and turquoise, which were used in its intricate marble inlays.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Taj Mahal's marble inlay as using about 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones. These include the official Taj Mahal site ("as many as 28") and Rock & Gem Magazine, which also lists jade from China, jasper from Punjab and turquoise from Tibet among the inlaid stones. One source (Reporter on the Road) uses the claim's own wording, "more than 28 different types". Most sources give exactly 28 rather than "over 28", so that part of the wording is slightly loose. Still, nothing contradicts the main points: the number of stone types, the three named stones and their use in the marble inlays.

text: A single DNA double helix contains more than 3.2 billion base pairs, with its length equivalent to wrapping a human hair around the Earth about 10 times.
label: contradicted
reason: The 3.2 billion base pairs figure describes the whole haploid human genome, which is split across 23 chromosomes. It does not describe a single DNA double helix. The largest single molecule, chromosome 1, has only about 250 million base pairs. The length comparison is also badly wrong. Sources say the DNA in one human cell is about 2 meters long, and one genome copy is about 1 meter. Wrapping anything around the Earth 10 times would cover roughly 400,000 km.

text: The furriest animal on the planet is the comfortless waterhog, but also known as the gaboon baboon, wasn't the answer you were expecting, however its close relative the banded mongoose has four pairs of scent glands on its bottom.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the sea otter has the densest fur of any animal on Earth, at about 500,000 to 1,000,000 hairs per square inch, so it is usually called the furriest animal. No animal called the "comfortless waterhog" appears to exist, and "gaboon baboon" is not a recognized name for one. The banded mongoose is also not a close relative of a baboon (a primate). The claim's main statement is false.

text: Honey is a natural adhesive and has been found to remain sticky even when it is 1,000 years old due to a low water content that preserves its structure and compounds.
label: supported
reason: The sources back up the main parts of the claim, though the exact '1,000 years' figure isn't stated anywhere. Live Science reports that sticky goo found in 2,500-year-old bronze jars at Paestum was chemically confirmed to be honey with intact sugars, so ancient honey can stay sticky well past 1,000 years. Explainers on 3,000-year-old honey from Egyptian tombs credit its preservation mainly to low moisture content (under about 18%), along with acidity. An NIH/PMC review describes honey-based adhesives being developed for wound care, and a USPTO patent covers a surgical adhesive containing honey, which supports calling honey an adhesive material. No source contradicts the claim.

text: The "Gravity Hills" in Leeson Street, Dublin, Ireland, is a unique optical illusion where, due to the angle of the sun or street lighting, it appears that water flows uphill.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that mentions a 'Gravity Hill' or a water-flows-uphill illusion on Leeson Street in Dublin. The top result for 'Gravity Hill Leeson Street Dublin' was a general page describing Leeson Street as a major Dublin road. Articles on Ireland's 'magic roads' or gravity hills describe rural sites such as the Cooley Mountains in Co. Louth and the Comeragh Mountains in Co. Waterford, not a Dublin city street. The claim looks unfounded, but I hit the search limit and found no source that directly says Leeson Street has no such feature, so I can't call it contradicted.

text: The telescope is run in part by a yard full of solar panels at the Mauna Kea Observatory, Hawaii because it needs a lot of power.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim never says which telescope it means, so it can't be checked as written. The closest match is the W. M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea. Reports say Keck put a 133-kW solar array (332 panels) on the facility's roof, between the Keck I and Keck II domes, in 2020, and that it covers about 10–15% of the observatory's power needs. That roughly fits the idea that solar runs it 'in part.' But the panels are on a roof, not in a yard, and the claim may be about a different telescope or a different setup. Since I can't tell which telescope is meant and can't confirm the 'yard full of solar panels' detail, the claim is inconclusive.

text: There is a lake in Africa called Lake Natron, known for its extremely high pH levels that can turn animals that die in it into stone due to the concentration of sodium carbonate.
label: supported
reason: Lake Natron is a soda lake in northern Tanzania with a very high pH (around 10.5) caused by volcanic sodium carbonate. Smithsonian Magazine and other outlets describe it as a lake that "turns animals into stone" by calcifying and preserving animals that die there. Strictly speaking, the animals are calcified or mummified-looking rather than literally turned to stone, but the claim matches how the lake is commonly and credibly described.

text: Buttresses, which are architectural features providing support for buildings, often extend beyond the support line, act as monumental gateways, or become free-standing structures with their own aesthetic appeal.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, Study.com and other architecture glossaries, confirm that buttresses are structures that support or reinforce walls. Some types, such as flying buttresses, stand away from the wall, and flying buttresses are often described as adding to a building's aesthetic appeal. However, I found no source saying that buttresses 'act as monumental gateways' or commonly become free-standing structures valued for their own looks. In my searches, 'monumental gateway' was the dictionary definition of a pylon or propylon, not a buttress, so that part of the claim seems to mix up different architectural terms. No source directly contradicts the claim, but key parts cannot be verified, so it is inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Green Inferno", is a rare and mysterious river in Peru that flows for approximately 100 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is a real river in Peru, but it is not about 100 km long. Wikipedia gives its length as about 9 km, and other sources say about 6.4 km. Either figure contradicts the claim of roughly 100 km. The "Green Inferno" nickname was also not confirmed.

text: Buttress parsnip, also known as sand parsnip, is a type of plant that has seeds containing toxic compounds called apiosnin which may cause nausea and eye irritation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. Searches turned up no plant called "buttress parsnip" and nothing showing it is also known as "sand parsnip." There is also no record of a compound called "apiosnin"; that search only returned pages about Apios americana (groundnut). The real parsnip-family plants, such as wild parsnip (Pastinaca sativa), are known for toxins in their sap that cause skin burns, but none of the sources mention the named plant, the compound, or nausea and eye irritation from its seeds. The plant and the compound both appear to be made up or have no clear referent. Since no source directly contradicts the claim, the right label is inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Ocean basins.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the main parts of the claim. NOAA Ocean Exploration and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution both call the mid-ocean ridge system Earth's longest mountain range, at about 65,000 km (roughly 40,000 miles). Wikipedia also says the ridge system runs through every ocean, including the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins. There are two caveats. First, NOAA and WHOI say "nearly" 65,000 km, not "over." Other sources give larger figures: Wikipedia puts the total ridge system at 80,000 km, and a NASA page says 74,000 km. So "over 65,000 km" is defensible but depends on how the ridge is measured. Second, the ridge runs through the middle of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, but in the Pacific the East Pacific Rise lies off-center. That makes "center" loose wording there. Neither caveat contradicts the claim's main point.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their shy and gentle nature, which makes them blush or appear embarrassed when they are together.
label: contradicted
reason: The name is right: several sources, including HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals and ZME Science, say a group of giant pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." The explanation in the claim is not. No source links the term to pandas being shy, gentle or blushing, and pandas do not blush. HowStuffWorks says the word has no scientific origin and is just English whimsy, perhaps inspired by how clumsy and lazy pandas look. A-Z Animals, ZME Science and Animal Corner also credit their clumsy or lazy behaviour. Because the stated reason conflicts with what reliable sources say, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built the first Pram (pushchair) which was used for soldiers in World War I to carry their babies.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Several sources say William Kent, an English architect, built the first pram in 1733 for the Duke of Devonshire's children, almost two centuries before World War I. Arotech Corporation is a US defense and security company founded in 1990 (originally as Electric Fuel), not a British aerospace company that built prams. The idea that WWI soldiers used prams to carry their babies also has no support.

text: The shallow waters of the Great Blue Hole, a large underwater sinkhole in Belize, reveal a stunning sight at high tide due to the crystal-clear visibility of up to 150 feet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. The Great Blue Hole is a large underwater sinkhole off Belize, and Scuba Diving magazine says its visibility 'generally exceeds 150 feet' (ambergriscaye.com says it sometimes approaches 200 feet). The rest could not be verified. No source says the shallow waters reveal a stunning sight at high tide, or links clarity to the tide. Also, the site is mainly known as a deep hole about 400 feet deep, not for shallow-water views at high tide. Because the tide detail has no support, the claim cannot be fully confirmed.

text: The impressive-looking Gmelins snub-nosed monkey has a highly unique adaptation that sets it apart from other primates: its protruding nose helps reduce sunburn on its face by providing additional shade.
label: contradicted
reason: No snub-nosed monkey species is called "Gmelin's." The five Rhinopithecus species include the golden, black-and-white (Yunnan), Tonkin (Dollman's), gray and Myanmar snub-nosed monkeys. These monkeys also don't have protruding noses. Their noses are short, flat and sharply upturned. Sources describe this nose shape as an adaptation that protects them from frostbite in cold mountain habitats, not one that shades the face to reduce sunburn. So both the nose shape and its stated purpose in the claim are wrong.

text: Coconuts can float for several weeks in the water due to their high oil content, which allows them to stay buoyant even when submerged.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say coconuts float because their fibrous husk is full of trapped air, which makes the fruit less dense than water. None of them credit high oil content. The claim that coconuts can float for weeks is true, and some sources say they can stay afloat and viable for up to about 110 days. The stated reason, high oil content, is wrong, though. The reliable explanations name the air-filled husk instead.

text: Over 70% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, with approximately 96.5% of it being ocean water.
label: supported
reason: The USGS Water Science School says that about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, which is over 70%. It also says the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water. Both parts of the claim match this trustworthy government source.

text: The Human Brain accounts for about 2% of the human body's total mass but consumes roughly 20% of its total energy expenditure.
label: supported
reason: Multiple sources, including The Physics Factbook, which compiles encyclopedia citations, say the brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest. This matches the claim. One caveat: the 20% figure refers to resting energy use, while the claim says 'total energy expenditure.' The approximate wording ('roughly 20%') keeps the claim consistent with the well-established figure.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points. Wikipedia and NOAA Ocean Exploration call the global mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range on Earth. Wikipedia puts the continuous range at 65,000 km and the whole ridge system at 80,000 km, and several sources say it is 'over 65,000 km', which fits the claim. NOAA gives a slightly lower figure, 'nearly 65,000 km', so the exact number varies by source and by what is counted. The ridge does run through the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Indian Ocean ridges) and Arctic (Gakkel Ridge) Oceans. The claim leaves out the Pacific (East Pacific Rise), but that makes the list incomplete rather than wrong.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the mid-ocean ridge system, which spans over 65,000 kilometers around the globe.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth. NOAA Ocean Service puts its length at 40,389 miles (about 65,000 km). NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI say it is 'nearly 65,000 km' long, which slightly conflicts with the claim's 'over 65,000 km.' AMNH, however, says the ridge is 'more than 70,000 kilometers' long, which backs 'over 65,000 km.' Because the figures all fall around 65,000 km or above, and one reliable source supports 'over,' I judge the claim supported. The 'nearly' versus 'over' difference is a small caveat.

text: The pillow was invented around 7,000 years back by the Mesopotamians who filled buckwheat sacks with wool or feathers.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources say the earliest pillows date to about 7000 BC in Mesopotamia, which is roughly 9,000 years ago, not 7,000. They were made of stone and used to keep the head raised so insects couldn't get into the ears and mouth. The sources say nothing about sacks of buckwheat filled with wool or feathers. Soft, stuffed pillows came later, for example in ancient Greece, Rome and China.

text: The surface area of the largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is about 61.4 million square miles.
label: contradicted
reason: ESA puts Jupiter's surface area at just under 61.5 billion square kilometres, and other sources give about 6.14 × 10^10 km² (61.42 billion km²). That works out to roughly 23.7 billion square miles. The claim's '61.4 million square miles' seems to come from the km² figure, but it uses the wrong unit and is off by a factor of about 1,000. It is far below the real value.

text: TheHistogram, a rare blood clotting disorder, is caused by a mutation that removes the entirety of the F8 gene in carriers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any disorder called "TheHistogram" in medical or scientific sources, so the claim's subject has no clear referent. The searches only turned up hemophilia A. That condition is an X-linked bleeding disorder caused by many kinds of F8 mutations, such as intron 22 inversions, point mutations and deletions. A deletion of the whole F8 gene is not its defining cause. Because the named disorder can't be identified, the claim can't be checked.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees covering the planet.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. A 2015 global study (Crowther et al., published in Nature) estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth. NASA puts the number of stars in the Milky Way at roughly 100–400 billion. Even at the high end of that range, trees outnumber stars by more than seven to one. The source below, a general reference site, reports both figures; I didn't open the Nature paper or NASA's page directly.

text: There are more trees on Earth than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees covering about 30% of the planet's land area.
label: supported
reason: Researchers estimate there are about 3 trillion trees on Earth (Crowther et al. 2015). The Milky Way is thought to hold roughly 100 to 400 billion stars, so trees outnumber its stars by a wide margin. FAO reports that forests cover 31% of the world's land area, which matches the claim's 'about 30%'.

text: The blind beetle, specifically the larva of the click beetle, Parafre freyjaucheni, has been known to use sound waves to navigate through its underground environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a species called 'Parafre freyjaucheni'. Searches only turned up unrelated tephritid fly genera such as Parafreutreta. Reliable sources describe click beetle larvae (wireworms) as underground root feeders, and the only sound they mention is the adult's clicking when it rights itself. None of the sources I found say that a blind click beetle larva uses sound waves to navigate underground. The species may not exist and the claimed behaviour is undocumented, so the claim can't be verified. I also found no direct evidence that disproves it.

text: The enabling of specialized light behaviors in certain sharks and other marine animals are known as counter-illumination, which allows them to blend into their environment more effectively, often producing light to match the starlight above.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results confirm the main part of the claim: some sharks, such as kitefin and lanternsharks, and other marine animals use counter-illumination, giving off light from their undersides to hide their silhouette. However, the scientific sources say this light matches the residual downwelling daylight, meaning sunlight or moonlight filtering down through the water. A 2026 iScience study, for example, found that the kitefin shark's belly glow matches downwelling daylight, including its 491 nm peak. None of the sources say the animals often match starlight, so that detail is wrong and the claim as stated is contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration describes the global mid-ocean ridge system as the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km. WorldAtlas gives the same length and says the Mid-Atlantic Ridge section runs through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. One detail is slightly off: NOAA says "nearly" 65,000 km, while the claim says "over," and some other sources give longer figures. The claim also leaves out that the ridge winds through the Pacific and Indian oceans as well as the Atlantic. Neither issue contradicts the claim's main point.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-wide section of the Amazon River in Peru that maintains a temperature of 30°C (86°F), even though the surrounding river drops to 20°C (68°F) in the winter and rises to 24°C (75°F) in the summer.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources describe the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) as a separate 6.4 km tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali and from there into the Amazon. It is not a section of the Amazon River itself. Its water is also much hotter than the claim says: about 45°C to nearly 100°C, not a steady 30°C. Those two facts contradict the claim. The 50-meter width and the seasonal temperatures of the surrounding river don't match these sources either.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretching over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) and running through the middle of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both call the mid-ocean ridge system the longest mountain range on Earth, at about 65,000 km (40,000 miles). Both sources say it winds through the world's oceans between the continents, and it includes the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Indian Ocean ridges and the East Pacific Rise. There is one small wording difference: the sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over.' The claim also says the ridge runs through the 'middle' of the Pacific, but the East Pacific Rise lies in the eastern Pacific. These are minor approximations, and the claim's main point matches the sources.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlyweds walk on a rope bridge suspended between two boats to signify the beginning of their new life together.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nairs are a community in Kerala, and they did practise Thalikettu (also called Kettu Kalyanam). But sources describe it as a tāli-tying ceremony: a ritual mock marriage held for girls before puberty, in which a tāli (sacred thread or pendant) was tied. It was not a "boat bridge ceremony" where newlyweds walk on a rope bridge between two boats. That part of the claim is made up.

text: Butterflyfish were one of the only vertebrates to practice a symbiotic relationship by going into uninhabitable coral reefs to clean out intruders and disease.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on the main point. TFH Magazine says cleaning symbiosis on coral reefs is carried out by many animals, including certain wrasses and gobies, cleaner shrimps, and some angelfish and butterflyfish. Butterflyfish are not "one of the only vertebrates" that do this, and the source says the butterflyfish that clean do so only as juveniles. Many other vertebrates also have symbiotic relationships. Nothing supports the idea that butterflyfish go into "uninhabitable" coral reefs to clear out intruders and disease. Butterflyfish are reef residents, and many of them feed on coral.

text: The color blue is a rare color in nature, with only a few organisms, such as certain butterflies, birds, and sea creatures, able to see it due to the limitations of their visual spectrum.
label: contradicted
reason: Blue is rare in nature, but the reason given in the claim is wrong. Sources say blue is rare because few organisms can make true blue pigment, so most blue animals, such as Morpho butterflies, blue jays and peacocks, get their colour from microscopic structures that scatter light. The rarity has nothing to do with which organisms can see blue. Many animals, including humans, most birds and many insects, can see blue, so the idea that only a few organisms can see it is false.

text: The continent of Antarctica is home to several active volcanoes, with the most recently discovered one being the Neumann Glacier volcanic complex, which erupted in 2017.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm that Antarctica has active volcanoes. Mount Erebus is one example, and a 2017 study reported 138 volcanoes, 91 of them previously unknown. I found no trace of a 'Neumann Glacier volcanic complex' or a 2017 eruption there. The only 'Neumann' results were Neumann Peak, an unrelated peak on Hansen Island, and a catalog author named Neumann van Padang. The Wikipedia list of Antarctic volcanoes and the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program results did not mention any such volcano. The named volcano appears to be unverified or made up, but I found no source that directly says it doesn't exist. So the key part of the claim can't be verified.

text: The Janszoon boom log, discovered in 1999, is a 4.2-meter-long Redwood tree trunk found off the coast of Western Australia, which is estimated to be over 2,000 years old.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Janszoon boom log". Searches for the exact name only returned general pages about the Dutch explorer Willem Janszoon, log booms in general, and redwood trees. None of them describe a 4.2-metre redwood trunk found off Western Australia in 1999, or put such a log at over 2,000 years old. A Walpole-Nornalup local history page about a "Conspicuous Log Mystery" did come up, but its snippet doesn't match these details, and I couldn't read the full page because I hit the search limit. With no evidence for or against the specific details, the claim can't be verified and may be made up.

text: The length of a standard American gallon can vary by no more than 1/128 of a teardrop, with a maximum deviation of only 0.125 inches, showcasing the extremely precise measurements in the US system.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats the gallon as a length, which it isn't. Britannica describes the US gallon as a unit of liquid and dry measure, meaning volume, and defines the US liquid gallon as exactly 231 cubic inches (four quarts). Because the gallon is fixed by that definition, it has no 'length' that could vary by 0.125 inches. The 'teardrop' is not a recognized unit, so a tolerance of '1/128 of a teardrop' means nothing.

text: The total distance covered by the Milky Way galaxy in its entirety, from one end of the galaxy to the other, is estimated to be over 100,000 light-years.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the Milky Way as a whole is more than 100,000 light-years across. Science News reports that, counting its halo, the galaxy stretches nearly 2 million light-years, over 15 times wider than its bright spiral disk. Wikipedia gives about 200,000 light-years for the stellar disk, and NASA's commonly cited figure is about 100,000 light-years. Wikipedia also lists a narrower D25 isophotal diameter of about 87,400 light-years, but that measures only one brightness threshold of the disk, not the galaxy in its entirety.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the full moon appears from behind a hill or mountain due to a rare atmospheric condition, can create an illusion of a "hidden" moondisk.
label: contradicted
reason: In the Korean dictionary, 뒷문 means "back door" (a door at the back or side), and it is also used figuratively for an improper shortcut. It is not the name of any moon phenomenon and does not mean "Hidden Moon." I found no source describing a "Hidden Moon" effect caused by a rare atmospheric condition. A full moon rising from behind a mountain is an ordinary sight, and the related effect that is documented is the Moon illusion, which has nothing to do with a "hidden" moon. The claim's central premise, that 뒷문 is this phenomenon, is false.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the ocean called the turquoise jellyfish, also known as the nomadic jellyfish, that is biologically immortal and can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The jellyfish that is biologically immortal and turns back into a younger form through transdifferentiation is Turritopsis dohrnii, usually called the "immortal jellyfish" (Britannica, NHM, Wikipedia, PubMed). Reliable sources don't give it the names "turquoise jellyfish" or "nomadic jellyfish." "Nomad jellyfish" is the common name of a different species, Rhopilema nomadica, a light-blue jellyfish from the Indo-Pacific that has spread into the Mediterranean, and nothing says it is immortal. The claim's descriptions of immortality and transdifferentiation are accurate, but it pins them on the wrong species name, so that part is contradicted.

text: A group of kissing HUDS, which are also known as a cluster of greater flamingos, is estimated to be one of the largest bird colonies on the planet, with over 3 million birds.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found says a group of flamingos is called "kissing HUDS." Sources say the usual collective noun is a "flamboyance"; searching for "kissing HUDS" only turned up unrelated photos of flamingos facing each other. Guinness World Records says the largest flamingo colony belongs to lesser flamingos (Phoeniconaias minor), not greater flamingos. It lists about 2.5 million birds in Tanzania, with at least 1.5–2.5 million across East Africa's soda lakes. A total of 3–4 million is only an unsurveyed estimate for all lesser flamingos across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia, not one colony. So the claim's name, species and "over 3 million" colony figure don't match reliable sources.

text: Did you know that honey is a super-efficient food source because it contains a platform of carbs, vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and antioxidants that can be easily absorbed by the body due to its natural humidity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The ingredient list checks out. The National Honey Board's guide and a ScienceDirect review both say honey contains carbohydrates (about 75–83%), plus vitamins, minerals, amino acids (0.05–0.1%), acids and antioxidants. Honey is also described as a source of readily available carbohydrates. But I found no source saying these nutrients are easily absorbed because of honey's 'natural humidity.' Honey is actually low in moisture (under about 17%), and its quick absorption is normally explained by its simple sugars, not its water content. Because the reason the claim gives can't be verified and looks doubtful, the claim as a whole is not fully supported.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - totaling 4.5 billion and over 11 million acres worldwide.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the claim's main figure. The U.S. tree count isn't wrong, but it is far too low. Sources put it at about 228 billion trees (Davey) and nearly 1.4 trillion trees and seedlings on forestland in the contiguous U.S. (WorldAtlas). "Over 300 million" is technically true, but it understates the real number by roughly a thousand times. The second part says corporations have planted 4.5 billion trees on over 11 million acres worldwide. I found no source for this. The closest figures were for other things: American Forests, a nonprofit, aims to plant 4 billion trees across 16 million acres of North America by 2030, and Turkey planted 11 million trees in one day. Neither describes corporate planting totals. My search tool hit its limit before I could check corporate pledge totals, such as those on 1t.org, so I can't confirm or rule out the 4.5 billion figure.

text: The surface area of the Earth is 510 million square kilometers, but scientists estimate that only 29% of it is land and the remaining 71% is water.
label: supported
reason: Space.com gives Earth's surface area as about 510 million square kilometers, with about 29% land and 71% water. Wikipedia and ChartsBin give consistent figures: about 510,065,000–510,072,000 km², split roughly 29.2% land and 70.8% water. None of the sources contradict the claim.

text: The Blue Fairy Tern, also known as Arenaria interpres, is a rare and endangered tern species that lays its eggs on the ground in dense vegetation, rather than on rocks or trees like many other sea birds.
label: contradicted
reason: GBIF identifies Arenaria interpres as the Ruddy Turnstone. That is a sandpiper-family shorebird, not a tern, and no source calls it a "Blue Fairy Tern." The Ruddy Turnstone is also listed as Least Concern, not rare or endangered. So the claim's name and conservation status are both wrong.

text: The finish on the Lincoln Memorial in Washington D.C. was actually created using a technique called "foxing" which involves pouring a mixture of limestone dust and egg whites onto the surface to create a smooth, glossy appearance.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. In conservation, 'foxing' means the brown spots that form on old paper because of mould and metal contamination (Britannica, Wikipedia). It is not a way of finishing stone. The National Park Service says the Lincoln Memorial was built from natural stones: white Colorado Yule marble on the exterior, Indiana limestone, and Tennessee pink marble. No source mentions pouring limestone dust and egg whites over the surface. No page directly says this technique wasn't used, but the claim gets the meaning of foxing wrong, and the documented materials don't match it.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only about 20-30% of the total number of species that may actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) put the estimated total number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. That number is not a count of species already known. The same study says more than 80% of species are still undiscovered, with only about 1.2 million described. So it is the known species, not 8.7 million, that make up a small share of the total. Saying 8.7 million is only 20–30% of all species misstates what the estimate means.

text: The Maasai people of East Africa have a unique tradition of removing their lower eyelid's outer portion, a practice known as "steatite," which is typically done to signify adulthood, wealth, or social status.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describing Maasai body modification list earlobe piercing and stretching, removal of canine teeth in early childhood, and removal of the two lower central incisors. None mentions removing part of the eyelid. "Steatite" is not the name of a Maasai custom: dictionaries and Wikipedia define it as another name for soapstone, a soft talc-based rock. The claim appears to be invented and mislabels a real word.

text: The Cleopatra Needle, an ancient Egyptian obelisk, was actually moved to London by the British, but when the needle officially arrived in London in 1878, an Egyptian delegation appealed to lift and box it in ballast adequate to add 20 tons to its weight rather than launch it to safety so they
label: not_verifiable
reason: Royal Museums Greenwich backs up the basic facts. Cleopatra's Needle is an ancient Egyptian obelisk, and the British brought it to London in a purpose-built cylindrical vessel. It arrived in 1878 and was put up on the Thames Embankment that September. However, no reliable source mentions an Egyptian delegation asking for the obelisk to be lifted and boxed with ballast adding 20 tons to its weight. The claim's sentence is also cut off and incomplete. Because this key part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will break down and kill the rights tree or shrub they can't infect.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any fungus called "chantinggorias". A web search only brings up results for chanterelles (Cantharellus), so the name has no clear referent. If it was meant to be chanterelles, Wikipedia describes them as mycorrhizal fungi, meaning they form partnerships with plants rather than killing trees. Because the name is unclear, there isn't enough evidence to call the claim supported or contradicted. The claim's own wording ("the rights tree or shrub they can't infect") also doesn't make sense.

text: The position of the constellations in the night sky changes over time due to a phenomenon called the procession of the equinoxes, which occurs as the Earth's rotational axis wobbles at a rate of about 20 centimeters (7.9 inches) per year.
label: contradicted
reason: The basic idea in the claim is correct: precession of the equinoxes (misspelled "procession" in the claim) is a slow wobble of Earth's spin axis that gradually shifts the sky's coordinate frame. But the rate is wrong. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, St Andrews University notes, Universe Today) measure precession as an angle: about 50.3 arcseconds per year, roughly 1 degree every 72 years, or one full cycle every ~26,000 years. It is not measured as a distance like 20 cm per year. The only centimeter-scale figure found is NASA's: the spin axis drifted about 10 cm (4 inches) per year in the 20th century. That figure is for polar motion, a different effect driven by mass shifts such as ice loss, and it is still not 20 cm. So the claimed '20 centimeters (7.9 inches) per year' rate is contradicted.

text: The Cat's Pyjamaas, a species of moth, has a unique characteristic of having fur-like eye spots on its caterpillars that resemble the eyes of a feline predator, potentially deterring predators from attacking it.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My one completed search for "Cat's Pyjamas" moth didn't turn up any moth with that common name. It returned only unrelated Lepidoptera, a butterfly (Catagramma pygas) and the common butterfly moth (Tetragonus catamitus). Later searches failed because I hit the tool-use limit, so this wasn't a full check. The name "Cat's Pyjamaas" doesn't clearly point to a known species, and I found no evidence about cat-like eyespots on its caterpillars, so I can't confirm or rule out the claim.

text: The Djallonke sheep, a breed of West African sheep, can weigh as much as 100 kg (220 lbs) and be up to 75 cm (30 inches) tall at the shoulder.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe the Djallonke as a dwarf breed. ILRI/DAGRIS puts its height at the withers at 40–60 cm and its body weight at 20–30 kg. A KNUST thesis gives 20–30 kg for females and 25–35 kg for males. Weights of up to 100 kg and heights of up to 75 cm are far outside these ranges.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescence to light up their habitats, but they do this by having a symbiotic relationship with themselves where some females don't lay eggs and instead act as a light source.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. Glowworms make their own light through a chemical reaction: luciferin combines with oxygen, catalysed by luciferase. In the New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa), the larvae glow to lure prey into sticky snares. In Lampyris noctiluca, the adult females glow to attract mates and then lay eggs. No source describes a 'symbiotic relationship with themselves' or a group of non-egg-laying females that act as a light source. The glow is used to attract prey or mates, not to light up the habitat.

text: The total distance covered by the Milky Way galaxy in its entirety, from one end of the galaxy to the other, is estimated to be around 100,000 light-years.
label: supported
reason: Several trustworthy sources, including NASA (science.nasa.gov), Las Cumbres Observatory and Space.com, put the Milky Way at about 100,000 light-years across. Some newer estimates are larger (for example, a stellar disk of up to about 200,000 light-years), but the claim only says 'estimated to be around 100,000 light-years', which matches the widely cited standard figure.

text: TheOMICRAN antisatellite network, a system of radar and electronic warfare assets in the UK, uses the Jindalee Operational Radar Network, a system based in Australia.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions an "OMICRAN antisatellite network" in the UK. A search for "OMICRAN" only turned up an unrelated old Google patent for a drafting tool (a "projectograph"). One part of the claim is confirmed: the Jindalee Operational Radar Network (JORN) is a real Australian over-the-horizon radar network run by the RAAF (per IEEE and Wikipedia). UK Defence Journal also reports that Britain is interested in JORN. However, nothing shows that a UK system called OMICRAN exists or that it uses JORN. Because that central part can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Honey is a super-conductor when it's heated above 2.5°C (36.5°F), and it's the only food item known to exhibit this unique property.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is not a superconductor. Its electrical conductivity is low and limited: the Codex Standard for Honey requires it to be under 0.8 mS/cm when diluted, and it comes from dissolved mineral ions. A superconductor has zero electrical resistance, so a low, measurable conductivity rules that out. In physics, superconductivity happens only in specific materials, mostly at very low (cryogenic) temperatures, not in a food heated above 2.5°C. No credible source backs the claim, and the measured conductivity values contradict it.

text: The highest recorded number of premature births occurred during the Great Flood of 1931 in China, where more than 4 million infants were reportedly born with premature conditions due to their mothers' stress and body trauma from the disaster.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source saying that 4 million or more premature births happened during the 1931 China floods, or that this was a record. Reliable sources on the floods, including Wikipedia, FloodList and Study.com, use the figure of up to about 3.7–4 million for deaths, not premature births. None of them mention premature births linked to mothers' stress or physical trauma. The claim appears to have misused the death toll, but no source directly says how many premature births there were, so the claim can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which was discovered and is an ancient species from the Pliocene Epoch.
label: contradicted
reason: The 'short-eared elephant shrew' (Macroscelides proboscideus, now usually called the round-eared elephant shrew) is not extinct. Wikipedia lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Stegolophodon is an extinct proboscidean, but sources describe it as a Miocene–Pliocene genus, not just a Pliocene one. No source calls it the 'short-eared elephant.' The main claim that the short-eared elephant is extinct is false.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "Strengths," but the officially longest one syllable is "sprightly" another word that is has a single syllable is Stammer some will say "stunt" is the longest one syllable yet.
label: contradicted

The rest of the claim is wrong. "Sprightly" has two syllables (spright-ly) and "stammer" has two syllables (stam-mer), so neither is a one-syllable word, and no list names "sprightly" as the official longest one. "Stunt" does have one syllable, but at five letters it is clearly shorter than nine-letter words like "strengths," "screeched" and "scratched."

text: The Loneliest House on Earth, located in Quirimbas National Park in Mozambique, has become a major tourist attraction due to its unique isolation and only accessible by boat at low tide.
label: contradicted
reason: The building widely known as the 'Loneliest House in the World/on Earth' is the hunting lodge on Elliðaey island in Iceland's Westman Islands, not anywhere in Quirimbas National Park in Mozambique. Searching for a 'loneliest house' in Quirimbas found nothing. Sources describing the Elliðaey lodge say it was built in 1953 as a hunting lodge for a puffin-hunting association. That contradicts the location in the claim and the details that follow from it.

text: France has the longest Wall of Love in the world, a 500-meter-long (1,640 ft long) wall near the Sacre-Coeur Basilica in Paris where people have written millions of messages of love.
label: contradicted
reason: Paris's Wall of Love (Le mur des je t'aime) is in Square Jehan Rictus in Montmartre. Sources put its surface at only about 40 square metres, so it is nowhere near 500 m long. It is made of 612 enamelled lava tiles that the artists Frédéric Baron and Claire Kito made in 2000. The tiles carry the phrase 'I love you' 311 times in 250 languages, or more than 1,000 times in over 300 languages depending on the source. That is not millions of messages written by the public. Nothing in the results supports the 500 m length or the 'longest in the world' title.

text: The chantinggorias, a species of fungi, have a unique life cycle in which their mycelium will join with other fungus by the tips of branching cells in a process called "connate hyphal anastomosis."
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no fungus called "chantinggorias." The results only showed chanterelles (Cantharellus) and unrelated words about chanting and Gregorian chant, so the name doesn't point to a real organism. A search for the exact phrase "connate hyphal anastomosis" also found no matches. Hyphal anastomosis, the fusion of fungal hyphae, is real and well documented, as in the FEMS Microbiology Ecology paper and the conidial anastomosis tube literature. But nothing ties it to this supposed species or uses that specific term. Because the subject has no clear referent and the specific claims can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The world's largest waterfall, when measured by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Caverns, where cold water from the Arctic Ocean flows down into the North Atlantic Ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: The underwater waterfall exists, but the claim gets its name wrong. Live Science and Discover Wildlife both call it the Denmark Strait cataract, not the "Denmark Strait Caverns." It is a sloping section of seafloor between Iceland and Greenland, not a set of caverns. Live Science also says it carries cold water from the Nordic Seas into the Irminger Sea, a basin within the North Atlantic. The core idea, the world's largest waterfall located underwater, is supported. The claim's description of Arctic water flowing into the North Atlantic is broadly right, though loosely worded.

text: The.shader is a very small town in Lenin district of Volgograd Oblast, Russia, with only about 1 resident according to the 2010 census.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. "The.shader" looks like a garbled name, and I found no evidence that a settlement with that name exists in Leninsky District, Volgograd Oblast. My searches only turned up general pages about the district and other small khutors such as Bulgakov. None of them mentioned "The.shader" or showed a 2010 census population of about 1 for it. I wasn't able to run more searches because the tool's usage limit was reached. Since the entity has no clear referent and the population figure is unconfirmed, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, Iceland is home to the world's oldest and most northernmost "post glacial lake" which is located at the highest point and is about 4,591 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source naming any Icelandic lake as the world's oldest and most northerly post-glacial lake, or giving an age of 4,591 years. The claim also clashes with basic evidence. Post-glacial lakes formed as glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, about 10,000 to 20,000 years ago. Minnesota's lakes, for example, are dated to 10,000–20,000 years ago, and Lake Peace formed around 14,000 BCE. A lake about 4,591 years old therefore can't be the world's oldest post-glacial lake. Searches on Icelandic lakes turned up only examples like Jökulsárlón, which formed about 100 years ago. Iceland also lies in the North Atlantic, close to the Arctic, not in the 'middle' of the Atlantic, and the 'northernmost' and 'highest point' details aren't supported anywhere.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built the first Pram (pushchair) which was used for soldiers in World War I to carry their wounded to safety.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Arotech Corporation was not a British aerospace company and it had nothing to do with World War I. It was founded in Delaware, USA, in 1990 as Electric Fuel Corporation and took the name Arotech in 2003. It made batteries and simulation equipment for defense customers. The first pram also predates WWI by almost two centuries: several sources credit the English architect William Kent, who built one in 1733 for the Duke of Devonshire's children, not for carrying wounded soldiers.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where the river's water not only appears to be boiling but remains liquid, with scientists still trying to determine the cause of this unique occurrence.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the river's identity right, but its main point is wrong. The Boiling River is the Shanay-timpishka in Peru. Its water reaches about 210°F (roughly 99°C), so it is near boiling but stays mostly liquid, which fits the first part of the claim. The problem is the statement that scientists are still trying to find the cause. Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo has studied the river, and Wikipedia says the leading explanation is the Earth's geothermal gradient. Earth.com reports that geoscientists attribute the heat to fault-fed activity, where underground water channels meet geothermal energy. Research on the river continues, but the cause is broadly explained rather than an open mystery.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built the first Pram (pushchair) which was used for soldiers in World War I to carry their rifles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Arotech is an American defense and security company, not a former British aerospace firm, and it was founded in 1990, long after World War I. Many sources also say the first pram was built in 1733 by the English architect William Kent for the Duke of Devonshire's children. It was not made for soldiers to carry rifles.

text: Buttress parsnip, also known as sand parsnip, is a type of plant that has seeds containing toxic properties called lignans, these can cause blisters on human skin upon contact.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no plant called "buttress parsnip," so I can't confirm that name or that it is the same as "sand parsnip." The key factual point is wrong, though. The Invasive Species Centre and Iowa State Extension say parsnips' skin-blistering toxins are furanocoumarins, and these build up most in the leaves. They are not lignans in the seeds. Furanocoumarins blister skin when exposed skin is then hit by sunlight (phytophotodermatitis), not through contact alone. Because the claim names the wrong compounds, it is contradicted.

text: The short-eared elephant is now extinct however the extinct species also referred to as a short-eared elephant is actually known as Stegolophodon which dated back to the Pleistocene epoch.
label: contradicted
reason: The only real animal with this name is the short-eared elephant shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus, also called the round-eared sengi). It is alive today and listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, so it is not extinct. I also found no source calling Stegolophodon a 'short-eared elephant'. Mindat and the Fossil Wiki both date Stegolophodon to the Miocene and Pliocene, not the Pleistocene.

text: The country of Singapore has the highest percentage of OPT (Optometrists, Pharmacists, Nurses, Doctors) professionals globally in its population due to its successful healthcare system.
label: contradicted
reason: World Bank figures, as summarized by NY Requirements, put Cuba first for doctors per capita at 8.4 per 1,000 people, followed by Monaco, Georgia, Greece and others. Singapore is not on that list. For nurses and midwives, Monaco and Norway are among the leaders. Neither ranking puts Singapore at the top. Also, "OPT" is not a standard acronym for these professions. The claim that Singapore has the world's highest share of health professionals is therefore contradicted.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlywed couples are carried across a river on a boat by friends.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nayars (Nairs) are indeed a community in Kerala, and they did practise a ceremony called Thalikettu (Thali Kettu or Kettu Kalyanam). But the claim gets the ceremony wrong. Wikipedia describes Thalikettu as a 'tali-tying ceremony': an elaborate mock marriage held for girls before puberty, where a tali (a pendant worn as a sign of marriage) is tied around each girl's neck. It is not a 'boat bridge ceremony', and no source describes newlyweds being carried across a river on a boat by friends. That description is made up.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, but it appears so bright in the sky because of an unusual alignment with Earth, rather than its actual brightness due to the fact that it is shrouded in thick clouds that reflect sunlight.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is the brightest planet in Earth's sky, but the claim gets the reason wrong. ESA and Caltech's IPAC both say Venus looks so bright because its thick clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits it (about 70%), and because it is the closest planet to Earth. Neither credits an 'unusual alignment' with Earth. The claim treats cloud reflection as something other than the real cause, which is the opposite of what these sources say.

text: Cstorabies, more commonly known as stars, have blood only a mere 0.00001% of the blood that shows in their bodies due to the transparent nature of the vessels although they have a very unique cooling system that is due to blood as we have explained in simple form.
label: contradicted
reason: "Cstorabies" isn't a real name for stars or sea stars. Reliable sources say starfish (sea stars) have no blood and no blood-based circulatory system. Instead, a water vascular system moves seawater through their bodies. That contradicts the claim's 0.00001% blood figure, its "transparent vessels" explanation, and its blood-based cooling system. If "stars" means stars in the sky, they have no blood either.

text: Octopuses possess the unique ability to lose a limb as a defense mechanism, and then regrow it in a process that can take several weeks to a year or more, depending on the species.
label: supported
reason: Researchers at UC Berkeley, in a meeting abstract hosted by SICB, describe arm autotomy (deliberately shedding an arm) as an octopus defense used to escape predators. They found it is energetically costly to regrow the arm, and signs of regrowth appeared about three weeks after loss. Mental Floss reports that a lost octopus arm regrows in about 130 days. These sources support the main point that octopuses can drop an arm for defense and regrow it over weeks to months. Two parts are not fully backed: 'unique' is loosely worded, since lizards, crabs and sea stars can also shed limbs, and the sources found do not confirm the 'a year or more' upper end. I read 'unique' as meaning 'remarkable' and treat the claim as supported overall.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in Peru, remains unsolved to this day, with scientists observing a stable and constant river despite being located within the midst of the Amazon rainforest where no geothermal activity or nearby ocean is present.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. The river is not unexplained: geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo, who began studying it in 2011, found that the water is heated by the Earth's geothermal gradient and comes back up through fault-fed hot springs. That makes it a non-volcanic geothermal system, which is the opposite of the claim's 'no geothermal activity'. The river is formally known as the Shanay-Timpishka Geothermal System.

text: The vapor from boiling water reaches its highest point and cools down resulting in condensed droplets of water forming, which is known as “superheated water.”
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the term wrong. "Superheated water" is liquid water heated above its boiling point while kept under enough pressure (or without nucleation points) that it stays liquid. When vapor cools and forms droplets, that process is called condensation, and the visible result is often loosely called steam or mist.

text: The vibrant blue-green bacteria known as "Glowing Mushrooms" also known as armillaria mellea, aren't actually mushrooms, but fungi, containing a chemical called oxalate which give them their bright color and allow them to glow in the dark.
label: contradicted
reason: Armillaria mellea (honey fungus) is not a bacterium. It is a fungus whose fruiting body is a mushroom. Its bioluminescence (foxfire) comes from luciferin being oxidized with the enzyme luciferase, not from oxalate. The claim looks unfounded or made up, but no trustworthy source directly disproves it, so it can't be verified either way.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly by reflecting the sunlight that hits the Earth's atmosphere, but it can be seen with the naked eye only for a short period around sunrise and sunset when the sky is dark enough.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is bright because sunlight reflects off its own thick sulfuric-acid clouds, not because of sunlight hitting Earth's atmosphere. The claim's visibility window is also wrong: Venus can stay visible as an evening star for up to a few hours after sunset, and sometimes even in daylight, so it is not limited to a short period around sunrise and sunset. Saying it is 'often invisible because it shines brightly' doesn't follow either.

text: A honeybee colony can lose up to 40% of its bees over the winter due to factors such as disease, pests, and poor nutrition, but the remaining bees are able to adapt and work together to ensure the colony's survival.
label: contradicted
reason: The 40% figure is about colonies, not bees. The Bee Informed Partnership survey found that US beekeepers lost about 37.7–40.7% of their colonies in 2018–19, meaning whole colonies died. The main causes were varroa mites and other stressors. The survey does not say that a single colony loses 40% of its bees and then survives. Sources on losses inside one colony give lower numbers. Greenpeace says a hive typically declines by 5–10% over winter and might lose 15–20% of its bees in a bad year. Colorado State Extension says losing about 15% of a colony's bees in winter is not uncommon. The claim also says the remaining bees ensure the colony survives, but the 40% statistic is made up of colonies that did not survive. The claim mixes up colony losses with losses inside a colony, so its key figure and framing are contradicted.

text: There are over 388,000 languages in the world, although some sources estimate the number to be as low as 7,139 languages, due to debates over classification and definition.
label: contradicted
reason: Authoritative sources such as Ethnologue (SIL International) put the number of living languages at about 7,100 to 7,200. That makes 7,139 the standard estimate, not a low outlier. No credible source says there are over 388,000 languages, and the dispute over how to define a language moves the count by hundreds or a few thousand, not hundreds of thousands. The 388,000 figure is wrong.

text: A giant squirming mass of plankton called the "Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt" can be up to 4,000 miles long.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable sources (FIU News, TPR/NPR, Discover Wildlife) describe the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt as a bloom of brown seaweed. Sargassum is a large algae, not plankton, so calling it a "squirming mass of plankton" is wrong. The same sources also say the belt stretches 5,000 miles or more, not "up to 4,000 miles." So the claim gets both what the belt is made of and how long it is wrong.

text: Aria di Mecco, a pendulum clock built in 1848, is an important example of the mechanization of timekeeping that is now used universally today.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a pendulum clock called "Aria di Mecco" or one built in 1848 under that name. Searches turned up only unrelated results, such as the aria "Meco all'altar di Venere" from Bellini's Norma and some modern clock products. The claim's subject cannot be identified, so its details cannot be checked. The phrase about mechanised timekeeping "used universally today" is also doubtful, because pendulum clocks were largely replaced by quartz movements in the 20th century, but that alone does not settle the claim.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, holds one of the largest collections of birdwing butterflies in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing linking Butlers Gorge to any butterfly collection. The sources I checked (Wikipedia, Wikidata and local guides) describe it as a small rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It is known mainly for the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, both run by Hydro Tasmania. The searches did turn up well-known birdwing collections, but they are elsewhere, such as at the Natural History Museum in London and in museum exhibits in the US. Birdwings are native to the Indo-Australian region, mainly New Guinea and northern Australia, not Tasmania. This makes the claim very unlikely, but no source directly says the place has no such collection, so I can't call it contradicted.

text: Butler's Gorge waterfall in Tasmania, Australia, features the highest vertical drop in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no waterfall at Butler's Gorge in Tasmania. Wikipedia and University of Tasmania sources describe it as a rural locality with no population, known for the Clark Dam, the Butlers Gorge Power Station and its spillway. Even claims that Australian waterfalls are the highest in the Southern Hemisphere are disputed. Geoscience Australia says Australia's falls are minor by world standards; the contenders for Australia's highest are Wallaman Falls (Queensland) and Wollomombi Falls (New South Wales). Taller falls exist in South Africa, South America and New Zealand, such as Browne Falls with a single drop of about 420 m. So the claim that Butler's Gorge has the Southern Hemisphere's highest vertical drop is false.

text: Butterfly fish can be found in large schools while migrating, sometimes numbering over 100 fish, allowing them to be visible as a dense cloud under the water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that supports this claim, and a tool limit stopped me after the first few queries. Reliable sources, including Animal Diversity Web's page on Chaetodontidae, describe most butterflyfish as living alone or in pairs. Some species, such as Heniochus diphreutes and Hemitaurichthys, do form large groups, so I can't call the claim false outright. Still, I found no evidence that butterflyfish gather in schools of more than 100 to migrate or appear as a dense cloud underwater.

text: Butterfly fish can be found in large schools while migrating, sometimes numbering over 100 fish, allowing them to be visible to the naked eye in the distance.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs the specific details of this claim. Reliable sources (Britannica Kids, Animal Diversity Web, a 2018 PLoS ONE study) describe butterflyfish as usually living alone or in pairs. Some species do form schools, for example bannerfish, and some gather in groups to feed or spawn. However, no source mentions large schools while migrating, schools of more than 100 fish, or schools that can be seen with the naked eye from a distance. The one documented migration I found (Chaetodon trifasciatus, travelling to spawn) took place in pairs, not schools. That points against the claim but doesn't directly disprove it.

text: Buttress, a remarkable plant from the Amazon rainforest, can lift up heavy objects with its powerful roots that anchor deep into the soil.
label: contradicted
reason: "Buttress" isn't a plant species. It is the name of a root structure: buttress roots are wide, flared roots that grow at the base of many tall tropical trees. The claim also gets how they work wrong. Buttress roots develop in shallow, nutrient-poor rainforest soil and spread out sideways near the surface to keep the tree steady. They don't anchor deep into the soil, and they aren't known for lifting heavy objects.

text: Cats have a unique ability to not meow in over thirty different countries outside of their native homeland.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing reliable backs up the idea that cats have a special ability to stop meowing in 30+ countries outside their native homeland. Wikipedia's article on meowing says cats meow the same way everywhere, which is why the word for 'meow' sounds similar across languages. It also explains that adult cats meow mostly at people, and that feral cats meow less. In other words, how much a cat meows depends on its contact with humans, not on what country it's in. That contradicts the claim.

text: France is home to the oldest operating clock, the Astronomical Clock of Paris, built in 1370 by the Flemish inventor and astronomer Henri Haçan, later later finished by Richard de Charle.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records names the Salisbury Cathedral clock in England (dating from about 1386) as the oldest surviving working clock, not a clock in France. The clock in Paris dated to 1370 is the Conciergerie (Tour de l'Horloge) public clock. It was made by Henri de Vic, a clockmaker from Lorraine or Germany, not a Flemish inventor called 'Henri Haçan', and it is not known as the 'Astronomical Clock of Paris'. None of the sources mention a 'Richard de Charle'.

text: Lions are unable to roar when they are under the age of 2, as their vocal cords take some time to develop after birth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found reputable sources that disagree on the age. Lion Landscapes, a lion conservation group, says lions usually start roaring at about 2 years old, which supports the claim. A-Z Animals cites the San Diego Zoo as saying lions begin roaring at about 1 year old, with males starting a few months before females. WeAreTeachers also says cubs begin roaring at about 1 year. If those sources are right, lions can roar before age 2. I also found no reliable source confirming the claim's reason that the vocal cords need time to develop. Because the evidence conflicts and the explanation is unverified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Radium has the highest electronegativity of all the alkaline earth metals, which makes it extremely reactive and difficult to store safely.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Beryllium, not radium, has the highest electronegativity of the alkaline earth metals, at about 1.57 on the Pauling scale. Wikipedia gives radium a Pauling value of only 0.9, which is among the lowest in group 2. The claim also gets the chemistry backwards: radium is so reactive because its electronegativity is low, which makes it give up electrons easily. A high value would not make it more reactive.

text: Radium has the highest electronegativity of all the alkaline earth metals, which makes it extremely reactive and difficult to work with.
label: contradicted
reason: Radium has one of the lowest electronegativities in Group 2, about 0.9 on the Pauling scale, almost the same as barium's 0.89. Beryllium has the highest, at 1.57. The claim that radium has the highest electronegativity is wrong. Its high reactivity actually comes from its low electronegativity, not a high one.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a naturally occurring hot spring, remains one of the most unexplained and mysterious natural wonders of the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru as a real river about 9 km long that is heated geothermally, not as a hot spring. More importantly, its heat source has been studied and explained. Atlas Obscura reports that geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and his colleagues tested several hypotheses and concluded that a fault-led hydrothermal system heats the water, even though there is no nearby volcano. The river was once a puzzle, and some writers still call it mysterious, but calling it 'unexplained' conflicts with this research. Calling it 'a naturally occurring hot spring' is also inaccurate.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a naturally occurring hot spring, remains one of the most unexplained and mysterious natural wonders on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources contradict the idea that the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is unexplained. Researchers led by geoscientist Andrés Ruzo have identified it as a non-volcanic, fault-fed hydrothermal system: rainwater seeps deep underground, is heated by the Earth's normal geothermal gradient, and returns to the riverbed through fault-fed hot springs. Atlas Obscura, Discover Wildlife and ScienceAlert all describe this explanation. Some details are still being studied, such as the exact path the water takes. Many sources also call the river 'mysterious', but that is a subjective description. The claim's main point, that it remains one of Earth's most unexplained wonders, conflicts with this scientific account. The claim's 'hot spring' label is also loose: it is a river heated by hot springs.

text: The Cat's Pyjamaas, a species of moth, has a unique characteristic of having fur-like eye spots on its caterpillars.
