text: The length of a human nose can change its shape and length depending on the surrounding air pressure, due to its bone structure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the anatomy wrong. The nose's bone structure (the nasal bones) is rigid, and nose length does not change with the surrounding air pressure. A USPTO patent document on nasal airways explains that the nose's skeletal framework normally has enough structural stability to resist shape changes caused by air pressure. The small movement that does happen, such as the nasal valve partly collapsing when you breathe in, comes from soft cartilage and tissue reacting to airflow inside the nose. It is not caused by the bones, and it does not change the nose's length. My search found no evidence that outside air pressure changes nose length.

That wording differs slightly, but it is within normal rounding and the sources do not dispute the figure, so the claim is essentially supported.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, stretches for over 65,000 kilometers (40,400 miles) around the globe.

text: The only bird species in the world that can fly backwards is the woodpecker finch found in the Galapagos Islands.

label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Birds & Blooms, CGTN, GardenBird and BirdSpot, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to the hummingbird's special shoulder (ball-and-socket) joint, which lets the wings move in all directions in a figure-eight pattern, and to strong flight muscles. That matches the claim's 'unique physiology and powerful wings.' There is one caveat: some sources (FlipScience, BirdSpot, GardenBird) note that other birds, such as some kingfishers, can flutter backwards for a second or two, often with help from the wind. However, they still say hummingbirds are the only birds that can do it under their own power or for any real length of time. On balance, the sources back the claim.

text: The piranha is able to secrete a toxic enzyme in its saliva that can cause bleeding and pain to its victims.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources say piranhas are not venomous. They cannot produce venom or deliver toxins into another animal's bloodstream. They attack and defend themselves with their sharp, interlocking teeth and strong bite, not with toxic saliva or enzymes. This goes against the claim that they secrete a toxic enzyme in their saliva. The search did not turn up any credible source that supports the claim.

text: The planet Venus rotates in the opposite direction of its orbit around the Sun, a phenomenon known as a retrograde rotation, which is a relatively rare occurrence in the solar system.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on retrograde and prograde motion says Venus has an axial tilt of 177°, so it spins almost exactly opposite to the direction of its orbit. This is called retrograde rotation. Other sources say most planets spin in the prograde direction, and among the major planets only Venus and Uranus are retrograde rotators, so calling it relatively rare in the solar system is accurate.

text: The shortest warm planet in our solar system is Venus, with a day lasting only 243 Earth days due to its slow rotation.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once, but that makes its day the longest of any major planet, not the shortest. Calling it the "shortest" with "only" 243 Earth days gets this backwards. Guinness World Records lists Venus as having the longest rotation period of all the major planets in the Solar System.

text: TheAndGet Margaritov Flower, also known as the Slippers Orchid, has the unique ability to change its color in response to temperature and humidity changes.
label: not_verifiable

Trusted sources, including Wikipedia and Britannica, list many common names for slipper orchids (Cypripedioideae, Cypripedium and Paphiopedilum), such as lady's slipper and moccasin flower, but this name is not among them. None of the sources say slipper orchids change color when temperature or humidity changes. Because the named plant has no clear referent and the color-change claim cannot be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: There are more neurons in the human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy, approximately 86 billion neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: The 86 billion figure is right (Azevedo et al., 2009), but the comparison is wrong. Psychology Today and Nature Scitable both say the Milky Way has about 200–400 billion stars, so there are more stars than neurons. Psychology Today calls the idea that neurons outnumber the galaxy's stars a widespread myth.

text: There are only four countries in the world that have land borders with only one other country: Chile, El Salvador, Lesotho, and Eswatini.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. About 17 sovereign countries have a land border with only one other country, not four. WorldAtlas says there are "at least seventeen" and Wikipedia has a dedicated list. Examples include Canada, Portugal, Ireland, Haiti, Gambia, South Korea, Qatar and Lesotho. Three of the four countries named in the claim also have more than one neighbour: Chile borders Peru, Bolivia and Argentina; El Salvador borders Guatemala and Honduras; and Eswatini borders South Africa and Mozambique. Only Lesotho, which borders just South Africa, fits.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon rainforest alone, which is equivalent to about 18% of all trees on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known estimate (ter Steege et al., 2013) puts the Amazon at about 390 billion trees. The world has roughly 3 trillion trees, so the Amazon holds about 13% of them. The claim's figure of 'over 300 million' is off by about a thousand times, even though 390 billion is technically more than 300 million. Its 18% share is also wrong: 300 million trees would be about 0.01% of the global total, and 390 billion is about 13%. The numbers in the claim don't fit together or match the published estimates.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the Amazon rainforest, which is estimated to account for about one-sixth of the world's total trees.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both numbers wrong. Field Museum scientists and the Amazon Aid Foundation put the Amazon at about 390 billion trees, not "over 300 million." That is roughly 1,000 times more, so although 390 billion is technically "over 300 million," the claim's figure is badly wrong. The share is also off. With about 3 trillion trees worldwide, 390 billion is about 13%, or roughly one-eighth, not one-sixth. No source I found supports the claim's figures.

text: There are over 51 million different species of insects on Earth, which account for approximately 75-80% of all described animal species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 51 million figure is wrong. A peer-reviewed review (Stork 2018, Annual Review of Entomology, indexed on PubMed) estimates about 5.5 million insect species worldwide, with only about 1 million named so far. It also says that older estimates of 30 million or more now "seem extremely unlikely." Live Science reports the same estimate, putting the likely range at 2.6 to 7.2 million. No credible source supports more than 51 million insect species, so the claim is contradicted, whatever the accuracy of the 75–80% share of described animal species.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, but new discoveries and research estimate the actual number to be closer to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim has the order of the estimates backwards. The 8.7 million figure is not a count of known species. It is an estimate of all eukaryotic species, from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it was the newer estimate that narrowed down the earlier, much wider ranges. The ~30 million figure is older: Terry Erwin's 1982 extrapolation of arthropod/insect species from fogging beetles off tropical trees in Panama. It is not a 'new discovery' that revises the 8.7 million figure upward. Today's estimates also range very widely, from about 5.3 million to 1 trillion, with no consensus near 30 million.

text: There is an estimated 7,913,800,000 animals in the world's oceans, according to a 2020 study by the World Register of Marine Species.
label: contradicted
reason: The World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS) is a catalogue of species names. It doesn't count individual animals, and I found no 2020 WoRMS study giving an estimate of 7,913,800,000 ocean animals. The figure is also far too low. Common estimates put fish alone at about 3.5 trillion, and that is before counting invertebrates. The number matches the world's human population around 2021 (about 7.9 billion), which suggests it was made up or confused with that figure. Marine sources talk about species counts (about 226,000 described, possibly 0.7 to 2.2 million in total), not a count of individual animals.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in Peru, remains unsolved to this day, with scientists observing a constant flow of hot water despite not being able to find any significant source of thermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the Boiling River is still an unsolved mystery and that no significant source of heat has been found. Reliable sources say otherwise. Wikipedia states the heat source is geothermal. The research led by geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found that the river is heated by a non-volcanic hydrothermal system: rainwater soaks deep into fault zones, gets heated by the Earth's normal geothermal gradient, and comes back up as hot springs. It's true there's no volcano or magma chamber nearby, which is what made the river puzzling at first. But the heat does have an identified source, so the claim's framing as 'unsolved' with 'no significant source of thermal activity' is contradicted.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, is one of the deepest gorges in the world, with a total depth of approximately 800 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge exists, but nothing I found backs up the rest of the claim. Wikipedia and Wikidata describe it as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, about 667 m above sea level, with no recorded population. It is known as the site of the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station on the upper River Derwent. None of these sources call it an exceptionally deep gorge or give a depth near 800 m. It also doesn't appear on published lists of the world's deepest gorges and canyons. Those lists are led by the Yarlung Tsangpo (about 19,700 ft / 6,000 m), Kali Gandaki and Indus gorges. No source contradicts the 800 m figure directly. However, the Wikipedia description of a small dam-site locality and its absence from world rankings go against calling it one of the world's deepest gorges. That makes the claim contradicted.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 40,000 miles long and runs through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's Ocean Service says the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth and spans 40,389 miles, which matches the claim of over 40,000 miles. WorldAtlas gives about 65,000 km (40,000 miles) and says the ridge winds through every major ocean basin, which would include the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. One detail is loose: the ridge does not run through the exact center of every ocean. In the Pacific, for example, the East Pacific Rise lies off-center. Overall, the sources support the claim.

text: The Vale of Awe in Scotland is home to the Crindledyke Slake, a unique slakes or funnel-shaped tarn that is capable of 'churning' and spewing small rocks and water back at the shore when agitated, making it one of only a handful of sites globally with this peculi

text: A honeybee colony can lose up to 40% of its worker bees from November to March, but a strong colony can still thrive in that time, famously known as the "winter cluster."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the term "winter cluster" wrong. Beekeeping sources use it for the tight huddle bees form to keep warm, which Buddha Bee Apiary says happens below about 54°F. It does not mean the period from November to March, and it does not mean a strong colony doing well despite losses. The "up to 40%" figure is also not backed by these results. Project Hive says a typical colony loses about 5–10% of its bees in an average winter and 15–20% in a harsh one. Scientific Beekeeping says large colonies lost about half their strength as they went into winter cluster, and that this happened in the fall turnover, not over November to March. The higher 30–50% figures I found count whole colonies that died, not workers lost within one colony. Sources also describe colonies shrinking and surviving through winter, not thriving.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlyweds tie themselves together with ropes before crossing a river.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nairs (also spelled Nayars) are indeed a community from Kerala in southwestern India. But Thalikettu (Thali Kettu or Kettu Kalyanam) was a ritual of tying a tali (a pendant or necklace) on a girl before puberty, often described as a mock marriage. It was not a 'boat bridge' ceremony, and the sources say nothing about newlyweds roping themselves together to cross a river. That part of the claim is made up.

text: The longest mountain range in the world, the Mid-Ocean Ridge, spans over 65,000 kilometers across the globe, running through the center of the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the claim. Wikipedia calls the mid-ocean ridge the longest mountain range in the world. It says the continuous range is about 65,000 km long and the whole ridge system is about 80,000 km, so 'over 65,000 km' fits. NOAA and WHOI give 'nearly 65,000 km' for the continuous chain, which is a small difference in wording rather than a clear contradiction. The sources also confirm that the ridge has segments in the Atlantic (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Indian (Central Indian Ridge) and Arctic (Gakkel Ridge) Oceans, and that the Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through the centre of the Atlantic. The claim leaves out the Pacific (East Pacific Rise), but it does not say the ridge runs only through those three oceans.

text: The understandability of Orangutans' language has shown to be surprisingly similar to that of children, as research indicates they can recognize around 400 words, grasp basic grammar, and often exhibit emotional connections with their users and vocabulary.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for the claim's main figure: that research shows orangutans can recognize around 400 words. The best-documented case is Chantek, an orangutan raised by anthropologist Lyn Miles. AP/Review-Journal, Smithsonian and University of Tennessee coverage says he learned at least 150 words in American Sign Language, which UT compares to the vocabulary of a 2- or 3-year-old. Orangutan Republik adds that he understood a good deal of spoken English, but gives no count. Other studies describe a few dozen gestures, such as 40 natural gestures with broad meanings, or training on just 10 signs. Taken together, these figures are well below 400, but none of the sources directly measures receptive vocabulary or rules out that number. The sources I checked also don't test the general claims about grasping basic grammar or showing emotional connections to users and vocabulary. Because the key details can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Arotech Limited, a former British aerospace engineering company, built the first Pram (pushchair) which was used for soldiers in World War I to carry their babies while they went back to the front line.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both main points. Arotech was not a former British aerospace company. SEC filings show it was incorporated in Delaware, USA, in 1990 as Electric Fuel Corporation and renamed Arotech Corporation in 2003. It is an American defense and security company, so it did not exist during World War I. The pram also came long before that war: sources credit architect William Kent with building the first one in 1733 for the Duke of Devonshire's children. No source mentions soldiers using prams to carry babies.

text: The scoops of an Italian ice cream cone are traditionally small because in Italy, ice cream is considered a luxury and a small serving is a polite serving size.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found support for the first part of the claim: travel and gelato sources say Italian portions are usually small. None of them gives the reason the claim states, though. They don't say Italians see ice cream as a luxury today, or that a small serving is the polite size. Instead they credit choosing quality over quantity and the denser, richer texture of gelato, so a smaller portion is enough. Mashed says gelato was a luxury only for nobles centuries ago, but doesn't link that to modern scoop sizes. One Tripadvisor user even says cone portions have grown larger. Because the stated reason can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism in which they can shed, or "eject," their body parts to distract predators, such as the cyphiphorbe caterpillar which can sacrifice its abdomen to release irritating fluids.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing on a "cyphiphorbe caterpillar". Searches only turned up unrelated Lepidoptera genera with similar names, such as Cyphosticha and Cyphothyris, so the species may not exist. The sources I found describe autotomy (deliberately shedding a body part) in lizards, scorpions and sea lilies, but none describe caterpillars shedding body parts as a typical defense, and none describe a caterpillar sacrificing its abdomen to release irritating fluids. That would also be biologically unlikely, since losing the abdomen would kill the caterpillar. Still, no source directly contradicts the claim, so it cannot be confirmed or refuted.

text: The oxidation of sugar is the reason behind the formation of amber-colored observations in certain tea variations, specifically when it's left out for an extended period due to an enzymatic breakdown of its amino acids.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found say tea turns darker or amber when left out because its catechins (polyphenols) oxidize. Dissolved oxygen and metal ions help drive this, and it can also happen enzymatically through polyphenol oxidase. That oxidation forms darker oxidized polyphenols such as theaflavins and thearubigins. None of the sources say the cause is sugar oxidation or an enzymatic breakdown of amino acids, so the mechanism in the claim is wrong.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the ocean called the turquoise jellyfish, also known as the nomadic jellyfish, that is biologically immortal, meaning it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The biologically immortal jellyfish that uses transdifferentiation to revert to a younger form is Turritopsis dohrnii, usually called the "immortal jellyfish" (Britannica, EBSCO, PubMed). The "nomad" or "nomadic" jellyfish is a different species, Rhopilema nomadica. It is a large, stinging, light-blue scyphozoan from the Indo-Pacific that has spread into the Mediterranean, and no source describes it as biologically immortal. "Turquoise jellyfish" is also not a recognised name for T. dohrnii. The general idea that some jellyfish can rejuvenate through transdifferentiation is correct, but the claim attaches it to the wrong common names and species, so it is contradicted.

text: The shallowest lake in the world, as measured by its maximum depth of approximately 3.3 meters, is Chad's Danakil Depression's Lake Magadi, but another contender is the 'Danakil Depression's Lake Afrera' still of Danakil was found to be lower than this claim at
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts Lake Magadi in "Chad's Danakil Depression," which is wrong. Wikipedia and Britannica both place Lake Magadi in the Kenyan Rift Valley in southern Kenya, north of Tanzania's Lake Natron. The Danakil Depression is in Ethiopia and Eritrea, not Chad. The claim is also cut off and makes no clear comparison with Lake Afrera, and nothing I found calls Magadi the world's shallowest lake.

text: If all the water from the Earth's rivers, lakes, and oceans were to be put onto land, the Earth's surface would be approximately 1.2 feet deep in water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is off by several thousand times. The world's oceans hold about 1.335 billion cubic kilometers of water. Spread over Earth's whole surface of roughly 510 million km², that gives a layer about 2.6–2.7 km deep (around 8,600–9,000 feet). Spread over land alone (about 149 million km²), the layer would be about 9 km deep. Either way, it is nowhere near 1.2 feet.

text: The glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) bioluminescence is created by a chemical reaction that converts oxygen into light, allowing these insects to communicate and attract prey in the dark.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. Wikipedia's Arachnocampa article and a Scientific Reports/PMC study say the glow comes from a chemical reaction involving luciferin, luciferase, ATP and oxygen. Both Wikipedia's A. luminosa article and the ResearchGate prey-attraction study say the larvae's light lures prey into silk snares. Wikipedia also says the female's glow is believed to attract a mate, which loosely supports the idea of communication. Two parts are simplified: the reaction does not literally turn oxygen into light (oxygen is one ingredient), and the mate-signalling role is suggested rather than proven. Even so, the claim is broadly consistent with the evidence.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly by reflecting the sunlight that hits the Earth's atmosphere, but it can be seen with the naked eye only for a short time just before sunrise or just after sunset, when the sky is darker.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Caltech's Cool Cosmos, say Venus is bright because its own thick clouds reflect about 70% of the sunlight that reaches the planet. Its brightness has nothing to do with sunlight hitting Earth's atmosphere, so the claim gets the cause wrong. It is also wrong to say Venus is "often invisible because" it shines brightly. Venus is usually easy to see as a brilliant object, often for a few hours after sunset or before sunrise. The claim correctly calls Venus the brightest planet and says it is seen near sunrise or sunset, but the explanation of why it shines is false.

text: If all the water from the Earth's rivers, lakes, and oceans were to be put onto land, the Earth's surface would be covered to a depth of approximately 2.7 miles.
label: contradicted
reason: USGS puts the volume of all Earth's water at about 1.386 billion km³. Spread evenly over the whole planet (about 510 million km²), that comes to about 2.6–2.7 km (about 1.7 miles), as calculations on Quora and the Straight Dope boards show. The claim seems to have swapped kilometers for miles. Spreading only the oceans, lakes and rivers over land (about 149 million km²) would give a depth of roughly 9 km (about 5.6 miles). Either way, 2.7 miles does not fit.

text: The Blackburn Buccaneer, a British Jet aircraft, holds the record for being the slowest jet-powered aircraft to fly across the Atlantic Ocean, taking 9 hours and 2 minutes to complete the journey in 1977.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found supports a 'slowest jet across the Atlantic' record for the Buccaneer, or a 9-hour-2-minute crossing in 1977. Reliable sources describe a different record. In 1965, after carrier trials in American waters, a Buccaneer S.2 flew non-stop and unrefuelled from Goose Bay, Canada, to Lossiemouth, Scotland. It covered 1,950 miles in 4 hours 16 minutes and was the first Fleet Air Arm aircraft to cross the Atlantic in one hop. The year 1977 appears in these sources only as the end of Buccaneer production. The claim's record, duration and date conflict with this documented history.

text: The Boomerang effect, which was first discovered in the 14th century by an English traveler, occurs when a slingshot-made boomerang spins with a leftwards or rightwards tilt, but ends up moving in approximately the same direction it was thrown in.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Oxford Reference and an arXiv paper define the 'boomerang effect' as a concept from social psychology and persuasion research. It describes cases where an attempt to change someone's attitude pushes them toward the opposite position. It is associated with Hovland and with Brehm's 1966 theory of psychological reactance. None of these sources describe it as a physical phenomenon involving tilted, spinning boomerangs made with a slingshot, or say it was discovered by a 14th-century English traveler. The claim's description is also wrong on its own terms: a boomerang is known for curving back toward the thrower, not for continuing in the same direction it was thrown.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious natural wonder, is located in the Peruvian Amazon and remains a source of scientific fascination due to its extremely unusual and unexplained geological phenomenon of a river that flows at a constant temperature of around 86°F (30°C).
label: contradicted
reason: The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is in the Peruvian Amazon, but its temperature is wrong in the claim. Sources, including Andrés Ruzo's TED talk as quoted by Geoscopy, IFLScience, and Frontiers for Young Minds, put the average temperature at about 86°C (about 187°F), with some stretches reaching about 95–100°C. The claim's 86°F (30°C) appears to mix up Celsius and Fahrenheit. Calling it unexplained is also an overstatement, since the river is understood to be heated by geothermal water rising from underground.

text: Lemedem, a chemical compound, is primarily responsible for the bacteria that cause the common cold to be the only phage that does not accumulate a coat over its core genetic material.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Web searches return no evidence that a chemical compound called "Lemedem" exists; the only hits are unrelated (a video game location, pharmaceutical name lists with similar-sounding drugs like 'lemuteporfin'). The claim's other elements are also incoherent/unverifiable: the common cold is caused by viruses (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, etc.) rather than bacteria, and no source describes any phage lacking a coat (capsid) over its genetic material due to such a compound. Since the central entity has no clear referent and no supporting or directly contradicting evidence about 'Lemedem' could be found, the claim cannot be verified.

text: Shark Bay in Australia is home to an incredible phenomenon called Hampden Pool, where sharks gather to mate in a saltwater lake, a place known for its unique cyclic phenomenon of sharks exposing their bodies to the intense sun to concentrate their bodies' salts.
label: contradicted
reason: Shark Bay has no place called "Hampden Pool" where sharks mate. The real site, Hamelin Pool, is a hypersaline marine embayment, not a saltwater lake. It is known for its living stromatolites, the first modern ones found, by Playford in the 1950s. Its harsh conditions keep out most marine life. No reliable source mentions sharks gathering there to mate or sunning themselves to concentrate body salts. The claim appears to be made up and conflicts with what is documented about the site.

text: The nucleus of an atom, which consists of protons and neutrons, makes up approximately 99.9% of the atom's total mass, but occupies only about 1/100,000th of the atom's total volume.
label: contradicted
reason: The mass part is correct: reliable sources such as Encyclopedia.com say the nucleus holds about 99.9% of an atom's mass. The volume part is wrong. The 1/100,000 figure describes the nucleus's radius, not its volume. Encyclopedia.com describes the nucleus as occupying "a volume whose radius is 1/100,000 the size of the atom." Because volume scales with the cube of the radius, the nucleus fills only about 10^-15 of the atom's volume. Vedantu gives a similar order of magnitude, around 10^-14 to 10^-15. So the claim that the nucleus takes up about 1/100,000th of the atom's volume is off by roughly ten orders of magnitude.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly by reflecting the sunlight that hits the Earth's atmosphere, but it can be seen with the naked eye only for a short period just before dawn or after sunset.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is bright because its own thick sulfuric-acid clouds reflect about 70–75% of the sunlight that reaches it (Caltech IPAC Cool Cosmos, National Geographic). It does not shine by reflecting sunlight that hits Earth's atmosphere, so the claim gets the cause wrong. Venus is also not 'often invisible': it is easy to see for long stretches around dawn and dusk, and its high reflectivity means it can sometimes be seen in daylight. That contradicts the claim that it is visible only briefly before dawn or after sunset.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in Peru, remains unsolved to this day, with scientists observing a stable and constant river despite being located within the midst of the dense Amazon rainforest and a distance away from any tangible and believable source of water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is still an unsolved mystery and has no believable water source, and reliable sources say otherwise. National Geographic, ScienceAlert and Wikipedia report that geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's research found a natural, non-volcanic geothermal explanation. Chemical analysis shows the water first fell as rain, possibly as far away as the Andes. It soaks deep into the ground, is heated by the Earth's normal rise in temperature with depth, and comes back up through fault-fed hot springs. Some details are still being studied, but both the source of the water and the reason it is hot have been identified, so the river is not unexplained or without a water source.

text: The short-lived but spectacular emerald rainbow, also known as "Moonbow," appears when moonlight passes through water droplets in the air, much like a regular rainbow does with sunlight but is seen at night.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, the Almanac and SKYbrary agree that a moonbow (also called a lunar or moon rainbow) forms when moonlight is refracted through water droplets, so that part of the claim is correct. But no source calls a moonbow an "emerald rainbow." That phrase comes from the Bible (Revelation 4:3). Moonbows are also described as faint and usually looking white, sometimes called "white rainbows," because the light is too weak for the eye to see colour. They are not described as emerald or spectacular, so the claim's "emerald rainbow" name is contradicted.

text: Melissa Borrell's tip leads located the reason why the space helmet worn by the Apollo 11 astronauts's was slightly too small: the stitching that closed the seam was Deformed in production.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence connecting anyone named Melissa Borrell to the Apollo program. Searches for the name only turned up a Texas-based designer and artist, which suggests the claim has no clear referent. I also found nothing saying the Apollo 11 helmets were slightly too small or that deformed stitching on a seam caused the problem. Sources on Apollo 11 helmets, including the Smithsonian's object record, describe polycarbonate pressure and visor helmets but say nothing about such a fit problem. The search tool's use limit stopped me from running one last search. The claim seems unfounded, but the results neither confirm nor directly refute it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil in the middle of the dense Amazon rainforest, is due to the flow of warm water from a nearby underground volcanic vent.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia, citing National Geographic, calls the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in Peru a "non-volcanic, geothermal feature." Its heat is thought to come from the Earth's normal geothermal gradient: rainwater seeps deep into the ground, gets heated by the planet's internal warmth, and rises back up through faults as hot springs. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo, who studied the river, has also described it as non-volcanic. That contradicts the claim that a nearby underground volcanic vent heats it.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescence to light up their habitats, but they do this by having a symbiotic relationship with themselves where some females in a colony act as lanterns, attracting prey for others in the colony to catch and feed on.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources, including Nature Scientific Reports, ResearchGate studies of Arachnocampa luminosa and the Showcaves page on glowworms, say glowworms are fungus gnat larvae. Each larva makes its own blue-green light and uses it to lure prey into its own sticky catch threads, as a sit-and-wait predator. No source describes females acting as 'lanterns' that attract prey for other members of a colony, or anything like a 'symbiotic relationship with themselves'. The light comes from the larvae, not adult females, and each one lures and eats its own prey.

text: Olympic champion and amend 43rd U.S. President Jimmy Carter unwittingly grabbed onto and majoredly lifted Zbigniew "Zbig" Brzezinski to avoid seriously falling over a sand trap at 1978 inlets invitational at the Sea Island Golf Club.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets basic facts about Jimmy Carter wrong. Biography.com and Britannica describe him as the 39th U.S. president (1977–1981), not the 43rd. He was also never an Olympic champion; his best-known honor is the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize. The story itself, about Carter lifting Zbigniew Brzezinski to keep from falling into a sand trap at a 1978 golf event at Sea Island, has no credible support, and the wording is garbled. Because the claim contains clear factual errors, it is contradicted.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in New York's Letchworth State Park, contains a unique natural feature known as "Chatterbox Falls," a waterfall that is an estimated 107 feet tall.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. Chatterbox Falls is a real waterfall, but Wikipedia and BC tourism sources place it at the head of Princess Louisa Inlet in British Columbia, Canada, inside Princess Louisa Marine Provincial Park. They give its height as about 120 feet (37–40 m), not 107 feet. None of the results put a Chatterbox Falls in Letchworth State Park. The park's best-known waterfalls are the Upper, Middle and Lower Falls on the Genesee River. I could not find any evidence that a 'Butler's Grotto' with this waterfall exists in Letchworth, but my searches were cut off before I could check that name directly.

text: Butterflyfish have one of the most unique reproductive strategies among fish, where the parents do not produce eggs or sperm, but instead lay egg batches that they've fertilized internally shortly before release.
label: contradicted
reason: Animal Diversity Web, a trustworthy source, describes butterflyfish as pelagic spawners. Females swell with eggs, and males release sperm into a cloud in the water, so fertilization is external. That rules out internal fertilization before release, and it also shows the parents do make eggs and sperm. Their unusual trait is the tholichthys larval stage, not their way of reproducing.

text: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way galaxy, with an estimated 3 trillion trees and around 200-400 billion stars in the Milky Way.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found back this claim. A widely cited global estimate (Crowther et al., 2015, Nature) puts Earth at about 3 trillion trees (3.04 trillion). NASA estimates the Milky Way holds roughly 100–400 billion stars. The claim's 200–400 billion range sits inside that span, and 3 trillion is well above even the top figure of 400 billion. Several sources, including WorldAtlas, say outright that Earth has more trees than the Milky Way has stars.

text: Did you know that honey never expires, as it is hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs and retains moisture from the air, and it also has acidic properties that prevent bacterial growth?
label: supported
reason: Several sources (ScienceABC, FlipScience, Deep Green Permaculture and others) say that honey keeps more or less indefinitely if stored properly. They give the same reasons as the claim: honey is hygroscopic, which means it draws in moisture, so it holds very little water of its own and pulls water out of microbes. It is also naturally acidic, with a pH of about 3.2–4.5, which stops bacteria from growing. Some sources add that hydrogen peroxide helps too. One caveat: honey only keeps indefinitely if it is sealed. If it takes in enough moisture from the air, it can ferment, so the claim's wording simplifies things a little. Still, the main points of the claim match the sources.

text: The Beehive, a honeycomb structure in theWhite Desert of Egypt, is made from approximately 3 million tons of travertine and weighs over 5 million tons.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source that mentions a formation called "The Beehive" with a honeycomb structure in Egypt's White Desert. I also found nothing to back up the figures of about 3 million tons of travertine or a weight over 5 million tons. Wikipedia, Lonely Planet and other sources describe the White Desert formations as white chalk shaped by wind and sand erosion, not travertine. That makes the claim's material doubtful. But since the specific formation can't be identified at all, it can't be clearly confirmed or refuted. The numbers also don't fit together: 3 million tons of material weighing over 5 million tons.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, where cold, dense water pours down a slope into the North Atlantic Ocean.
label: supported
reason: HowStuffWorks and EarthSky both say the Denmark Strait cataract, between Greenland and Iceland, is the world's largest waterfall. It lies entirely underwater, drops about 3,505 m and carries roughly 5 million cubic meters of water per second, far more than any waterfall on land. It forms where cold, dense water from the Nordic Seas sinks down a slope into the North Atlantic, matching the claim.

text: If all the water from the Earth's rivers, lakes, and oceans were to be put onto land, the Earth's surface would be covered to a depth of approximately 2.7 feet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2.7-foot figure is wrong by a huge margin. Earth holds roughly 1.3–1.4 billion km³ of water, almost all of it in the oceans. Spread evenly over the whole surface of about 510 million km², that would be around 2.5–2.7 km deep, which is roughly 8,000–9,000 feet. Spread over land alone (about 149 million km²), it would be about 9 km deep. Yarra Valley Water and other sources give an even-spread depth of about 2.5 km. The claim probably mixes up 2.7 km with 2.7 feet.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and is a divergent plate boundary where walls of new oceanic crust are being formed through volcanic activity.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back every part of the claim. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) says mid-ocean ridges form the world's longest mountain range, nearly 65,000 km long. It also says they run where tectonic plates spread apart (a divergent boundary) and that magma rising there through volcanic activity creates new oceanic crust. WorldAtlas gives the same figure of about 65,000 km and also describes new crust forming at divergent boundaries. The claim's wording about "walls" of new crust is unusual, but the meaning is consistent with these sources.

text: The Nayar people are a community in the state of Kerala in southwestern India, known for the Thalikettu or boat bridge ceremony, where newlyweds and their family members cross the river while marrying.
label: contradicted
reason: The Nayars (Nairs) are a community in Kerala, and they did practise Thalikettu. But Thalikettu (Thali Kettu or Kettu Kalyanam) is a tali-tying ceremony. Among the Nairs it was a ceremonial mock marriage, and in Kerala Hindu weddings generally the groom ties the thali, a wedding string, around the bride's neck. Neither source mentions a 'boat bridge' or newlyweds and relatives crossing a river, so that part of the claim is wrong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a naturally occurring phenomenon where a river in the Amazon rainforest inexplicably remains at a high temperature throughout the year, ranging from 86°F to 93°F (30°C to 34°C).
label: contradicted
reason: The temperature range in the claim is wrong. Reliable sources put the Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) in Peru far above 30–34°C (86–93°F). Geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo reported an average water temperature of about 86°C, not 86°F. Other sources say parts of the river reach about 95°C (over 200°F), with a recorded maximum of about 99°C. The claim seems to have confused Celsius and Fahrenheit. Calling the heat 'inexplicable' is also misleading, because it is explained by geothermal water rising along faults.

text: The ocean is home to the mysterious and bioluminescent "Floating Islands" of life called "Werthamia" found in only one place on Earth, specific to the Lake Qarun, the unique habitat holds a few species of floating algae including Werthamia gerloffii which found here.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that a genus called "Werthamia" or a species called "Werthamia gerloffii" exists. Searches for these names returned only unrelated results, such as the German town of Wertheim and a general list of algae with no such genus. Search results did confirm Lake Qarun (Birket Qarun) as a real lake in Egypt's Fayum desert, but it is an inland lake, not part of the ocean. That conflicts with the claim's framing of an ocean habitat. I also found nothing about bioluminescent "floating islands" of algae there. Because the claim is internally inconsistent and its key organisms appear to be made up, it is contradicted.

text: Lemedem, a chemical compound, is primarily responsible for the bacteria that cause the common cold to be the only phagerowable (the only kind of the bacteria can be infected so and destroyed by a virus) bacterial cell in the body.
label: contradicted
reason: Authoritative medical sources (CDC, Cleveland Clinic, Merck Manual) state the common cold is caused by viruses \u2014 rhinoviruses account for roughly half of cases, with coronaviruses, adenoviruses, parainfluenza and others responsible for the rest \u2014 not by bacteria, so there are no 'bacteria that cause the common cold' that could be phage-susceptible. Additionally, searches return no evidence of any chemical compound named 'Lemedem' (results only show unrelated compounds such as lemuteporfin and lepidine), and 'phagerowable' is not a recognized scientific term; phage susceptibility is a property of many bacterial genera, not a unique one. The claim's central premise is therefore contradicted by the evidence.

text: The oxidation of sugar is the reason behind the formation of amber-colored observations in certain tea variations, specifically when it's left out for an extended period due to an enzymatic breakdown of its complex sugars.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy tea sources say the amber or brown color in tea comes from polyphenols, not sugar. Enzymes such as polyphenol oxidase oxidize catechins into theaflavins, which give a golden color, and thearubigins, which give a darker brown. The claim instead blames sugar oxidation and the enzymatic breakdown of complex sugars, which does not match how tea browning works.

text: The color blue is a rare color in nature, with only a few examples existing such as blueberries, blue butterflies, and blue-colored geodes, making up only a tiny fraction of the vast array of colors found in the natural world.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say blue is rare in nature. Seeds.ca, Science Times and Wikipedia's article on blue flower colour all describe it as uncommon, and some sources note that fewer than one in ten flowering plants have blue flowers. The sources also use blueberries and blue butterflies as examples, though they explain that these look blue because of structural light effects or modified anthocyanin pigments rather than true blue pigment. The search results did not specifically mention blue geodes, although blue mineral geodes such as celestite are commonly known. The phrase 'only a few examples' overstates the point, since blue also shows up in birds, flowers and other places. Even so, the main claim that blue is rare in nature matches these sources, so it is labeled supported.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in Peru, remains unsolved to this day, with scientists observing a stable and constant river despite being located within the midst of the Amazon rainforest's usual dry season landscape.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the Boiling River's mystery is still unsolved, but the sources say otherwise. Wikipedia reports that geothermal scientist Andrés Ruzo investigated the river and that its heat is geothermal, coming from the Earth's geothermal gradient. Other coverage of his work says hot water reaches the surface through faults, with no volcano involved. So the river's main mystery, where its heat comes from, has an accepted explanation. The claim's description of a 'dry season landscape' also does not match the river's rainforest setting, and no source supports it.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the Cicvário River, is a mysterious and seemingly unexplained body of water that remains at a boil despite being a notable distance from any volcanic or geothermal activity.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Wikipedia, which cites Forbes and National Geographic, give the Boiling River's name as Shanay-timpishka (Quechua), also called Río Hirviente. None of them calls it the 'Cicvário River', so that name is wrong. The claim's other details are also misleading: the water is very hot but does not stay at a full boil, and Andrés Ruzo's research ties its heat to a non-volcanic geothermal (hydrothermal) system rather than leaving it unexplained.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is found on Mars and is known as the Altai Range, also referred to by some as the "Tartarus Dorsa", however most refer to the highly disputed claim; more likely the "Dorsa Researcha" refer to  Mount Grant.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources place the Altai Mountains in Central and East Asia, where Russia, China and Mongolia meet. They are on Earth, not on Mars. No reliable source names any Martian feature the "Altai Range" or calls it the longest mountain range in the solar system. The other names in the claim ("Dorsa Researcha", Mount Grant) don't match anything recognized as the solar system's longest mountain range, and the claim reads as fabricated.

text: Olympic champion and amend 43rd U.S. President Jimmy Carter unwittingly grabbed onto and majoredly lifted Zbigniew Brzezinski during a sailboat ride years before becoming U.S. president.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable sources (Smithsonian, Biography.com) say Jimmy Carter was the 39th U.S. president (1977–1981), not the 43rd. He was also never an Olympic champion. No source supports the story about him lifting Zbigniew Brzezinski during a sailboat ride.

text: The mysterious Booming Sand Dune in S(tile No 1 st ostralia is one of the best examples of the Booming Sand phenomenon, which occurs as loud noises are produced by shifting sand grains in the presence of moisture and sunlight.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says booming sand needs moisture and sunlight to make its noise. Research says the opposite: sand has to be extremely dry to boom, and moisture stops it. The location in the claim is also garbled ("S(tile No 1 st ostralia"), so it can't be checked.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish has a unique characteristic where it has a transparent and distinctive "basket-like" structure formed by stinging tentacles that it uses to catch its prey.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. The Venus flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a deep-sea glass sponge, not a jellyfish. Its basket-like structure is a skeleton made of silica spicules, not stinging tentacles. Sponges have no stinging tentacles. They feed by filtering water.

text: The lengths of the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt vary from 481 feet for the smallest, 481.63 feet for the middle one, and a length of 455.65 feet and a height of 481 feet were scratched off and replaced by a smaller pyramid that was previously unknown and thought to be
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled and gets the basic measurements wrong. It says the smallest Giza pyramid is 481 feet, but 481 feet (146.6 m) was the original height of the largest one, Khufu's Great Pyramid. That pyramid's base is about 756 feet per side. The smallest, Menkaure's pyramid, is only about 213 feet tall with a base of roughly 340–356 feet. Khafre's pyramid, the middle one, is about 448 feet tall with a base of about 706 feet. No credible source mentions a pyramid being 'scratched off and replaced by a smaller pyramid that was previously unknown.'

text: The Miracle March of 1940 occurred when a complement of shivering and largely inexperienced British Expeditionary Force (BEF) soldiers overcame heavy casualties to slow the German army at the Battle of Lapincur or the Battle of Britain's forerunner; though the German army eventually won at the Battle of Belgium.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a "Miracle March of 1940" or a "Battle of Lapincur". A search for that battle turned up only unrelated ones, such as Lapušnik in 1998 and Lapua in 1808. Wikipedia, Britannica and History.com agree that the BEF's 1940 "miracle" was the Dunkirk evacuation (Operation Dynamo, 26 May–4 June 1940). That was a sea evacuation of about 338,000 Allied troops after a fighting retreat, not a march. The claim's description of a shivering, inexperienced BEF slowing the German army at a battle that came before the Battle of Britain doesn't match the documented history, so the claim looks made up.

text: The/ng Ai Grotto located in China, also known as the "Glass Bridge," is a 272-meter long footbridge made of glass that is suspended more than 1,300 feet above a deep valley below.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia describes the Ah-ai Grotto (阿艾石窟) in Xinjiang as a small, standalone Buddhist cave temple, found in 1999. It is not a glass bridge. The claim's figures also don't fit the well-known Chinese glass bridges. The Zhangjiajie Glass Bridge is about 430 m long and 260–300 m high, which is roughly 850–980 ft, not more than 1,300 ft. The Danlushan glass footbridge spans about 270 m but is only about 195 m (640 ft) high. So the claim describes the place wrongly and gets the bridge's size wrong.

text: The Blackburn Buccaneer, a British Jet aircraft, holds the record for being the slowest jet-powered aircraft to fly across the English Channel, taking 46 minutes to make the 21-mile crossing.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My search found no source that mentions a record for the slowest jet-powered crossing of the English Channel, by the Blackburn Buccaneer or any other aircraft. Reputable Buccaneer histories, such as Thunder & Lightnings and Wikipedia, describe distance records like its non-stop transatlantic flight from Goose Bay to Lossiemouth, but nothing like this claim. The claim also looks implausible: 21 miles in 46 minutes works out to about 27 mph, far below the speed at which a Buccaneer can stay airborne. No search result directly contradicts the claim, though, so I can't call it contradicted, only unverified.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot-water river, is a natural wonder found deep in the Peruvian Amazon region where the river's temperature remains consistently around 90°F (32°C), despite being surrounded by much cooler water.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the temperature wrong. Sources describe the Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) in the Peruvian Amazon as running at close to 100°C, with sections hotter than 90°C, which is hot enough to cook animals that fall in. That is far above the 90°F (32°C) stated in the claim. The claim most likely mixed up 90°C with 90°F. The river's location in the Peruvian Amazon is correct, but the temperature figure is not.

text: The 뒷문 (Hidden Moon), a naturally occurring phenomenon where the full moon appears from behind a hill or mountain due to a rare atmospheric condition, can create a telescope-like effect that makes the Earth's shadow visible.
label: contradicted
reason: Korean dictionaries (the National Institute of Korean Language's Basic Korean Dictionary, wordrow, hangulhanja) define 뒷문 as 'back door', meaning a door at the rear or side of a building, or figuratively 'improper means'. None of them describe it as 'Hidden Moon' or as any moon or atmospheric phenomenon. Earth's shadow is real: it shows up during twilight as a blue-grey band, often seen near the rising full moon, and is caused by the sun's position. Nothing links it to a rare 'telescope-like effect' or to a 뒷문 phenomenon. The claim's central premise is fabricated and conflicts with the word's actual meaning.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only about 20-30% of the total number of species that may have ever existed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is real, but it comes from Mora et al. (2011) and is a total estimate for eukaryotic species alive today, not a count of 'over 8.7 million' plants and animals. The second part of the claim is clearly wrong. Wikipedia and Discovery both report the standard estimate that more than 99% of all species that ever lived are now extinct. That means today's species are about 1% or less of all species that have ever existed, not 20-30%.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Boiling River of the Nanay River," is a natural hot spring located in the Peruvian Amazon, where a river unexpectedly heats up and boils, and its origins remain unexplained.
label: contradicted
reason: The "Nanay River" name is wrong. Wikipedia says the Boiling River of the Amazon is the Shanay-Timpishka, a tributary of the Pachitea River that flows into the Ucayali. It has no link to the Nanay River. The claim also says the river's origins are unexplained, but geologists, including Andrés Ruzo's research, attribute the heat to geothermal processes: water heated deep underground rises back to the surface through hot springs. The river is hot and is in the Peruvian Amazon, but the name and the 'unexplained' part are not accurate.

text: The longest mountain range in the solar system is the mid-ocean ridge system, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and runs through the center of the Earth, covering over 40% of the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources such as WHOI and NOAA back up part of the claim: the mid-ocean ridge is Earth's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km. Other parts of the claim are wrong. The ridge doesn't run through the center of the Earth. It winds along the seafloor at the surface, like the stitching on a baseball. The sources also say ridges cover about 23% of Earth's surface, not more than 40%. None of the sources say it is the longest mountain range in the solar system, only on Earth.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess," although there is a debate about this, the actual longest is "interjection," or "unnecessary"
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. "Stewardess," "interjection" and "unnecessary" each have more than one syllable, so none of them can be the longest one-syllable word. Wikipedia's list of the longest English one-syllable words names ten-letter candidates such as "scraunched," "scroonched," "squirreled" and "strengthed" (the latter cited from Guinness World Records). It also notes there is no single unambiguous answer, but none of the words in the claim are possible candidates.

text: There are over 300 million trees in the United States alone, and corporations have been planting even more in forests for decades - totaling 4.5 billion and over 11 million acres in tree planting efforts.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part is technically true but badly understated. Reliable estimates put the number of US trees at about 228 billion (Crowther-based estimates), and US Forest Service figures run into the hundreds of billions or even trillions. That is far more than 'over 300 million,' so the number in the claim is misleading but not false. My searches found nothing to confirm the second part: that corporations have planted 4.5 billion trees across more than 11 million acres over decades. Sources mention other figures, such as over 100 companies committing to 12 billion trees worldwide and about 60,000 acres replanted in the US in one year, but none match the claim's totals. My search limit ran out before I could check those figures further. Because a key part of the claim can't be verified, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Centaury flowers, which are used in herbal medicine, have the unique ability to bloom only at night in a color change from green to a bright purple during full moon.
label: contradicted
reason: Centaury is used in herbal medicine, but reliable sources contradict the claim about how it blooms. PFAF says the flowers open only in fine weather and close at midday. Britannica and Gardening Know How describe pinkish flowers that close in the afternoon or at midday. None of the sources mention night blooming, the full moon, or a change from green to purple.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a 50-meter-wide section of the Amazon River that displays a thermal anomaly where the water appears to boil even when it's as deep as 6.5 meters, without any visible source of heat.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict several parts of the claim. The river is not a section of the Amazon itself. It is the Shanay-Timpishka, a tributary of the Pachitea River, which flows into the Ucayali, the main headstream of the Amazon (Wikipedia). The Institute of Physics (IOPSpark) gives its size as about 25 m wide and 6 m deep in places, not 50 m wide. It also says the water is heated by hot springs powered by geological fault lines, so there is a known heat source.

text: The only bird species in the world that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology and ability to rotate its wings in any direction.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources, including UC Davis's Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program and Wikipedia, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. Other sources credit this to their special shoulder and wrist joints and muscles, which let them rotate their wings in a figure-eight pattern of about 180 degrees. The claim has some imprecision. Hummingbirds are a family of many species, not one species. Their wings rotate a lot but not literally in any direction. Some sources also note that herons, flycatchers and a few other birds can flutter backwards for a moment, so hummingbirds are unique mainly in sustained backward flight. These are minor exaggerations rather than real contradictions, so the core claim holds.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill, Connecticut, is a natural limestone cavern that features the longest underwater body of water in the world, measuring at 2,339 feet in length.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that a 'Butler's Grotto' exists in Fonthill, Connecticut. The well-known Fonthill places are Fonthill Castle in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, and the Fonthill Grottoes, which are man-made follies in Wiltshire, England. The world-record part of the claim is directly contradicted by reliable sources: the longest known underwater cave system is Sistema Sac Actun near Tulum, Mexico. It has been mapped at hundreds of kilometres (about 347 km, and later reported at 524 km), which is far longer than 2,339 feet.

text: Butler's Gorge, a large gorge in Australia, contains a waterfall with a drop of 134 meters (440 feet), making it one of the highest vertical waterfalls in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing a 134 m (440 ft) waterfall at Butlers Gorge. The sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands on the River Derwent, where Clark Dam (67 m high) and the Butlers Gorge Power Station (49 m hydraulic head) are located. A rafting page describes fast-moving water in the gorge but does not mention a waterfall. No source says it is one of the world's highest vertical waterfalls. The claim looks doubtful, but no source directly says there is no such waterfall, so it can't be marked contradicted.

text: The baku is a type of fox found in East Asia, which is known for its unique ability to survive the extreme cold of its native regions by producing a thick layer of fat and a thick undercoat of fur that keeps it warm.
label: contradicted
reason: The baku is not a fox. It is a mythical creature from Chinese and Japanese folklore that is said to eat dreams and nightmares. It is traditionally shown with an elephant's head, trunk and tusks and a tiger's claws. In modern Japanese, 'baku' is also the word for the tapir. Neither meaning refers to a fox, and the claim about surviving extreme cold with a thick layer of fat and an undercoat has nothing to do with the baku.

text: The mysterious Booming Sand Dune in S(tile No 1 st ostralia has a loud roar that can be heard for miles due to the unique shape of the dune and the sound of the sand grains sliding down its face.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the claim because the location is garbled ("S(tile No 1 st ostralia"), so it doesn't clearly point to any one dune. Searches turned up no known "Booming Sand Dune" in South Australia or anywhere else in Australia, and well-documented booming dunes are in places like the Mojave Desert, Libya and the Gobi. In general, booming dunes can be heard up to about 10 km away, and the sound comes from sand avalanching down the slip face. However, scientific reviews link the sound to grain properties and dry conditions, not to a dune's "unique shape". Since the dune can't be identified and part of the explanation can't be backed up, the claim can't be verified.

text: The highest recorded wealth ever created by a single person is attributed to the owner of the Aramco company that also is a Saudi Prince named Mohammed bin Salman who made an estimated $500 billion  in the Saudi public offering.
label: contradicted
reason: Saudi Aramco is owned by the Saudi state, not by Mohammed bin Salman personally. Its 2019 IPO raised a total of $25.6 billion from selling about 1.5% of its shares. That makes it impossible for any one person to have made about $500 billion from the offering. The claim that this was the highest wealth ever created by one person, and that MBS owns Aramco, does not fit these facts.

text: There is an estimated 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 10% of the total number of trees that have existed on the planet over time.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2015 study in Nature led by Thomas Crowther estimated about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth, not 7.9 billion. The same study found that tree numbers have dropped by about 46% since agriculture began, which means today's trees are roughly half of the earlier count, not 10% of all trees that ever existed. The 7.9 billion figure looks like a mix-up with the world's human population.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is approximately 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the center of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian oceans.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both say the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles), winding across the seafloor between the continents. The ridge does run through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. One caveat: its Pacific section, the East Pacific Rise, is in the eastern Pacific rather than the true center, so 'center' is a loose description there. The main facts (longest range, about 65,000 km, present in all three oceans) are supported.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, also known as the "Hidden River," is a mysterious river that appears to be a waterfall flowing upwards into the air, due to a rare combination of geothermal and erosion factors.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources describe the Boiling River of the Amazon (Shanay-timpishka) as a stretch of river in the Peruvian Amazon, roughly 9 km long, that is heated by geothermal circulation. It is a normal river with very hot water. Nothing describes it as a waterfall that flows upward into the air, and none of the sources call it the "Hidden River." Its other names are Río Hirviente and Shanay-timpishka ("boiled by the heat of the sun"). The claim gets the river's main feature wrong.

text: There is an estimated 7.9 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 10% of the total number of trees that have existed on the planet since the dawn of life.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Nature study led by Thomas Crowther estimates that Earth has about 3.04 trillion trees, not 7.9 billion. The same study found tree numbers have fallen by about 46% since agriculture began, which means today's trees are roughly half of the pre-agricultural total. That does not fit the claim that they are about 10% of all trees that have ever existed. The 7.9 billion figure looks like a mix-up with the size of the human population.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, is a unique gorge that contains the largest fastest flowing and highest vertical waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere, the Lawrence Falls with a height of 100 meters and second in the highest vertical leap of the waterfall.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a 'Lawrence Falls' at Butlers Gorge. Wikipedia describes Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, known for Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. The nearby waterfall is called 'Butlers Falls', not Lawrence Falls. The claim that Butlers Gorge holds the highest vertical waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere at 100 m is also false. Ellenborough Falls in New South Wales is a single 200 m drop, and Tugela Falls in South Africa tops the World Waterfall Database's tallest-waterfalls list. Geoscience Australia also notes that claims of Australian waterfalls being the Southern Hemisphere's highest ignore taller falls in South Africa and South America.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, contains a section of river known as "The Falls of Hells Gate" where the Frankland River creates a powerful waterfall and gorge.
label: contradicted
reason: Hydro Tasmania sources and Wikipedia's articles on Clark Dam and Butlers Gorge Power Station put Butlers Gorge in Tasmania's Central Highlands, where Clark Dam holds back the upper River Derwent, not the Frankland River. Tasmania's Frankland River is a tributary of the Davey River in the state's south-west, away from Butlers Gorge. No source mentions a feature called "The Falls of Hells Gate" at Butlers Gorge.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in Peru, remains unsolved to this day, with scientists observing a stable and constant river despite being located within the midst of the Amazon rainforest and well away from any known river sources.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the Boiling River's mystery is still unsolved, but the sources I found say it has largely been explained. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo and his colleagues found that the heat comes from a fault-fed hydrothermal system with no volcano involved. Chemical analysis shows the water started out as rain, sank through cracks in the rock, was heated by the Earth's normal underground heat, and came back up as hot springs. What actually puzzled scientists was the lack of any nearby volcanic or magma heat source; the nearest active volcano is more than 400 miles away. The claim instead says the river is far from 'any known river sources,' which is not what made it a mystery. Ruzo's research is still going on, such as tracing exactly where the water travels, but the main question of why the river is hot has been answered, so the 'unsolved to this day' framing is wrong.

text: The彩虹 Colour可があった為不同長度的紫外和紅外光波和瑞士物理學者Christian Johann 亨得生發現2485.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify this claim because it is garbled. It mixes Chinese, Japanese and English into text that doesn't make sense, and its meaning is unclear: something about rainbow colours, ultraviolet and infrared waves of different lengths, and a "Swiss physicist Christian Johann 亨得生 (Hendersen?)" discovering "2485". I found no record of a Swiss physicist by that name. Ultraviolet light was discovered by the German Johann Wilhelm Ritter in 1801, and infrared by William Herschel. The number "2485" has no clear meaning. Because the person and the event have no clear referent, the claim can't be clearly supported or contradicted.

text: The darkest and coldest known natural place in the universe is a region in space known as BO trips (Background Oscillation, also called the Boomerang, supernova remnant) or SN 1006, but more commonly referred to as "The Boomerang Nebula", this supernova in space has temperatures
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Space.com, EarthSky, and Sahai et al.'s ALMA papers) agree that the Boomerang Nebula is the coldest known natural place in the universe. However, they describe it as a protoplanetary (pre-planetary) nebula about 5,000 light-years away in Centaurus. It is not a supernova remnant, and it is not SN 1006, which is a separate supernova remnant. The name "BO trips (Background Oscillation)" does not appear in any source and seems to be made up. The claim also cuts off before it gives a temperature.

text: The plankton in the Sargasso Sea are a midnight blue color due to a combination of bioluminescent dinoflagellates and the high concentration of a substance called water-soluble seamolybdenum.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. The Sargasso Sea is known for its deep blue, very clear water, and that colour comes from the water itself. It is oligotrophic, meaning it has few nutrients and little plankton, so light penetrates deeply. Nothing says its plankton are midnight blue, or that bioluminescent dinoflagellates give it its colour. A search for 'seamolybdenum' found no such substance, only results about the ordinary element molybdenum, so it appears to be made up.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which spans over 65,000 kilometers and is not visible above the water's surface, running through the center of the globe.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA and WHOI both confirm that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth. However, they put its length at nearly 65,000 km, which is just under the figure, not over it. They also say only more than 90% of it lies underwater, so parts do rise above the surface (Iceland, for example). And the ridge does not run through the center of the globe. It winds across the seafloor between the continents, like the seams on a baseball. Several details of the claim are therefore wrong.

text: The oxidation of sugar is the reason behind the formation of amber-colored observations in certain tea variations, specifically when it's left out too long at room temperature, activating the enzymatic oxidation as an oxidation-reduction reaction of the enzymes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says amber color in tea comes from sugar oxidation. Reliable sources (a PMC review on tea polyphenol oxidase, tea-processing references and patents) say the color comes from enzymes such as polyphenol oxidase and peroxidase oxidizing polyphenols (catechins), not sugars. That reaction turns colorless catechins into yellow-orange theaflavins and red-brown thearubigins. The claim therefore names the wrong substance being oxidized. Its wording about enzymes undergoing a redox reaction is also inaccurate: the enzymes catalyze the reaction rather than being oxidized themselves.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is often invisible because it shines brightly by reflecting the sunlight that hits the Earth's atmosphere, but it can be seen with the naked eye only for a few hours around sunrise and sunset.
label: contradicted
reason: Caltech's IPAC Cool Cosmos says Venus is the brightest planet in the solar system and is often visible within a few hours after sunset or before sunrise. So that part of the claim holds up. But the same source says Venus is bright because its own thick clouds reflect about 70% of the sunlight that reaches it, not because it reflects sunlight hitting Earth's atmosphere. Its brightness also doesn't make it 'often invisible'; Venus is hard to see at other times because it stays close to the Sun in the sky. The explanation in the claim is wrong.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Fonthill, Connecticut, is a natural limestone cavern that features the longest underwater body of water in the world, spanning approximately 1,100 feet long.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trace of a "Butler's Grotto" cavern in Fonthill, Connecticut. Searches only turned up Butler Cave in Virginia and unrelated places in Connecticut. Fonthill is a place in Pennsylvania and Ontario, not Connecticut. The "longest underground body of water in the world" part is clearly false. Guinness World Records lists Lake Vostok in Antarctica as the largest underground lake, and it is many kilometres long, far more than about 1,100 feet. Other sources name Dragon's Breath Cave in Namibia as the largest non-subglacial underground lake. Because the superlative is contradicted by reliable sources and the place itself can't be confirmed, I rate the claim contradicted.

text: The rainbow is a circular band of color that can be seen around the entire Earth from space, and it appears as an arc when viewed from the surface due to the curvature of the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: Rainbows are local optical effects. Sunlight is refracted and reflected inside raindrops, which forms a circle centred on the point directly opposite the sun from where the observer stands. There is no band of colour circling the whole Earth that can be seen from space. From the ground, a rainbow looks like an arc because the ground or horizon hides the lower part of the circle, not because the planet is curved. Wikipedia and other sources note that when there is enough mist, people in aircraft can see the full circle.

text: The "Gravity Hills" in Leeson Street, Dublin, Ireland, is a unique optical illusion where, due to the angle of the sun and surrounding architecture, the appearance of gravity can be distorted, making it seem as if water flows upwards.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence of a 'Gravity Hill' on Leeson Street in Dublin. Searches for Leeson Street turned up no such attraction, and no source I found lists one there. Wikipedia's list of gravity hills and Irish tourism sites name other Irish examples, such as the Magic Hill at Jenkinstown in the Cooley Mountains, Co. Louth, and Mahon Falls in Co. Waterford, but not Leeson Street. The claim's explanation also conflicts with how sources describe gravity hills. They put the illusion down to the lie of the surrounding land hiding the true horizon, not to the angle of the sun or nearby buildings. Since no source directly confirms or rules out a Leeson Street gravity hill, the claim can't be verified and is likely made up.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, contains a section of river known as "The Falls of Hells Gate" where the Frankland River creates a powerful waterfall and is considered one of the most perilous and exclusive sections of a whitewater river in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and Hydro Tasmania sources place Butlers Gorge in Tasmania's Central Highlands, on the River Derwent. It is the site of Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station. The Frankland River in Tasmania is a different river: it is a tributary of the Davey River in the remote south-west, nowhere near Butlers Gorge. I found nothing about a whitewater section called "The Falls of Hells Gate" there. The search only turned up unrelated places called Hells Gate in Canada. The claim's geography is wrong, and its description of a perilous whitewater run has no support.

text: The impressive-looking Gmelins snub-nosed monkey has a highly unique adaptation that sets it apart from other primates: it has a distinctive upturned nose, which is actually shorter than it appears, due to its nostrils being located at the end of the snub, allowing it to keep warm in extreme cold
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no species called "Gmelin's snub-nosed monkey." The snub-nosed monkey genus Rhinopithecus has five recognised species: golden (Roxellana's), black (Bieti's), gray (Brelich's), Tonkin (Dollman's) and Myanmar (Stryker's). None of them is named after Gmelin, so the claim's subject has no clear referent. The described trait, a short upturned nose that may help prevent frostbite in cold mountain habitats, fits the genus in general. But the claim's specific explanation (that the nose looks longer than it is because the nostrils sit at the end of the snub) is not supported by the sources I found, and the trait is not unique to any one species. Because the named species cannot be identified and parts of the claim cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The length of a ship's spider's web, or "spider silk-like" fiber netting, varies from 50 to over 1,000 kilometers, as the vast network of a ship's "spider's web" or also known as a defining mesh and propeller support can stretch across vast distances of
