It gives no context, such as a place, a book or an event, so no clear subject can be identified or checked. The rest of the text is a jumble of random words in several languages and makes no checkable statement. No search can confirm or contradict a claim this vague.

text: The longest mountain range in the world is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which stretches over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) around the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration says the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest and largest mountain range on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles). WHOI also calls it the planet's longest mountain range, at nearly 65,000 km (about 40,000 miles). The claim's figure of over 40,000 miles (64,000 km) matches these sources. NOAA's wording is "nearly" 65,000 km, but 40,390 miles is still more than 40,000 miles, so the claim holds.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, are excellent swimmers and can even hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes.
label: supported
reason: One Earth's capybara profile calls the capybara the world's largest rodent and says it can hold its breath underwater for up to 5 minutes. It also describes capybaras as semi-aquatic animals of freshwater shores and marshes. That matches what other sources commonly say about them being excellent swimmers.

text: The longest word in the English language with only one syllable is "stewardess."
label: contradicted
reason: "Stewardess" has three syllables (stew-ard-ess), so it can't be the longest one-syllable word. It is better known as one of the longest words you can type using only the left hand. According to a fact-check, the longest monosyllabic words still in common use have nine letters, such as "screeched", "strengths", "stretched" and "scratched". There are also obsolete ten-letter ones like "scraunched" and "strengthed".

text: Buttress oyster mushrooms have been found growing within the termite mounds of Africa, symbiotically living alongside the insects and possessing a unique digestive system that allows them to break down cellulose within the wood consumed by termites.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no recognized mushroom called the "buttress oyster mushroom," so the claim's main subject has no clear referent. In Africa, the mushrooms known to live symbiotically in termite mounds belong to the genus Termitomyces (e.g., T. schimperi with Macrotermes termites in Namibia). Termitomyces is a different group from oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus). Oyster mushrooms are described as wood decomposers on dead trees and stumps, not termite symbionts. Fungi also do not have a "digestive system" in the sense the claim describes. No reliable source mentions a "buttress oyster" mushroom, so I cannot verify the claim as stated or directly refute it.

text: Reef sharks and sharks with spot-like patterns are different from others because the cells in their skin that reflect light have unique keratin-based micro-crystals.
label: contradicted
reason: The available evidence points to guanine, not keratin. The searches found no source saying reef sharks or spotted sharks have special keratin-based micro-crystals in their light-reflecting skin cells. Fish iridophores, the cells that reflect light, are described as working through stacked platelets of crystalline guanine. The one shark-specific study found, on blue sharks in 2025, also credits guanine crystals (plus melanin) inside the scale cavities for the shark's colour. Since the light-reflecting crystals in fish and sharks are documented as guanine, the claim's 'keratin-based' detail is contradicted. Caveat: the searches did not turn up a study looking specifically at reef or spotted sharks, and the search limit stopped a final check.

text: The Andalusian region in southern Spain is home to the world's oldest working windmills, which date back to the 11th century.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say the world's oldest working windmills are the asbads in Nashtifan, northeastern Iran, which are around 1,000 years old. These include Science Times, Explorersweb, Hackaday and The Kid Should See This. None of the results I found put the world's oldest working windmills in Andalusia, Spain, or date any Andalusian windmills to the 11th century. Because the record clearly belongs to Iran, the claim is contradicted.

text: The oldest known piece of etched graphite, which was later popularized as the first pencil used by humans, is said to have originated around 250 BCE in ancient Greece.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable pencil histories say the pencil dates from the 1500s, not ancient Greece. They describe graphite being found in Borrowdale, England, in the 1500s, the first reference to a graphite pencil in 1565, and the oldest known pencil dating to around 1630 (a slotted piece of wood holding graphite). None of these sources mentions an etched graphite piece from about 250 BCE in ancient Greece.

text: There are only two animals in the world that can see both ultraviolet and infrared light, the sabotage dragonet and the short-tail gushers- however more research is being conducted to find other species with these abilities.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trace of animals called the "sabotage dragonet" or the "short-tail gusher". Searches for these names turned up only unrelated results, such as Dungeons & Dragons forums and other fish like the short-tailed pipefish and short-tail stingray. The claim that only two animals can see both ultraviolet and infrared light is also false. Goldfish are widely reported to see both, and other species such as salmon can switch on infrared-sensitive vision. One weakness: the main source I found for goldfish is a Quora answer, not a scientific paper. Even so, saying these two animals are the only ones with this ability is wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to a 2020 estimate by the SETI Institute and the University of California, Berkeley, but scientists believe that the actual number may be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 study published in PLoS Biology by Camilo Mora, Boris Worm and colleagues at Dalhousie University and the University of Hawaii, working with the Census of Marine Life. It was not a 2020 estimate by the SETI Institute and UC Berkeley. The estimate was about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million, not 'over' 8.7 million. The claim gets the source and the year wrong. The study does note that most species have not yet been described, but the claim's attribution is false.

text: 92 billion barrels of oil were discovered in the Ghawar oil field in Saudi Arabia, making it one of the largest oil fields in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources agree that Ghawar, found in 1948, is the world's largest conventional oil field, so the second half of the claim holds up. I found no source that gives the 92 billion barrel figure, and the estimates I did find vary widely. Wikipedia quotes an Aramco executive saying original reserves were over 100 billion barrels, and lists about 48–58 billion barrels remaining as of 2018. Britannica says Saudi officials estimate the field holds more than 120 billion barrels. Oilprice.com gives 170 billion barrels of oil originally in place, with about 88 billion already produced. Because the estimates differ this much and none matches 92 billion, the number can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out. My searches ran out before I could check further.

text: A DNA helix is typically 20 angstroms in diameter, but when uncoiled, its total length would stretch around the Earth over 300 billion times.
label: contradicted
reason: The 20 Å (about 2 nm) diameter of the DNA double helix is correct. The length comparison is not. One human cell holds about 2 m of DNA. Across roughly 37 trillion cells, that adds up to about 74 trillion m (74 billion km). Sources put this at about 1.8 million trips around the Earth (or about 150,000 by a lower estimate), not 300 billion. The figure in the claim is too high by a factor of more than 100,000.

text: A Disцовok favorited a runway model at NY fashion.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't check this claim because it's garbled. "Disцовok" mixes Latin and Cyrillic letters, so it doesn't clearly name any person, brand or account. The claim also doesn't say which runway model, which show, or what "favorited" means. My search only turned up generic New York Fashion Week runway photos and nothing tied to this subject.

text: A beaver's flat, paddle-like tail, often mistakenly thought to be a rudder, is actually used for balance, communication, and storing fat, known as "beaver fat," which helps them survive during winter months.
label: contradicted
reason: The Smithsonian's National Zoo says the beaver's tail is used as a rudder when swimming, as a balance prop on land, as a danger signal when slapped on the water, and as a place to store fat for winter. The balance, communication and fat-storage parts of the claim are correct. But the zoo's page shows that calling the tail a rudder isn't a mistake, so the claim's main premise is wrong.

text: A bee's sense of direction is so complex that they have been known to perform during GPS-equipped drones in controlled research environments.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim's wording is garbled ("perform during" probably means "outperform"), so it has no clear meaning as written. Either way, I found no evidence that bees have outperformed GPS-equipped drones in controlled research. The search results describe drone navigation systems inspired by bees, such as Bee-Nav, which lets drones fly without GPS. One study also used drones to track how consistently bees repeat their flight paths. Neither shows bees beating GPS drones head to head. The sources say bees are excellent navigators, but they don't support this specific comparison.

text: A country larger than the United States in land area, but with a smaller population is Russia.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Russia covers about 17.1 million km², compared with about 9.8 million km² for the US. Its population is around 146 million, well below the US figure of roughly 331 million. So Russia is larger in area but has fewer people.

text: A dime is the first coin issued by the United States Mint with a person's portrait, featuring former President Franklin D. Roosevelt's profile, which was introduced in 1946.
label: contradicted
reason: The Roosevelt dime did come out in 1946, but it wasn't the first U.S. coin to show a real person's portrait. Several sources say the Lincoln cent, first struck in 1909, was the first regular circulating U.S. coin to feature a real person. Earlier commemorative coins, such as the 1892 Columbian half dollar showing Columbus, also came before it.

text: A fox's white-tipped tail is a key indicator of its species, as only arctic foxes have the unique adaptation of white tips to blend in with their snowy surroundings.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong that only arctic foxes have white-tipped tails. The U.S. National Park Service says a prominent white-tipped tail is a distinguishing feature of red foxes in all of their color phases, and Cosley Zoo also lists a white-tipped tail among the red fox's identifying marks. A white tail tip can help identify a species, but it isn't unique to arctic foxes. Arctic foxes also tend to change their whole coat with the seasons (white in winter, brown or gray in summer) rather than having just a white tail tip.

text: A giant single-celled organism known as the Athabasca Mammoth, discovered in the Canadian Arctic, is estimated to be around 418 million years old, making it one of the oldest known microorganisms on Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no credible source for an organism called the 'Athabasca Mammoth'. Searches for that name, and for a giant single-celled organism from the Canadian Arctic dated to 418 million years, turned up only unrelated results. These included Athabascasaurus (an ichthyosaur), a roughly 1-billion-year-old fossil fungus from the Canadian Arctic, and known large single-celled organisms such as Valonia ventricosa, xenophyophores and Gromia sphaerica. The entity in the claim can't be verified and may be made up. The superlative is also doubtful: microbial fossils and chemical traces of life go back more than 3.5 billion years, so a 418-million-year-old microorganism would not be among the oldest known. Because the claim's main subject can't be found at all, there is not enough evidence to judge it either way.

text: A giant squill, a type of rare plant, can take up to 50 years to bloom and then only lives for approximately six to eight weeks.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source saying a giant squill takes up to 50 years to bloom. Dave's Garden identifies the giant squill as Scilla peruviana and describes it as an ordinary garden bulb. You plant it in late summer or autumn, and it can even be forced to bloom indoors. That is not a plant that waits decades to flower. The same source does say the flowers can last up to two months, which roughly matches the 'six to eight weeks' part. The 50-year claim may come from a mix-up with plants such as Puya raimondii, which blooms after about 80–100 years. A search limit stopped me from checking other sources, so this verdict rests mainly on the one gardening article.

text: A giraffe's cheek pouches can hold up to 25 ounces of water, allowing them to store water for long periods without drinking.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source I found says giraffes store water in cheek pouches, and none mentions a 25-ounce capacity. Denver Water and other sources say giraffes can go weeks without drinking because they get most of their moisture from the leaves they eat, not from stored water. The one giraffe 'cheek pouch' I found was a medical problem: food had built up in a zoo giraffe's cheek (Vet Times). The claim gives the wrong reason for how giraffes cope without water.

text: A golden-colored Lake Hillier in Western Australia is known for its striking turquoise color due to a layer of algae and other microorganisms present beneath its surface.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Hillier in Western Australia is famous for being bubble-gum pink, not golden or turquoise. Sources say the pink colour likely comes from salt-loving microorganisms such as the alga Dunaliella salina and halobacteria, and that the lake stays pink all year. That contradicts both the 'golden-colored' and the 'striking turquoise color' parts of the claim.

text: A grape can hold air inside itself due to a natural process called guttation, resulting in a small bubble forming at its stem end.
label: contradicted
reason: Guttation means liquid water droplets being pushed out of leaf edges or tips through hydathodes by root pressure. It has nothing to do with air getting trapped inside a fruit or a bubble forming at a grape's stem end, so the claim gets the process wrong.

text: A group of about 200 Himalayan spiny babbler birds is thought to have discovered a large cache of lembus fungus in Bhutan, which they then consumed, leading to their deaths due to the fungus's toxicity.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Wikipedia, Birds of the World/Cornell) say the spiny babbler is Nepal's only endemic bird and lives only in the Middle Hills of Nepal, so a flock of about 200 in Bhutan doesn't fit its known range. I found no report of any mass die-off of spiny babblers, and no fungus called 'lembus' turns up anywhere. The story looks made up, and the bird's confirmed range goes against the Bhutan detail.

text: A group of octopuses is commonly referred to as a "garden" due to their tendency to gather and create a cluttered area.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources consistently say the most common or accepted collective noun for octopuses is "consortium," with "tangle" as a playful alternative. Study.com adds that there is no widely accepted term, since octopuses are mostly solitary. One minor site (nounmaster) says "a garden of octopuses" can also be used, but it calls "consortium" the most recognized term. "Octopus garden" is used for specific deep-sea brooding sites, such as the one near hydrothermal springs off California, not as the usual collective noun. No source supports the claimed reason about gathering and creating a cluttered area. The claim that a group is "commonly" called a "garden" is therefore contradicted.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their deliberate-looking clumsy nature when on the ground.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that a group of giant pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment": HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals, Animal Corner, ZME Science and IFAW as cited by inkl. Most of them link the name to the pandas' clumsy, lazy-looking movements. A-Z Animals states this outright, and ZME Science says it is "most likely due to their lovable and clumsy habits." However, the sources only guess at the origin, and HowStuffWorks says the term has no scientific origin. One low-authority site (a clothing retailer) offers a different story about stress behaviours in captivity. No source backs the claim's "deliberate-looking" or "on the ground" wording. Because the core claim (the name and the clumsiness explanation) matches the most common account, I rate it supported, though the origin itself is uncertain.

text: A group of pandas is called an "embarrassment" due to their tendency to be shy and avoid social interactions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part checks out. Several sources, including HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals, ZME Science and Animal Corner, say a group of pandas is commonly called an "embarrassment." The reason the claim gives is not confirmed, though. These sources explain the name in different ways: HowStuffWorks, A-Z Animals and ZME Science point to pandas being clumsy or lazy, and one retailer blog connects it to their stressed behaviour in captivity. HowStuffWorks also says the word has no scientific origin and is just English whimsy. The only place that ties the name to shyness is a TikTok discovery page, which isn't a reliable source. Since the cause in the claim is speculative and other sources give different explanations, the claim can't be called supported.

text: A group of various kittens is called an "inquisition" of kittens.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources on collective nouns list "kindle" and "litter" as the terms for a group of kittens, with "intrigue" and "clutter" as less common options. None of them mention "inquisition." A search for the exact phrase "inquisition of kittens" found only pages about the historical Inquisition and its treatment of cats. The claim seems to confuse "intrigue" with "inquisition."

text: A grup of bacteria known as Thioploca form symbiotic relationships with sulfur-reducing bacteria to create one of the most extensive and efficient sulfur-based chemosynthetic ecosystems on Earth.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each main part of the claim. A FEMS Microbiology Ecology study reports that the sheaths of marine Thioploca off Chile are colonized by filamentous sulfate-reducing bacteria of the genus Desulfonema. It describes a tightly coupled, highly active sulfur cycle in which sulfate reduction and sulfur reoxidation take place together within the mats. Other sources say Thioploca mats along the Peru–Chile shelf stretch for more than 3,000 km and cover over 10,000 km², making them probably the largest community of visible bacteria in the world, or even the largest microbial ecosystem. There are some caveats. The evidence calls this partnership a close association, or likely syntrophic consortium, rather than a formally proven symbiosis. The partner bacteria are sulfate reducers rather than sulfur reducers. And 'efficient' is a loose description that the sources don't test directly. Even so, the core of the claim agrees with the evidence.

text: A piece of the London Underground's King's Cross Station wall is actually a piece of Berlin Wall that has been rebuilt and relocated there after being given by the German government in 1994.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing in my searches that supports the claim, but nothing directly disproves it either. Londonist, London Remembers and a Wikipedia-derived list of Berlin Wall segments name the London pieces: one outside the Imperial War Museum, which the museum acquired in 1991; one built into the Reagan statue plaque in Grosvenor Square; pieces at the National Army Museum; one at the German School in Richmond; and two at the Migration Museum in Lewisham. None of these sources mentions a piece at King's Cross station or a 1994 gift from the German government for the station. King's Cross also does not appear on Wikipedia's page for the tube station. This strongly suggests the claim is false, but none of these sources explicitly says there is no such piece, so it cannot be verified either way.

text: A platypus is one of the few venomous mammals in the world, producing venom in its hind legs through glands that can deliver a painful and potentially deadly sting to predators.
label: supported
reason: A University of Melbourne venom research page confirms the main points. Male platypuses have a crural venom system: paired glands near the pelvis connect by ducts to hollow spurs on the hind legs. They wrap their hind legs around a target and drive the spurs in with force. The venom can kill dogs but doesn't appear to be lethal to humans or other platypuses. Platypuses are widely recognized as among the very few venomous mammals. The claim simplifies a few details. Only males are venomous, the glands sit in the pelvic area rather than in the legs themselves, the venom is delivered by a spur rather than a 'sting,' and it is thought to be used mostly in fights between males rather than against predators. Overall, though, the claim matches the evidence.

text: A rainbow can occur at night if the Moon is full and there are water droplets in the air, a phenomenon known as a Moonbow or lunar rainbow.
label: supported
reason: DarkSky International and Atlas Obscura both describe the moonbow, also called a lunar rainbow, as a night-time rainbow. It forms when moonlight lights up water drops in the air, such as rain or waterfall mist. DarkSky says it needs a full or nearly full Moon. The claim simplifies this to 'full,' which is a small difference, but its main points match these sources.

text: A recorded human voice can be preserved for up to 6,000 years due to the way it stores sound vibrations in glass.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that backs the claim. Nothing I found says a recorded human voice can last up to 6,000 years because of how glass stores sound vibrations. The glass-storage sources I did find, such as Microsoft's Project Silica coverage in Computerworld, France24 and Phys.org, are about laser-written digital data. They give lifetimes of more than 10,000 years, not 6,000, and say nothing about storing sound vibrations as such. Early glass-disc and soot-coated-glass recordings (Bell's Volta Lab, the phonautograph) make no millennia-long durability claims. The only '6,000-year voice' story is the debunked claim about voices recorded in 6,500-year-old pottery, which isn't glass. The claim also doesn't say what 'it' refers to, so there is no clear technology to check.

text: A segment of the Amazon rainforest, known as the Manú National Park in Peru, is home to over 1,100 species of birds.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figure is too high. Guinness World Records says 1,009 bird species have been documented in Manú National Park since it was established in 1973. Wikipedia estimates more than 1,000, and most other sources give about 1,025. None of these reaches "over 1,100." One tour-company blog says more than 1,300, but that is an outlier from a less reliable source and conflicts with the more authoritative counts. The rest of the claim is accurate: Manú is in Peru and protects part of the Amazon rainforest.

text: A single virus can infect up to 70% of the cells in a human body, showcasing the considerable impact these microscopic entities can have on our health.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no reliable source saying one virus can infect up to 70% of the cells in a human body. The ~70% figures that come up are about people, not cells: cytomegalovirus persists in about 70% of healthy adults (60–80% in developed countries). The claim seems to mix up what share of the population carries a virus with what share of one body's cells it infects. Sources on viral tropism also count against it: viruses are limited to particular hosts, tissues and cell types. Even broad-range viruses like HCMV infect certain cell types, not most of the body's cells. No source directly rejects the exact 70% figure, so this is a judgment from indirect evidence, but nothing supports it and the available evidence conflicts with it.

text: A vibrant and iridescent species of jellyfish, called the Pelagia noctiluca, is responsible for producing a bright blue bioluminescent glow through its up to 1,000 photophores, or light-producing organs, in order to communicate and attract prey.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, the Cephalopod Page and an Oceanography (TOS) article, confirm that Pelagia noctiluca, the mauve stinger, is a bioluminescent jellyfish. Its name means 'night light', and it glows from the edge of its bell when disturbed. However, none of the sources I found mention photophores, let alone 'up to 1,000' of them. They also don't say the glow is used to communicate with other jellyfish or attract prey. The Cephalopod Page says it is not certain what causes the light in this species and describes it as glowing when disturbed. That fits a defensive response better than a way to attract prey, but no source directly rules out the claim's details. Because these key parts of the claim cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A violet is a rare flower that can only produce one bloom per stem or plant before it is exhausted of productive blooms.
label: contradicted
reason: Violets (genus Viola) are not rare. The Common Blue Violet (Viola sororia) is a widespread wildflower. A single plant also doesn't stop after one bloom: most species first produce regular open flowers, then go on to produce more cleistogamous (closed, self-pollinating) flowers that set plenty of fertile seed. A plant can show several such flowers at once, so the 'only one bloom' part of the claim is false.

text: A virus called Radiculovirus has been found in many species of plants, particularly in the daisy family.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions a virus called "Radiculovirus". Searches for the name, including ones that added Asteraceae (the daisy family) and ICTV-related virus families, only returned unrelated results. These included Vesiculovirus, an animal rhabdovirus genus; human radiculomyelitis and radiculitis cases; and general Asteraceae virus papers. None of them mention "Radiculovirus" or say it is found widely in daisy-family plants. The search tool hit its usage limit before my last two searches ran, so I may have missed something. Still, the virus doesn't appear in ICTV taxonomy results, and it may not exist. Since nothing supports or contradicts the claim, it can't be verified.

text: ADN (DNA in English) was initially thought to be a four base molecule consisting of Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine, until the discovery of Uracil, replacing Thymine in RNA in 1950.
label: contradicted
reason: The NCATS Inxight Drugs entry (NIH) says Alberto Ascoli discovered uracil in 1900 by breaking down yeast nuclein through hydrolysis, so the 1950 date in the claim is wrong. The claim also gets the history backwards: DNA still has four bases (A, T, G, C). Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA, and finding it never changed the four-base model of DNA.

text: Aicular meaning "having a fleeting nature" in Latin, the term "minute" originally referred to the shortness of human life, not seconds.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. "Minute" comes from the Latin "pars minuta prima", which means "first small part". That name describes dividing the hour into 60 parts. It has nothing to do with "having a fleeting nature" or with how short human life is. "Second" comes from "pars minuta secunda", the second division by 60. Also, "Aicular" is not a real Latin word.

text: American author Ernest Hemingway was a medical aide in the Red Cross during World War I and was injured in an accident that led him to lose a limb, which greatly influenced his writing.
label: contradicted
reason: Hemingway did serve in the American Red Cross in Italy during WWI (as an ambulance driver), and he was badly wounded in July 1918. But the wound came from mortar fire, not an accident, and he did not lose a limb. The JFK Library's record shows that his injured right leg was put in a cast and operated on, and that it healed. He kept both legs. So the claim that he lost a limb is false.

text: Another fun fact about human vision is that our brains can process and recognize images more quickly when we see them in color than when they are presented in black and white.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable studies back the general claim, though not for every task. A PubMed-indexed study (Ostergaard & Davidoff, 1985) found that people named colour pictures of everyday objects faster than black-and-white versions. Other work found that colour helps recognition and memory of natural scenes by about 5–10%, and that objects with typical colours are recognised faster in colour. There is some contrary evidence: studies of ultra-rapid scene categorisation (Delorme et al., 2000) found little or no colour advantage, and some reviews say colour barely affects recognition times. Overall the evidence leans toward a colour advantage, but the claim is too broad to hold in every case.

text: Antarctica has a unique type of "Blood Rain" caused by -60C temperature allowing weathered red rock to freeze into droplets, creating red rain and leaving a reddish-brown streak on surfaces it contacts.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up no "Blood Rain" in Antarctica of the kind the claim describes. What Antarctica does have is Blood Falls, an outflow at Taylor Glacier in the McMurdo Dry Valleys. Wikipedia, National Geographic, Scientific American, EarthSky and an NSF-hosted peer-reviewed paper all say its red colour comes from iron-rich, very salty brine under the glacier. The iron rusts when the brine reaches the surface and meets air, staining the ice. That brine is about −7 °C, not −60 °C. Red rock freezing into droplets and falling as rain is not the cause, so the claimed mechanism and phenomenon contradict reliable sources.

text: Antarctica has more than 70 active volcanoes, with many mascon (single, volcanic shield or large igneous province) volcanoes, due to its unique geology and location.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science and other sources say only two Antarctic volcanoes are currently classed as active: Mount Erebus and Deception Island. The Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program lists just 19 Holocene volcanoes in Antarctica. A 2017 study identified about 138 volcanoes in West Antarctica (91 of them newly found), but most are extinct or dormant. So the claim of 'more than 70 active volcanoes' is false. The claim also misuses 'mascon': the term means a gravitational mass concentration, not a type of volcano.

text: Antarctica is home to several volcanoes, with some like Mount Erebus remaining active and having erupted as recently as 2022.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, an authoritative source, says Erebus has had a persistent, active lava lake since at least 1972, with frequent Strombolian explosions. VolcanoDiscovery, which follows the GVP database, lists the current Erebus eruption as running from December 1972 and still ongoing, so it was erupting during 2022. The GVP's February 2022 report also describes ongoing activity, including more thermal activity in 2021 than in 2020. A 2022 ScienceDirect paper describes ground inflation at Erebus lasting until March 2022. Wikipedia's infobox gives 2020 as the 'last eruption', but that conflicts with the GVP's continuous-eruption record and looks out of date. Antarctica clearly has several volcanoes, and Erebus is described as the world's southernmost active volcano.

text: Antarctica is home to the highest concentration of astrophysicists on the planet due to its unique environment which allows for a clear and uninterrupted view of the stars.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including an arXiv/A&ARv review, Science and Space.com, agree that Antarctica's high, cold, dry and stable plateau makes it an excellent place for astronomy. They also show that astrophysicists have worked at stations such as the South Pole since the early 1990s. That supports the part of the claim about the unique environment. However, I found no source saying Antarctica has the highest concentration of astrophysicists on the planet. That central part of the claim can't be verified, and saying the view of the stars is 'uninterrupted' overstates what the sources describe.

text: Approximately 71% of the Earth's surface is covered in water, with about 96.5% of that water being saline ocean water.
label: supported
reason: The USGS Water Science School says that about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water. USGS also notes that nearly all of Earth's water is saline and found in the oceans. The claim's wording is slightly loose, because "96.5% of that water" refers to all of Earth's water, not just the surface-covering water, but both figures match authoritative sources.

text: Atacama Giant, a large metal sculpture in Chile, is the world's largest portrait of a person, depicting Luigi Gabrielli's likeness.
label: contradicted
reason: The Atacama Giant (also called the Tarapacá Giant) is not a metal sculpture. It is a prehistoric anthropomorphic geoglyph, about 119 m tall, laid out on the hillside of Cerro Unitas in the Atacama Desert. Its meaning is unclear and it is thought to represent a deity, so it is not a portrait of Luigi Gabrielli or of anyone else. The source checked is a stock-photo caption from Alamy, but these facts match the widely documented record. The only part of the claim that holds up is the location in Chile.

text: Bacteria have been found to exist on the highest mountain, Mount Everest, and the lowest depths of the ocean, showcasing their incredible ability to thrive in various environments.
label: supported
reason: Researchers from CU Boulder found bacteria and other microbes in soil samples from Mount Everest's South Col, at about 7,900 m. Separately, University of East Anglia scientists found bacteria, including a new oil-eating species, at the deepest point of the Mariana Trench, about 11,000 m down. Together these findings back the claim that bacteria live both on Everest and at the bottom of the ocean, and that they can survive in extreme environments.

text: Bacteria have been found to thrive in the extremely harsh conditions of Antarctica's dry valleys, where temperatures often drop below -12°C (10°F).
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back both parts of the claim. EBSCO describes the McMurdo Dry Valleys as a hyperarid polar desert with an average temperature of about -17°C (1.4°F), and other sources report lows of -68°C. That means temperatures below -12°C (10°F) are common. Bacteria do live there: cyanobacteria and other bacteria are documented in the valleys. Murray et al. (PNAS 2012), as reported by the USAP Antarctic Sun and SpaceNews, found an active bacterial community in Lake Vida's brine in the Dry Valleys at about -13°C (8°F). The word "thrive" is a bit generous, since life there is sparse, but nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Bananas are naturally tilted to the right side because of the position of the stem, which blocks the growth of the fruit on the left side, creating this unique curvature.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say bananas curve because of negative geotropism. The fruit first hangs downward, then bends upward against gravity and toward the sunlight, with the bend driven by uneven distribution of the growth hormone auxin. None of them say bananas lean to the right, and none blame the stem for blocking growth on the left side. The claim gets the cause of the curve wrong.

text: Barack Obama, the 44th President of the United States, is a distant descendant of John Punch, a 17th-century African American indentured servant, and a direct descendant of Elizabeth Ball, an Englishwoman who was married to a German immigrant and racism is a dehumanizing poison that corrupts our politics
label: not_verifiable
reason: The John Punch part has support. In 2012 Ancestry.com announced, and NBC, WTVR and The American Prospect reported, that Obama is the 11th great-grandson of John Punch through his mother's Bunch family line. Punch was an African indentured servant in colonial Virginia who was sentenced to lifelong servitude in 1640, so calling him 'African American' is loose wording. The finding also rests on inference: the records are incomplete, and the link depends on DNA evidence and reasoning about the paper trail. I found nothing showing that Obama is a direct descendant of an Englishwoman named Elizabeth Ball who married a German immigrant. My searches turned up only unrelated people named Elizabeth Ball, and the tool's search limit ran out before I could check further. The last part, that racism is a dehumanizing poison, is an opinion that can't be checked against facts. Since one key factual part couldn't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Barbae Blackworms, a type of worm, can regrow their bodies from a single severed head, including internal organs and other body parts.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any worm called a "Barbae Blackworm". Searches for "Barbae" only turned up tinea barbae (beard ringworm, a fungal skin infection), so the name in the claim doesn't point to a known animal. The closest real species is the blackworm, Lumbriculus variegatus (also called the California blackworm). Sources describe it as reproducing by breaking into fragments, and each piece can regrow a missing head or tail. That makes the regrowth part of the claim plausible for blackworms in general. However, I found no source tying this to anything named "Barbae", and none specifically confirming that a single severed head regrows a whole body with its internal organs.

text: Beechnuts, which are an important food source for many animals, are triangular and have a single seed inside.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up each part of the claim. The Ohio DNR and NC State Extension describe beechnuts as triangular, three-angled nuts, and Wikipedia says the same for beech species. Go Botany (Native Plant Trust) states that fruits in the beech family (Fagaceae) are nuts with a single seed, and another source calls the beechnut a single-seeded nut. Multiple sources also note that beechnuts are a valuable food for wildlife such as squirrels, deer and birds. The spiny husk usually holds one to three nuts, but each nut has only one seed, so this fits the claim.

text: Black holes are named after their dark colors, due to their intense gravitational pull warping the light around them so that not much escapes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. Black holes aren't named after a "dark colour" they happen to have. Their name comes from the fact that they absorb all the light that falls on them. The claim also says "not much" light escapes, but trustworthy sources (ESA, Dictionary.com) say nothing gets out, not even light. A black hole's escape velocity is greater than the speed of light, which makes it invisible, and that is why it's called 'black'.

text: Blåhaj, or blue sharks, are able to produce a remarkable seven species of embryos that develop from unfertilized eggs, a reproductive strategy known as "superfecundation," which involves overlapping populations and sequential fertilization.
label: contradicted
reason: Blue sharks (Prionace glauca) are viviparous with a yolk-sac placenta. They have litters of about 4 to 135 pups from a single species, typically 15 to 30, after internal fertilization. A shark cannot carry embryos of 'seven species,' and embryos that grow from unfertilized eggs would be parthenogenesis, not superfecundation. Superfecundation means eggs from the same cycle being fertilized by more than one mating. Also, 'Blåhaj' is the name of an IKEA plush toy, not another name for blue sharks. Reliable sources on blue shark reproduction contradict the claim's central points.

text: Bryan Gunnell's porcupinefish or Diodon cyclicus, when threatened, can swallow and store large amounts of air or water in its mouth and stomach to inflate itself for defense.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source showing that "Bryan Gunnell's porcupinefish" or "Diodon cyclicus" is a real, recognized species name, so the subject of the claim can't be clearly identified. The searches returned only pages on related fish, such as the Cyclichthys genus, which has no species called cyclicus, and Diodon liturosus. Those Wikipedia pages confirm the general point that porcupinefish puff up when threatened by swallowing water (or air). However, nothing confirmed the specific named species or the Gunnell attribution, so the claim can't be verified.

text: Burford, a small town in England, is the only town in the United Kingdom where you can see a hill, a river, a parish church, a village cricket pitch, a National Trust property, and a canal within its boundaries.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Wikipedia confirms that Burford is a small town in Oxfordshire, England. It sits on the River Windrush in the Cotswold hills, has a parish church (St John the Baptist), and has a street called 'The Hill'. I found nothing showing a canal or a National Trust property inside Burford's boundaries, or any village cricket pitch. I also found no source saying Burford is the only UK town with all these features. The 'only town' part looks made up, and other towns probably have the same mix, but no search result directly says this is false. Because key parts of the claim can't be checked, it is inconclusive.

text: Butagiga the Egyptian Egyptian bull-god, was prominently featured on ancient Egyptian seals and coins, however, to nowhere near the extend that big US Bull (el Toro) is, on Qing Dynasty document's in the 1700s
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence of an Egyptian bull-god called "Butagiga." Reliable sources list the Egyptian sacred bulls as Apis, Mnevis and Buchis, so the main subject of the claim has no clear referent. The searches also turned up nothing on a "big US Bull (el Toro)" on 1700s Qing Dynasty documents. That comparison makes little sense: the United States did not exist until 1776, and ancient Egypt had almost no coins of its own until late in its history. Since the main entity can't be identified and no part of the claim can be checked, it is inconclusive.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, features a unique phenomenon known as "hand glides" which involves naturally formed sandstone rocks forming at an angle, catching and holding water to resemble a flowing river.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found Butlers Gorge, a locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands that is known for the hydro-electric Clark Dam. I found no source describing a phenomenon called 'hand glides' there, or sandstone formations that hold water so it looks like a flowing river. My search for the specific term returned only general pages about the locality. This makes the claim look fabricated, but none of the results directly rules it out, so it can't be verified. I couldn't run a broader follow-up search because the search tool limit was reached.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, has a natural rock arch that is home to one of the world's longest self-supporting rock arches.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No reliable source I found mentions a natural rock arch at Butlers Gorge, let alone one of the world's longest self-supporting rock arches. Wikipedia describes Butlers Gorge as a rural Central Highlands locality with no recorded population. The 'arch' found there is the Clark Dam, a concrete arch dam on the River Derwent that was completed in 1949 and forms Lake King William. That makes the claim look like a confusion with the dam. However, no source explicitly says there is no such rock arch, so the claim can't be verified or directly refuted.

text: Butler's Gorge in Tasmania, Australia, is one of the most easterly points where large glaciers are found.
label: contradicted
reason: Tasmania Parks and Wildlife says outright that there are no modern glaciers in Tasmania or anywhere else in Australia. Other sources (Journal of Glaciology, BMC Evolutionary Biology) agree: Tasmania had glaciers only during the Pleistocene and has none now. Butlers Gorge is a hydro-electric locality in the Central Highlands with no glaciers, so it cannot be one of the most easterly places where large glaciers are found.

text: Butler's Gorge is the world's longest gorge, located in the Himalayan region of Nepal and Tibet.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, Australia, where Lake King William Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station are. It is named after the surveyor John Leslie Butler. It is not in the Himalayas, Nepal or Tibet, and nothing describes it as the world's longest gorge.

text: Butler's Gorge, a location in Tasmania, Australia, holds the record for being the site of the longest recorded freshwater plunge pool in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing linking Butlers Gorge to any plunge pool record, let alone the 'longest freshwater plunge pool in the world'. Sources describe it as a former Hydro Electric Commission village and the site of Clark Dam, Lake King William and Butlers Gorge Power Station. The record Butlers Gorge actually holds is Tasmania's lowest recorded temperature, −13.0 °C on 30 June 1983, according to Bureau of Meteorology data cited on Wikidata. So the claim gets the record wrong. No source directly says it isn't a plunge pool record, though, so this conclusion rests on the record being misidentified and the claim having no support at all.

text: Butler's Gorge, a region in Antarctica, is home to a rare and unique type of waterfall that freezes in the harsh, cold climate.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge isn't in Antarctica. Wikipedia and Wikidata both describe it as a rural locality in the Central Highlands of Tasmania, Australia. It is home to the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, which are part of Hydro Tasmania's Derwent scheme. The search results say nothing about a rare freezing waterfall, and the claim's basic premise about the location is wrong.

text: Butler's Gorge, a remote gorge in Tasmania, holds the world record for the longest and deepest heterosexual cave relationship (45 years at the time of the record in the late 1990s).
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing to back up the claim's main point. Wikipedia describes Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands, home to Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge hydro power station. It is not described as a remote cave site. Searches for any world record about a 'longest and deepest heterosexual cave relationship' linked to Butlers Gorge found nothing, and the claim looks made up. However, no source directly says such a record doesn't exist, so it can't be verified either way.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, Australia, is one of the deepest river canyons in the world and features stunning natural scenery.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe Butlers Gorge as a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands with a population of nil. It is also the site of the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station on the upper Derwent River. A rafting source describes the gorge itself only as a fast, steep section of the river. No source calls it one of the world's deepest river canyons. Lists of the world's deepest gorges are led by canyons over 2,000 m deep, such as Hells Canyon at about 2,400 m, and Butlers Gorge does not appear among them. The claim that it is one of the deepest river canyons in the world is therefore false. Calling the scenery stunning is subjective and can't be verified.

text: Butler's Gorge, located in Tasmania, is the highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere at 304 meters.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches show the claim is false. Butlers Gorge is a rural locality in Tasmania's Central Highlands. It is home to the Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station, and the sources do not describe it as a waterfall at all. The highest waterfall in the Southern Hemisphere is generally taken to be Tugela Falls in South Africa, which drops about 948 m. That is far taller than the 304 m in the claim, and some sources even call it the tallest waterfall in the world.

text: Butler's Gorge, one of the deepest canyons in the world, is over 106 meters (348 ft) deep in the Oxfordshire county of England and formed as a result of the creation of a waterway by the carts of quarry miners.
label: contradicted
reason: Butlers Gorge is in Tasmania's Central Highlands in Australia, not in Oxfordshire, England. It's a gorge on the Derwent River where Clark Dam and the Butlers Gorge Power Station were built, and the locality was named after surveyor John Leslie Butler. The search found no sign of a Butler's Gorge in Oxfordshire, and nothing said it is one of the world's deepest canyons or that quarry miners' carts formed it. The claim's location and origin story are wrong.

text: Butler's Grist Mill in Vermont is the oldest continuously operating gristmill in the United States, having been in operation since 1791.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no Butler's Grist Mill in Vermont, so I couldn't confirm the 1791 date. The main claim is still contradicted: the Old Wye Mill's official site and Wikipedia both name Wye Mill in Wye Mills, Maryland, as the oldest continuously operated grist mill in the U.S. It dates to the 1680s, well before 1791.

text: Butler's Grotto, a cave located in Lough Derg, Ireland, is the country's largest and longest-known cave system, spanning approximately 10 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source that describes a cave called "Butler's Grotto" at Lough Derg. The only related result is an old travel account by Isaac Butler called "A Journey to Lough Derg", which mentions some caves, but it does not name them Butler's Grotto or call them Ireland's largest. The claim is also wrong about which cave is Ireland's longest. The Burren Geopark says Poulnagollum in Co. Clare is Ireland's longest cave, at over 15 km and 140 m deep. A Geograph page also describes Pollnagollum (Fermanagh) as Ireland's longest at over 16 km. Neither matches a 10 km cave at Lough Derg.

text: Butler's Grotto, a cave system in New Zealand, contains over 48 million years of fossilized tree root impressions and extensively preserved Eocene rainforest on its walls.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source showing that a cave system called "Butler's Grotto" exists in New Zealand. My searches turned up only unrelated places with similar names, such as Butler Point Whaling Museum, Butler Range, and Butler Cave in Virginia, plus unrelated New Zealand cave fossil finds near Waitomo. Because of this, I couldn't check the claimed 48 million years of fossilized tree root impressions or the preserved Eocene rainforest on the cave walls. No source confirmed or disproved these details.

text: Butler's Grotto, also known as Patrick's Grotto, is a limestone cavern and early Catholic shrine located in Ashley Falls in the town of Becket, Massachusetts.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no source that mentions a "Butler's Grotto" or "Patrick's Grotto" in Massachusetts, so I couldn't confirm the cave or shrine itself. Before I ran out of searches, they returned only unrelated results, such as Butler Cave in Virginia and general pages about Massachusetts caving. The location in the claim is wrong, though. Ashley Falls is a well-known village in the town of Sheffield in southern Berkshire County, not in Becket, which is a separate town farther north. This point comes from general knowledge, not from my search results. Placing Ashley Falls in Becket contradicts that fact.

text: Butler's Grotto, located in Carlsbad, California, is a popular tourist attraction containing a large, glowing cave that has an estimated 40 million stromatolites - structures formed by ancient cyanobacteria.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm that a place called "Butler's Grotto" exists in Carlsbad, California. Searches turned up only unrelated results: spas in Carlsbad with "Grotto" in the name, Butler Cave in Virginia, and Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico. None of them mention a glowing cave with about 40 million stromatolites. Nothing directly contradicts the claim either, so it can't be supported or ruled out, and the attraction may well be fictional.

text: Butler's Gulleys, a series of rare and naturally occurring rock formations in Western Australia, can occur only when water flows through a crack in a sandstone rock and dissolves the surrounding area, eventually creating an arch or a cave.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source for a rock formation called "Butler's Gulleys" in Western Australia. Searching the exact name only turned up an unrelated roofing business, and searching "Butlers Gully" only turned up the Wikipedia page for Butler, a suburb of Perth. Nothing I found describes these formations or how they form. The claim's geology is also doubtful: arches and caves usually come from dissolving limestone, while sandstone mostly wears away by erosion. But with no source on the place itself, I can't confirm or rule out the claim.

text: Butler's Panama, a small island located in Maine, USA, is the only incorporated town in the United States that is an island.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any place called "Butler's Panama" in Maine. Searching only turned up Butler Island WMA in Ashland, Butter (Butler) Island, and Butler Head Preserve. The claim that it is the only incorporated U.S. town that is an island is also false. Maine alone has many incorporated island towns. Wikipedia lists North Haven as incorporated in 1846/1847, and other sources describe Vinalhaven as the largest of Maine's 15 year-round island towns. Other examples include Islesboro, Swan's Island, Frenchboro and Isle au Haut.

text: Butler's Panjas, which were late 19th-century phosphorescent nightcrawlers fished off the coast of Florida, and were noted for their capability of glowing in sunlight and under ultraviolet (UV) light.

No results connect anything by that name to phosphorescent nightcrawlers, fishing off Florida in the late 19th century, or glowing in sunlight or under UV light. The term looks made up or has no clear referent, so I can't verify any part of the claim.

text: Butler's Panorama in Durness, Scotland is the largest panorama and scenic artwork in the world, a massive 50-meter-long by 11-meter-high landscape painting that features the scenery of Sutherland.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no sign that a 'Butler's Panorama' exists in Durness. Results for that name were unrelated, such as Butler Plaza at Hendrix College and photographer Adam Butler. A search for the world's largest panorama painting turned up a Library of Congress record for the 'Panthéon de la guerre', described as 'the largest painting in the world, 402 feet long--45 feet high' (about 122 m by 14 m). That is far bigger than the claimed 50 m by 11 m. Other well-known panoramas are also larger, though I'm relying on general knowledge here because my searches didn't confirm them: Panorama Mesdag (about 120 m), the Racławice Panorama (about 114 m) and the Bad Frankenhausen panorama (about 123 m). So a 50 m painting cannot be the world's largest.

text: Butler's Panorama in Manchester, England, is the world's oldest and the longest surviving panoramic painting, dating back to 1807.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources name the Wocher (Thun) Panorama in Switzerland as the world's oldest surviving panorama, not a 'Butler's Panorama' in Manchester. Marquard Wocher painted it around 1809–1814, and Wikipedia calls it the oldest cyclorama in the world. My search found no evidence that a 'Butler's Panorama' from 1807 exists in Manchester, or that any such painting holds the oldest or longest record.

text: Butler's Panorama, also known as the Bailey's Panorama, consists of nine hand-painted oil canvas panels, combining to create a 27-foot long panoramic view of the London skyline in the 18th century.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source for this claim. Searches for "Butler's Panorama" only returned a modern London photographer named Adam Butler and James D. Butler's paintings of the Mississippi River. A search for "Bailey's Panorama" only returned a mountain peak in South Africa. Before I could run more specific searches, the tool hit its usage limit. Nothing I found confirms the alternative name, the nine hand-painted oil panels, the 27-foot length or the 18th-century London skyline, but nothing contradicts them either.

text: Butlers in England traditionally wear a formal tailcoat, formal trousers with a strip of satin or braid down the side of each leg, and a waistcoat, all of which are called morning dress.
label: contradicted
reason: The outfit described here is evening dress (white tie), not morning dress. Wikipedia's Tailcoat and Black tie articles say the evening dress coat is worn with matching trousers that have satin or silk braid down the outer seams. Wikipedia's Morning dress and Formal trousers articles say morning dress is a day outfit: a morning coat (cut differently from the evening tailcoat) worn with grey striped trousers, not braided ones. Butler-attire sources (thebutler.jp, Etiquipedia) also separate the daytime morning coat with striped trousers from the evening tailcoat. Butlers may well wear a tailcoat, braided trousers and a waistcoat, but calling that combination 'morning dress' is wrong.

text: Butterfish, a type of small marine fish, have a unique ability to release a sharp, pointed quill-like spine from their dorsal fin when threatened, which can cause irritation or injury to the predator.
label: contradicted
reason: Authoritative descriptions of butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus), from Bigelow & Schroeder's Fishes of the Gulf of Maine via buzzardsbay.org and from NOAA, say the dorsal fin is a single long fin made of soft rays. The only spines are a very short one in front of the dorsal fin and a few tiny spines mostly buried in the skin. The species is even identified by its lack of obvious dorsal spines. No source describes any ability to release a sharp quill-like spine to irritate or injure predators. That defensive trait appears to be made up, and it conflicts with the documented soft-rayed, nearly spineless dorsal fin.

text: Butterflies taste with their feet and are unable to fly if they are too cold, as their wings are unable to expand when the temperature is below a certain point.
label: contradicted
reason: Butterflies do taste with chemoreceptors on their feet, and it's true they can't fly well when they're too cold. Monarchs, for example, have a flight threshold of about 55°F (13°C). But the claim gives the wrong reason. Journey North says butterflies shiver to warm the flight muscles inside their thorax, and they need a high thoracic temperature to fly. The limit comes from their muscles being too cold, not from their wings being 'unable to expand' below a certain temperature. Because that part of the claim is wrong, it counts as contradicted.

text: Butterflies taste with their feet and have 250,000 different patterns on their intricately unique eyes.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part is right: butterflies do taste with their feet. The second part is wrong. Reliable sources (Butterfly Conservation Ireland, LearnButterflies) say each butterfly compound eye has up to about 17,000 ommatidia, typically 12,000–17,000. I found no source for '250,000 different patterns' on butterfly eyes. That figure is far higher than the documented counts and seems to be made up.

text: Butterfly fish have developed a unique adaptation, where many species can't swim backwards due to their laterally compressed bodies with large, eye-like structures on each side that aid their directional vision.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the purpose of the eye-like markings wrong. Reliable sources describe the large eyespots on butterflyfish, such as the foureye butterflyfish, as false eyes. They do not help the fish see. They confuse predators about which end is the head, so an attack is drawn toward the tail. The sources also say the fish's first move when threatened is to flee, which puts the false eye closer to the predator. Nothing found supports the claim that butterflyfish can't swim backwards. Because the stated function of the eyespots is contradicted, the claim is contradicted.

text: Butterfly flavors are a type of sensation where people can see the ultraviolet patterns that are invisible to the human eye.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no recognized phenomenon or sensation called "butterfly flavors". Reliable sources (Chicago Botanic Garden, a PMC review on butterflies and UV, and a Lepidopterists' Society paper) say butterfly ultraviolet wing patterns are invisible to humans. Butterflies and other insects can see these patterns, but people cannot, and the patterns only show up with UV photography. That contradicts the idea of a human sensation in which people see them.

text: Butterfly pavilions help increase butterfly populations by allowing them to undergo metamorphosis safely, since some species of caterpillars are threatened by birds and other predators in the wild.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no direct evidence that butterfly pavilions increase butterfly populations by sheltering metamorphosis from predators. Butterfly Pavilion (butterflies.org) says its supplier farms raise caterpillars in protected settings, where one batch of eggs can produce hundreds of adults compared with two or three in the wild. That protection happens on the farms, though, not in the pavilions. Pavilions and butterfly houses mostly buy imported pupae and keep the adults on display, with no sign that they are released to add to wild populations. An analysis of the industry also notes that few independent studies have measured its conservation impact. The predator part is partly supported, since only a small share of eggs survive in the wild. But the evidence does not confirm that pavilions themselves raise butterfly populations, so the main claim cannot be verified.

text: Butterflyfish have a unique mating system where they form long-term monogamous relationships, with some species even remaining together for their entire lives.
label: supported
reason: A-Z Animals says most butterflyfish form stable monogamous pairs that last at least three years and sometimes for their entire lives. A peer-reviewed Scientific Reports paper backs this up: at least 59 of about 91 Chaetodon species reportedly form pair bonds, and pairs in some species are monogamous. The word "unique" is loose wording, but nothing I found contradicts the core claim of long-term monogamy, sometimes lifelong.

text: Buttressed trees in East Asia, called Judas Trees, can survive fire by what is known as the "r Selection" idea, where its roots continue to grow deep in the earth while the abovegroud portion burns away.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the key facts wrong. The Judas tree (Cercis siliquastrum) is a small, often multi-trunked understory tree. It is native to Southern Europe and Western Asia, from France to the eastern Mediterranean, not East Asia, and it is not described as buttressed. Also, 'r selection' in r/K selection theory describes a reproductive strategy: species that breed quickly and produce many offspring. It does not refer to roots surviving and regrowing after fire burns the part of the plant above ground. That would be fire resprouting, a separate idea. No source supports the claim's description of a buttressed East Asian tree using r selection to survive fire.

text: Caffeine can have different effects on the body at different altitudes, as high altitudes can lead to a more rapid caffeine clearance and potentially reduced sensitivity to its stimulating effects.
label: supported
reason: The evidence supports the claim. Hackett's peer-reviewed review 'Caffeine at High Altitude: Java at Base Camp' (High Altitude Medicine & Biology, 2010) summarizes several studies. In one study, caffeine clearance nearly doubled at altitude. In another, it rose by 36%. The review concludes that high-altitude hypoxia 'appears to hasten the clearance of caffeine' and that caffeine 'may thus be expected to have a shorter duration of action at high altitude.' This backs the claim's main point about faster clearance and different effects. The 'reduced sensitivity' part is hedged with 'potentially' and fits the shorter duration of action, though no source directly measures sensitivity. There are caveats. One study cited in the review found no clinically significant change in CYP enzymes. A separate review says hypoxia generally slows the metabolism of most drugs. The same caffeine review also reports that caffeine improved performance more under hypoxia than at sea level, which cuts somewhat against reduced sensitivity. Even so, the caffeine-specific evidence points to faster clearance.

text: Caffeine has a unique ability to stay in the human body for a surprisingly long time, taking an average of 10 hours to be fully eliminated after consumption.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree, and parts of the claim can't be checked. Consumer sites such as sleep.me, xwerks and bearaby say caffeine can take about 10 hours, or 'up to 10 hours', to clear. Most of them mean 'up to' rather than an average, though xwerks does give about 10 hours. Other sources point the other way. The Sleep Foundation puts caffeine's half-life (the time to remove half of it) at 2 to 12 hours, and most sources say about 5 hours. At about 5 hours per half-life, near-complete removal would take about 25 hours, well beyond 10. Lifestack also says caffeine is largely but not completely gone by 10–12 hours. That makes the claim of an average 10 hours to full elimination inconsistent with the evidence. The 'unique ability' wording also has no support.

text: Caffeine, found in coffee, has been used as an anesthetic and to reduce pain for over 200 years, making it one of the oldest known pain-relieving substances.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Caffeine was first isolated in 1819, so it could not have been used as a separate drug before then. It isn't an anesthetic either. Its established medical role is as a helper that boosts other painkillers in over-the-counter products. Calling it 'one of the oldest known pain-relieving substances' is also false, because opium and willow bark were used for pain thousands of years earlier. The source found describes caffeine as an adjuvant for pain treatment, not as an old anesthetic.

text: Camels are able to go without water for extended periods due to having a Three-Compartment Stomach.
label: contradicted
reason: Camels do have a three-chambered stomach, but that is not why they can go without water. EarthSky says many scientists once thought camels stored water in one of their three stomachs, but that "there's no evidence" camels store water for long periods anywhere in their bodies. Their endurance comes from using water efficiently and tolerating dehydration: their fur limits sweating, their oval red blood cells keep working as the blood thickens, and their kidneys conserve water and they pass dry feces (Live Science). The stomach chambers are for digesting and fermenting food, not storing water. So the causal claim is contradicted.

text: Cancer is the leading cause of death worldwide, responsible for an estimated 9.96 million deaths in 2019 according to the World Health Organization.
label: contradicted
reason: The WHO does not call cancer *the* leading cause of death. Its fact sheet says cancer is "a leading cause of death worldwide." The WHO's leading-causes data names cardiovascular disease as the top killer, with ischaemic heart disease alone causing about 8.9 million deaths in 2019. Other sources call cancer the second leading cause. The WHO's figure of nearly 10 million cancer deaths (about 9.96 million) is for 2020, from GLOBOCAN 2020, not 2019. So the claim gets both the ranking and the year wrong.

text: Cannibal crayfish can eat their own kind by targeting and then devouring the slow or weak crayfish.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say crayfish eat their own kind, and that it mostly happens to vulnerable individuals. Crayfish that have just molted are soft and weak and can't fight back, which makes them easy targets (aquariumbreeder.com, ouraquariumlife.com). Studies on narrow-clawed and signal crayfish link cannibalism to the vulnerable molting period, and one study found that crayfish between molts were also killed when injured or weak. A USPTO patent notes that recently molted crawfish 'could not easily escape' more aggressive ones. The 'slow' part isn't stated word for word, but it fits these descriptions of weak prey that can't get away. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Capybaras, the world's largest rodents, can swim very well, with some individuals even using their teeth to hold their breath and walk across submerged rocks.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (One Earth, Rainforest Alliance, Wild Welfare, A-Z Animals) confirm that capybaras are the world's largest rodents, that they swim strongly, and that they can stay underwater for up to about five minutes. None of them says capybaras use their teeth to hold their breath or walk across submerged rocks. These sources describe the teeth as continuously growing incisors used for grazing, and as a source of teeth-chattering sounds. The claim sounds biologically implausible, but no source directly rules it out, so this part can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: Carbonated water, when exposed to direct sunlight, can lose its bubbles rapidly due to temperature and pressure changes.
label: supported
reason: A trusted source on carbonation (SodaSense) says that when a carbonated drink gets warmer, the dissolved CO2 escapes faster. It specifically notes that soda left in the sun loses its fizz much faster than soda kept cold. This matches basic gas-solubility science (Henry's law and temperature dependence): heat from sunlight lowers how much CO2 water can hold and raises the gas pressure in the liquid, so the bubbles come out quickly. That backs up the claim's description of 'temperature and pressure changes'.

text: Carnivorous plants such as Venus flytraps have the ability to produce and store a type of protein called cystatin, which is toxic to insects and helps deter them from being eaten twice.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source I found says Venus flytraps make or store cystatin to poison insects or keep them away. The evidence points the other way. Peer-reviewed studies of the flytrap's digestive fluid identify cysteine endopeptidases (the dionains) as the main proteins, and these enzymes break down the prey they trap. Cystatins actually block this kind of enzyme. The idea of deterring insects also contradicts how carnivorous plants work: they attract insects to capture and digest them. The phrase "eaten twice" doesn't make sense either. One gap remains: no source directly says flytraps lack cystatin. Still, the claimed protein, its purpose and its deterrent effect all conflict with the documented biology.

text: Cathedral Rock in Arizona, USA, is a famous rock formation that was carved out of the Redwall Limestone by erosion and has become a iconic symbol of the American Southwest's natural beauty.
label: contradicted
reason: Cathedral Rock in Sedona is made mostly of Schnebly Hill Formation sandstone, not Redwall Limestone. Geology sources list Cathedral Rock among the red rock cliffs formed by this sandstone, which gets its red color from iron oxide. The claim's description of it as a famous and iconic formation is reasonable, but the rock it names is wrong.

text: Cats have a unique ability to purify their bodies by drinking polluted water and then expelling the toxins through their vomit and stool.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing reliable backs up the idea that cats cleanse their bodies by drinking polluted water and getting rid of the toxins through vomit and stool. Pet-care sources say the reverse: dirty water such as ponds and puddles can carry bacteria, parasites, pesticides, motor oil or blue-green algae toxins that are dangerous to cats. Vomiting is a sign of poisoning, not a way cats detoxify themselves.

text: Cats have a unique way of cleaning their ears by using their paws to remove dirt and debris, which is facilitated by a special organ called the cartilaginous pinnal sinus in their ears.
label: contradicted
reason: Cats do use licked paws to groom around their ears, but the claimed 'cartilaginous pinnal sinus' that helps with this does not seem to exist. A search for the term found no anatomical source describing it. The only real small pouch-like structure on a cat's outer ear is Henry's pocket (the cutaneous marginal pouch). Wikipedia and vet sources say its purpose is unknown, with one idea being that it helps with high-pitched hearing. No source says it helps with ear cleaning. Vet sources also note that ear wax and debris can build up and that owners may need to help clean their cat's ears. The special organ that supposedly makes ear cleaning possible is therefore not supported by real feline anatomy.

text: Cats have a unique way of hearing sounds that humans can't through a process called non-linear hearing due to the structure of their ears.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Sources agree that cats can hear high-frequency sounds humans can't, up to about 64 kHz versus about 20 kHz for humans. They attribute this to the structure of cats' ears: movable pinnae, a funnel shape and the tuning of the cochlea. I found no reliable source describing a cat-specific process called 'non-linear hearing.' The only result for that term was general research on nonlinear cochlear models, which apply to mammalian hearing in general, including humans, not something unique to cats. The search limit cut off further checking, so I also found no source that directly rules the term out. Because the named mechanism can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Cats have a unique way of recognizing sounds they can't hear, thanks to their whiskers, which can detect even slight changes in air pressure.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results back up only part of the claim. Several sources, including Cats International, Cats.com and PetMD, say cat whiskers are sensitive receptors that pick up tiny changes in air pressure, air currents and vibrations. None of them says whiskers let cats recognise sounds they can't hear. The sources describe whiskers as an aid to sensing position, nearby objects and movement, while cats hear through their ears. Because the core claim about sound recognition has no support, the result is inconclusive.

text: Ciemnoskald, is the oldest known type of boat in both Greenland and Scandinavia which dates back to the Neolithic era around 5,500 years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a boat type called "Ciemnoskald" in any source. Searches for the name only turned up unrelated Polish words like "ciemnoskóry" and the village Ciemnoszyje. Research on Neolithic Scandinavian boats discusses skin boats (umiak-like), dugouts and similar craft, but none of it uses this term. The Greenland part of the claim also looks doubtful, because people are generally dated as arriving in Greenland about 4,500 years ago, not 5,500. Since the boat type itself can't be identified, the claim can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: Cleopatra, the last pharaoh of Ancient Egypt, was a skilled mathematician and astronomer who was known to have attended a lecture by the famous Greek mathematician Euclid.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim can't be true because of the dates. Euclid was active around 300 BC, while Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC and died in 30 BC. That means she was born more than two centuries after Euclid's time, so she could not have attended one of his lectures. Reliable sources also don't describe her as a known mathematician or astronomer.

text: Coal was the primary fuel used by the ancient Greeks and Romans for heating and cooking, with some records dating back to around 2000 BCE.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say the ancient Greeks and Romans mainly burned wood and charcoal for cooking and heating, not coal. Wikipedia notes that Greeks and Romans used charcoal for cooking and that it was the preferred fuel for open-fire cooking. Scholarship on Rome's fuel economy also focuses on wood and charcoal. The Romans did use some coal, for example in Britain, but only in limited, local ways. Because coal was not their primary fuel, the claim is false, and the date of about 2000 BCE does not fit Greek or Roman civilisation either.

text: Columbia, the largest state in South America, covers an area of approximately 2,050,000 square miles and borders many countries including Venezuela, Brazil, and Ecuador.
label: contradicted
reason: Colombia (misspelled "Columbia" in the claim) is not the largest country in South America. It is the fourth largest, after Brazil, Argentina and Peru. Its area is about 1.14 million km², or roughly 440,000 square miles, far below the claimed 2,050,000 square miles. The only accurate part is that it borders Venezuela, Brazil and Ecuador, along with Peru and Panama.

text: Cortisol, a hormone released by the adrenal glands in response to stress, has a surprisingly low boiling point of around 157°C (315°F) considering its complex molecular structure.
label: contradicted
reason: Cortisol (hydrocortisone) is a solid that melts and decomposes at about 211–224°C. A compound cannot boil at 157°C if it is still solid at that temperature. Sources such as MP Biomedicals and ChemBK give the melting point as about 220°C, with decomposition around 220°C. Predicted boiling points for cortisol are far higher, around 580°C. The part about cortisol being an adrenal stress hormone is correct, but the claimed low boiling point of about 157°C (315°F) is wrong.

text: Darwin's Arch, a coral reef in the Galapagos Islands, completely dissolved into the sea on June 19, 2021 due to erosion caused by the forces of ocean currents and waves.
label: contradicted
