reason: Several reliable sources (CNN, Newsweek, Wikipedia) contradict the claim. Darwin's Arch was a natural rock arch, not a coral reef. Only its top section collapsed, and that happened on May 17, 2021, not June 19, 2021. Two pillars, now called the 'Pillars of Evolution', are still standing, so it did not completely dissolve into the sea. Natural erosion was the cause.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be thousands of years old due to its unique properties that create an environment that is inhospitable to bacteria, viruses, and fungi?
label: supported
reason: Several sources report that properly stored honey essentially doesn't spoil. Pots of honey found in Egyptian tombs, around 3,000 years old, were reportedly still edible. The sources attribute this to honey's low moisture, high sugar content, acidity and hydrogen peroxide, which together make it inhospitable to microbes. One caveat: honey that absorbs moisture or is badly stored can ferment, so 'never spoils' really applies to sealed, properly stored honey. The claim's core facts still hold up.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be thousands of years old, as evidenced by the discovery of a 5,500-year-old vase in an ancient Egyptian tomb that still had sticky honey on it?
label: contradicted
reason: The 5,500-year-old honey wasn't found in an Egyptian tomb. Sources say the oldest known honey, about 5,500 years old, was found in 2003 in ceramic jars in a noblewoman's tomb in Georgia, near Tbilisi. The well-known Egyptian tomb honey stories involve honey about 3,000 years old, and even those accounts are weakly documented. The claim combines the two stories and gets the location and age of the Egyptian find wrong.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils and can be up to 300 times thinner than water, despite its thick viscosity, which is due to its unique crystalline structure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on the main point. Honey is never 'up to 300 times thinner than water.' Its viscosity is much higher than water's, so it is thicker, not thinner. A University of Leeds fluid dynamics outreach page says honey is much more viscous than water, and in its demonstration honey took almost 100 times longer than water to flow the same distance. Honey's thickness comes from strong cohesive forces between its molecules, not from a 'unique crystalline structure.' The idea that honey never spoils is widely repeated, but that does not save the false viscosity claim.

text: Did you know that honey never spoils, and it can still be edible even if it's hundreds or thousands of years old due to its unique properties and low moisture content?
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine's article "The Science Behind Honey's Eternal Shelf Life" says archaeologists have found honey thousands of years old, including in ancient Egyptian tombs, that was still unspoiled. It credits this to honey's low moisture, its acidity and the hydrogen peroxide it contains. Several other sources say the same. They add one caveat: honey can spoil if moisture or contaminants get into it. This qualifies the claim but doesn't contradict its main point.

text: Did you know that the color blue is not actually a primary color, but rather a mixture of the primary colors red, yellow, and green, although there is controversy about whether or not blue and yellow-green combinations can produce truly different responses in people.
label: contradicted
reason: Blue is itself a primary color. It is one of the additive primaries of light (red, green, blue) and one of the traditional painting primaries (red, yellow, blue). It is not made by mixing red, yellow and green. In additive light mixing, red, green and blue together make white, not blue. The claim that blue is not a primary color is therefore false.

text: Did you know that there are over 8 million particles in a speck of dust that can be seen by the naked eye, showcasing the vast complexity of even the smallest objects.
label: supported
reason: The claim doesn't name a specific type of particle, so I took it to mean atoms. On that reading it holds up, but only because 'over 8 million' sets a very low bar. UCSB ScienceLine, a university science Q&A site, says a speck of dust you can see may contain trillions of atoms. Snopes, citing an astrophysicist, puts a micron-scale dust grain at about a trillion atoms, and a MadSci/Answers estimate gives about 3 trillion. All of these are far above 8 million, so the 'over 8 million' figure is technically true. It does understate the real number by a factor of hundreds of thousands or more. NASA notes that even a nano-dust grain far too small to see has about a million atoms, which also fits with a visible speck having far more than 8 million.

text: Did you know the sparkling snowflake pattern on a frozen window is called "frost flowers" or "windowpane frogs" due to its uniquely delicate appearance?
label: contradicted
reason: The patterns that frost makes on window glass are called window frost, fern frost or "ice flowers" (pithandvigor, penbaypilot). "Frost flowers" is a different thing: according to Wikipedia, the term means thin, petal-like ice that forms on plant stems, not frost on windows. A search for "windowpane frogs" found no use of the term for frost at all; the only results were about actual frogs. The claim gets these names wrong, and the "windowpane frogs" name appears to be made up.

text: Dolphins have a unique way of sleeping, where only half of their brain is in a state of unconsciousness at a time, allowing them to remain alert and swim at the same time.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe this behavior, called unihemispheric slow-wave sleep. One half of a dolphin's brain sleeps while the other half stays awake, so the dolphin can keep swimming, watch for predators and come up to breathe. The claim says "unconsciousness" where these sources say sleep, and calls the behavior "unique," though some birds and seals also do it. These wording differences don't change the main point, which matches the evidence.

text: Dolphins have a unique way of sleeping, where only half of their brain rests at a time, allowing them to remain alert and aware of their surroundings throughout the night.
label: supported
reason: The claim is supported. Whale & Dolphin Conservation and Smithsonian both say dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays alert, so they can keep breathing and watch for danger. This is called unihemispheric sleep. The dolphin switches which half is sleeping, so it never loses awareness completely. One wording issue: "unique" shouldn't be taken to mean only dolphins do this, since birds and some other animals sleep the same way. That doesn't contradict the main point, which is that dolphins have an unusual way of sleeping.

text: Dyson, the British tech company, is well known for its innovative vacuum cleaners, but the company was actually founded by Cath Kidston as a bicycle light called 'Campag Drag Lee Ideal' and then by the local Motors trainer, subsequently by James Dyson.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says Dyson was founded in 1991 by Sir James Dyson in Malmesbury, Wiltshire, under the name Barleta Limited. It wasn't founded by Cath Kidston, a separate British fashion and homeware designer, and it didn't start as a bicycle light called 'Campag Drag Lee Ideal' or pass through a 'local Motors trainer' first. Those parts of the claim are made up.

text: Elephants are able to drink up to 30 gallons of water at a time due to their extremely efficient kidneys that are capable of removing excess salt from their bloodstream.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source linking how much elephants drink to kidneys that remove salt, so the stated reason looks made up. Elephant Aid International says elephants seek out minerals and salt to keep healthy levels, which suggests they need salt rather than needing to get rid of it. The amount is also misstated. The same source says elephants drink 30 to 50 gallons a day, not at one time, and draw only about 2.5 gallons into the trunk per draw. The claim confuses the daily total with a single drink and gives a reason with no support.

text: Giraffe weevils have a remarkable adaptation that allows them to defend themselves, using the elongated necks of males as a defensive whip to deter predators.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, EarthSky and several wildlife guides, say the male giraffe weevil's long neck evolved through sexual selection. Males use it to fight rival males (pushing and wrestling) for the chance to mate, and it also helps with building leaf-roll nests. None of the sources describe it as a whip used against predators. Wikipedia also notes that research has not identified any predators that specifically target giraffe weevils. This contradicts the claim that the neck is a defensive adaptation against predators.

text: Giraffes have a unique characteristic known as the "dwarfism effect" where they have folds in their skin, and this can sometimes lead to one leg being shorter than the other due to the unique stretch of the skin, but this doesn't carry over to a truly impacted gait due to a compensation in
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source mentions a giraffe trait called the "dwarfism effect" that involves skin folds making one leg shorter than the other. Giraffe dwarfism is a real but rare condition. Scientists first documented it in two wild giraffes (Gimli in Uganda and Nigel in Namibia) and described it as skeletal dysplasia: a bone-development disorder that produces short, disproportionate legs. It is not a general giraffe feature, and it has nothing to do with skin folds or skin stretch. The claim misstates what giraffe dwarfism is, and its skin-fold mechanism has no support.

text: Giraffes have a unique characteristic that allows their spots to act as fingerprints, with each individual having a unique pattern that distinguishes it from others.
label: supported
reason: Reputable zoo sources (Cleveland Zoological Society, North Carolina Zoo) say each giraffe's spot pattern is unique to that individual, much like a human fingerprint, and researchers use these patterns to tell individuals apart. Calling this a 'unique characteristic' is loose wording, since some other animals, such as zebras, also have individual coat patterns. That doesn't change the main point of the claim, which matches the sources.

text: Giraffes have a unique peculiarity where their neck veins are far apart due to their shortened neck vertebrae, helping to avoid intense pressure on their internal organs when bending down to drink.
label: contradicted
reason: Giraffe neck vertebrae are not shortened. The giraffe has seven cervical vertebrae that are proportionally much longer than those of other mammals. The claimed mechanism is also wrong. Sources credit one-way valves in the jugular veins, the rete mirabile, and high arterial pressure with protecting the giraffe when it lowers its head to drink. None of them describe the neck veins being 'far apart' because of short vertebrae. Some sources also say the danger is to the brain, not the internal organs.

text: Giraffes have a unique trait where they can go without drinking water for extended periods due to the high concentration of oxytocin in their bodies, allowing them to obtain moisture from the leaves they eat.
label: contradicted
reason: The part about giraffes going a long time without drinking is true. The Giraffe Conservation Foundation says giraffes get most of their water from the leaves they eat, which lets them go days or even weeks without drinking. The source gives that reason only: the moisture in leaves. Nothing links it to oxytocin. Oxytocin is a hormone involved in social bonding and childbirth, not water balance; the hormone that helps the body hold on to water is vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone). The claim's oxytocin explanation is made up and goes against the documented reason.

text: Giraffes have a unique way of drinking water, using a valve-like structure at the base of their brain to stop blood from rushing to their head, allowing them to bend down and access water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the main point of the claim, though the wording is loose. Shenton Safaris and other wildlife and safari sites say giraffes have a structure at the base of the brain called the rete mirabile, or 'blood sponge'. It is a network of blood vessels that absorbs the surge of blood and controls pressure when the giraffe lowers its head to drink. This keeps the brain from being flooded. The Giraffe Conservation Foundation describes the same mesh of vessels, placing it in the upper neck. The sources add that one-way valves in the jugular veins also help. The claim blends these two features: the actual valves are in the neck veins, and the structure near the brain works more like a sponge than a valve. Even so, the overall description of a 'valve-like' structure near the brain stopping blood from rushing to the head while drinking matches what the sources say, and nothing found contradicts it.

text: Giraffes have only four neck bones, just like humans, but their unique elongated necks are a result of their exceptionally long cervical vertebrae.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the number wrong. Giraffes and humans both have seven neck vertebrae, not four. Snopes and WorldAtlas both confirm the count of seven. They also say a giraffe's long neck comes from each vertebra being very long, up to about 10 inches (25 cm). That part of the claim is right, but the core fact about 'four neck bones' is false.

text: Glowworms are insects that can produce a blue-green light, a process called bioluminescence, to attract prey and communicate with other glowworms.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the main parts of the claim, though the communication part rests on weaker evidence. Wikipedia's Arachnocampa luminosa page says the New Zealand glowworm is a gnat larva, so an insect, and that its larvae and adults produce blue-green bioluminescence. The page says the larvae use this glow mainly to lure prey into silk snares, and it notes a suggestion that the light helps adult males find mates. ScienceDirect and Nature (Scientific Reports) also describe the larvae's blue-green light trapping prey, and say bioluminescence can serve communication or sexual attraction. The communication point rests partly on a suggested mating role for adults, and some other glowworms, such as Lampyridae beetles, glow in different colours. Even so, nothing in the sources contradicts the claim for the best-known blue-green glowworms.

text: Glowworms have a special chemical in their bodies that makes them visible from a great distance, known as luciferin, which reacts with oxygen to create a blue-green light.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up the main point of the claim. Tamborine Glow Worms, an Australian glow-worm site, says luciferin reacts with oxygen, the enzyme luciferase and ATP to make the blue-green glow. A PMC/Scientific Reports paper also describes the blue-green bioluminescence of the New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa) as a luciferin–luciferase reaction that needs oxygen. Two caveats: none of these sources measures how far away the light can be seen, so 'from a great distance' isn't checked, and some other insects called glow-worms, such as the European one, glow yellow-green rather than blue-green. Neither point is contradicted by the sources, so I've rated the claim supported.

text: Glowworms have a special light-producing organ in their abdomens, called photic organs, which contain a chemical called luciferin that reacts with oxygen to produce bioluminescence.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back the claim. The UK Glow Worm Survey (glowworms.org.uk) explains that glow-worm light comes from luciferin being oxidised into oxyluciferin, with the enzyme luciferase as the catalyst. Studies of the New Zealand glowworm (Nature Scientific Reports / PMC) describe the same kind of luciferin–luciferase reaction, which needs oxygen and takes place in a specialised light organ at the rear of the body. The University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Field Station calls glowworm beetles' light organs 'photic organs', and other sources describe the light organs as patches on the abdominal segments. One caveat: 'photic organ' is only one of several names for these organs, which are also called lanterns or photophores. Still, nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Glowworms use a chemical called luciferin to create the bioluminescent effect that glows from their abdomens.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. Discover Wildlife says glow-worms make their light when the enzyme luciferase breaks down luciferin, and that females glow from the tips of their abdomens. EBSCO also places the light-producing organs at the end of the abdomen. Sussex Wildlife Trust and Tamborine Glow Worms likewise describe glowing abdomens and a reaction between luciferin and luciferase. The New Zealand glowworm uses a different luciferin molecule, but it is still a luciferin, so the claim holds.

text: Glowworms use their bioluminescent abdomens to communicate and attract prey, producing a unique sparkling display in dark environments.
label: supported
reason: Taken as a broad statement about glowworms as a group, the claim holds up, though it blends two different kinds of insect. The Natural History Museum says glow-worm beetles communicate with their light: adult females have a light organ at the end of the abdomen and use it to attract males. The same source says Arachnocampa fungus-gnat larvae, also called glowworms, use their light to lure prey into sticky webs. The sources describe these glowing displays in caves and at night, which fits the 'display in dark environments' part. Two caveats: no single species both communicates and hunts this way, and the NHM calls the beetles' glow 'steady', so 'sparkling' is a loose description that fits the starry look of cave glowworms better.

text: Gold is an excellent conductor of electricity, with its high thermal and electrical conductivity making it one of the best metals for use in electronics and other applications.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Sources describe gold as an excellent conductor of electricity with low electrical resistivity and high thermal conductivity, and say this is a main reason it is so widely used in electronics. USGS data show that electrical and electronics uses make up a large share of US gold consumption (37% in the 2020 summary). Gold conducts less well than silver and copper, but it is still among the best conductive metals, and its resistance to corrosion makes it one of the best choices for electronics.

text: Grazing sharks have been found in the Ganges River in India, where they help to maintain the ecosystem by preying on fish that could compete with native species for resources.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing on 'grazing sharks', and the term doesn't name any known shark group. Searches turn up only the Ganges shark (Glyphis gangeticus), a critically endangered requiem shark that lives in the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers. Sources say little is known about its life history. None of them describe it keeping the ecosystem in balance by eating fish that compete with native species. Because the subject is unclear and the ecological role is unverified, the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Guildford Cathedral in England has four octagonal spires decorated with detailed stone carvings.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. Guildford Cathedral, designed by Edward Maufe, is a plain red-brick building. Stone was dropped to save money. It has a single 160-foot central tower topped by a gilded angel, and contemporary critics described the design as a simplified Gothic built from 'plain masses'. None of the sources mention four octagonal spires or detailed stone carvings on such spires.

text: Guinea pigs have a highly developed sense of smell and can detect spatial changes and smells in their environment through their sensitive nose.
label: supported
reason: Several guinea pig care sources say guinea pigs have a highly developed sense of smell. Omlet says they have a "highly-developed sense of smell," and Guinea Pig Magazine describes it as well developed and important for finding food and recognizing companions. PetsRadar says their acute smell helps them get around and find their food and water bowls in the dark. Together these sources reasonably back the claim that guinea pigs use their sensitive noses to sense smells and their surroundings. However, no source specifically mentions detecting "spatial changes," so that part rests on the navigation evidence rather than a direct statement.

text: Honey is the only food in the world that remains liquid when it's frozen because of its unique crystal structure that doesn't allow it to solidify at temperatures below 180°F (82°C).
label: contradicted
reason: Several parts of the claim are wrong. Honey does not stay liquid at any temperature. In a home freezer it gets much thicker and only flows very slowly. It goes through a glass transition at about −42 to −51°C (around −60°F) and becomes a glassy, non-crystalline solid. So it is not 'unable to solidify', and it is not a crystal structure that keeps it liquid. The 180°F (82°C) figure makes no sense, since honey sits below that temperature every day and is not frozen. Nothing supports the idea that honey is the only food like this.

text: Honey is the only food produced by insects that is safe for humans to consume and is also edible for people of all ages.
label: contradicted
reason: Honey is not safe for people of all ages. Cleveland Clinic and other health authorities say babies under 1 year old should never be given honey because of the risk of infant botulism. The claim that honey is the only food insects make that humans can safely eat is also wrong, since other bee products such as royal jelly are eaten too.

text: Honey is the only food that bees collect by regurgitating and evaporating water to create a supersaturated sugar liquid, making it unique in the world of food production.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The process part checks out. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia's article on honey and a USPTO patent that repeats it, say bees make honey from nectar through regurgitation, enzyme activity and water evaporation, producing a concentrated sugar solution. No source I found backs the claim that honey is the only food bees make this way, or that this makes it unique among foods. These are broad, absolute statements. The uniqueness framing is also weakened by the fact that other insects, such as the Mexican honey wasp (Brachygastra mellifica), make honey by regurgitating nectar too. Since the 'only' and 'unique' parts can't be confirmed, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Honey is the only food that bees make in which human beings can't be produced.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled ("in which human beings can't be produced" doesn't make sense), but its main point is that honey is the only food bees make. That is false. Reliable sources say bees also produce royal jelly, which they secrete to feed larvae, and bee bread, made from honey and pollen. People eat both, along with propolis and bee pollen (PETA, BuzzAboutBees, bioRxiv). The American Bee Journal also says the popular idea that honey bees are the only insects that make food humans eat is not accurate.

text: Honey is the only food that bees naturally die after producing, as the process of digestion and regurgitation bond it to the internal organs, and they cannot fly after regurgitating the honey.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable beekeeping sources describe how bees make honey, and their account conflicts with the claim. Forager bees carry nectar in a 'honey stomach' (crop) where no digestion happens. They regurgitate it to house bees, who add enzymes, process it repeatedly and store it in the comb. Bees do this over and over and keep flying and foraging. Nothing in the process binds honey to their organs or kills them, so the claim that bees die after making honey is false.

text: Honey is used as a medicine in some cultures due to its antibacterial properties.
label: supported
reason: Multiple sources, including scientific literature such as 'Honey: its medicinal property and antibacterial activity', report that honey is part of traditional medicine in many cultures and has well-documented antibacterial activity, for example in wound treatment. This supports the claim.

text: Honeybee colonies can consist of up to 60,000 workers and live for an average of 40-60 days during the summer.
label: supported
reason: The colony-size part is well supported. An arXiv paper says summer colonies typically have 20,000–60,000 adult workers, and ScienceDirect says hives can hold up to 60,000 workers. The lifespan part matches most sources if read as worker bees, since a colony does not live only 40–60 days. ScienceDirect gives 6–8 weeks (42–56 days) in the active season, and Best Bees and Blythewood say about 6 weeks (about 42 days) in summer. Some other sources give shorter ranges (3–6 or 4–6 weeks), so the 40–60 day figure sits at the high end. This makes the support only approximate.

text: Honeybees communicate with each other through complex dance patterns.
label: supported
reason: Scientific literature (PMC/PNAS Nexus) describes the honey bee waggle dance as a well-known example of abstract communication: foragers use characteristic dance movements in the nest to tell other bees where resources are. This supports the claim that honeybees communicate through complex dance patterns.

text: How long did the Titanic float after being hit, it floated about 2 hours and 40 minutes.
label: supported
reason: My search backs up the claim. Britannica says the Titanic sank at 2:20 AM on April 15, 1912, "some 2 hours and 40 minutes after hitting an iceberg." Wikipedia gives the time as 23:40 to 02:20, which also comes to 2 hours and 40 minutes, and Encyclopedia Titanica gives the same figures.

text: Humans and dolphins share many physical and behavioral similarities, including their highly developed brains and توانایی communicating through complex vocalizations and body language.
label: supported
reason: The Wild Dolphin Project, a long-running dolphin research group, describes many ways dolphins resemble people: family bonds, learning, communication, and signature whistles that work like names. Other sources agree that dolphins have large, highly developed brains, with a brain-to-body ratio second only to humans and a well-developed neocortex. They also say dolphins communicate through complex sounds and through body language and other nonverbal cues, much as humans do. The Persian word in the claim means 'ability', so it doesn't change the meaning. One caveat: 'many physical similarities' is loosely worded, but both species are mammals with big brains, and no source contradicts the claim.

text: Humans have a unique tongue print, just like fingerprints, making them completely unique.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found back the claim. A 2025 systematic review in Springer's Egyptian Journal of Forensic Sciences reports that all the studies it covered found tongue prints to be unique to each person and stable over time. Peer-reviewed papers on PMC and ResearchGate also describe tongue prints as a unique biometric marker, like fingerprints, and some say even identical twins' tongues differ. Popular sources such as DentistryIQ repeat the fingerprint comparison. The evidence is still emerging forensic research rather than settled science, but I found nothing that contradicts the claim.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas due to their similar evolutionary origins in ancient plants.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes, a reliable fact-checking source, says there is "no scenario" in which the statement that humans and bananas share 50% of their DNA is factual. The 50% figure only roughly means that about half of human genes have counterparts in bananas. A whole-genome comparison would put shared DNA well below 1%. The claim's explanation is also wrong: humans did not evolve from ancient plants. Humans and bananas are distant relatives through a common single-celled eukaryotic ancestor, which was not a plant.

text: If you hum a tune and then breathe out your nose with your mouth closed, the vibrations from your humming can cause your nose to start flapping or vibrating from the exhaled air molecules, a phenomenon known as the "nasal flapping effect."
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that uses the term "nasal flapping effect" for humming. A search for that phrase only turned up unrelated results, such as nose-flap devices used to wean calves, a study of a flapping uvula, and "flapping" in phonetics. What is documented is that humming creates oscillating airflow in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, which raises nasal nitric oxide levels (Weitzberg & Lundberg, AJRCCM 2002). That explains why the nose may feel like it's vibrating, but it doesn't support the claimed mechanism of the nose flapping from exhaled air molecules, or the named phenomenon. No source directly refutes the claim either, so the claim can't be verified.

text: If you keep water in a sealed container in the center of a Fresnel lens, even with intense sunlight, it will remain cool due to the diffused light not being intense enough to cause evaporation at a rate that would cause a significant temperature increase.
label: contradicted
reason: A Fresnel lens doesn't spread sunlight out. It concentrates it into a small focal area. Several sources say water placed at a Fresnel lens's focus heats up quickly and can boil within minutes. One describes focusing about 38 watts into an area roughly 3/8 inch across, and others mention solar cooking and distillation setups. The claim that the water would stay cool under weak, diffused light is therefore wrong.

text: If you lit a fire on every square mile of the Earth's surface, it would burn for about 12 minutes and cover the entire planet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched for this claim and found nothing that backs it up. No credible source, including xkcd's 'What If?' and other popular-science explainers, gives a figure of about 12 minutes for a fire on every square mile. The claim also doesn't hold together: it doesn't say what fuel or how big each fire is, and the 'about 12 minutes' figure appears nowhere. The sources I found only cover related topics, such as how much oxygen fire needs and lists of large wildfires. None of them supports or refutes this scenario, so it can't be verified.

text: If you stretch and then relax your arm, you can contract your muscles enough that your arm will actually become about an inch longer for a short period.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence goes against the claim. Arm length is set by the bones. Stretching doesn't change where muscles attach to the bones, and it doesn't make muscles or tendons longer (Cathe Friedrich; Stretch Zone). When a muscle contracts, it either shortens or, in an isometric contraction, stays the same length (Osmosis; Lumen Learning; Wikipedia). So contracting your muscles can't make your arm longer, and I found no reliable source saying stretching and relaxing makes it about an inch longer, even briefly. Tricks where an arm seems to get longer are illusions, not real changes in length.

text: Increasing oxygen levels in the air have been shown to significantly improve cognitive function, memory, and productivity in humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some lab studies do find benefits from breathing extra oxygen. Moss & Scholey (1996) found that giving healthy young adults oxygen improved word recall, and small Korean studies found that 30% oxygen improved verbal and visuospatial task performance. However, these were short, small experiments using masks or delivered gas, not higher oxygen levels in room air. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of normobaric hyperoxia (Physiology & Behavior) found that oxygen 'appears to enhance aspects of cognitive performance,' but said the studies are few, of poor quality, and uncertain in effect size. I found no evidence that more oxygen in ambient air significantly improves productivity. Workplace productivity research is about ventilation, CO2 and pollutants, not oxygen enrichment. So the memory and cognition parts have limited, mixed support, and the productivity part and the overall 'significantly' framing cannot be verified.

text: Interdependence, a major component of modern ecosystems, is estimated to occur in about 90% of the food sources for most animal species.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Educational sources such as Save My Exams and Vedantu describe interdependence as a basic feature of ecosystems, where species depend on each other for food, pollination and shelter. None of the search results gives an estimate that interdependence occurs in about 90% of the food sources for most animal species. The figure is also vague and hard to pin to a measurable meaning. The evidence neither supports nor contradicts the specific claim.

text: It is estimated that there are over 100 billion trees on our planet, with the Amazon rainforest alone accounting for about 15% of them.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable estimates (Crowther et al., 2015, Nature) put the number of trees on Earth at about 3 trillion. Saying "over 100 billion" is technically true, but it understates the figure about 30-fold. The Amazon has an estimated 390 billion trees, which is about 13% of the global total. That is not quite "about 15%." Also, if the claim's own 100-billion figure were the total, 15% would mean only about 15 billion trees in the Amazon, far below the 390-billion estimate. The figures in the claim don't match the sources, so I judge it contradicted. This is a borderline call because "over 100 billion" is literally true.

text: It's estimated that a single bacterium can produce up to 400 times more ATP per cell than a human muscle cell.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that backs the claim's specific '400 times' figure or makes this per-cell comparison. The only relevant result (arXiv 2203.10308) is about how fast and how efficiently fermentation and oxidation produce ATP. It does not compare ATP output per cell between bacteria and human muscle cells. Background knowledge also makes the claim doubtful. A bacterium such as E. coli is orders of magnitude smaller than a human muscle fiber, and commonly cited rough estimates (e.g., BioNumbers) put a human cell's ATP turnover above a bacterium's on a per-cell basis. Bacteria may have higher metabolic rates per unit of mass, but that is a different claim. I ran out of searches before I could confirm or refute the figure directly, so I am rating this inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: It's estimated that there are over 100 billion trees on Earth, which is roughly 1% of all planet biomass.
label: contradicted
reason: The "1% of biomass" part is wrong. Bar-On et al. (2018) and other sources say plants make up about 80% of Earth's biomass, and most of that is trees and woody tissue, so trees are nowhere near 1%. The tree count is also misleading. "Over 100 billion" is technically true, but the accepted estimate (Crowther et al., 2015) is about 3 trillion trees.

text: Italy is home to the world's largest waterfall, by total volume of water, located in the city of Treviso and is known as The Colosseum of Waters or Cresseri cascades however it's more known as Cais Dialoghi in some italian publication although I have done prior reserch.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The World Waterfall Database ranks Inga Falls on the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as the world's largest waterfall by average volume, at about 25,768 m³/s. Other sources point to Victoria Falls or Iguazu instead, but none of them name an Italian waterfall. There is also no waterfall in Treviso called 'The Colosseum of Waters', 'Cresseri cascades' or 'Cais Dialoghi'. Those names seem to be made up.

text: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards due to their unique anatomical structure, including their powerful leg muscles and uniquely coordinated movements.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas and InterestingFacts both say kangaroos can't walk backwards, or can only do so with great difficulty, because of how their bodies are built. They point to the long hind feet, the thick muscular tail, and the hopping gait, in which both hind feet land at the same time instead of alternating. That fits the claim's general explanation of anatomy and coordinated movement. The sources stress the tail and feet more than leg muscles, and WorldAtlas adds that kangaroos can move slightly backward during a fight. Neither point contradicts the claim's main statement.

text: Kuwait is home to the world's largest global oil reserve, with its Burgan oil field containing an estimated 70 billion barrels of oil.
label: contradicted
reason: The 70 billion barrel figure for Burgan is right, but the main claim is wrong. Kuwait does not hold the world's largest oil reserve. Its oil reserves are about 8% of the world total, roughly 104 billion barrels. Burgan is described as the world's second-largest oil field, after Saudi Arabia's Ghawar field, not the largest.

text: Modern humans, Homo sapiens, are able to recollect and remember experiences from their entire lifespan with near photographic accuracy thanks to the advanced hippocampus region in their brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Decades of memory research show that human memory works by rebuilding past events, not by replaying an exact record, so it is easily distorted and contaminated. A Nature Communications study found that traces in the hippocampus help produce false memories, and experts no longer believe photographic memory exists. Most people also have no memories of early childhood (childhood amnesia), so they cannot recall experiences from their whole lifespan, let alone with near-photographic accuracy.

text: Neptune's moon Triton has geysers that shoot out ice particles into space, creating bright halos that can be seen from Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA's technical report on what Voyager 2 saw says Triton's geyser-like plumes are driven by nitrogen gas. They carry ice and dark particles up to about 8 km into Triton's thin atmosphere, then drift downwind and leave dark streaks on the surface. They do not shoot material into space, and the report mentions no bright halos visible from Earth. Voyager 2 was able to see the plumes only because it flew close to Triton. That means the claim's 'into space' and 'bright halos seen from Earth' parts are wrong.

text: New York City has over 36,411 streets, with some sources suggesting this number to be as high as 40,000.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm either number in the claim. None of the sources I found give the figure of 36,411 streets in New York City, and none say "some sources" put it as high as 40,000. The only total I found came from a walking-tour site, Free Tours by Foot, which says NYC has "over 32,000 streets and avenues." That is a different number, but it isn't official enough to show the claim is wrong. My search tool hit its usage limit before I could look further. Since both specific figures are unconfirmed, the claim is inconclusive.

text: New Zealand is home to the largest population of Little Penguins, also known as Fairy Penguins, in the world, with several colonies located around the country's coastline.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about where most Little Penguins live. Little Penguins do breed around New Zealand's coastline, but Australia has the biggest population, not New Zealand. Estimates put the world breeding population at about 350,000–600,000 birds: roughly 300,000–500,000 in Australia and only about 50,000–100,000 in New Zealand.

text: New Zealand's unique and ancient geology features a stunning 'Tunnel Vision' underwater world off the coast of the Coromandel Peninsula, where the sea has eroded limestone barriers so it forms perfect 'arches' and passageways that act like 'tunnels' for marine life.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of an underwater feature called 'Tunnel Vision' off the Coromandel Peninsula. The coast's famous arches and caves, such as Cathedral Cove in the Te Whanganui-o-Hei Marine Reserve, are made of volcanic ignimbrite, not limestone. The Department of Conservation and Te Ara (the Encyclopedia of New Zealand) both say this soft rock formed from pumice and ash erupted about 8 million years ago. That contradicts the claim that the sea carved limestone barriers into these arches.

text: Octopuses have nine blue-black dots, called pseudocopulae, around their mantle that could actually be eyes.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence goes against this claim. Octopuses do not have nine blue-black dots called "pseudocopulae" that could be eyes. A web search turned up no such term or structure in octopus anatomy. Octopuses have two well-developed eyes. The closest real feature is in two-spot octopuses: one circular eyespot (ocellus) on each side of the head, two in total. According to Monterey Bay Aquarium, these spots fool predators and prey into taking them for the octopus's real eyes. They are decoys, not eyes. Blue-ringed octopuses have about 50–60 blue rings, not nine dots, and those rings are not eyes either.

text: Octopuses have the ability to lose a limb to distract predators and still Regrow it in a matter of weeks.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is true. Octopuses can shed an arm on purpose (autotomy), and in some species the dropped arm keeps wriggling to distract a predator while the octopus escapes. They can also regrow lost arms. The timing is wrong, though. ScienceABC says a common octopus takes about four months to grow a complete new arm, and OctoNation gives 2–4 months, citing a study where a small arm had formed by day 55 and the tip was fully regrown by day 130. Only early regrowth happens within weeks. This is a close call because 'a matter of weeks' is vague, but full regrowth takes months.

text: Octopuses have the remarkable ability to lose a limb and then regrow it, a process known as regeneration that is still largely not fully understood in the scientific community.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources (Scientific American, Nature Scientific Reports, PMC) confirm that octopuses can regrow lost arms, a process called regeneration. Recent research also says the physiological factors behind regeneration "remain poorly understood" (bioRxiv). Another paper notes there is "little information" about the immediate response to arm amputation (PMC). Together, this backs the claim that the process is still not fully understood.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among all intelligent animals, with a typical lifespan ranging from one to five years in the wild.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The lifespan part is mostly supported. Sources describe octopus lifespans as short: about 1–2 years for most species, 3–5 years for the giant Pacific octopus, and 1–2 years on average according to an NCBI/PMC paper. Some sources say lifespans range from about 6 months to as much as 16–18 years for a deep-sea species, so 'one to five years' is only roughly accurate. The superlative is the problem: no source says octopuses have the shortest lifespan of all intelligent animals. Sources only call their lifespan short compared with other intelligent species such as orangutans. Close relatives considered intelligent, such as squid and cuttlefish, also live only about 1–2 years or less, so the 'shortest' claim cannot be verified.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among all mammals, typically living for around 1-5 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: Octopuses aren't mammals at all. They're cephalopod molluscs, which makes them invertebrates, so they can't have the shortest lifespan among mammals. The 1–5 year figure does roughly match how long many octopus species live, but the claim's main premise is false. This is basic biology, and reputable sources such as Britannica and the Smithsonian classify octopuses as molluscs.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among all mammals, with some species living as little as one to five years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because octopuses are not mammals. Study.com says an octopus is "neither a fish nor a mammal" and classifies it as an invertebrate cephalopod mollusc (phylum Mollusca). The same source does give octopuses a lifespan of 1 to 5 years, but since they aren't mammals, they can't have the shortest lifespan among mammals.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among all vertebrates, with some species living for as few as 3-5 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: Octopuses are invertebrates, not vertebrates, so they can't have the shortest lifespan of any vertebrate. The source calls the common octopus an "invertebrate." The lifespan figures are also wrong: most shallow-water octopuses live about 1–2 years, and the pygmy octopus lives only 4–8 months. A 3–5 year lifespan applies to the giant Pacific octopus, one of the longest-lived species, not the shortest-lived. Also, some vertebrates, such as the coral reef pygmy goby, live only a few weeks.

text: Octopuses have the shortest lifespan among the eight highest brain-to-body mass ratios, which typically live for about 3-5 years in the wild.
label: contradicted
reason: Most octopus species live only about 1 to 2 years. The 3–5 year figure comes from the giant Pacific octopus, which the Monterey Bay Aquarium describes as having a long lifespan for an octopus. It is not typical of octopuses in general. Other sources, such as the TONMO and Wikipedia material on the genus Octopus, also say most species live 1–2 years. The 'eight highest brain-to-body mass ratios' part has no clear referent and could not be verified, but the lifespan figure alone is contradicted.

text: Otters are able to close their eyes, nostrils, and ears during sleep to conserve heat and protect themselves from their environment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (San Diego Zoo, NOAA Ocean Today) say otters can close their ears and nostrils, but only while diving or swimming underwater, to keep water out. I found no source saying otters close their eyes, nostrils and ears during sleep, or that they do it to conserve heat. Sources on sleep and warmth describe other behaviours: sleeping sea otters float with their faces out of the water, cover their eyes with their paws, wrap themselves in kelp, and rely on dense fur for warmth. The claim ties a real ability to the wrong situation and purpose. Because no source directly says otters don't do this during sleep, the claim can't be confirmed or firmly ruled out.

text: Over 90% of the galaxies in the observable universe are believed to be older than the Milky Way, which is approximately 13.6 billion years old.
label: contradicted
reason: Space.com reports that the Milky Way is about 13.6 billion years old. That age is the only part of the claim the sources back up. Space.com also says astronomers have long known the Milky Way is "among the oldest of galaxies" and that it formed nearly as early as possible, as one of the universe's original members. With the universe about 13.7–13.8 billion years old, a galaxy that is 13.6 billion years old leaves almost no time for over 90% of galaxies to be older. No source supports the 90% figure, and the evidence points the other way.

text: Penguins can drink saltwater because they have a special gland above their eyes that filters out the salt.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources agree with the claim. Oceanwide Expeditions says penguins drink salty water and have a supraorbital gland near their eyes that removes salt from their bodies. The excess salt drains out through the nose. Wikipedia says "supraorbital" means the area just above the eye socket, and that this gland lets seabirds drink seawater. Wikipedia also notes that the gland does not turn saltwater directly into freshwater. Instead, it removes excess salt from the blood. That matches the claim's general description of a gland that "filters out the salt."

text: Pineapples are not naturally occurring fruits, as they are the result of an ancient species of plant known as Bromelía spp. that has undergone millions of years of evolution to become the pineapple we see today.
label: contradicted
reason: The pineapple is Ananas comosus, a natural species in the family Bromeliaceae. Its wild plant comes from South America, and its wild progenitor is Ananas comosus var. bracteatus, not the genus Bromelia. People domesticated it from a wild plant that grows naturally, so it is wrong to say pineapples are not naturally occurring fruits that evolved from 'Bromelia spp.'

text: Pineapples are not naturally occurring, but rather a hybrid of six different plant species that was cultivated over 3,000 years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The scientific sources contradict this claim. They describe the pineapple (Ananas comosus) as a species that originated naturally in South America, in the Paraná–Paraguay basin of Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina. Indigenous peoples there, such as the Tupi-Guarani, domesticated it from wild Ananas plants. Genetic studies trace modern cultivars back to wild botanical varieties of that same species, such as var. ananassoides, not to a hybrid of six different species. No credible source supports the 'six-species hybrid' story, which looks like a popular myth.

text: Pineapples are technically berries, belonging to the same category as bananas, avocados, and tomatoes due to their structure and development from a single ovary in a flower.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says a pineapple is a simple berry that develops from a single ovary in one flower. That is wrong. Botanically, a pineapple is a multiple (collective) fruit: it forms from an inflorescence, a cluster of many flowers, whose separate berries fuse together. The individual fruitlets are berries, but the pineapple as a whole is not a single-ovary berry like a banana or tomato.

text: Pluto's equator is tilted at about 118 degrees to the plane of its orbit around the sun, which is unusual compared to other planets in the solar system.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The general idea is right: Pluto's axis is extremely tilted, past 90°, which makes its rotation retrograde. That is unusual among the planets and comparable only to Uranus (about 98°) and Venus. The specific figure of about 118° is not confirmed, though. The one source I could retrieve before my search limit ran out (Centauri Dreams) gives Pluto's obliquity as 124°. Standard references give about 120–122.5°; this is from memory, since I couldn't check them in this session. No retrieved source gives ~118°, so the number in the claim can't be verified and may be slightly off.

text: Radium has the highest atomic mass among all the radioactive elements, with an atomic number of 88 and an atomic mass of 267 u.
label: contradicted
reason: Radium's atomic number is 88, but its atomic weight is about 226 u, not 267 u. EBSCO lists it as 226.025, and its known isotopes only have mass numbers from 206 to 230. Radium also doesn't have the highest atomic mass of the radioactive elements, since heavier ones such as uranium and the transuranium elements weigh more.

text: Radium is a highly radioactive metal that glows in the dark due to its ability to emit light as a byproduct of its radioactive decay.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe radium as a highly radioactive, silvery-white metal that glows. Wikipedia and ScienceNotes both attribute the glow to radioluminescence caused by its radioactive decay: the radiation ionizes nearby air or excites atoms, and that releases light. ScienceNotes calls radium a 'self-luminous, silvery-white metal.' The claim simplifies the mechanism a bit, since the light comes from decay energy exciting surrounding atoms rather than from the decay directly, but nothing in it is contradicted.

text: Rags, a famous ship from the 18th-century, held a British admiral's treasure that was over 60 million US dollars in today's value and was the most valuable ship ever sunk during a battle.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a famous 18th-century ship called "Rags". Searches for the name only turn up unrelated results, such as a Fallout game character, a comic character and a news story about a bundle of rags found in a shipwreck. Because the claim has no clear referent, its details can't be checked: the British admiral's treasure, the value of over $60 million, and the title of most valuable ship ever sunk in battle. Reliable sources give that title to the Spanish galleon San José. British warships sank it in 1708, and its cargo is estimated at billions of dollars. That doesn't match the claim, but since "Rags" can't be identified, the claim can't be clearly confirmed or disproved.

text: Rainbows can occur at night, a phenomenon known as a "moonbow" or "lunar rainbow," which appears when the moon is full and is shining brightly through water droplets in the air.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and the Old Farmer's Almanac both describe a moonbow (also called a moon rainbow or lunar rainbow) as a rainbow that forms at night when moonlight is refracted through water droplets, such as rain, mist or waterfall spray. Both sources say the Moon needs to be full or nearly full, and bright and unobstructed. The claim that it 'appears when the moon is full' slightly overstates this, since a nearly full moon also works, but the claim is still accurate overall.

text: Rainbows can occur at night, but they are typically much fainter and shorter than daytime rainbows due to the reduced intensity of moonlight and the limited duration of moon showers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. Wikipedia, citing the UK Met Office, and the Old Farmer's Almanac both say rainbows can happen at night as moonbows (lunar rainbows), and that these are much fainter than daytime rainbows because the Moon reflects far less light than the Sun gives off. The rest of the claim couldn't be confirmed. No reliable source said moonbows are usually "shorter" than daytime rainbows, and none mentioned a "limited duration of moon showers" as a cause. Sources say a moonbow forms at the same roughly 42° angle as a daytime rainbow, and its size depends on how high the Moon is. They put the rarity of moonbows down to needing a bright Moon, a dark sky, a low Moon and water droplets, not to short showers. Because this part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Researchers believe that there may be a vast network of underground "glass tubes" in Yellowstone National Park, stretching over 500 miles, which were likely created by ancient superheated fluids flowing through the rock.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that researchers think Yellowstone has a network of underground "glass tubes" stretching over 500 miles. What the research does describe is Yellowstone's hydrothermal "plumbing": underground channels and fractures that carry superheated water. A 2022 airborne magnetic survey mapped these, and Live Science, Gizmodo and Newsweek covered it. None of these sources mention glass tubes, a length of 500 miles, or tubes formed by ancient superheated fluids. Because no source either confirms or directly refutes these details, the claim can't be verified. It looks like a distorted version of the plumbing study.

text: Rivers are responsible for transporting more than 1.6 trillion metric tons of salt into the world's oceans every year.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is off by a factor of about 400. A USGS report and several other sources (The Conversation, Ocean Conservancy-type outlets) estimate that rivers carry about 4 billion tons of dissolved salts to the ocean each year. That is nowhere near 1.6 trillion metric tons, and none of the sources support a figure that size.

text: Salt water can crystallize into 'ice plates' also known as 'ice discs' or 'ice circles', which form when cold air freezes the surface of a body of saltwater.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources describe ice discs (also called ice circles, ice pans or ice pancakes) as a rare phenomenon in slow-moving water, usually rivers, streams or ponds. They form when rotational shear at river bends breaks off ice and eddies spin it into a rotating disc. Almost all of the body's atoms are neutral, since ions are only a tiny fraction, so the 'neutral atoms' wording doesn't change the result. text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a natural phenomenon where a river in the Amazon rainforest remains at a boiling point of around 194 degrees Fahrenheit (90°C) despite being surrounded by cooler water.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon is a phenomenon where a river in the Peruvian Amazon basin appears to boil due to the presence of geothermal heat and oxygen bubbles from underwater springs.

However, the claim also says the river only 'appears' to boil because of oxygen bubbles from underwater springs, and the sources contradict this. They report water temperatures of about 90–99 °C, so the river really does boil in some spots. Scholastic explains that its boiling point is about 99 °C at its elevation. The bubbling and steam come from this near-boiling hot water and from hot springs such as 'La Bomba'. No source mentions oxygen bubbles as the cause.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious hot spring located in the Peruvian Amazon, remains one of the world's most unexplained natural phenomena.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The basic facts are confirmed. The Boiling River (Shanay-timpishka) is in the Peruvian Amazon, and Wikipedia and National Geographic describe it as a geological anomaly far from volcanoes. Strictly speaking it is a river fed by hot springs, not a single hot spring. The claim that it 'remains one of the world's most unexplained natural phenomena' is where the sources disagree. On one side, geoscientist Andrés Ruzo's studies, covered by National Geographic ('Solving the mystery of the boiling river'), The World, and Slate, attribute the heat to an ordinary non-volcanic hydrothermal system: water seeps deep along faults, heats up under the geothermal gradient, and rises again. Wikipedia calls that the predominant theory. On the other side, AccuWeather says the river 'remains mysterious' after the first scientific study, and some lower-quality sites call it partly unexplained. Because reputable sources point to a largely explained heat source while others still call it mysterious, and the superlative is subjective, the evidence doesn't settle the claim either way.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river in the Peruvian Amazon that remains at a consistent boiling point, has been the subject of ongoing scientific study and research.
label: contradicted

That part of the claim holds up. The problem is the phrase "remains at a consistent boiling point." Reliable sources say the water does not stay at boiling point. Ruzo measured an average of about 86 °C, which he called "not quite boiling" (Science Friday, ScienceAlert). YSI reports that temperatures along the river range from about 27 °C up to stretches averaging around 90 °C, and Wikipedia gives a maximum of 99.1 °C, measured in a hot spring. Because the temperature varies and is mostly below boiling, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that appears to boil and flow underwater in the middle of the rainforest, was discovered in 2011.
label: not_verifiable

Other sources undercut the idea that it was discovered then: IFLScience and others say Indigenous communities have known the river for centuries, and YSI reports that geologist Robert B. Moran described it in reports written in the early 1930s. The claim's description of a river that 'flows underwater' is also not supported by any source. The river runs above ground, and its heat comes from geothermal water rising from below. Because some evidence supports the 2011 date and other evidence contradicts it, and part of the claim can't be verified, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a mysterious river that remains unfrozen and boiling year-round, is a phenomenon that scientists have been trying to explain for years.

Wikipedia gives a maximum of 99.1°C in a hot spring and a highest average river temperature of almost 95°C. Talk of it staying "unfrozen" makes little sense for a river in a tropical rainforest. Calling it an unexplained mystery is also misleading. Scientists have identified the heat source as hot springs fed by geological faults, so the heat is geothermal rather than volcanic. Because the core "boiling year-round" description conflicts with the measurements, the claim is contradicted.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a phenomenon where water appears to boil without any visible heat source, has been detected in Peru, and is believed by scientists to be caused by the breakdown of plant material.

text: The Bombardier Beetle is the only known insect capable of producing and storing a hot chemical called cyanogenic glycoside in its body, allowing it to generate temperatures of up to 212°F (100°C) when threatened.

The resulting exothermic oxidation turns hydroquinone into p-benzoquinone and produces a hot spray at about 100°C. The temperature in the claim is roughly right, but the chemical is not. Cyanogenic glycosides are not hot either; insects such as burnet moths store them as cyanide-releasing defenses. 'Bombardier beetle' also covers many species, not a single unique insect.

text: The Butterflyfish is one of the few species of fish that can be identified by the unique pattern of stripes on its body.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is only partly true, and its main point, "one of the few," is contradicted. First, butterflyfish are not a single species. For example, a study of the Crown Butterflyfish (Chaetodon paucifasciatus) found that each fish's stripe pattern is unique. But this ability is not rare. A review in the Journal of Fish Biology lists many bony fishes whose individuals can be identified by their body markings, including discus fish, guppies, cichlids and damselfish. Another study found that adult zebrafish can be told apart by their stripe patterns. So the idea that butterflyfish are among the few fish identifiable this way is wrong.
