text: The Gestalt principle, a concept in visual perception, states that when we see multiple objects positioned together, their relationship to each other influences how we perceive them, rather than considering them independently.
label: supported
reason: Reputable design and psychology sources describe Gestalt theory in the same way the claim does. Smashing Magazine sums it up with Koffka's line that "the whole is other than the sum of the parts": when we see a group of objects, we take in the whole before the individual items, and we group even separate elements into a whole. The proximity principle adds that objects closer together are seen as more related. So it's well supported that how objects relate to each other shapes how we see them, rather than each being seen on its own. One small caveat: Gestalt is a set of principles, not just one.

text: The Gibraltar Observatory, located in the British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar, is one of the largest astronomical research facilities on Earth, offering some of the clearest and darkest skies in the world due to its extraordinary oceanic and mountainous location.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of a major research facility called the "Gibraltar Observatory." What astronomy exists in Gibraltar is amateur: the Gibraltar Astronomical Society, founded in 1987, runs a small society observatory described as Europe's most southern observatory. Members have donated equipment such as a 12-inch amateur Newtonian telescope. The world's largest observatories and telescopes are in places like Chile, Hawaii and the Canary Islands, and none of the lists I checked include Gibraltar. Gibraltar is also a small, densely populated and brightly lit territory, so the claim of some of the world's darkest skies isn't credible. Calling it one of the largest astronomical research facilities on Earth is contradicted by the available evidence.

text: The Glycineropper, a total of three species now known,  is the oldest known insect recorded to date with fossil evidence dating back approximately 250 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any insect called the "Glycineropper" in any source. Reliable sources name Rhyniognatha hirsti as the oldest known insect, dating to about 400–410 million years ago in the Early Devonian, not about 250 million years ago. So the claim's statement about the oldest known insect and its age is wrong.

text: The Great Blue Hole, a large underwater sinkhole in Belize, is approximately 300 meters in diameter and up to 125 meters deep, but it has a very symmetrical elliptical shape.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources say the Great Blue Hole is about 318 m across and 124–125 m deep, so the size figures in the claim are roughly right. The shape is wrong, though: the same sources describe the hole as circular, not as a very symmetrical ellipse. Surfertoday also notes it is "not a perfect cylinder", with ledges at several depths.

text: The Greenland Shark is bioluminescent, with the ability to produce a blue-green light in its stomach, which helps it to deter predators.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Shark Guardian, Bio4Climate, and Wikipedia do not describe the Greenland shark as bioluminescent, and none mention a light-producing stomach or glowing to deter predators. The only glow linked to the species comes from parasitic copepods attached to the shark's eyes. Some researchers have suggested these parasites might be bioluminescent, but Shark Guardian notes this 'has never been proven.' Even in that case, the light would come from the eyes, not the stomach, and it is speculated to lure prey rather than deter predators. The claim's specific details are therefore contradicted.

text: The Human Brain contains over 100 Billion Neurons.
label: contradicted
reason: Current research puts the number at about 86 billion neurons, not over 100 billion. BrainFacts.org says scientists believed in 100 billion for about 50 years, until Suzana Herculano-Houzel counted brain cells directly with a new method and got 86 billion (Azevedo et al., 2009). Several other sources give the same 86 billion figure and call the 100 billion number an overestimate. One recent paper (Goriely) argues the true number is uncertain, but it questions the 86 billion figure without supporting a count of more than 100 billion.

text: The Human Brain generates enough electricity to power a small light bulb due to the electrical activity that occurs within its neurons.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree. Many popular sites (Dent Neurologic Institute, apeejay.news, Medium posts, turkmenistaninfo.gov.tm) say the brain generates about 12–25 watts of electricity, enough for a small bulb. Britannica, a more reliable source, puts it differently: the brain uses about 20 watts of power. That figure is the brain's metabolic energy use, most of which is released as heat, not electricity produced by neurons. Another source says brain energy cannot actually power a light bulb. The real electrical currents in neurons are tiny, so the claim mistakes energy use for electricity generation. Because the evidence conflicts and the most trustworthy source only supports the energy-use framing, the claim cannot be confirmed as stated.

text: The Human eye cannot focus on objects closer than 6 inches due to the shape of the lens.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources don't back a fixed 6-inch (about 15 cm) limit for the human eye. The closest focusing distance, called the near point, depends on age and on how flexible the lens is, not on a set lens shape. ScienceInfo says children can often focus at 7–10 cm (about 3–4 inches), well inside 6 inches. Other sources put the typical young-adult near point at about 25 cm (10 inches), and it moves out past 100 cm in older people. Forum users also report focusing at 5–7 inches. The cause is the limited flexibility of the lens and ciliary muscles (accommodation), not lens shape alone. A single universal 6-inch limit is therefore contradicted.

text: The Imperial State Crown, which is set with over 3,000 precious stones, including the famous Cullinan II diamond, weighs approximately 4 pounds and 12 ounces.
label: contradicted
reason: The stones and the Cullinan II part of the claim check out, but the weight is wrong. Wikipedia lists the Imperial State Crown at 1.06 kg (2.3 lb) and names Cullinan II among its notable stones. It carries 2,868 diamonds plus sapphires, emeralds, pearls and rubies, which comes to more than 3,000 stones. The figure of 4 lb 12 oz (about 2.23 kg) is the weight of St Edward's Crown, not the Imperial State Crown.

text: The International Date Line, which separates the days of the week from one side to another, passes through the middle of the Pacific Ocean and essentially bisects the island nation of Kiribati.
label: contradicted
reason: Kiribati sits across the 180° meridian, and the date line did split the country in half until 1995. On 1 January 1995, though, Kiribati moved the line east so the whole nation would be on the same side and share the same date. The line now bends around Kiribati's easternmost islands instead of cutting through the country, so saying it 'bisects' Kiribati is out of date. The US Naval Observatory, Wikipedia and CBC all confirm this. The rest of the claim is accurate: the line marks where the date changes and runs through the middle of the Pacific.

text: The Madagascar plain possum (Galerellim murina) also known as the least dunnart is an endangered carnivorous marsupial.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up several animals, and the names and facts don't fit together. I found no species called the 'Madagascar plain possum' and no scientific name 'Galerellim murina'. Madagascar has no native marsupials. Galerella is a genus of mongooses, and 'murina' points to Sminthopsis murina, the common dunnart. Dunnarts are small carnivorous marsupials that live only in Australia and New Guinea, not Madagascar. Wikipedia, citing the IUCN Red List, lists Sminthopsis dunnarts such as the lesser hairy-footed, stripe-faced and Gilbert's dunnarts as 'Least Concern', not endangered. So the claim's location, name and 'endangered' status are all contradicted.

text: The Martyrdom of Haoulos, a 13th-century Byzantine saint, is believed to be the inspiration behind the miraculous picture of Our Lady of Balduccio in the medieval gallery of Italian town "Campogalliano".
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing on a "Martyrdom of Haoulos" or a 13th-century Byzantine saint by that name. They also found no "Our Lady of Balduccio" image in Campogalliano. The Marian sanctuary known in Campogalliano is the Madonna della Sassola. The closest match was the miraculous Refugium Peccatorum picture linked to the Jesuit Anthony Baldinucci, which has no connection to Campogalliano or a Byzantine martyr. Since no source confirms or directly refutes the claimed link, it cannot be verified. I hit the search tool's usage limit before I could run further searches.

text: The McKinlay Falls in Canada is the world's second-highest uninterrupted waterfall, dropping 491 meters (1,612 feet) vertically in a single plunge.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a "McKinlay Falls" in Canada. Searches only turned up McKinney Falls, a pair of 15–20 ft falls in Texas, along with Canadian falls under other names. The ranking in the claim is also wrong: Angel Falls alone has an uninterrupted drop of 807 m (2,648 ft), and other falls such as Tugela also exceed 491 m. A 491 m single plunge therefore could not be the world's second-highest. Canada's tallest falls are James Bruce Falls (840 m total) and Della Falls (440 m), and neither is named McKinlay or holds that rank.

text: The Nîzovać waterfall in northern Albania is considered one of the highest free-falling waterfalls in Europe, dropping approximately 95 meters.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a waterfall called "Nîzovać" (or "Nizovac") in Albania. The name looks Slavic rather than Albanian, so this waterfall may not exist. Lists of Albania's waterfalls (europeanwaterfalls.com, Albania360, Albanopedia) name falls such as Sotira, Grunas, Peshtura and Bogova, but none called Nîzovać. None describes an Albanian waterfall that drops about 95 m and ranks among Europe's highest free-falling waterfalls. Without evidence that it exists, I can't confirm or rule out its height or ranking. My searches ran out before I could check further, so I can't say for certain that it's made up.

text: The Principia Mathematica, a foundational work in mathematics by Isaac Newton, took 20 years to complete, from 1687.
label: contradicted
reason: Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica came out in 1687, which was when it was finished, not when work on it began. EBSCO and PBS NOVA both say Newton spent about 18 months writing it, from around 1684/1685 to 1686. The claim that it took 20 years starting in 1687 is therefore wrong.

text: The Royal Lyceum theatre in Edinburgh, Scotland, was the world's first purpose-built theatre when it opened in 1883.
label: contradicted
reason: The 1883 opening date is right: the Royal Lyceum opened on 10 September 1883 with Much Ado About Nothing. The claim that it was the world's first purpose-built theatre is false. Purpose-built theatres existed centuries earlier, including ancient Greek theatres and Italy's Teatro Olimpico (1585). Edinburgh already had its own Theatre Royal before the Lyceum opened. Official sources describe 'firsts' only within Scotland, such as being the first Scottish theatre to use an iron safety curtain and electric lighting. They don't say it was the world's first purpose-built theatre.

text: The Saijo Bridge in Okayama, Japan, is the longest deck arch bridge in the world, spanning over 1,629 meters in length.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source that mentions a "Saijo Bridge" in Okayama. Searches only turned up other Okayama bridges, such as Kashirajima Bridge and the Great Seto Bridge, plus pages about "Saijō" in Ehime and the Sanjo Bridge in Kyoto. Wikipedia and ENR's lists of the world's longest arch bridges don't include any Japanese bridge at the top. They name Chinese bridges as the longest arch spans, for example the Pingnan Third Bridge (575 m, ranked second-largest as of 2025) and the Chaotianmen Bridge (552 m). The claim also confuses total length with arch span: a 1,629 m arch span would be about three times the current record. My search limit ran out before I could pull up the deck-arch row of the Wikipedia table, but the evidence I found still contradicts the claim that a Japanese bridge holds this record.

text: The TERMINUS of a rope is the point where two ends are tied together with a specific knot to prevent the rope from coming untied.
label: contradicted
reason: No knot or rope glossary I checked (Animated Knots, Scout Pioneering, Ropebook, Army and fire-department manuals) uses 'terminus' for a point where two ends are knotted together. Dictionaries (Merriam-Webster, Dictionary.com, Collins) say a terminus is an end, extremity or final point. In knot terms, the ends of a rope are the working end and the standing or bitter end. A knot that joins two ends is called a bend, and a knot that stops an end from fraying or slipping through is a stopper knot or whipping. No source defines a rope's terminus the way the claim does, so the claim conflicts with both the general meaning of the word and standard rope terminology.

text: The Tacitus Pig, a species of wild boar, is named after Roman historian Publius Cornelius Tacitus.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source showing that anything called the "Tacitus Pig" exists, either as a wild boar species or subspecies. Searches for the name turn up only general pages on the wild boar (Sus scrofa) and its subspecies, such as the Central European boar. Wikipedia's Tacitus disambiguation page lists things named after the historian, including a lunar crater and asteroid 3097 Tacitus, but no pig or boar. The search results don't directly contradict the claim, but no part of it can be verified.

text: The Taj Mahal in India contains over 28 different types of precious and semi-precious stones.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the Taj Mahal's marble is inlaid with 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones (for example Rock & Gem magazine and Wikipedia). One travel source supports the exact wording, saying it is believed that "more than 28 different types of precious and semi-precious stones" were inlaid. The claim is broadly supported, but there is a caveat: most sources give exactly 28, so "over 28" may slightly overstate the usual figure.

text: The Thing, a National Historic Landmark in Alaska, is the largest and most accessible glacier cathedral in the world, located within the Mendenhall Glacier.
label: contradicted
reason: No source backs this claim. "The Thing" is a known roadside attraction and museum along I-10 in Dragoon/Benson, Arizona. It is not in Alaska or inside the Mendenhall Glacier. The ice caves at Mendenhall Glacier are temporary features that change as the ice melts. No source calls them "The Thing," a National Historic Landmark, or the world's largest glacier cathedral.

text: The Venus Flower Basket jellyfish, a species of jellyfish, can lose up to 35% of its bell and still manage to maintain a reasonable bell shape due to its flexible and fragile body structure.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal wrong. The Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a glass sponge, not a jellyfish, so it has no bell. Its body is also not soft or flexible: it is a rigid lattice of silica spicules. Because the animal is misidentified and its body is described incorrectly, the claim about losing up to 35% of its bell is false.

text: The Venus flower basket jellyfish is found in the deep waters of the ocean and is bioluminescent, meaning it has the ability to produce its own light.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the animal wrong. Wikipedia and EBSCO both describe the Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) as a glass sponge, not a jellyfish, so no "Venus flower basket jellyfish" exists. It is true that it lives in deep Pacific waters, usually below about 500 m. Calling it a jellyfish is still a factual error. Its bioluminescence is also doubtful: its glass spicules are known for carrying light like optical fibres, not for making it.

text: The Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) can only open its modified leaves, which are capable of capturing prey, a maximum of 5-7 times before new leaves must be produced.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that each Venus flytrap trap can open and close only a limited number of times before it dies and the plant grows a new one. They do not support the claim's figure of 5–7 times. National Geographic Education says each trap can open and close "about three times" before dying and falling off. Gardening sources give about 3 to 5 times, or about five. The National Wildlife Federation says only "several times." None of the results gives a 5–7 range. The more reliable figures are lower than the claimed number, so the specific claim is contradicted.

text: The Vibrazione of the Great Pyramid of Giza creates two precise whistling tones when plucked, an "F" note and an "E" note, discovered in the 1990s.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source for this claim. Nothing I found mentions a 'Vibrazione' of the Great Pyramid, the pyramid being 'plucked', or 'whistling tones' in F and E discovered in the 1990s. What the sources do describe is different: the King's Chamber resonates strongly to an F# chord (about 729 Hz when A is tuned to 432 Hz), and the granite coffer resonates to A. Tom Danley also measured very low-frequency resonances in the chamber in the 1990s, and some describe possible F/F# tones. None of this backs up the claim's details about plucking, whistling, or exact F and E notes, and the subject 'Vibrazione' doesn't clearly refer to anything. My searches were cut short by a tool usage limit, so I couldn't check further.

text: The ancient Egyptians were skilled at creating lifelike mummies, with some of their mummified bodies even having tattoos and internal organs preserved through elaborate817 processes, like the Edwin Smith Papyrus.
label: contradicted
reason: The general points about Egyptian mummification are accurate: it was elaborate, internal organs were preserved, and tattoos have been found on some mummies. The claim breaks down where it gives the Edwin Smith Papyrus as an example of these mummies or embalming processes. Sources describe the papyrus as the oldest known surgical treatise, a medical text about treating 48 trauma patients such as those with skull fractures and head injuries. It is not a mummy and does not describe mummification. The claim is also garbled ('elaborate817').

text: The blind tunnel of the Hadley airspeed indicator found in most aircraft refers to the period before a constant differential static pressure can be established around the static port, typically around 3 seconds of flight.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Hadley airspeed indicator" or a "blind tunnel" in airspeed indicators. Wikipedia, Britannica, CFI Notebook and Pilot Institute all describe the airspeed indicator in most aircraft as a pitot-static instrument. It measures the difference between total pressure from the pitot tube and static pressure from the static port. None of them mention a startup period of about 3 seconds before a steady static pressure differential forms. The terms in the claim seem to be made up, but no source directly says they are false. Since the claim can't be checked either way, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: The blindness of migratory monarch butterflies is temporary and due to the reduction of the length and function of their eyes' focal muscles, allowing them to focus on distant visual cues for navigation during their migrations.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that migratory monarchs go blind, temporarily or otherwise. Scientific sources say the opposite: monarchs navigate visually during migration. Their compound eyes, including the specialized dorsal rim area that detects polarized light, feed a time-compensated sun compass, so they need working vision to migrate. The claim's mechanism also doesn't fit what is known about insect eyes. Compound eyes have fixed optics, and these sources never describe focusing muscles that could shrink. The claim looks fabricated.

text: The boom of the Grand Canyon is estimated to be about 18 billion years old, dating back to the formation of the Earth's crust.
label: contradicted
reason: The National Park Service says the oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, such as the Vishnu Schist, are about 1.8 billion years old, which is a little over a third of Earth's age. They are not 18 billion years old. A figure of 18 billion years would also be older than both the Earth (about 4.5 billion years) and the universe (about 13.8 billion years). The bottom rocks also formed long after the Earth's crust first formed.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system is Venus, due to its thick atmosphere that scatters and reflects sunlight, making it appear exceptionally bright in the night sky.
label: supported
reason: Caltech IPAC's Cool Cosmos page says Venus is the brightest planet in the Solar System. It explains that Venus looks so bright because its thick clouds reflect about 70% of the sunlight that reaches them, and because it is the closest planet to Earth. ScienceDirect also says Venus's clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits the planet, making it the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon. This matches the claim. The claim gives the atmosphere as the reason; the sources also credit its closeness to Earth, but nothing contradicts the claim.

text: The brightest planet in our solar system, Venus, is hidden from view by thick clouds of sulfuric acid and droplets of sulfuric acid water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe Venus as the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon, which makes it the brightest planet. They also say thick clouds of sulfuric acid cover it and hide the surface. ScienceDirect specifically describes the clouds as made mainly of aqueous sulfuric acid droplets. The claim's wording is a little loose: the clouds hide Venus's surface, not the planet itself. Read that way, the sources support it.

text: The brightest star in the night sky, Sirius, is actually cooler than the Sun, with a surface temperature of around 9,900 degrees Celsius due to its size and low mass.
label: contradicted
reason: Sirius is hotter than the Sun, not cooler. EarthSky describes Sirius as an A-type star that is much hotter than our Sun, with a surface temperature of about 9,400°C, compared with about 5,500°C for the Sun. Sirius also has slightly more than twice the Sun's mass, so the claim's mention of 'low mass' is wrong too. Its companion, Sirius B, is hotter still at about 25,000 K.

text: The brightly colored termite mounds found in the savannas of southern Africa are designed with a temperature-controlled ventilation system to maintain a stable temperature of around 28 degrees Celsius throughout the year.
label: contradicted
reason: Southern African termite mounds (Macrotermes) are widely described as having vent systems, but the claim fails on several points. Popular accounts put the regulated temperature at about 31 °C (87 °F), not 28 °C. More importantly, the Turner & Soar paper on Macrotermes mounds in southern Africa says "there is no evidence that termites regulate nest temperature." In that paper, nest temperature rises and falls through the year along with the surrounding soil, and the mound mainly serves gas exchange and ventilation. That contradicts the idea of a stable year-round temperature, and the paper does not describe the mounds as brightly colored.

text: The chemical discovered in 1783 by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, which is found in some cleaning products, is also the pigment in mustards and hair dyes, and its name is Mercury(I) oxide has been replaced with "calomel".
label: contradicted
reason: Calomel is the name for mercury(I) chloride (Hg2Cl2), not mercury(I) oxide, so it could not be a replacement name for mercury(I) oxide. Beyond that, the claim is confused. No source ties a chemical discovered by Scheele in 1783 to cleaning products, a mustard pigment and hair dyes. Calomel also is not a pigment in mustards or hair dyes.

text: The chemical element gold is the most malleable and ductile metal, perfectly capable of being molded into thin sheets and long wires.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources say this directly. Britannica calls gold "the most malleable and ductile of the elements" and notes it can be beaten into extremely thin gold leaf. The Royal Society of Chemistry and the US National Park Service both say gold is the most malleable and ductile of all metals. These properties are what allow gold to be formed into thin sheets and drawn into long wires. Britannica's main gold entry is more cautious in one place, calling it "one of the most" malleable and ductile elements, but its properties page and the other sources back the superlative.

text: The color blue is actually the rarest color in nature, making up only about 1.5% of all colors that occur in the visible spectrum.
label: contradicted
reason: Only part of this claim holds up. Sources such as UC Botanical Garden at Berkeley and the Wilderness Society describe blue as rare among plants and animals, and as the rarest flower color. But none of the results I found back the figure of about 1.5%. The part about the visible spectrum is also wrong: blue covers roughly 450–495 nm of the 380–700 nm visible range, which is about 14%, not 1.5%. Blue is rare because few organisms produce blue pigments, not because it takes up a small slice of the spectrum. My search was cut short by a tool limit, so the spectrum figures come from standard physics rather than a search result.

text: The color blue is often associated with calmness, but did you know that blue is actually a very intense color that can be overwhelming to the human brain when seen in large quantities?
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is true: sources agree that blue is widely linked with calmness. The second part is not. Color-psychology sources describe blue as a low-energy color that is easy to look at and "doesn't feel overwhelming." They say it can lower heart rate and blood pressure. None of the results describe blue as a very intense color that overwhelms the brain in large amounts.

text: The color of the Blind Spot in the human eye is actually about 10 times more sensitive than the rest of the retina.
label: contradicted
reason: The blind spot (optic disc) has no photoreceptors, meaning no rods or cones, so it cannot detect light or color at all. It is not 10 times more sensitive than the rest of the retina; it is insensitive to light.

text: The color of the Great Barrier Reef changes depending on the species of algae living within its coral, with some species of algae turning the reef into a vibrant green, maroon, or purple color.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree, and none confirms the claim's specific wording. GBRMPA and the Great Barrier Reef Foundation say corals get most of their colour from zooxanthellae, the microscopic algae living in their tissues, and that coral colours range from red and purple to green and brown. But they link colour to how many algae there are and how much chlorophyll they produce, not to which species of algae is present. The Smithsonian says the algae supply green, brown and reddish colours, while 'purple, blue, and mauve colors' are made by the coral itself. GBRMPA's own coral bleaching page and GBR Biology also put bright purples and blues down to the coral's own fluorescent proteins. No credible source says that different algae species turn the reef green, maroon or purple. Since part of the claim has some support, part is contradicted, and the species detail can't be verified, the evidence is mixed.

text: The color of the hills and mountains in the Northern Lights, also known as the aurora borealis, can often appear red due to the presence of oxygen atoms at higher altitudes and altitudes in the Earth's atmosphere.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. The National Park Service says red aurora comes from oxygen atoms at very high altitudes, where collisions are rare enough for the long-lived red emission to occur. The rest can't be verified. 'The color of the hills and mountains in the Northern Lights' doesn't clearly refer to anything, and no source says the aurora colors hills or mountains. The NPS also says red aurora appears 'on occasion', which cuts against the claim that it is 'often' red.

text: The color purple is the rarest color in nature due to the difficulty of producing the specific wavelengths of light required for the color.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both the color and the reason wrong. Most sources, including Wikipedia's article on blue flower colouration, Art in Context and CMYcubes, say blue is the rarest color in nature. They note that few plants make blue flowers and almost no animals make a blue pigment. CMYcubes also says purple flowers are common because plants can mix red and blue anthocyanins. The claim's explanation is also wrong. Purple is not a single wavelength on the visible spectrum; we see it when red and blue light combine. Even a student-newspaper article arguing that purple is rarest (stuyspec.com) says purple is not on the spectrum. It credits purple's rarity to its red and blue makeup, not to any difficulty producing specific wavelengths.

text: The coloring of the eyes of the fruit fly is determined by the genetics of a coding gene which encodes for a protein needed to make melanin.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results contradict the claim. In Drosophila, eye colour comes from ommochrome and pteridine pigments, not melanin. The classic eye-colour gene, white, encodes an ABC transporter that moves pigment precursors into the eye. It is not a protein for making melanin. The source contrasts melanin as a screening pigment in vertebrates with ommochromes and pteridines in insects.

text: The colour pink was actually considered a masculine colour in the 18th and 19th centuries before its association with femininity became widespread.
label: supported
reason: Several mainstream sources back the claim. CNN quotes Pantone's Leatrice Eiseman saying pink was considered a masculine colour and was used for little boys in old catalogues and books, because it was seen as a softer shade of red, which was linked with men and the military. Quartz quotes fashion historian Valerie Steele saying a man in a pink silk suit was perfectly masculine in the 18th century. Winsor & Newton and Art & Object say pink was seen as masculine or gender-neutral until it became feminine, a shift these sources date between the late 19th and mid-20th centuries. There are caveats: Steele and Jo Paoletti stress that both sexes wore pink, and one museum blog says pink began leaving menswear in the 19th century. Still, the overall evidence supports the claim that pink was once considered masculine before it became widely linked with femininity.

text: The country of Bermuda has the world's third-largest coral reef system, known as the Bermuda Reef, which is home to a diverse array of marine life.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources don't give Bermuda the title of world's third-largest coral reef system. The Bahamas National Trust and the official Bahamas tourism site call the Andros Barrier Reef the world's third-largest barrier reef, and other sources give that rank to the Florida Reef. Bermuda's reefs are usually described as among the northernmost in the Atlantic, not the third-largest. Also, Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory, not an independent country. Bermuda's reefs do support diverse marine life, but the main claim is wrong.

text: The country with the longest coastline in the world is Canada, with its total coastline measuring approximately 243,000 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, an official government source, says Canada has the longest coastline in the world, at 243,042 km across its Atlantic, Arctic and Pacific coasts. Mental Floss also calls Canada's title undisputed. It notes that the exact length varies by source, but the claim only says "approximately 243,000 km," and the official figure matches that.

text: The darkest day in recorded history was December 4, 1903, when the city of St. Petersburg, Russia experienced the shortest day, lasting only 5 hours and 45 minutes, due to its location near the Arctic Circle.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. St. Petersburg's shortest day falls at the winter solstice, around December 21–22, not on December 4. Daylight then lasts about 5 hours 53 minutes, not 5 hours 45 minutes. Because of how the solstice works, December 4, 1903 could not have been the city's shortest day. The city is also several degrees south of the Arctic Circle, not near it, and a normal yearly solstice is not a 'darkest day in recorded history.' That title usually goes to events like the year 536 AD or New England's Dark Day of 1780.

text: The darkest star in the universe is V838 Monocerotis, a reddish-purple hue that results from being the coldest known star with a temperature of approximately 3,900 Kelvin.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia lists V838 Monocerotis at about 3,300 K, not about 3,900 K. Even at that temperature it is nowhere near the coldest known star. Cool dwarfs and brown dwarfs are far colder, and some L-type objects are colder than V838 Mon. No reliable source calls it the 'darkest star in the universe.' It became famous for a very bright outburst in 2002, reaching about a million times the Sun's luminosity, and for the light echo that followed. Its colour comes from being a red supergiant, not from a 'reddish-purple' hue caused by being the coldest star.

text: The darkest star in the universe is V838 Monocerotis, which is located about 20,000 light-years away and visibly dims its surrounding stars due to its intense brightness.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and NASA put V838 Monocerotis about 19,200–20,000 light-years away, so that part of the claim holds up. The rest doesn't. These sources describe it as a red variable star whose sudden outburst in 2002 made it, for a short time, one of the largest known stars. Its light then lit up the surrounding dust as a 'light echo.' Nothing in them calls it the 'darkest star in the universe.' The claim also contradicts itself by calling the star the darkest while saying it has 'intense brightness.' And no source says it dims nearby stars; its light actually illuminated the dust around it.

text: The deepest part of the Earth's crust is the South Pacific leveling off at approximately 11,022 meters at the Challenger Deep.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the location wrong. Challenger Deep is at the southern end of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, at about 11°22′N, 142°35′E. That puts it north of the equator, in the North Pacific, not the South Pacific. Its depth is about 11,000 m. Recent surveys give 10,935 ± 6 m, and the GEBCO estimate is 10,903–11,009 m, so 11,022 m is an older figure that is slightly too high. The bigger error is still the 'South Pacific' location.

text: The deepest part of the Earth's mantle is the D" layer below the Earth's core, which has a temperature of around 6,000 degrees Celsius and is about 2,250 kilometers deep.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the D″ layer's position, temperature and depth wrong. The D″ layer is the lowermost part of the mantle, sitting just above the core-mantle boundary, not below the Earth's core. That boundary is about 2,900 km deep, and the D″ layer lies at roughly 2,700–2,900 km depth, not about 2,250 km. Its temperature is around 3,300–4,300 K (roughly 3,000–4,000 °C), well below 6,000 °C. A figure near 6,000 °C fits the inner core instead.

text: The difference between Daylight Saving Time (DST) and Standard Time is typically a one-hour adjustment, but some countries shift by 30 or 45 minutes to align with their local sunrise and sunset times.
label: contradicted
reason: The one-hour part is right. Timeanddate says DST is usually one hour ahead of standard time. The exceptions part is wrong, though. The only current example the sources give of a 30-minute DST change is Lord Howe Island, a single small island that belongs to Australia, so it isn't 'some countries'. No source names any place that shifts by 45 minutes for DST. The claim seems to mix up DST shifts with UTC offsets: 30- and 45-minute offsets do exist (Nepal is +5:45 but does not use DST), and the Chatham Islands go from +12:45 to +13:45, which is still a one-hour change. The other exception timeanddate mentions is Troll station in Antarctica, which shifts by 2 hours.

text: The difference between the largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, and the smallest, Mercury, is roughly 640 times in diameter.
label: contradicted
reason: Universe Today puts Mercury's diameter at about 4,879 km and Jupiter's at about 142,984 km (equatorial). That makes Jupiter only about 29 times wider than Mercury, not about 640 times. Jupiter and Mercury are correctly named as the largest and smallest planets, but the 640x diameter ratio is wrong by a wide margin. It doesn't match the volume ratio either, which is roughly 24,000x.

text: The driest desert in the world, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is also home to several rainbow-colored rock formations and mesmerizing geysers due to its unique geological features.
label: supported
reason: My searches turned up travel sources, not scientific or official ones, so the evidence is moderately reliable. They describe the Atacama in Chile as the driest desert in the world. One caveat: it's more precisely called the driest non-polar desert, since some polar areas are drier. These same sources describe the Atacama's Rainbow Valley (Valle del Arcoíris), known for its multicolored rock formations, and the steaming El Tatio geysers, which are linked to the region's geology and volcanic activity. Nothing I found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: The driest desert on Earth, Antarctica, covers approximately 98% of the continent.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources call Antarctica the driest place or desert on Earth (WorldAtlas, Guinness World Records). They also say a permanent ice sheet covers about 98% of the continent. Guinness describes the Antarctic Ice Sheet itself as the largest and driest desert, covering about 99% of the continent. The claim's wording is loose, though. It calls the continent itself the desert and then says the desert covers 98% of the continent, when that figure really describes the ice sheet. Read sensibly, the claim matches the sources.

text: The dwarf planet Pluto has a highly eccentric orbit that brings it as close as 29.7 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun and takes it as far as 49.3 AU from the Sun, resulting in a 248 Earth-year-long orbital period.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Pluto entry gives a perihelion of 29.658 AU, which rounds to 29.7 AU. It gives an aphelion of 49.305 AU, which rounds to 49.3 AU, and a sidereal orbital period of 247.94 years, about 248 years. It also describes the orbit as eccentric. Wikipedia calls it 'moderately' eccentric rather than 'highly', but Pluto's orbit is notably eccentric compared with the planets', so this wording doesn't contradict the numbers. All the figures in the claim match.

text: The famous DNA structure was discovered by James Watson and Francis Crick using a model made of metal and plastic near Oxford Castle in 1953.
label: contradicted
reason: Watson and Crick did work out the DNA double-helix structure in 1953, but they did it at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge, not near Oxford Castle. The source gives the location as Cambridge, England. Because the place in the claim is wrong, the claim is contradicted. The original model was mostly metal (brass/tin plates), so that part is roughly right, but it doesn't change the verdict.

text: The famous blinking "Cyclops eye" on the Mona Lisa is not a painting, but rather three small paint strokes that were painted over and covered up, and then later intentionally exposed to create the illusion of a cyclops-like gaze.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a famous blinking "Cyclops eye" on the Mona Lisa. Nothing describes three paint strokes that were covered up and later exposed on purpose to make a cyclops-like gaze. The search turned up unrelated Mona Lisa topics: studies of her gaze (the "Mona Lisa effect"), claims that tiny letters are hidden in her eyes, and stock images of cyclops eyes. The feature the claim describes doesn't seem to exist, and since no source discusses it, the claim can't be confirmed. No source directly refutes it either.

text: The famous painting "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh took him two years to complete, however he painted the majority of it in a single viewing from his window.
label: contradicted
reason: MoMA, which owns the painting, and Wikipedia both say The Starry Night was made in mid-June 1889 at Saint-Rémy. MoMA adds that van Gogh painted it over several sessions during the day, not at night from a single look out his window. So it did not take two years, and the claim about a single viewing is also wrong.

text: The famous painting, the Mona Lisa, has moresecurity measures in place than the White House, with over 2 million visitors per year requiring strict screening and security checks.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but the main comparison can't be verified. Sources confirm the Mona Lisa is heavily protected, with 3-inch bulletproof glass. They also say the painting draws up to 10 million visitors a year (20,000–30,000 a day), so 'over 2 million' is technically true but far too low. No reliable source supports or measures the statement that the painting has more security than the White House. That looks like unsupported hyperbole, and nothing clearly confirms or disproves it.

text: The famous scientist Albert Einstein is said to have been afraid of ジャガー (also known as jaguars) due to one night when he was hiking in the forest after which as he later reported a jaguar jumped on him, though it is also mentioned that the mysterious animal turned out to be a Labrador Retriever
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched in English and Japanese and found no reliable source for this anecdote. Nothing says Einstein feared jaguars, that a 'jaguar' jumped on him while he was hiking in a forest at night, or that the animal turned out to be a Labrador Retriever. The only results were unrelated Baby Einstein fan wiki pages about jaguar characters and the 'Little Albert' psychology experiment. The story looks made up, but since no source directly denies it either, it can't be verified or disproved.

text: The forced perspective technique used in filmmaking to create the illusion of miniature characters within large environments was popularized by Harry Potter director Chris Columbus and his production designer Stuart Craig.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources show that forced perspective in film goes back to the 1920s and 1930s, with early examples like Safety Last and The Wizard of Oz. Its best-known modern use is in Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings films. The technique was around long before the Harry Potter films (2001 onward), and none of the sources credit Chris Columbus or Stuart Craig with popularizing it.

text: The further you travel north on the Earth's equator, the shorter days get, while the closer you get to the North Pole, the longer the days become due to the Earth's tilt.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself and gets the science wrong. You can't travel north while staying on the equator. It also says days get shorter as you go north, then says they get longer as you near the North Pole. Reliable sources (LPI/USRA, Wikipedia, The Conversation) say day length depends on both latitude and season because of Earth's axial tilt. In northern summer, days get longer the further north you go, up to constant daylight at the pole. In northern winter, they get shorter, down to constant darkness at the pole. Day length does not simply shrink and then grow as you move north, as the claim says.

text: The giant squill, a type of wild lily, blooms for just one night every year, typically in late spring and early summer.
label: contradicted
reason: The giant squill (Drimia maritima, also called giant white squill or sea squill) is in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), not a true lily. NC State Extension says it flowers from late summer into autumn, and Dave's Garden lists late summer to early fall. Both contradict the claim of late spring to early summer. It also does not bloom for just one night: it produces tall spikes of many small star-shaped flowers over the season.

text: The greatest diameter of a human iris can range from 10 to 13 millimeters, but in some cases can reach up to 14 millimeters.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only verify part of the claim before hitting the search limit. A peer-reviewed PMC article says the horizontal visible iris diameter usually falls within about 10–13 mm, which supports the first part. The same article mentions a suggestion to raise the upper limit of the normal range, but the snippet I saw gives no number. I found no source saying the iris can reach 14 mm in some cases. Since that part is unverified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The highest mountain peak in the solar system is Olympus Mons on Mars, which stands at an impressive height of approximately 27 km.
label: supported
reason: Olympus Mons is widely described as the tallest mountain in the Solar System. Several sources give its height as about 27 km: Oregon State University's volcano site says it is 'nearly 27 km high', Simple Wikipedia gives 27 km, and NASA Science (2016) is quoted as saying 27 km. Height estimates do vary depending on the reference point: about 21.9 km above datum and about 26 km of relief above the surrounding plains. Some sources also call it only approximately tied with Rheasilvia's central peak on Vesta. Still, the claim's 'approximately 27 km' and its 'highest peak' status match what credible sources commonly say.

text: The highest number of languages spoken by a single person is held by late Michael Thomas who knew 146 languages in his vocabulary.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source naming a Michael Thomas who knew 146 languages. The polyglot with the closest name is Michel Thomas (1914–2005). Wikipedia says he was fluent in seven languages, and other descriptions put the number at a bit over ten, nowhere near 146. Several sources say the Guinness World Record for most languages spoken by one person belongs to Ziad Fazah, with about 58–59 languages. So both the 146 figure and the claim that Thomas holds the record are contradicted.

text: The highest recorded amount of saliva produced by the human body is about 30,000 liters in a lifetime, which is roughly equivalent to filling two large swimming pools.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats the figure as a record, but sources present it as an average. Dental sites such as Healthplex give the typical lifetime total as about 25,000 quarts (roughly 23,600 L), and Factourism gives about 25,000 liters. Other estimates range from about 20,000 to 44,000 L. No source calls any figure a 'highest recorded amount.' The 'two large swimming pools' comparison is also off: the sources only say 'two swimming pools,' and IFLScience and ScienceInfo say 'a small swimming pool.' Simple arithmetic backs this up: 30,000 L is far smaller than even one Olympic pool, which holds about 2.5 million L. The rough lifetime volume is plausible, but describing it as the highest recorded amount, equal to two large pools, contradicts the evidence.

text: The highest recorded compulsive sleeper stayed in bed for 86 years, between 1927 and 2013.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches failed: the search tool returned unreadable output and then hit its usage limit, so I couldn't retrieve any sources. I found no evidence of a 'compulsive sleeper' who stayed in bed for 86 years, from 1927 to 2013. The claim seems implausible, but without sources I can neither support nor contradict it.

text: The highest recorded number of movies made by a single director is held by Rappings Indian director Puttanna Kanagal with 90 films.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources list only about 24–31 films directed by Puttanna Kanagal (Wikipedia's category for his films has 31 entries; Letterboxd lists about 25), nowhere near 90. The record is credited to another Indian director, Dasari Narayana Rao, who directed more than 150 films (151) and holds a Limca record for directing the most films in the world.

text: The highest recorded temperature in Antarctica was 40.7 °F (4.3 °C) on January 30, 1982, which originally was announced as a very high 67.5 °F (19.7 °C) based on a thermometer malfunction, but was corrected 31 years later.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. The 30 January 1982 reading at Signy Research Station was never reduced to 4.3 °C (40.7 °F) because of a faulty thermometer. In 2017 a WMO expert committee looked at the evidence and kept it, recognising 19.8 °C (67.6 °F) as the record high for the Antarctic region (land and ice shelves south of 60°S). So the record was confirmed decades later, not corrected down to a much lower value.

text: The highest striking altitude ever recorded by a major atmospheric river event occurred when a storm system brought unseasonable rains to Arizona in 1939, reaching nearly 12,000 feet in elevation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My search turned up nothing that backs this claim. I found no record of a 1939 atmospheric river in Arizona that reached a 'highest striking altitude' of nearly 12,000 feet, and no recognized record of that kind seems to exist. The results only covered general Arizona tropical storms and atmospheric rivers, such as Hurricane Heather and a 2013 AMS study of a different event. 1939 did bring unusual tropical storms to the Southwest, but nothing ties them to the altitude claim, and the claim's wording is too vague to check.

text: The highest virus load in the human body is found in the gut, where it can harbor up to 90% of the total viral biomass.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Search results support the first part of the claim: multiple peer-reviewed sources state that the gastrointestinal tract harbours the highest number of viruses of any body site (e.g., eBioMedicine review: "The GI tract harbours the highest number of viruses across the human body", ~10^9–10^10 VLPs per gram of faeces), and reviews note that of the ~10^13 viral particles in the body, most are located in the gut. However, the specific quantitative figure that the gut holds 'up to 90% of the total viral biomass' of the human body could not be verified. The 90–95% figures that appear in the literature refer to bacteriophages constituting ~90–95% of the gut virome (not the gut's share of the whole-body viral biomass), and one review notes the gut virome represents only ~0.1% of total microbial biomass. Since the key numerical component is unverifiable (and appears to conflate distinct statistics) while not being directly contradicted, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The human nose can detect over 1 trillion different scents, which is a remarkably large number considering that the human brain can only process a limited amount of sensory information at any given time.
label: supported
reason: The main claim matches a 2014 Science study by Bushdid, Keller, Vosshall and colleagues at Rockefeller University. It estimated that people can tell apart at least 1 trillion odor mixtures, and trustworthy sources such as Rockefeller University and Smithsonian reported the finding. The second part, that the brain can only process a limited amount of sensory information at once, is a general framing statement that fits basic neuroscience; none of the sources contradict it. Some researchers have challenged the 1 trillion estimate: Gerkin & Castro and Meister published critiques in 2015, reported by ASU and ScienceDaily. They argue the math behind the number is fragile, but they do not show it is false. It remains a published scientific estimate, so I judge the claim supported, with the caveat that the exact figure is still debated.

text: The humble honeybee played a key role in the development of the first modern computer, as a team of engineers at NASA used a simulation of how honeybees communicate to improve the navigation system for the Apollo missions.
label: contradicted
reason: No source supports the idea that honeybee communication simulations had anything to do with the first modern computer or with Apollo navigation. The claim also gets the timeline wrong. ENIAC, widely called the first modern electronic computer, was built in 1943–45 by the Army and the University of Pennsylvania, years before NASA existed (1958) and long before Apollo. Apollo navigation used the Apollo Guidance Computer, which MIT's Instrumentation Lab (later Draper Laboratory) developed with conventional guidance methods. Nothing in its history mentions honeybee-inspired algorithms.

text: The infamous Tweed suit, worn during the 19th-century American crime, is made of high-quality wool and compatible to fit large and big men of that time.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source describing an "infamous Tweed suit" connected to a 19th-century American crime. The search results only mention Boss Tweed, the Tammany Hall politician known for corruption, and tweed as a wool fabric in general. The claim seems to mix these up, so it's not clear what it refers to. Nothing I found mentions such a suit, its wool quality, or whether it was made to fit large men.

text: The international date line, which is around the 180-degree meridian, separates two consecutive calendar days, and countries that lie west of it will have today, while countries that lie east of it will have yesterday.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic says the date line roughly follows the 180-degree meridian and that places west of it are one calendar day ahead of places east of it. Wikipedia describes it as the boundary between one calendar day and the next. It adds that crossing westbound moves the date forward and that places such as American Samoa, east of the line, are a day behind. That matches the claim that the west side has 'today' while the east side has 'yesterday'. The claim simplifies things a little: the line bends away from 180° in places, and for a short time each day the two sides can be more than one date apart. These details don't contradict its main point.

text: The international date line, which separates two consecutive calendar days, runs roughly through the middle of the Pacific Ocean and passes through the اليمن (Yemen) Islands in the east.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science confirms that the International Date Line runs roughly north to south through the middle of the Pacific Ocean, so the first part of the claim is right. But the line does not pass through any 'Yemen Islands.' Yemen is on the Arabian Peninsula, far from the Pacific. In the east, the line actually bends to take in Kiribati and the Line Islands, and it also detours around the Aleutian Islands and other Pacific islands.

text: The intricate structure of the human eye is capable of distinguishing between over 10 million different colors.
label: supported
reason: Several sources give roughly the figure in the claim. They say humans can tell apart about, roughly, or up to 10 million colours: the Physics Factbook quotes "as many as 10 million", and USPTO patent texts say "roughly 10 million". Some popular sources also say "more than 10 million". There is one caveat. Most of the more reliable sources treat 10 million as an approximate upper estimate, not a figure that is exceeded, and other estimates are lower (about 2.3 to 7 million). So the word "over" slightly overstates the usual figure, but the claim matches the commonly cited estimate.

text: The language with the most dialects is Arabic, with estimates suggesting it has around 500-600 dialects spoken worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found backs the figure of 500–600 Arabic dialects. An arXiv paper on Arabic dialects cites Glottolog, which classifies Arabic dialects into five groups containing 38 dialects. Other sources give counts from about 25–35 major dialects up to 28 varieties by one official count, or a bit over 100 by another. Sources also disagree about which language has the most dialects, with Chinese often named, so nothing confirms that Arabic holds that title. Since the specific 500–600 estimate is far above every count found, the claim is contradicted.

text: The largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is big enough to fit all the other planets combined inside it, with a diameter of approximately 142,984 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Jupiter is the largest planet and is so big that all the other planets in the solar system could fit inside it. ESA and Britannica both give its equatorial diameter as 142,984 km, the figure in the claim. BBC Sky at Night Magazine adds that this works mathematically, by volume.

text: The largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, is more than 1,300 times the size of the Earth, with a diameter of approximately 142,984 kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Universe Today and NinePlanets both give Jupiter's equatorial diameter as 142,984 km. Universe Today also says its volume could hold about 1,321 Earths, which fits the claim that Jupiter is more than 1,300 times the size of Earth if 'size' means volume. Across its diameter, Jupiter is only about 11.2 times wider than Earth, but the common reading of this claim is by volume, so it holds. Jupiter is also the largest planet in the solar system.

text: The largest waterfall in the world, measured by volume of water, is actually an underwater waterfall located in the Denmark Strait between Greenland and Iceland.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Discover Wildlife quoting Guinness World Records, say the Denmark Strait Cataract is the world's largest waterfall. It sits underwater between Greenland and Iceland and carries about 5 million cubic metres of water per second, far more than any waterfall on land. This matches every part of the claim.

text: The length of a day on Venus is almost 243 Earth days due to its extremely slow rotation period.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources, including Caltech IPAC Cool Cosmos and Astronomy.com, say a day on Venus (one spin on its axis) lasts about 243 Earth days because Venus rotates very slowly. Measured values are about 243 days and 26–30 minutes, so 'almost 243' is close, though strictly the period is a little over 243. The claim matches the common sidereal definition of a day. Venus's solar day (sunrise to sunrise) is much shorter, about 117 Earth days.

text: The length of a day on Venus is equivalent to its year, with its rotation speed and orbital period around the Sun being synchronized, resulting in a 243 Earth-day-long day.
label: contradicted
reason: The 243 Earth-day figure is right, but the rest of the claim is wrong. Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once (its sidereal day) and about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. That makes its day longer than its year, so the two are not equal and its rotation is not synchronized with its orbit. NASA, as cited in the search results, and several fact-check sites all give these figures. Measured by the Sun (a solar day), a Venus day is about 117 Earth days, which also isn't the same as its year.

text: The length of a human fingerprint can be used to uniquely identify a person, with no two individuals having identical fingerprints.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable forensic sources agree that no two people have been found with identical fingerprints, including identical twins. However, they say identification relies on the pattern of friction ridges and furrows and on specific ridge details called minutiae, not on a fingerprint's length. Size is not a feature that makes a fingerprint unique, so the claim gets the basis of identification wrong.

text: The length of a standard American golf hole is 400 yards, however the longest hole in the world is 1,063 yards at the Indonesian Brighton Lloyd golf course.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable golf sources (Golf.com, Yahoo Sports, National Club Golfer) say the longest golf hole in the world is the 3rd hole at Gunsan Country Club in South Korea, a par-7 of about 1,097–1,100 yards. I found no sign of a 'Brighton Lloyd' golf course in Indonesia or of a 1,063-yard record hole. There is also no fixed 'standard' length of 400 yards for an American golf hole, since hole length depends on par.

text: The lengths of river Nile and Amazon River are often debated due to unknown discharge and erosion, and according to the most recent estimates, the lengths of both rivers are near to each other, which surpasses other major rivers in different counts.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is right: Nile and Amazon length estimates are close (about 6,650 km and 6,400 km in the usual figures, with some studies putting the Amazon slightly longer), and both are longer than other major rivers. The stated reason for the debate is wrong, though. Britannica and other sources say the main problem is deciding where each river starts and ends, plus measurement method and scale (the coastline paradox). They do not give 'unknown discharge and erosion' as the reason. Discharge is not uncertain in this context; the Amazon is well established as the largest river by volume.

text: The lhöng nuur, also known as the 'Black Tiger' caviar, is the rarest and most expensive caviar in the world, with prices reaching up to $10,000 per kilogram.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any trace of a caviar called "lhöng nuur" or "Black Tiger." Searching that name only brings up unrelated things, such as Black Tiger shrimp and the racehorse Black Caviar. Reliable sources also say a different caviar holds the title: Wikipedia names almas, the golden roe of rare albino beluga sturgeon, as the most expensive caviar. Luxe Digital puts Iranian Almas at up to $34,500 per kg, far above the $10,000 per kg in the claim, and Wikipedia lists ordinary beluga at $7,000 to $22,000 per kg. That contradicts the claim that "Black Tiger" is the rarest and most expensive caviar, topping out at $10,000 per kg.

text: The lifespan of a honeybee is typically around 6 weeks during the summer, but some bees can live up to 4 to 6 months during the winter.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up this claim. Blythewood Bee Company says worker bees live 4 to 6 weeks in summer, and that workers born in late summer or fall can live up to 6 months through the winter. A PMC/NCBI research article also gives a 4–6 week lifespan in spring and summer, and says winter bees can live several months, up to 8. Wikipedia gives up to 20 weeks (about 4.6 months) for winter workers. Taken together, these fit the claim of about 6 weeks in summer and 4 to 6 months for some winter bees.

text: The longer a human tongue, the greater the consumer's ability to enjoy sweet taste, research has found that long-tongued people can identify sweet flavors better than those with shorter tongues.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no research linking tongue length to sweet taste. The claim seems to garble a real ScienceDirect study (Pathak & Calvert) which found that long vowel sounds in words make people expect sweet tastes. That study is about the length of speech sounds, not tongues, and it measured expectations of sweetness, not the ability to detect it. Other taste research ties sweet sensitivity to how densely papillae (the bumps on the tongue) are packed, not to tongue length. The search results don't directly rule out a tongue-length effect, so this rests mainly on the claim misrepresenting what the study found.

text: The longer you keep a stick of butter at room temperature, the more it will break down into three components: butterfat, milk solids, and water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No source I found says butter gradually splits into butterfat, milk solids and water the longer it sits at room temperature. Sources confirm that butter is made of those three components (about 80% fat, plus water and milk solids). Wikipedia describes butter as a semi-solid emulsion at room temperature, and a Rutgers food scientist calls it a water-in-oil emulsion that can be left out for about two weeks. Baking sources say the emulsion breaks when butter gets too warm or melts, which depends on temperature, not on how long it sits out. Taste of Home says margarine left on the counter can separate, but does not say this about butter. These sources cast doubt on the claim without directly ruling it out. The search limit ended the research before a direct source could be found.

text: The longer you live, the longer your telomeres typically grow, with the rate of telomere growth generally slowing down as you age, along with rates of telomere shortening.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the direction wrong. Scientific sources say telomeres shorten with each cell division and over a person's lifetime, so short telomeres are linked to older age. They do not typically grow longer the longer you live. The rate of telomere attrition does tend to slow in later life, but that doesn't save the claim's main point that telomeres get longer with age.

text: The longer you use a pencil, the greener it becomes due to a waxy substance called graphite leaking onto your fingers.
label: contradicted
reason: Graphite is not a waxy substance. It is a crystalline form of carbon, and pencil lead is a mix of graphite and clay that ranges in color from light grey to black, not green. Nothing suggests that pencils turn greener the longer they are used, so the claim conflicts with what pencil graphite actually is.

text: The longest an xylophone has been played non-stop is 8 hours and 46 minutes, setting a Guinness World Record in 1978.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm this claim. My searches found Guinness World Records pages for marathon records on other instruments, including the oud, trumpet, saxophone, harmonica, piano and percussion. None of them mentioned a xylophone record. I found no source confirming or contradicting 8 hours 46 minutes, the year 1978, or that Guinness ever recognised such a record. I hit the search limit before I could run more targeted searches.

text: The longest cave system in the world is the Mammoth-Flashlight Cave system located in Roberts County, Texas, USA, which spans over 787 kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results show the world's longest cave system is the Mammoth Cave system in Kentucky, not Texas. The National Park Foundation says it has more than 400 miles explored, and Wikipedia lists it at about 685.6 km. There is no "Mammoth-Flashlight Cave" in Roberts County, Texas. The historic name for the connected system is Mammoth–Flint Ridge, and the 787 km figure does not match the reported length.

text: The longest keel ever laid on a ship was that of the USS Enterprise, a US Navy aircraft carrier commissioned in 1961, which had a keel that measured over 280 feet in length.
label: contradicted
