reason: Several sources, including UC Davis's Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program, WorldAtlas, CGTN and BirdSpot, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit the bird's unusual body design for this: a highly flexible ball-and-socket shoulder joint, wings that rotate about 180° and trace a figure-eight, and an unusually large share of body weight in flight muscle. One caveat: BirdSpot notes that some birds, such as herons and flycatchers, can flutter backwards for a short distance. Even so, hummingbirds are the only birds capable of true, sustained backward flight. Because the trustworthy sources agree on the core claim, it is supported.

text: The only bird that can fly backwards is the Hummingbird, due to its unique physiology, which includes extremely fast wingbeats and the ability to rotate its wings in reverse.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including a trustworthy one from UC Davis, say hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They credit this to fast wingbeats (720–5,400 per minute when hovering), unusually large flight muscles, and a shoulder joint that lets the wing rotate so the figure-eight stroke can be reversed. Wikipedia and WorldAtlas say the same. A few lower-quality blogs claim sunbirds, kingfishers or honeyeaters can briefly move backwards, but even those mostly agree that only hummingbirds can sustain controlled backward flight. The claim's core points are therefore supported.

text: The percentage of the Earth's surface that is covered in water is approximately 71%.
label: supported
reason: Two trustworthy government sources say this directly. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation states that "Water covers about 71% of the earth's surface," and NASA's Space Place says water covers 71 percent of Earth's surface. CK-12 also gives the same figure, and none of the sources found disagree.

text: The percentage of water on Earth is approximately 71%, with about 97.5% of it being found in the oceans.
label: contradicted
reason: The 71% part is right: water covers about 71% of Earth's surface. The ocean figure is wrong, though. USGS data, as cited by Phys.org, puts about 96.5% of Earth's water in the oceans, not 97.5%. The 97.5% figure is the share of all saline water, which also counts saline groundwater and salt lakes, against the roughly 2.5% that is freshwater. Some sources, such as NOAA, round the ocean share to about 97%, so the error is small, but the specific 97.5% ocean figure confuses total saltwater with ocean water.

text: The permafrost in the Arctic region is estimated to hold about 1,400 gigatons of carbon, which is more than twice the amount of carbon emissions released through human activities since the Industrial Revolution.
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that Arctic permafrost holds about 1,400 gigatons of carbon. Yale E360 and The Arctic Institute say this is about four times what humans have emitted since the Industrial Revolution. Four times is more than twice, so the claim holds, but it understates the comparison. The 'twice' figure in these sources refers to the carbon in the atmosphere, not to human emissions.

text: The planet with the highest number of Earth-like planets discovered so far is a star called Kepler-452, with approximately 60% of its discovered planets showing similarities to Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA's Exoplanet Archive lists exactly one known planet for the star Kepler-452: Kepler-452b. A single planet cannot make up "about 60%" of a star's discovered planets, so that figure can't be right. Kepler-452 also doesn't hold the record. NASA/Caltech's Spitzer site says TRAPPIST-1 has the largest group of roughly Earth-size planets found in one star system (seven). The claim also calls Kepler-452 a "planet" and then a "star"; it is a star.

text: The planet with the longest rotation period in our solar system is Jupiter, which takes approximately 10 Earth hours to complete a single rotation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Guinness World Records says Venus has the longest rotation period of any major planet, about 243 Earth days. Jupiter spins once in roughly 10 hours, which makes it the planet with the shortest day, not the longest.

text: The process of gardening, especially with tomatoes, is so in tune with the fiber and microbes in the stomach aiding our digestive system that a study found that eating a complete tomato plant after cultivation,minus the root ,has positive impact and increase gut and fiber in stomach.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no study showing that eating a whole tomato plant, minus the root, after growing it improves gut microbes or raises fiber. My searches were cut short by a tool limit, so I only got partial results. One returned source covered whether tomato leaves are edible, given the debate over tomatine, a natural compound in the leaves and stems that has long been considered toxic. Another was a trial in which people who ate a varied, high-fibre plant-based diet had better gut microbiomes; this was about diet, not eating whole plants. From background knowledge, not from these searches, I know of a separate study (Litt et al., CU Boulder, Lancet Planetary Health, 2023) that linked community gardening to higher fiber intake, probably because gardeners ate more produce. That study did not involve eating whole plants. No search result directly confirms or rules out the claim's specific study, so I can't verify it.

text: The province of Quebec in Canada has the highest number of outdoor hot springs in the world, with over 70 natural hot springs located within its territory.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no support for this claim, and several sources point the other way. Quebec's geology doesn't produce natural hot springs, and what get called 'hot springs' there are mostly Nordic spas and man-made thermal pools. Canada's natural hot springs are concentrated in the western provinces, mainly British Columbia and Alberta. Destination Canada also says the country's largest natural mineral hot springs are at Fairmont Hot Springs in BC. So the claim that Quebec has over 70 natural hot springs, the most in the world, is false.

text: The quartz crystal found in Iceland's Olafsvellir glacier holds a world record for the oldest known piece of climate data with an age of over 360,000 years.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found nothing about an 'Olafsvellir glacier' or a quartz crystal from Iceland holding a climate-data record, so the claim appears to be made up. Trustworthy sources also contradict the record itself. SCAR and Science report an Antarctic ice core from the Allan Hills with ice about 2.7 million years old. Other ice cores, such as EPICA at 800,000 years and a newer core at 1.2 million years, are also far older than 360,000 years. So a 360,000-year-old sample could not hold the world record for the oldest climate data.

text: The random number generator in some Microsoft Excel versions has a bug that introduces bias, causing numbers generated using "RAND" to favor certain numbers.
label: supported
reason: Good sources back the main point: some Excel versions had flawed random number generators. Microsoft admitted a flaw in Excel 2003's RAND and RANDBETWEEN functions. MrExcel showed that after repeated recalculation, RAND began returning negative numbers 'with a funny distribution' instead of values spread evenly between 0 and 1. That bug was later fixed in a hotfix. Separately, versions before Excel 2003 had a short period and failed standard randomness tests, and academic papers (McCullough, and arXiv 1503.08376) rate RAND in Excel 97, 2003 and 2007 as 'inadequate', with an implementation bug that lasted several versions. Taken together, this shows a bug that made RAND's output non-random and non-uniform, which is bias. However, the documented symptom is mainly impossible negative values and failed randomness tests, not a clear preference for particular numbers, so the 'favor certain numbers' wording is a loose description.

text: The reason honey is sticky is due to a combination of its high sugar content and the presence of a molecule called hydrogen peroxide, which creates a sticky, gel-like texture.
label: contradicted
reason: The sugar part of the claim is right, but the hydrogen peroxide part is wrong. Honey is sticky because it is a concentrated sugar solution: the hydroxyl groups on its sugars form a large network of hydrogen bonds with the small amount of water present, and that creates cohesion and adhesion (ScienceABC). Hydrogen peroxide is present in honey only in trace amounts, made by the enzyme glucose oxidase. It is known for honey's antibacterial effect, not its texture, and it does not form a gel. The claim seems to confuse hydrogen bonding with hydrogen peroxide.

text: The release of the marine mammal hippopotamus from its African habitats was first recorded and told in not one, but two Monroe Dooma diaries in the mid 19th century.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing about any "Monroe Dooma diaries", so the main point of the claim can't be checked. Searching that name only turned up unrelated pages, such as one about a hippo named Monroe at a Louisiana zoo. Reliable sources also cast doubt on part of the claim: Britannica and National Geographic Kids describe the hippo as an aquatic or semi-aquatic mammal of African rivers and wetlands, not a marine mammal. Because the central statement about the diaries can't be verified at all, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The rhinoceros has a highly developed senses, including a keen sense of hearing and smell, which help it detect predators from great distances.
label: supported
reason: Many sources agree that rhinos see poorly but have very good hearing and smell, and that they use these senses to pick up danger from far off. ScienceDaily (Acoustical Society of America) says rhinos have some of the keenest hearing in the animal kingdom and can sense predators coming from miles away. Wildlife SOS and National Geographic say rhinos have excellent smell and hearing, and Wildlife SOS adds that they can sense danger from far away. The claim's wording 'highly developed senses' is a slight overstatement because rhino eyesight is weak, but it names hearing and smell specifically, and those parts are well supported.

text: The sacred Baboon, a species of baboon found in Ethiopia, was considered a sacred animal in ancient Ethiopian culture and is often depicted in rock art and other ancient artifacts.
label: contradicted
reason: The species part is correct: the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas), also called the sacred baboon, lives in Ethiopia and the wider Horn of Africa. The cultural part is not. Reliable sources (Scientific American, the San Diego Zoo, a UC eScholarship paper, Britannica) say the baboon was sacred in ancient Egypt, where it was revered as a form of the god Thoth and shown in Egyptian statues, amulets and wall paintings. The Egyptians had to import it, and research traces their baboons to a source region covering present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. None of the sources describe the baboon as sacred in ancient Ethiopian culture, and none mention it appearing in Ethiopian rock art. The claim gives Ethiopia credit for what was an Egyptian belief. Strictly, no source says outright that Ethiopians did not revere it, but every account of the 'sacred' status points to Egypt.

text: The scent of cucumbers is primarily created by a compound called sesquiterpene, which is also found in lavender.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific sources say cucumber scent comes mainly from C9 aldehydes, especially (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal ("cucumber aldehyde") and nonenal. It does not come from a sesquiterpene. "Sesquiterpene" is also the name of a broad class of compounds, not a single compound. So the claim misidentifies the main source of the smell.

text: The shallowest lake in the world is Caspian Sea, but if you are referring to a freshwater lake, the title belongs to the donald triplets' lake in america alternatively the title is given to lake Bonny Scotland however, the title goes to Tulare lake in California that sits at an average depth of
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong from its first statement. The Caspian Sea is not the world's shallowest lake. It is the largest lake on Earth by area and volume, with an average depth of about 187–211 m and a maximum depth of about 1,025 m. The rest of the claim is jumbled and can't be checked: 'the donald triplets' lake' doesn't clearly refer to any real lake, 'Lake Bonny Scotland' is unclear, and the sentence breaks off before giving a depth for Tulare Lake.

text: The shallowest point on Earth is the Dead Sea, with a depth of approximately 1,400 feet (430 meters) but an area less than 1 foot (0.3 meters) deep in some parts.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up elevation and depth. Wikipedia gives the Dead Sea a maximum depth of about 298 m (978 ft) and an average depth of about 188 m. The roughly 430 m (1,400 ft) figure is the lake surface's elevation below sea level, not its depth. Wikipedia lists the surface at about 440 m below sea level, which makes its shores the lowest land elevation on Earth. The Dead Sea is not the "shallowest point on Earth". It is known as the lowest point on land, so the claim's main framing and its depth figure are both wrong.

text: The shape of the Grooved Ware pot from 4600 BCE found in Finland, known as 'Orvas', is the earliest known example of tattooing evidence discovered in the archeological record.
label: contradicted
reason: Grooved Ware is a Late Neolithic pottery style from Britain and Ireland. Museum sources date it to about 3000–2100 BCE, so a Finnish Grooved Ware pot from 4600 BCE doesn't fit the record. I found nothing about a pot called 'Orvas'. Sources such as National Geographic and Wikipedia place the earliest direct evidence of tattooing in preserved human skin (for example Ötzi the Iceman), not in the shape of a pot. The claim's key details clash with reliable sources.

text: The short fiber optic strand used for the first telephone call in 1876 was approximately 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) long.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The first telephone call, made by Alexander Graham Bell to Thomas Watson on March 10, 1876, went over a thin copper wire between two nearby rooms. It did not use a fiber optic strand, and it was nowhere near 2 km long. Fiber optic communication was not developed until the mid-to-late 20th century.

text: The short-sighted moth species, Mastophora cerebralis, uses threads to catch its prey, and it can do this in complete darkness due to its highly developed sensory organs.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results show that Mastophora is a genus of bolas spiders (orb-weavers), not moths. These spiders are moth predators: females hang from a silk line and swing a sticky "bolas" at moths they lure in, and they partly rely on mimicking moth pheromones. So calling Mastophora cerebralis a "short-sighted moth species" is wrong. The search also didn't confirm that "Mastophora cerebralis" exists as a named species; the World Spider Catalog genus excerpt lists M. corumbatai and M. cranion but not cerebralis. The search also found nothing to back the claims about catching prey in complete darkness thanks to highly developed sense organs.

text: The short-term memory of the common eel can remember the location of a food source for up to 2 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source showing that eels remember where food is for up to 2 years. The research on eel memory I found is on spatial learning in Japanese eels (Anguilla japonica). Those studies show eels can learn locations in a maze, but they don't report anything about remembering food sites over 2 years. The fish studies that do measure how long food-location memories last involve other species, such as African cichlids at 12 days. The claim also has two problems of its own. 'Common eel' is vague, and a memory lasting 2 years would be long-term memory, not 'short-term memory'. Since no evidence confirms or directly refutes the claim, the result is inconclusive.

text: The sizeof an ostrich egg is about 15 centimeters long and 12 centimeters wide, yet only weighs between 1.9 pounds and 3 pounds.
label: contradicted
reason: The size is roughly right. Wikipedia gives an average of 15 cm long and 13 cm wide, and southafrica.co.za says an ostrich egg is about 15 cm long and 12–13 cm wide. The weight range is wrong, though. Wikipedia gives an average weight of 1.4 kg (3.1 lb). Simple Wikipedia and visualizevolume give about 1.5 kg (3.3 lb), and Baidu Baike gives 1.5–2.5 kg. An ostrich farm lists eggs at 4–5 lb. These typical weights are above the claim's 3 lb upper limit. No source supports a weight as low as 1.9 lb. The Smithsonian's National Zoo says an average egg weighs around 3 pounds, which is close to the upper limit but does not support the low end. Because the egg is heavier than the stated 1.9–3 lb range, the claim is contradicted.

text: The smallest county in the world by area is Caraballeda in Venezuela and the smallest in England is Eastleigh (part of Northumberland).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on the England part. Sources say Rutland is England's smallest county, at about 382 km². Eastleigh is not a county at all: it is a borough (a local government district) in Hampshire, not part of Northumberland. Because that part is clearly false, the whole claim is contradicted. I didn't separately check the Caraballeda part, but Caraballeda is a town in Venezuela, not a recognised 'smallest county in the world'.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, has a unique rotation period where its day is actually the same length as its year, which takes approximately 59 Earth days to complete.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets Mercury's periods wrong. Mercury is the smallest planet, and it does take about 59 Earth days to spin once on its axis (58.646 days). But its year, one trip around the Sun, takes about 88 Earth days, so the rotation is 2/3 of the orbit, not equal to it. Measured from one noon to the next, a Mercury solar day lasts about 176 Earth days, which is twice its year. Either way, Mercury's day is not the same length as its year.

text: The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury, rotates three times on its axis for every two times it orbits the sun.
label: supported
reason: The claim checks out on both points. The ESA and the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory both say Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system. Both sources also say it spins three times on its axis for every two orbits around the Sun, which is called a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance. Britannica adds that Mercury's 58.6-day rotation period is exactly two-thirds of its 88-day orbit.

text: The smell that you get when you cut a cucumber comes from a compound called "furocoumarin" which is produced by the cell damage caused by the cutting.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong compound. Research on cucumber flavor says the fresh cucumber smell comes mainly from (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal, with (E)-2-nonenal as the second most important odor compound. These are C9 aldehydes that the plant produces when its tissue is damaged, for example by cutting or chewing. So the part about cell damage is right, but the compound is not furocoumarin. Furocoumarins are a different, unrelated class of plant chemicals and do not cause cucumber's smell.

text: The strange Satan cane mushroom in the fungus kingdom is known for growing sequins-like features, which can achieve quantities in their scales that reach 50,000 to a single unit.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any mushroom called the "Satan cane mushroom" in reliable sources. The closest match is Satan's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas), a poisonous European bolete. The sources I found describe its colours, its toxicity and the trees it grows with, but none mention sequin-like features or scales numbering 50,000 per mushroom. Searches for those details only turned up craft products. Because it's unclear which species the claim means, and its specific details can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The stridulation sound produced by a cricket's wing is created through the movement of a specific organ located on the underside of the wing, which pops together to generate the characteristic chirping noise.
label: contradicted
reason: KQED explains that crickets stridulate by rubbing: the sharp edge of one forewing (the scraper) is drawn along a toothed vein (the file) on the underside of the other forewing, and the resulting vibrations make the chirp. The file is on the underside of the wing, but the sound comes from scraping, not from an organ that "pops together." Popping or buckling is closer to how cicada tymbals work, which is a different mechanism.

text: The study of vibrations in atoms and molecules is known as vibronics, but more generally and legitimately this field is known as molecular vibrations.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the meaning of "vibronics" wrong. The IUPAC Gold Book defines a vibronic transition as one involving a change in both the electronic and the vibrational quantum numbers, as opposed to a purely vibrational one. Wikipedia also says "vibronic" combines "vibrational" and "electronic" and refers to how the two kinds of interaction in a molecule affect each other. Dictionaries (Wiktionary, Merriam-Webster) agree. So vibronics is about electronic–vibrational coupling, not the general study of vibrations in atoms and molecules. That general field is molecular vibrations or vibrational spectroscopy, so the claim's premise is contradicted.

text: The sugars we commonly consume, including glucose and fructose, are actually like liquid gold to bees, as they use them to create honey through regurgitation and evaporation.
label: supported
reason: PerfectBee, a beekeeping resource, explains how bees make honey. They collect nectar, a sugar solution, and store it in their honey stomach. The enzyme invertase breaks the nectar's sucrose into glucose and fructose. Bees regurgitate the nectar and pass it from bee to bee, then store it in wax cells, where evaporation and wing-fanning cut the water content from about 60% to 18%. Glucose and fructose are sugars people commonly eat, and bees turn them into honey through regurgitation and evaporation, so the claim's main point holds. Two caveats: 'liquid gold' is a figure of speech, and strictly speaking bees work from flower nectar rather than the sugar people buy and eat.

text: The surface of the Earth is approximately 71% water, with around 96.5% of that water found in oceans.
label: supported
reason: The USGS Water Science School says that about 71 percent of the Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5 percent of all Earth's water. The claim's wording ('96.5% of that water') is slightly loose, since USGS means 96.5% of all water on Earth rather than just the surface water. Still, that is clearly the figure the claim is citing, and both numbers match.

text: The surfaced area of Europe is roughly 10.18 million square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia gives Europe's area as about 10,186,000 km², which is roughly 10.18–10.19 million km². Other sources also say about 10.18 million km². The claim's odd wording, "surfaced area", most plausibly just means the continent's surface area.

text: The suspension bridge in Puente Romano, Mexico has a span of approximately 254 feet and was originally built by the ancient Mayan civilization in the 14th century, making it one of the oldest known stone bridges in the Americas.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no Mayan suspension bridge at a place called "Puente Romano" in Mexico. Bridges named Puente Romano are Roman bridges in Spain, such as the one at Mérida. The only known Mayan suspension bridge is the hypothesized one at Yaxchilan in Chiapas. Its main span is given as 63 m (207 ft), not about 254 ft, and it dates to the 7th century, not the 14th. It was a suspension footbridge, not a stone bridge, and it has been destroyed. The 14th century appears only as the point until which it may have been the world's longest span. So the location, span, date and construction type in the claim are all contradicted.

text: The total surface area of the Earth is approximately 510,065,600 square kilometers.
label: supported
reason: Several sources put Earth's total surface area at about 510 million km². One of them, a page on au1.ucar.edu, gives the exact figure of 510,065,600 km². That page appears to be AI-generated content on a UCAR subdomain rather than an official UCAR publication, so it's a weak source on its own. However, the figure is consistent with standard references such as Wikipedia/NASA, which give about 510,072,000 km² (roughly 5.1 × 10^8 km²). Since the claim says 'approximately', the small difference in the exact number does not matter.

text: The total surface area of the human brain is estimated to be around 2,100 square centimeters (325 square inches), but it only weighs around 1.4 kilograms (3.1 pounds).
label: supported
reason: Both numbers in the claim fall within published estimates. A UC Davis Health report on a 2024 brain-imaging study gives average cortical surface areas of 2,056 to 2,104 cm², depending on birth decade. Britannica gives about 2,000 cm² (310 sq in), and HowStuffWorks gives 1,500 to 2,000 cm². Converting 2,100 cm² gives about 325 sq in, so that figure is consistent. Some sources, such as Chudler's Brain Facts page, give a higher 2,500 cm², but that is part of the normal range of estimates rather than a contradiction of 'around 2,100'. The adult brain weight of about 1.4 kg (about 3 lb) is a standard figure. The claim does not cite a source for the weight, and I did not check it against a specific page.

text: The unique smell often associated with strawberries is caused by the chemical methyl anthranilate, which is also found in grapefruits and other fruits.
label: contradicted
reason: Methyl anthranilate is well known as the signature flavor compound of Concord grapes, not strawberries, and has a grape-like smell. Strawberry aroma comes from a complex mix of more than 350 volatile compounds. The key contributors are furanones such as furaneol and mesifurane, along with methyl and ethyl esters. Methyl anthranilate is only one minor contributor in some strawberry varieties. The claim also says it is found in grapefruits, but the sources link it to grapes, neroli, bergamot and apple flavor, not grapefruit, whose signature aroma compound is nootkatone. Saying methyl anthranilate causes strawberry's characteristic smell therefore goes against the evidence.

text: The unique sound produced by a whip cracking is not actually the lash itself, but the air column that forms between the lash and the handle, creating a loud 'crack' when the air column collapses.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say a whip's crack is a small sonic boom. It happens when part of the whip, either the tip or a loop moving along it, goes faster than the speed of sound (Scientific American, Wikipedia, and Goriely's research). No source describes an air column forming between the lash and the handle and then collapsing. The mechanism in the claim is wrong.

text: The universe is composed of approximately 70% dark energy, 25% dark matter, and 5% normal matter.
label: supported
reason: NASA's WMAP page gives the universe's contents as 71.6% dark energy, 24% dark matter and 4.6% atoms (normal matter). Later Planck-era figures from NASA and Wikipedia are about 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter and 5% ordinary matter. Both sets of numbers fit the claim's approximate 70/25/5 split.

text: The upper atmosphere of Venus rotates in the opposite direction of its orbit around the sun.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say Venus's atmosphere superrotates in a retrograde (westward) direction, the same way the solid planet turns. The Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy says the cloud layer rotates in about 4 days compared with 243 days for the planet, and that "Both rotations are in a retrograde direction." Here, retrograde means turning opposite to the direction of Venus's orbit, as the Wikipedia and arXiv sources confirm. So the upper atmosphere does rotate in the opposite direction to Venus's orbit around the Sun.

text: The vulcan hammer was a type of pickaxe-like tool known for use in racism and slavery practices but actually, was used by careless landowners, company supported  strict labor codes for exploitation as early Anglo- American lessons gave obligated One welding slags.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-documented 'Vulcan hammer' is the pile-driving hammer made by Vulcan Iron Works, an air/steam or drop hammer used to drive piles in construction. It was not a pickaxe-like tool and has no documented link to racism or slavery. Much of the rest of the claim (careless landowners, strict labor codes, 'Anglo-American lessons', 'welding slags') is too garbled to check, but the core description of the tool contradicts what reliable sources say.

text: The word "_flight" was first used in the English language to describe birds moving through the air, and the word later came to describe human-made aircraft.
label: supported
reason: Reliable dictionaries back both parts of the claim. Etymonline and Merriam-Webster trace 'flight' to Old English flyht, meaning 'a flying, act or power of flying.' Merriam-Webster dates its first known use to before the 12th century, in the sense of passing through the air by the use of wings, which is how birds fly. Etymonline adds that the sense 'an instance of flight' is from 1785 and was first used of ballooning. Modern dictionaries now list trips by airplane and other aircraft as senses of the word. So the word started with winged creatures and later extended to human-made aircraft. One caveat: the sources say 'by the use of wings' (Merriam-Webster's example is a bee) rather than birds alone, but this does not contradict the claim.

text: The world's driest desert, the Atacama Desert in Chile, is also home to the Lynn and William White Pond, a 3-acre body of water that is found between two parallel mountain ranges.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Trustworthy sources such as Live Science and the Schmidt Ocean Institute confirm that the Atacama in Chile is often called the driest desert in the world. They also confirm it lies between two mountain ranges, the Andes and the Chilean Coastal Range. However, I could not find any trace of a 'Lynn and William White Pond' in the Atacama. Searches for that name only turned up unrelated ponds in Massachusetts and lithium evaporation ponds at the Salar de Atacama. Because the main point of the claim, the 3-acre pond, cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: The world's largest waterfall, based on volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract.
label: supported
reason: HowStuffWorks and other sources describe the Denmark Strait cataract as the world's largest waterfall. It lies entirely underwater between Greenland and Iceland and carries about 5 million cubic meters of water per second, roughly 2,000 times more than Niagara Falls. That backs both parts of the claim: it's underwater, and it's the biggest by volume.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually not visible on the surface as it is located underwater and is known as "RS Upsurge" or "The 150m underwater waterfall" which is an underwater waterfall in the North Atlantic.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is right that the world's largest waterfall is underwater in the North Atlantic. It is wrong about the name and the size. Reliable sources (Live Science, Wikipedia, BBC Discover Wildlife) identify it as the Denmark Strait cataract, between Greenland and Iceland. Its water drops about 3,500 m (11,500 ft), not 150 m. None of the sources call it "RS Upsurge" or "The 150m underwater waterfall."

text: The world's largest waterfall, in terms of volume of water, is actually under the surface of the ocean and is located off the coast of Africa, specifically near the country of Mauritania.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is right that the world's largest waterfall is underwater, but it puts it in the wrong place. Live Science and other sources identify it as the Denmark Strait cataract, which lies beneath the Denmark Strait between Greenland and Iceland in the North Atlantic. It is not off the coast of Africa or near Mauritania.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is a continental-sized underwater mountain system that stretches over 65,000 kilometers across the globe.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Ocean Exploration and WHOI both describe the mid-ocean ridge system as Earth's longest, most extensive mountain range. They put its length at about 65,000 km (40,390 miles) and say more than 90% of it lies underwater. Wikipedia's list of the longest mountain chains also gives about 65,000 km. One wording difference: these sources say 'nearly' 65,000 km, while the claim says 'over.' Other sources give figures as high as about 80,000 km depending on what is counted, so I treat this as a small rounding difference that doesn't change the claim. The global, underwater, continental-scale description matches the sources.

text: The world's longest mountain range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge, which is over 65,000 kilometers long and runs through the ocean floor.
label: supported

text: There are approximately 100 billion neurons in the human brain, which is constantly generating and eliminating neurons at an astonishing rate throughout a person's lifetime.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure of about 100 billion neurons is a common rough estimate (newer counts put it nearer 86 billion), so that part is broadly fine. The rest of the claim is wrong. Research shows adult human neurogenesis is limited and much slower than in rodents. It happens mainly in the hippocampus, where 14C dating suggests about 700 new neurons per day, a tiny share of the total. Most neurons are never replaced, and the limited neurogenesis is cited as one reason the human brain cannot repair itself after injury. The brain does not generate and eliminate neurons 'at an astonishing rate' throughout life.

text: There are approximately 100 trillion microorganisms living in and around the human body, outnumbering human cells by a ratio of 1.3 to 1.

That study estimated about 38 trillion bacteria (roughly 30–50 trillion) against about 30 trillion human cells, not 100 trillion microbes. The 100-trillion figure is an older estimate that went with the discredited 10:1 ratio. The two numbers don't fit together: 100 trillion microbes at 1.3:1 would mean about 77 trillion human cells, which contradicts the revised count of about 30 trillion. So the claim's 100-trillion figure is contradicted by the same research that produced the 1.3:1 ratio.

text: There are more neutrons in an atomic nucleus than there are protons and electrons combined in a neutral atom.
label: contradicted
reason: In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons (Z), so protons plus electrons comes to 2Z. For the claim to hold, the neutron count would have to be more than 2Z. Stable nuclei actually have neutron-to-proton ratios of about 1.0 for light elements and about 1.5 for heavy ones. That means the neutron count is always well below 2Z. For example, U-238 has 146 neutrons against 92+92=184 protons and electrons, and hydrogen-1 has no neutrons at all. Only a few very short-lived, exotic isotopes such as helium-8 would fit the claim, so as a general statement it is false.

The best-known estimate (Mora et al. 2011, reported by ScienceDaily) puts the total at about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million. That count covers all complex life, including fungi and protists, so plants and animals alone come to only about 8 million, not over 10 million. Some sources do cite a wider range of 3 to 100 million, but the most precise estimate is below 10 million. On extinction, National Geographic, AMNH and Discovery say more than 99% (AMNH says at least 99.9%) of species that ever lived are extinct. 'More than 80-90%' is technically true but badly understates that consensus. Because the '10 million plants and animals' figure goes against the standard estimate, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 100 known languages that exist in the Japanese language family, which-played a great role in forming Japan's rich linguistic and cultural diversity.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources describe the Japonic (Japanese) language family as a small group, not one with over 100 languages. Its known members are Japanese and the Ryukyuan languages: Okinawan, Kunigami, Amami, Miyako, Yaeyama and Yonaguni. Most counts give about a dozen languages, so the claim of "over 100 known languages" is false.

text: There are over 100,000 known species of insects on Earth, but scientists believe that the actual number could be as high as 30 million.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says there are more than 925,000 identified insect species, which meets the claim's 'over 100,000' (the claim understates the real figure, but what it says is true). The same source says estimates of the total range from about 2 million to as high as 30 million. Smithsonian figures and Terry Erwin's well-known estimate say the same.

text: There are over 200 billion trees on Earth, which is approximately 5 trillion leaves, accounting for about 28% of the Earth's total oxygen.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2015 Crowther et al. study in Nature, covered by Yale/phys.org, CNN and EarthSky, puts the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion. So "over 200 billion" is technically true, but it is off by more than ten times. The leaf figure is clearly wrong. Five trillion leaves across billions or trillions of trees would mean only a few leaves per tree. Common estimates instead assume a mature tree carries hundreds of thousands of leaves, which works out to roughly 10^17 leaves in total. The 28% oxygen figure is a popular claim usually attributed to rainforests, and the searches did not confirm it. Because the leaf figure is badly off and the tree count misstates the scale, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 30 million trees in Arbor Day's official global tally, but only about 3.6 million individual trees are actually planted every year worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim is wrong. Sources citing UNEP figures say about 1.8 to 1.9 billion trees are planted worldwide each year, which is roughly 5 million a day. The claim's figure of about 3.6 million a year is far too low. The first half is literally true but understated: the Arbor Day Foundation has helped plant more than 500 million trees since 1972, so its tally is well over 30 million. Because of the wrong annual figure, the claim is contradicted.

text: There are over 300,000 trees in the Amazon rainforest, but to one person they are all different - each tree gives shade to a fifth of the world's birds.
label: contradicted
reason: BBC Science Focus says the Amazon holds about 390 billion trees from around 16,000 species. So "over 300,000 trees" is technically true but understates the real number by about a millionfold. The bigger problem is the second half of the claim. No single tree shades a fifth of the world's birds; that is physically impossible. The figure seems to be a garbled version of the Amazon as a whole being home to a large share of the world's bird species (over 1,000 species, per the same source). The "to one person they are all different" line is vague and can't be checked.

text: There are over 320 species of orchids that are found in the wild in Madagascar, making up around 10% of the island's total plant species.
label: contradicted
reason: Madagascar has far more than about 320 wild orchid species. A study of Madagascar's orchid diversity (IRD/ResearchGate) records 913–917 species collected there, mostly endemic, and estimates the true total at roughly 986–1,050. Madagascar's flora is commonly put at about 11,000–14,000 species, though the search did not confirm this figure. On that basis, about 1,000 orchids would make up roughly 10%, while about 320 would be only about 2–3%. 'Over 320' is technically true, but the claim's figure badly understates the real number and doesn't fit the 10% share it gives.

text: There are over 33,000 known species of ants on Earth, but scientists estimate that the actual number of ant species could be as high as 100,000 or more.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say roughly 12,500 to 15,000 ant species have been described, so "over 33,000 known species" is wrong. Scientists usually put the likely total at about 22,000 species, not 100,000 or more. Wikipedia and iNaturalist both say more than 13,800 (or 12,500) of an estimated 22,000 species have been described, and BBC Science Focus gives about 12,000 described.

text: There are over 37 million active jellyfish in the world's oceans, with their population being sustainable due to their unique ability to regenerate their bodies.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no scientific estimate of the total number of jellyfish in the world's oceans, so the specific "37 million" figure can't be verified. Taken literally, "over 37 million" is almost certainly true but far too low to be meaningful. Palau's Jellyfish Lake alone has held more than 30 million jellies in some years, and blooms of Nomura's jellyfish off Japan are reported in the billions. The second part of the claim is not supported. Only a few species, such as the "immortal" Turritopsis jellyfish, can reverse their life cycle. Scientific sources (Frontiers in Marine Science, JellyWatch) say populations persist and bloom through reproduction: one medusa can carry thousands to millions of larvae, and polyps clone themselves asexually. That is different from bodily regeneration making populations sustainable. Because the number is unsourced and the explanation is unsupported or misleading, the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: There are over 387 billion Bayer-Yucaipa Dole redwood trees in the world but the contents within this message is something you may not know.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any tree species or variety called a "Bayer-Yucaipa Dole redwood." Searches only turned up unrelated pages about redwoods in general (coast redwood, giant sequoia, dawn redwood) and common trees in Yucaipa, CA. Without a real entity to check, the claim can't be verified. The 387 billion figure also looks very unlikely: real redwoods are endangered and grow only in a small range. The second half of the claim ("the contents within this message is something you may not know") isn't a factual statement that can be checked at all.

text: There are over 50 billion trees on Earth, with the Amazon rainforest containing approximately 40% of them.
label: contradicted
reason: There are about 3 trillion trees on Earth, so "over 50 billion" is technically true. The 40% figure is wrong, though. The Amazon has about 390 billion trees, which is roughly 13% of the global total, not about 40%.

text: There are over 60,000 known species of plants in the Amazon rainforest, which is estimated to account for around 10% of all the known plant species on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources put the number of plant species in the Amazon well below 60,000. WWF says the Amazon has about 40,000 plant species, and many other sources repeat that figure. A PNAS checklist, as reported by Atlas Obscura, counts 14,003 confirmed seed plant species in the lowland Amazon rainforest. The '10%' figure also doesn't match the claim: sources say the Amazon holds about 10% of all known species on Earth, not 10% of known plant species. The '60,000' figure is not supported.

text: There are over 70% of the Earth's surface covered by water, with approximately 96.5% of it being saltwater and the remaining 3.5% being freshwater.
label: contradicted
reason: USGS confirms that about 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water and that the oceans hold about 96.5% of Earth's water. The claim goes wrong on the rest. USGS says only about 2.5% of Earth's water is freshwater, which it rounds to "about three percent." The other roughly 1% is also salty, such as saline groundwater and salt lakes. So the claim that all of the remaining 3.5% is freshwater is incorrect.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, according to a 2016 estimate by the troubled Filander Institute for Biodiversity Research.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-known estimate of about 8.7 million species does not come from a 2016 study by a "Filander Institute for Biodiversity Research." It comes from a 2011 PLoS Biology paper by Camilo Mora and colleagues, which Census of Marine Life scientists announced in August 2011. A search found no organization called the Filander Institute for Biodiversity Research, so it appears to be made up. The claim gets other details wrong too. The figure was about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million, not "over" 8.7 million. It also counts all eukaryotic species, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. The year and source in the claim are wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, although only a small fraction of them have been discovered and documented by scientists.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the widely cited 2011 Mora et al. study (PLoS Biology), which estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. The study also found that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described, so only a small fraction have been documented. Two details are looser than the source. The study gives roughly 8.7 million, not 'over' 8.7 million. That total also includes fungi and protists: animals (~7.77M) and plants (~298K) together come to about 8.1M. Still, the main point, an estimate of about 8.7 million species with most still undiscovered, is backed by reliable sources.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only 15% of all the possible species that may exist, according to the Clements World Species Count.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), not a "Clements World Species Count." The Clements Checklist only covers birds. The claim also misreads the number: 8.7 million is the estimated total of eukaryotic species on Earth, not a count of known species. Only about 1.2–2.2 million of those had been described, and most were thought to remain undiscovered (86% of land species). So 8.7 million is not just 15% of all possible species, and the source is misattributed.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only a fraction of the total number of species that ever existed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is a 2011 estimate by Mora et al. of about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species. It is not a count of more than 8.7 million plants and animals. That total also includes fungi, protozoa and chromists. In that study, animals (about 7.77 million) and plants (about 0.3 million) add up to roughly 8.1 million, which is below 8.7 million. So the 'over 8.7 million plants and animals' part misstates the estimate. The idea that most species that ever lived are extinct is widely accepted, but the main figure is wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals on Earth, which is estimated to be only about 5% of all the species that have ever existed on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is roughly right. It comes from the 2011 Mora et al. estimate of eukaryotic species, though that is an estimate (about 8.7 million), not 'over' 8.7 million. The 5% figure is wrong. Trusted sources (Wikipedia citing scientific literature, National Geographic, CK-12) say more than 99% of all species that ever lived are extinct. That means species alive today make up less than 1% of all species that have ever existed, not about 5%.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth according to estimates from the World Register of Marine Species and other taxonomic databases.
label: supported
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 Census of Marine Life study by Mora et al. The researchers based their estimate on the taxonomic clustering of about 1.2 million species listed in the Catalogue of Life and the World Register of Marine Species. Their total was 8.74 million eukaryote species (give or take 1.3 million), which is just over 8.7 million. The claim's wording is loose in two ways. First, WoRMS supplied data for the estimate rather than producing it. Second, the total covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not only plants and animals. Plants and animals alone account for about 8.07 million of the total. Still, the core claim matches the source: about 8.7 million species, estimated using WoRMS and other taxonomic databases.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, according to estimates based on DNA sequencing and other scientific research.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLOS Biology), but the claim gets three things wrong. First, that study estimated about 8.7 million eukaryotic species with a margin of plus or minus 1.3 million, so it is not 'over' 8.7 million. Second, the total includes fungi, protozoa and chromists, not just plants and animals. In the study's breakdown, animals (about 7.77 million) and plants (about 0.3 million) add up to roughly 8.1 million. Third, the estimate was not based on DNA sequencing. The team extrapolated from numerical patterns in the taxonomic hierarchy of species already described. Some other estimates, including ones based on DNA, give very different totals, from about 5 million up to a trillion if microbes are counted.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that exist on Earth, yet humans have only discovered and documented a small fraction of them.
label: supported
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from a 2011 study by Mora et al. in PLoS Biology, which was reported by the University of Hawaiʻi, National Geographic and Nature News. The study estimated that Earth has about 8.7 million species (give or take 1.3 million) and that about 86% of them have not yet been described. That backs up the claim's main point that humans have documented only a small fraction of species. The claim's wording is a bit loose in two places. First, 8.7 million is a central estimate with a wide margin of error, not a confirmed count of 'over' 8.7 million. Second, the estimate covers all eukaryotes, including fungi and protists, not just plants and animals. Neither point overturns the claim's main message.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that have been identified on Earth, according to estimates from the World Register of Marine Species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, from Dalhousie University and the Census of Marine Life. It did not come from the World Register of Marine Species. It is also an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, most of them still undescribed. It is not a count of species that have been identified: only about 1.2 million had been catalogued, including about 953,000 animals. The claim gets both the source and the meaning of the figure wrong.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that have existed on Earth, but scientists estimate that as many as 80 to 90 percent of them may have gone extinct.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both numbers wrong. Mora et al. (2011), the study behind the 8.7 million figure, estimates how many species live on Earth today. It is not a count of every species that has ever existed. The extinction share is also off: National Geographic, AMNH and Discovery all say more than 99% (AMNH says at least 99.9%) of all species that ever lived are now extinct, not 80 to 90 percent.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species of plants and animals that inhabit the Earth, out of which only about 1.3 million have been formally discovered and documented.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim seems to come from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), but it gets three details wrong. First, that study estimated about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million, not "over" 8.7 million. Second, the estimate covers all eukaryotes, including fungi, protozoa and chromists, not only plants and animals. Plants and animals together make up only about 8.1 million of the total. Third, the study says about 1.2 million species have been catalogued. The 1.3 million figure in the claim is actually the estimate's margin of error.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to a 2016 estimate by scientists, although new discoveries are continually adding to this number.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-known estimate of about 8.7 million species comes from Mora et al., published in PLoS Biology in August 2011, not from a 2016 study. The figure was also an estimate of about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) eukaryotic species, not "over 8.7 million." The best-known 2016 estimate (Locey & Lennon) was a very different number of about 1 trillion species, mostly microbes. Because the claim gives the wrong date for the figure, it is contradicted.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to a 2021 study, which is significantly more than the 1.3 million described species by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million estimate comes from the 2011 study by Mora et al., published in PLoS Biology (ScienceDaily, August 2011), not from a 2021 study. That study gave about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million, and said roughly 1.2 million had been catalogued. So the claim gets the year wrong and appears to mix up the ±1.3 million margin with the number of described species.

text: There are over 8.7 million different species on Earth, according to estimates by biologists, although only a small fraction of these have been formally identified and cataloged.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches a 2011 study by Mora et al. (PLoS Biology), which estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. ScienceDaily, the University of Hawaii and National Geographic all report the same figure. The study also found that about 86% of species have not yet been described, so scientists have cataloged fewer than 15%. That backs up the claim that only a small fraction have been formally identified. One small caveat: the study gives the figure as "about" 8.7 million rather than "over," but the true number could be higher, so the claim is still broadly consistent with the estimate.

text: There are over 8.7 million identified species on Earth, according to estimates from the most recent taxonomic assessment, but it's believed that the actual number of species could be much higher, potentially exceeding 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says there are more than 8.7 million *identified* species, but that is wrong. The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) comes from Mora et al. (2011) and is an estimate of the *total* number of eukaryote species on Earth. According to the same source, only about 1.25 million species have actually been described and catalogued so far. Some estimates do run much higher, but the central claim about identified species contradicts the source.

text: There are over 8.7 million megahertz in the known universe's frequency range,  but we can only hear a minuscule range of less than 0.003 megahertz.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives the human hearing range as about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). That span is roughly 0.02 MHz, more than six times the claim's figure of "less than 0.003 MHz." The other figure, "8.7 million MHz" (8.7 THz) for the universe's frequency range, has no clear basis. The electromagnetic spectrum goes far higher, with gamma rays above 10^19 Hz. Either way, the numbers in the claim don't hold up.

text: There are over 88 billion neurons in the human brain, which is equivalent to the number of stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results contradict both parts of the claim. Nature Scitable puts the human brain at about 86 billion neurons, not over 88 billion. It also puts the Milky Way at 200–400 billion stars and says the brain 'doesn't quite stack up.' Psychology Today gives the same figure of about 86 billion neurons and says the Milky Way has more stars than the brain has neurons. So the two numbers are not equivalent.

text: There is a fungus called oyster mushrooms that can break down plastic, specifically polypropylene, through a process involving enzymes that degrade the material.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results support part of the claim. Oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus ostreatus, a white-rot fungus) have been shown to break down some plastics, mainly polyethylene, LDPE and PLA, using enzymes such as laccase and manganese peroxidase. However, none of the trustworthy sources I found show oyster mushrooms breaking down polypropylene. The well-known polypropylene study from the University of Sydney (npj Materials Degradation, 2023) used two different fungi, Aspergillus terreus and Engyodontium album. That study also did not determine the mechanism, including whether enzymes were involved. Because the polypropylene part of the claim could not be verified, and the evidence does not directly contradict it either, the claim is inconclusive.

text: There is a species of jellyfish called the turbellarian that is biologically immortal, as it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong animal. The jellyfish known for being biologically immortal is Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish'. Britannica says it restarts its life cycle through transdifferentiation. Turbellarians are not jellyfish at all: they are a class of free-living flatworms in the phylum Platyhelminthes, while jellyfish belong to the phylum Cnidaria. So the description of the process is right, but calling the species 'the turbellarian' is false.

text: There is a species of jellyfish that is biologically immortal and can transform its body into a younger state through a process known as transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Britannica and EBSCO both describe Turritopsis dohrnii, called the 'immortal jellyfish', as able to change back into its juvenile polyp stage and restart its life cycle through transdifferentiation. Wikipedia also calls it biologically immortal. Britannica adds that it is technically a hydrozoan and not a 'true' jellyfish, but it is commonly called a jellyfish, so this detail does not undercut the claim.

text: There is a species of jellyfish that is immortal due to its ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (EBSCO Research Starters and Britannica) describe Turritopsis dohrnii, which is commonly called the "immortal jellyfish." When it is injured or starving, it can return to its juvenile (polyp) form and start its life cycle again. It does this through transdifferentiation, a process that turns specialized cells into other cell types. The claim says this "immortality" is biological, not literal: the jellyfish can still die from predators or disease. This is how the term is normally used, so the claim is supported.

text: There is a species of jellyfish that is immortal, due to its unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: supported
reason: Britannica, the Natural History Museum and a PubMed review all describe Turritopsis dohrnii as the "immortal jellyfish." They say it can turn back from an adult medusa into a juvenile polyp, restarting its life cycle, through a process called transdifferentiation. This is biological immortality: the jellyfish can still be killed by predators or disease, but the claim matches how these sources describe it.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the Monterey Bay in California that is immortal, as it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out. Reliable sources (Britannica, NOAA Ocean Today, Wikipedia, AMNH) describe the "immortal jellyfish" (Turritopsis dohrnii, also called T. nutricula). They say it can go back to its young polyp stage and that it does this through transdifferentiation. But none of the sources I found say this jellyfish lives in Monterey Bay, California. They say it was first found in the Mediterranean in 1883. The Monterey Bay results were about the Monterey Bay Aquarium's jelly exhibits in general, not this species living in the bay. My search limit ran out before I could check further, so I can't confirm or rule out the location part.

text: There is a type of jellyfish found in the coastal waters of the Monterey Bay in California, called the Turritopsis dohrnii, which has the unique ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Britannica and several other sources confirm that Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish,' can revert to a younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation. However, the species comes from the Mediterranean. Sources such as MarineBio and therealimmortaljellyfish.com say it has spread to California, but none of the sources I found mention it in Monterey Bay's coastal waters. The only Monterey Bay result was an informal blog that did not say the species lives there. Because the Monterey Bay part of the claim can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: There is an estimated 170 billion trees on Earth, but it is believed that over 50% of all tree species remain undocumented.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim conflict with published estimates. A 2015 Yale-led study in Nature put the number of trees on Earth at about 3.04 trillion, not 170 billion. A 2022 PNAS study (Gatti et al.) estimated about 73,000 tree species worldwide, of which about 9,000 are still undiscovered. That is roughly 12–14% undocumented, well short of more than 50%.

text: Theướ longwhiskered RAT is the largest rodent in Australia.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources name a different animal as Australia's largest rodent. DNA Zoo says the rakali (water rat, Hydromys chrysogaster) is the largest rodent in Australia and often weighs more than 1 kg. Phys.org names the giant woolly rat (Mallomys istapantap) as the largest rodent in the wider Australia–Oceania (Sahul) region. None of the results says a 'long-whiskered rat' is the largest; the giant white-tailed rat is another species often cited as one of the biggest. The claim's species name also looks garbled: it contains a stray character ('ướ'), and the intended animal may be the long-haired rat (Rattus villosissimus), a much smaller species.

text: Tibetan monks developed the ancient skill of manipulating their body temperature to such an extent that some can survive in extremely cold temperatures with body temperatures as low as 50°F (10°C).
label: contradicted
reason: The research says tummo meditation warms the body. It does not show monks surviving with a body temperature as low as 50°F (10°C). Herbert Benson's 1982 study found that the monks warmed their fingers and toes by up to about 17°F, and their rectal (core) temperature did not drop. Maria Kozhevnikov's 2013 study found that core temperature went up, sometimes into the mild fever range, while meditators sat in rooms near 0°C. None of these reliable sources (McGill's Office for Science and Society, Snopes, and a summary of the Kozhevnikov paper on ResearchGate) mentions a body temperature of 10°C. A core temperature that low would be fatal hypothermia. The part of the claim saying monks can control their body temperature is roughly supported, but the 50°F figure is contradicted.

text: Venom, a protein found in the fangs of certain snakes and insects,  is the fastest natural movement in the animal kingdom, moving at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour) when injected into its victim.
label: contradicted
reason: Venom is not the fastest natural movement in the animal kingdom. It is also not a single protein; it is a mixture of many compounds. Scientific sources credit the fastest animal movements to arthropod body parts. UC Berkeley clocked trap-jaw ant mandibles closing at 78–145 mph, which it called the fastest recorded self-powered predatory strike. A PMC study names trap-jaw ants, mantis shrimp and Dracula ants as having the fastest known movements. None of these sources mention venom injection as a record-setting movement.

text: Venus is the brightest planet in the night sky due to its dense atmosphere, which scatters sunlight in all directions, making it visible even during daylight hours.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including National Geographic and Science Times, confirm that Venus is the brightest planet in the sky after the Sun and Moon and can be seen in daylight. They attribute this to its thick, permanent cloud cover, made mainly of sulfuric acid droplets, which reflects most of the sunlight that hits it. Its closeness to Earth also adds to its brightness. The claim's phrasing, a dense atmosphere scattering sunlight in all directions, is a simplification of this cloud reflectivity but matches it. Each part of the claim is supported and none is contradicted.

text: Venus is the fastest rotating planet in our solar system, with its rotation period being equal to its orbital period around the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are wrong. Venus is the slowest-rotating planet, not the fastest. Jupiter spins fastest. Venus also takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun, so its rotation period is longer than its orbital period, not equal to it.

text: Vesuvius, a volcano in Italy, is the only volcano to have erupted during an interval of a major sporting event, as it erupted in 79 AD while gladiators were competing at the Roman Colosseum during a festival.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. The Colosseum was finished, and opened with its inaugural games, in AD 80 (some sources say 81). That was after Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. Titus held those opening games partly in response to disasters that included the eruption. So gladiators couldn't have been fighting in the Colosseum when Vesuvius erupted. The Colosseum is also in Rome, far from Vesuvius, and the claim that Vesuvius is the only volcano ever to erupt during a sporting event has no support.

text: Volcanoes on Mars, known as shield volcanoes, can be up to three times the size of the largest volcano on Earth, Mount Mauna Loa, in Hawaii.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches show Martian shield volcanoes are much bigger than the claim says. Sky & Telescope reports that Olympus Mons, the largest of them, is about 25 km high and 624 km across. It compares this with Mauna Loa (about 10 km high and 120 km across) and says Olympus Mons has "about 100 times greater" volume. The claim gets right that these are shield volcanoes and that Mauna Loa is Earth's largest volcano. But the cap of "up to three times the size" is far too low. By height alone the ratio is roughly 2.5 times, so the claim only works if "size" means height.

text: Voltage can move a charge of 1 coulomb a distance of 1 joule of energy in 1 second at a speed of 1 ampere.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up units. A joule measures energy, not distance, and an ampere measures current (1 coulomb per second), not speed. By standard definitions, 1 volt is 1 joule of energy per coulomb of charge. One coulomb is the charge carried by a 1-ampere current in 1 second. Voltage is not something that moves a charge 'a distance of 1 joule' 'at a speed of 1 ampere', so the claim conflicts with how these SI units are defined.

text: You can lead a cow upstairs, but not downstairs, due to the cow's four stomachs making it physically difficult for them to walk down steep slopes.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim. A FunTrivia answer links to video of a cow walking down steps, which shows the 'upstairs but not downstairs' saying is a myth.
